title: Druze experts condemn Tom Barrack's accusations against Syrian Druze, warn of sectarian violence
body: US envoy Tom Barrack's claims that the area between Sweida and Daraa was “the captagon manufacturing operation of the world” and that a Druze sheikh was using perceived American and Israeli backing to “persecute other Druze” have drawn criticism from the Druze community, with some Israeli experts telling The Jerusalem Post on Sunday that the remarks had led them to question his suitability for the role.Speaking in an interview with Lebanese-Australian podcaster Mario Nawfal on Friday, Barrack alleged that Druze in the area were living off the manufacture and sale of illicit drugs.“It's not Israel that worries me. It's a particular Druze sheikh who utilizes the perception of Israeli backing of some alignment with America to persecute other Druze,” Barrack said.Although Barrack did not name the sheikh, his comments have been widely interpreted in Arab media as referring to Sheikh Hikmat al-Hijri, a spiritual leader of the Druze community who has called for Israeli support and independence from Syria.Growing calls for Syrian Druze independence Calls for independence and Israeli support among Syria's Druze community have grown more frequent since Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa came to power in late 2024.Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham, the formerly designated terrorist organization led by Sharaa, has a documented history of persecuting Druze, while the sectarian massacres in July 2025 and sporadic violence since have further fueled fears of Damascus's Islamist government.Against this backdrop, Israeli Druze diplomat and historian Dr. Reda Mansour criticized Barrack's remarks in a post on X/Twitter, describing his attribution of the global Captagon trade to the Druze region and his criticism of its local leadership as “highly irresponsible” and untruthful.“By baselessly criminalizing an entire ethnic minority, these statements put the vulnerable Druze community in southern Syria at direct risk of sectarian violence and targeted jihadi attacks. Painting a minority enclave as an illicit hub paints a dangerous target on their back for extremist networks,” Mansour wrote.“Diplomacy demands accuracy, not reckless generalizations that compromise human lives. We stand in solidarity with the Druze community in Syria.”Concerns rise amid ongoing violence against Druze communityMansour's concerns come amid continued violence against the community. More than 1,300 Druze were killed in the July 2025 massacres in Sweida and surrounding villages, according to UN figures, while subsequent outbreaks of sectarian violence have continued to see civilians abducted and killed.Civilians have also been killed in Jordanian military strikes on facilities Amman alleges are used for weapons storage and drug manufacturing. In a strike on January 18, 2024, for example, Jordan killed sisters Farah and Dima, aged three and five, along with their parents and other members of their extended family.Dr. Mordechai Kedar, a research fellow at the Begin-Sadat Center for Strategic Studies, told the Post that Barrack's comments and “lack of understanding” of the region have “brought a lot of damage to the whole Middle East.”Barrack sounds confident about diplomatic progress, but at the same time he accuses an entire population without evidence. Being optimistic about diplomacy does not give him the right to make false accusations. And a political agenda does not turn an accusation into a fact. If Mr. Barrack cannot prove his claims, he should stop using his position to attack Sweida and its people. Bashan will not be attacked and defamed to serve anyone's agenda.— Zéna Mansour ܙܺܝܢܵܐ ܡܲܢܨܘܪ (@ZeinaMansour1) October 25, 2026Doubting Barrack's knowledge of the issue of Sweida or the sectarian violence, Kedar said that he thought Barrack was relying on information provided to him and not the information on the ground or from the people affected by the violence.Jonathan Hessen, a senior fellow at the Jerusalem Institute for Strategy and Security, added that Barrack's remarks were not just “dismaying” because they showed a disregard for the safety and security of a community that has already been subjected to multiple massacres but because his statements were factually unfounded.“Even when the Jordanians launched airstrikes in southern Syria, the majority of the targeted warehouses were actually in Daraa, the province south of Sweida, where the Bedouins reside,” he said.“One warehouse was also targeted in Sweida, although I am not aware of its contents. However, those targets were provided to the Jordanians by Damascus, so there are certain aspects that need to be taken into account.”He noted that Barrack has a pattern of minimizing the suffering of those across the Middle East where the impact would disrupt his broader plans, referencing both Barrack's comments last week, where he insisted that the Islamic regime was “not evil,” and past commentary on Syrian violence.

title: Israel needs unity: Why Herzog must bring Netanyahu, Eisenkot together - opinion
body: I am a right-wing religious Zionist, an Ethiopian-born Israeli-American, and a father raising four children in Jerusalem, and I am frightened.Not because Israelis disagree, disagreement is part of democracy, but because our politics increasingly teaches us to hate one another more passionately than we love the country we share, while our enemies watch, our international standing collapses, and the wounds of October 7 remain open.I know where I stand politically. I believe in secure borders, Jewish sovereignty, and Israel's unquestionable right to defend its citizens. Hamas must never again govern Gaza. Iran and its terrorist proxies must be deterred. The Jewish people cannot subcontract their survival.Right-wing and left-wing are equal owners of the same countryBut being right-wing does not require me to treat left-wing Israelis as enemies. Their children serve beside ours. They run into shelters when the sirens sound. They bury loved ones, pay taxes, and worry about the future of the same country. They are equal owners of it. The same is true in reverse.Supporting a change in government does not justify dismissing millions of traditional, religious, or conservative Israelis as primitive, dangerous, or morally inferior. Netanyahu's voters will not disappear if he loses an election, just as his opponents will not disappear if he wins. Israel belongs to all of us.That truth should guide President Isaac Herzog after the election. Current polls show Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party and Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party competing for leadership, while neither bloc appears certain to command the 61 Knesset seats needed to govern. Israel may awaken to another divided parliament and another invitation to paralysis. We cannot afford it.October 7 was not only a military and intelligence catastrophe. It was a warning about what happens when leaders become distracted by internal warfare, institutions lose public trust, and citizens begin viewing one another as threats. Hamas crossed a physical border after we had already allowed hatred to cross every political and social border within Israel.Our enemies study us. They hear our leaders call one another traitors, fascists, and enemies of democracy. They see clashes among secular, religious, right-wing, left-wing, Jewish and Arab citizens.They do not interpret our division as healthy democratic debate. They interpret it as weakness and wait for the next fracture.Israel's diplomatic position is also in danger. The Jewish state is increasingly portrayed not as a democracy defending itself, but as the source of every regional crisis. Antisemitism and propaganda drive much of this campaign, but our poisonous politics makes it easier. A country that cannot speak respectfully to itself will struggle to speak persuasively to the world.This is why Herzog must become more than a ceremonial observer after the election. He cannot dictate a coalition, overturn the voters' decision, or force rivals to trust one another. But he possesses something rare in Israeli public life: an office intended to represent the entire nation. Herzog should invite Netanyahu and Eisenkot to the president's residence and keep bringing them back until they seriously consider a broad Zionist unity government.Not a government without disagreement. Not a government designed to rescue political careers. A government of limited national repair.Such a coalition should begin with a clear program: restore security and border readiness; establish an independent state commission to investigate the failures surrounding October 7; confront Iran and its proxies; rebuild Israel's international diplomacy; reduce the cost of living; require meaningful military or national service across society while respecting genuine Torah scholarship; and protect every law-abiding citizen from terrorism, organized crime and political violence.It must also address Israel's excluded communities. Ethiopian Israelis should not be remembered only during elections or cultural ceremonies. Arab citizens who reject terrorism and accept the laws of the state should not be treated as a permanent fifth column. Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) citizens should not be spoken about as if they are strangers to the Jewish future.Rights bring responsibilities, but responsibilities must also bring belonging. Unity does not mean moral confusion. Israel must distinguish democratic disagreement from support for its destruction.Leaders who excuse terrorism cannot be trusted with national security. But disagreement over courts, settlements, religion, or Gaza does not make an Israeli disloyal.Becoming protectorsRabbi Jonathan Sacks, of blessed memory, taught that society is the home we build together. A home cannot survive when family members would rather burn it down than allow a rival to sit at the head of the table.Netanyahu has devoted much of his life to Israel's security and international standing. Eisenkot served the country as a soldier, commander, and chief of staff, and he paid the unbearable price of losing family members in war.Each man represents citizens who love Israel. Each also carries responsibilities greater than his personal grievances. They do not have to admire one another. They do not have to erase their disagreements. They must decide whether their hatred and mistrust are more important than the country they both claim to serve.I made aliyah with my wife and four children shortly before October 7 because I believe in Israel, not merely as a refuge, but as the shared moral project of the Jewish people. I did not bring my children home so they could inherit a nation divided into tribes that no longer recognize one another.The next October 7 must never happen. Preventing it will require weapons, intelligence, and secure borders. It will also require Israelis to become protectors of one another again.Herzog, bring Netanyahu and Eisenkot to the same table. Ask them to place Israel above ego, party, and personal history. The election will determine who wins seats. Leadership will be measured by whether they can save the house we all share.The writer is a former New York City Supreme Court detective, an investigator and educator in conflict resolution and restorative peace, and a moral diplomacy expert. His upcoming book, Moral Diplomacy for a Broken World, is inspired by the late Rabbi Jonathan Sacks.

title: Why Netanyahu's supporters remain loyal to him despite his failures - opinion
body: For over a decade, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has demonstrated an extraordinary ability to retain the loyalty of his supporters despite profound failures under his leadership. He has been described as Israel's most successful politician, the greatest political survivor, and the leader of a personality cult.Millions of Israelis vote for Netanyahu because they genuinely share his political worldview that Israel must be exceptionally strong, distrust the Palestinians, fear Iran, oppose territorial concessions, and regard the Israeli Left as naïve, all legitimate political positions.The more puzzling question is why personal loyalty to Netanyahu remains so resilient even when events appear to contradict the image of him as Israel's indispensable protector.What does Netanyahu offer his followers beyond policy? Perhaps the answer lies in something deeper than politics. He offers psychological security through powerful rewards: security, identity, certainty, conviction, and collective struggle. To reinforce these bonds, he has also used the divisions within Israeli society with remarkable effectiveness, creating a powerful distinction between “us” and “them.”Understanding these psychological dynamics may help explain Netanyahu's extraordinary political resilience, and why his most devoted followers remain loyal even when the facts appear increasingly difficult to reconcile with his image.Netanyahu's most powerful political appealNetanyahu's most powerful political appeal has long been security, not merely security as policy but as an emotional promise. Israelis live with a profound awareness of vulnerability shaped by the Holocaust, wars, terrorism, Iran, Hamas, and Hezbollah.Netanyahu has built his political persona around the image of an experienced leader who recognizes dangers and can protect Israelis. During Operation Protective Edge in 2014, he said, “The ultimate responsibility for your security and peace is mine, as prime minister.”The message is not only about trusting his security policies but more about trusting him with their security. Security is identified not with a government or policy but with Netanyahu himself. The question is no longer whether Netanyahu made mistakes, but who can protect us if not Bibi.Netanyahu also offers identity. His rhetoric often blurs the distinction between himself, his supporters, and the nation. In October 2025, he told the Knesset: “We are Jews, we are Israelis, we are strong.”This framing makes opposition to Netanyahu appear to some supporters not just as political disagreement but as opposition to the country and its security. It also taps into longstanding resentment toward Israel's traditional elites.Netanyahu has been remarkably effective at turning that resentment into solidarity with himself. Politics shifts from a contest between competing ideas toward an “us versus them” struggle. Once politics becomes an identity conflict, evidence is less powerful.Another characteristic is Netanyahu's projection of certainty. In July 2026, describing a change in Israel's security doctrine following October 7, he said: “I am taking the reins, and I am changing it.” Netanyahu consistently presents himself as someone who sees what others cannot see and possesses the experience to provide the solution. His implicit message is reassuring.Since people dislike uncertainty, particularly when it feels existential, they want someone who appears to understand what's happening, knows what must be done, and is confident to act.Another mechanism sustaining Netanyahu's following is his ability to turn criticism into conviction. In 2021, he said: “The test of leadership requires that the right decisions be made even when they are not understood at any given moment and their justification becomes clear later on.”Netanyahu has created a protective shield around him. If events prove him right, he was right. If they prove him wrong, it means history has not caught up with him. Therefore, he is never wrong, as it may simply be too early to know. This creates a remarkably resilient form of loyalty.The fifth element is the sense of permanent external collective threat. Iran has occupied a central place in Netanyahu's political narrative for decades, while Hamas, Hezbollah, and other enemies reinforce the perception that Israel is surrounded by hostile forces. The threats are real and Netanyahu's uncompromising strength is presented as the only reliable means of protection.In January 2024, Netanyahu declared: “No one will stop us, not The Hague, not the axis of evil, and not anyone else.” Such language positions him as the leader standing between his people and a hostile world. And his followers feel they cannot afford to weaken the person protecting them. As long as the threat remains, the protector is indispensable.The phenomenon of cognitive dissonanceNetanyahu's political success cannot be separated from his ability to turn political disagreement into questions of identity and belonging. Israeli society has long contained profound ideological, religious, ethnic, and social divisions. The crucial question is what political leaders do with those divisions.When opponents are portrayed as dangerous rather than simply mistaken, compromise becomes harder. Disagreement can become disloyalty, and defending the leader can become a way of defending one's own side.This helps explain the phenomenon of cognitive dissonance. When reality conflicts with a deeply held belief, people may reinterpret reality, so the belief can survive. Political attachment can become intertwined with identity, fear, and belonging. After years of defending a leader, acknowledging that he failed can mean reconsidering one's own judgment.That may be the deepest source of Netanyahu's resilience. For some devoted supporters, letting go of Netanyahu may feel like letting go of a part of their identity, security, and certainty that he has come to represent.The writer is an Israeli Canadian, formerly an economist and senior policy adviser in the Ontario Public Service, Canada. She is active in Jewish community life in Toronto and Miami, and writes about Israel, Zionism, and the relationship between Israel and the Diaspora.

title: ‘Extra, extra!’ New book brings ancient Talmudic texts to life for readers of all ages - review
body: Educator, lecturer, and writer Zalman Eisentstock brings stories from the Talmud to life by providing them to readers in a “newspaper” format accompanied by cartoon drawings.The Talmud Chronicles: Bringing Talmudic Events to Life covers significant historical events from around 100-200 CE and breathes life into characters from the Talmud. The “editions” included in this publication trace the history of the Jewish people through Ancient Rome, the Parthian Revolt, and the Bar Kochba rebellion as the sages of the time lay the foundations for the creation of the Mishnah.An entertaining journey through topics ranging from astronomy to the OlympicsCombining real events with pockets of insightful humor, the author takes the reader on an entertaining journey through topics ranging from astronomy and archaeology to the arts and Olympic events, all set in their particular geopolitical context.Talmud Chronicles is an ideal coffee table book. Picking it up provides an opening for learning, whether directly from its stories or through the questions that arise from reading it, which can lead to further study and/or fascinating discussions.It appears to be aimed at both adults and children, and there is something for everyone in its varied sections, inspired by real newspapers.TALMUD CHRONICLES: BRINGING TALMUDIC EVENTS TO LIFEBy Zalman EisenstockUrim Publications112 pages; $35

title: Settler violence is a political blind spot in Israel’s election campaign - opinion
body: Even as settler violence grows increasingly prominent abroad, Israelis seem somewhat ambivalent. According to a recent survey, 78% of the public call Judea and Samaria and a Palestinian state important or very important. But asked to prioritize, they rank it dead last: cost of living at 35%, haredi (ultra-Orthodox) conscription at 18%, the Iran war at 17%, judicial reform at 16%, and the future of Judea and Samaria at just 7%.Before accusing Israelis of monstrous disregard, remember that in the Israeli political system they have only one vote to decide the prime minister, judicial reform, and security policy all at once. If you had only one dollar to invest, where would you place it?Israelis will faithfully recite the cost of living – but as Naftali Bennett has discovered, to his dismay, they are not being honest. His comprehensive economic plan, released in early July, landed somewhere between negligible and nil. By contrast, the cost of living barely features in Gadi Eisenkot's campaign, yet that hasn't stopped the exodus from the one party to the other. The real number-one concern for Israeli voters has always been, and continues to be, security.To an outsider, the correlation between settler violence and security looks weak, if not negative. The vigilantism rampant in the West Bank doesn't make Israelis safer – but for a certain sector, cracking down on it represents the opposite. That is why the opposition hasn't capitalized on the seeming "wild west" created, largely by government incompetence, 20 minutes from the capital. They will mention the issue when a particularly egregious event occurs, but don't expect a poster reading “If he can't secure Judea and Samaria, can he secure Tel Aviv.”Such an ad would collide with two associations of settler violence, both of which the movement itself reinforces. In the Israeli political dictionary, the antonym of the settlements is the Palestinian state: Speak harshly of the movement's excesses, and you are heard as lending a hand to the people trying to bring one about.Settler violence tied to claims to Palestinian statehoodMeir Deutsch, director-general of the prominent settlement NGO Regavim, drew that connection explicitly not long ago, arguing that the “settler violence” narrative is a foreign-funded campaign engineered “to create the tool that will force the State of Israel to establish a Palestinian state.” The second association is folded into that same charge: foreign. Regavim's report casts the campaign as EU-financed and amplified by hostile voices abroad, and Deutsch points to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's own acknowledgment that settler violence helped justify a partial American arms embargo in the middle of the war. To make settler violence a headline issue, then, is to risk sounding at once obtuse about the real threat and faintly foreign in one's preoccupations.All of this is built on a fundamental truth: Israeli elections run in only one direction – rightward.That's why the self-styled “right-wing defense minister,” Israel Katz, fired the head of IDF Central Command on live TV for continuing to hold a violent settler, Tal Yinon Dardik, in custody and why even now he flatly rejects reinstating administrative detention for what he insists are a “handful of Jewish rioters.” The stunt ended in a swift and humiliating walk-back, but it captures a broader perception on the Right: Taking on the campaign against settler violence is a winning cause. If there is internal polling on the issue, it has not been leaked. The truth is no one knows how many votes such actions secure, but it certainly secures a flank.Right-wing politicians rarely hesitate when red lines are clearly crossed: A direct assault on IDF troops, like the violence seen last April, triggers immediate outrage across the political spectrum, while an indefensible action against Palestinian civilians, such as the Jit rampage, forces even figures like Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich to disavow perpetrators as rogue “criminals” divorced from mainstream Zionism.But when the focus turns to the daily friction, political calculus changes. Leaders find it far safer to dance around the problem than to risk getting launched leftward for stepping on a partisan landmine. Settler violence won't be the wedge issue of the election. It won't even be a widely discussed one – it'll feature in attacks on the government as second fiddle at best. Not because people think settlers are right, but because attacking them makes one sound left-wing.The writer serves as the English director of the Ribo Center and the editor of Amit Segal's newsletter, It's Noon in Israel.

title: UAE’s Lana Nusseibeh receives more support in bid to become next UN secretary-general
body: Cypriot Foreign Affairs Minister Constantinos Kombos said on Friday that he supports UAE Ambassador Lana Nusseibeh as the next United Nations secretary-general.Kombos wrote on X/Twitter that he has known Nusseibeh for years, noting that she "is an experienced, highly effective and well-respected diplomat, with an approach focusing on dialogue, compromise and tangible outcomes, while also having a strong track record in supporting multilateralism and the United Nations."I have known and worked with @Lana_Nusseibeh for some time. Lana is an experienced, highly effective and well respected diplomat, with an approach focusing on dialogue, compromise and tangible outcomes, while also having a strong track record in supporting multilateralism and the United Nations. I firmly believed, and continue to do so, that it is time for female leadership in important multilateral organisations. Qualified candidates have not been endorsed so far for the position of the @UN Secretary-General, under the rules of the UN system. It is becoming time sensitive to ensure that the selection process proceeds. I therefore wish Lana strength in this demanding endeavour, and every success in paving new pathways. @mofauae- Constantinos Kombos (@ckombos) October 23, 2026He also noted that it was time for a woman to become the next secretary-general, saying, "it is becoming time-sensitive to ensure that the selection process proceeds."On Thursday, Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) Secretary-General Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi said member states unanimously endorsed the United Arab Emirates' nomination of the ambassador for the position, according to the Saudi Gazette.This is important as support for Nusseibeh grows, with Albudaiwi attributing the unanimous support to the GCC countries' commitment to strengthening multilateral cooperation and reinforcing the UN's role in maintaining international peace and security in accordance with the principles and objectives of its Charter, the Saudi Gazette reported.The Maldives, BoP's Nikolay Mladenov support Nusseibeh's nominationThe Maldives said on Sunday that it welcomed Nusseibeh's nomination. In addition, Nikolay Mladenov, who is a key official with the Gaza Board of Peace and formerly served as Bulgaria's defense minister and Foreign affairs minister, wrote on X that "Lana Nusseibeh has always understood that the #UN works when someone is willing to systematically build the bridges nobody else wants to build."Lana Nusseibeh has always understood that the #UN works when someone is willing to systematically build the bridges nobody else wants to build. In the Security Council she did that quietly and consistently and with great profesionalism. She now has the chance to take that same spirit and ethos to the UN Secretariat. Wishing you courage and strength for the journey ahead and much success!— Nickolay E. MLADENOV (@nmladenov) October 22, 2026"In the Security Council she did that quietly and consistently and with great professionalism," said Mladenov. "She now has the chance to take that same spirit and ethos to the UN Secretariat. Wishing you courage and strength for the journey ahead and much success!"Nusseibeh has served as the UAE's foreign affairs minister and as the UAE's permanent representative to the UN in New York from 2013 to 2024. She also served for four years as foreign affairs assistant minister for political affairs.Since the organization was founded in 1945, the UN has had ten secretaries-general, including an acting leader from 1945 to 1946, though some have been more memorable than others. Sweden's Dag Hammarskjöld, who served from 1953 to 1961, was an energetic leader who sought to achieve a ceasefire in the Congo. He died in a plane crash while on his way to Zambia.U Thant, who served in the 1960s, was the first non-Western secretary-general. He was followed by Kurt Waldheim in the 1970s. Waldheim was an intelligence officer under Nazi Germany, which made his appointment strange, considering the UN was founded after the defeat of the Nazis. In the 1990s, former Egyptian diplomat Boutros Boutros-Ghali became the head of the UN. He was largely seen to have failed at key moments, such as during the Rwandan genocide.In the last decades, the UN has seen secretaries-general who appeared relatively ineffectual, such as Kofi Annan, Ban Ki-moon, and current UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres. As part of a complex election process, an informal straw poll of officials in the deciding UN Security Council last week gave [former Costa Rican vice president Rebeca] Grynspan a narrow lead over her closest competitors: Guyana's former Foreign Minister Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett and Argentina's International Atomic Energy Agency Director-General Rafael Grossi, Euro News reported.The report notes that the winner needs at least nine votes from the 15-member UN Security Council without a veto from any of the five permanent members - the US, the UK, France, China and Russia - and they have until the end of December to choose the successor to Gutteres, before the UN General Assembly confirms the appointment.Euro News also noted other candidates, including former Ecuadorian foreign minister Maria Fernanda Espinosa, former Senegalese president Macky Sall, former UN under-secretary-general Olara Otunnu of Uganda, and Ecuadorian diplomat Ivonne A-Baki.Nusseibeh currently serving as UN Women Executive Board presidentAccording to a UN biography of Nusseibeh, the ambassador currently serves as UN Women Executive Board president and was recently appointed co-facilitator of the Ad Hoc Working Group on the Revitalization of the UN General Assembly by the General Assembly president.A website that appears to have been created for her candidacy notes that Nusseibeh is currently on leave from government responsibilities to focus on her UN secretary-general candidacy.The website also includes a statement attributed to Nusseibeh, in which the ambassador says she is "stubbornly optimistic about the future of our world and the important role multilateralism will play in it.""I am offering active, hands-on leadership on peace and security: acting earlier, bridging divides and pursuing practical first agreements that save lives now and create space for broader peace," she said, adding that she "will bring that same urgency and focus on results to development and human rights – building a more focused, responsive UN that delivers for the people it serves."Nusseibeh was born in 1978, is married, and has two children. She has a BA and MA from Queens' College at the University of Cambridge. She also has an MA in Israeli and Jewish Diaspora Studies from the School of Oriental and African Studies (SOAS), University of London.Prior to her UN role, she established the UAE Foreign Affairs Ministry's Policy Planning Department in 2009 and served as its first director for three years. She also served as the UAE's Co-Special Envoy to Afghanistan and Pakistan. She also headed the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) task force at the ministry.French-language media platform and digital news outlet IsraJ noted Nusseibeh's important family background, saying her family originally lived in Jerusalem and that her Emirati citizenship came from her father, Emirati President Cultural Advisor Zaki Nusseibeh.It added details about the family's rich academic and intellectual background and its long roots in Jerusalem and the region, with relative Anwar Nusseibeh having been a prominent figure in Palestinian and Jordanian politics.Wounded in 1948, Anwar Nusseibeh served as Jordanian Defense Minister and later as Jerusalem Governor under Jordanian rule. After 1967, he conducted discreet contacts between Israel and Jordan regarding the future of the West Bank.IsraJ further noted that the ambassador's uncle, Sari Nusseibeh, is a former president of Al-Quds University in the West Bank. He wrote several important books, including Once Upon a Country about his family and Palestinian issues.

title: Marvel plans to collaborate with Israeli writers on new 'Zodiac' series draws online backlash
body: Another Israeli success story in Hollywood is drawing online backlash, as Marvel is set to collaborate with two Israeli writers on a new series, with the announcement already sparking hostile reactions on social media before filming even begins.According to a report Deadline published on Friday, Ron Leshem and Amit Cohen have been tapped to write Marvel's upcoming espionage series, Zodiac, currently in development for Disney+. However, some social media users have already declared that they will boycott the series solely because its writers are Israeli.The announcement quickly drew criticism online, with some users attacking Marvel's decision to hire the Israeli writers. One user accused the company of prioritizing political messaging over its existing shows, writing, "You canceled the second season of Wonder Man and the future of Daredevil just to shove Zionist propaganda down our throats."Similar reactions appeared on Reddit, where one user suggested that the involvement of Israeli writers meant the series would serve as Israeli intelligence propaganda."Another show going straight into the trash. Espionage and Israelis in the same series. You might as well have advertised it as Mossad propaganda," the user wrote.Some criticize backlash as undermining new series prior to debutOthers criticized the backlash, arguing that the controversy had already undermined the possibility of discussing the series on its own merits."And just like that, there goes any chance of having a positive discussion about the series online," another user wrote.Leshem and Cohen are established figures in the television industry, with a track record of creating Israeli and international productions. Leshem was among the creators of the original Israeli version of Euphoria, which later became an international hit through HBO's American adaptation starring Zendaya.The two writers have collaborated on several television series, including The Gordin Cell, Valley of Tears, Traitor, Red Skies, and Bad Boy, as well as the international drama No Man's Land. Their experience developing security and espionage thrillers could now bring a new perspective to the Marvel Cinematic Universe.There is currently no indication that Zodiac will address Israel, the Middle East, or the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Nevertheless, the writers' Israeli nationality has already become a source of controversy, despite the fact that no cast members, characters, or significant plot details have been announced.For some viewers, even a superhero series seems to have become a political issue.

title: October 7 should have changed Israeli politics, yet we are voting for the same leaders - opinion
body: We are down to crunch time. With Tuesday's elections approaching, a significant portion of the Israeli electorate is still struggling with a fundamental question: Who deserves our vote?But perhaps we should be asking a different question: How did we end up with essentially the same political leadership that brought us to October 7?Think back to the days immediately following the greatest catastrophe in modern Israeli history. Amid the shock, grief, and anger, there was one sentiment that seemed to unite Israelis across the political spectrum: Enough.We promised ourselves that things would change.We spoke about a new generation of leadership emerging from the battlefield. Men and women who had dropped everything on October 7, left their families and businesses, and rushed to defend their country. People who demonstrated that leadership was not about political survival, television appearances, or accumulating power, but about responsibility, sacrifice, and service.Political initiatives began forming around this very idea. Perhaps those who fought together in Gaza and Lebanon, despite their political and religious differences, could also govern together in Jerusalem.They might disagree about judicial reform, religion and state, or economic policy. But they understood something our politicians seemed to have forgotten: You can disagree with someone without treating him as your enemy.  You can disagree and still work together for the nation.For a brief moment, it seemed that October 7 might produce a genuine political revolution.So what happened? Somewhere along the way, the political establishment and much of the media convinced us that new leadership was too risky. That experience, even experience associated with catastrophic failure, was preferable to fresh faces and fresh ideas.And so here we are, once again being asked to choose among the very people who helped shape the security and political systems that failed us.Israel's leaders responsible for October 7 failureConsider the four prominent figures seeking to lead Israel: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Gadi Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett, and Avigdor Liberman.Netanyahu bears the greatest responsibility. He was prime minister on October 7. The bottom line is that the buck stops with him.He deserves substantial credit for Israel's military achievements since October 8. But those accomplishments cannot erase his responsibility for what happened the day before. He can argue that he relied on the intelligence community and the military establishment. That may be true. But leadership means accepting responsibility for the institutions under your command, especially when they fail catastrophically.Yet Netanyahu's challengers cannot simply present themselves as innocent bystanders. Eisenkot served as IDF chief of staff. Bennett and Liberman both served as defense ministers. Each occupied positions of enormous influence over Israel's military preparedness, strategic priorities, and defense establishment.True, they did not all hold office on October 7, and their individual responsibilities are certainly not identical. Nevertheless, each played a significant part of the system whose assumptions and shortcomings demand serious examination.Remember what happened when reservists reported for duty after the massacre? Many discovered that their units lacked essential equipment: modern protective vests, helmets, tactical uniforms, drones, and other basic necessities.Instead of receiving everything they needed from the military establishment, reservists and their families scrambled to raise money. Jewish communities abroad opened their wallets. Volunteers organized emergency shipments. Private citizens worked around the clock to equip soldiers heading into battle.It was an extraordinary demonstration of Jewish solidarity. It was also an indictment of our military preparedness. How could a country that spends so much on defense find itself relying on private donations to equip soldiers going to war?The shortages raised serious questions about procurement, budgeting, inventory management, and readiness. These questions cannot be directed only at the government in office on October 7 or the prime minister. They must also be directed at those who previously led the defense establishment who were derelict in their responsibility of making sure that our soldiers have the equipment and ammunition they need to fight our enemies.Accountability cannot be selective. We cannot demand Netanyahu's resignation because of October 7 while automatically exempting former defense ministers and chiefs of staff from scrutiny simply because they now oppose him.If October 7 taught us anything, it should be that titles, experience, and impressive military résumés are not substitutes for accountability.Fortunately, there are alternatives worth examining.People of Israel, headed by Ofer Winter; Haredi Public, headed by Moti Leitner; and the Reservists-Economic Party, headed by Yoaz Hendel, represent attempts to bring different voices and approaches into Israeli politics.These parties should be judged seriously, including on their policies, leadership, competence, and ability to govern. Newness alone is not a qualification, and voters must also consider whether smaller parties can cross the electoral threshold. But surely, we owe new political movements more than automatic dismissal.We desperately need leaders whose first instinct is cooperation rather than confrontation, whose loyalty is to the country rather than their political careers, and who understand that national unity is not merely a slogan reserved for wartime.The men and women who defended Israel after October 7 demonstrated extraordinary courage, initiative, and responsibility. Why should we assume that the people capable of leading soldiers under fire are incapable of helping lead the country? Why should we assume that new voices are incapable of solving the issues that the current political class continues to kick down the road?October 7 was supposed to be a turning point in Israeli history. It should also have been a turning point in Israeli politics.We cannot keep complaining about the same politicians, the same divisions, and the same failures, only to return them to power election after election.If we truly meant what we said after October 7, then it is time to give a new generation of leaders a chance. In the immortal words of Hillel from Ethics of the Fathers 1:14: “If not now, when?”Israel deserves more than another election between yesterday's failures. It deserves a new beginning.The writer is the managing partner of Dekel Capital Management, a resident of Beit Shemesh, and an avid Zionist who cares deeply about the future of the State of Israel and the Jewish people.

title: High Court strikes down petition to end sperm donor anonymity
body: The High Court of Justice has struck down a petition seeking to allow children conceived through sperm donation to learn the identity of their biological father, leaving in place the rule that keeps donors anonymous. The issue was raised in a High Court petition by the organizations Choosing Family and B'Tzalmo, which oppose anonymous donation, and the court asked to hear the ministry's position. The panel can either leave the current anonymous-only system in place or allow two parallel tracks, anonymous and non-anonymous; adopting its recommendations would require changes to existing legislation. The petitioners argued that the provision guaranteeing donor anonymity violates children's right to know who their biological parents are.Israel currently permits only anonymous sperm donation. Under the Public Health Regulations, disclosing identifying donor details is prohibited.A woman who wants to conceive with a man she knows must present a parenting agreement between them that overrides any other arrangement, meaning there is no route to an identified donation without a commitment to fatherhood behind it. Who regulates sperm donation in Israel?Sperm donation in Israel is not regulated by primary legislation; every donor signs a form confirming the donation is anonymous and that no identifying detail will be passed to the woman purchasing the sample.Last year, the Justice Ministry published regulations for a database registering egg donations that will also record whether the mother was fertilized with a sperm donation, in which case the donor's code will be registered.The move followed a petition filed five years earlier by Choosing Family and B'Tzalmo demanding a registry to prevent marriages between relatives, given that a man can donate at several sperm banks and there was no orderly registration of donors.

title: Jewish billionaire Bill Ackman calls for Ben-Gvir, Smotrich to be excluded from next government
body: Jewish billionaire Bill Ackman condemned National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich in a Sunday Twitter/X post, just days before the Israeli election, saying a new government should not include them."Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich have caused Israel enormous reputational damage with their statements and actions, which are presented in the global media as representing the voice and will of all Israelis," Ackman said."As such, a government formed without Ben-Gvir and Smotrich will send a message to the rest of the world that Israel is turning a new page."I said I wasn't going to weigh in on who should be prime minister of Israel as that is a decision for Israeli citizens. I did, however, want to share one point of view from the perspective of someone who has an understanding of how Israel is perceived in America. Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich have caused Israel enormous reputational damage with their statements and actions which are presented in the global media as representing the voice and will of all Israelis. As such, a government formed without Ben-Gvir and Smotrich will send a message to the rest of the world that Israel is turning a new page. This will allow Israel to rebuild lost credibility, increase the opportunity for an expansion of the Abraham Accords, and enjoy a better relationship with Democrats and Republicans and Americans at large.— Bill Ackman (@BillAckman) October 25, 2026Ackman said he was presenting this perspective as someone who understands how Israel's perceived in the United States.He added that excluding Ben-Gvir and Smotrich would allow Israel to "rebuild lost credibility, increase the opportunity for an expansion of the Abraham Accords, and enjoy a better relationship with Democrats and Republicans and Americans at large."Ben-Gvir acknowledges importance of diplomatic relations, prioritizes soldiersBoth Ben-Gvir and Smotrich have been highly controversial internationally, drawing ire from many of Israel's allies for their extremist views and statements, including in the US.Earlier this month, during an English-language election campaign event, Ben-Gvir acknowledged that Israel's international diplomacy matters to the country's national security, but asserted it shouldn't take precedence over the nation's soldiers.“I think there's a great importance to our diplomatic relations and connections,” Ben-Gvir said in response to a question submitted by The Jerusalem Post. “It's important that we look good on the world stage. But not at the expense of our fighters and our soldiers.”Sam Halpern and Keshet Neev contributed to this report.

title: Iraq braces for renewed Iran conflict after 1,000 strikes on Kurdistan, 600 militia attacks
body: Iraq is on edge over the prospect of renewed fighting with Iran after Tehran carried out some 1,000 strikes on the Kurdistan Region in northern Iraq. Additionally, Iranian-backed militias launched roughly 600 attacks inside Iraq, most of them on US diplomatic facilities. Iraq closed some border crossings with Iran, including the Al-Sheeb crossing in southern Iraq, on Wednesday, saying it needed upgrades to security and technical infrastructure. Iran criticized the decision, saying Baghdad failed to provide advance notice and rejected allegations that narcotics and counterfeit currency are being smuggled into Iraq through border crossings, according to a Rudaw report. This crossing, also known as Al-Shaib, was the first targeted for closure in Maysan Governorate. This crossing is believed to be near an area where an Iranian-backed militia in Iraq launched a drone strike on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline in September. Rudaw also reported that, in retaliation, Iranian businessman Babak Zanjani called for restrictions on Iraqi oil tankers passing through the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile, the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) has denied reports that Ukrainian forces, military units or drones are operating from its territory. The KRG Interior Ministry issued a statement on Thursday rejecting the allegations as baseless, according to the Iraqi News Agency (INA). However, the source of the reports remains unclear.The ministry emphasized that the Kurdistan region maintains a policy of neutrality in regional and international conflicts. It said it would not allow its territory to serve as a base for hostile military operations against other countries. The statement reflects the KRG's efforts to avoid being sucked into conflicts involving Iran, as Tehran has been pressuring Iraq to expel Kurdish-Iranian opposition groups that are present in the Kurdistan region of northern Iraq.Iraq, Jordan move to strengthen bilateral security In another development, Iraq and Jordan have emphasized the importance of strengthening bilateral security cooperation. According to the Iraqi News Agency (INA), Iraqi Interior Minister Yasser al-Maliki spoke by telephone on Wednesday with his Jordanian counterpart, Mazen al-Faraya. Faraya congratulated Maliki on assuming his new position, and the two officials discussed expanding coordination between their interior ministries. The Iraqi Interior Ministry said the conversation reflected the two countries' commitment to strengthening security and stability through closer cooperation. The discussion comes as Baghdad seeks to manage security along its borders. While Jordan and Iraq have positive historic ties, the desert area near Jordan and Syria in Iraq's Western Anbar area has been a source of threats in the past. This is a largely tribal, sparsely populated area that could become a security vacuum following the US withdrawal from Iraq and Syria.Iraq is also focusing on security along its western border with Syria. According to the Iraqi News Agency (INA), Defense Minister Nayef Mukayif al-Shammari conducted an aerial inspection tour on Saturday of Iraqi military units deployed along the Iraq-Syria border in Nineveh province. The Iraqi Defense Ministry said the visit aimed to review force deployment and positioning along the border and assess operational readiness.

title: Women’s futsal team to compete in China tournament
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 25 (MNA) – Iran’s women’s national futsal team will participate in a four-nation tournament in China as part of their preparations for the 2026 Asian Indoor and Martial Arts Games.
The Iranian squad will depart for China on Nov. 2, to take part in the tournament, scheduled to be held from Nov. 4 to 9.
Iran, China and Hong Kong have been confirmed as participants, while the fourth team are expected to be announced soon.
The Iranian team will compete under the guidance of head coach Shahrzad Mozafar, who will use the tournament to assess her players and fine-tune the squad ahead of the continental competition.
The event will provide Iran’s women with valuable international experience as they continue their preparations for the Asian Indoor and Martial Arts Games.
The seventh edition of the Asian Indoor and Martial Arts Games is scheduled to take place in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, from Dec. 11 to 22, 2026.
The multi-sport event is expected to bring together athletes from 45 countries competing across 18 sports.
Iran’s women’s futsal team will be aiming to make the most of the China tournament to strengthen their preparations and build momentum ahead of the Games in Riyadh.

title: Democrat Scott Colom aims for deep-red Mississippi Senate seat
body:
Colom would be Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction.
Why are major Democrats and Republicans flocking to Mississippi in recent weeks?
In a climate where polls show President Donald Trump's approval ratings cratering, Democrats are unusually optimistic about Scott Colom's chances of flipping the Senate seat held by incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith -- even in deep-red Mississippi.
"We got to have a senator that looks out for Mississippi, that puts Mississippi farmers first, Mississippi small businesses first, represent our values by not allowing corruption to ruin our country and actually delivers on the commitments to put America first," Colom told ABC News in an interview earlier this week.
The incumbent's campaign dismisses the Democratic push as the last-ditch effort of a campaign that will fall short.
Colom is a district attorney for four counties along the Mississippi-Alabama border and a former nominee to become a U.S. district judge. He would be Mississippi's first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction.
Democrats have argued that Colom's prominent credentials, as well as voter pushback against Republican incumbents and motivation among Democratic-leaning Black voters, could help boost him. Mississippi's population is around 36% Black, according to U.S. Census data .
Colom faces an uphill battle, as Mississippi has not elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1982 and voted for Donald Trump in 2024 by around 20 points. ABC News rates the race solid Republican.
But he has gotten the attention of national Democrats; major party figures such as former former Vice President Kamala Harris and Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock have campaigned with him. Former President Barack Obama also recorded an ad for him released earlier this month.
Harris, during a rally with Colom on Thursday, told attendees, "I've been in those rooms where there's no cameras, it's senators talking to each other... When you have a voice like his in that room, just think about the impact that's going to have on the decisions coming out of that room. Think about that. This is no ordinary time, and this is no ordinary man."
Colom also went viral online last week after a social video he posted showed Hyde-Smith, during a local news interview from February, saying "You have so many proteins to choose from" while discussing how to deal with higher prices on meat and other goods. In the interview, Hyde-Smith also spoke about working on regulations that would help energy production, and tax incentives to help development.
But it was the proteins part that Colom's campaign seized on, with a punchy video that featured voters mocking the senator's words, with one saying, "Pick another protein ... I'd rather pick another Senator instead." (The campaign has confirmed to ABC News that the video has been turned into a campaign ad.)
One concrete sign of confidence among Democrats over Colom's chances came on Tuesday, when the Senate Majority PAC, an outside group aligned with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, announced it would spend $1.2 million on an ad campaign across broadcast TV and digital for ads for Colom.
Asked what signs the group sees in Mississippi that makes it worth investing in, spokesperson Lauren French wrote, "Cindy Hyde-Smith has spent a decade in Washington without passing a single piece of legislation, and Mississippians have noticed."
Hyde-Smith has cosponsored legislation that has passed into law but legislation she initially sponsored or reintroduced has not become law, according to congressional records . Asked to respond to Senate Majority PAC, Hyde-Smith's campaign pointed to how bills from lawmakers "are often passed as part of larger legislative packages," and that has been true for some of Hyde-Smith's bills, including the first one she introduced. The campaign also pointed out that she is running for only her second full term.
French said Colom is running a "disciplined campaign" with messages resonating with voters.
Colom and Hyde-Smith have some history, as she blocked his nomination for federal judge in 2023. She cited his support for transgender rights and having previously been boosted by a George Soros-linked PAC, according to the Mississippi Free Press .
He insists his bid for Senate is not motivated by a desire to get back at her.
"It has nothing to do with the run for me ... as a Christian, I forgive her. It's about the people in Mississippi," Colom told ABC News.
"We are confident that Mississippians will once again send Cindy Hyde-Smith back to the U.S. Senate on November 3rd. This is simply Washington insiders making a last ditch effort to give life to Scott Colom's failing campaign," campaign manager Jake Monssen told ABC News in a statement.
Hyde-Smith's supporters may be more motivated after a boost from President Donald Trump, who's set to hold a rally in Mississippi on Monday as part of a swing of campaign rallies mostly in red states.
The Republican National Committee announced the rally around a week after Colom's social video went viral, although Trump and the group have not indicated why they are doing the rally there and Trump has expressed confidence in Hyde-Smith.
"Cindy Hyde-Smith's very popular ... So if I need to get her over the top, I would go there [to Mississippi]. She's great. Cindy Hyde-Smith is great," Trump told reporters when asked Thursday about the Senate election.
Hyde-Smith will be attending the rally, according to her campaign.
24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

title: Why are dance clubs disappearing? Because half of Gen Z avoids dancing for fear of humiliation
body:
There was a time when I spent hours in dance clubs. I never saw a single episode of the first run of Seinfeld, because for eight straight years, I left the house at 9 p.m. to oversee a club gig in Hamilton.
I called 1995 “the summer of clubs.” As a lowly afternoon radio announcer, I was always looking for ways to boost my income. The easiest way was to host an alt-rock night at a club. Owners were always looking for ways to get people in the door every night of the week. That summer, I hosted nights on Mondays, Wednesdays, Thursdays and Fridays, which involved a long trip to Buffalo, a last call at 3:50 a.m. and an arrival back home at around 7 a.m. Other announcers at the station had similar schedules.
It was exhausting, but the income helped us toward the down payment on a house. And it was gratifying, too, presiding over an evening that featured hundreds of people dancing like no one was watching.
When I was program director of 102.1/The Edge about 20 years ago, live-to-air broadcasts from local dance clubs were big, big business. At one point, we had events on Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, two on Saturday and one on Sunday night. These broadcasts brought in hundreds of thousands of dollars every year, were highly rated and attracted hundreds of people each night.
We weren’t alone. Other contemporary music stations in Toronto were doing the same thing. If you scanned across the dial on a Friday or Saturday night, you could eavesdrop on what was happening in clubs across the city. If you cared to step out, the west end of downtown, along King and Richmond streets, had every second door leading to a club. Some were tiny holes in the wall. Others, like Lucid on John Street, were massive. It stretched over four floors and 53,000 square feet. It was later taken over by Ontario-born New York City club legend Peter Gatien (The Limelight, Palladium, Tunnel) and turned into CiRCA.
Sidewalks were jammed with lines of people waiting to get into each one. Toronto cops patrolled the Entertainment District area on horseback until dawn and city council was constantly getting complaints about crowds, noise and the inevitable idiot behaviour. Meanwhile, we’d hear insane stories about club scenes in places like New York, London, Berlin and Ibiza.
This was in addition to all the raves happening in Toronto at the time, which made the city one of the two or three biggest rave capitals on the planet.
It was truly the best of times and the worst of times. You could disappear into the mysterious darkness of a dance club and lose your mind for a little bit. Many bad decisions were had, but at least most went unrecorded for posterity.
Today, though, the dance club scene everywhere is a shadow of its former self. Yes, gentrification was a factor. Shifting musical tastes can be blamed too, as can local authorities who saw clubs as the enemy and did what they could to make conducting business as difficult as possible. And when COVID-19 came along, that was the death knell for whoever was left. It also resulted in a two-year hiatus when it came to those all-important ages, 18 to 21, who were finally old enough to go out with all the adults. They never got into the habit.
But I have a theory that the biggest killer of dance clubs was the smartphone.
Before smartphones and you wanted to meet someone new, you had to leave your home, travel through time and space, endure the dignities of rude doormen, pay an extortionate cover charge, another charge for coat check and then empty the rest of your wallet on drinks. For that, you got a whole lot of social interaction (both good and bad), exposure to great music at high volumes and a chance to dance away your cares.
With smartphones, none of that is necessary. Want a hookup? Call up Tinder, Grindr or any number of other dating apps and order in. Music? You have 250 million songs at your fingertips through streaming music services. Social interaction? That’s what texting, WhatsApp and social media are for, isn’t it?
There’s one other smartphone factor to consider, something that has just been confirmed by a study conducted by LifeStance Health, a U.S. mental health-care provider. It suggests we’ve gone from FOMO that might occur when we stay home to the fear of accidentally going viral.
This survey asked 1,000 American adults about attitudes toward going out to dance. Almost half (49 per cent) said that dancing in public made them too anxious. The idea of dancing like no one is watching (there’s that saying again) fills them with such fear of being recorded on a smartphone and humiliated on social media that they’d rather just stay home. Gen Z (43 per cent) fears “acting silly” will turn them into social media jokes. About 40 per cent says that this anxiety stops them from being in the moment and just enjoying themselves. And lest you think that it’s just Gen Z, the survey reported that 30 per cent of adults in this survey felt exactly the same way.
Some are strangers shooting surreptitiously while club promoters and influencers have no problem sticking cameras in the faces of patrons, all in the name of creating “content.”
It’s not just in America, either. A British study says that Gen Z is “hyper aware” of what’s going on around them in nightclubs and constantly watch for strangers taking pictures and video. They know that one bad decision will live on the internet forever and perhaps impact important things in the future. Perhaps just sit on the sidelines. And if they do decide to dance, few people decide to really let loose. Self-consciousness rules the dance floor.
Some clubs are taking precautions. In Berlin, many clubs provide customers with a sticker that they must put over their camera lens. Hey, it’s something.
Smartphones and fear of TikTok or Instagram infamy after a few drinks is one thing. Now, though, we’re moving into the era of smart glasses with built-in cameras like Meta’s Ray-Bans. Gee, what could possibly go wrong there?
Dance like no one is looking? Expressions of pure joy in public? Not caring about what other people think? Thanks, but maybe just best stay home, yeah?

title: Al Nassr v Al Wasl Asian Champions League clash in Riyadh postponed
body: The Asian Champions League (ACL) clash between Cristiano Ronaldo's Al Nassr and Dubai club Al Wasl has been postponed. The ACL Elite match was originally scheduled to take place at the King Saud University Stadium in Riyadh on Monday. However, the match has been postponed to a later date. The Asian Football Confederation stated that “the new match date and kick off time will be confirmed and communicated in due course”. While no official reason for the postponement was provided, travel issues related to regional disturbances are believed to be a factor. However, other Asian Champions League matches are scheduled to go ahead as planned. Saudi Arabia club Al Qadsiah are scheduled to host Qatari side Al Sadd at the Prince Mohammed Bin Fahd Stadium in Dammam. Also, high-flying UAE side Al Ain are set to host Iranian team Tractor FC at the Hazza Bin Zayed Stadium in Al Ain on Monday. Matches and events in Saudi Arabia have been affected amid intense fighting between the kingdom and Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels. A Saudi Pro League match between Al Nassr and Asian champions Al Ahli was postponed. The Six Kings tennis tournament featuring the likes of Carlos Alcaraz, Novak Djokovic and Alexander Zverev in Saudi Arabia was postponed due to attacks on Riyadh. Elsewhere, the Riyadh Fashion Week and Future Investment Initiative conference were also postponed. More to follow …

title: Russia creating favorable conditions for Western companies — Putin
body:
MOSCOW, October 25. /TASS/. Russia is creating favorable conditions for Western companies that have remained in the country, Russian President Vladimir Putin said.
"We strive to create appropriate, favorable conditions for them," he told Vesti reporter Pavel Zarubin.
Some companies were practically in tears as they left Russia under pressure from Western European governments, he added.
"When certain companies left under pressure from Western European governments, our friends from those countries were practically in tears," Putin said.

title: Russia prepared to export as much of diesel fuel as US may need — deputy PM
body:
MOSCOW, October 25. /TASS/. Russia is prepared to deliver whatever volume of diesel it requires to the United States as part of the diesel deal, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said.
"Frankly speaking, we will export as much as our partners would want. We can delivered as much as needed," told Vesti reporter Pavel Zarubin when asked how much of diesel fuel Russia is prepared to supply.
Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump held a phone call on October 9, during which they discussed, among other things, petroleum product supplies. The Russian president said that Moscow had reiterated its readiness to supply oil and petroleum products to the United States and global markets.

title: Previous winner of Mustafa Prize donates $160,000
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 25 (MNA) – A previous winner of the Mustafa Prize donated some $160,000 to Mustafa(PBUH) Foundation through the Rasul Medal to support young scientists across the Islamic world.
Mehmet Toner, a 2025 Mustafa(pbuh) Prize laureate, endowed his prize money to contribute to the advancement of the Rasul(pbuh) Medal.
Toner, one of the three laureates of 2025 Mustafa Prize, has requested that his cash prize be devoted to supporting young scientists through the Rasul Medal. Under the statutes of the Mustafa Prize, the cash prize of 500,000 dollars was shared among Toner and the two other laureates. In previous years, Ugur Sahin (2019), Omid Farrokhzad (2023), and Vahab Mirrokni (2025) have donated their cash prize to help establish and advance the Rasul Medal.
Born in 1958 in Turkey, Mehmet Toner is a professor of biomedical engineering at Harvard Medical School. He won the 2025 Mustafa Prize for the development of nano/microfluidic devices with clinical applications. His technology enables the isolation of cancer cells from blood, supporting early diagnosis, monitoring, and designing precise treatments for patients.
The Rasul Medal Previously known as the Young Scientist Medal, the Rasul Medal was founded based on the endowments made by Mustafa Prize laureates, Ugur Sahin, Omid Farrokhzad, and Vahab Mirrokni. It is awarded to scientists under the age of 40 residing in Islamic countries. The inaugural edition of the Medal was held alongside the 6th Mustafa Prize in 2025.
The Medal is awarded to impactful works in the fields of Life and Medical Science and Technology, Basic and Engineering Sciences, and Computer Science by young scientists from Islamic countries. The candidates must be nominated by a third-party scientific or technological body, such as universities and research centers, reputable scientific and technological associations and institutions, academies of sciences, or science and technology parks. The candidates for the Rasul Medal must be under 40 years old at the end of the year in which the medal is awarded. This means that candidates for the 2026 Rasul Medal must be born in 1987 or later.
The winners are bestowed a medal, a certificate, and a $10,000 cash prize in each category.
Established as a symbol of excellence and scientific merit of the young generation of scientific talent, the Rasul Medal promotes scientific and technological breakthroughs by young scientists in the Islamic world and recognizes their influential achievements.

title: EPL: Carrick bench Bruno Fernandes after Como outburst
body: Manchester United boss Michael Carrick said it was a “pure football” decision to drop captain Bruno Fernandes to the bench despite the Portugal midfielder’s criticism of his manager’s tactics in a 4-1 thrashing by Como. Without a win in seven games in all competitions, Carrick badly needs a victory against Bournemouth at Old Trafford on Sunday to quell speculation over his future and has made a bold call. The Red Devils begin the day 15th in the table with just seven points from their opening seven league games. Fernandes hit out at United’s passive approach out of possession as Champions League debutants Como ran riot in Italy on Wednesday. “When you have options it’s always a difficult decision. We have to make the right one for today and the team to get that performance we want,” added Carrick as he dismissed the decision was taken as a response to Fernandes’s outburst. Fernandes won a clean sweep of individual awards last season after breaking the Premier League record for assists with 21 as United finished third in the table. But the 32-year-old’s impact has been much more limited so far this season, bar a hat-trick against Ipswich back in August. Carrick made four changes in total with Matheus Cunha, Matthijs de Ligt and Noussair Mazraoui also dropping out for Ayden Heaven, Leny Yoro, Carlos Baleba and Amad Diallo. Fernandes’s comments came just over a week after Lisandro Martinez took aim at the club’s board for not doing enough to strengthen Carrick’s squad in the transfer window. Martinez was not dropped for his remarks but was replaced at half-time in a 1-1 draw at Leeds last weekend with an injury and is only fit enough to return from the bench against Bournemouth. “You can say whether Bruno was right or wrong in what he said but you have to take responsibility on the pitch. You have to take responsibility as a group of players,” said United’s all-time leading goalscorer Wayne Rooney. He added: “These players, they’re selfish. They don’t care about their team-mates, don’t care about the manager, the staff or the fans, they care about themselves. “If they’re not getting what’s right for them, they’re like babies and just throw their toys out of the pram and go and deflect the blame on to anyone else but themselves.” Vanguard News The post EPL: Carrick bench Bruno Fernandes after Como outburst appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: FRSC identifies persistent safety violations among tanker drivers
body: The Federal Road Safety Corps (FRSC) has identified speeding, driver fatigue, overloading and driving against traffic as persistent violations among petroleum tanker drivers. The FRSC spokesman, Osondu Ohaeri who told the News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) on Sunday in Abuja, warned that such practices continue to threaten road safety despite enforcement efforts. Ohaeri further discussed the challenges associated with the transportation of petroleum products and other goods by articulated vehicles. He said some tanker drivers exceeded recommended speed limits in attempts to meet delivery schedules, despite the difficulty of bringing heavily loaded vehicles to a safe stop. He explained that the size and weight of tankers required drivers to exercise caution, particularly when approaching bridges, bends and congested sections of highways. He also identified fatigue as a major risk, noting that some drivers attempted to cover long distances, including journeys from Kano to Lagos, overnight without adequate rest. “Driving while fatigued could impair concentration and reaction time, increasing the likelihood of losing control of vehicles. “Also, driving against traffic is another serious violation. Some operators overload their vehicles or use them to carry additional goods alongside petroleum products. “These practices can compromise vehicle stability and expose drivers, passengers and other road users to danger,” he said. Ohaeri attributed the persistence of the violations partly to drivers’ attitudes and the pressure to meet delivery schedules, stressing that compliance with traffic regulations remained essential regardless of operational demands. He said the FRSC had continued to intensify safety education and enforcement while working with operators and other stakeholders to improve compliance. He disclosed that the corps had achieved about 75 per cent success in issuing the appropriate Class G driver’s licences to relevant operators, as part of efforts to ensure that drivers possessed the required qualifications. He said the agency was also engaging petroleum marketers and other industry stakeholders to strengthen safety standards across the transportation chain. He urged tanker drivers and operators to prioritise safety over delivery schedules, warning that violations involving vehicles conveying highly flammable products could have devastating consequences. He called for improved driver discipline, adequate rest, proper vehicle maintenance and strict adherence to speed limits to reduce crashes involving articulated vehicles. The post FRSC identifies persistent safety violations among tanker drivers appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Overnight Russian attack damages homes in two districts of Vinnytsia
body:
According to Ukrinform, the Vinnytsia City Council reported this on Facebook .
"Damage to residential buildings has been recorded in two neighborhoods of the city – Zamostia and Mali Khutory. There were no fatalities. Two people are in hospital. The other injured people received medical assistance at the scene and declined hospitalization," the statement said.
In Zamostia, a residential apartment in a high-rise building was directly hit. Fortunately, the woman who lives there was not at home that night. The strike destroyed the panel partitions between floors. Rescue workers are now clearing the rubble, while construction specialists are inspecting the building's structures to determine the next steps. The blast wave also damaged neighboring buildings.
In Mali Khutory, a drone completely destroyed a two-story garage. Around ten neighboring houses were damaged, with windows shattered and roofs and utility networks affected.
As Ukrinform reported, Russian forces struck a five-story apartment building in Vinnytsia with a drone overnight into Sunday, October 26, injuring six people.

title: Bosnia Deserves Better Than Permanent Probation
body:
When the war in Bosnia ended in 1996, the Dayton Peace Agreement provided for a high representative, an international figure appointed by the 55 member Peace Implementation Council. The high representative has powers to impose or annul laws and to remove elected officials. The position was intended to be temporary and critics say that it has become an obstacle to the development of democracy in Bosnia and Herzegovina.
The fight over who should replace Bosnia and Herzegovina’s High Representative has exposed a deeper divide between Washington and Brussels: what to do with an international protectorate that was meant to have evaporated decades ago. The United States is right that Bosnia needs to move beyond open-ended foreign supervision. But if Washington wants a Bosnia that welcomes American investment and commercial engagement, simply weakening the machinery that has governed the country for three decades will not get it there.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
The impasse proves the point. Europeans remain reluctant to dismantle the Office of the High Representative (OHR), empowered to impose laws and remove officials under its “Bonn Powers”; Washington has grown impatient with what it sees as an unaccountable brake on sovereignty. Europeans suspect an American bid to muscle into institutions that Brussels has spent years building; Americans suspect a European bid to preserve a protectorate past its purpose. Both suspicions contain some truth, and neither side gains from paralysis.
The immediate dispute concerns a person; the deeper problem is a system with no clear end in sight. Christian Schmidt resigned as high representative on July 1, charging the Peace Implementation Council (PIC) – the 55-odd states and organizations overseeing the 1995 Dayton settlement – with urgently finding a successor. His deputy, the American diplomat Louis Crishock, became acting high representative: for now, an American is running the apparatus his own government wants scaled back.
The July 14 deadline for a new high representative passed without agreement – not because of Bosnian obstruction, but because PIC ambassadors failed to reach a compromise. That should matter to Washington. If the objective is a Bosnia more sovereign and commercially open, the question is not whether the OHR should last forever – plainly it should not – but how to leave behind a state capable of standing without it.
A managed exit offers more leverage than passive disengagement; the alternative is a vacuum in which entrenched interests exploit ethnic divisions while outside powers less aligned with Bosnia’s sovereignty compete for influence. Washington’s instinct, articulated in its broader Western Balkans policy, is to empower local actors over open-ended supervision; European officials say much the same, even if distrust of American intentions has kept them from acting on it.
Thirty years ago, the Dayton Peace Accords stopped a war by dividing power among Bosniak, Serb and Croat blocs rather than building a fully functioning unified state – an achievement in itself, but a peace agreement drafted at speed to stop the killing, not a constitution designed to elaborate a functioning state. Bosnia remains suspended between that emergency architecture and the normal life of a sovereign nation.
It is tempting, particularly in Washington, to conclude that Bosnia’s institutions are themselves the obstacle and that the PIC and OHR are simply failed mechanisms best left to wither. But the deeper problem is horizonless oversight, which neither drives reform nor pushes politicians to take responsibility when they can hide behind an administrator’s extraordinary powers instead.
That drift has been compounded by neglect – as one senior European diplomat put it wearily, few in Brussels know much about Bosnia any more, and fewer really care – and by dysfunction: the PIC has not met at ministerial level for nearly 20 years, and the OHR has become entrenched to the point of paralysis.
Russia’s presence in the PIC, too, is a particular absurdity: a state waging war on one European neighbor sitting in judgment on the peace of another. Its 2021 bid to force the issue through the UN Security Council failed, and it has since largely boycotted the Council’s work on Bosnia.
None of this excuses Bosnia’s own political class, too many of whom remain trapped in the past and act provocatively precisely because the high representative’s powers shield them from consequences. But the protectorate has entrenched a culture in which responsibility is always someone else’s: Bosnia’s divisions have been curated, in part, by the very structures meant to heal them.
The OHR was meant to close in 2007, then 2008. Instead that deadline morphed into the “5+2” agenda: five objectives and two conditions with no date attached, several still unmet two decades later.
