On the scale of the world, the greatest risk is Chinese aggression in Taiwan. By defending itself, Ukraine has demonstrated the difficulties in offensive operations and made such a war more likely.
Ukraine is making a nuclear war less likely. Russia is a nuclear power. Ukraine is not. If Russia is allowed to defeat Ukraine, other middle powers will likely draw the conclusion that they need to build nuclear weapons in order to defend themselves. By holding back Russia, Ukraine is also holding back nuclear proliferation.
Ukraine is defending us all from oligarchy, from the rule of the very wealthy. Putin’s idea that Ukraine is not a real country is the example of an oligarchic fantasy, the kind of centibillionaire nonsense that can take lives and destroy the planet. By resisting Russian aggression, Ukraine is showing that democracy can defend itself.
Ukraine is providing an example of freedom. In Ukraine, even during conditions of war, civil society functions, and people speak their minds. Under Russian occupation, an entirely different mode of life prevails: Women are raped ; children are deported to Russia to be assimilated; local activists are murdered; young men are forced into the Russian army to die; total uniformity is imposed.
And so what Trump says is wrong in the very broadest of senses. Ukraine is doing work for our security and for our liberty. Ukrainians have held off the worst and bought the rest of us time.
And Trump’s claim is also wrong in the narrow sense. Ukraine has been providing battlefield intelligence to the United States from the beginning of the war. It has shared its experience of modern warfare with American institutions. It even sent – in these most trying of times inside Ukraine – hundreds of its own experienced air defense troops to the Near East to help protect Americans and their allies from Iranian drones.
Imagine what those Ukrainian crews, separated from their embattled country to defend Americans, are thinking right now, as their contributions are denied, and as their own families are put in greater danger by US policy.
Trump’s statement is not only unjust. It is not only a lie. It is a big lie, whose purpose is not to describe the world but to change it, to blame the victim and assist the aggressor, to betray the ally and destroy the alliances, to create a world in which everyone must feel unsafe except the wealthy and powerful, a world in which all that matters are the personal feelings and personal dealings of a handful of oligarchs and dictators.
Reprinted from the author’s blog Thinking About. See the original here .
The views expressed in this opinion article are the author’s and not necessarily those of Kyiv Post.

title: Must we destroy the evidence of our past to build our future?, By Lande Ọmọ Ọba
body:
And I asked myself: Must we destroy the evidence of our past in order to celebrate our freedom from it? Surely, preserving a colonial building does not mean celebrating colonialism! It simply means acknowledging that this was part of our history. Whether we like that history or not, it happened. I am told that even the fountain that replaced the courthouse is no longer functional. We lost an important historical building for a water fountain that is not functional. The list goes on and on.
On Tuesday, I had the privilege of listening to former President Olusegun Obasanjo speak at Harvard University Institute of Politics and Centre for African Studies. He had come to discuss peacekeeping in Africa and beyond, but there was something he said about our identity and history that has stayed with me. There were quite a number of young Nigerians in the room, many from the diaspora.
A young man, about 26 years old, asked a question about the Nigerian Civil War. He wanted to know whose account of the war was correct, considering that different people had different versions of what happened. As he spoke, I sensed that he was leaning towards finding fault with one ethnic group over another and allied to the current heated polity. President Obasanjo was not having it!
He gave examples of heroic acts by individuals from different ethnic groups and equally troubling acts by people from those same groups. In fact, he told a story of how he was saved from an assassination plot by a Hausa, Hassan Katsina. Then he uttered the words that I will hold dear for a long time. “There are only two types of Nigerians: good Nigerians and bad Nigerians. Not good tribes and bad tribes.” I thought that was profound.
But I also kept thinking about that young man. He is 26. He was not born when the civil war happened. So, whose version of history is he listening to? His grandfather’s? His parents’? Someone who experienced the war? Or perhaps something he read on social media? And what if the version he has heard is incomplete or coloured by someone’s personal experience or prejudice? How would he know? Which is why many like me worry about our attitude to history in Nigeria.
We talk a lot. We argue endlessly about our past, our leaders, the civil war, ethnicity, corruption, and everything in between. But how much do we actually document and, more importantly, how much do we learn so that we do not keep making mistakes? History is not just about remembering what happened. It is about understanding why it happened, what went wrong, what worked, and how we can do better. We cannot keep making the same mistakes and expecting different results. As President Obasanjo spoke about peacekeeping across Africa, I found myself thinking about Nigeria. We have played important roles in keeping peace in other countries, but today we are struggling with insecurity and divisions within our own borders. Surely, understanding our history must be part of finding lasting solutions.
And I found myself asking, why are we not doing more of this in Nigeria? Our history did not start from our independence in 1960. I was recently told a story about the old courthouse at Tinubu Square, near Kakawa Street on Lagos Island. Apparently, the site once housed the Court of Assizes, an important part of our judicial history during colonial rule. The building was demolished and replaced with a fountain commemorating Nigeria’s independence .
Not too long ago, I visited Concord, Massachusetts and had the opportunity to spend some time at the historic Colonial Inn, a building dating back to 1716! Nearby, British forces and American colonial militiamen fought during the Revolutionary War in 1775. The area has been carefully preserved, with buildings, monuments and records that tell the story of what happened. I stood there taking it all in. Here was a country preserving a history that is over 250 years old. Generations have come and gone, but the story remains accessible. Of course, people may disagree about how historical events should be interpreted. But the evidence is there to be examined.
And I found myself asking, why are we not doing more of this in Nigeria? Our history did not start from our independence in 1960. I was recently told a story about the old courthouse at Tinubu Square, near Kakawa Street on Lagos Island. Apparently, the site once housed the Court of Assizes, an important part of our judicial history during colonial rule. The building was demolished and replaced with a fountain commemorating Nigeria’s independence. A friend was telling me about how Professor Wole Soyinka has also commented critically on the loss of that historic building. The argument, as the story was told to me, was that we needed to put the memories of colonial rule behind us, and we replaced this site with a water fountain!
And I asked myself: Must we destroy the evidence of our past in order to celebrate our freedom from it? Surely, preserving a colonial building does not mean celebrating colonialism! It simply means acknowledging that this was part of our history. Whether we like that history or not, it happened. I am told that even the fountain that replaced the courthouse is no longer functional. We lost an important historical building for a water fountain that is not functional. The list goes on and on.
In the West, they have lectures on the life of Christopher Marlowe and William Shakespeare born in 1564! At one of the lectures, I felt an inner voice asking how many times I have attended or been invited to a lecture on the life of any outstanding African born even 100 years ago, but here I was listening with rapt attention to this lecture. Sometimes we are too eager to move on, to forget, to start afresh, without asking ourselves what we should have learnt from what came before.
What about the ordinary Nigerians who lived through those difficult years? The mothers, teachers, civil servants, journalists, and families whose lives were changed forever? Who is recording their stories? Who is listening to them? And who is making sure that the next generation has access to these accounts? We need to preserve our history, especially the difficult and uncomfortable parts.
We forget that progress is often about improving on yesterday, not pretending yesterday never happened. We are not only losing our living history, but we are also gradually losing the generation that witnessed some of the most important periods in Nigeria’s history. Those who experienced independence, the civil war and the early years of military rule are getting older. Many have already passed away. Every time one of them dies, we risk losing stories that may never have been properly documented. These people are living libraries. And I am not talking only about former presidents, governors, or military leaders.
What about the ordinary Nigerians who lived through those difficult years? The mothers, teachers, civil servants, journalists, and families whose lives were changed forever? Who is recording their stories? Who is listening to them? And who is making sure that the next generation has access to these accounts? We need to preserve our history, especially the difficult and uncomfortable parts. Not in order to keep old wounds open or pass blame from one generation to another, but to understand how we got here and what we must do differently.
I keep thinking about that young man at Harvard and President Obasanjo’s response. The young boy whispered to many around him: “He didn’t answer my question,” and someone else said “Our African parents avoid uncomfortable truths with long tales and proverbs.” I smiled. Will they act differently when they become elders? We owe future generations the truth about our history, not simply the version that suits our beliefs, our families, or our ethnic affiliations. Because if we genuinely want a better Nigeria, we must be willing to learn from the Nigeria that came before us. We cannot erase our past and then expect to learn from it.
By the way, I paid $15 to the tour guide to tell me about the revolutionary war and my brunch at the Colonial Inn cost $65. There is money to be made for history and tourism.
‘Lande Omo Oba , a lawyer, writes from Lagos.

title: Adnoc prepares new wave of oil and gas tenders for 2027
body: Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (Adnoc) plans to tender contracts for offshore sour gas developments, an export gas pipeline and enhanced oil recovery projects in 2027, as the state energy giant prepares a new wave of engineering and construction work. "The demand is real, and the timeline is set," Adel Al Yafei, Adnoc's senior vice president for group commercial operations and execution, told suppliers on Sunday at the second Make it with Adnoc Forum in Abu Dhabi, before the Adipec energy conference. Adnoc has awarded 10 major engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) projects so far this year, along with more than 8,000 requisitions, contracts and purchase requests involving more than 1,500 suppliers, he said. The offshore sour gas development includes wellhead towers and pipelines, while the export gas pipeline project involves new wells and an offshore cluster to expand capacity, according to presentation slides. The enhanced oil recovery project will use alternating injections of carbon dioxide and water to increase production. Downstream projects scheduled for tender in 2027 include refinery residue upgrading and additional export berths for natural gas liquids and sulphur. The tender pipeline also covers a long-term development project involving new wells, a processing island and offshore platforms, alongside onshore and offshore power distribution, an island power link and offshore field connections. For 2028, Adnoc outlined onshore and offshore oilfield developments, an integrated onshore gas project, gas storage, digitalisation and infrastructure upgrades. The company did not disclose project values. Adnoc is seeking to raise its oil production capacity to 5 million barrels a day by 2027, from 4.85 million bpd. The tender pipeline comes as Adnoc seeks to expand domestic manufacturing, unveiling more than Dh60 billion ($16.3 billion) in opportunities for UAE suppliers through 2030 at the same forum. The initiative covers more than 200 essential products and critical spare parts, many currently imported, as the company seeks to reduce its exposure to global supply disruptions. "Adnoc will expand and grow in all of its assets," Mr Al Yafei said. Beyond major construction projects, the company plans to tender drilling and upstream services in 2027 and 2028, including downhole completion, drilling fluids and cementing. Operational contracts will cover inspection and maintenance of compressors, turbines and pumps. The plans come as Adnoc changes how it procures equipment and services, aiming to reduce tender cycle times by 40 per cent without cutting the time suppliers have to prepare bids. "That's the time we save from our process, not the time we take from what you need to deliver a good technical and commercial offer," Mr Al Yafei said. Bidding periods will be aligned with market conditions, while project schedules will take account of urgency, complexity and supplier capacity. Companies will also receive feedback after tenders to help improve future bids. Adnoc has doubled its EPC contracting principles to 20 from 10, seeking greater flexibility and competition. Unit-rate contracts will be negotiated against market median prices rather than unusually high or low bids. For EPC tenders, the company will prioritise the most competitive offer and negotiate exclusively with that bidder if it meets Adnoc's benchmark. First-time bidders will also be assessed on their capacity to deliver. Adnoc is also revising its in-country value (ICV) procurement framework. From November 1, bids will be assessed using a formula weighted 70 per cent towards commercial terms and 30 per cent towards ICV, said Salama Alawadhi, senior vice president for group commercial, ICV and industrial development.

title: Mother, child killed as 2 trucks crash in Lagos
body: A mother and her child have been killed after two heavily laden container trucks overturned at Mile 2, near Freeman Market, inward Apapa, Lagos State. The Lagos State Traffic Management Authority disclosed this in a statement issued by its Director, Public Affairs and Enlightenment Department, Adebayo Taofiq. The statement said the victims were trapped beneath the overturned trucks and their containerised cargoes, sustaining fatal injuries. LASTMA’s rescue and recovery personnel responded to the scene, cordoned off the affected road and diverted motorists through an adjoining service lane to prevent further accidents and ease traffic congestion. The agency deployed a crane and a high-capacity tow vehicle to remove the overturned trucks and their containers, while officers of the Nigeria Police Force provided security during the recovery operation. The remains of the victims were subsequently taken to the Police Mortuary in Yaba for necessary procedures. The General Manager of LASTMA, Olalekan Bakare-Oki, expressed sadness over the incident and extended his condolences to the bereaved family. He called on relevant security agencies to conduct a thorough investigation to establish the immediate and underlying causes of the crash. Bakare-Oki said the investigation should determine whether mechanical defects, overloading, improper cargo distribution, driver negligence or other factors contributed to the accident. He urged operators of articulated vehicles to ensure their trucks were roadworthy, secure their cargoes properly and comply strictly with established road safety regulations. The LASTMA boss also advised motorists, particularly commercial truck drivers, to exercise caution and prioritise the safety of other road users. He stressed that regular mechanical inspections, proper cargo handling and responsible driving were essential to preventing avoidable road crashes and fatalities in Lagos State.

title: Miri Regev's unfulfilled promises: Eight transportation reforms that never happened
body: Miri Regev returned to the Transportation and Road Safety Ministry on December 29, 2022, and her second term has so far failed to reduce road-accident fatalities.In 2024 and 2025, road deaths hit a two-decade high, and 2026 shows no sign of change except a slight decline, driven only by a sharp drop in March, when the country was in shelters and safe rooms during Operation Roaring Lion.Evidence of the minister's major failure came from the European Transport Safety Council (ETSC). At the end of 2025, the council announced it was suspending Israel over government measures that, the organization said, were incompatible with its basic commitment to saving lives. The organization formally ended Israel's participation in its Road Safety Performance Index (PIN) program, with no clear path back.The ETSC decided to suspend Israel's National Road Safety Authority (RSA) from the program until further notice: “The recent actions of the current Israeli government are not consistent with the fundamental commitment of ETSC and the PIN program to protecting human life.” Israel's Transportation Ministry claimed the move was political, but the surge in the number of people killed and injured on Israel's roads, in contrast to most European countries, Regev's lack of interest in road safety, and the departure of key figures in the field, such as Avi Naor, who served as chairman of the RSA, and Erez Kita, who served as the authority's director general, suggest otherwise.Despite the poor results and scant action, the transportation and road safety minister delivered a stream of media statements meant to benefit Israel's citizens and the road safety community. A comprehensive check by Walla Cars and the Or Yarok road safety association reveals the minister's main statements and promises during her term, and how much of them were carried out.Ride-sharing in Israel: Didn't happen“Uber will be in Israel. Period.” That was Regev's reply on October 22, 2025, to a parliamentary question from MK Eitan Ginzburg on advancing shared transportation.The approval was meant to allow private drivers to carry paying passengers in their own cars, aiming to increase competition in the passenger transport market and lower prices for consumers. The bill initiated by Ginzburg (Blue and White, Beyachad) passed a preliminary reading in the Knesset and even a first reading, but went no further.As of October 2026, ride-sharing is not legal in Israel, but the Transportation Ministry rarely acts against private drivers who pick up paying passengers, mainly in the Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) community, where they are known as “drivers.”They are not subject to the high insurance costs and licensing fees charged to legal cab drivers, or to the other regulatory requirements the state imposes on official taxis, such as buying a “green number” taxi license for more than 200,000 shekels, or leasing one.Higher fines for a range of offenses, especially cellphone use: Didn't happenRegev supplied the quote and announced the move at the Yedioth Ahronoth transportation conference: “Police will catch someone texting, and they'll immediately give him a 10,000-shekel fine the first time. He won't go to court. The second time, it will be confiscation of the vehicle.” On December 2, 2025, the minister declared on her Facebook account and on X that she would raise the fines.As of October 2026, the stiffer fines have not yet materialized.Scrapping the internal driving test: Didn't happenIn another attempt to present itself as fighting the cost of living, the Transportation Ministry promoted abolishing the internal test, which pre-test driving instructors administer before the official exam and costs learners and their parents between 150 and 400 shekels. The move was even formally included in the 2026 state budget agreements, and an official circular stated that the abolition would take effect on June 18, 2026.The move was never completed because of protests by driving instructors and technical problems and failures, leading the ministry to announce, just one day before implementation, that it had decided to postpone the amendment's entry into force for an in-depth reexamination.No new date was set.Approval for Tesla full self-driving: Didn't happenRegev addressed the issue after Tesla drivers in Israel submitted a petition, posting the following on her official accounts. On October 29, 2025, she wrote on her Facebook page and on X: “I've received the many appeals from Tesla drivers in Israel! Tesla drivers? Soon you won't have to hold the wheel.”In a conversation with Tesla CEO Elon Musk at the Smart Mobility conference, Regev also promised to speed up approval in Israel for FSD and equivalent systems from other carmakers.Since then, a long list of European countries, from the Netherlands to Belgium, Denmark and the Czech Republic, have approved its use. But in Israel, the Transportation Ministry has not yet updated the regulation requiring drivers to keep their hands on the wheel throughout the drive, nor has it worked with the Commissioner of Insurance to settle liability for an accident that occurs while the vehicle is in autonomous mode.Multi-year national road safety plan for 2026–2030: Didn't happenGovernment Resolution 3491 of November 16, 2025, states that “with the aim of reducing the rate of road accident casualties, reducing the economic damage caused by road accidents and strengthening the government's commitment to improving road safety,” the government approved a multi-year national road safety plan for 2026–2030.Under the plan, the rate of road accident casualties is to be cut by 25% within five years of the resolution's approval and funding, compared with the 2021–2025 average, a lower target than had been set in the past. The ministry also set a goal for Israel to rank among the seven leading countries in road safety, measured by casualties relative to population size.On December 14, 2025, the ministry declared: “Stopping the carnage on the roads: 350 million shekels a year have been budgeted for saving lives and restoring road safety in Israel. The most dramatic road safety move in a decade: a comprehensive, budgeted and measurable national plan will get underway as early as 2026.”“We are launching a dramatic national move to save lives. This is a significant moment of taking national responsibility, in which the State of Israel is changing direction and putting the safety of road users at the top of its priorities,” Regev boasted in a press release at the time. “After years in which road safety received no systemic, comprehensive response, we are bringing a comprehensive, budgeted and focused plan to save lives, which means fewer families receiving the terrible news at the door. The state is taking responsibility.”As of October 2026, the money has not been transferred to fund the plan.Fewer required driving lessons: Didn't happenIn August 2024, Regev proposed a new procedure that would dramatically reduce the minimum number of driving lessons required before taking the road test, from 28 lessons to just 22 for automatic vehicles, to lower the cost of getting a driver's license. Or Yarok opposed it, as did the ETSC, which issued a formal warning that cutting initial training would harm the safety of young drivers, who are defined as a high-risk group. Professionals at the RSA, to whom the initiative was referred to assess its implications, also objected. The move never went ahead.Annual vehicle inspections at garages: Didn't happenOn June 6, 2023, the minister posted on her page on X (formerly Twitter): “ONE STOP SHOP – who doesn't know the hassle when it's time for the annual vehicle inspection. You clear half a day, if not more, going to a licensed testing center; if the car fails, you drive to a garage to fix the faults, then back to the center, and so on. Wasting time, fuel, workdays, and more. “I have instructed the relevant parties in my ministry to put an end to this, and they are now working on it, setting professional standards, with supervision and oversight and preserving the safety and consumer aspects, so that licensed garages will be qualified to carry out the annual vehicle inspection. Quickly and efficiently, and all this as part of my plan to fight the cost of living in Israel.”The following day, the ministry released a statement reading: “This is a historic move that will significantly shorten the long lines and reduce the load on testing centers, encourage inspections to be carried out on time, accessibly and close to drivers' homes or workplaces, alongside lower costs as part of the fight against the cost of living in Israel.”Regev claimed the move was based on a professional opinion that she refused to disclose, and ignored the fact that the law had once allowed inspections at garages but was changed because of the garages' conflict of interest: a single body that looks for faults in a vehicle on behalf of the state and can immediately offer to fix them for the customer on the premises.Such an arrangement could also lead to vehicles that are not fully roadworthy being approved in return for the customer having other, non-safety maintenance work done there.As of October 2026, the plan is stuck in the legislative process and under review by professional staff. Drivers in Israel must still go in person to official licensed testing centers for the annual inspection.Shorter waits for medical exams: Didn't happenRegev pledged to shorten long waiting times at the Medical Institute for Road Safety (MIRS) by outsourcing the institute's services and decentralizing its powers to private bodies.As of October 2026, the move has not been completed, and the institute still operates at a sluggish pace, to the detriment of tens of thousands of drivers a year whose licenses are revoked on medical grounds and who are forced to wait months for an examination at the only institute authorized to restore their licenses.Ministerial committee on road safety: Met three times in two yearsOn November 24, 2024, Regev announced the formation of a ministerial committee on road safety. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was appointed chairman, and the committee includes the government's most senior ministers.The committee held its first meeting on May 4, 2025, about six months after the government announced its establishment. The second was held on October 26, 2025, and the third on February 8, 2026.Netanyahu did not attend a single session.The committee's deliberations led to no significant road-safety decisions.Attorney Yaniv Yaakov, CEO of Or Yarok: “The Israeli public deserves a road safety minister who understands the weight of the responsibility and the purpose for which he works every day — to save lives. Minister Regev made many promises, but at the end of her term, only a small portion of them served road safety, as the grim figures also show. The minister's biggest failure is her refusal to approve a multi-year national plan, even though she requested it and it already exists."The wrong priorities have led us to the worst figures in two decades and to our removal from the European Transport Safety Council's annual performance report. Inaction costs human lives. The next transportation and road safety minister will have to change the priorities and put saving lives first. That is his duty and his privilege.”

title: First Nations, Carney, premiers to gather for ceremony ahead of historic meeting
body:
Prime Minister Mark Carney says this week’s meeting with First Nations leaders will help forge new relationships as his government pursues a major projects building boom.
First Nations leaders are meeting with Carney and some of the country’s premiers in Ottawa.
Carney said Monday it’s the first time in two decades the first ministers have met in person with First Nations leaders.
“Our task is twofold. First is to work together to create opportunities for all our peoples, while building a country that is stronger, more sovereign and more independent,” Carney said.
“And secondly, our task is to live our values fully of a fair and inclusive Canada.”
National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak said First Nations fought hard for this meeting and it should not be the last such gathering with first ministers.
“We have a mandate to seek political and technical tables that will advance constitutional discussions, recognize and implement First Nations’ inherent treaty and human rights,” Woodhouse Nepinak said.
“The prime minister has said that Canada is built on the bedrock of three peoples, First Nations, French and British. But there is no getting around the fact that First Nations have inhabited these territories long before any colonial borders were established.”
The meeting comes as Carney’s government works to speed up major project approvals and development — efforts some First Nations chiefs say threaten their rights.
The premiers of Alberta, British Columbia and Quebec are not attending the meeting.

title: Understanding Your Milk Options: A Dietitian’s Guide to Choosing the Right Milk
body: By Tito Ipinmoye Buying milk used to be simple. You walked into a supermarket, reached for a familiar tin or sachet, and carried on with the rest of your shopping. Today, that same trip can leave many people standing in the dairy aisle far longer than they expected. I remember shopping at one of the large supermarkets when I noticed a young couple standing in front of the milk shelf. They had been there for what felt like ten minutes, carefully picking up one product after another, turning the packs over to read the labels before placing them back. The wife was scrolling through Instagram, almost desperately, as though she hoped someone had recently posted the answer to the question they were trying to solve. “Which milk should we buy?” I couldn’t help but overhear parts of their conversation. Interestingly, they weren’t comparing brands or prices. They were trying to understand the different options available. Should they choose dairy milk or a non-dairy alternative? And if dairy was the right choice, what exactly was the difference between Full Cream Milk and Filled Milk? They wanted to make the right choice but weren’t sure what those terms meant. Eventually, I smiled and walked over. “Hello,” I said. “I’m sorry to interrupt. I’m a dietitian, and from what I’ve overheard, I think I can help explain the differences.” Within a few minutes, what had seemed like a complicated shopping decision suddenly became much clearer. They thanked me, picked the product that best suited what they were looking for and continued with the rest of their shopping. That encounter reminded me of something I have observed repeatedly throughout my years of practice: many consumers assume that milk is simply… milk. Yet today’s supermarket shelves tell a very different story. Before deciding which milk to buy, many consumers are first faced with an important question: Should I choose dairy milk or a non-dairy alternative? For those who choose dairy milk, there is another decision to make. Understanding the difference between Full Cream Milk, Filled Milk and age-appropriate milk products is key to choosing the option that best meets their needs. The challenge is that these differences aren’t always obvious to the average shopper. As a result, many people make their decisions based on familiarity, price or attractive packaging rather than understanding what the product was designed to do. Making informed food choices doesn’t always begin with eating something different. Sometimes, it begins with simply understanding what you’re buying. And that’s exactly where we’ll begin. Understanding the Two Main Milk Options When we think about the milk aisle, it can sometimes feel as though there are endless options. The first decision is much simpler than many people realise. Broadly speaking, there is Dairy milk and non-dairy milk Dairy milk comes from animals, most commonly cows, although goat’s and sheep’s milk are also consumed in many parts of the world. It naturally provides high-quality protein, calcium and several essential vitamins and minerals that support growth, bone health and overall wellbeing. For consumers who choose dairy milk, there is one more decision to make. Not all dairy milk products are the same. Within the dairy category, the two most common options consumers will come across are Full Cream Milk and Filled Milk . While both are dairy products and both provide important nutrients, they differ in their fat composition and are designed to meet different nutritional needs and consumer preferences. Understanding these differences is the next step in choosing the milk that’s right for you. Understanding Your Options Standing in that supermarket, I realised the couple weren’t just trying to choose a brand. They were trying to understand which type of dairy milk best suited their needs. Once you’ve decided that dairy milk is the right choice for you, the next step is understanding the different dairy products available. Peak’s dairy range, for example, includes Full Cream Milk, Filled Milk and Peak 456 Growing-Up Milk . Although they all contain dairy ingredients, each has been developed to meet different nutritional needs and life stages. Rather than thinking of these as different versions of the same product, it helps to think of each one as serving a different purpose. Peak Full Cream Milk is designed to provide complete dairy nutrition for everyday family use. Peak Filled Milk, on the other hand, offers consumers another dairy option with a different fat composition while still providing important nutrients such as protein and calcium. Peak 456 Growing-Up Milk is specially formulated to support the nutritional needs of children aged four to six years. Understanding what each product is designed to do makes choosing the right one much easier. Let’s take a closer look at each one. Peak Full Cream Milk When most people think of milk, Full Cream Milk is usually what comes to mind. Made from whole cow’s milk, it naturally contains milk fat, giving it the rich, creamy taste many people enjoy. It also provides complete dairy nutrition by supplying high-quality protein, calcium and a range of essential vitamins and minerals that contribute to bone health, muscle function and overall wellbeing. One example within this category is Peak Full Cream Milk, which is available in both powdered and evaporated formats. Its versatility makes it suitable for drinking, breakfast cereals, smoothies, tea, coffee, cooking and baking, making it a practical choice for everyday family use. Best suited for: Families looking for complete dairy nutrition for everyday use. Peak Filled Milk Filled Milk is a dairy milk product in which part or all the natural milk fat has been replaced with vegetable oils. While this gives it a different fat composition from Full Cream Milk, it continues to provide important nutrients such as high-quality protein, calcium and essential vitamins. Peak Filled Milk offers consumers another dairy milk option that combines these nutritional benefits with a different fat composition to suit varying dietary preferences. Rather than thinking of Filled Milk as “better” or “worse” than Full Cream Milk , it is more helpful to understand that each product has been developed to meet different consumer needs. The right choice depends on your nutritional requirements, health goals and personal preferences. Best suited for: Consumers looking for a dairy milk option with a different fat composition. Peak 456 Growing-Up Milk Children have different nutritional needs at different stages of growth, which is why age-appropriate milk products have an important role in supporting a balanced diet. Peak 456 Growing-Up Milk is specially formulated for children aged four to six years. In addition to providing high-quality protein and calcium, it is fortified with essential vitamins and DHA, an omega-3 fatty acid that supports normal brain development during childhood. By providing nutrients tailored to this stage of growth, Peak 456 helps support the nutritional needs of young children as part of a healthy, balanced diet. Best suited for: Children aged 4–6 years. A Simple Guide to Choosing the Right Milk Choosing the right milk doesn’t have to be complicated. Once you understand what each product is designed to do, the decision becomes much simpler. If you’re looking for… A suitable option is… Complete dairy nutrition for the family Peak Full Cream Milk A dairy milk option with a different fat composition Peak Filled Milk Nutrition designed for children aged 4–6 years Peak 456 Growing-Up Milk Before adding any dairy milk product to your shopping basket, ask yourself three simple questions: Which dairy milk do I need? Full Cream or Filled milk Who am I buying this product for? Does this product meet my nutritional needs and suit how I intend to use it? Answering these questions can help you move beyond attractive packaging or familiarity and choose the product that best suits your needs and those of your family. Choosing with Confidence Standing in that supermarket, I realised the young couple weren’t looking for the “best” milk. They were looking for clarity. Like many consumers, they simply wanted to understand the options available, and which one best suited their needs. Their questions weren’t unusual. They reflected the uncertainty many shoppers experience when faced with more choice than ever before. The good news is that having more options isn’t a problem. In fact, it’s an advantage. The first step is to know that there is dairy milk and non- dairy milk. For those who choose dairy milk, understanding the difference between Full Cream Milk , Filled Milk and age-appropriate milk products makes choosing the right option much easier. The key is understanding the purpose of each product. Once we understand those differences, choosing milk becomes less about guesswork and more about making informed decisions for ourselves and our families. After all, making informed nutrition decisions doesn’t begin when we pour milk into a cup. It begins with the knowledge and confidence to choose wisely. So, know your milk. The post Understanding Your Milk Options: A Dietitian’s Guide to Choosing the Right Milk appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: EU fails to instill values in migrants, allows those values to crumble at home — Putin
body:
MOSCOW, October 25. /TASS/. European elites have lost their own traditions and culture and are no longer able to instill them in the migrants who have arrived in their countries, Russian President Vladimir Putin told Vesti reporter Pavel Zarubin.
"How can one introduce European traditions and customs into this environment when they themselves are dismantling their own traditions and customs," he said, adding that "nothing definitely reaches this environment of migrants and their children."
"Many have arrived and lived there for decades, yet they do not speak the language of the host country," Putin added.

title: Nigeria Woos Korean Investors As Seoul Highlights Youth Initiatives
body: Michael Olugbode in Abuja Nigeria has urged South Korean companies to increase investment in manufacturing, agriculture, technology and shipbuilding, seeking to leverage Korea’s industrial expertise to boost local production, create jobs and accelerate economic growth. The appeal was made by the Chief of Protocol at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Babagana Wakil, who represented the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Ambassador Bianca Odumegwu-Ojukwu, at a reception to mark Korea’s National Day in Abuja, weekend. Speaking on behalf of the minister, Wakil said Korea’s achievements in industrialisation, technology and infrastructure offered valuable lessons for Nigeria as it pursued economic diversification. He urged Korean firms to explore opportunities in local manufacturing and assembly, shipbuilding and other industries capable of expanding Nigeria’s industrial base. He said Nigeria was interested in Korean expertise in agricultural mechanisation, particularly rice production and processing, to improve productivity and support food security. Other priority areas included digital technology, infrastructure, education, technical training, maritime security and fisheries. Wakil reaffirmed the Nigerian government’s appreciation for Korea’s contributions to the country’s economic growth and skills development, stressing the need to expand trade and investment for mutual benefit. South Korean Ambassador to Nigeria, Jeong Yoan, highlighted initiatives supported by his country in youth entrepreneurship, education and agricultural employment, describing Nigeria’s young population as a major asset. He disclosed that the Korea International Cooperation Agency (KOICA), the Small and Medium Enterprises Development Agency of Nigeria (SMEDAN) and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) broke ground in September on the Abuja Centre for Entrepreneurship. The centre is expected to support hundreds of young entrepreneurs and start-ups in turning business ideas into viable enterprises. Jeong also said Korea’s Smart School project, implemented with the Universal Basic Education Commission (UBEC), had reached 8,000 children and trained more than 300 teachers and school leaders. In agriculture, KOICA and the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) are implementing initiatives aimed at creating green jobs for young Nigerians. Approximately 2,000 Nigerian officials have also received training in Korea through KOICA programmes, he said. “Our shared goal is simple: more opportunities for young people, stronger local businesses, and better lives for our people,” Jeong said. The ambassador named Daewoo Engineering & Construction, LG, Samsung, Hyundai and Solpia among Korean companies operating in Nigeria’s energy, manufacturing, clean water and digital technology sectors. He said the Korean Embassy, working with the Korea Trade-Investment Promotion Agency (KOTRA), would continue to promote investment, technology transfer and local employment. Jeong said Korea respected Nigeria’s development priorities and sought to work with the country as an equal partner, adding that stronger commercial ties could create jobs, strengthen local businesses and generate shared prosperity. Nigeria and South Korea established diplomatic relations in 1980, with ties spanning trade, investment, education and technical assistance. Nigeria is seeking to build on those relations to attract more capital and expertise for industrial expansion and employment generation.

title: Russia Open to US-Ukraine Trilateral Talks After Nov. 4
body:
Russia is prepared to resume trilateral negotiations with Ukraine and the US after Nov. 4, following Russia’s National Unity Day holiday, Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov announced on Sunday, Oct. 25.
Speaking to Russian state media, the senior Kremlin adviser confirmed Moscow’s willingness to re-engage in working-level consultations, while refraining from setting a definitive calendar date for the next diplomatic round.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“Right now the next deadline is Nov. 4, our major holiday,” Ushakov said in an official dispatch reported by news agencies. “After that, we will be ready to resume negotiations.”
Ushakov tempered expectations regarding immediate breakthroughs, characterizing the prospective tripartite session as an exploratory, range-finding engagement designed to test positions rather than conclude definitive agreements.
Substantial diplomatic work remains necessary before any comprehensive settlement framework can materialize, the aide added.
The timeline outlined by the Kremlin places prospective trilateral consultations in early November, coinciding with preparations for broader international summitry.
Earlier on Sunday, Ushakov confirmed that Moscow, Beijing, and Washington have agreed in principle to convene a three-way summit between Russian President Vladimir Putin, US President Donald Trump, and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders’ summit scheduled for Nov. 18-19 in Shenzhen, China.
Ushakov indicated that operational progress achieved during working-level consultations and the Shenzhen summit would directly dictate whether Vladimir Putin attends the Group of 20 (G20) summit in Miami, Florida, scheduled for December.
The post-Nov. 4 timeframe also follows high-level shuttle diplomacy conducted by White House special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who met with Putin in St. Petersburg on Oct. 21 after holding consultations with Ukrainian and European leadership in Oslo on Oct. 20.
Previous diplomatic reporting indicated that working delegations from Kyiv, Washington, and Moscow could convene in Abu Dhabi or Switzerland to lay the groundwork for high-level meetings.
While Moscow has signaled conditional openness to resume tripartite talks, fundamental divides persist regarding the baseline principles of any settlement.
President Volodymyr Zelensky affirmed in recent remarks that Kyiv is prepared to freeze combat operations along the existing line of contact to bring an immediate halt to active hostilities, but firmly ruled out the formal surrender of sovereign territory or legal recognition of occupied regions as Russian land.
Zelensky has demanded binding security guarantees, minimum ten-year international defense funding, and an enforceable ceasefire as prerequisites for any enduring peace.
At the same time, European capitals have raised alarms over great-power diplomacy brokered without direct continental participation.
Former Ukrainian Prime Minister Arseniy Yatsenyuk and European leaders have cautioned that tripartite arrangements excluding affected partners risk partitioning European security structures , while the EU continues to explore mechanisms – including the potential appointment of a dedicated European peace envoy – to ensure continental interests are defended at the negotiating table.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: NVIDIA’s Jensen Huang Receives Honorary Judo Black Belt in Astana
body: NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang received an honorary black belt from the International Judo Federation (IJF) in Astana on October 23. The federation said the award recognized his contributions to technology and innovation and the values he shares with the sport. The presentation came during Huang’s visit to Kazakhstan for talks on the country’s AI development . Following the World Judo Championships in Baku, IJF President Marius Vizer traveled to Astana to assess preparations for the 2027 championships, which the city will host. During his visit, Vizer presented Huang with the belt, according to NVIDIA’s account of the ceremony . Timur Kemell, the federation’s director of promotion and development and an Executive Committee member , then presented Huang with the Code of Judo. Its eight values include respect, courage, modesty, and self-control. From left: IJF Executive Committee member Timur Kemell, NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang, and IJF President Marius Vizer at Huang’s honorary black belt ceremony in Astana. Image: IJF The honorary black belt is a symbolic distinction rather than a rank earned through judo training and technical grading. The IJF has made similar awards to prominent figures outside competitive judo, including Pope Francis in 2022 and Italian Economy Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti in 2024 . Vizer described Huang’s award as “a symbol of respect, commitment and belonging to the international judo family.” NVIDIA also promoted the award through its Newsroom account on X on October 24, publishing a photograph of Huang alongside Vizer and Kemell. “The black leather jacket wasn’t the final form,” the company wrote, referring to Huang’s familiar attire. Huang discussed martial arts during NVIDIA’s AI Summit in Mumbai in October 2024. In a conversation with actor and martial artist Akshay Kumar , he said both of his children held second-degree black belts. “When you’re good at anything, it gives you confidence to do everything else,” Huang said. Kazakhstan’s traditional wrestling sport, qazaq kuresi , was inscribed on UNESCO’s Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2016. At the 2024 Paris Games, Yeldos Smetov became Kazakhstan’s first Olympic judo champion, following silver at Rio 2016 and bronze at the Tokyo Games.

title: Moscow ready to resume trilateral talks with Ukraine, US after Nov. 4, Kremlin aide says
body:
The Kremlin is ready to resume trilateral talks with Ukraine and the U.S. after Nov. 4, when Russia celebrates National Unity Day, Russian President Vladimir Putin's foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov told state-controlled outlet Vesti on Oct. 25.
The statement follows Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky 's Oct. 23 remarks that a new round of trilateral talks is expected in the first half of November, with Abu Dhabi a possible venue.
"The next deadline is now Nov. 4, our major holiday. After that, we will be ready to resume negotiations," Ushakov said.
The Kremlin has repeatedly rejected ceasefire proposals, demanding instead that Kyiv cede the only partially occupied Donbas, a strategically important region in eastern Ukraine. Such a concession would give Moscow territory that Russian forces have been unable to capture on the battlefield. Ukraine, in contrast, has agreed to multiple ceasefire proposals put forward by the U.S.
Ushakov said he did not expect the first trilateral meeting after the pause to yield significant results, calling it a "trial run." A peace agreement between Russia and Ukraine "still needs work," he added.
On Oct. 20, U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and European partners, including Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store.
The following day, Witkoff held a three-hour meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg, after which the Kremlin said it was ready to resume trilateral talks in November.
Witkoff said on Oct. 21 that discussions among Ukrainian, U.S., and Russian representatives would "continue at the technical level."
Putin has long avoided meeting with Zelensky. Instead, the Kremlin chief is reportedly seeking a meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump in China next month in an effort to secure a favorable peace deal without Ukraine's participation .
In recent weeks, Trump has also lashed out at Zelensky, unilaterally announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine that ultimately failed, threatened to cut off intelligence-sharing with Kyiv, and eased sanctions on Russian oil exports.
Trump has defended the sanctions relief, arguing that it could encourage Moscow to take part in peace negotiations with Kyiv.

title: Top10 Magazine Names Umaru Kwairanga As Man of the Year 2026
body: The Group Chairman, Nigerian Exchange Group (NGX Group), Alhaji Umaru Kwairanga, has been named the Top10 Magazine’s Man of the Year 2026. He emerged from among many other distinguished personalities in a multi-stage rigorous selection and screening process. He succeeds the Chairman of Casiva Ltd, Alhaji Nasiru Haladu Danu, who was the magazine’s Man of the Year for 2025. He joins a club of distinguished Nigerians who have won the crown since the inception of the award over 10 years ago, with the late Group Managing Director of Access Bank, Dr. Herbert Wigwe, as the pioneer winner of the award in 2016. Also on the magazine’s roll of honour are the Chairman, Cosgrove Group (2020), Umar Abdullahi; Chairman of Peace Mass Transit (PMT) and Founder of Maduka University (2022), Chief Samuel Onyishi; former Chairman, Federal Inland Revenue Service, FIRS (2023), Muhammad Nami and Senator George Akume (2024), among others. In a letter conveying Alhaji Kwairanga’s selection as the Man of the Year 2026, the Board of Editors of the Magazine said it was in recognition of his towering leadership as custodian of Nigeria’s capital market, his role in driving national economic development, his championship of corporate governance, transparency, integrity and influence that defined Nigeria’s economic narrative in 2026. These, the givers of the award said, clearly stand him out as a man of excellence worthy of celebration, “hence the decision of our management to accord you this special recognition as the Top 10 Magazine’s Man of the Year 2026,” the letter said. In a year marked by economic reforms, market volatility and renewed investor search for trust and transparency, Kwairanga stood tall as a symbol of stability, integrity and visionary leadership. Under his watch, the Nigerian Exchange has emerged as one of Africa’s best performing markets, restoring investor confidence, attracting foreign inflows and providing capital for enterprise growth that creates jobs for millions of Nigerians. As overseer of NGX Regulation, he has championed board accountability, shareholder protection, ESG compliance and global best practices, elevating Nigerian corporate governance to world standard. His influence goes beyond the trading floor of Marina. He is a trusted counsel to regulators, a respected voice in the Presidency’s economic circle, a bridge between the private sector and government, and a mentor to a generation of investors and entrepreneurs who see in him the embodiment of ethical capitalism. A man of unblemished integrity, quiet philanthropy and profound intellect, Kwairanga represents the best of Northern and Nigerian leadership – humble yet powerful, principled yet pragmatic, traditional yet globally minded. In a nation in search of role models who prove that one can be successful without cutting corners, powerful without being oppressive and wealthy without losing humanity, Kwairanga stands as a beacon. “For his towering leadership as custodian of Nigeria’s capital market, his role in driving national economic development, his championship of corporate governance and transparency, his integrity and influence that defined Nigeria’s economic narrative in 2026, the Board and Management of the Top10 Magazine unanimously select Alh. (Dr.) Umaru Kwairanga as Man of the year 2026,” stated the publishers of the Top10 Magazine. The Top10 Magazine is a monthly publication established over 10 years ago as a platform to celebrate excellence and people of excellence from all human endeavours. The Top10 Man of the Year Award was also instituted the same year as an annual award by the magazine as the highest honour reserved annually for one distinguished Nigerian whose leadership, integrity, influence and national impact have defined the year. This year’s recipient, Kwairanga, a man of untainted character and impeccable reputation, is renowned for his unwavering commitment to success. Kwairanga has 25 years’ cognate experience in the banking, pensions, investment, manufacturing and commercial sectors. He has served previously as a council member of the Nigerian Stock Exchange and is currently a council member of the Institute of Directors of Nigeria; and an active director on the boards of many quoted/listed and unquoted companies including Ashaka Cement Plc where he served for over 10 years, first as a director and later as chairman of the Board. He is currently the GMD/CEO of Finmal Finance Services Limited. He is a Fellow of the Chartered Institute of Stockbrokers, Fellow of Certified Pension Institute Nigeria (2005) and Fellow of Institute of Directors of Nigeria. He is Chairman – Commerce, Trade and Investment subcommittee of Gombe State transition committee. Kwairanga has a B.Sc (Hons) Business Administration (1991) and MBA (1995) both from University of Maiduguri and M.Sc. Finance & Governance from Liverpool John Moores University (2007). Publisher/Editor-In-Chief of the Top10 Magazine, Mr. Tony Iji, said the award will be presented to Kwairanga at the Top10 Magazine’s Annual Excellence Awards night slated for November 22, 2026 which will be graced by the crème de la crème of the society. To mark this high-profile event, the magazine is putting together a special award edition to celebrate him and other awardees. The edition which will comprehensively chronicle his achievements, leadership journey, and contribution to Nigeria’s capital market and the economy in general.

title: Drones attack plant owned by Russia’s largest titanium producer in Perm Krai, media report
body:
According to Ukrinform, this was reported by The Moscow Times .
Perm Krai Governor Dmitry Makhonin stated that, as a result of the drone attack, “an industrial facility in the north of the region sustained minor damage and continues to operate normally.”
According to preliminary information, five employees of the plant were injured, three of whom were taken to the hospital for examination,
According to the Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+, the chemical and metallurgical plant “Avisma” in Berezniki was targeted.
Its products are used in the manufacture of military aircraft, aircraft engines, and rocket and space technology. Local residents in online chat rooms confirm the attack on the facility.
The plant is owned by the VSMPO-Avisma Corporation—the world’s largest titanium producer and a key supplier of this metal to Russian defense industry enterprises.
According to publicly available data, the facility produces sponge titanium (with a capacity of 44,000 metric tons per year), metallic magnesium (60,000 metric tons per year), and magnesium-based alloys. The company employs over 7,100 people.
As reported by Ukrinform, on Saturday in Omsk, Russia—located more than 2,500 km from Ukraine— drones attacked a local industrial compl ex.

title: Stranded Ghanaian fishermen survived on fresh fish, burnt canoe wood at sea
body: A 29-year-old Ghanaian fisherman has recounted how he and six colleagues survived nearly two weeks at sea after their canoe’s outboard motor broke down, leaving them without adequate food and drinking water. Kwamena Nkum said the fishermen’s provisions ran out five days after the engine failure, forcing them to depend on fish they caught and eventually burn parts of their canoe to prepare meals. The seven men, all from Sekondi, embarked on a fishing expedition to Axim in the Western Region on October 9, 2026, aboard a canoe named Second Chance. Their journey took a dangerous turn three days later when the outboard motor stopped working. Efforts to repair the engine proved unsuccessful, leaving them stranded at sea. “We usually spend five days at sea, but this time, our motor became faulty on the third day. It just went off. We tried to fix it, but it didn’t work. Our food and water got finished,” Mr Nkum recounted. He said the fishermen resorted to drinking seawater after their supplies were exhausted, boiling it in an attempt to reduce its salt concentration. They initially ate fish from their catch, but some of the fish spoiled and had to be discarded. The men subsequently used hooks and lines to catch fresh fish for food. Mr Nkum said the fishermen had fuel and matches to make fire but eventually ran out of charcoal, compelling them to burn wood taken from their canoe to cook. After drifting for several days, the men eventually sighted land during the night. One fisherman who was still awake alerted the others. They switched on their mobile phones and later received a call from a friend, Kingsley, who was in contact with people back home. Mr Nkum said they contacted their fishing leaders and attempted to establish their location. Although they initially believed they were in Togo, they later discovered they had drifted into Beninese waters. “We had no food left. We were very hungry,” he said. According to him, Kingsley and the fishing leaders contacted the chief fisherman in Benin, who provided the stranded men with food and water. The fishermen subsequently received assistance from local fishing communities and the Beninese and Togolese navies. They were eventually handed over to the Ghana Navy by a Togolese naval vessel at the Ghana-Togo maritime border on October 21, 2026. The men later arrived safely at the Fishing Harbour in Tema following a joint search-and-rescue operation. The fishermen were identified as Kofi Emmanuel, 32; Uncle Amoah, 45; Kwamena Nkum, 29; Kofi Aboagye, 36; Doboa, 35; Agya Badu, 42; and Kwamena Akyem, 40. Reflecting on the ordeal, Mr Nkum said carrying a second outboard motor could have helped prevent the emergency from escalating, stressing the importance of having backup equipment for fishing expeditions.

title: Enugu traders reaffirm support for Gov Mbah’s second term
body:
Market traders and leaders across Enugu State have assured Governor Peter Ndubuisi Mbah of their support for a second term in office, declaring that his administration’s development strides, market-friendly policies and interventions in the trading sector have strengthened their confidence in his leadership.
The traders, under the umbrella of the Enugu State Market Amalgamated Traders Association (ESMATA), led by its President, Chief Chinwuba Igwesi, gave the assurance on Friday, 23 October during a high-level market stakeholders’ meeting with the governor.
The meeting, which brought together chairmen and secretaries of more than 50 markets across the state, provided an opportunity for the traders to express their appreciation for the administration’s development initiatives, highlight improvements in the business environment and discuss measures to further expand commercial activities across Enugu State.
Speaking on behalf of the association, Igwesi said traders across the 17 local government areas were prepared to support Governor Mbah’s re-election, citing what he described as visible development, improved business conditions and the administration’s responsiveness to the concerns of the market community.
He particularly commended the governor for ending the illegal Monday sit-at-home disruption that had previously forced traders to lose substantial income by shutting their businesses on Mondays. According to him, the restoration of normal commercial activities throughout the week has enabled traders to open their shops daily and improve their earnings.
The ESMATA president said the return of regular market activities had brought relief to traders, whose businesses had suffered from repeated disruptions, uncertainty and lost trading opportunities.
Igwesi also expressed gratitude to Mbah for approving the provision of transformers to markets without adequate electricity, the asphalting of road networks within several markets and the installation of solar-powered streetlights to improve visibility, security and commercial activities.
He noted that these interventions were helping to address long-standing infrastructure challenges that had affected traders and customers, while making the markets more accessible and conducive to business.
The market leaders further appreciated the governor for the construction of toilet facilities in markets, the release of utility vehicles to market leadership and the appointment of some market leaders into his administration. They also commended him for approving pilgrimage opportunities for some market leaders during the year, describing the gestures as indications that the government recognises and values the contributions of traders to the state’s economy.
Igwesi said the traders were particularly proud that Mbah understood their challenges because of his background in business, adding that they considered his performance in office a source of pride for the market community.
According to him, the governor’s understanding of the realities of trading had been reflected in policies and decisions aimed at improving the business environment, strengthening commercial activities and supporting the livelihoods of traders and their families.
The ESMATA president also addressed concerns surrounding taxation, dismissing rumours of a general increase in taxes. He explained that the administration’s approach had involved the unification of taxes into a single account, rather than the alleged increase being circulated.
He said traders were willing to pay their taxes because they could see development projects and public infrastructure being delivered across the state. He maintained that the visible use of public revenue for development had strengthened traders’ confidence in the government and its management of resources.
Igwesi further observed that business activities in Enugu were thriving, particularly in the building materials sector, which he said had experienced improved commercial prospects under the current administration.
He attributed part of the growth to the governor’s directive requiring contractors handling projects in the state to purchase construction materials from local suppliers in Enugu instead of sourcing them from outside the state where such materials were available locally.
According to him, the policy had helped retain more business transactions within Enugu, increased patronage for local traders and contributed to the growth of businesses dealing in building materials and related supplies.
The ESMATA president also praised the administration’s investment in healthcare infrastructure, recounting his experience during a visit to the international hospital project. He said the facility was so impressive that he momentarily felt as though he had travelled to Dubai.
He described the project as evidence of the scale of development taking place in the state and said such investments were helping to reshape perceptions of Enugu while improving the prospects for economic growth.
In a strong declaration of support, Igwesi said Mbah’s record of performance had given him an advantage over opposition candidates ahead of the next governorship election.
He assured the governor that the market community would stand firmly behind his re-election bid, urging him to remain focused on delivering development and improving the welfare of residents.
“When the time comes, your work will speak for you,” he said, while reiterating the traders’ position with the declaration: “No opposition in Enugu State.”
The market leaders, speaking in unison, also assured the governor that he could remain confident in the support of traders, insisting that the development taking place across the state had strengthened their resolve to back his administration for another term.
They maintained that the market community was encouraged by the governor’s approach to governance and the recognition given to traders as important partners in Enugu’s economic development.
Responding, Governor Mbah thanked the market leaders for the visit and for acknowledging his administration’s efforts, assuring them that the state would witness even greater development if they renewed his mandate by voting him back into office.
The governor said his administration remained committed to expanding the state’s economic opportunities, improving infrastructure and positioning Enugu as a leading destination for business, investment and commercial activities.
He outlined several initiatives intended to strengthen the trading sector, including plans to develop a cargo terminal at the Akanu Ibiam International Airport, Enugu, to improve the movement of goods and connect businesses in the state to international markets.
Mbah explained that the cargo terminal would help open Enugu to the world, facilitate the movement of goods and create opportunities for traders and businesses to participate more directly in international commerce.
He also disclosed plans for direct cargo operations between Enugu and China, which he said would soon commence, enabling Enugu traders to import goods directly from China at more affordable rates.
The governor said the initiative was designed to reduce the difficulties traders encounter when sourcing goods, improve access to international supply chains and strengthen the competitiveness of businesses operating in Enugu.
He further highlighted the ongoing construction of the International Market at Idodo, describing it as part of the administration’s broader strategy to expand commercial infrastructure and create more opportunities for traders, investors and other economic players.
According to him, the government is deliberately expanding Enugu’s business space through infrastructure, connectivity and strategic investments that will enable the state to attract more commercial activities and create opportunities for its people.
Mbah also spoke about his efforts to reconnect Enugu to the centre of national activities, noting that the state had been losing some of its historic prominence as the capital of the former Southern Region and a leading political and administrative centre in the South-East.
He said the construction of the International Conference Centre (ICC), Enugu, was part of the strategy to restore the state’s standing by providing a modern venue for major national events, conferences and gatherings.
The governor explained that hosting such events would bring participants, visitors and businesspeople into Enugu, creating opportunities for hotels, restaurants, transport operators, traders and other service providers to benefit from increased economic activities.
He stressed that the government’s investment in security was equally important to this ambition, noting that a safe environment was necessary to attract thousands of visitors and ensure that businesses could operate without fear.
Mbah said the administration was working to provide a secure environment supported by an effective security system, adding that safety, infrastructure and economic planning must work together to make Enugu an attractive destination for business and investment.
On the state’s economic future, the governor reaffirmed his ambition to grow Enugu’s economy from an estimated $4 billion to a $30 billion economy, stressing that the target was linked to his administration’s determination to expand productivity, attract investment, strengthen local businesses and create more opportunities for residents.
He described Enugu as a state with significant economic potential and expressed confidence that ongoing and planned investments would help accelerate its growth.
The governor also reassured the traders that their interests would remain a priority in his administration, declaring that he would not support policies designed to undermine the trading community.
Mbah said his personal experience in business had given him an understanding of the challenges traders face, including the demands of running businesses, sourcing goods, meeting financial obligations and sustaining livelihoods.
He assured the market leaders that he would continue to consider the implications of government policies for traders and ensure that the administration’s economic agenda supported rather than hindered their activities.
The governor’s remarks reinforced the administration’s position that traders and other business operators are central to Enugu’s development strategy and must benefit from policies intended to grow the state’s economy.
The meeting was attended by key government officials, including the Senior Special Assistant to the Governor on Market Liaison, Dr Chinedu Mbah; the Senior Special Assistant to the Governor on Security, Mr Vincent Onyeaboor; and the Special Adviser to the Governor on Political Matters, Chief Frank Anioma. The three officials accompanied the governor in receiving the market leaders.
The engagement underscored the importance of sustained dialogue between the state government and the market community, with traders expressing appreciation for completed interventions while the governor outlined further plans aimed at improving infrastructure, expanding access to international trade and strengthening Enugu’s commercial position.
With the ESMATA leadership and representatives of more than 50 markets expressing confidence in the administration, the meeting highlighted the growing significance of the trading sector in the state’s economic and political conversations ahead of the next governorship election.
For the traders, the central message was that market infrastructure, reliable security, access to goods, improved business opportunities and visible development would remain important measures of government performance. For Governor Mbah, the meeting provided an opportunity to reaffirm his commitment to building a more connected, secure and commercially vibrant Enugu State.

title: Bilateral meeting between Putin, Trump at APEC not arranged but possible — Kremlin aide
body:
MOSCOW, October 25. /TASS/. Russia and the United States have not arranged a bilateral meeting between Presidents Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump on the sidelines of the APEC summit where a three-way interaction involving Chinese President Xi Jinping is planned, Russian Presidential Aide Yury Ushakov said, adding that such an encounter is possible.
"We haven’t agreed on this meeting yet because, up until now, the discussion has focused on this trilateral contact," he told Vesti reporter Pavel Zarubin.
"If two presidents happen to be in the same place, they will at least greet each other and have a conversation <...>. Major international summits like these create significant opportunities for such interaction," Ushakov added.

title: Trump Eyes Post-War Business Ties With Both Ukraine and Russia
body:
US President Donald Trump said that Washington plans to conduct commercial business with both Ukraine and Russia once the war between the two nations concludes.
Speaking to journalists on Saturday, Oct. 24, Trump outlined his expectation of normalized economic engagement with both countries following a cessation of hostilities.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“I think that after this war ends, we’ll do business with Ukraine and with Russia, I would think,” Trump told reporters.
The remarks reflect Trump’s transactional approach toward foreign policy and international economic engagement, positioning post-war trade reconciliation as an element of future bilateral ties.
Trump on Ukraine: We'll do business with Ukraine and with Russia after this war ends, I would think. pic.twitter.com/bjxgf4l8cw
Trump’s statements arrive shortly after comments delivered at a campaign rally in Florida on Friday, Oct. 23, in which the US president suggested that imposing 200 percent import tariffs on Ukraine and Russia could theoretically pressure both parties toward a diplomatic settlement.
However, Trump conceded that direct trade measures would likely have minimal impact due to limited bilateral trade volumes.
“We ended five wars thanks to tariffs. I said, ‘If you continue to fight, we’re going to put a 200 percent tariff on you,’ and they stopped,” Trump told supporters in Florida.
“We should probably immediately do it with Ukraine and Russia. Never thought of it. But we don’t buy enough to do it to them, so it doesn’t work.”
The administration has increasingly utilized trade restrictions, tariff waivers, and commercial agreements as central instruments in its diplomatic maneuvering ahead of the Nov. 3 US midterm elections.
Trump’s focus on future commercial engagement with Moscow and Kyiv unfolds amid continuing friction regarding Washington’s economic tools to influence the conflict.
President Volodymyr Zelensky previously stated that the US president possesses statutory leverage to compel Russian President Vladimir Putin to negotiate , emphasizing that bipartisan sanctions approved by the US Congress remain unenacted at the White House.
“Trump could very easily bring Putin to the negotiating table, because he has the means to do so. The way he speaks about me – President Trump should speak about Putin in the same way,” Zelensky said.
“Sanctions are sitting on his desk. He didn’t vote for them – Congress voted for strong sanctions. He has the power to act.”
Ukraine’s head of state also rejected assertions by the Trump administration linking retail fuel price increases in the United States to Ukrainian long-range drone interdiction strikes on Russian oil refineries.
While Trump justified a bilateral commercial arrangement to facilitate Russian diesel sales on global markets to lower consumer costs, Zelensky stated that domestic US diesel benchmarks operate independently of Russian export volumes.
The debate over commercial relations arrives after Trump’s recent decision to suspend statutory sanctions and trade duties codified under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 .
On Oct. 16, Trump signed an executive order invoking Section 115 of the Graham Act to waive mandatory 500 percent tariffs on Russian imports and 100 percent secondary duties targeting global buyers of Russian hydrocarbons, just 48 hours before the measures were scheduled to take statutory effect.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended the suspension as a 60-day pause to assess the broader economic fallout of tariffs on both the US and international economies, citing third-party dependencies such as India’s reliance on Russian crude.
