title: Art can give ecological restoration a local voice – World Resources Institute
body: The World Resources Institute (WRI) says art and culture can help make ecological restoration more meaningful to local communities. This is according to the institute’s Landscape Restoration Manager for the Ghana Cocoa Belt, Eric Lartey, who made this known at the inaugural Climate x Culture Summit in Accra on Thursday, October 22. “Restoration is more about people,” Mr Lartey said, explaining that music, oral traditions, festivals and customary practices shape how many Ghanaian communities relate to land, forests, water and biodiversity. He said integrating culture can connect restoration to community identity and make use of traditional ecological knowledge, which “can also inform more effective restoration practices.” Mr Lartey highlighted the Restoration Artists Network (RAN), a global initiative under the WRI that brings together musicians, visual artists, storytellers and cultural leaders to make ecological restoration more accessible. “Artists are powerful storytellers and cultural influencers,” he said, describing their ability to translate technical restoration concepts into simple, engaging messages. He cited a collaboration between Ghanaian and American artists that produced six songs drawing on Ghanaian musical traditions and local languages. The project aims to give landscape restoration “a local and a human voice,” he said. “Art is an access point. It can invite attention, stimulate conversation,” Mr Lartey said. He added that art can help people see themselves in a story that might otherwise feel technical or distant, while cautioning that it cannot replace investment, science or policy. @theculturejoint Okyeame Kwame at the Climate x Culture Summit 2026 which brought together voices from sustainability, the creative industries and culture to explore how we can make climate action more practical, inclusive and part of everyday life. Together, we can turn creativity into climate action. ♬ original sound – Culture Joint “If we want restoration effort to endure, it must be locally led and culturally grounded,” he said, pointing to Restore Local as a framework for the approach. The summit, themed “Designing Sustainable Creative Experiences For Africa,” was organised by Culture Joint Media in partnership with Ghana’s Minister of State for Climate Change & Sustainability at the Presidency. It brought together stakeholders from the climate, creative, business, media and technology sectors to explore how culture and creativity can contribute to climate action and sustainable development. Minister of State for Climate Change and Sustainability at the Office of the President, World Resources Institute (WRI) Africa, Centre for CSR, West Africa, Climate and Development Knowledge Network (CDKN), Ghana Youth Environment Movement (GYEM), 365Mustang, Dobiison, JoyNews and Myjoyonline.com.

title: Netanyahu's crypto plan could cause 'irreversible damage' to Israeli economy, business leaders warn
body: A group of 109 economists, business leaders, high-tech entrepreneurs, and former senior public officials issued a strongly worded statement expressing "deep anxiety and concern" over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's conduct, warning of irreversible damage to Israel's economy if international sanctions are imposed.The letter followed an interview in which Netanyahu made clear that he was not concerned about sanctions, said that US military aid "is not something that will last forever and will eventually end," and revealed that he had requested a plan to circumvent banking sanctions using cryptocurrencies and blockchain technology."The prime minister's remarks demonstrate a fundamental lack of understanding and ignorance in the face of Israel's collapsing standing in the international arena," the 109 signatories charged in their letter. "Netanyahu is knowingly leading the State of Israel toward an international economic boycott and isolation, and all he has to offer is a bizarre solution commonly used by criminal organizations that will be of no help whatsoever."The economists warned that restrictions on Israel's banking system would lead to soaring unemployment, the complete disappearance of foreign investment, and the paralysis of the economy's primary growth engine, the high-tech sector.They also warned of severe consequences for Israelis' daily lives, including the inability to use credit cards, the loss of access to online shopping platforms such as Amazon and AliExpress, the departure of foreign workers, and serious difficulties for the healthcare system in purchasing medicines and medical equipment.The signatories compared the potential scenario to countries that have faced severe sanctions, including South Africa, Iran, and Russia, warning of a dramatic decline in living standards and devastating damage to Israel's ability to finance its defense needs.The statement was signed by a long list of prominent figures, including two Nobel Prize laureates, Prof. Joel Mokyr (Economics) and Prof. Aaron Ciechanover (Chemistry).Other signatories include Israel Prize laureate and former Bank of Israel governor Prof. Jacob Frenkel; former deputy governors Prof. Zvi Eckstein and Dr. Nadine Baudot-Trajtenberg; and former supervisors of banks Yair Avidan and Rony Hizkiyahu.The list also includes many former senior Finance Ministry officials, including former directors-general Yarom Ariav, Prof. Avi Ben-Bassat, David Brodet, Haim Shani, and Prof. Manuel Trajtenberg, who also previously chaired the National Economic Council.Also signing were former chief economist Shira Greenberg and former budget director Udi Nisan.Prominent figures from the high-tech industry and business community include CyberArk founder Alon Cohen, Check Point co-founder Marius Nacht, G City founder Chaim Katzman, BIG Shopping Centers CEO Hai Galis and chairman Eitan Bar Zeev, high-tech entrepreneur Gigi Levy-Weiss, Fireblocks co-founders Idan Ofrat, Dov Moran, and Roy Vermus, and many others.Bank of Israel emphasizes importance of maintaining economic relationsThe wave of economic criticism followed an unusual response from the Bank of Israel, which clarified over the weekend that "cryptocurrencies cannot serve as a means of circumventing sanctions on Israel."The central bank emphasized that "the right thing for Israel's economy is to preserve our economic relations with our main trading partners and focus on preventing sanctions."Netanyahu responded to the remarks in an interview with Channel 14, saying, "I thank the Bank of Israel for its advice, but I do what I think is right."The business sector also strongly rejected the proposal.Galit Miran, CEO of the Israel-America Chamber of Commerce, warned against "adopting financial models characteristic of isolated and excluded countries," noting that such mechanisms could undermine investor confidence and Israel's credit rating.The Manufacturers Association of Israel emphasized that the Israeli economy is built on free trade and the free movement of capital, and that maintaining these conditions is the only way to ensure economic resilience.Netanyahu's election opponents condemn economic planThe economic controversy quickly became a central issue in the election campaign, which will culminate on Tuesday.Yashar party chairman Gadi Eisenkot issued his own stark warning: "If Netanyahu continues, there will be no savings, no international investments, and you will not be able to pay by credit card online or abroad. For Netanyahu, the conversation has shifted from prosperity to survival. After another term under him, we will long for the days of austerity."Opposition leader Yair Lapid also attacked Netanyahu, saying, "Netanyahu admits in his own words that if his government is reelected, military aid will be finished and sanctions will be imposed, leading to insane price increases and irreparable damage."B'Yachad party chairman Naftali Bennett said he was appalled by Netanyahu's vision. "This means the destruction of Israeli high-tech, the loss of livelihoods for hundreds of thousands of families, poverty for millions of Israelis, and a threat to security. Netanyahu is placing Israel in the same category as Iran, North Korea, and Russia."

title: Issue of Putin’s trip to G20 in Miami to be considered after APEC summit — Kremlin aide
body:
MOSCOW, October 25. /TASS/. Russia is preparing for the APEC summit in Shenzhen now, Russian Presidential Aide Yury Ushakov said, adding that only after that the issue of the G20 summit in Miami will be considered.
"For now, we are discussing the November summit in Shenzhen, but we have received an invitation [to the G20 summit]," he told Vesti reporter Pavel Zarubin.
When asked whether a great deal would depend on the success of this summit, Ushakov answered in the affirmative. "Naturally. But as I said: first comes November, and then December," he said.

title: Choosing humanity over harm: A National Assembly’s duty to protect life, By Margaret Uddin Ojeahere
body:
This moment, however, presents an opportunity to demand the leadership Nigerians deserve. Nigeria does not need more punishment; it needs leaders that understand the weight of human suffering. The first step is clear: Attempted suicide must be decriminalised. People in crisis deserve care, not constraints. Criminalisation only worsens stigma, mental health problems, and hinders access to appropriate care. Equally urgent is the full implementation of the National Mental Health Act.
Those were the words my late teacher, Professor Albert Anjorin, repeated to us in medical school decades ago. They are simple, humane, and rooted in the belief that every life is worth protecting. It is heartbreaking that in 2026, I am hearing the opposite sentiment echoed from the hallowed chambers of Nigeria’s National Assembly.
Less than four days after the commemoration of the 2026 World Mental Health Day, a week filled with stories of lived experiences, awareness campaigns, and calls for compassion for persons struggling with mental health challenges and their caregivers, Nigerians were confronted with a statement that shook the conscience of the nation. Words attributed to the Senate President, Godswill Akpabio, went viral: “If you attempt suicide, make sure you die. Anyone who attempts and fails will go to jail.”
Words, once spoken, cannot be recalled, and these remarks landed like a blow on the progress Nigeria has made from repealing the Lunacy Act of 1958 to enacting the National Mental Health Act in 2022. For years, advocates have tried to help Nigerians understand a simple truth: anyone with a brain can develop a mental health condition. Mental health conditions do not respect tribe, class, religion, or political office. Research shows that one in four to five Nigerians live with a mental health condition, and with worsening governance, insecurity, unemployment, and collapsing amenities, the numbers may be even higher. The story below is not an outlier but it reflects the broader reality captured in these statistics.
“ At twenty-eight, Daniel often felt older than his age, as trauma ages people in ways birthdays never do. Fifteen years had passed since the night insurgents descended on his village, leaving behind ashes and sad memories. Daniel remembered the sound of his father’s voice , firm, resisting the attackers. He also remembered how quickly courage could be swallowed by gunfire. His mother’s fate was worse. Daniel had seen what no child should ever witness. He survived only because his father had shoved him beneath a heap of rusted roofing sheets moments before the attackers reached their home. He lay there listening to the horror unfolding above him, praying for a miracle that never came. Thereafter, Daniel has lived with survivors’ guilt, depression and post‑traumatic stress disorder, words he learned much later. He tried to rebuild his life, but trauma clung to him like a second skin. Jobs slipped through his fingers. Relationships dissolved under the weight of memories he could not silence. Even the cost of his medications became a burden too heavy to carry. His aging uncle and cousin did what they could. They offered shelter, food, and reassurance. They sat with him through episodes, prayed with him when he felt lost, and accompanied him to therapy. His faith community embraced him, reminding him that survival was not weakness but a testimony. Still, there were times when Daniel felt like a burden. Nights when he wondered if the last vestiges of life were worth holding at all. But each time he dipped, someone pulled him back – a cousin’s hand on his shoulder, a therapist’s gentle words, a pastor’s reminder that healing is slow but possible. These small acts of care kept him going. Then one afternoon, while sitting outside the clinic waiting for his appointment, Daniel heard a statement on his phone, a voice from a trusted person who swore to protect him saying that anyone who attempted suicide should ‘ make sure they die, ’ and that those who survived should be jailed. For a moment, Daniel felt himself slipping again. But then he remembered his uncle’s voice, his cousin’s laughter, his therapist’s steady encouragement, his community’s prayers. He remembered that survival was not a crime. It was courage. He whispered to himself, ‘ I am still here, ’ and in that moment, he chose again to hold on. ”
For years, advocacy efforts focused on educating the less informed, assuming that misunderstanding drove stigma. But the landscape changes entirely when a senior lawmaker suggests jailing people who survive suicide attempts. What message does that send to Nigerian youths who comprise over 60 per cent of our population? To the adolescents battling suicidal thoughts? To the adult drowning in depression, overwhelmed by economic hardship, or shattered by trauma and insecurity?
Suicide is the third leading cause of death among young people aged 15–29. Nigeria records an estimated 15,000 suicide deaths annually, and for every life lost, 20 to 25 more people attempt suicide. Each suicide also leaves about 135 people deeply affected, contributing to over two million suicide loss survivors. These figures are considered conservative, especially in countries like Nigeria where suicide remains misunderstood, stigmatised, and criminalised, leading to significant under‑reporting. Nigeria remains one of the few countries where surviving a suicide attempt can still lead to prosecution. Under Section 327 of the Criminal Code and Section 231 of the Penal Code, individuals may face up to 12 months’ imprisonment, despite the Federal Government’s reaffirmation of its commitment to decriminalising attempted suicide.
For years, advocacy efforts focused on educating the less informed, assuming that misunderstanding drove stigma. But the landscape changes entirely when a senior lawmaker suggests jailing people who survive suicide attempts. What message does that send to Nigerian youths who comprise over 60 per cent of our population? To the adolescents battling suicidal thoughts? To the adult drowning in depression, overwhelmed by economic hardship, or shattered by trauma and insecurity? Sadly, vulnerability is being treated as a criminal offence. Can this then be described as a governance deficit or profound moral failure? Interestingly, a kind of reaction formation plays out here. With mental health problems rising and at least a quarter of Nigerians affected, it is not surprising that some of the lawmakers who laughed during plenary may later seek mental health care quietly like Nicodemus in the night, when they or their relatives become vulnerable and need urgent support to prevent dire consequences. The hypocrisy cuts deep.
This moment, however, presents an opportunity to demand the leadership Nigerians deserve. Nigeria does not need more punishment; it needs leaders that understand the weight of human suffering. The first step is clear: Attempted suicide must be decriminalised. People in crisis deserve care, not constraints. Criminalisation only worsens stigma, mental health problems, and hinders access to appropriate care. Equally urgent is the full implementation of the National Mental Health Act. Three years after its passage, it remains largely dormant, leaving millions without the protection, services, and funding it promises. Nigerians should not wait indefinitely for a law designed to safeguard their wellbeing. Our youth, who represent Nigeria’s future, need safe spaces, mentorship, opportunities, and accessible mental health support. Real progress also requires investment in mental health infrastructure. Community treatment centres, crisis helplines, trained professionals, and integration of mental health services into primary healthcare should be national priorities, not punchlines.
To paraphrase Senator Asuquo Ekpenyong’s view: When a person gets to the point of throwing in the towel and tries to end it all, we should protect, support, and never punish. The future of this nation depends on how seriously we take the mental wellbeing of its people. It is past time for our lawmakers to rise to that responsibility. Governance should never laugh at pain, and policies must not criminalise suffering, they should strengthen systems that uphold healthcare, dignity, and protection from despair.
Mental health does not exist in isolation. It is shaped by the conditions people live in: security, employment, education, and access to basic amenities. Addressing these social stressors would significantly reduce the rising cases of mental health conditions, and lawmakers must treat it as a core governance requirement. National awareness campaigns led by government can help reduce stigma and encourage help-seeking. And none of this should occur in siloes. Collaboration is essential. Nigeria has psychiatrists, other experts and civil‑society organisations already doing the work. Lawmakers should collaborate with them, not undermine their efforts. Nigeria deserves leaders who understand that mental health is a national development issue, leaders who speak with empathy, legislate with wisdom, and act with urgency. Leaders who know that when someone reaches the point of giving up, survival should be celebrated not prosecuted.
To paraphrase Senator Asuquo Ekpenyong’s view: When a person gets to the point of throwing in the towel and tries to end it all, we should protect, support, and never punish. The future of this nation depends on how seriously we take the mental wellbeing of its people. It is past time for our lawmakers to rise to that responsibility. Governance should never laugh at pain, and policies must not criminalise suffering, they should strengthen systems that uphold healthcare, dignity, and protection from despair. It may also be worth exploring a functional‑fitness assessment for anyone seeking political office to ensure those entrusted with millions of lives have the judgment, cognitive capacity, and emotional regulation required for public responsibility.
We cannot rewrite the past, but we can choose a kinder future. A future where survival is honoured, vulnerability is supported, and every Nigerian knows their life is worth holding on to.
Margaret Uddin Ojeahere is the founder of Noetic Minders Health Initiative and a consultant psychiatrist with Jos University Teaching Hospital, Plateau State, Nigeria.

title: Drones Strike Russian Titanium Producer Avisma in Urals
body:
Long-range strike drones struck the “Avisma” titanium and chemical-metallurgical plant in the city of Berezniki in Russia’s Perm region overnight into Sunday, Oct. 25, targeting one of the world’s largest titanium production facilities, The Moscow Times and independent monitoring groups reported.
The enterprise operates as a subsidiary production division of VSMPO-Avisma Corporation, the world’s leading manufacturer of titanium sponge, specialized titanium alloys, and raw magnesium.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Perm Region Governor Dmitry Makhonin acknowledged the aerial incursion on Sunday, stating that an industrial enterprise situated in the northern sector of the province sustained “minor damage” following an attack by unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs).
Makhonin claimed that the damaged facility continues to operate under standard routines and reported no casualties.
However, Ukrainian open-source intelligence (OSINT) monitoring channel Exilenova+ reported that the drone strikes engaged the production grounds of the Avisma chemical-metallurgical facility in Berezniki.
Local residents similarly reported hearing multiple drone engines followed by detonations and the sound of air defense engagements in the vicinity of the plant’s industrial perimeter.
The Berezniki metallurgical complex functions as an irreplaceable industrial node within the Russian Federation’s defense-industrial supply chain.
Avisma specializes in the chemical processing of ilmenite ore into titanium tetrachloride and the subsequent thermal reduction of titanium sponge, alongside refining metallic magnesium and magnesium-based master alloys.
The refined titanium sponge and intermediate billets produced at Berezniki are transported to VSMPO’s primary smelting and mechanical processing facilities in Verkhnyaya Salda, Sverdlovsk region, to manufacture high-strength forgings, rolled sheets, and structural sub-assemblies.
The enterprise’s titanium alloys are critical structural materials utilized across Russian aerospace manufacturing, combat aviation, jet engine production, and missile systems.
Components fabricated from Avisma’s metals are integrated into fuselage airframes and turbine components for Su-35 and Su-57 fighter aircraft, fuselage mountings for tactical bombers, heavy armor assemblies, and missile airframes for cruise and ballistic platforms.
Beyond conventional defense hardware, specialized titanium castings and corrosion-resistant alloys from VSMPO-Avisma are supplied directly to Roscosmos for space rocket propulsion casings and to naval shipyards constructing nuclear-powered submarines.
The strike in Berezniki – located approximately 1,500 kilometers (930 miles) from Ukrainian borders in the Ural Mountains – forms part of an expanding Ukrainian asymmetric campaign systematically targeting Russia’s deep-rear defense metallurgy and strategic chemical supply lines.
The incident in Perm region coincides with long-range drone strikes conducted across Siberia on Saturday, where unmanned platforms struck the Omsky Kauchuk chemical enterprise in Omsk – over 2,500 kilometers from Ukraine – igniting a large-scale blaze at a facility supplying synthetic rubbers and chemical binders used in solid rocket propellant for Iskander-M and intercontinental ballistic missile platforms.
Concurrently overnight into Sunday, Ukrainian strike drones engaged industrial and logistics infrastructure in central Belgorod, damaging the closed MegaGRINN commercial facility, while previous precision missile and drone interdictions hit the Proton defense microelectronics plant in Oryol and the Tolyattikauchuk petrochemical plant in Samara region .

title: Mother, child die as two container trucks overturn in Lagos
body:
A mother and her child have died after two container-laden trucks overturned at Mile 2, near Freeman Market, inward Apapa, Lagos.
Vanguard newspaper reported on Sunday that the victims were trapped beneath the trucks and their containers in the accident, which occurred over the weekend.
The Lagos State Traffic Management Authority (LASTMA) said its rescue team evacuated the victims and cleared the wreckage. Traffic was diverted through an adjoining service lane while a crane and a heavy-duty tow vehicle were used to remove the overturned trucks and containers. Police officers secured the scene during the operation.
The victims’ remains were taken to the police mortuary in Yaba.
LASTMA General Manager, Olalekan Bakare-Oki, called for an investigation to determine the cause of the crash, including whether mechanical faults, overloading, improper cargo distribution or driver negligence played a role.
He urged truck operators to ensure their vehicles were roadworthy and their loads properly secured.
The accident comes weeks after another crash involving two trucks, a commercial bus and nine motorcycles at First Gate, inward Mile 2, along the Mile 2-Seme Expressway, left four people critically injured.
The 6 October crash involved two Mack trucks, one carrying a 20-foot container. LASTMA said preliminary findings suggested that one of the trucks might have suffered brake failure, causing the driver to lose control and collide with the other vehicles.
The injured victims, three men and a woman, sustained multiple fractures to their arms and legs and were taken to hospital for treatment.
LASTMA said the drivers involved in that crash were handed over to the police for investigation and possible prosecution.
The cause of the latest accident has not been established.

title: Dialogue with EU on Ukraine necessary as Europe wants to continue war — Kremlin aide
body:
MOSCOW, October 25. /TASS/. The Kremlin considers it necessary to continue the dialogue with the European Union, given that it is precisely in Europe that there is a commitment to continuing the conflict in Ukraine, Russian Presidential Aide Yury Ushakov said.
"It is not enough to talk only with Kiev, it is necessary to talk with all of Europe, which fully supports Kiev," he told Vesti reporter Pavel Zarubin.
"Perhaps Europe’s position is of key importance here," Ushakov added.

title: EPA takes Styrofoam ban campaign to five northern regions ahead of January 1, 2027 deadline
body: The Environmental Protection Authority (EPA) is intensifying its nationwide public education campaign on Ghana’s impending ban on polystyrene foam products, taking the campaign to five northern regions as the January 1, 2027, implementation deadline approaches. The week-long campaign, scheduled for Monday, October 26, to Sunday, November 1, 2026, will cover the Northern, Upper East, Upper West, Savannah and North East regions, targeting consumers, manufacturers, distributors and other stakeholders ahead of the ban. The EPA announced the ban on polystyrene foam products as part of efforts to address their environmental and adverse health impact and promote more sustainable alternatives. The nationwide awareness campaign is designed to prepare the public and industry players for the transition. The campaign has been organised across three geographical zones; the southern belt, centred on Accra; the middle belt, centred on Kumasi; and the northern belt, centred on Tamale. The Accra and Kumasi campaigns were held in July and August respectfully, with the Tamale campaign scheduled for October 29, 2026, bringing together stakeholders from all five northern regions for a major public awareness event. Led by the EPA’s Chief Executive Officer, Professor Nana Ama Browne Klutse, the delegation will hold mini-durbars in Bolgatanga, Nalerigu, Damongo Wa among other communities thought the week before culminating the northern belt campaign in Tamale. The Tamale event will feature an inter-school environmental quiz involving five second-cycle institutions namely the Ghana Senior High School, St. Charles Minor Seminary, Tamale Islamic Science Senior High School, Kalpohin Senior High School and Tamale Senior High School. The competition will test students’ knowledge of environmental issues, the health dangers associated with polystyrene foam products, their impact on the environment, the benefits of the ban and the lifestyle changes required before and after its implementation. The initiative is expected to deepen environmental awareness among young people and encourage them to become advocates for responsible consumption and environmental protection. The campaign will also feature a debate between the University for Development Studies (UDS) and Bagabaga College of Education under the motion; BEYOND THE BAN: Can Ghana Turn the Polystyrene Foam Products Phase-Out into a Public Health, Environmental and Economic Benefits? The UDS team will comprise Angela Ansah as principal speaker, Adu Michel Chibaley as supporting speaker, and Shakiratu Cheltima Fuseini as summarising speaker. Bagabaga College of Education will be represented by Joseph Maadi Sagulo as principal speaker, Mbowura Clement Samira as supporting speaker, and Fuseini Abdul-Hakeem Tunteiya as summarising speaker. The debate will provide a platform for the tertiary institutions to examine the implications of the ban and explore practical alternatives to polystyrene foam products. Both institutions are also expected to showcase innovative alternative products they have developed to help bridge the supply gap that could emerge following the ban. The event is expected to attract traditional authorities, school heads, students and other stakeholders. It will also be broadcast live across major television channels to extend its reach beyond the immediate audience. Ahead of the main event, public awareness floats will be held in the five regional capitals to mobilise residents and draw attention to the impending ban. The EPA will also intensify media engagements and stakeholder consultations throughout the week, while its regional, area and district offices have been directed to step up public education as the implementation date draws closer. Speaking in an interview, EPA Chief Executive Officer Professor Nana Ama Browne Klutse reaffirmed the Authority’s commitment to ensuring effective implementation of the ban in accordance with the directive of President John Dramani Mahama. She said the extensive public education campaign was intended to give consumers, manufacturers and distributors sufficient notice to prepare for the transition and adopt appropriate alternatives. “The EPA is taking its time to create public awareness on the ban to prepare consumers, manufacturers and distributors for what is coming, effective January 1 2027, so they can prepare and make the right lifestyle adjustments.” “No one should have the excuse that they were not aware of this ban. There will be no excuses by January 2027. The EPA is fully ready to carry out His Excellency’s orders to root this out from our country.”she added. Other EPA officials are also on the ground leading various campaign teams, engaging communities and consulting relevant stakeholders on the impending restrictions. With the January 1, 2027, deadline approaching, the Authority says it is stepping up public education to ensure that consumers and businesses understand the ban, prepare for the transition and embrace environmentally sustainable alternatives.

title: The betrayal of the ones we trusted
body: There is a loneliness that has nothing to do with being alone. It is the loneliness of knocking on the door of the institution that was built for you, and hearing only the echo. Ghana’s citizens are learning that loneliness this October. Nineteen girls, and a house on the hill At Obuasi Senior High Technical School, the number of students who have come forward with allegations of sexual abuse against the suspended headmaster has risen from 16 to 19, according to investigative journalist Manasseh Azure Awuni, who says more may follow because some did not report. The allegations, which include rape, sexual assault and threats, are contained in his documentary. They remain subject to investigation. The headmaster has not been convicted of anything, and the Constitution says he is presumed innocent until proven guilty. That principle protects all of us, and I hold to it. But presumption of innocence is a shield for the accused. It was never meant to be a blindfold for the system. Look at what the reports say about who knew, and when. The Municipal Chief Executive for Obuasi has confirmed she was told last year, after a former sports master reported that the headmaster had slept with a student. A recording in the documentary reportedly captures the school’s housemistress describing how a female student was taken away at night after an allegation of sexual assault, and how the housemistress confronted the headmaster, who asked only how the girls were. One political statement says some incidents were brought to school authorities as far back as March 2026, without meaningful action to protect the students. Reports also indicate the Ghana Education Service initially recommended only a transfer. A transfer would have moved the problem to another school. It would have done nothing to protect the girls already harmed, or the ones he might meet next. Manasseh says this is not even his first visit to that school over such claims. By his account, his first visit, in 2018, was about allegations of sexual assault there too. Only after the documentary did the machinery move. The Interior Minister told Parliament’s Public Accounts Committee that the police will conduct a thorough and impartial investigation, and that the matter will not be swept under the carpet. The headmaster resigned as constituency secretary of his political party and withdrew from its chairmanship race. It is good that they moved. But why did it take a camera, a journalist and a national outcry? What was a child supposed to do in March, or in 2025, when she told the adults whose job it was to listen? A girl who is abused by the person who holds the highest authority over her school has nowhere to run, because the system is built so that he is the one she must report to. When every door she knocks on opens onto someone who knows him, someone who fears him, or someone who votes with him, she learns something no child should learn. She learns that being believed is a privilege. A student, a motorbike, and nineteen days Ivan Apprey Baidoo was 20, a law student, on his way to play football. Prosecutors allege that a police corporal on traffic duty pursued the motorbike he was riding as a passenger, kicked it during the chase so that the rider lost control and crashed into a concrete barrier, and then left without arranging medical help. Baidoo was pronounced dead on arrival. The corporal was charged with murder on 15 September, about three weeks after the 27 August incident. Those are the prosecution’s allegations, and the officer is entitled to his day in court. I will say honestly that this case has seen movement. The officer was interdicted, the homicide unit took over, and charges were brought. But the family had to demand transparency, and a father had to say publicly that his son did not die in an ordinary accident. A young man who spent years studying the law died at the hands of someone who is paid to enforce it. Imagine what his mother thinks every time she hears the words “rule of law.” “No bed” Then there are those who die before the courts ever hear their names. On the night of 6 February, Charles Amissah, a 29-year-old engineer, was alive, stabilised and breathing. By dawn he was dead, after nearly three hours in an ambulance, denied admission at three of Accra’s most prominent hospitals because there was “no bed available”. The investigating committee concluded that his death resulted from multiple system failures, including delays in emergency response, lack of proper stabilisation, and weak coordination between the major hospitals. Nothing about this was new. In 2024, Korle Bu had to suspend referrals to its surgical and medical emergency unit because it was housing 60 patients in a 36-bed unit. Ghana’s ratio of roughly 0.9 hospital beds per 1,000 people is far below what the World Health Organization recommends. A person can fail by a system that never intended to hurt them. When failure is predictable, repeated and left uncorrected, it becomes a choice. Due process is sacred. But justice delayed is justice denied, as every law student, including Ivan, was taught. A case that takes years leaves a victim waiting while her abuser keeps his title, his salary and his neighbors. It leaves a widow paying lawyers’ fees out of grief. In practice, the people who can afford to wait are the ones who need justice least. That is how selective justice works. No one must announce it. It comes through who gets believed first, who gets a hearing, who can afford the lawyer, who has someone in the right office to call. The poor and the powerless are left with a thin version of the same Constitution. The loneliest word in our language Nineteen girls, a young man on a motorbike, an engineer in an ambulance. Different stories, one feeling. The people who trusted us to be ready, to be fair and to be fast found that the door was shut. If we want to repair this, we must start by honoring what the Constitution says quickly. Investigate the Obuasi allegations transparently and protect the girls who spoke from retaliation. Create independent reporting channels in every school. Make emergency care a legal duty that does not depend on a vacant bed. Hold officers to the same law they enforce on everyone else. And let no victim in Ghana ever again must wait for a journalist before an institution decides to care. So, what is freedom, if a girl is not free from fear in her own school? What is justice, if it must be asked for in the right accent, from the right family, with the right lawyer and the right party card? Freedom is not only the absence of chains. It is the confidence that if someone breaks you, the state will stand on your side of the room. We are better than this. But only if we act like it.

title: Fourteen years after genocide, Yazidis may see stability in Iraq - analysis
body: Fourteen years after ISIS invaded the Sinjar region of Iraq and targeted the Yazidi minority in a genocidal campaign, the group may finally see some stability in northern Iraq.Yazidis are one of several minority groups in Iraq, and most live in the Sinjar region of northern Iraq and in some towns in the Kurdistan Regional Government's governorates. In August 2014, ISIS invaded Sinjar and massacred thousands of Yazidis. ISIS also kidnapped thousands and sold them into slavery. It was one of the most horrific crimes that ISIS committed.Sinjar, which Yazidis also call Shingal, was liberated in November of 2015. Sinjar refers to the entire region, including a long mountain and a city with the same name. Numerous Yazidi villages and towns to the north and south of the mountain.During the genocide, many Yazidis fled to the mountain, and many were also saved by the Kurdish People's Protection Units (YPG) in Syria, who helped open a corridor for them to flee. Since then, many of the group have lived in IDP camps in the Kurdistan region or slowly made their way back to poverty-stricken livelihoods in Sinjar.The Yazidi region was largely abandoned by Iraq. In 2017, the Kurdish Peshmerga, who had helped liberate the area from ISIS, were pushed out by Iraqi federal troops and by Iranian-backed militias of the Popular Mobilization Forces. The Yazidis remained, but they were divided.Some Yazidis targeted by Turkey after joining PKK-linked groupSome Yazidis had joined the Shingal Protection Units (YBS), a group that is linked to the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK). As such, the Yazidis found themselves in the crosshairs of Turkey, which views the PKK as a terrorist group.Now things are changing again. Rudaw, a Kurdish media outlet, noted on October 24 that Murad Ismael, a Yazidi activist and Iraqi lawmaker who has spent many years seeking to help his community, said on Saturday that members of the Shingal Protection Units (YBS) would be integrated into several Iraqi security institutions, including the police, rejecting suggestions that all fighters would join the Shiite-dominated Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF).This matters because, for several weeks, there has been talk of a deal between Baghdad and the YBS to integrate the group into the security forces. The goal of Iraq is to rein in all the independent militias in Iraq. This also includes disarming the Iranian-backed militias. However, those groups are stronger and more influential. The Yazidis are a group that Iraq feels it can work with and possibly have a model for integrating an independent armed group into the security forces.However, there is some controversy about how the group might be integrated. If it is integrated as a brigade within the PMF, concerns remain about how it might operate. The report indicates that the YBS integration will be more multi-layered.Ismael's remarks followed Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi's Friday interview with state media, where the leader said the YBS would be integrated into the PMF as part of an agreement to restore federal control over Shingal (Sinjar), Rudaw reported.“The integration process is not limited to the PMF, only a portion of it, with part of it being integrated into the police and part of it into other security structures,” said Ismael of the plan.It now remains to be seen how quickly the integration process will happen. Ismael appeared to indicate that it will begin in the next several days. Iraq has said it wants the other militias integrated by June 2027. According to Rudaw, Ismael said he expected members of the YBS's all-female force to be integrated into the Iraqi Interior Ministry's Community Police.This matters because it mirrors a similar process on the other side of the border with the Syrian Democratic Forces. This mostly Kurdish group is integrating into the Syrian security forces. As a result, a swath of Iraq and Syria is now changing. This will allow stability and investment on both sides of the border.Region in dire need of investmentThe region is badly in need of investment. This includes basic infrastructure, as well as schools and other facilities. It has been badly neglected for many years. Part of the neglect has been due to the uncertainty of what might come next. Yazidis have been wary of returning in the past unless they feel that ISIS and its supporters will be prevented from returning.At the same time, the different armed groups, such as the YBS and also Iranian-backed militias, make it impossible for investment to flow into the area, or for people to feel that stability will return.The decision by Baghdad to seek to normalize the situation in Sinjar and work on security is important. The issue now will be whether the details of the agreement lead to change. Iraq has successfully revived Mosul, which is between Sinjar and the Kurdistan Region. That large city of 2 million people was once occupied by ISIS until it was liberated in 2017. Now, it's possible that the stability in Mosul might radiate out to Sinjar.

title: Shortage of oncology nurses threatens cancer care delivery in Nigeria
body: Nursing professionals have called for improved welfare, increased training opportunities and greater inclusion in health sector decision-making, warning that the shortage of oncology nurses is undermining cancer care in Nigeria. They made call in separate interviews with the News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) in Abuja. According to the National Institute for Cancer Research and Treatment (NICRAT), Nigeria records 102,000 to 127, 763 new cancer cases and approximately 72,000 to 79,542 cancer related deaths annually. The professionals noted that the country lacked sufficient specialists to meet the increasing demand for cancer care, added that the migration of trained nurses to other countries further worsen the situation. Prof. Khadijat Musah, Dean of the Faculty of Nursing Sciences, Federal University Otuoke, Bayelsa State, estimated that Nigeria had about 300 oncology nurses. Musah expressed concern over the migration of trained nurses and urged the government to address their welfare. “I am using this opportunity to thank the leadership of Nigeria and everybody in government. But they should try and look into the welfare of oncology nurses,” she said. She said only two institutions in Nigeria trained oncology nurses, with each admitting up to 50 candidates depending on available resources and capacity. According to her, some universities have introduced postgraduate programmes in oncology nursing, including masters and doctoral degrees. “Our voices need to be heard because we are patient advocates. We see them go through the pain,” Musah said. She said nurses’ close contact with patients gave them first-hand knowledge of the challenges people faced during cancer treatment and recovery. Also speaking, an oncology nurse, Ann Joachim, described the shortage of trained specialists as a major challenge. “We are short-staffed. We have limited number of trained oncology nurses. “You find out that a nurse will sacrifice her time, her talent, her skill just to acquire the specialty she needs as an oncology nurse,” Joachim said. She said oncology nurses were not adequately rewarded for their specialised skills and also faced occupational risks associated with cancer care. In spite of the challenges, Joachim encouraged young nurses to specialise in oncology. “I will advise them to come into the profession. If not for anything, for the love, for the compassion, for the ability to participate in curtailing this disease called cancer,” she said. Fatima Adam, Vice-President of the Oncology Nursing Society of Nigeria, underscored the critical role oncology nurses played in cancer treatment. Adam, who works at the Federal Teaching Hospital, Katsina, said no multidisciplinary cancer care team was complete without an oncology nurse. “In cancer care today, we talk about the multidisciplinary team (MDT), which is never complete without an oncology nurse, who is always at the bedside of the patient 24/7,” she said. She also advocated early exposure of nursing students to oncology to encourage more young professionals to specialise in the field. “Catch them young,” Adam said. Similarly, Nanre Mampak, an oncology nurse and educator with more than 20 years of experience, called for nurses to be included in decisions affecting healthcare delivery. “People who know nothing about nurses go to take decisions and ask nurses to implement. “My advice for Nigerian government is that let us make nurses fully inclusive in decision-making in the health sector,” she said. (NAN)

title: NDLEA arrests South African woman with 36.65kg cocaine, Lagos car dealer
body:
The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) has arrested a South African woman with 36.65kg of cocaine at Lagos airport and a Lagos-based car dealer accused of receiving and arranging accommodation for her.
The agency also arrested a Nigerian-American woman with 9.45kg of cannabis known as loud after she arrived in Nigeria from the United States.
In a statement shared with PREMIUM TIMES on Sunday, NDLEA spokesperson Femi Babafemi identified the South African woman as Qhina Beauty, 34.
He explained that she was arrested on 7 October at the departure hall of the Murtala Muhammed International Airport, Ikeja, Lagos, while preparing to board a Qatar Airways flight to South Africa via Doha.
A search of her two bags uncovered 30 blocks of cocaine weighing 36.65kg, the NDLEA said, adding that the drugs were wrapped in Sellotape, divided into seven parcels and laced with dried pepper.
Ms Beauty reportedly told investigators that she arrived in Nigeria on 30 September to collect the consignment. She said another South African woman recruited her and promised to pay her 20,000 rand after delivery.
She also identified two other people allegedly involved in the operation: one based in the United States and the other a Lagos car dealer, the statement said.
The agency said it arrested the dealer, Uchenna Victor Umunnakwe, 46, on 14 October at Apple Junction, Ago Palace Way, Lagos, after keeping him under surveillance at his residence in Shasha.
Mr Umunnakwe reportedly admitted receiving Ms Beauty at the airport and arranging her stay at Santiago Hotel in Amuwo-Odofin.
The agency noted that he later moved her to Cynarisso Hotel near the airport ahead of her departure.
The arrests come about two months after the NDLEA announced the seizure of 184.5kg of cocaine, valued at an estimated N39 billion, in Lagos.
PREMIUM TIMES reported that the cocaine was intercepted while being prepared for export through a courier logistics company. The operation led to the arrests of Kazeem Afolabi, popularly known as KC Luxury, and Lawal Kehinde, a logistics company employee.
The NDLEA described Mr Afolabi as the alleged Nigerian coordinator of an international drug trafficking syndicate.
It said the network used Nigeria as a transit point to move cocaine from South America to the United Kingdom, other parts of Europe and Asia.
The agency described the seizure as the largest interception of cocaine through a courier channel in its history.
In a separate operation, NDLEA operatives arrested Anetor Gloria Ubong, 62, a realtor based in Richmond, Texas, at Lagos airport on 21 October after she arrived on a United Airlines flight from Houston.
Ms Ubong, who holds Nigerian and United States passports, had 18 parcels of Loud weighing 9.45kg in one of her two checked-in boxes. The drugs were concealed in a box covered with gift-wrapping paper.
According to the agency, she told investigators that her daughter and her daughter’s future brother-in-law had delivered the box to her home in the US. She said she was to deliver it in Nigeria to her daughter’s fiancé, identified as Jibola.
In another operation in Lagos, a special unit of the agency arrested Eletu Rasheedat, 41, in the Eti Osa area on 23 October.
The operatives recovered 5,820 pills of diazepam, 780 tablets of tramadol, 3.7kg of skunk and 230.25 litres of skuchies.
In Delta State, operatives arrested Peter Ugochukwu, 51, in Warri and recovered thousands of opioid capsules and tablets, bottles of codeine syrup and other substances.
The seizures included 29,350 capsules of tramadol, 6,620 tablets of tramadol 200mg, 4,116 bottles of codeine syrup, 11,340 tablets of Rohypnol and 3,500 tablets of diazepam.
Officers also recovered 300 ampoules of pentazocine injection, 200 ampoules of diazepam injection, and quantities of tramadol 225mg, Molly and Cocodamol.
The NDLEA said the suspect and a white Hummer bus were handed over to the agency by the Nigeria Police Force in Delta State.
In a separate operation at Enhere Junction, Warri, officers arrested Helen Bakporo Samson, 46, on 19 October with 6kg of skunk.
In Oyo State, operatives arrested Fajana Dada Oluwaseyi, 41, in the Adamasingba area of Ibadan on 19 October. The agency said he had escaped arrest after officers seized 197.8kg of cannabis from his house on 16 September.
In Kano State, a raid in Gerawa on 22 October led to the arrest of Murtala Lawan, 30, and the seizure of 159 blocks of cannabis weighing 97.2kg.
In Taraba State, operatives arrested Raiyanu Misa, 39, at the Lankaviri checkpoint in Yorro Local Government Area on 23 October with 95 blocks of compressed cannabis weighing 60.175kg.
On the same day, the police handed over another suspect to the NDLEA after arresting him at Dakka village in Bali Local Government Area with 112 blocks of cannabis weighing 81.49kg.
In Niger State, officers arrested Emmanuel Ekene, 26, on the Sabo-Kainji Road in Borgu Local Government Area on 19 October with 64,000 opioid pills, including tramadol and diazepam.
In Bauchi State, operatives arrested Jamilu Mustapha, also known as Last Card, 45, at Nasaru Town in Ningi Local Government Area on 21 October. They recovered 379kg of cannabis packed in seven sacks.
In Ondo State, operatives raided a farm at Board-Ala, Akure South, on 20 October and recovered 56 abandoned bags of cannabis weighing 583kg.
In Edo State, the agency destroyed two cannabis farms in Ugbada Forest, Uzebba, Owan West Local Government Area, on 18 October. The farms had an estimated yield of 2,023.14kg.
The operatives burnt 450kg of processed cannabis at the site and took another 97kg as exhibits.
In a separate operation at Ewe community in Owan West, officers arrested Mary Edokhai, 42, with 35kg of cannabis.
The NDLEA chairman, Buba Marwa, commended the officers involved in the operations and urged them to sustain efforts against drug trafficking and substance abuse.
The agency also said its commands continued public awareness campaigns under its War Against Drug Abuse programme, including sessions for students and school staff.

title: Aref asks Azeri girls facing bans to continue studies in Iran
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 25 (MNA) – Iranian First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref has called on Azerbaijani girls and women that face hijab restriction in their country to continue their education Iran.
In a post on X, Aref thanked the Ministry of Science for announcing the readiness of Iranian universities to admit Azerbaijani girls who wear hijab. He also urged other education officials and university authorities to take steps to ensure that these students can continue their studies.
The request follows reports of hijab-related restrictions in educational institutions in the Republic of Azerbaijan. Earlier reports indicated that some female students and teachers who wear hijab had faced restrictions on attending educational institutions, prompting protests in response.
The Basij Student Organization of the University of Tehran had previously protested the reported restrictions by displaying a banner outside the Embassy of the Republic of Azerbaijan.

title: European authorities not analyzing causes of unrest, looking for those to blame — Putin
body:
MOSCOW, October 25. /TASS/. European authorities who blame Moscow for the unrest in their countries, do not analyze the underlying causes of the events, but look for someone to hold responsible instead, Russian President Vladimir Putin said.
In an interview with Vesti reporter Pavel Zarubin, the head of state noted that such accusations reveal the weakness of leaders in a number of European countries.
"And that’s bad for them. Why? Because instead of analyzing the events unfolding or looking for the underlying causes, they simply pin the blame on someone else, first on the US, and now on Russia," Putin said.

title: Police arrest suspect over railway vandalism in Ogun, recover 16 iron rods
body: By James Ogunnaike Abeokuta The Ogun State Police Command has arrested a 36-year-old man, Shobande Taofeek, over alleged vandalism and theft of railway infrastructure in the Arigbajo area of the state. The police also recovered 16 railway iron rods and two gas cylinders suspected to have been stolen during the operation. The arrest was carried out by operatives of the Special Weapons and Tactics (SWAT) unit of the command following intelligence reports about the alleged vandalism and theft of railway materials in the area. In a statement issued on Sunday, the Police Public Relations Officer, Ogun State Command, DSP Oluseyi Babaseyi, said the operatives intensified surveillance and patrols in the affected area on Friday October 23, leading to the suspect’s arrest. According to the statement, the suspect subsequently led the operatives to an uncompleted building where the recovered items were found. “On 23 October 2026, SWAT operatives intensified surveillance and patrols in the affected area, leading to the suspect’s arrest. He subsequently led the operatives to an uncompleted building where the stolen items were recovered as exhibits,” the statement said. The police further disclosed that preliminary investigations indicated that the suspect had allegedly admitted involvement in similar offences on three previous occasions. However, the command said investigations were ongoing to establish the full circumstances surrounding the alleged crime and identify other individuals who might have been involved. “Efforts are ongoing to apprehend other suspects connected with the crime and recover any additional stolen property,” the statement added. The State Commissioner of Police, Bode Ojajuni, reiterated the command’s commitment to protecting public assets and critical infrastructure, warning that those responsible for vandalism would be brought to justice. Ojajuni, according to the statement, reaffirmed the command’s “unwavering commitment to protecting public assets, safeguarding critical infrastructure and bringing perpetrators of economic sabotage to justice.” He also called on residents to support security agencies by providing credible and timely information that could help prevent crime and protect public infrastructure across the state. The police urged members of the public to cooperate with law enforcement agencies, stressing the importance of community participation in crime prevention and the maintenance of safer communities. The post Police arrest suspect over railway vandalism in Ogun, recover 16 iron rods appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Government allocates nearly UAH 188M to repair 33 homes damaged by Russian attacks
body:
Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi announced this on Facebook , according to Ukrinform.
“The government has allocated 187.6 million hryvnias for the restoration of 33 apartment buildings damaged as a result of Russian aggression in the Dnipropetrovsk, Sumy, and Kyiv regions. Funds from the Fund for Eliminating the Consequences of Armed Aggression will be transferred to local budgets,” Koretskyi said.
According to him, the funding will be used to restore three buildings in Kryvyi Rih, 20 in Sumy, and 10 in the Kyiv region.
This will help more than 4,000 residents return to their homes as quickly as possible.
As reported by Ukrinform, on September 21, the government announced that it was allocating 150 million hryvnias for the restoration of 11 apartment buildings in the Zaporizhzhia region that were damaged by Russian attacks.

title: Dubai Fashion Week: The best runway looks, biggest moments and designers to know
body: Dubai Fashion Week closed its spring/summer 2027 season with a reminder that the region’s fashion ambitions extend well beyond the runway, with shows and presentations by designers from far and wide, underlining the importance of the Middle Eastern market within fashion. Tarun Tahiliani Indian couturier Tarun Tahiliani closed Dubai Fashion Week in grand style on Monday, October 26 , sending Lebanese singer Maya Diab down the runway in an embellished silver lehenga (skirt) and choli (blouse). Called Many Moods of Tarun Tahiliani and described as “a celebration of the cultural ties that bring India and the Arab world together”, the collection combined modest pieces in rich peacock tones, burnt orange and mocha with traditional South Asian silhouettes, showcasing the delicate draping that has become Tahiliani’s signature. Surface decoration ranged from intricate handwork that moulded fabric to the body to featherlight embellishments framing necklines. Tightly cinched gowns shimmered in champagne colour, exquisitely draped skirts flowed in liquid gold, and swing coats were finished with burnished bronze detailing. Already a celebrated name in India, Tahiliani made his Dubai Fashion Week debut with a collection that bridged Indian craftsmanship and the tastes of the modern Arab woman. After the recent opening of his first boutique outside India, in Dubai, the show marked a confident arrival in the region. Designed with his new clientele in mind, it brought together two distinct sartorial traditions with an elegance that should win him plenty of new admirers. Onori Backstage at her Onori runway show on Day Four of Dubai Fashion Week, Emirati entrepreneur Sharifa Al Hashemi admitted she was exhausted. “I'm the founder, the designer, the micromanager, the accountant, the finance, the inventory manager, and I source material,” she laughed. Her fatigue, however, was nowhere to be seen in a collection inspired by a recent holiday in Sardinia. From the hotel interiors and flowers to the style of women on the island, Al Hashemi translated her memories into a wardrobe of relaxed Mediterranean elegance. A 1950s-inspired duster coat was reimagined as a strapless dress, while a fitted midi dress was softened with fabric flowers. Patterned Capri pants were paired with a babydoll top, which reappeared in baby blue alongside a long sheer skirt. Making her Dubai Fashion Week debut, Al Hashemi was equally keen to celebrate her Emirati roots. “I'm proudly Emirati and so inspired by my country, by Dubai, how it is top in everything,” she said. “It inspires me to become more ambitious, more hardworking.” That heritage was woven into every look through a subtle reference to the region's pearling history. “We have the dangling monogram, and there's a pearl attached to each piece, and it is part of the culture.” The show closed with a bridal look: a sheer cream dress beneath a long veil edged with golden beaded fringe. Shimmering like the inside of an oyster shell, it spoke of patience and longevity. Kuni Couture View this post on Instagram A post shared by kuni couture (@kuni.couture) The brainchild of Jordanian architect-turned-designer Sara Mousa, Abu Dhabi-based Kuni Couture delivered a sumptuous runway show with The Art of Becoming, a collection rooted in the brand’s name, derived from the Arabic for “be yourself”. Speaking backstage, Mousa described it as a “journey of women exploring their personality and themselves”, expressed through an evolving colour palette. “Starting with beige colours, which is soft, feminine and light, and then blue colours as she's starting to explore herself and her personality.” The progression unfolded through a drop-waist bisque gown embellished with bronze beading, a fitted sand-coloured dress with a billowing periwinkle cape, and a sheer silk corseted look adorned with silvery-blue beads. A hooded magenta satin gown featured a crystal-encrusted bodice, while a mini dress shimmered with cascading black beads. The darker palette marked the culmination of the journey: “This is a woman who knows who she is. She's bold, she's strong, she's unstoppable.” Mousa's architectural background was evident in the interplay of structure and softness. “I tried to put (big crystal) stones with silk. It's feminine, and at the same time it's strong.” The message became personal when Mousa took her final bow alongside her young daughter. “Everything I'm doing is for her,” she said. “You have to be strong, you have to be unstoppable, you have to be bold and just go ahead.” Nafsika Skourti The highlight of day two was undoubtedly the Dubai Fashion Week debut of Palestinian-Greek label Nafsika Skourti, which closed the day with a runway show called Sisters by Choice. The brand was started by sisters Nafsika, the creative director, and Stephanie Skourti, the business lead. "I was thinking that there is no official way to celebrate your friends ... and the energy really matched having a happy protest," Nafsika explained backstage. "So, we have slogans saying things like No Wrong Turns, and Sisters by Choice, and all these affirming statements that I really connected with." Returning to the runways after a nine-year hiatus, the collection was relaxed and built around daytime silhouettes in light, easy-to-wear fabrics. It was, she said, an exploration of "daywear, more activewear, and really leaning into the busy women we are." Stephanie explained the shift away from occasion-wear. "Anyone who has been following the brand will notice that we used to do high and low before, and now it’s a lot more intentional, while at the same time, staying true to our brand codes, like corsetry and detailing," she said. This was seen as sleeves and skirts trimmed with ribbons and open back tops made from woven beading, and mixed with roomy floral skirts, and sporty zip through tops. The result was lightweight pieces, cut for movement, that placed the demands of women's lives front and centre. Amid endless shows of beautiful, yet restrictive evening wear, this felt revolutionary. "Where we are from is something we are always thinking about and exploring. We feel very Arab. We grew up in the Middle East,” Stephanie said. Yousef Al Jasmi The runway programme of the week opened with Kuwait’s Yousef Al Jasmi, a designer well-versed in dressing for the spotlight. Having created looks for Lady Gaga, he understands the appeal of theatrical excess, and this collection delivered it in abundance. Crystal-encrusted dresses skimmed the body, long strands of crystals cascaded from shoulder to floor, and sculpted bodices were paired with sheer, close-fitting skirts. Moving from barely-there nude to dramatic black, the collection was designed to catch the light from every angle. Sara Pedram Next came self-taught designer Sara Pedram, whose collection, Simurgh, drew inspiration from The Conference of the Birds , the 12th-century epic poem by Attar of Nishapur. Exploring transformation, spirituality and Persian cultural heritage, Pedram translated the story into a series of sculptural silhouettes. A ballerina opened the show, followed by sheer creations with wing-like extensions at the shoulders. A richly embellished burnt-amber column gown gave way to a shimmering cascade of swaying paillettes, while a Prussian-blue velvet gown featured a Swarovski-crystal Tree of Life traced across its train, symbolising growth and renewal. Most arresting was a voluminous, full-skirted creation in rough hessian, hand-painted with a scene inspired by Persian poet Hafez , whose work, Pedram explained, was “close to my heart”. “Simurgh is a legendary bird that represents rebirth, transformation and rising again,” Pedram said backstage. “This collection is very personal to me, especially this year. Fashion is more than a beautiful dress; I love to explain the story behind each piece.” Pallavi Puri Indian designer Pallavi Puri followed with Beyond Borders, a collection exploring cultural exchange through a wardrobe designed for women across the region. Drawing inspiration from family and friends, their tastes and the way they dress, Puri reworked traditional Indian beadwork for a contemporary audience, citing Emirati, Asian and Moroccan women among her most inspirational clientele. Horses were another recurring motif, reflecting both the designer’s long-standing fascination with the animals and Dubai’s enduring equestrian culture. Indian model Lisa Haydon opened the show, while Lebanese actress Cyrine Abdel Nour closed it wearing an embellished bridal look. “Did you realise one is from India and one is Arab?” Puri said, highlighting the collection’s cross-cultural message. “My show is Beyond Borders, so it is about mixing and coming together.” It was Haydon's first appearance for Puri and a return to opening a runway show after a lengthy break. “When you open a show, you set the tone, so I was extra nervous,” she admitted. “This is [Puri’s] debut show [at Dubai Fashion Week], so it was quite a special moment to be part of. I have walked in Dubai Fashion Week before, but today was a lot of firsts.” Kresha Bajaj Closing the evening was Kresha Bajaj, who returned with a collection showcasing the designer’s signature beadwork. Applied to daywear, it trailed across delicate crocheted tops, framed the necklines of street-style tank tops and formed striking zebra-skin patterns. As the collection moved into evening wear, the embellishment became increasingly elaborate, forming latticework across torsos, looping around hips and swaying across legs with every step. It was glamour with an edge. The Showroom Before the first models took their places on Thursday, a showroom in Dubai Design District previewed emerging talent from around the world and introduced several designers to the UAE market. Among them was Bahrain’s Touchless, whose 3D-printed handbags have already attracted the attention of British Vogue , Selfridges, Level Shoes and Fashion Trust Arabia, as well as making an appearance in the Bridgerton universe. Egyptian jeweller-turned-eyewear designer Amr Saad brought a precious touch with bespoke gold and silver frames finished with jewellery-like detailing along the arms and bridge. Tunisian footwear label Balga drew on traditional metalworking techniques for its sculptural heels. Leather mules featured hand-hammered metalwork, including a tapered heel etched with graphic lines reminiscent of baklava. Kuwaiti designer Kochylia, whose name means seashells in Greek, offered a considered take on wardrobe classics, from reworked trench coats to tuxedo jackets finished with handmade porcelain buttons fashioned from Kuwaiti mud.

title: Injured Chukwueze set to miss crucial AFCON qualifiers
body: Nigeria international Samuel Chukwueze is expected to miss the upcoming Africa Cup of Nations AFCON 2027 qualifiers. The AC Milan wingback is still nursing a hip injury and will likely not recover in time to feature for the Super Eagles in the must-win double header. Chukwueze suffered the injury during his side’s 3-2 win over Atalanta, in a match he was substituted due to the complaint. He was expected to recover within two weeks, but reports in Italian media says the explosive dribbling wizard is expected to spend more time on the sideline. He is one of three AC Milan players expected to remain in the treatment room until after the international break. This indicates Chukwueze is not expected to join up with his colleagues for the crucial matches against Tanzania in Uyo and Dar es Salaam. Nigeria host Tanzania on November 13, and visit the AFCON 2027 co-hosts for matchday four. Nigeria are second in Group L with three points from two matches, three points behind Guine-Bissau who shocked the continent with a 3-0 win over the Super Eagles. Both countries vie for the solitary AFCON slot in Group L, and further drop of points could see Nigeria miss AFCON for the first time since similar failure in 2017.

title: Armed Forces bravery in upholding Hormuz symbol of Iran power
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 25 (MNA) – The commander of Iran's Army Navy has said that the valor and braveries of the naval personnel of the Armed Forces in safeguarding the strategic Strait of Hormuz is a symbol of Iran’s power on the international stage.
Speaking during a visit to the 3rd Naval Zone (Nabovvat), Rear Admiral Shahram Irani hailed the role played by the brave naval personnel of the Armed Forces in safeguarding the Strait of Hormuz and the Sea of ​​Oman as a symbol of the authority of the Islamic Republic of Iran on the international stage.
Referring to the self-sacrifice, valor, and braveries of the Army Navy personnel during the 40-day war [Ramadan War], Rear Admiral Irani stated, “Through their effective and responsible presence in strategic maritime regions, the brave sailors of the Army Navy have taken giant steps toward safeguarding the nation’s maritime borders and upholding Iran’s maritime security and authority."
The valor displayed by the seafaring personnel of the Armed Forces in defending the Strait of Hormuz and the Sea of ​​Oman reflects their high spirit of self-sacrifice and sense of responsibility; it serves as a manifestation of their commitment and dedication, a testament to their maritime might, and a symbol of the authority of the Islamic Republic of Iran, he emphasized.

title: Real Madrid’s Courtois to miss El Classico due to illness
body: Real Madrid have suffered a major setback ahead of their El Clasico clash against Barcelona after goalkeeper Thibaut Courtois was ruled out of Sunday’s La Liga encounter due to illness. The Belgian goalkeeper has contracted the flu and will miss the Matchday 10 fixture at Camp Nou, forcing Madrid to turn to Ukrainian shot-stopper Andriy Lunin. The development comes at a crucial time for Real Madrid, who trail Barcelona by six points in the La Liga standings and need a positive result to strengthen their title challenge. Real Madrid confirmed Courtois’ late withdrawal in a statement released hours before kick-off. “Courtois is a last-minute withdrawal from tonight’s LaLiga matchday 10 game between Real Madrid and Barcelona due to a bout of the flu,” the club said. “Illia Voloshyn has been called up to the squad in his place.” Courtois’ absence represents a significant blow for Madrid, given his importance to the team and his recent performances. The 34-year-old was in action during Madrid’s recent Champions League outing, in which the club reportedly secured a 4-1 victory over RB Leipzig. His late withdrawal leaves Lunin with the responsibility of guarding Madrid’s goal in one of the most important fixtures of the season. Lunin is expected to start in goal in place of Courtois as Madrid prepare to face their fierce rivals. The 27-year-old has served as Courtois’ deputy in recent seasons and gained valuable experience during Madrid’s run to the Champions League final in 2024. He will now face a major test against a Barcelona side that has enjoyed an impressive start to the domestic campaign. Barcelona head into the encounter looking to maintain their strong league form, while Madrid will be eager to close the gap at the top of the standings. Madrid’s preparations have been further complicated by the absence of forward Vinícius Júnior, who remains unavailable as he serves a four-match domestic suspension. The Brazilian’s absence deprives Madrid of an important attacking option for the high-profile encounter. Madrid have also suffered two league defeats this season, against Real Betis and Atletico Madrid, increasing the pressure on the team to secure a result against Barcelona. With Courtois ruled out at the last minute and Vinícius unavailable, Madrid face a difficult challenge as they seek to reduce Barcelona’s six-point advantage in the La Liga title race. title: Taraba Govt mobilizes emergency relief, food supplies to Binnari after bandit attack
body: By Femi Bolaji JALINGO — The Taraba State Government has deployed emergency relief materials to Binnari community in Karim Lamido Local Government Area, less than 24 hours after a deadly bandit raid left more than forty residents dead and several households displaced. The rapid humanitarian intervention was executed on the direct directive of Governor Agbu Kefas, who mandated immediate state assistance to cushion the hardships faced by survivors of the Friday afternoon incursion. A high-powered government delegation led by the Executive Secretary of the Taraba State Emergency Management Agency (TSEMA), Dr. Audu Echuseh, arrived in the community on Saturday to coordinate the distribution of relief items and assess the extent of property destruction. The assessment team included the members representing Karim Lamido Constituencies at the Taraba State House of Assembly, Hon. Anas Shuaibu Didango and Hon. Abner Shittu; the Vice Chairman of Karim Lamido Local Government Council, Alhaji Uba Munyarda; alongside traditional rulers and community stakeholders. Addressing grieving residents during the distribution of supplies which included food grains, mattresses, blankets, and essential non-food items, Dr. Echuseh conveyed Governor Kefas’s deepest condolences to the bereaved families. She stated: “We are here on behalf of the Taraba State Government to show solidarity and provide immediate succour to our brothers and sisters in Binnari. His Excellency has directed that no victim of this dastardly act be left unattended to. “This is just the first phase of our intervention. The government is fully committed to providing necessary humanitarian support while collaborating with security agencies to ensure long-term stability and security in the area.” Reacting to the prompt response, the lawmakers commended the state government for its swift action, pledging total grassroots cooperation with security formations deployed to comb the area and forestall future attacks. Although the police claimed ten persons were killed, residents of the community said more than forty residents were lost to the attack.
