title: Jared Kushner, the Bank of Israel, and the difference between allegations and facts - opinion
body: I know Jared Kushner. I have spoken with him personally on several occasions. I know that he worked hand in hand with Steve Witkoff to bring the Israeli hostages home from captivity in Gaza. I know that Kushner cares deeply about the future of the State of Israel. I also believe that he is one of the few people with real influence in the Trump administration who genuinely cares about the future and welfare of the Palestinian people.I cannot speak about Kushner's private business dealings, his financial affairs, or every aspect of his work in the Middle East. I have no firsthand knowledge of those matters, and I will not pretend otherwise.I can speak to his involvement in efforts to help Israelis and Palestinians. I have witnessed an evolution in his thinking, and in my judgment, that evolution has been for the better. I believe he increasingly understands that Israel's future cannot be separated from the future of the Palestinian people.That is why I read with particular interest the extraordinary allegations published in Vanity Fair on October 22, in an article by Matthew Cole concerning Kushner's alleged secret financial arrangements in the Middle East.One allegation immediately caught my attention. The article claims that approximately $1 billion was transferred into an account at the Bank of Israel, supposedly connected to Kushner and, according to one source, intended for his personal benefit.This story has a fundamental problem.The Bank of Israel is not a commercial bank. It is Israel's central bank. Private individuals cannot simply open accounts there.This is not a matter of opinion. It is how the Israeli banking system operates. The Bank of Israel maintains accounts for the government, banking institutions, certain financial entities, and authorized foreign central banks and financial institutions. It does not offer private banking services to individuals, whether they are Israeli citizens, American businessmen, or presidential advisers.Allegations of private Kushner account incompatible with bank rulesIf the allegation is that Kushner personally opened or controlled a private account at the Bank of Israel, it is incompatible with the bank's published rules.Could money have moved through an institutional account? That is a different question and would require specific evidence. But the published allegation raises an obvious question that should have been answered before publication: Who was the legal account holder, and how could Kushner supposedly control the funds?I do not know whether the other financial allegations in the article are true or false. But when an investigation makes an extraordinary claim involving a central bank without adequately explaining how such an arrangement could exist, it raises serious questions about the reliability of its reporting.Extraordinary allegations require extraordinary scrutiny. They should not be accepted simply because they make sensational headlines.My defense of Kushner is not based on political loyalty. I have disagreed with American administrations, including this one, on fundamental questions concerning Israel and Palestine. I judge people by what I know of their actions and by whether they contribute to a better future.In Kushner's case, I have seen someone willing to engage with difficult realities and to reconsider positions. I have seen someone who understands that diplomacy requires more than repeating established formulas. Most importantly, I believe he recognizes that a sustainable future for Israel must also offer Palestinians dignity, opportunity, and hope.After decades of working for Israeli-Palestinian peace, I have learned to recognize the difference between people who speak about peace and people who may actually help make it possible.Kushner increasingly an ally of those seeking peace between Israelis, PalestiniansIn my personal judgment, Kushner is increasingly an ally of those of us who have devoted our lives to achieving Israeli-Palestinian peace.That does not place him above criticism or scrutiny. No one should be above either. But criticism must be grounded in facts, and serious journalism must distinguish between evidence and speculation.The claim about a private account at the Bank of Israel deserves a clear explanation. Until one is provided, I see no reason to accept it – and every reason to question the credibility of that part of the story.The writer is the Middle East director of the International Communities Organization and the co-head of the Alliance for Two States.

title: Russia Launche 1,600 Bombs and 2,300 Drones Over Past Week
body:
Russian forces launched approximately 1,600 guided aerial bombs, nearly 2,300 strike drones , and 48 missiles of various types against Ukraine over the past week, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced on Sunday, Oct. 25.
In a statement on Facebook and reported by state news agency Ukrinform, Ukraine’s head of state outlined the human and material toll of the relentless aerial campaign, emphasizing that strikes have inflicted fatal and non-fatal civilian casualties on a near-daily basis.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“During this week alone, Russia launched around 1,600 guided aerial bombs, 48 missiles of various types, including ballistics, and almost 2,300 strike drones against Ukraine,” Zelensky stated.
“Unfortunately, almost every day there are dead and wounded from these brutal strikes.”
Zelensky highlighted the operational breadth of recent Russian strikes, confirming that overnight bombardments damaged critical infrastructure and civilian facilities across nine administrative regions.
Adversary munitions struck thermal power plants, electrical substations, coal mining enterprises, grain storage facilities, commercial shopping centers, and a postal terminal.
The president reviewed the casualties caused by the weekend’s standoff attacks, pointing to the deadly drone strike on the city of Synelnykove in Dnipropetrovsk region , which killed four civilians and wounded 22 others, including an 11-year-old girl.
Zelensky also referenced the strike on a five-story residential building in Vinnytsia that injured six people and forced the evacuation of an adjacent nursing home, alongside the assault on Kharkiv , where Russian forces struck a construction hypermarket and subsequently launched a secondary strike targeting arriving emergency rescue workers.
Addressing the geopolitical dimension of the ongoing bombardments, Zelensky observed that Moscow’s intensified attacks reflect its actual response to international diplomatic initiatives and efforts to end its isolation.
“This is precisely how Russia reacts to diplomacy and de-isolation,” Zelensky emphasized, stressing that Western partners must not permit military assistance to decline while diplomatic tracks are explored.
The president urged European allies to expedite defense support, calling specifically for the immediate release of surface-to-air interceptors that have already received political clearance from partner governments.
“It is necessary to unblock the supplies of Patriot interceptors already agreed upon by the Europeans ,” Zelensky said.
“It is necessary to further support Ukrainian combat aviation to protect against jet-powered Shaheds. Every such defense package, especially ahead of winter, helps save lives.”
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Lagos SWAN inaugurates seven-member electoral committee ahead of elections
body:
The Lagos State chapter of the Sports Writers Association of Nigeria (SWAN) has inaugurated a seven-member electoral committee to organise elections for a new executive committee.
The committee, known as the SWAN Electoral Committee (SWANECO), was inaugurated on Friday at the Teslim Balogun Stadium, Surulere, Lagos, during the chapter’s Extraordinary Congress.
Patrick Omorodion, chairman of the chapter’s caretaker committee, inaugurated the electoral body, which is chaired by Mozez Praiz, with McAnthony Anaelechukwu as secretary.
Other members are Abdul Rahmone Abulore, Soliu Adeyemo, Tega Onajaife, Jovita Ekeh and Suo Chapele.
Mr Omorodion said the committee’s establishment was part of the mandate given to the caretaker committee by the national body to strengthen the chapter’s administration and facilitate a credible election.
He said the process was intended to help restore stability and ensure the chapter had a substantive executive committee.
Speaking on behalf of the electoral committee, Mr Praiz pledged to carry out the assignment responsibly and help usher in a new executive committee capable of revitalising the chapter.
He cited activities such as the now-dormant SWAN Cup as examples of initiatives the chapter could revive to strengthen its engagement with members.
Enitan Obadina, SWAN’s national welfare officer, who represented the national executive at the congress, described the inauguration as a positive development for the Lagos chapter.
“As one of the country’s leading chapters, we are happy that Lagos is on the right path, and national SWAN, led by its president, Isaiah Benjamin, is providing support to ensure the process follows the constitution and is inclusive for members, to avoid the challenges of the past,” he said.
Veterans of the association who attended the ceremony included Mitchel Obi, Kunle Solaja, Felix Awogu, Godwin Enakhena, Emma Jemegah, Joe Apu, Pius Ayinor, Mike Mayaki and Smart Ebhodaghe.
The national body established the Lagos SWAN caretaker committee on 9 October with Mr Omorodion as chairman, Oni Afolabi as secretary and Anulika Menanya as a member.
The electoral committee is expected to oversee the process of electing a new executive for the Lagos chapter.

title: Taraba Community Puts Death Toll From Binnari Attack at 50, Govt Delivers Relief Materials
body: The death toll from a suspected bandit attack on the Binnari community in Karim Lamido Local Government Area of Taraba State has risen from the 10 initially reported by the police to 50, according to community accounts. Gunmen invaded the community on Friday, shortly after Jumu’ah prayers, shooting sporadically, looting food items and residential houses, and setting shops and motorcycles ablaze. In a statement issued on Saturday, the Taraba State Police Command confirmed that 10 bodies bearing gunshot wounds had been recovered from the scene. The Police Public Relations Officer, ASP Victor Mshelizah, said the attackers were large in number and invaded the village with heavy gunfire, causing panic among residents. “Upon receipt of the report, police operatives were immediately mobilised to the scene, where ten (10) bodies bearing gunshot wounds were recovered,” Mshelizah said in a statement. “The corpses were subsequently handed over to the families for burial in accordance with Islamic rites.” The police said additional personnel had been placed on red alert, while joint reinforcement teams comprising the Police Tactical Units, Police Mobile Force, conventional police, the Nigerian Army and other security agencies had been deployed to the area. However, community accounts put the death toll at 50 following further searches in nearby bushes and a river. More Bodies Recovered According to the community’s account, after the initial 10 bodies were found, 27 more were recovered following an intensive search of the surrounding bushes. Another 13 bodies, mostly those of children, were subsequently found in a river and nearby bushes. Some had reportedly drowned, while others were hit by stray bullets. Residents said the attackers crossed into the community from neighbouring Plateau State with sophisticated weapons. The community also alleged that Binnari had been attacked three times by armed groups. The Commander of the Hunters Association, Babangida Ibrahim, said police officers and Nigerian Army personnel responded after the alarm was raised, forcing the attackers to flee as security operatives approached. He said the intervention helped limit the casualties. Ibrahim, however, expressed concern about the challenges faced by local hunters, saying conventional security agencies arrest them even when they carry pump-action guns. He called on the government to provide hunters with sophisticated weapons to help them confront future attacks. Community Seeks Improved Security, Road Access A community stakeholder, Tanko Bobbo Andemin, called on the government to treat the recurring attacks on Binnari as a special security concern. He also appealed for improved road access to Karim Lamido, saying poor connectivity makes it difficult for security personnel to reach affected communities. “We call on His Excellency to link Karim Lamido with road network because this thing happens due to lack of access roads, even if the security agents want to come, there is no road,” Andemin said. He urged residents to remain law-abiding and protect themselves while awaiting further government action. The member representing Karim II State Constituency in the Taraba State House of Assembly, Anas Shuaibu, described the attack as “one attack too many” and called on the neighbouring Plateau State Government to strengthen security along the border. “I want to appeal and plead with the Plateau State Government to take drastic measures because the bandits are destroying lives and property in Taraba State,” he said. Shuaibu added that he would report the incident to the Taraba State Governor and expressed hope that the governor would engage his Plateau State counterpart to ensure stricter border patrols. Governor Condemns Killings Taraba State Governor, Agbu Kefas, condemned the killings and called on security agencies to take urgent steps to restore calm, protect lives and property, and bring those responsible to justice. In a statement issued by his Special Adviser on Media and Digital Communications, Emmanuel Bello, the governor said every effort must be made to identify and apprehend the perpetrators, regardless of their status or position. Kefas reaffirmed his administration’s commitment to addressing insecurity and restoring lasting peace in Karim Lamido. He also highlighted ongoing efforts to facilitate the safe return of displaced persons and rebuild confidence among residents affected by previous crises. As part of the broader peacebuilding efforts, the governor recently approved ₦1bn for the Taraba State Bureau for Peace and Conflict Management to address the aftermath of previous crises and support initiatives aimed at restoring peace in Karim Lamido. The governor sent condolences to the victims’ families and urged residents to remain calm and cooperate with security agencies. Relief Materials Meanwhile, the Taraba State Emergency Management Agency has delivered relief materials to the affected community, where thousands of residents have reportedly been displaced and are seeking refuge in neighbouring communities. The agency also assessed the extent of the damage to determine further humanitarian assistance required. The Executive Secretary of Taraba SEMA, Echuseh Audu, appealed for calm, assuring residents that the state government would not abandon them. She said the government and security agencies were taking measures to restore normalcy and improve security in the area. “As we provide humanitarian support in the form of food and non-food items, I want to counsel the residents of the area to be calm and vigilant and work closely with security operatives to provide credible information that will assist in halting a recurrence,” Audu said. The state government also said it was deploying additional security personnel to prevent further attacks and ensure that those responsible were brought to justice. The victims have been buried in a mass burial as residents continue to assess their losses and await further measures to prevent a recurrence. title: ‘My daughter, my biggest priority’ – Naomi Osaka considers quitting tennis
body: Former world number one Naomi Osaka cast doubt on her future Sunday saying she would consider quitting tennis if her three-year-old daughter asked her to. The four-time Grand Slam champion from Japan took 15 months away from the sport after the birth of her daughter Shai, before returning in 2023. She is in Tokyo to play at the Pan Pacific Open this week and said becoming a mother had reshaped her priorities. “I wouldn’t say I’m part-timing it but my entire day doesn’t consist of that,” said the 29-year-old, now ranked 19 in the world. “It’s tough, sometimes I look towards my future and I often wonder how long I’m going to play. “Because if my daughter did say she didn’t want me to travel as much, I’m not the type of person to ignore that.” Osaka also stepped away from tennis in 2021 to prioritise her mental health. She said her “mindset is changing a lot” with age. “My daughter is my biggest priority,” she said. “I try my best to put as much energy as I can into tennis. “If I think about it in certain ways, I’m really proud of where I am now because it’s not like I can dedicate my entire time to the sport.” – Online abuse – Osaka said juggling her duties as a player and a mother was something she was “figuring out little by little”. She also offered support to the American Coco Gauff, who said she had received an “insane” amount of racist abuse on the internet at this month’s China Open. World number five Gauff, who is Black, said the experience had been “kind of draining”. Osaka, whose mother is Japanese and father from Haiti, said “nobody should have to go through that”. “It’s sad but I’m used to it on my end,” she said. “I feel like for me, I’ve dealt with that my entire career through decisions that I make that seem to make some people upset. It’s tough.” Osaka said efforts made by women’s tennis governing body the WTA to combat social media abuse did not “ever seem to fully work all the way”. “I know that some people are like, OK, if it bothers you that much, stay off social media,” said Osaka. “But sometimes that’s the best way to connect with your fans. “From my end, what I do about it is I don’t really go on social media at all.” Osaka is seeded seven in Tokyo and plays Italy’s Jasmine Paolini in the first round. World number one Elena Rybakina of Kazakhstan and Philippines sensation Alexandra Eala are also competing. Osaka said she was “not far off” refinding her best form and was “optimistic for next year”. title: Russian titanium plant in Urals reportedly hit by Ukrainian drones, 1,500 km from Ukraine
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); A drone attack damaged an industrial facility in Russia’s Perm Krai early on 25 October, injuring five workers, Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ reported. Exilenova+ identified the target as the AVISMA chemical and metallurgical plant in Berezniki, around 1,500 km from Ukraine’s border. The reported strike highlights Ukraine’s ability to reach industrial facilities deep inside Russia that support its military-industrial complex. AVISMA produces titanium materials used in aviation and aerospace manufacturing, including military aircraft, aircraft engines, missiles, and space technology, according to Exilenova+. Regional governor Dmitry Makhonin said the industrial facility sustained damage but continued operating normally. He said five workers were injured in the attack. A target deep inside Russia Perm Krai lies in Russia’s Ural region, roughly 1,500 km from Ukraine’s border. The distance places the reported strike far beyond Russia’s border regions, where Ukrainian drone attacks have frequently targeted military and industrial infrastructure. The reported attack follows a broader Ukrainian campaign against Russian industrial and energy facilities linked to the country’s war effort. Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed that air defenses intercepted and destroyed 532 Ukrainian drones overnight across 23 Russian regions and over the Sea of Azov, according to Russian state news agency TASS. The reported interceptions included drones over Perm Krai, as well as regions around Moscow and areas in southern and western Russia. The figures have not been independently verified. The extent of damage at AVISMA and any impact on its operations have not been independently established. title: Hormuz management to never return to pre-war era: Araghchi
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 25 (MNA) – Iranian Foreign Minister Seyyed Abbas Araghchi has declared that “nothing will be the same” as before the US-Israeli war of aggression on Iran, including the administration of the Strait of Hormuz.
He made the remarks during the inauguration ceremony of the documentation center and museum of martyred diplomat Kamal Kharrazi, who was assassinated in a terrorist US-Israeli strike earlier this year.
He said that fundamental and strategic changes have taken place in West Asia and that nothing will be the same as it was before the 40-day imposed war (also known as the Ramadan war).
“For decades, the Strait of Hormuz has remained open, and neither Iran nor Oman, the two coastal states bordering the waterway, has imposed any restrictions on maritime traffic. On the contrary, both countries have helped ensure security and safety and protect the marine environment,” he added.
“However, the current war has changed everything. We must acknowledge that new realities have emerged. The shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz will no longer be the same as before, nor will the Strait be managed as it was in the past.”
Iran restricted transit through the Strait of Hormuz in response to the criminal US-Israeli aggression that began on February 28.
On June 17, Tehran and Washington signed aPakistan-brokered Memorandum of Understanding (MoU), whose Article 5 places responsibility for reopening and managing the Strait squarely in Iran’s hands.
However, Washington attempted to undermine Iran’s sovereignty over the Strait and imposed a naval blockade in violation of the war-ending deal, prompting Tehran to declare the vital global energy chokepoint closed to all traffic.
Additionally, in his remarks, the foreign minister said that if the aggressors have any sense of reason, they will not try another military assault against the Iranian nation, noting, “They’ve tried twice, and they’ve seen the results.”
The US and the Israeli regime waged their first criminal war against Iran, which lasted 12 days, in June 2025. Their second aggression began on February 28, 2026, and came to a halt in early April after 40 days.
In both wars, Iran’s resistance and successful retaliatory operations forced the aggressors to accept a ceasefire.
Araghchi also stressed that regional security must be ensured by the countries of the region themselves, without relying on or requiring the presence of foreign forces.
Iran and the regional states should live together in peace, without foreign interference, he said. “This is the only way to achieve peace, security, and stability in our region.”
Iran maintains relations with all the Persian Gulf countries while working to reach a shared understanding on a new regional security framework, he continued, Press TV reported.
“Our neighborliness policy is based on peaceful coexistence with our neighbors… Another important point is that, in our view, all regional issues are interconnected. It is not possible to have war and conflict in one part of the region while expecting peace and calm in another.”
“That is why, in all our negotiations with the US side, mediated by Pakistan, Qatar and other friendly countries, we have emphasized that any end to the war must encompass all fronts and bring an end to hostilities on every front. Otherwise, we will not see stability in the region.”

title: Vucic's mission: Can Serbia's longtime leader secure new mandate? - analysis
body: As Serbs headed to the polls on Sunday in one of the most consequential elections in the country's recent history, Aleksandar Vucic asked voters to place their confidence once again in a leader who has dominated the Balkan country for more than a decade, overseeing a period of considerable economic development while pursuing a distinctive foreign policy that has allowed Serbia to maintain productive relations with the US, Russia, China, and Israel, among others.Vucic, who resigned as president on September 27, seeks to return to the prime minister's office, having served as prime minister between 2014 and 2017 before winning the presidency.This election provides an opportunity to secure a fresh public mandate following almost two years of political unrest, after student-led demonstrations that began after the collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad in November 2024, which killed 16 people and prompted widespread accusations of corruption, negligence, and a failure of public accountability.Vucic is the head of a list called United Serbia, made up predominantly of his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), a party he helped found almost two decades ago, and the Serbian Radical Party, PUPS, the Serbian People's Party, the Workers' Party, the People's Peasant Party and the United Peasant Party.Despite the two-year-long demonstrations, Vucic enters Sunday's contest with advantages, particularly among voters who associate his leadership with the modernization of Serbia's infrastructure, alongside improvements in living standards, and the stability of a country whose recent history since the breakup of Yugoslavia has been marked by conflict and economic uncertainty.United Serbia coalition leading student-backed list, survey showsAn Ipsos survey published on Thursday placed his United Serbia coalition at 47.4% against 40% for the student-backed list, suggesting the governing bloc retains a sizable electoral base despite the sustained campaign against it. The survey, conducted among 3,624 respondents, was commissioned by Vucic's coalition, while other opinion polls have suggested a considerably closer race or an opposition lead.The outcome remains uncertain, although the figures do indicate somewhat the continuing appeal of a leader whose critics have repeatedly predicted that his political dominance was approaching its end – a situation one may apply to Israel as the country heads to the polls on Tuesday.From an Israeli perspective, Vucic's continued leadership would preserve an important and valued relationship with a European country that has maintained close diplomatic and defense ties with Israel, frequently taking positions at odds with those of other European governments.During an exclusive interview with The Jerusalem Post at the Presidential Palace in Belgrade last year, Vucic spoke candidly about Serbia's decision to supply Israel with military equipment almost immediately following the October 7 massacre, despite criticism from European leaders.“I am the only one in Europe today dealing in military ammunition with Israel,” he told this writer at the time. “And it is why I am often criticized by colleagues.”Vucic said that Serbia had moved quickly to assist Israel in the days following the Hamas attacks, expediting the necessary government approvals to enable the transfer of urgently needed military supplies. The relationship has since deepened, with the two countries expanding cooperation in defense technology and military production, including plans for a joint drone manufacturing facility involving Israel's Elbit Systems.The relationship also goes beyond defense cooperation. Trade and investment have grown considerably in recent years, while the two countries have also deepened their diplomatic engagement, culminating in the establishment of a formal strategic partnership earlier this year, which Foreign Minister Marko Djuric told the Post was an “historic step forward.”Vucic: Serbia-Israel relationship rooted in shared history, security challengesVucic has consistently emphasized that Serbia's relationship with Israel is rooted in a shared history and an understanding of the security challenges facing both countries, sentiments he expressed during the interview in Belgrade.“Our ties with Jews and Israelis – this is something different from a historical perspective up to the present day,” he said. “This isn't policy or current politics, no. This is our politics of all times, and it will always have to remain so.”With regard to the United States, Serbia's affinity with President Donald Trump since his reelection is seen among its population, with a 2024 Gallup International survey finding that 59% of respondents would have supported him over Kamala Harris, the highest figure recorded in Europe. Earlier this month, Trump praised the Serb-US relationship, telling Newsmax Balkans that the two countries enjoyed “very good relations.”Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Djuric also launched a strategic dialogue in July covering economic cooperation, security, and energy infrastructure. For Vucic, closer relations with the US are a major development given the troubled history between the two countries, particularly NATO's bombing of Serbia in 1999, while potentially helping Belgrade diversify its dependence on Russia.Serbia has also developed an increasingly close relationship with the United Arab Emirates, where investment and trade, alongside energy cooperation, have strengthened diplomatic ties between Belgrade and Abu Dhabi.Vucic's friendship with UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed al-Nahyan has become an important component of that relationship, with the Serbian leader expressing solidarity with the Emirates following the outbreak of the war with Iran in February.One can see through these relationships the diplomatic approach Vucic has pursued throughout his leadership: cultivating close ties with Israel, the US, and Arab partners while maintaining longstanding connections with Russia and China, whose investments in Serbian infrastructure and industry remain important to the country's economic development.Sunday's election will also determine whether Vucic can successfully navigate a considerable personal political transition.Having served as prime minister between 2014 and 2017 before winning the presidency, his resignation last month opened the way for a return to the office through which he first consolidated his leadership of Serbia. His decision does carry some political risk, particularly given the strength of the opposition movement, but it is also a reflection of Vucic's confidence that his electoral appeal remains sufficiently strong to secure another governing mandate.For a country of approximately 6.5 million people, Serbia has established a diplomatic presence considerably greater than its demographic or economic weight might suggest, cultivating relationships with major powers and influential Middle Eastern partners while continuing to pursue its own national interests.

title: Israel Police arrest four women in tax-refund scam that hit some 500 victims
body: Police arrested four women in northern Israel on Sunday on suspicion of defrauding some 500 people who had sought help claiming tax refunds, in a scheme that allegedly netted hundreds of thousands of shekels.Northern District police officers and Border Police troops raided the suspects' homes early Sunday, took the four into custody and seized items linking them to the alleged offenses, police said. The suspects are a mother and her two daughters from Kafr Kanna and a woman from Ilut, both localities near Nazareth.According to the Northern District's fraud unit, three of the suspects, the mother, one of her daughters, and the woman from Ilut, worked together at a legitimate tax-refund company.They approached clients who wanted to check whether they were eligible for a refund and had them pay a fee to open a file into the suspects' private bank account, then later into a fictitious account the suspects had set up.Many of the roughly 500 victims never filed a complaint, and investigators contacted them on their own initiative, police said.In recent months, the suspects also contacted the clients' pension funds and had them cashed out, police said, costing the victims both money and accrued benefits.Fraud from the insideIn July, a major corruption investigation led to the arrest and questioning of several current and former Israel Tax Authority employees suspected of accepting bribes over an extended period in exchange for facilitating the submission and approval of fraudulent tax reports and refunds worth an estimated 80 million shekels.The affair is believed to have continued for more than 20 years at tax assessor offices in the central region, including the Petah Tikva and Netanya branches, with the suspects alleged to have collected between 10 million and 15 million shekels in bribes.

title: 2027: Tinubu has lost touch with reality, unaware he’s president — Shaibu
body: The Director of Strategic Communication of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) Presidential Campaign Council, Phrank Shaibu, has accused President Bola Tinubu of losing touch with reality, alleging that he is disconnected from the economic hardship facing Nigerians. Shaibu made the allegation during an interview on ARISE News on Sunday, faulting the president for blaming the opposition for hunger despite spending three and a half years in office. “He has lost touch with reality. Bola is not aware of his environment. He is not aware of what Nigerians are going through. He’s not even aware that he’s president,” Shaibu said. He described Tinubu’s explanation of the country’s hunger crisis as delusional, arguing that the president should take responsibility for the economic situation under his administration. “I watched him yesterday and my eight-year-old son who was beside me said, what’s this man talking about? He has been in office for three and a half years. And he’s talking about hunger being created by the opposition. I think it is delusional,” he said. Shaibu challenged Tinubu to compare the cost of living when he assumed office on May 29, 2023, with the current situation, arguing that Nigerians should not be worse off under his leadership. He cited the removal of petrol subsidy as a major factor behind rising prices, saying the policy triggered sharp increases in the cost of goods and services. “Bola Tinubu claimed the podium, and announced that subsidy was gone. And boom, what happened? Everything rose astronomically. The Nigerians cannot afford three square meals today,” he said. The ADC campaign official also alleged that higher university fees had forced some students out of school, despite the establishment of the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND). He further criticised Tinubu for continuing to blame the opposition, noting that the All Progressives Congress governed the country for eight years under former President Muhammadu Buhari before handing over power in 2023. Shaibu said Tinubu’s remarks on hunger raised questions about his understanding of the hardship experienced by ordinary Nigerians. He argued that the president should be held accountable for his administration’s economic policies rather than attributing the crisis to political opponents. title: Google’s AI search changes upended online publishing
body:
This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more about AI’s impact on the web, follow Emma Roth. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.
How it started
The digital publishing industry has relied on Google for a very long time. Many outlets spent time and money optimizing their webpages to show up at the top of the search engine, with the goal of getting readers to click on their articles or discover their websites for the first time. For years, the relationship between Google and publishers was largely reciprocal; online publishers filled out Google’s search index with content, while Google supplied publications with exposure and traffic.
But that relationship has changed. The launch of Google’s AI search features — coupled with changes to the way it ranks search results — has made it harder for publishers to survive on traffic from Google alone. In 2024, Google rolled out AI Overviews, a feature that slots an AI-generated search result summarizing pages from across the web at the very top of Google Search, with links to sources its AI system determines to be the most useful placed below the summary. Instead of vying for clicks on the first page of Search, publishers became beholden to an AI system that regurgitates results, with no guarantee that users will actually click on the source of that information.
Though Google’s AI Overviews got off to a shaky start, the feature immediately raised concerns among publishers, with the News/Media Alliance saying it will be “catastrophic” to web traffic. A 2024 investigation from the Press Gazette found that Google’s AI Overviews appeared for almost a quarter of news-related searches in May 2024. By August, the outlet found that AI Overviews had begun impacting the visibility of publishers by replacing media sites that previously held the top spots on Google’s search engine for certain queries.
A future where Google could eventually stop sending traffic to outside sites on the web has only gotten closer as the company builds out its vision for an AI-powered search. In May 2025, it launched AI Mode, a feature that replaces Google’s standard search engine with a chatbot-like interface that provides detailed summaries from results on the web.
How it’s going
The concerns raised by the News/Media Alliance were real: Traffic to online publishers tanked following the launch of Google’s AI search features. A June 2025 report from The Wall Street Journal revealed how traffic to Business Insider, The Washington Post, HuffPost, and the WSJ itself has declined since 2022. Data from analytics company Similarweb suggested that search traffic to The New York Times sank from 44 percent to 35.5 percent in three years, the WSJ reported.
A report from Digiday pointed to similar dips at Digital Content Next (DCN), a trade association that represents outlets and media companies like Bloomberg, The Associated Press, The New York Times, Condé Nast, and Vox Media. Between May and June 2025, DCN says 19 of its members experienced a traffic loss on Google, ranging from 1 to 25 percent, Digiday reported. DMG Media, which owns Daily Mail and Metro, told the UK’s Competition and Markets Authority that click-through rates dropped by up to 89 percent between June and July 2025, citing impacts from AI Overviews. On top of all of this, Pew Research found that people are “less likely” to click on links to other websites when they see an AI Overview.
These numbers starkly contrast with Google’s claims that its AI search features are helping the web. Last year, Google Search head Liz Reid said click volume from the search engine remained “relatively stable,” adding that AI search is sending more clicks to different types of websites — especially those “with forums, videos, podcasts, and posts” from other users. Nick Fox, Google’s senior vice president of knowledge and information, told the BBC, “From our point of view, the web is thriving.”
In addition to scrutiny from regulators, publishers from around the globe have filed lawsuits against Google, claiming the company’s AI search features have negatively impacted traffic. Many lawsuits haven’t been successful. US District Judge Amit Mehta dismissed an antitrust case from Chegg and Penske Media, which owns The Rolling Stone, Billboard, The Hollywood Reporter, and The Verge. The same judge also rejected a proposed class action lawsuit surrounding AI Overviews filed by Arkansas newspapers.
What happens next
Online publishers have had to adjust their strategies in the wake of falling search traffic, with many leaning on social media, newsletters, and subscriptions to promote and make money from their work. Others are using a toggle that allows them to opt out of appearing in AI Mode and AI Overviews without affecting their visibility in search — an option Google broadly rolled out following an order from the UK. But this still doesn’t fix sinking traffic.
Pushback from online publishers appears to have resulted in some changes to Google’s AI search features. The company has begun to make sources more prominent in AI Mode and AI Overviews, as hovering over a link in either feature will show a pop-up with a list of articles and accompanying images. Another AI search change puts in-line links “higher up in responses more frequently.”
Google will likely continue making changes to how it presents sources in AI search, while coming up with ways to compensate publishers that inform its results. The company says 400 publishers, including The Washington Post, CNN, Axios, and the Financial Times, are now part of its News AI pilot program, which licenses content to develop new AI features. It’s also testing a program that pays publishers for the use of their content in AI Overviews and AI Mode, according to reports from The Information and Digiday. Whether this program is enough to repair Google’s relationship with publishers remains to be seen.
By the way
* Google is burying blue links even further beneath AI Overviews. The search summaries have started to automatically expand for some queries, instead of requiring users to manually click a “Show more” button.
* The Wall Street Journal reports that Reddit is also considering cutting off Google due to dropping traffic.
* It’s not just publishers and online forums that are concerned about AI Overviews — the nonprofit Common Sense Media claims the search summaries pose an “unacceptable” risk to kids by failing to respond appropriately to children in crisis.
Read this
* This Decoder interview with Google CEO Sundar Pichai sheds a lot of light on the company’s vision for the future of search.
* This write-up from The New York Times shows how Google’s AI Overviews still struggle with accuracy.
* A survey from Nieman Lab reveals how more people are relying on AI chatbots to get their news.

title: Greek Banks Earn €2.6 Billion in Six Months as Bad Loans Climb to €6.2 Billion
body: Greek banks profits reached €2.6 billion in the first half of 2026, yet bad loans on their books rose to €6.2 billion over the same period. Both figures come from the Bank of Greece’s latest Financial Stability Review, published on 22 October. Greek banks profits keep rising According to the Bank of Greece , Greek banking groups posted after-tax profits of €2.6 billion between January and June, up 3.8% on the first half of 2025. Interest and fees drove the result. Net interest income rose 5.6%, helped by loan growth and larger holdings of foreign government bonds. At the same time, net fee and commission income jumped 18.5%. Together, these core revenues grew 8.3% year on year. Banks also set aside far less money for bad debts, with loan-loss provisions down 27.8%. On the other hand, operating costs rose 9.3% and trading gains fell. Overall, the sector’s return on equity stood at 12.1%. Capital buffers eased slightly. The CET1 ratio fell to 14.8% in June from 15.4% in December 2025, while the total capital ratio slipped to 19.6% from 19.8%. What the €6.2 billion actually means The €6.2 billion figure is the stock of non-performing loans (NPLs) held on Greek banks’ own balance sheets, on a solo basis. Therefore, it excludes the legacy bad debts that banks have already sold or securitised, which loan servicers now manage. That stock rose by €529 million, or 9.3%, from €5.7 billion in December 2025. As a result, the NPL ratio edged up to 3.4% of all loans from 3.3%. According to the report’s detailed figures, reported by SKAI and Ta Nea, €1.7 billion of loans turned bad during the half-year. By contrast, only €388 million returned to performing status, and banks wrote off just €73 million. Households felt the strain most. Household bad loans rose 14% from December, mainly in mortgages and, to a lesser extent, consumer loans. The household NPL ratio reached 8.6%. Business NPLs rose 5.4% to about €3.2 billion, with the sharpest increase among self-employed professionals and micro-businesses (12.5%). Meanwhile, bad loans to shipping companies fell 7.3%. Even so, the central bank stresses that NPLs remain 94%, or €101 billion, below their March 2016 peak. Are high interest rates part of the problem? The Bank of Greece links part of the rise in bad mortgages to the recent legislative settlement for Swiss franc loans, as well as to bank initiatives targeting restructured mortgages of vulnerable households, Powergame reports. However, borrowing costs are clearly climbing. The European Central Bank raised its key rates twice in 2026, by 25 basis points in June and again in September. Consequently, the average rate on new loans to Greek businesses rose to 4.5% in August from 3.7% in December 2025. The report also points to sharply higher energy prices and inflation, which reached 3.8% in Greece in January–September. According to Powergame, the central bank flags two risks in particular: rising interest rates, and fast-rising property prices combined with accelerating mortgage lending. Neither threatens financial stability for now, but both could push more households and businesses into arrears. Still, with Greek banks profits holding up, the Bank of Greece concludes that the sector remains resilient. “Current challenges leave no room for complacency,” it said, urging banks to keep supporting investment and growth through new lending. title: €400 for Pensioners on 30 November: Who Gets It and Who Misses Out
body: Greece’s €400 pensioner payment is set to land on 30 November, with about 2.2 million people expected to receive it. However, not every pensioner qualifies. Here is a simple guide to the new rules. A permanent annual boost, not a one-off The payment is an annual support that Greece now pays every November. Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis announced the rise to €400 at the Thessaloniki International Fair (TIF) in September. By comparison, eligible pensioners received €250 last year, and in April 2026 the government had planned €300. The rules sit in Article 19 of a Ministry of National Economy and Finance bill containing the TIF support measures. The bill is in public consultation until 1 November, and the government aims to pass it in November, ERT reports . As a result, the details below reflect the draft law and could still change. Who qualifies for the €400 pensioner payment Under the bill, the following groups qualify: Pensioners aged 65 and over who received a main pension in September. For this first payment, they must have turned 65 by 31 December 2025. Pensioners aged 60 and over who receive only a survivor’s (widow’s) pension , without their own old-age pension. People with disabilities of any age who receive the relevant disability pensions or welfare benefits. Uninsured elderly people who receive the relevant OPEKA benefits. Crucially, there are no longer any income or property tests. Previously, a single pensioner earning more than €25,000 a year, or a couple earning more than €35,000, could miss out, according to Capital.gr. Property limits of €300,000 and €400,000 also applied. Now a retired couple who both qualify will receive €800 between them. Who misses out Two main groups will not receive the money this year: Old-age pensioners under 65 , unless they fall into one of the special categories above. Pensioners who turn 65 during 2026. Even someone who turned 65 in January 2026 misses out this time. Instead, they should receive the payment in November 2027. Critics say the age-only test creates new unfairness. For example, Newsit points out that a 70-year-old with an income of €30,000 will get the €400, while a 64-year-old pensioner on just €8,000 a year will not. When and how it is paid Labour Minister Niki Kerameus has said the €400 will be paid at the end of November, together with December pensions. The date given is 30 November, although the money may appear in bank accounts a few days earlier, depending on the official payment schedule. Importantly, nobody needs to apply for the €400 pensioner payment. The money goes automatically into recipients’ bank accounts, and e-EFKA will offer an online service to check eligibility. The amount is paid net, without tax or deductions. It also cannot be seized or offset against debts to the state, social security funds or banks. Moreover, anyone who fits more than one category receives the payment only once. What it costs Overall, the measure costs €879 million a year, according to figures reported by SKAI. Most of that, €712 million, goes to about 1.78 million pensioners aged over 65. title: Adnoc offers $16.3bn in manufacturing opportunities to UAE suppliers
body: Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (Adnoc) is offering more than Dh60 billion ($16.3 billion) in local manufacturing opportunities through 2030, as the state energy giant overhauls procurement to cut supplier onboarding time by as much as 80 per cent. The opportunities, covering more than 200 essential products and critical spare parts, were unveiled on Sunday at the second Make it with Adnoc Forum in Abu Dhabi, before the Adipec energy conference. The inaugural forum was held in May. Adnoc aims to replace imports with local production to shorten delivery times and reduce exposure to global supply disruptions. “We are inviting companies to build capabilities in the UAE that will serve our industry and country for years to come,” said Dr Sultan Al Jaber, Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology and managing director and group chief executive of Adnoc The push follows disruption to global energy supply chains, which has highlighted the importance of domestic manufacturing , said Omar Al Nuaimi, Adnoc’s group chief for commercial and in-country value (ICV). “It was our suppliers and vendors and partners who enabled us to continue pushing our products to the world and energy to the world,” he told the forum. Adnoc has already achieved Dh80 billion of its Dh90 billion local manufacturing target for 2030, supporting the localisation of more than 130 products and the establishment or expansion of 95 factories, Mr Al Nuaimi said. The latest opportunities span drilling equipment, electrical and automation systems, chemicals, catalysts, piping and heavy machinery. Products targeted for local production include electrical submersible pumps, oil country tubular goods, seamless pipes and compressors. “These are not 200 products only. These are opportunities, partnerships, industries, and a whole value chain,” Mr Al Nuaimi said. Adnoc is also simplifying how suppliers compete for contracts, aiming to shorten purchasing cycles by up to 40 per cent, halve documentation requirements and remove prequalification for 60 per cent of service categories. From November 1, commercial and ICV offers will be assessed together in a single evaluation weighted 70 per cent towards commercial terms and 30 per cent towards ICV. The change retires Adnoc’s previous bid-matching approach, encouraging suppliers to submit their most competitive offers from the outset. Contracts below Dh2 million will be exempt from ICV requirements, while those below Dh50 million will no longer face ICV retention obligations, said Salama Al Awadhi, Adnoc’s senior vice president for group commercial, ICV and industrial development. Supplier registration, previously taking weeks, can now be completed within a day, she said. Artificial intelligence will also be used to verify documents through a consolidated supplier platform. The revised procurement rules could have a wider impact across the UAE’s industrial supply chain, particularly among smaller companies working under major contractors, said Osama Fadhel, assistant undersecretary for industrial accelerators in the Ministry of Industry and Technology. Zero bureaucracy is in our DNA today Osama Amir Fadhel, Ministry of Industry and Technology In an interview with The National , he said the 30 per cent local-content weighting would create a “ripple effect” through the energy sector and could serve as a model for other major buyers. “Zero bureaucracy is in our DNA today,” Mr Al Fadhel said, describing how efforts to automate government services are spreading to private and state-linked businesses. The national ICV programme has redirected more than Dh473 billion into the UAE economy, including Dh126 billion last year, and created 28,000 jobs for Emiratis, he said in his address to the forum. Adnoc’s own programme has redirected more than Dh307 billion since 2018, with its annual contribution reaching Dh65 billion in 2025, up from Dh18 billion in its first year. The company is working with the ministry, Abu Dhabi Investment Office and other partners to connect manufacturers with investment opportunities and financing through the National Industrial Resilience Fund. It also expanded its Local+ programme to more than 100 UAE manufacturers, from 70 at its launch in May, requiring contractors bidding on new projects to source eligible products from approved local suppliers. Abu Dhabi Oilfield Services Company, which participated in the inaugural Make it with Adnoc Forum in May, has doubled its UAE manufacturing capacity since the ICV programme began eight years ago and now exports globally from Abu Dhabi, said Mazen Shehada, its director of business development. He said the latest changes would make it easier for manufacturers to access Adnoc’s procurement pipeline, while giving them greater certainty over future demand. “With their offtake agreements, they’re giving us a commitment to enable us to invest more and be able to be confident in our investments,” Mr Shehada told The National .

title: ‘Trump Is Cooked’: Republicans Clash Over Ukraine as Midterms Loom
body:
“I think Trump is cooked in the midterms, unless literally every poll is disgustingly wrong.”
This assessment came from a Republican-adjacent Washington source speaking to Kyiv Post on condition of anonymity as US President Donald Trump’s handling of Russia’s war against Ukraine draws unusually public criticism from his own party.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“I don’t think [Trump’s] efforts to scapegoat Ukraine will make that worse, but he’s also not getting away with it,” the source added. The latest sentiment comes on the heels of Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff traveling to St. Petersburg to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin for a new round of negotiations, during which he referred to Putin as a “humanitarian” . Meanwhile, Russian forces continued attacking Ukrainian cities and Kyiv reported restricted access to satellite communications essential to frontline operations and intercepting Russian drones.
For Republican commentators and politicians who had spent months pushing the Trump administration to increase pressure on Moscow, this was an unpleasant sight. They found themselves watching the US offer Russia economic relief while pressing Ukraine for concessions and restricting its defense capabilities.
Beyond immediate moral discomfort and questions on Washington’s foreign policy priorities, there’s also the practical aspect as they seek re-election during the Nov. 3 midterms. With all 435 House seats and roughly a third of the Senate contested, the Republican party’s chances of preserving a majority in both chambers risks slipping away as Trump’s approval rating continues to plunge.
In late July, conservative MAGA commentator Laura Loomer made headlines. Formerly a fierce critic of Ukraine, she traveled to Kyiv to interview President Volodymyr Zelensky , publicly acknowledging that she had repeated Russian propaganda before realizing Moscow’s support for Iran in its confrontation with Israel and the US – a circumstance that helped change her position.
This is how she became part of an emerging pro-Ukraine conservative camp alongside figures such as Ben Shapiro, who had also interviewed Zelensky, as well as Mark Levin and other prominent Trump-adjacent commentators.
For a country often presented to some Republican audiences as a burden on American taxpayers, this was a significant opening and a promising one as well, since the renewed enthusiasm reinforced the case for the sanctions championed by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham . The logic was that if Russia would not agree to a ceasefire or a negotiated end to the war, it should face a heavier economic cost for continuing the invasion.
The momentum bore fruit: Congress passed the bill, and Trump signed it into law on Sept. 18. Key provisions were due to take effect by Oct. 18 , although the legislation also gave the president broad waiver powers.
Yet what appeared to be a breakthrough soon became a full-fledged retreat.
Instead of imposing those additional penalties, Trump abruptly announced his diesel agreement with Moscow on Oct. 9 .
A week later, he waived major new sanctions and duties under the Graham legislation (though leaving existing sanctions in place) and launched what Susan B. Glasser of The New Yorker coined as a pre-election campaign against Zelensky , toward whom his antipathy is long documented.
Trump blamed Ukraine’s refinery attacks for aggravating fuel shortages and suggested that a settlement would require different Ukrainian leadership, while thanking Putin for presumably being “the reasonable one” in the illegal war he started.
This time, however, the pressure went beyond personal attacks: intelligence sharing, satellite access and weapons deliveries had become part of the dispute, accompanied by a considerably more Moscow-friendly rhetoric than in spring when the US resorted to similar ways of pressuring the victim of Russia’s aggression.
Glasser’s description of Trump’s actions might be easy for his supporters to dismiss as criticism from a familiar opponent. The reaction from Republicans themselves, however, was harder to explain away with freshly-converted Loomer saying : “Buying Russian oil puts money back into the coffers of the Islamic regime of Iran that chants Death to America. We know this.”
While disagreements with Zelensky, including concerns about corruption and oversight, were not unusual for many Republicans, restricting Ukraine’s ability to defend itself while offering economic relief to Russia was another.
“What is interesting is that his recent, unveiled support for Putin has finally seen some anger from Congressional Republicans,” the source told Kyiv Post, warning that some of them “are leaving office.”
Reacting to Witkoff’s salute to Putin in St. Petersburg as a “humanitarian” for releasing American detainee Stephen Hubbard , another Republican-adjacent source privately told Kyiv Post: “I so hate Witkoff.”
The anger, however, was not limited to private conversations. Republican Sen. Thom Tillis responded in very strong terms to Witkoff’s flattery, asking:: “WTF, Steve?” Separately, Sen. John Cornyn described Putin as a “stone cold killer.”
Hours after the meeting, Russia launched another attack on Kyiv.
The backlash followed strong objections to the privately-struck diesel deal. Tillis, Susan Collins and Mitch McConnell joined a bipartisan letter urging Trump to reverse the agreement , arguing that it would offer limited relief to American consumers while supplying revenue to Moscow.
Republican Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, standing for reelection in Pennsylvania’s 1st Congressional District pursued legislation to block Russian energy purchases . European governments also rejected following Washington’s lead on sanctions relief .
Then came the reports of restrictions on intelligence and satellite communications that only served to intensify the tensions on Capitol Hill.
Zelensky said on Oct. 20 that US intelligence sharing had resumed . Satellite access took longer to improve: restrictions on SpaceX’s Starlink and defense-tailored Starshield services had disrupted connections on fast-moving equipment, including Ukrainian drones.
On Oct. 24, Ukrainian defense specialists reported that terminals were operating above the previous 161 km/h limit . Later that morning, Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara reported stable connections above 400 km/h .
But Patriot interceptor deliveries remained delayed , according to Zelensky’s remarks reported that day. Restored intelligence and communications did not resolve the shortage of missiles needed to intercept Russian attacks.
For Republicans seeking re-election, these developments leave an awkward question to answer: what has Washington attained by this and how it does affect them?
Despite the existing notion among some that the Republicans are Russia-friendly, the evidence paints a different picture.
Earlier Pew polling found that 47% of Republicans regarded Russia as an enemy. Across Americans, 83% viewed Russia unfavorably.
The real partisan Ukraine disagreement lies in two distinct domains: US budgetary and culture wars. The former comes down to the idea of spending and how it affects the average person’s ability to fulfill the basic American idea of buying a home, which, unlike today, used to be a largely affordable endeavor.
The latter is more poignantly about which way American society should be heading: toward a more secular group with the progressive agenda dominating the mainstream view, or the opposite.
Ukraine got trapped in both as it needs money from an already heavily indebted society and the idea, often spread by Russian propagandists and other malign agents, that it’s a Democratic stronghold of progressive thought .
Both affect the Republican stance toward Kyiv, even if they view Ukraine’s resistance as a legitimate fight at large, which is reflected in the Republican polling ahead of the looming midterms.
University of Maryland surveys , conducted between July 21 and Aug. 17, found Republican majorities supporting continued military assistance to Ukraine in 31 of 39 battleground states and congressional districts surveyed.
The question covered equipment, ammunition, training and intelligence — including capabilities subsequently drawn into October’s disputes.
To understand what that means practically for Republicans, beyond the question of why deal with Putin in the first place, requires consideration of what House members must do when they return to their districts: explain not only why they supported or opposed a particular bill, but also the direction of their party’s policies.
This is what happened to Ukraine-born Republican Rep. Victoria Spartz who encountered an angry crowd at a March 2025 town hall in Indiana , where questions about Ukraine accompanied criticism of federal spending cuts and other Trump policies.
Republican lawmakers thus face a two-sided task. On the one hand, attacking their party’s leader risks alienating his supporters. On the other hand, defending him without qualification means explaining policies that some of their own constituents oppose – including what Kyiv Post’s source described as “unveiled support for Putin.”
Nor can they simply rely on the “Trump effect,” hoping his endorsement will improve their prospects: A New York Times/Siena survey released on Oct. 21 put Trump’s approval at 36%, against 59% disapproval. Approval of his handling of the cost of living stood at 29%; on gas prices, it was 24%.
Even if candidates can persuade their core supporters that the diesel deal, admittedly, supported by over 50% of the Republican voters, was necessary, winning a competitive election requires more than securing the loyalty of the core base.
In majoritarian systems, which operate on the “winner takes it all” principle, candidates also need voters who are not reliably behind their party. That includes swing voters and independents, although the two groups are not interchangeable.
Here is where Republicans face less encouraging news.
Independents opposed the diesel deal by 71% to 10% , while opposition among all respondents stood at 63%.
“The diesel fuel deal does almost nothing to help diesel prices, but it does damage Republicans politically. Trump needs Independents to vote Republican,” Steven Moore recently wrote .
Moore is a former Republican congressional chief of staff and founder of the Ukraine Freedom Project, which has worked to build conservative support for Kyiv.
Depending on how much weight these voters give foreign policy, their dissatisfaction could help Democratic candidates or weaken Republican turnout. The survey does not measure whether the deal will change their votes, but the gap between Republican and independent opinion is substantial and cannot be ignored.
They could still vote Republican for other reasons, from economic policy to cultural issues.
Or, they could opt for a Democrat if they choose to show at the polling stations at all, given that fewer than half of eligible Americans voted in recent midterms .
If there’s anything to learn from Trump’s handling of electoral defeats, it’s that he strongly rules out such possibilities per se. This is why the recent actions aimed at preparing to contest the outcome if they’re not favorable to the Republican Party should be taken into consideration – even if they do not result in substantial practical and societal repercussions.
Yet any hope in Kyiv, or in some European capitals, that a Democratic victory would automatically restore generous and predictable funding, would be misplaced.
Ukraine appears to have a difficult time navigating the American political landscape and how to approach it – an impression stemming from Zelensky’s former right-hand man Andriy Yermak’s confession that he does not wish to understand Washington’s political ins and outs. He’s resigned due to alleged involvement in a large-scale corruption scandal .
The former US Ambassador Oksana Markarova’s perceived Democratic sympathies coupled with the corruption allegations involving her recently-resigned successor Olha Stefanishyna and today’s absence of a newly-appointed ambassador further complicate Kyiv’s positions on Capitol Hill, which bears little resemblance to its 2022 version when both the Democrats and the Republicans voted in favor of providing aid to Ukraine.
What would change more immediately if the Democrats take over is the political pressure on the administration.
If Democrats take the House, they would be positioned to replace Mike Johnson as speaker, control committees and pursue investigations. Ukraine would almost certainly feature in that confrontation, as Kyiv Post’s source predicts: “Democrats with both houses will be launching a salvo of investigations and even impeachment hearings. Trump’s nonsense toward Ukraine will definitely be part of that.”
In fact, the scrutiny of the administration’s decisions is already underway.
On Oct. 22, Sen. Richard Blumenthal announced an inquiry into restrictions on Starlink and Starshield , seeking information from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Musk about who authorized the changes and how they were implemented.
The inquiry also examines the Pentagon’s dependence on SpaceX and whether US forces could face similar disruptions. Restoring Ukraine’s access does not settle who restricted it or why.
A Democratic House would give those investigations greater institutional backing, including control over hearing agendas and the pursuit of documents and testimony. The sanctions waivers and diesel agreement would offer further subjects for scrutiny.
But scrutiny and the reversal of current aid-absent policy aren’t identical endeavors.
Some Democrats, like Ilhan Omar voted against Graham’s sanctions , and even if Democrats initiate another Ukraine aid package, or if Fitzpatrick-initiate bipartisan Ukraine Support Act, which passed the House on June 4 and proposed additional assistance for Kyiv alongside sanctions against Russia, appears on the Senate floor with enough “yays,” it would still need Trump’s signature.
Little suggests that the man who thanks Putin, has his envoy call him a humanitarian, and floats 200% tariffs on both Ukraine and Russia to force them into a peace deal, will do just that.
The views expressed in this opinion article are the author’s and not necessarily those of Kyiv Post.
Lesia Dubenko is a Ukrainian political scientist and analyst. A graduate of Lund University (MSc in European Affairs), she covers issues relating to international affairs, migration, and disinformation.

title: Falakro Villages: Rivers, Lakes and Stone Lanes in Drama
body: The Falakro villages, spread across the slopes of a 2,232-metre mountain, pair stone houses and old customs with rivers, lakes and forest. Mount Falakro ranks among the most beautiful mountains in Greece, rising above Drama . Its slopes hold abandoned settlements, marble quarries and alpine meadows full of wild orchids, crocuses, thyme and primroses. Pine, oak, chestnut and beech cover its forested sides. Rare butterflies live here, while wild horses graze freely higher up. You can start from Prosotsani, Petrousa or the city of Drama. Still, it pays to stay in the Falakro villages perched on the slopes rather than those at the foot. Volakas, a base for the Falakro villages Among the Falakro villages, Volakas makes the best base for a tour of the mountain. Built at 830 metres, it greets visitors with pigs, hens, cows and horses near its entrance. Don’t expect a picture-postcard village like Papingo. Instead, this is an authentic farming community, with stone houses, lanes and marble quarries just outside. On its shady, slightly raised square stands the old church of Profitis Ilias, a timber-roofed basilica from 1841. Since a new church went up next door, it rarely opens, so ask the priest to let you in. At Epiphany, Volakas comes alive with the Arapides custom , when men blacken their faces and wear bells and animal skins. It revives an old Dionysian ritual. Later, at the feast of the Holy Spirit, riders and walkers carry the Holy Trinity icon up to the chapel of Agios Pnevma. A feast on the mountain follows, and a summer music festival also keeps Volakas lively. Riverside calm around Potamoi The Falakro ski centre lies 15 kilometres from Volakas. On the north side, about 17 kilometres away, Potamoi sits beside the Nestos River with views of the snowy summit. Until the 19th century, Greeks and Turks lived here together, and two or three Ottoman-style houses survive. Below spreads a lake formed by the Nestos and the Despatis River behind the Thisavros dam . First, though, head 3 kilometres north to the chapel of Agios Rafail, among towering plane trees, hornbeams, elms and alders. Here the Despatis meets the Maloustas stream. Sit on the bench on the small wooden bridge and listen to the water. Then follow the trail to the Maloustas waterfall, another enchanting corner of the Falakro villages. Pagoneri and the trails of Granitis Heading west, you reach Pagoneri, once called Tseresovo, an amphitheatre-shaped listed traditional settlement. Like other Falakro villages, it works as a balcony facing the mountain. Its raised church of the Presentation of the Theotokos also overlooks the square. Below it, a café serves as the information office and even knows who holds the key to a small folklore collection. South-west of Volakas, at 760 metres, Granitis sits among beech, chestnut, fir, walnut and hazel trees. A stone fountain marks its centre, and its tavernas often sell local beans, because Drama is famous for them. From the village church of the Taxiarches, a trail enters dense forest, stopping first at the chapel of the Panagia. In addition, Granitis offers about 30 kilometres of waymarked paths. Each year it also hosts the Granitis Trail, with 21-kilometre and 9-kilometre routes plus a children’s course. No wonder walkers love this corner of the Falakro villages. Fort Lisse and Lake Lefkogeia Ten minutes west, the village of Ochyro guards Fort Lisse, the largest fort of the Metaxas Line in the area. Set inside a granite rock at 771 metres, its galleries hold living quarters, an infirmary and ammunition stores. Straight north lies Kato Nevrokopi , the main village. Although it isn’t especially pretty, it has banks, shops and good tavernas. Stock up on beans and the famous potatoes of Nevrokopi here. From there, a road leads to Lefkogeia, whose charming artificial lake is a highlight near the Falakro villages. Holding back two streams that once flooded the plateau created it, and it now covers about 90 hectares. You can walk or cycle its 14-kilometre perimeter among pines, willows and poplars. Storks, cormorants, grey herons and moorhens also feed in its waters. Taxiarches and the road back to Volakas On the southern foothills, tiny Taxiarches is famous for the Holy Monastery of the Ascension of the Saviour. Elder Georgios Karslidis, the newest recognised saint of the Orthodox Church in Greece, founded it in 1930. Most of the monastery went up gradually from 1970, but the original small church still stands at its heart. The sparse, green village suits anyone seeking quiet, like all the Falakro villages. Further north, Dendrakia looks like a ghost village, with only a handful of residents. However, its lively cultural association joins nearby Livadero for chestnut-gathering walks. Livadero, at 647 metres, suffered during the Bulgarian occupation and later the civil war. Before the war, it served as a summer resort for the people of Drama. From Livadero, a road runs about 8 kilometres north to Lake Thisavros on the Nestos. Then cross the Papades bridge and climb to Sidironero, known for its mushrooms. To return, the best route back to Volakas runs through Livadero and Taxiarches. You can also split your stay between Volakas or Granitis and Taxiarches to explore both sides of the Falakro villages.
