title: The College of Magic turns ordinary kids into confident, top-hat wearing magicians
body:
Lubelo Mthenjana, who's 11, performs a magic trick involving fire during the annual junior magic contest at the College of Magic in Cape Town, South Africa. Tommy Trenchard for NPR hide caption
Dressed in a sharp black three-piece suit and a dapper yellow bow tie, Lubelo Mthenjana stands alone on a dark stage, taking in the last few seconds of quiet before the curtain opens. He takes a deep breath as his name is announced. Then he opens his arms wide and flashes a bright smile.
"Hello everyone! My name is Lubelo Mthenjana, and I will be performing for you … some magic!"
The audience of about 30 children and parents is spellbound. They laugh out loud as he makes a string of paper clips vanish into a plastic cup and gasp with surprise as the clips reappear inside a matchbox. Then comes his best trick: He conjures sweets out of thin air and tosses them into the crowd. The room erupts. As Lubelo takes his final bow to thunderous applause, his mom beams a proud smile at the 11-year-old apprentice magician.
On this cloudy Saturday morning in September, Cape Town's College of Magic is buzzing with energy as dozens of students are competing in the annual junior magic contest. Heading to their classrooms, children in top hats, crisp white shirts and ties dash up and down a staircase decorated with a riot of brightly colored posters. On every floor, display cabinets overflow with magic wands, sparkly hats, silk scarves, handcuffs, dice, Rubik's Cubes, toys, photographs and dozens of trophies earned by students in competitions all over the world.
Students examine a set of trick playing cards during a class at the College of Magic, whose pupils are ages 10 to 18. Tommy Trenchard for NPR hide caption
Aspiring magician Sibabalwe Sibaj, 17, juggles while riding a unicycle. Tommy Trenchard for NPR hide caption
Outside the old red-brick Victorian mansion, framed by palm trees, two teenage boys zip around the car park on unicycles. Balls, clubs and diabolos shoot up into the air as a handful of kids practice juggling on the porch.
Tucked away in a peaceful suburb, this extraordinary school is a real-world Hogwarts: Africa's only school for youthful stage magicians and illusionists. Every Saturday morning, about 190 starry-eyed students ages 10 to 18 attend classes in everything from puppetry, mime and clowning to juggling, card tricks, illusions, mentalism, stage magic, theater production and escapology. "All the skills that will make a good magician," sums up David Gore, the school's founder.
In 1980, Gore was studying law and paying his way by performing at private magic shows when he and a friend came up with the idea of starting a magic school.
David Gore founded the Cape Town College of Magic in 1980, defying apartheid era laws by teaching multiracial classes. In the decades since, the college has trained thousands of magicians, illusionists and performers. Tommy Trenchard for NPR hide caption
"We walked into our local newspaper house with our top hats and tails, told our story about how we were starting the College of Magic, did magic for the journalists in the newsroom, and they published an article," he recalls. "From that article, we had 34 young people who started attending formal weekly classes studying magic."
At the time, South Africa was still in the grip of apartheid, a brutal system of racial segregation that dictated almost every aspect of daily life. State schools were strictly segregated. Students of different races could not even share park benches, some building entrances or take the same public transport to school. Yet the College of Magic was multiracial from day one.
The College of Magic Students are entranced by a class on close-up magic. Tommy Trenchard for NPR hide caption
"When we started out, our organization was illegal," says Gore, referring to its no-segregation policy. "This was an opportunity for young people from all backgrounds to come together around a common interest in magic, to learn about each other and understand each other."
Nearly 50 years later, the school continues to stand out in a city still deeply divided along racial and economic lines.
"Many of our young people remain siloed in their socioeconomic groups, very often along either language or racial lines," Gore explains. "Some arrive in very fancy cars, others have taken an hour in a collective taxi to get here. But when they're here, they work with the same equipment, the same classes, the same stages and get the same food."
Though the six-year course costs a fee, about 80% of the students cannot afford to pay and are sponsored, mostly through private donations.
How do you master the arts of juggling and spinning plates? Practice, practice, practice. Tommy Trenchard for NPR hide caption
"Magic is such a wonderful companion for our young people here in South Africa," says Gore. "They're able to carry it in their pockets, into the communities and the marginalized areas where most of our students come from. It's an art form that can be performed without being wealthy or needing very expensive instruments."
Multiple studies have found that learning magic can help children develop self-esteem, curiosity, lateral thinking, fine motor skills and problem-solving abilities. A 2021 study conducted by researchers at the Universities of Hertfordshire and Edinburgh found that children who learned and performed a magic trick showed greater improvements in creative fluency and originality than those who completed a similar art activity.
Themba Van der Westhuizen, 12, practices a magic trick on a schoolmate at the College of Magic. Van der Westhuizen says he enjoys impressing friends and family with his tricks and that learning to become a magician has boosted his self-confidence. Tommy Trenchard for NPR hide caption
Even watching a magic trick can challenge our assumptions about the world and stimulate more original thinking. In another study, researchers found that it stimulated areas of the brain associated with cognitive flexibility and processing unconventional information.
In this photo from 2021, Anele Dyasi, a former student and now teacher of at the College of Magic, reaches out to a white dove at the school's dove enclosure. The college has since stopped using animals in its performances. Tommy Trenchard for NPR hide caption
"Many of our graduates don't become performers or magicians. But one of the skills that this young generation is most going to need for their careers is creativity," adds Gore. "That is what's so fantastic about magic: Nothing's impossible for us."
For 11-year-old Lubelo, magic has "opened up a new world." After watching a family friend perform a trick, he was determined to join the College of Magic. He had to wait until he turned 10 to enroll. Now, he's hooked.
At home in Makhaza township, about 40 minutes from the college, Lubelo spends his free time watching magic shows online and practicing tricks on his brothers and parents. He keeps his props, tools and other secrets in a box hidden away in his room. He's even chosen a stage name: Spade Boy — after his favorite card suit.
Aspiring magician Lubelo Mthenjana is clearly the family star as they stand outside their home in the Khayelitsha neighborhood of Cape Town. Tommy Trenchard for NPR hide caption
"If my mom is cooking and asks me to pass the potatoes, I'll start juggling with them," he says mischievously.
Lubelo has also persuaded several friends to join the school, becoming something of an ambassador in a community where magic is often frowned upon and associated with witchcraft.
"Many people are afraid of magic. But at the College of Magic, we don't do dark magic," he explains. "We just do the kind of magic that makes somebody smile, makes them happy and takes the stress away."
Sometimes, he says, other children ask whether he can turn people into pigs. "Then I just say: 'Let me start with you!' and they run away," he laughs.
Lubelo's mother, Yandiswa, says the magic lessons have boosted her son's confidence. They have brought another kind of relief, too. "It keeps him occupied and away from this environment and everything that's happening outside," she says.
With nearly 60 murders per day, South Africa has one of the world's highest crime rates, and several of Cape Town's townships are among the areas hardest hit by violent crime. From his home in Makhaza, Lubelo often hears gunshots. He says boys his age are drawn into using and selling drugs.
The magic community hasn't been spared. Just a few weeks before our visit, the school held a memorial service for Duma Mgqoki, a promising young magician, former student and volunteer teacher who was killed in a shooting in July. He was 22.
In this photo from 2021, Duma Mgqoki tries his hand at a card trick at the Cape Town College of Magic. In 2026, Mgqoki was killed in a shooting in the Philippi neighborhood of Cape Town. Many of the College's students come from neighborhoods marked by unemployment and violent crime. Tommy Trenchard for NPR hide caption
"On a weekly basis, some of our young people come to us saying they've experienced crime on a firsthand basis," says David Gore. "These things need to change, and we're very hopeful that the younger generation of today are going to be the force of change to bring about the society which we all would like to live in."
Students from the Cape Town College of Magic do their magic trick homework in the Mfuleni neighborhood where they live. Tommy Trenchard for NPR hide caption
Back at the college, after finishing his show, Lubelo steps off the stage to a chorus of fist bumps and backslaps from his excited friends.
"He was so good! We're swimming in happiness!" one teenager beams. Without skipping a beat, the boys run outside, pick up colorful leather balls and launch into a juggling competition.
Lubelo Mthenjana begins his performance during the annual junior magic contest at the College of Magic. Spoiler alert: He won in his age class! Tommy Trenchard for NPR hide caption
By now, a light drizzle has set in, but the two unicyclists are still making their rounds in the car park, seemingly undeterred. "Even when the storm comes, even when the world ends, I'll never stop unicycling," declares 14-year-old Joshua Clyde as he whizzes past.
Inside the cafeteria, a wide-eyed crowd has gathered around a teacher showing off a magic trick. With a snap of his fingers and what seems like a touch of superhuman power, he makes a coin disappear from a student's closed fist. It reappears beneath the student's watch.
Others have opted for the puppeteering class, upstairs, where pairs of students are taught to bring their humanoid puppets to life.
Puppets are part of the curriculum at the College of Magic. Teacher Jesse Brooks shares his puppet mastery with 12-year-old Okuhle Ntshutshe. Tommy Trenchard for NPR hide caption
Footsteps drum up and down the staircase as the remaining performers in this Saturday competition rehearse their routines, nerves and excitement mounting. "Why am I so nervous? I've got this!" says bubbly Kungentando Ndenetya, 12, repeating the mantra to herself.
Aspiring magician Kungentanda Ndenetya performs during the annual junior magic contest at the Cape Town College of Magic. Tommy Trenchard for NPR hide caption
Once every child has performed, the jury retires to a quiet office to deliberate. All four judges are former students or teachers at the College of Magic. Twenty-five-year-old Caitlin Hutchison, who comes from "a long line of magicians," says the school taught her "resilience training." Monica Nyakatya graduated in 2009 and now works in logistics but has remained close to the institution that, she says, "shaped" her.
The judges at the annual junior magic contest applaud after a performance at the College of Magic in Cape Town, South Africa. Tommy Trenchard for NPR hide caption
The deliberations are strictly confidential. When the judges return, everyone gathers in the small theater. The young magicians hold hands, waiting anxiously as the results are announced. Then comes Lubelo's age group.
Prestidigitation pupil Lubelo Mthenjana adjusts his bow tie. Many of the College's students sport traditional magician attire like bow ties and top hats. Tommy Trenchard for NPR hide caption
Beaming, he strides onto the stage to shake each judge's hand — then runs into his mother's arms.
As soon as he gets home, he will practice his newest tricks.
For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.
Julie Bourdin is a freelance journalist based in South Africa and France. She covers human rights and climate-related stories across Africa and beyond.
Tommy Trenchard is an independent photojournalist based in Cape Town, South Africa. He has previously contributed photos and stories to NPR on the Mozambique cyclone of 2019, Indonesian death rituals and illegal miners in abandoned South African diamond mines and won a World Press Photo prize for the images in his story for NPR on clashes between elephants and people in Zambia.
NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.

title: 2027: Engaging APC data boys, insult to my integrity — Pat Utomi
body: A chieftain of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Professor Pat Utomi, has described engaging social media users he accused of being All Progressives Congress (APC) supporters paid to troll critics as an insult to his integrity. Utomi said the users began attacking him after he raised concerns about the living and working conditions of Nigerian soldiers, whom he said were poorly paid despite risking their lives to protect the country. In a post on X on Sunday, the economist alleged that some of those who criticised him were APC supporters benefiting from what he described as “stomach infrastructure”. “Yesterday, we talked about the poor living and working conditions of Nigerian soldiers compared to their counterparts in the US, and how senators are fattening their pockets with billions of naira while the soldiers who risk their lives every day to protect us are underpaid heavily,” he wrote. He said some social media users attacked him after he raised the issue, prompting him to examine their profiles. “Then, some fellows benefiting from stomach infrastructure began to bash us. I took a quick look at their profiles, and it became obvious to me that they were APC data boys trolling anyone who dared to speak up,” Utomi said. He added that he would not engage with the accounts, saying, “Engaging with any of them is an insult to my integrity.” In a separate post, Utomi also accused APC politicians of attempting to intimidate Nigerians ahead of the 2027 general election. He said Nigerians should not allow such actions to discourage them from participating in the electoral process. “We have seen videos of APC politicians trying to intimidate Nigerians ahead of the 2027 general elections,” he wrote. Utomi urged Nigerians to unite and resist what he described as attempts to instil fear ahead of the polls. “Nigerians need to understand that these fellows are powerless when we stand united. Do not allow them to sow seeds of fear in you,” he said. He also called on voters to participate in the election and protect the integrity of their votes. “Come out, vote, and defend your votes,” Utomi added. title: 2026 Ballon d’or ceremony: date, time and how to watch
body: Football fans around the world are preparing for the 2026 Ballon d’Or ceremony, which will take place on Monday, October 26, in London, England. The 70th edition of the prestigious football awards will bring together leading players, coaches and other figures in the game as organisers announce the winners of the men’s and women’s Ballon d’Or and other individual and team awards. For the first time in the award’s history, the ceremony will be held outside Paris, with the London Palladium selected as the venue in a tribute to Sir Stanley Matthews, the inaugural winner of the men’s Ballon d’Or in 1956. Here is everything you need to know about the date, start time and how to watch the 2026 Ballon d’Or ceremony live. When is the 2026 Ballon d’Or ceremony? The 2026 Ballon d’Or ceremony will take place on Monday, October 26, 2026 , at the London Palladium in London. The main ceremony is scheduled to begin at 8 p.m. UK time , with the red-carpet arrivals and interviews expected to start earlier in the evening. The event is expected to run until approximately 10 p.m. UK time, followed by a press conference featuring the winners. What time does the Ballon d’Or ceremony start in Nigeria? For viewers in Nigeria, the main ceremony is scheduled to begin at 9 p.m. West Africa Time (WAT) on Monday, October 26. The event’s schedule in selected locations is as follows: Nigeria: 9 p.m. WAT United Kingdom: 8 p.m. BST The red-carpet coverage in London is scheduled to begin at 6 p.m. UK time, giving fans an opportunity to follow the arrival of nominees and other guests before the main ceremony. How to watch the 2026 Ballon d’Or ceremony live Football fans can follow the ceremony through the official Ballon d’Or website and its designated broadcast partners. The official Ballon d’Or website will also provide live updates, ceremony information, statistics and results. Who are the favourites for the 2026 Ballon d’Or? England captain Harry Kane and Barcelona forward Lamine Yamal are among the leading contenders for the men’s award. Kane is seeking to become the first Englishman to win the men’s Ballon d’Or since Michael Owen in 2001, while Yamal is hoping to claim the prestigious individual honour after another notable campaign with Barcelona. Other prominent nominees include defending champion Ousmane Dembélé of Paris Saint-Germain, Real Madrid forward Kylian Mbappé and Manchester City striker Erling Haaland. The men’s shortlist also features Lionel Messi, an eight-time winner of the award, alongside several other leading players from European and international football. In the women’s category, Barcelona midfielder Alexia Putellas is among the nominees seeking to add to her previous Ballon d’Or Féminin victories. The award will recognise the standout performer in women’s football over the relevant assessment period. What other awards will be presented? In addition to the men’s and women’s Ballon d’Or, the ceremony will recognise achievements across several categories. These include the Kopa Trophy for young players, the Yashin Trophy for goalkeepers, the Johan Cruyff Trophy for coaches, the Gerd Müller Trophy for goalscorers and the Club of the Year awards. The ceremony will also feature the Sócrates Award, which recognises football-related solidarity initiatives and contributions to social causes. With the event marking the 70th anniversary of the Ballon d’Or, this year’s ceremony is expected to attract considerable attention as the football world gathers in London to celebrate individual and collective achievements from the 2025–26 season. title: Can the media announce election results before INEC’s official declaration?, By Samson Itodo
body:
…media organisations can responsibly share and aggregate officially announced results as part of their public information role, but they must be careful not to present such reporting as a final declaration of the election outcome. Until INEC officially declares and returns a winner, all reported figures should be understood as part of an ongoing results management process.
To address this issue, it is important to understand the election results management process. Election results are first announced at the polling unit level and immediately made public through verbal declaration and the posting of result sheets. The purpose of this public announcement is to promote transparency. Once results are announced at the polling unit, they become public information.
Furthermore, the introduction of the INEC Result Viewing Portal (IReV) was designed to deepen transparency in the electoral process. The objective is to make results accessible to citizens and stakeholders, enabling them to follow the results management process, while reducing opportunities for manipulation during collation. In that context, the media can report results that have already been officially announced at polling units because those results are already in the public domain.
This is particularly important given the widespread concerns and distrust surrounding the results management process. Historically, the collation stage has often been viewed as the weakest link in the electoral process and the point at which political actors may seek to compromise outcomes. Media and citizen oversight therefore serve several important purposes:
INEC is the constitutional authority empowered to declare election results and return a candidate as duly elected. Declaration goes beyond publishing polling unit outcomes; it is the formal legal pronouncement that a candidate has won an election and has been returned as the winner. Until INEC makes that declaration, no candidate can legally be regarded as having won the election.
At the same time, it is important to distinguish between announcing results and declaring a winner . INEC is the constitutional authority empowered to declare election results and return a candidate as duly elected. Declaration goes beyond publishing polling unit outcomes; it is the formal legal pronouncement that a candidate has won an election and has been returned as the winner. Until INEC makes that declaration, no candidate can legally be regarded as having won the election.
However, reporting or aggregating results that have already been officially announced at polling units does not amount to declaring a winner. The media may report and analyse such publicly available results, provided this is done responsibly, accurately, and within established professional and ethical standards. That said, media organisations must remain conscious of the realities of the results management process. During collation, several factors can affect the final outcome. INEC may cancel results where there is confirmed over-voting, while adjustments may also arise from polling units where elections did not hold, were postponed, or were disrupted by violence or other incidents. These considerations are taken into account during the collation process and can ultimately influence the final results.
For instance, there are constitutional thresholds that candidates must satisfy before they can be declared and returned as winners. It is therefore possible for election results to be announced without an immediate declaration and return of a winner, if those constitutional requirements have not been met. In presidential and governorship elections, for example, the Constitution requires not only that a candidate secure the highest number of lawful votes cast, but also that s/he obtain at least 25 per cent of the votes cast in no fewer than two-thirds of the states in a presidential election, or two-thirds of the local government areas in a governorship election.
The publication of false, inaccurate, or misleading results can undermine public trust and attract legitimate institutional sanctions. However, where the media responsibly reports and analyses results that have already been officially announced by INEC, such reporting enhances transparency, strengthens public oversight, and contributes to democratic accountability without encroaching on INEC’s exclusive constitutional mandate to declare and return a winner.
Determining whether these conditions have been satisfied requires a comprehensive assessment of the final collated results, a responsibility that rests exclusively with INEC. This underscores the distinction between reporting results and declaring a winner. While the media may responsibly share and aggregate results that have already been officially announced at polling unit, ward, local government, and state levels, only INEC has the constitutional authority to determine whether all legal thresholds have been met and to formally declare and return a candidate as the winner of an election.
This is precisely why all actors, including the media, should avoid declaring winners before INEC completes the collation process and makes its official declaration. Reporting results that have already been announced by INEC at the polling unit, ward, local government, or state level is entirely different from declaring an electoral outcome. The former promotes transparency and public oversight, while the latter remains the exclusive constitutional responsibility of INEC.
Therefore, media organisations can responsibly share and aggregate officially announced results as part of their public information role, but they must be careful not to present such reporting as a final declaration of the election outcome. Until INEC officially declares and returns a winner, all reported figures should be understood as part of an ongoing results management process. Ultimately, all actors, including the media, civil society organisations, and observers, must operate in accordance with the principles of integrity, professionalism, accuracy, and ethical conduct.
The publication of false, inaccurate, or misleading results can undermine public trust and attract legitimate institutional sanctions. However, where the media responsibly reports and analyses results that have already been officially announced by INEC, such reporting enhances transparency, strengthens public oversight, and contributes to democratic accountability without encroaching on INEC’s exclusive constitutional mandate to declare and return a winner.
Samson Itodo is an election, democracy, and public policy enthusiast. Itodo serves as the Executive Director of Yiaga Africa, Principal Partner of the Election Law Center and Chairperson of the African Union Advisory Group on AI in Peace, Security and Governance. He is also a member of the Kofi Annan Foundation board and the Board of Advisers of the International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance (IDEA).

title: Bookworm urges schools to embrace extracurricular activities to develop pupils’ talents
body: The Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of Bookworm, Nelson Kofi Poku, has urged parents and teachers to encourage children to participate in extracurricular activities to help them develop their talents and improve their chances of accessing educational opportunities. He said academic performance in the classroom alone was no longer sufficient to prepare children for the opportunities available in an increasingly competitive world. Speaking on the sidelines of the Bookworm Greater Accra Season 13 grand finale on Saturday, October 24, Mr Poku said educational competitions and other public activities provided platforms for children to demonstrate their abilities and attract opportunities beyond the classroom. “We are living in a society where your performance in the classroom alone is not enough to excel,” he said. He encouraged parents and teachers to expose children to activities that would build their confidence, improve their communication skills and enable them to showcase their abilities. Mr Poku cited the example of a female student from Keta in the Volta Region who, according to him, made history by reaching the final stage of a National Science and Maths Quiz competition, an achievement that helped her secure an opportunity to continue her education abroad. He said such opportunities demonstrated the importance of allowing children to participate in competitions that could open doors to further education and personal development. “Parents and teachers should adapt this kind of learning and enrol children in public activities. By so doing, society will begin to know what the children have and what they can offer,” he said. Bookworm expands educational competition Mr Poku said Bookworm, which has operated for nearly a decade, had expanded its activities to about 10 regions across the country. He disclosed that the Greater Accra competition began with approximately 74 schools, with 33 qualifying for the grand finale. The competition, held on October 24, featured three categories: lower primary, upper primary and junior high school (JHS), with winners to be crowned in each division. He said the Greater Accra event was the third regional finale organised by the programme in October, following competitions in the Eastern Region on October 10 and the Ashanti Region on October 16. According to him, Bookworm remains open to pupils from both public and private schools, providing an opportunity for children from different educational backgrounds to participate. He described the participation of public schools as encouraging, noting that the programme was designed to accommodate all interested pupils. “We open our hands to all students. Anyone who develops an interest in joining the programme is welcome. We take them through the process, and we do it together,” he said. Scholarships, laptops and international exposure Mr Poku said Bookworm had introduced incentives to reward outstanding participants and motivate children to improve their academic and personal development. He explained that winners receive 50 per cent scholarships for one year, while ultimate winners are also presented with laptops. Additionally, sponsors support selected top performers to undertake trips to Dubai, covering 50 per cent of the cost, with the level of support varying according to their positions in the competition. He said the international exposure was intended to broaden the children’s perspectives and introduce them to opportunities and experiences beyond Ghana. Mr Poku added that corporate partners, including Trillium Industry, Choco and Floral Tissue, also provide souvenirs and other items for participants and winners. Beyond reading and comprehension The Bookworm CEO said the competition was designed to develop a broad range of skills rather than focus solely on reading. He explained that participants undergo several stages, including storytelling, summarising passages and answering comprehension questions. Another segment, known as Knowing Your Parents , is designed to strengthen relationships between children and their parents by helping them understand their family backgrounds, preferences and behaviour. Mr Poku said the segment was introduced to encourage parents to spend more time with their children and strengthen family bonds. He expressed confidence that the different activities would help participants develop critical thinking, communication and interpersonal skills while building their confidence. He said Bookworm would continue to provide platforms through which children could discover their strengths, demonstrate their abilities and prepare for future opportunities.

title: Saudi says Riyadh airport partly reopens despite ongoing fighting with Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis
body: Saudi Arabia said its main airport had partially resumed operations at two terminals on Sunday despite renewed threats to target it from Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis, as the kingdom intercepted another wave of missiles and drones amid continued fighting with the group.The Houthis have continued their daily attacks on the kingdom, the world's largest oil exporter, despite Saudi strikes against the group, with the airport's partial reopening coming after a deadly attack earlier this month that forced it to suspend operations.The conflict has become an increasingly destabilizing element in the US-Israeli war with Iran, turning US ally Saudi Arabia into a pressure point in the wider war.Flight tracking data shows little trafficAfter Saudi authorities announced the partial resumption of operations at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree early on Sunday renewed a warning to airlines, airport staff and travelers against using it, saying it remained a "military target" and would "never be safe."Late on Saturday, the airport said Terminal 1 would be designated for domestic flights and Terminal 2 for international flights operated by national carriers starting Sunday.Despite the announcement, flight tracking data from Flightradar24 showed little traffic at the airport on Sunday.The airport had halted operations on October 10 following an attack claimed by the Houthis that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade.The Saudi-led coalition said earlier this month that the Houthis had carried out 20 attacks on King Khalid International Airport between October 1 and 11.Missile, drone attacks continueSaudi civil defense authorities issued emergency alerts for Riyadh and the cities of Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran on Sunday, before saying minutes later that the danger had passed.The coalition said two drones and a ballistic missile were launched towards Riyadh, and a cruise missile towards the southern city of Khamis Mushait. It later said it intercepted 10 ballistic missiles fired towards southern Saudi Arabia.The Houthis said they attacked the airport and Saudi oil facilities on Saturday. Saudi authorities did not comment directly on the Houthi statements.Saudi Arabia has stepped up its strikes against the Houthis after the group seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month, closing in on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait – a global maritime chokepoint and shipping route for Gulf oil producers on the opposite side of ​the Arabian Peninsula to the Strait of Hormuz.The renewed fighting in Yemen has shattered a UN-brokered truce that had largely held since 2022. Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen's civil war in 2015 at the head of a coalition supporting the internationally recognized government, after the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, a year earlier.

title: Luminate Group visits CJID, praises partnership on AI governance
body:
A delegation from Luminate Group , led by its Chief Executive Officer, Melanie Hui, visited the Centre for Journalism Innovation and Development (CJID) at its new office in Abuja on Friday, reaffirming the partnership between the two organisations.
During the visit, CJID Chief Executive Officer Dapo Olorunyomi called for greater scrutiny of technology companies, arguing that their control over digital communication platforms had created new accountability challenges for journalists and civil society.
He illustrated the problem with the case of Mohammed Yusuf, a trader in Ilorin, Kwara State, who lost about ₦150,000 after responding to a sponsored TikTok advertisement offering a grant from OPay, a payment company.
Mr Olorunyomi said the trader lost almost all the capital for his business after following the instructions in the advertisement.
“The advertisement Mohammed saw was not hidden in some dark corner of the internet. It was placed, paid for and approved inside the systems of one of the most powerful companies in the world,” he said.
“Had a newspaper run that advertisement, we would know whom to hold responsible, from the editor and the publisher to the regulator who licenses them. With a platform, those lines are much harder to draw, and the citizen who has been wronged is often left with nowhere to turn.”
He said CJID’s accountability work had increasingly focused on technology platforms because they determine what users see, remove content and enforce rules governing public speech, often through systems that are difficult for citizens to scrutinise.
Mr Olorunyomi said Luminate’s support had helped CJID expand investigative reporting across West Africa and develop its work on digital technology, artificial intelligence and information disorder.
He said applications for the Centre’s Platform Accountability Reporting Fellowship had risen from about 800 in 2025, when only 15 fellows could be selected, to more than 1,000 this year.
The programme trained 35 fellows and commissioned 18 investigations, he said.
The investigations were compiled in a report titled “Digital Harms in Nigeria,” which documents cases of online fraud, abusive digital lending practices and harmful content on social media platforms.
He said a fake electoral commission portal was also suspended, while Citizens’ Gavel initiated legal action against Telegram based on findings about exploitation networks.
However, he cautioned that such responses did not necessarily mean the underlying problems had been resolved.
“A deleted account or a lawsuit tells us that evidence produced a response. It does not yet tell us that the harm has stopped, that Mohammed has his money back, or that the system that failed him has changed,” he said.
He said CJID planned to return to cases documented in the report and send specific, dated requests to Meta, TikTok, X and Telegram, with the responses to be published.
Mr Olorunyomi also highlighted the centre’s work on artificial intelligence through DUBAWA’s audio verification tool, a WhatsApp fact-checking chatbot and the Nigeria AI Collective, which brings together civil society organisations, journalists, academics and technology professionals.
He said more than 600 people from the media, civil society, universities and the technology sector were involved in the collective, while seven civil society organisations had received advocacy grants and 70 communication lecturers had received support to incorporate AI into their teaching.
He said CJID was also working with partners across West Africa to digitise newspaper archives and develop models that understand Nigerian Pidgin and Ghanaian English.
“The systems now being built will increasingly shape how the world understands Nigeria, Ghana and the Sahel. They will draw on someone’s archive and learn someone’s language, and we would like at least some of those archives and languages to be ours,” he said.
In her reflection, Malanie Hui, Luminate’s chief executive officer, commended CJID’s work on artificial intelligence innovation, research and governance, while identifying transparency, accountability and misinformation as continuing challenges.
She said Luminate would continue supporting the Nigeria AI Collective and efforts to develop Nigeria’s artificial intelligence ecosystem.
Ms Hui said African countries should have the capacity to shape the global AI economy rather than remain consumers of technologies developed elsewhere.
She pointed to the role of regulators, workers and innovators in shaping the continent’s digital future and said Luminate would support their efforts.
She also called for equitable ownership of digital infrastructure and institutions, arguing that meaningful participation in the technology sector must extend beyond access to include influence over decisions that shape the continent’s future.
Ms Hui said equity means moving beyond participation alone. It means having meaningful influence over the infrastructure, the institutions, the partnerships, the choices that will determine Africa’s digital future, she said.
CJID works with Luminate on artificial intelligence research, innovation and governance through the Nigeria AI Collective. The centre coordinates the collective’s AI governance efforts, working with civil society organisations and the media to examine the effects of artificial intelligence on the information ecosystem and society.

title: National Guard Drones Deliver 600 kg of Aid to Occupied Oleshky
body:
Ukrainian National Guard operators have deployed unmanned aerial vehicles to deliver over 600 kilograms of humanitarian aid, infant food, and toys to families trapped in the Russian -occupied city of Oleshky, Minister of Internal Affairs Ivan Vyhivskyi announced on Sunday, Oct. 25.
The aerial resupply mission was executed by service members of the “Bolharychi” special purpose company, a subordinate unit of the 11th Mykhailo Hrushevskyi Brigade of the National Guard of Ukraine, state news agency Ukrinform reported.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Writing on Facebook, Vyhivskyi confirmed that unmanned aerial platforms transported 15 individual cargo containers across contested airspace into the isolated Dnipro left-bank enclave in the southern Kherson region.
“Despite the Russian occupation and the severe conditions confronting the residents of Kherson region, our units continue to support the people,” Vyhivskyi stated in an official dispatch.
The delivered cargo focused primarily on life-sustaining supplies for households with young children facing acute shortages of infant nutrition and basic necessities.
According to the internal affairs minister, the 15 airdropped consignments contained baby milk formula, breakfast cereals, dried foods, developmental games, and toys for infants and toddlers isolated under military occupation.
“Among the children who remain in blocked Oleshky are those born during the full-scale war who have known no life without terror,” Vyhivskyi said.
“We support these families and deliver essential basic goods to them.”
Vyhivskyi expressed formal gratitude to the volunteer logistics networks that assembled the care packages, the drone operators who navigated contested electronic warfare corridors, the armed detachments providing fire cover, and local contacts on the ground who risked their lives to recover and distribute the supplies within the occupied perimeter.
The drone delivery underscores the desperate conditions in Oleshky, situated approximately five kilometers southeast of liberated Kherson on the east bank of the Dnipro River .
The municipality has remained under Russian military control since the opening days of the full-scale invasion in February 2022 and has been entirely severed from authorized overland cargo deliveries and international humanitarian missions since late May.
Roughly 1,700 civilians remain trapped in the municipal center amid destroyed municipal heating networks, severed running water, and intermittent electrical supply ahead of freezing winter temperatures.
Ukrainian officials have repeatedly described the municipality as under virtual siege, noting that exit roads and river transit points are heavily mined and subjected to continuous loitering drone reconnaissance.
Ukrainian defense units have intermittently utilized heavy multi-rotor transport drones to air-drop rations and pharmaceuticals into residential yards as diplomatic negotiations to secure an overland corridor continue.
The aerial relief mission coincides with preparations for a synchronized, localized ceasefire framework scheduled to take effect across Oleshky on Tuesday, Oct. 27, at 3:00 a.m. Kyiv time (4:00 a.m. Moscow time).
Finalized during bilateral consultations between Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets and Russian negotiating lead Yana Lantratova – mediated with assistance from US First Lady Melania Trump – the framework establishes a phased humanitarian operation to deliver larger medical and food consignments and begin civilian evacuations.
President Volodymyr Zelensky affirmed that Kyiv will adhere strictly to operational commitments to unblock the city, emphasizing that opening humanitarian access to Oleshky remains vital to preventing catastrophic civilian loss ahead of winter.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: MacArthur Foundation visits CJID, Premium Times, reaffirms support for media accountability
body:
The MacArthur Foundation has reaffirmed its commitment to supporting accountability journalism and digital accountability in Nigeria. The leadership of the foundation stated this during a visit to the offices of the Centre for Journalism Innovation and Development (CJID) and PREMIUM TIMES in Abuja on Friday.
During the visit, Dapo Olorunyomi, chief executive officer of CJID and publisher of PREMIUM TIMES, highlighted the impact of the organisation’s support on investigative journalism, fact-checking, press freedom and efforts to hold technology platforms accountable in Nigeria.
The MacArthur Foundation delegation also officially opened CJID and PREMIUM TIMES’ head offices in Nigeria.
Speaking during the MacArthur Foundation’s visit, Mr Olorunyomi said the foundation’s support had helped build CJID’s capacity since its establishment in 2014, when it was known as the Premium Times Centre for Investigative Journalism.
“MacArthur believed in us in 2014, the year we were founded, when we were still the Premium Times Centre for Investigative Journalism, a small team beside a young newsroom, trying to report on the 2015 elections, on human rights abuses and on the money committed to the war against insurgency,” he said.
He said the foundation’s subsequent support helped establish DUBAWA, a fact-checking platform, and UDEME, a civic technology initiative that enables journalists and citizens to track public spending.
“Those two ideas became DUBAWA and UDEME. Everything that has grown from them since, from our verification work and AI tools to our budget tracking, our press freedom work and the young journalists we train, carries the mark of that early faith,” he said.
Mr Olorunyomi cited UDEME’s reporting on an abandoned general hospital in Ukanafun Local Government Area of Akwa Ibom State as an example of how sustained investigative journalism can contribute to public accountability.
He said the hospital, which successive governments had left unfinished for about 20 years, was commissioned in November 2025, giving the community its first functioning general hospital.
“Somewhere in that story are the young reporters of UDEME, who kept going back to that building and kept asking where the money had gone, long after everyone else had stopped asking. And somewhere further back in the same story is the MacArthur Foundation,” he said.
Mr Olorunyomi said the foundation’s support had also contributed to legal action to protect press freedom. He recalled that CJID joined the Socio-Economic Rights and Accountability Project (SERAP) to challenge fines imposed on four broadcasters over a documentary about banditry in Zamfara State.
In June 2024, he said, the Federal High Court set aside the fines, ruling that the broadcast regulator could not sanction independent media on its own authority.
The foundation also supported initiatives to improve the sustainability of local newsrooms and train young journalists, including the Campus Reporter programme, which he said had expanded from 15 Nigerian universities to 49 institutions across six countries.
Mr Olorunyomi said the opening of the new office represented the centre’s commitment to sustaining its work beyond individual grants.
“When the On Nigeria programme came to an end, many people expected organisations like ours to shrink. We chose instead to put down roots,” he said. “This building is about permanence, not size. It is our way of saying that the institution you helped to raise intends to stay here and keep doing this work, long after any single grant has closed.”
He said CJID was preparing for emerging threats to public information ahead of Nigeria’s 2027 general elections, including synthetic media and coordinated influence operations.
The centre is also digitising historical records of the Nigerian press, with more than 13,000 newspaper pages processed so far, and aims to train 10,000 young Africans in artificial intelligence, digital technology and media technology by 2030, he said.
In his remarks, the MacArthur Foundation President, John Palfrey, said the organisation has been very proud to support the work of CJID over the years. “Our support has exceeded $6 million. Anywhere in the world, that represents a substantial investment by our foundation in a single organisation,” Mr Palfrey said.
“It demonstrates that we believe in what you are doing and recognise its profound importance to the values we uphold around the world. At the MacArthur Foundation, we consider our mission to be the advancement of justice, vibrancy and peace around the world. I believe all these values are represented as we walk through your building.”
He noted that the new office would represent several things beyond being a physical building. It is a facility and a studio where stories are produced. “We also see it as a boardroom where partnerships are forged. You have told us about the incredibly important work of connecting with INEC and television networks,” he said.
“Ultimately, I love the idea that you are recording the first draft of history, ensuring that events are documented and that we do not forget them. We know that the arc of history does not always bend towards justice. Sometimes, we need reminders of that, and your work helps ensure that we are continually reminded.
“We also understood that this building would provide workspaces, and it is wonderful to see every seat filled, alongside the talent being developed here and the talent that is already present. Fundamentally, I believe this is a strong sign that a civic organisation such as yours can build resilience, both within itself and across the broader Nigerian society,” Mr Palfrey said.
Also speaking at the event, Supreme Court Justice Olubunmi Oyewole commended MacArthur’s support for judicial reforms in Nigeria, including the legislation of the Administration of Criminal Justice Act, which has strengthened criminal justice in the country.
Mr Oyewole also commended CJID and PREMIUM TIMES for staying true to accountability journalism and advocacy.

title: 1,314 protesters arrested in France over unrest
body: Police arrested 1,314 people in weekend protests across France, the interior ministry said Sunday, adding that 53 officers were hurt in clashes. The arrests occurred as violence broke out on the margins of mass demonstrations in major cities on Saturday over the high cost of living. It was the second consecutive weekend of unrest in France, which is heading to presidential elections in April and May to choose a successor to Emmanuel Macron, who is reaching his two-term limit. The interior ministry said police responded to 75 fires during Saturday’s protests, adding that 24 shops were looted. “Several investigations have been opened,” it said in a statement, without giving details. It said that the rest of Saturday night, after the clashes had died down, was “calm”. The ministry statement on Sunday did not say how many protesters were hurt. Late Saturday, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez spoke of two serious injuries among protesters: one in Toulouse and one in Clermont-Ferrand. – Protesters hurt – The Toulouse prefecture, which reports to the interior ministry, told AFP that a 20-year-old man was seriously hurt with a wound to his hand. A street medic who tended demonstrators told AFP, on condition of anonymity, that the man had “several fingers” blown off his right hand. The prefecture covering Clermont-Ferrand said a man there also had a hand hurt, but did not suffer the loss of any fingers. A French regional daily, La Nouvelle Republique, reported that a man in Poitiers was hurt in his left eye, showing a photo of a man holding his face. The newspaper’s photographer told AFP he was a 19-year-old who was wounded during a charge by riot police firing stun grenades and tear gas. There have been several instances in recent weeks, during student protests in France, of people being maimed by police stun grenades or tear gas grenades. It was not known if the injuries reported from Saturday were from those police weapons. Officials said investigations had been opened in at least some of the cases. mk/rmb/sbk The post 1,314 protesters arrested in France over unrest appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Kuwait’s defence dilemma. Modern weapons and vulnerable supply routes
body:
Kuwait is investing in modern combat aircraft and ground-based air defence, but its security also depends on keeping that equipment operational. Access to spare parts, repairs and external support becomes particularly important when a crisis affects the entire region. At the same time, the country must retain its ability to export oil and receive supplies. The effectiveness of its defence therefore also depends on how long its economy and armed forces can continue functioning under pressure.
The US State Department’s October approval of a possible sale of Patriot missile repair and return services to Kuwait illustrates a less conspicuous dimension of military modernisation. The package has an estimated value of $400 million and also covers spare parts, transport, training and technical support. The approval concerns a potential transaction; it does not confirm that the services have been provided or that a new batch of missiles has been delivered.
The significance of the notification extends beyond its financial value. It shows that sustaining existing capabilities requires further decisions and continued cooperation with suppliers. It does not establish how many missiles remain serviceable, how many have been expended or whether shortages exist. The implication for assessing defence capability is narrower but important: an arsenal must be examined alongside the arrangements that sustain it.
Iraq’s invasion on 2 August 1990 and Kuwait’s liberation by a US-led coalition in 1991 remain the fundamental historical reference points. They demonstrated the difference between securing international support and possessing forces able to stop aggression in its opening phase. They do not, however, establish that contemporary threats must take the same form.
Pressure can now be directed at the continuity of exports, the functioning of infrastructure or the ability to sustain operational readiness. In such a scenario, an adversary does not need to occupy territory to raise the costs of a government’s policies. Responding requires military protection to be combined with preparedness across public administration, infrastructure operators and businesses.
Kuwait was designated a US Major Non-NATO Ally in 2004. The status facilitates defence cooperation and access to certain military cooperation arrangements. It does not, in itself, create a US obligation to defend the designated country. This should not be read as evidence that Washington has no interest in Kuwait’s security. It is a distinction between a legal designation and specific decisions on assistance.
For defence planning, the substance of that assistance matters most: its scope, availability and sustainability during a crisis involving several US partners. Strong political relations facilitate cooperation, but they do not replace arrangements for supplies, maintenance and the reception of support.
Kuwait ordered 28 Eurofighter Typhoons in 2016 and 28 F/A-18E/F Super Hornets in 2018. The first two Typhoons were delivered in December 2021. These figures describe the scale of procurement programmes, rather than the number of aircraft available for operational missions in October 2026.
Diversifying suppliers provides access to different technologies and industrial partnerships. It also entails maintaining separate training, maintenance and supply arrangements. The benefit of acquiring two aircraft types therefore depends on the country’s ability to provide adequate support for both. Equipment diversity alone does not establish resilience to supply disruption.
In a statement issued on 25 September 2025, Leonardo announced an extension of support for Kuwait’s Eurofighters until December 2029. The services are to include local logistics support and training at Salem Al Sabah Base. At the time, the manufacturer stated that most of the aircraft on order had been delivered and were in service. That statement describes the position at the date of publication without establishing the fleet’s current operational availability.
In-country support can shorten some maintenance processes and facilitate training. It does not amount to full self-sufficiency. Component deliveries, access to specialist expertise and work requiring manufacturer involvement remain relevant. A useful measure of progress is therefore the range of tasks performed locally and the time required to return equipment to service.
Further procurement makes sense when the capacity to employ the equipment grows alongside it. An additional aircraft expands potential capability, but cannot substitute for a trained crew, effective support or available weapons. Any assessment of modernisation should account for these interdependencies.
The October package is not the only notification concerning the sustainment of Kuwait’s Patriot systems. On 14 January 2026, the US Defense Security Cooperation Agency announced approval of a possible sale of programme sustainment and follow-on technical support, together with related equipment. Its estimated value was $800 million.
These figures should not be added together as confirmed expenditure or treated as the price of new batteries. The notifications concern potential transactions with specified scopes. They nevertheless show that maintaining the system entails a financial and organisational commitment extending over many years.
For Kuwait, coordination between ground-based air defence, combat aviation and intelligence and surveillance capabilities is essential. The effectiveness of individual assets depends on the threat, the information available and the circumstances of each engagement. Possessing Patriot systems does not establish comprehensive territorial protection. Public procurement announcements also provide no basis for calculating how long the country can sustain its defence at a given intensity of attack.
Military protection must therefore be complemented by the ability to limit the consequences of strikes. Effective warning, emergency response and the restoration of services remain important even when some threats are successfully intercepted. Their quality helps determine whether an individual incident becomes a prolonged disruption to national life.
A second constraint on resilience lies beyond Kuwait’s territory. On 3 July 2026, Reuters reported that Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates had diverted some exports through pipelines bypassing the Strait of Hormuz during the conflict, while Iraq and Kuwait had far more limited access to that option.
This creates a distinct strategic problem. Protecting installations and terminals is necessary, but does not ensure that cargo reaches its destination. Secure domestic infrastructure can coexist with disruption further along the route. Increasing the number of aircraft or air defence systems does not, by itself, remove this dependence.
Maritime cooperation is consequently part of Kuwait’s defence policy. Its significance encompasses information sharing, operational coordination and the conditions under which shipping companies are willing to sail. Even a reduction in the military threat does not necessarily produce an immediate return to regular commercial traffic.
There is a dual dependence: the state needs exports to sustain revenue, while the armed forces need supplies to remain effective. A transport crisis can place pressure on both simultaneously. Stockpiles and alternative transport arrangements should therefore be assessed in terms of the time they give the government and military to respond, alongside the practical ability to replenish supplies.
For Kuwait, financing military support and securing its delivery during a crisis are different problems. American and European procurement programmes provide access to advanced capabilities, while leaving important maintenance and supply functions outside national control. Operating two fighter types also requires Kuwait to sustain two support systems. Splitting purchases between suppliers offers limited protection if access to the country becomes the common constraint.
The practical negotiation with suppliers concerns which repairs can be completed in Kuwait, which components need to be stocked there and how technical assistance will continue under attack. Extending a support contract is useful when it also reduces the work that must wait for personnel or parts to arrive from abroad. Local maintenance consequently has political value. It reduces the urgency with which Kuwait has to seek assistance while its partners are responding to demands elsewhere.
The dependence of oil exports on passage through Hormuz places a further limit on what national rearmament can achieve. Kuwait can improve the protection of its terminals and the availability of its forces, while access to overseas markets still depends on conditions farther down the Gulf. Maritime cooperation therefore deserves a place alongside procurement in defence diplomacy. Without reliable shipping, the country may preserve much of its arsenal and still face economic pressure strong enough to influence its political choices.

title: General Staff: Ukrainian forces destroy Russian radar systems, command post and personnel
body:
According to Ukrinform, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported this on Facebook .
According to the General Staff, the Russian army’s radar stations were struck in the areas of the settlements of Gostishchevo and Kurganne in the Belgorod Oblast of the Russian Federation.
“Striking the radar stations creates gaps in the enemy’s radar coverage and expands the capabilities of the Ukrainian Defense Forces to deploy unmanned systems at all levels,” the statement reads.
The General Staff also confirmed the destruction of a command post for an occupying unit near the town of Tarasivka in the Zaporizhzhia region and a command and observation post near Hola Prystan in the Kherson region.
“This disrupts the Russian aggressor’s command and control of its troops and complicates the coordination of its units on the battlefield,” the General Staff noted.
There are also reports of strikes on enemy troop concentrations near the towns of Mykolaivka and Novoukrainka in the Donetsk region, as well as in the areas of Berdiansk, Okhrimivka, and Tarasivka in the Zaporizhzhia region.
“Operations against key enemy military targets will continue until Russia’s armed aggression against Ukraine comes to a complete end,” the General Staff stated.
As previously reported, on October 23 and during the night of October 24, the Ukrainian Defense Forces carried out strikes on key targets within Russian territory. It has been confirmed that the main production building of JSC “Proton-Elektrotex” in Orel, the “Tolyattikauchuk” plant in Tolyatti, and an aircraft at the Yeysk airfield were destroyed.

title: Sudan drone strikes kill 306 in three weeks, UN rights body says
body: Drone strikes across Sudan killed at least 306 people in the first three weeks of October, a United Nations rights body said on Friday, warning that attacks attributed to both warring sides are increasingly devastating civilian areas. The UN Human Rights Office documented hundreds of injuries as strikes hit homes, markets, hospitals, displacement sites, power stations and water sources in Darfur, Kordofan, Blue Nile, Khartoum and other states. Drones have accounted for the majority of conflict-related civilian deaths in Sudan this year, UN human rights chief Volker Türk said, urging the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) to respect international humanitarian law. Among the deadliest incidents, at least 139 people were killed on Oct. 18 when a transport truck was struck in a repeat attack in Dibab, West Kordofan, an area controlled by the RSF, the UN rights body said. Alleged SAF drone strikes on shelters for internally displaced people in Ghubeish and El Nuhud, West Kordofan, killed at least 25 civilians and injured 31 between Oct. 6 and 10. In Blue Nile state, an alleged RSF drone strike killed at least 31 displaced people, mostly women and children, near an artisanal gold mining site in Abu Shendi on Oct. 9. Two alleged RSF strikes on the Bajaun gold mining area in South Kordofan on Oct. 9 and 16 killed 42 civilians and injured 25 others, the UN said. Drone strikes on markets in North Darfur, South Darfur and West Kordofan killed another 23 civilians, while an alleged RSF strike on Um Darfa hospital in Blue Nile injured two health workers and forced the facility to close. The UN body also warned of retaliatory strikes, saying RSF-attributed drone attacks around Khartoum airport were reportedly carried out in response to alleged SAF aerial strikes on Nyala, South Darfur. Türk said attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure are deepening displacement and worsening Sudan’s humanitarian crisis. He called for an end to arms transfers used in violations of international humanitarian law and urged both sides to agree to a ceasefire. Sudan has been at war since April 2023, when fighting erupted between the SAF and RSF, displacing millions and devastating infrastructure across the country. The post Sudan drone strikes kill 306 in three weeks, UN rights body says appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: Ghana Tennis Federation congratulates Wheelchair champions after Ga Mantse Tournament
body: The Ghana Tennis Federation (GTF) has congratulated wheelchair tennis players and officials for their commitment, sacrifice and participation in the Ga Mantse Tennis Tournament, highlighting the growing development of wheelchair tennis in Ghana. The tournament featured competitive men’s and women’s wheelchair tennis divisions, providing athletes with an opportunity to showcase their skills, resilience and sportsmanship. In the men’s division, Bernard Yawson emerged champion, while Daniel Laryea finished as runner-up. In the women’s division, Stacy Konadu Mensah claimed the title, with Bridget Nartey finishing as runner-up. The Federation commended all four finalists and every participating athlete for contributing to an exciting and competitive tournament. The GTF expressed its appreciation to the organisers, Abusua, for including wheelchair tennis in the Ga Mantse Tennis Tournament. According to the Federation, initiatives of this nature are essential to the development of para sport in Ghana, as they provide athletes with valuable competition, greater public visibility and opportunities to assess their progress. The Federation also expressed hope that future editions of the tournament would be bigger and create an even greater impact on wheelchair tennis development. Speaking on behalf of the Board, Henry K. N. Larbi, National Coordinator of Ghana Wheelchair Tennis, congratulated the players and officials for their dedication and commitment to the sport. He stressed the importance of securing sponsorship to enable Ghanaian wheelchair tennis players to compete in international tournaments and improve their chances of qualifying for the LA2028 Paralympic Games. Larbi noted that despite the talent and determination demonstrated by the athletes, limited financial resources remain a major obstacle to their international participation. Qualification for the Paralympic Games in wheelchair tennis depends significantly on international rankings, which players build through participation in recognised tournaments. However, the cost of international travel, accommodation, tournament entry fees and specialised sports wheelchairs continues to pose a challenge for Ghanaian athletes. With the LA2028 Paralympic Games approaching, the Ghana Tennis Federation is appealing to corporate organisations, government agencies, development partners and individuals to support the country’s wheelchair tennis players. Beyond competition, the Federation believes wheelchair tennis plays an important role in promoting inclusion, building confidence and changing public perceptions of persons with disabilities. The Ghana Tennis Federation and Ghana Wheelchair Tennis have reaffirmed their commitment to expanding the sport nationwide, identifying emerging talent and creating opportunities for athletes to compete at the highest level.

title: 12 injured, including 6 children, in shooting near Florida university, police say
body:
At least 11 of those injured had gunshot wounds, police said.
At least 12 people were injured, including six children, amid a Saturday evening shooting in Tallahassee, near the campus of Florida A & M University, officials said.
Eleven of those who were injured had gunshot wounds, Tallahassee Chief of Police Lawrence Revell told reporters during a late-night press conference.
"Six are adults and six are juveniles," he said. "We know our youngest victim is 11 years old. At least three of our victims have sustained serious injuries and one of those is in critical condition. Eight of those are reported to be in stable condition."
The person who was injured but not from a gunshot was "a grandmother of one of the victims," the chief said, adding that she "injured herself fleeing from the scene."
In a Sunday morning update, the Tallahassee Police Department (TPD) said that six of the victims remain hospitalized, with one in critical condition. Five other victims have been released from the hospital, police said.
No arrests had been announced as of Sunday morning. Police said they are working to identify those responsible for the shooting and sought the public's help, asking anyone with information about the shooting to contact investigators immediately. Police also asked that anyone with photos or video share them with investigators.
"We will determine what happened, identify those responsible, and get answers for all of the victims, their families and everyone impacted by this tragedy," Revell said in a statement released on Sunday. "We know there are people who saw something, heard something or may have video that could help us piece together exactly what happened."
"We need our community's help. No detail is too small, and no piece of information should go unreported," Revell added. "If you know something, please share it with our detectives. Your information could be the key to holding those responsible accountable."
Police described the shooting as an "altercation [that] occurred between individuals" near the intersection of Perry and Manatee Streets, just outside Florida A & M University's Bragg Memorial Stadium.
FAMU President Marva B. Johnson released a video statement Sunday afternoon, describing the shooting as an "evil act."
Johnson said that while the shooting did not occur on her campus, the school is offering care and support to "members of our FAMU family who were injured in the tragic incident."
She did not say if any students or faculty were among those injured.
"To our Rattler family and our surrounding Tallahassee community, I share your outrage and profound sadness at the senseless and despicable shooting that took place near our FAMU campus last night," Johnson said in the statement.
She added that free counseling support will be offered to students, saying, "A horrific act of violence like this is traumatizing for our students, whether you were near the event or not."
