Did the world learn from that episode or did we treat it like it was nothing? Were there things we did in Africa that made us less-susceptible to dying from COVID-19? Are there African remedies that could benefit the world? Or is there subtle racism or classism involved in these matters?
Another recent example came from geography but was also profoundly linked to economics. Flemish geographer Geraldus Mercator developed a map of the world in 1569, which was convenient and suitable for navigational purposes. But it minimised the size of the African continent especially. I recall a young white American guy speaking about that matter on social media about three years ago. I shared his video on my social media timelines. But he was ignored and made to look like a fraud. Until Togo took the matter up, pursued it through the United Nations, and got the World Map rightsized. Still a lot of African analysts said it doesn’t matter. That victory itself was another opportunity for self-deprecation, self-minimisation, and the heaping of blame on ourselves in what has now become ‘learned helplessness’.
Some asked if that was going to help us manage our resources better. Others answered that it was not, since we were destined to be this way. In their minds, everything could be explained away with corruption and our relative backwardness. They ignored the principle behind it. They justified the miseducation that has defined our thinking and destinies so far. They would rather work with wrong information in all spheres, in all disciplines, rather than take the effort to research the truth about ourselves and the world, or support and affirm those who do. The simple questions are: Would Africa have been taken more seriously if the true size was known since 1569? Would we have fought colonialism more stridently if we knew the true size of the land annexed? Could we have a bigger say in world fora like the United Nations? Could our own understanding of our own potentials be more enhanced? And why teach the untruth to our children for so long? It is this same type of tragedy that has us relying on economic theories propounded by Adam Smith, with Scottish data and realities in 1776, or David Ricardo’s Comparative Advantage theory of 1820, till today. We must think for ourselves!
There are many observations around the subject of economics that African economists are better suited to understand. We could write about informality, for instance, for we have the world’s largest informal economies, products of past dislocations and distrust of imported systems of government. We could write and research around the impact of history on economies, or the paucity of data to make economic decisions. What about the calculation of domestic investment in informal economies, where capital formation at the informal level is more rapid and exceedingly more robust but largely ignored? We could even research about how relatively low levels of literacy and underdeveloped political systems affect economics or conduct new research around resource dependency. The point is that we must never assume that all the research work relevant to our situation and to the study of economics have already been done, or that only non-Africans are better suited to think and postulate about peculiar issues. That will be the worst defeat that we would have conferred upon ourselves. African economists must be bold, must be articulate, and daring. The earlier we start along these lines, the earlier we will get the required recognition, but more importantly, our economies and people will be most positively impacted.
For the year 2026, Robert E Hall and Michael Woodford won the Sverige Riksbank Prize for research that generated a paradigm shift in ‘stabilisation’ policy. New Keynesian models, a result of their research, allow us to explain and quantify how stabilisation policy affects business cycles and are now used by central banks and finance ministries around the world. The achievements of Nigeria’s Central Bank under Olayemi Cardoso should be documented along these lines and it was a practical deployment in real time, not of Hall and Woodford’s ideas but our own organic thinking, which repositioned our economy.
Let us now look at those topics which have earned people around the world the best prizes in economics, with a view not to denigrating any, but to draw inspiration that we too can do this. I will select just a few:
For the year 2026, Robert E Hall and Michael Woodford won the Sverige Riksbank Prize for research that generated a paradigm shift in ‘stabilisation’ policy. New Keynesian models, a result of their research, allow us to explain and quantify how stabilisation policy affects business cycles and are now used by central banks and finance ministries around the world. The achievements of Nigeria’s Central Bank under Olayemi Cardoso should be documented along these lines and it was a practical deployment in real time, not of Hall and Woodford’s ideas but our own organic thinking, which repositioned our economy. In 2025, Joel Mokyr, Phillipe Aghton and Peter Howitt got the Nobel in Economics for demonstrating how innovation and new technology drive sustained economic growth and counteract historical stagnation. This should be an African story, really. And should not be so difficult for a bunch of African economists to put together. I believe it piggybacks on Joseph Schumpeter’s ideas of Creative Destruction and Innovative Entrepreneurship, which were the bedrock of my PhD dissertation.
In 2024, Daron Acemoglu and Simon Johnson got the Nobel in Economics for studies of how institutions are formed and affect prosperity. Their chunky book, Why Nations Fail , is a testimony to their world. I personally find the book onerous and cumbersome, and many economists around the world have now criticised their logic. In 2023, Claudia Goldin received the Nobel for ‘advancing our understanding of women’s labour market outcomes.’ I believe we have female economists in Africa that could have a lot to say about female contributions to the GDP, to entrepreneurship, to the family unit and general development of nations, even from a historical angle. I conclude that the world now suffers from a deficit of African opinions.
Other awardees include Ben Bernanke, Philip Dybvig and Douglas Diamond in 2022 for research into banks and financial crises; David Card, Joshua D Angrist, and Guido W Imbens in 2021 for contributions to labour economics and the analysis of causal relationships; Paul R Milgrom and Robert B Wilson in 2020 for improvements to auction theory and new auction formats; Abhijit Banerjee, Esther Duflo, and Michael Kremer in 2019 for research into experimental approach to alleviating global poverty; Richard H Thaler in 2018 for contributions to behavioural economics, and so on. I don’t think any of these topics upon which the prizes were given were esoteric. I think they all tell human stories around the discipline, and by now, Africa has more human stories to tell. African economists, rise up, speak up, and boldly showcase your work. Our time is now!
‘Tope Fasua is the special adviser to the President on Economic Matters.

title: What the US Movement Against Data Centers Can Learn From Abroad
body:
“I certainly didn't predict that it was all going to kind of come to a head as my book was coming out,” he says with a laugh.
While data centers are playing a role in shaping US elections—they’re one of the issues that could decide key midterm races in less than two weeks—there’s a history of struggle around the world. Marx’s book takes the reader on a tour of the tech industry’s quest for power and its opposition, from antiwar protests targeting American computers during the Vietnam War, to more recent resistance in Ireland and Chile, and an alternative vision for the future of data centers in New Zealand.
I caught up with him this week to talk about what he’s seen, and what could happen if the AI bubble pops.
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.
MOLLY TAFT: When did you decide to write a book about data centers?
PARIS MARX: In the Netherlands and Singapore, they had moratoriums going back to 2019. But in 2022, there was a growing recognition of the demands of data centers in Ireland, on the energy grid in particular. There were huge quantities of electricity that data centers were starting to consume over there.
The other story that really got on my radar was what happened with Google in The Dalles, Oregon. Google was really trying to hide its water use figures, to the degree that it got the city council to try to keep its water use figures secret. They kept that going for the better part of a year before the community finally got the actual numbers and found out that Google was using 29 percent of the water in the community.
ChatGPT came out at the end of 2022. It became apparent that there's going to need to be a lot more data centers for generative AI. These places were already feeling the effects of significant data center construction, and it felt like that was going to start coming to a lot more communities very soon.
I feel like a lot of Americans think data centers just came out of the blue in the US over the past year or two, just in time to be this huge midterms issue. One thing I like about your book is that it shows us how other countries and communities served as early warning signs.
Ireland was a real example of what can happen. Dublin had a moratorium passed back in 2021. It was actually the grid operator that said, “Hey, there are too many data centers. We do not have the grid capacity to connect any more of them.”
In response to that, you had the industry moving to make sure it can still build data centers in Ireland. They can't get grid connections in Dublin, so they start looking at building in other parts of Ireland. They also looked at starting to tap into the gas network so they can use generators. Eventually, they start building dedicated gas power plants to power their data centers instead of connecting to the grid.
The Irish energy grid is a public grid—only the public utility can build electricity lines. And data center companies actually lobbied for legislation that essentially allows private companies to build electricity cables. That obviously concerns a lot of people and presents questions about equity in the system.
The gas stuff looks so prescient with what’s happening in the US now, where companies are racing to build these massive private gas power plants for data centers.
[Data center operators] were getting these emission licenses from the Irish Environmental Protection Agency to be able to burn all these fossil fuels. The agency was warning that climate targets are going to be a lot harder to achieve now.
When I started to see that happen in the US, I wasn’t surprised. I’d already seen the story play out before. But the scale of it is staggering, and how quickly it’s escalated.
What happens to the physical infrastructure—from the gas plants to the data centers themselves—that's getting built out if this industry falls apart? Is there historic precedent for that?
I think we're in an AI bubble. But what does the collapse of that bubble look like? They're planning to add all these data centers and all of these gas power plants in order to power the data centers. But there are issues with getting turbines, with getting chips, with getting different kinds of pieces of the puzzle for the data center itself. Are these even going to get built out before there’s a reassessment of the demand for AI?
We often talk about the excess build-out of fiber capacity back in the dotcom boom and bust. But there was also a build-out of data centers—obviously a much earlier stage than what we're at now. A lot of data center companies went under. Companies like Equinix, which did survive, bought up a ton of data centers to be ready for when that capacity returned.
But the issue we have now is that if data centers are being planned for AI use, and we’re operating under the assumption that the chips are going to have to be cycled out within a few years. Even if the data center is there, what makes it most valuable is potentially not going to be useful by the time that demand returns.
Inevitably, even if the data centers don't come, then those gas plants will exist. They will be looking for new customers to justify their existence. I'm sure that people are not building them with the intention to just shut them down.
You ended the book with a specific example in New Zealand of a community-led effort to create a more accurate speech-recognition model of the Māori language, using local cloud providers to host the data. I really liked this alternative vision of a non-extractive way to harness the powers of AI. Have you thought about what we could do to make some changes and how this build-out is going?
I would like to see governments go really hard on actually putting firmer regulations on the development of data centers. But those should also be paired with regulations on the AI products themselves. We had a lot of promises about what generative AI was going to deliver that haven't been realized. There has also been a long list of harms that have arisen from these technologies that we were not told would come along with them. Our governments do not seem to be so willing to actually take that on. They're buying the narrative that generative AI is still what Sam Altman sold it to be in early 2023 rather than what it has become today.
I think that we do need to be thinking of how we do technology differently, especially in this moment where we're dedicating so many resources to the infrastructure to enable generative AI. We should be asking, how much computation do we really need? How many resources are actually justifiable to put into this project? What are we actually getting out of it, right?  Does what we're getting from what Silicon Valley is creating really justify the resources that we are collectively sacrificing in order to realize it? If we actually did the assessment, I think that we would very clearly find that there's no way to justify what we are doing right now—from a financial perspective, but also from a social and environmental one.
What We’re Writing
Speaking of those climate targets, it’s not just the Irish government that’s thinking about them. My colleague Joel Khalil covers how the European Union’s thirst for AI is running into European countries’ climate goals. Joel tells me he wouldn’t be surprised if data centers become a political flash point in Europe, like they are in the US, as countries go to the polls next year. “The fascinating thing about the European data center build-out is the collision of competing interests: national-level policy butts up against local priorities, ambitions for economic growth stand in conflict with climate objectives, and planning bureaucracy foils attempts by AI companies to rapidly expand their fleets,” he says. “It’s hard to see how Europe could possibly have it all.”
What We’re Reading

The New York Times covers how the AI and data center boom is boosting a surprising commodity: gray paint.
The massive build-out of data centers in Texas threatens years of progress in the state cutting air pollution. The Texas Tribune has more.
Google has apologized for clearing more than 800 acres of forest in Finland without getting the necessary environmental permits to build part of a €13 million data center project. The Guardian reports that the tech giant is facing backlash in the country that could bleed into elections next spring.

title: When a teen posts a selfie, how much filter is 'too much' filter?
body:
How much filter is too much filter for kids and teens posting selfies on social media?
That is the question state attorneys general across the country are grappling with following a landmark settlement with Meta this summer. As part of the agreement, the social media giant agreed to block some digital beauty filters for minors — specifically those mimicking extreme transformations like cosmetic procedures or heavy makeup.
Now, the burden falls on state officials to tell Meta where to draw the line. But defining where harmless fun ends and harmful manipulation begins is far from straightforward.
For teenagers navigating the digital landscape, the pressure of online perfection is a daily reality. Much of that pressure has been driven by online beauty trends like "Instagram face." Coined in 2019 by The New Yorker writer Jia Tolentino , the phrase refers to a look characterized by a small button nose, high cheekbones and pouty lips. While traditionally only achievable in real life through plastic surgery or extreme makeup, it can be applied instantly online using beauty filters.
Mia Lerner, a 17-year-old high school senior in California and a youth body image activist, knows the toll these digital tools can take. She told NPR experimenting with beauty filters contributed to her eating disorder and left her struggling with her self-image.
"I've even tried to fix my nose with AI," Lerner said. "My face looks a lot better, I think, in [the] photo that I manipulated with these beauty filters. But I'm still living with this nose that I see in the mirror."
Lerner welcomes the aspect of the Meta settlement that aims to restrict beauty filters for minors. "It's a very important step in the right direction," Lerner said.
However, the agreement reached in August between Meta and 47 U.S. states — plus Washington D.C. and three territories — does not institute a blanket ban on all digital effects.
Filters that transform users into playful characters, like elves or puppies, will remain available for young people. But so will filters offering subtle beautification effects — such as smoothing skin tone or adding a slight eye glow.
It is this category of relatively minor editing that particularly concerns Lerner.
"When I see something that has been so obviously AI-generated, it's very easy for me to logically say, 'Well, that's obviously been manipulated so I can't compare myself to that,'" Lerner said. "But when I see these videos of people who are just slightly edited, it's a lot easier for me to go down that comparison path."
Meta has previously implemented measures to manage beauty filters, which are increasingly powered by artificial intelligence.
The tech giant has already banned filters that explicitly promote cosmetic surgery, such as those overlaying pre-surgery marker lines onto skin. It has also shut down its platform for third-party creators of these tools, introduced mandatory labels for AI-generated content, and deployed automated AI detection systems . Despite these systems, harmful aesthetic filters and features that keep children trapped in an endless cycle of scrolling, clicking, and staying online persistently slipped past these guardrails, as a federal judge wrote in a summary judgement denying Meta's defense this summer.
Meta is not the only tech company grappling with teen access to beauty filters. TikTok also restricts users under the age of 18 from using them. Snapchat does not restrict teen access to filters. Neither company responded to NPR's request for comment. YouTube told NPR it does not have any filters. But there's nothing stopping users from posting images or videos made with third party filters to the platform — or onto TikTok and Instagram, for that matter.
Meanwhile, state attorneys general are reaching the end of a two-month window they set themselves to provide Meta with guidance in the form of a letter on what constitutes a bannable filter — and what does not.
They face a moving target, as digital beauty standards evolve rapidly.
"If the states want to define what is a beauty filter, they should define what is beauty," said Florencia Solari, a creative technologist who has spent years developing AI and augmented reality experiences for global brands.
Solari noted that trend cycles move quickly. "Instagram face" is already falling out of favor. "People are starting to move away from that because it's starting to look a bit clownish," Solari said. "Now it's going towards extreme thinness. So that's another problem."
As a result, the tools that are used to achieve the latest look are therefore also changing. So what might be branded by lawmakers as an "extreme" beauty filter in 2026 will likely be different in 2027.
While beauty standards are changing quickly, so is technology.
Instead of sitting in boardrooms debating pixel thresholds for cheekbones, Kelly Frasier, the co-author of a recent study highlighting the negative impacts of social media on body issues in adolescents, said legislators should consider the fact that teens will soon be able to use AI to create entire fake universes around themselves, not just change the way they look. So they should focus on broader AI regulation for minors.
"I think that legislators are asking the wrong question if they're asking where to draw the line for beauty filters," said Frasier. "And to be honest, filters will probably become completely obsolete within the next few years."
On top of the technological and cultural challenges, legal experts warn that individual states may struggle to reach a consensus on what does and does not constitute what the settlement agreement describes as a "cosmetic procedure filter."
"What we don't really have a sense of is what happens if the states disagree with each other?" said David Greene, senior counsel at the Electronic Frontier Foundation. "What if one state finds, you know, eyebrow lifting to be completely acceptable and another one thinks it's awful?"
NPR reached out to the attorneys general offices in all four plaintiff states that led the trial — California, Colorado, Kentucky, and New Jersey — for an update on the guidelines. But officials either declined to comment or did not respond.
Beyond the U.S., some international regulators are hoping to avoid discussions around beauty filter definitions entirely.
In Europe, the proposed KIDS Act — designed to regulate youth social media usage — takes a sweeping approach.
In that plan, "Beauty filters – not extreme beauty filters; beauty filters full stop – are forbidden for minors," said European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier. Regnier said EU legislators are closely watching the implementation of the U.S. settlement. "We want child-friendly services for our children. A beauty filter has nothing to do with a child-friendly service," Regnier said.
Meta says that it plans to enforce the ban on "cosmetic procedure filters" by early next year.
For youth activists like Lerner, the hope is that tech companies and regulators will include teens in these discussions. "So often it's just the government or these companies in these conversations," Lerner said. "The company should be asking us for our actual perspectives, like 'Are people actually using these extreme AI filters or is that not going to make a difference?' 'Do we need to target something else?'"
Meta said the company has partnered with teens over the years, but did not respond to NPR's question asking if it is doing so currently.
NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.

title: Trump wants 'business with both' Ukraine, Russia after war ends
body:
U.S. President Donald Trump said on Oct. 24 that he sees the U.S. doing business with both Ukraine and Russia after the war ends, despite criticism of efforts to restore commercial ties with Moscow.
The statement comes as the first tanker carrying Russian diesel is heading to New York from the Baltic port of Primorsk, set to deliver 40,000 metric tons of fuel following a supply agreement Trump announced on Oct. 9.
Soon after the announcement, Moscow partially lifted restrictions on its diesel exports, permitting the sale of 500,000 metric tons.
"Certainly, we'll do business with Ukraine and with Russia after this war ends, I would think," Trump said.
Trump added that he wanted to "get back to life where Russia and Ukraine make a deal, and then we'd be able to do business with both."
The U.S. president also argued that Washington should have secured greater financial returns in exchange for the billions of dollars in aid provided to Kyiv during Joe Biden's presidency.
"I feel foolish because all you had to do is ask them, and they would have paid. Meaning the EU would have paid," Trump said.
Plans to import around 900,000 metric tons of Russian diesel in the coming months have drawn criticism of the Trump administration from European allies, Ukraine, and members of Congress, as the shipments would circumvent sanctions imposed on Moscow over its war against Ukraine.
The shipment would mark the first Russian diesel deliveries to the U.S. since 2022, when then-President Joe Biden banned imports of Russian oil and petroleum products in response to Russia's war against Ukraine.
The deal comes amid a growing rift between Kyiv and Washington, as Ukraine faces restrictions on Starlink access and reported delays in deliveries of Patriot air defense interceptors .
Trump has also stepped up his criticism of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, accusing him of being unwilling to end the war and calling for his replacement.
The decision to resume Russian diesel imports coincides with a challenging political landscape for Republicans ahead of the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections, with recent polls showing declining support for Trump.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll found that just 31% of Americans approve of Trump's performance, marking the lowest approval rating of either of his presidential terms.
Meanwhile, 47% of registered voters said they would vote for Democrats if congressional elections were held today, compared with 35% who favored Republicans, giving Democrats a 12-point lead — their largest of the current election cycle.

title: Hundreds gather at funeral of Jordan church attack victims
body: Hundreds of Jordanians attended a funeral service for the nine Christians killed by gunmen in Jordan on Sunday, at the same church as the attack took place. On Friday, assailants opened fire in the compound of the St George's Greek Orthodox church, in the village of Hamoud in Karak governorate, the country's Public Security Directorate directorate said. Jordanian King Abdullah II called it a “terrorist attack.” Karak, about 100km south of Amman, is home to a Christian minority in the mainly Muslim kingdom. The attack took place during a funeral. On Saturday, authorities revised the death toll from seven to nine and said none of the three assailants had been captured. Security officials briefed the king “on the latest developments in the investigation into the attack”, the Royal Palace said, without giving details. King Abdullah called the attackers “outlaws of Islam” and ordered the government to “review policies for countering extremist ideology and to intensify efforts to eradicate its root causes”. Jordanians from across the Kingdom participated in the funeral, with tribes sending representatives from the north, centre and south of the country. Some were part of organised associations and unions while others attended spontaneously. Kamal Al Rawashdeh, a Muslim in his 80s, drove his beaten Hyundai from the nearby village of Al Taybeh to take part in the processions. “I felt it was my duty, this was a heinous act.” Members of the gendarmerie were present while other security forces and armoured vehicles drove into surrounding remote and desert areas. Checkpoints were set south of Amman on the main motorway leading to Karak as authorities hunt for the three suspects. Security forces were stationed at churches across the country during Sunday services, in an unprecedented tightening of security at Christian sites. At the main Orthodox church in Amman, many people attended Sunday mass. “The attack does not dissuade anyone, it makes us stronger,” said the priest. There was an armoured vehicle stationed at the entrance to the church. Such incidents are very rare in Jordan, which is relatively stable but has come under Iranian attacks since the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in February. The kingdom is home to ​several biblical sites that attract Christian pilgrims from around the world.

title: Troops neutralise 6 terrorists, arrest 11 suspected collaborators in Borno
body: Troops of the Nigerian Army have neutralised six terrorists, arrested 11 suspected collaborators and received the surrender of a Jama’atu Ahlis Sunna Lidda’awati wal-Jihad (JAS) member in Borno. This is contained in an operational report made available to the News Agency of Nigeria (NAN), on Sunday in Abuja. The report said the operations, conducted by troops of the Joint Task Force North-East, Operation Hadin Kai (OPHK), targeted terrorist fighters and suspected support networks in Kaga and Gwoza Local Government Areas. It said troops of 29 Task Force Brigade Garrison, supported by Hybrid Force personnel, ambushed suspected Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP)/JAS terrorists along the Targejeri axis of Kaga at about 12:37 a.m. on Oct. 25. According to the report, six terrorists were neutralised during the encounter, while troops recovered an AK-47 rifle, three magazines and 169 rounds of 7.62mm special ammunition. “Other recovered items included two Android phones, three button phones and charms. “In a related development, troops arrested six additional suspected terrorist collaborators during a follow-up raid in Benisheikh, Kaga, at about 6:20 a.m. on Oct. 24. “The arrests brought the number of suspects apprehended in connection with the investigation to 11, including five earlier arrests. “Items listed as recovered during the raid included an AK-47 rifle, three empty magazines, 169 rounds of 7.62mm special ammunition, three terrorist uniforms, a turban, a head mask, two Android phones, three button phones and charms,” it said. The report said the suspects were undergoing investigation to establish their alleged involvement in terrorist activities and identify possible links to other members of the network. It added that troops of 192 Battalion (Main), supported by Hybrid Force personnel at Hambagda Internally Displaced Persons (IDP) Camp in Gwoza, received a JAS member who surrendered at about 9:20 p.m. on Saturday. According to the report, preliminary investigation indicated that the individual had escaped from a terrorist enclave in the Mandara Mountains area of Gwoza and decided to abandon terrorism. “The individual surrendered with an AK-47 rifle and a magazine containing 28 rounds of 7.62mm special ammunition,” it added. The report said the defector was in custody undergoing further investigation and processing in line with established procedures. It said the operations underscore OPHK’s continued efforts to disrupt terrorist activities, dismantle support networks and encourage defections through sustained, intelligence-led operations. The military urged members of the public to provide credible and timely information to security agencies to support efforts to restore peace and enable displaced communities to return safely. The post Troops neutralise 6 terrorists, arrest 11 suspected collaborators in Borno appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Top 68 concerts and events coming to the UAE, from Jennifer Lopez to Mariah Carey
body: From pop and rock to stand-up comedy, ballet, opera and musicals, the UAE’s live events season is in full swing, with the months ahead offering a packed line-up across Abu Dhabi, Dubai and Sharjah. Mariah Carey will return to Abu Dhabi with her Christmas-time show in December, while Wasla Festival brings regional acts, including Marcel Khalife, Le Trio Joubran, TootArd and Fatima to Expo City Dubai in November. Najwa Karam will bring her greatest hits to Dubai’s Coca-Cola Arena, while Abu Dhabi Comedy Season has announced shows led by Palestinian-American star Mo Amer and US comic Aries Spears. Abu Dhabi Grand Prix weekend will feature Jennifer Lopez , with the pop star completing the after-race concert line-up at Etihad Live alongside Lewis Capaldi, Zara Larsson, Alex Warren, Imagine Dragons, The Chainsmokers and The Script. Looking ahead to 2027, Shah Rukh Khan curate the inaugural Unifyd festival at Etihad Live, with Arijit Singh, Karan Aujla and Sonu Nigam among the first artists announced. Here, we round up the concerts and live events still to come in the UAE. 1. The Fridge Concert Series Season 50 Special: October 27 at The Fridge Warehouse, Alserkal Avenue, Dubai The Fridge marks the 50th season of its concert series with a reunion night featuring former performers from across its 20-year history. The line-up is being kept under wraps, with collaborations and jam sessions planned for the limited-capacity show. Free; pre-registration required 2. Titize: A Venetian Dream: October 29 to 31 at Dubai Opera Venice is the inspiration for this show mixing circus, theatre, dance and live music. The 10-member cast use acrobatics, clowning and physical theatre to create a dreamlike version of Venice through its masks, waterways and carnival traditions. Shows at 2pm and 8pm; tickets from Dh275 3. Nass: October 30 at The Arts Centre at NYU Abu Dhabi French-Moroccan choreographer Fouad Boussouf brings together seven male dancers in a work connecting hip-hop movement with the ritual dimensions of North African music. The title takes inspiration from Moroccan group Nass El Ghiwane and draws parallels between their search for identity and the origins of hip-hop. Show starts 7.30pm; tickets from Dh52.50 4. Abdul Majeed Abdullah: October 31 at Coca-Cola Arena, Dubai Saudi singer Abdul Majeed Abdullah returns to Dubai with a catalogue spanning decades of Khaleeji and Arabic pop. Known for a distinctive vocal style that has helped shape Gulf music, his songs include Mn Mithlek , Tetnafasek Denyaay , Yabn Elawadem and Ghazal Ma Yensady . Show starts 9.30pm; tickets from Dh495 5. Riverdance: October 31 and November 1 at Etihad Arena, Abu Dhabi Riverdance returns to the UAE with a production marking the Irish dance show’s 30th anniversary. The staging retains Bill Whelan’s Grammy Award-winning score while introducing updated choreography, costumes, lighting, projection and motion graphics. Performance times vary; tickets from Dh215 6. Benjamin Clementine: November 1 at Dubai Opera British singer, pianist and composer Benjamin Clementine performs a programme combining experimental pop, contemporary classical music, jazz and poetry. His debut album, At Least for Now , won the Mercury Prize, while later recordings include I Tell a Fly and And I Have Been . Show starts 8pm; tickets from Dh500 7. Jony: November 4 at Coca-Cola Arena, Dubai Russian-Azerbaijani singer Jony is a star Russian pop and built a following with songs including Kamin , Kometa and Ty Besposhchadna . Show starts 9pm; tickets from Dh295 8. Mo Amer: November 6 at Etihad Arena, Abu Dhabi Palestinian-American comedian Mo Amer performs as part of Abu Dhabi Comedy Season. Born in Kuwait to Palestinian parents and raised in the US, his comedy draws on displacement, immigration and life between cultures. Those experiences also shaped Mo , the semi-autobiographical Netflix series he created with Ramy Youssef, which won a Peabody Award in 2023. Show time and ticket prices to be announced 9. Maz Jobrani: November 7 at Etihad Arena, Abu Dhabi Iranian-American comedian Maz Jobrani returns to Abu Dhabi with material exploring immigrant experiences, cultural misunderstandings and family expectations. He previously performed at the inaugural Abu Dhabi Comedy Week in 2024 on a shared bill with Bassem Youssef. Show time and ticket prices to be announced 10. Ministry of Sound Classical: November 7 at Dubai Opera Club anthems are given an orchestral spin as Ministry of Sound Classical brings dance music into the concert hall. Conducted by David Mahoney, the show combines a full orchestra and vocalists with electronic music, lighting and visuals, drawing on tracks associated with decades of club culture. Show time and ticket prices to be announced 11. Abdelkader Secteur: November 8 at Emirates Theatre, Dubai Algerian comedian Abdelkader Secteur returns to Dubai with a stand-up show drawing on family life, cultural traditions and everyday situations. Known for storytelling rooted in North African humour, he follows a previous Dubai appearance last year. Show starts 7.30pm; tickets from Dh195 12. American Ballet Theatre: November 20 at Emirates Palace, Abu Dhabi Dubbed one of the world's greatest dance companies, the American Ballet Theatre will perform works including Frederick Ashton’s Birthday Offering , Jiri Kylian’s Nuages , Brady Farrar’s Trio Elegiaque and Paquita , staged by Natalia Makarova after Marius Petipa. Show starts 8pm, tickets from Dh125 13. Aries Spears: November 21 at Etihad Arena, Abu Dhabi American comedian Aries Spears brings more than three decades of stand-up, impressions and crowd work to Etihad Arena. A former Mad TV cast member, he is known for his celebrity impersonations that include Michael Jackson, Eddie Murphy and Shaquille O'Neal. Doors open 9pm; show starts 10pm; tickets from Dh120 14. Synthony x Faithless: November 21 at Bla Bla by McGettigan's, Dubai Synthony makes its Middle East debut with a full orchestra reworking electronic dance anthems through live instrumentation, vocals and visual production. The night will also feature Faithless Sound System, led by Sister Bliss, with tracks including Insomnia and We Come 1 . Doors open 6pm; tickets from Dh295 15. Trevor Noah: November 25-26 and November 28 and 29 at Dubai Opera Trevor Noah brings a new stand-up show to Dubai across four nights. The Emmy Award-winning South African comedian and former host of The Daily Show has released several Netflix specials, hosts the podcast What Now? with Trevor Noah and is the author of Born a Crime and Into the Uncut Grass . Show starts 8pm; tickets from Dh295 16. Algarabia: November 26 at Emirates Palace, Abu Dhabi Algarabia presents a theatrical production blending flamenco with Arabic poetry, performed by musicians from Spain’s University of Navarra Symphony Orchestra alongside dancers and actors. The work follows the journey of an Arab girl drawn to ancient botanical theory and poetic tradition. Show starts 8pm; tickets from Dh100 17. Bader Saleh: November 27 at The Hive, Dubai Saudi comedian Bader Saleh brings his Bliss of Ignorance stand-up show to Dubai. He rose to prominence through the YouTube series EyshElly and has since worked across television, online comedy and live performance. Show starts 9pm; tickets from Dh175 18. Hiba Tawaji and Ibrahim Maalouf: November 27 at Dubai Opera Hiba Tawaji and Ibrahim Maalouf will unite for a one-night performance at Dubai Opera, with the programme drawing on French musical heritage through a blend of chanson, jazz and contemporary composition. Tawaji’s emotive vocals and Maalouf’s genre-crossing trumpet work make this one of the more distinctive concert pairings on the calendar. Show starts 8.30pm; tickets from Dh355 19. Atif Aslam: November 27 at Coca-Cola Arena, Dubai Atif Aslam returns to Coca-Cola Arena after five consecutive years of sold-out Dubai concerts. The Pakistani singer’s programme will move between Bollywood songs, pop-rock and devotional music, with hits including Tajdar-e-Haram , Jeena Jeena , Pehli Nazar Mein , Dil Diyan Gallan and Aadat . Doors open 9pm; tickets from Dh350 20. Tarkan: November 27 at Etihad Arena, Abu Dhabi Known internationally for the global hit Simarik and a catalogue that has defined Turkish pop for more than two decades, Tarkan is making his Abu Dhabi debut is further proof of Turkish’s pop growing popularity in the region. Show starts 8.30pm; tickets from Dh295 21. Wasla Festival: November 28 at Jubilee Park, Expo City Dubai Lebanese composer and oud player Marcel Khalife headlines the return of Wasla Festival, alongside Palestinian ensemble Le Trio Joubran, Syrian duo TootArd and Emirati-Honduran singers Fatima . Starts 6pm; tickets from Dh350 22. Ramy Sabry: November 28 at Etihad Arena, Abu Dhabi Egyptian singer Ramy Sabry comes to Abu Dhabi with a catalogue of romantic Arabic pop and ballads. His songs include Lama Bywhashny , alongside a wider repertoire centred on love, memory and heartbreak. Doors open 7.30pm; show starts 9pm; tickets from Dh295 23. Artbat Present Upperground: November 28 at Ushuaia Dubai Harbour Experience Ukrainian electronic duo Artbat bring their Upperground event series to Dubai, joined by Miss Monique, R3hab and Italian DJ and producer 7 Skies. The show follows Artbat’s recent reworking of Gotye's Somebody That I Used to Know with David Guetta. Doors open 8pm; tickets from Dh150 24. Verdi’s Opera Gala: November 29 at Emirates Palace, Abu Dhabi Marking 125 years since Giuseppe Verdi’s death, this programme is led by soprano Maria Agresta and tenor Giorgio Berrugi, and includes selections from Nabucco , I Vespri Siciliani , Otello and La Traviata , alongside overtures and duets drawn from Verdi’s wider catalogue. Show starts 8pm; tickets from Dh125 25. Ghostly Kisses: November 29 at Etihad Arena, Abu Dhabi Canadian singer-songwriter Margaux Sauve brings her Ghostly Kisses project to Abu Dhabi as part of her 2026 regional tour. Her music combines atmospheric pop, understated electronic production and intimate vocals, with songs including The City Holds My Heart . Show starts 8pm; tickets from Dh215 26. Andrea Bocelli: December 2 at Etihad Arena, Abu Dhabi Italian tenor Andrea Bocelli brings his 30th Anniversary Romanza World Tour to Abu Dhabi as part of Yasalam Classics. The concert celebrates Romanza , the album that helped establish him internationally and includes songs such as Con te partiro and Vivo per lei . Doors open 6pm; tickets from Dh295 27. The Tsar's Bride by the Bolshoi Theatre: December 2 at Dubai Opera The Bolshoi Theatre begins its first official UAE tour with Rimsky-Korsakov's The Tsar's Bride . Set during the reign of Ivan the Terrible, the opera centres on Marfa, a young woman whose selection as the tsar's bride sets off jealousy, rivalry and political intrigue. Show time and ticket prices to be announced 28. Bolshoi Theatre Orchestra, December 3 The Bolshoi Theatre Orchestra takes centre stage for a symphonic concert on the second night of the company’s first official UAE tour. Showtime and ticket prices TBC 29. Lewis Capaldi and Zara Larsson: December 3 at Etihad Park, Abu Dhabi Lewis Capaldi and Zara Larsson will open the Abu Dhabi Grand Prix 2026 after-race concert series with separate sets at Etihad Park. Capaldi returns to the capital following his Saadiyat Nights performance in January, bringing a catalogue that includes Someone You Loved , Before You Go and Forget Me . Larsson joins the bill with pop staples such as Lush Life , Never Forget You and Symphony , offering a high-tempo contrast to Capaldi’s ballad-driven set. The show launches the four-night programme running alongside the race weekend at Yas Marina Circuit. Showtime yet to be announced; access exclusive to Abu Dhabi Grand Prix ticket holders 30. Jennifer Lopez and Alex Warren: December 4 at Etihad Live, Abu Dhabi Jennifer Lopez returns to Abu Dhabi for the second night of the Grand Prix after-race concert series, sharing the bill with US singer-songwriter Alex Warren. Lopez's catalogue includes If You Had My Love , Waiting for Tonight , Jenny from the Block and On the Floor . Warren makes his UAE debut after the international success of Ordinary . Access exclusive to Abu Dhabi Grand Prix ticket holders 31. Shimza: December 4 at 16/360, Yas Marina Circuit, Abu Dhabi South African DJ Shimza brings his percussion-heavy Afro-tech sound to 16/360 as Abu Dhabi Grand Prix weekend gets under way. Known for extended, hypnotic sets, he has performed across Europe and Africa and collaborated with fellow South African DJ Black Coffee. Access exclusive to selected 16/360 Grand Prix hospitality ticket holders; packages from Dh1,250 32. Mont Rouge and Moojo: December 4 at Bagatelle, W Abu Dhabi, Abu Dhabi Swiss duo Mont Rouge and French DJ Moojo share the Friday bill at Bagatelle's rooftop pop-up during Abu Dhabi Grand Prix weekend. Mont Rouge are known for their Afro-house version of Voyage Voyage , recorded with Francis Mercier and Coco, as well as their remix of Axwell and Sebastian Ingrosso's More Than You Know . Tables from Dh7,000 33. The Nutcracker by the Bolshoi Theatre: December 4 to 6 at Dubai Opera The Nutcracker has become a Dubai Opera tradition, and this year's production will feature the Bolshoi Theatre, with Tchaikovsky's ballet performed by the company's dancers and orchestra. Yuri Grigorovich's choreography follows Marie from a family Christmas celebration into a fantasy world of toys and magic, set to a score containing some of Tchaikovsky's best-known music. Show times and ticket prices to be announced 34. Anyma: December 4 at Yas Gateway Park, Abu Dhabi Italian-American DJ and producer Anyma will perform at Yas Gateway Park as part of the official Abu Dhabi Grand Prix after party concert series. Known for large-scale audiovisual shows and melodic techno, he brought his dazzling live production to the Pyramids of Giza in 2025 and has become one of electronic music’s most distinctive live acts through his work as a solo artist and as one half of Tale of Us. Abu Dhabi Grand Prix ticket holder presales begin on September 10, with general sales opening on September 11; show time and ticket prices to be announced 35. Imagine Dragons: December 5 at Etihad Live, Abu Dhabi Imagine Dragons will headline the Abu Dhabi Grand Prix after-race concert series on Saturday night. Fronted by Dan Reynolds, the US band are known for songs including Believer , Radioactive , Demons , Thunder and It’s Time . The group last performed in Abu Dhabi in 2023, when they sold out Etihad Arena. Showtime yet to be announced; access exclusive to Abu Dhabi Grand Prix ticket holders 36. CamelPhat: December 5 at 16/360, Yas Marina Circuit, Abu Dhabi British electronic duo CamelPhat take over the trackside 16/360 venue on the second night of its Grand Prix programme. Dave Whelan and Mike Di Scala broke through internationally with the Grammy-nominated Cola , while their catalogue also includes Panic Room with Au/Ra and Breathe with Cristoph and Jem Cooke. Access exclusive to selected 16/360 Grand Prix hospitality ticket holders; packages from Dh1,250 37. Gordo: December 5 at Bagatelle, W Abu Dhabi, Abu Dhabi DJ and producer Gordo, formerly known as Carnage, joins Bagatelle's race-weekend programme with his house-focused sound. He contributed to Drake's 2022 album Honestly, Nevermind and released his debut album Diamante in 2024, featuring collaborations with Drake and Maluma. Tables from Dh10,000 38. The Chainsmokers and The Script: December 6 at Etihad Live, Abu Dhabi The Chainsmokers and The Script will close the Abu Dhabi Grand Prix after-race concert series with separate sets on race day. Irish band The Script are known for songs including Breakeven , The Man Who Can’t Be Moved , For the First Time and Hall of Fame . US electronic duo The Chainsmokers bring a catalogue that includes Roses , Don’t Let Me Down , Closer , Paris and Something Just Like This . Showtime yet to be announced; access exclusive to Abu Dhabi Grand Prix ticket holders 39. Black Coffee: December 6 at 16/360, Yas Marina Circuit, Abu Dhabi Grammy-winning South African DJ Black Coffee closes the three-night 16/360 programme on race day with his blend of deep house, African percussion and soulful vocals. His album Subconsciously , featuring collaborations with Pharrell Williams and David Guetta, won the Grammy Award for Best Dance/Electronic Music Album. Access exclusive to selected 16/360 Grand Prix hospitality ticket holders; packages from Dh1,250 40. Carl Cox: December 6 at Bagatelle, W Abu Dhabi, Abu Dhabi British DJ Carl Cox closes Bagatelle's Grand Prix weekend programme. A pioneer of Britain's acid-house movement, he has spent more than four decades playing house and techno and held a 15-year residency at Space Ibiza. His links with motorsport extend beyond the weekend through Carl Cox Motorsport, which he founded in 2013. Tables from Dh10,000 41. Enrico Macias: December 10 at Dubai Opera More than six decades of chanson and Mediterranean music feature in Enrico Macias’s latest Dubai concert. The French-Algerian singer is known for Adieu mon pays , Les filles de mon pays and Enfants de tous pays . The concert is reportedly among his final international appearances. Show starts 8pm; tickets from Dh295 42. Lisa Batiashvili and Giorgi Gigashvili: December 10 at The Arts Centre at NYU Abu Dhabi Georgian musicians Lisa Batiashvili and Giorgi Gigashvili will perform works by Beethoven, Bartok and Franck, alongside a contemporary piece by composer Josef Bardanashvili. Show starts 8pm; tickets from Dh150 43. Minsoo Sohn: December 11 at The Arts Centre at NYU Abu Dhabi Pianist Minsoo Sohn will perform Book One of Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier , presenting the 24 preludes and fugues that explore every major and minor key. The recital highlights both the intellectual depth and emotional breadth of the landmark work. Show starts 8pm; tickets from Dh150 44. Sole DXB: December 11 to 13 at The Square, Nad Al Sheba, Dubai Sole DXB returns with three days of live music, DJ sets, fashion, art and street culture. The line-up includes British singer Lola Young, electronic duo Overmono, jungle producer Nia Archives, Malian musician Fatoumata Diawara, Matthew Herbert, Peter Cat Recording Co, Hajaj, Gia Fu, and Maii and Zeid. Runs from 4pm to 2.30am each day; three-day tickets from Dh495 45. Bamboo and Cup of Joe: December 11 at Dubai World Trade Centre, Dubai Filipino acts Bamboo and Cup of Joe share the stage for a night of OPM at Dubai World Trade Centre. Bamboo brings songs including Masaya , while Cup of Joe's catalogue includes Multo . Show starts 7pm; tickets from Dh129 46. Guy Manoukian: December 11 at Dubai Opera Guy Manoukian marks Dubai Opera's 10th anniversary by returning for his own milestone 10th performance at the venue, following nine sold-out shows. The Lebanese-Armenian pianist and composer blends original work with Arabic melodies and contemporary arrangements, with his repertoire also drawing on the music of Fairouz and Abdel Halim Hafez. Show starts 8pm; tickets from Dh330 47. Mariah Carey: December 12 at Etihad Arena, Abu Dhabi Mariah Carey returns to Abu Dhabi with her Christmastime show, featuring festive songs including All I Want for Christmas Is You , Santa Baby and Christmas (Baby Please Come Home) alongside hits from her wider catalogue. The concert will be her second Abu Dhabi performance of the year, following her Saadiyat Nights show in February. Doors open 7pm; tickets from Dh249 48. Mahmut Orhan: December 12 at Ushuaia Dubai Harbour Experience, Dubai Turkish DJ and producer Mahmut Orhan returns to Dubai Harbour after performing there on New Year's Eve. His sound moves between deep house and indie dance, and he has performed at festivals including Coachella, Ultra Europe and Awakenings. Doors open 8pm; tickets from Dh150 49. Chicago the Musical: December 16 to 20 at Coca-Cola Arena, Dubai The Broadway production of Chicago comes to Coca-Cola Arena for eight performances over five days. Set during the Jazz Age, the musical follows nightclub performer Roxie Hart and vaudeville star Velma Kelly as they compete for public attention while awaiting trial for murder. The score includes All That Jazz , Cell Block Tango and Razzle Dazzle . Performance times vary; tickets from Dh49 50. Denis Matsuev: December 16 at Dubai Opera Russian pianist Denis Matsuev moves between classical repertoire and jazz in a concert titled Classics and Jazz . Show starts 8pm; tickets from Dh350 51. Abracadabra: December 18 and 19 at Dubai Opera Gulf theatre comes to Dubai Opera with Abracadabra , an Arabic language suspense comedy about two struggling theatre groups trying to save their careers. Their plan to stage a new show inside an abandoned theatre is disrupted by strange events, unexpected twists and a series of comic situations. The production runs for about an hour and blends Gulf theatre, suspense and entertainment. Show times vary; tickets from Dh230. 52. Dopa World: December 18 to 20 at Jubilee Park, Expo City Dubai Dopa World is a three-day festival focused on young Arab music, culture and creative businesses. Saint Levant is the first announced artist, with the Palestinian-Algerian performer known for blending Arabic, English and French across songs including Very Few Friends and Deira . The remaining artists are yet to be announced. Doors open 4pm daily; tickets from Dh245 53. Dhafer Youssef: December 19 at The Arts Centre at NYU Abu Dhabi Oud maestro Dhafer Youssef will perform with his quintet, bridging sounds from the East and West through jazz, Arab and North African traditions, as well as European classical and electronic elements. He is expected to perform material from his latest album Shiraz , described as his most personal work to date. Show starts 8pm; tickets from Dh150 54. Yassar Lemghari: December 25 at Emirates Theatre, Dubai Moroccan comedian Yassar Lemghari brings his Lamhayab show to Dubai, performed in Moroccan Darija. His stand-up draws on Moroccan culture and everyday life and follows a series of international performances. Doors open 8pm; show starts 8.30pm; tickets from Dh169 55. Rahat Fateh Ali Khan and Shah Zaman Ali Khan: December 26 at Coca-Cola Arena, Dubai Rahat Fateh Ali Khan returns to Coca-Cola Arena for his eighth appearance at the venue, joined by Shah Zaman Ali Khan. The concert brings together Qawwali, Sufi music and contemporary South Asian songs, with Shah Zaman continuing the musical tradition of the family into a new generation. Show starts 8pm; tickets from Dh95 56. Katy Perry: December 31 at Atlantis, The Palm, Dubai Katy Perry returns to the UAE to headline the New Year's Eve gala at Atlantis The Palm, a year after closing the 2025 Abu Dhabi Grand Prix. The American pop star brings a catalogue including Teenage Dream , Roar , Dark Horse and Firework . The black-tie gala also features a 30-piece live band, entertainment throughout the evening and a midnight fireworks display across Atlantis Dubai on Palm Jumeirah. Doors open 7pm; tickets from Dh6,500 for children and Dh8,500 for adults 57. Vessbroz: December 31 at Cavo, Ramee Dream Hotel, Dubai Vessbroz headline Cavo’s New Year’s Eve party with a set built around electronic house music and Middle East-inspired sounds. The line-up also includes Bazz Key, Qtee Rue, Taina and Hellfox. Doors open 10pm; tickets from Dh150. 58. Tony Ann: January 12, 2027, at Dubai Opera Canadian pianist and composer Tony Ann makes his Dubai debut with a programme blending contemporary piano and classical influences. Known for his viral #playthatword series and the Emotionally Blue, Orange and Red EP trilogy, Ann has also co-written The Chainsmokers tracks Sick Boy and Call You Mine . 59. Swan Lake on Ice: January 14 to 17, 2027, at Dubai Opera Tchaikovsky’s Swan Lake is reimagined on ice by the Imperial Ice Stars, with 24 skaters bringing together figure skating, ballet, aerial movement and theatrical choreography. The production follows the story of Odette, Prince Siegfried and Rothbart, with snowfall, fog, pyrotechnic effects and elaborate costumes adding to the staging. Show times vary by date; auditorium doors open 30 minutes before each performance; tickets from Dh300 60. Buena Vista Social Club Legacy Concert: January 24, 2027 at Dubai Opera Cuban music takes over Dubai Opera with a concert featuring Ibrahim Ferrer Jr, son of Buena Vista Social Club singer Ibrahim Ferrer, alongside veteran laud player Barbarito Torres Billed as Una Noche En La Habana , the show draws on son, bolero and other Cuban traditions associated with the musicians who brought Buena Vista Social Club to international audiences in the late 1990s. Show time and ticket prices to be announced 61. Tamaas Festival: January 29, 2027, at The Arts Centre at NYU Abu Dhabi Tamaas Festival returns with three acts moving between traditional forms and club-orientated production. Moroccan-Swiss musician Sami Galbi combines rai and chaabi with electronic music, while Nigerien guitarist Bombino performs Tuareg desert blues and rock. British collective Ibibio Sound Machine close the evening with West African rhythms, post-punk, disco and electronic music. Festival starts 7pm; free pass upon registration 62. Harry Potter Film Concert Series: February 5 to 6, 2027, at Etihad Arena, Abu Dhabi The UAE National Orchestra accompanies two Harry Potter films across consecutive nights. John Williams’ stirring score for Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban is performed on February 5, followed by Patrick Doyle’s music for Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire on February 6. Doors open 6.30pm; shows start 7.30pm; tickets from Dh120 63. Ramadaniyat – The Handover: February 17, 2027, at The Arts Centre at NYU Abu Dhabi Egyptian oud player Aly Eissa, Alexandrian violinist Ayman Asfour and Belgian-Norwegian keyboard player Jonas Cambien make their UAE debut as The Handover. The trio bring the ritual and folk music of rural Egypt into contact with free improvisation, psychedelic rock and electronic textures. Show starts 9.30pm; tickets from Dh52.50 64. The Phantom of the Opera: March 10 to 28, 2027 at Etihad Arena, Abu Dhabi Andrew Lloyd Webber's The Phantom of the Opera makes its Abu Dhabi debut with a three-week run at Etihad Arena. Based on Gaston Leroux's novel, the musical follows the masked phantom who lives beneath the Paris Opera House and becomes obsessed with soprano Christine Daae. The score includes The Music of the Night , All I Ask of You and the title song. The Abu Dhabi run comes during the musical's 40th anniversary year, following its West End premiere in 1986. Runs from March 10 to 28; tickets from Dh240 65. Unifyd: March 20, 2027 at Etihad Live, Abu Dhabi Arijit Singh, Karan Aujla and Sonu Nigam lead the inaugural Unifyd music festival curated by Bollywood star Shah Rukh Khan. The one-day event will feature more than 15 artists across several stages, spanning Hindi film music, Punjabi music and other strands of Indian culture. General sale opens October 20 at 10.30am through the District app; ticket prices to be announced 66. Tribute to Ziad Rahbani by Faraj Suleiman: March 26, 2027, at The Arts Centre at NYU Abu Dhabi Palestinian composer and pianist Faraj Suleiman returns with a programme dedicated to Lebanese composer, pianist and playwright Ziad Rahbani. Rather than reproducing the original recordings, Suleiman re-orchestrates and re-harmonises the material through contemporary piano, jazz and Arabic composition. Show starts 7.30pm; tickets from Dh78.75 67. A1 and Music Travel Love: April 17, 2027, at Coca-Cola Arena, Dubai British-Norwegian pop group A1 and Canadian duo Music Travel Love will share the stage for the first time in Dubai. A1 are known for hits including Everytime , Caught in the Middle and Like a Rose , while Music Travel Love, formed by twin brothers Bob and Clint Moffatt, are known for acoustic covers and originals including Nothing’s Gonna Change my Love for You . Show starts 8pm; tickets from Dh295 68. Richard Marx: June 6, 2027 at Coca-Cola Arena, Dubai American singer-songwriter Richard Marx comes to Dubai with a catalogue spanning more than four decades. His best-known songs include Right Here Waiting , Hazard , Hold On to the Nights and Satisfied , while his songwriting credits include hits recorded by artists such as Luther Vandross, Keith Urban and NSYNC. Show starts 8pm; tickets from Dh225

title: NPFL Preview: Rivers United face Bendel test as Ikorodu City, Shooting Stars clash in Lagos
body:
The 2026/2027 Nigeria Premier Football League (NPFL) season enters another crucial phase, with Matchday 10 serving up a stern test for unbeaten leaders Rivers United. A fiercely contested Southwest derby between the Oga boys, Ikorodu City, and Ibadan landlords, Shooting Stars, plus several key battles that could reshape the standings, are also on the cards.
Port Harcourt-based Rivers United will test their impressive defensive record against Bendel Insurance in Benin City, while former champions Enyimba face a tough trip to Nasarawa United. In Umuahia, Abia Warriors welcome Niger Tornadoes, with both sides seeking valuable points as the campaign gathers momentum.
The matchday has already produced its first result, with Katsina United and Plateau United sharing the points in a 2-2 draw in an all-northern encounter. The result leaves both sides with reasons to reflect on a contest that offered goals but denied either team maximum points.
With several clubs separated by only a handful of points, Sunday’s fixtures could prove significant in the race for the top positions and the struggle to establish consistency.
Rivers United head into Matchday 10 at the top of the NPFL table, level on 17 points with Enugu Rangers, who have two games in hand and have played one game fewer. The Port Harcourt club, however, remain unbeaten after nine matches, with four wins, five draws, and only two goals conceded.
That defensive record has made Rivers one of the most difficult teams to beat this season, but their tendency to share the points means Finidi George’s side cannot afford to become complacent.
Their latest outing ended in a goalless draw against Barau FC, extending their unbeaten run but also representing another opportunity to collect maximum points that slipped away.
Standing in their way this time are Bendel Insurance, who will welcome the league leaders to the Samuel Ogbemudia Stadium with ambitions of delivering a statement victory on home soil.
The Benin Arsenal have been inconsistent, alternating between wins and defeats, but their attacking threat makes them a dangerous opponent. With 14 goals scored in their opening eight matches, Bendel possess the firepower to test even the league’s most disciplined defence.
For Rivers, the challenge will be to maintain their defensive organisation while turning possession and chances into goals. Another draw would preserve their unbeaten record, but a win could strengthen their grip on top spot and warn their title rivals.
Bendel, meanwhile, have the opportunity to end Rivers’ unbeaten run, climb the log as a result, and announce themselves as serious contenders for a place among the leading teams.
The Southwest derby between Ikorodu City and Shooting Stars at the Mobolaji Johnson Arena in Lagos promises another intriguing encounter, with local bragging rights and crucial league points at stake.
Both teams will be eager to build momentum, although their recent fortunes have differed.
Ikorodu City have struggled for consistency, falling 2-1 to Niger Tornadoes in their last league outing. They will be determined to respond in front of their supporters and avoid allowing another result to derail their campaign.
Shooting Stars, on the other hand, head into the contest after ending their winless run with a 3-1 victory over Ranchers Bees in Ibadan. The Oluyole Warriors had gone five matches without a win before that result, and the victory should provide a timely boost ahead of their trip to Lagos.
The Oluyole Warriors will hope the win marks a turning point in their season, but an away trip to Ikorodu City presents a different challenge.
For Ikorodu City, the derby offers a chance to restore confidence and climb the standings. For Shooting Stars, it is a chance to build on their recent recovery and prove their victory over Ranchers Bees was more than a reprieve.
Enyimba will travel to Lafia to face Nasarawa United in a fixture with important implications for both clubs’ ambitions this season.
The People’s Elephant have endured an inconsistent campaign at best, and will be keen to collect points on the road as they attempt to establish themselves among the leading sides.
Their last league outing ended in a goalless draw against Warri Wolves, leaving them with work to do up front. Enyimba will need a sharper edge in front of goal if they want to leave Lafia with maximum points.
Nasarawa United, meanwhile, will look to make the most of home advantage. Their 2-0 victory over Inter Lagos in their previous match provided a positive result, and they will be eager to maintain that momentum against one of Nigerian football’s most decorated clubs.
The hosts have an opportunity to strengthen their position with another victory, but Enyimba’s experience makes them a difficult opponent to underestimate.
For both teams, the encounter represents more than a routine league fixture. It is an opportunity to build consistency and avoid losing further ground as the table begins to take shape.
Abia Warriors will welcome Niger Tornadoes in another fixture that could shape both clubs’ campaigns.
The Umuahia side will look to capitalise on home advantage and take all three points, while Niger Tornadoes arrive with confidence after defeating Ikorodu City 2-1 in their last league outing.
That victory gave the Ikon Allah boys a much-needed boost, and they will hope to carry the momentum into another challenging away fixture.
Abia Warriors, however, will be determined to make life difficult for their visitors. Home performances could prove crucial to their ambitions this season, especially as the competition for points intensifies.
Niger Tornadoes have already shown they can hurt opponents, but maintaining that attacking threat away from home will be essential if they want to leave Umuahia with a positive result.
Warri Wolves will host Kano Pillars in the “Sai Masu Gida”, a contest between two sides looking to strengthen their positions and build momentum.
The Sai Masu Gida will be hoping to return to winning ways after their recent results, while Warri Wolves will look to make their home advantage count.
The fixture offers both teams a chance to secure valuable points, but the side that manages the key moments better could come away with the advantage.
Kano Pillars possess the experience to make the contest uncomfortable for their hosts, but Warri Wolves will be determined to avoid surrendering points on home soil.
Barau FC will take on Kwara United in another important encounter, with both sides looking to improve their standings.
Barau have shown they can compete with the league’s leading teams, as shown by their goalless draw with Rivers United. They will now look to turn that defensive resilience into a winning performance against Kwara United.
The visitors, meanwhile, will be eager to bounce back after Abia Warriors held them to a 1-1 draw in Ilorin. Dropping points at home would have been frustrating, and they will hope to respond with a stronger away performance.
The contest could come down to which team makes better use of its opportunities, particularly if both sides approach the game cautiously.
Kun Khalifat FC will welcome Inter Lagos in a fixture that offers both clubs an opportunity to improve their fortunes.
Kun Khalifat have shown flashes of competitiveness this season, but they will need greater consistency to move away from the lower reaches of the standings.
Inter Lagos, meanwhile, travel in search of a response after losing 2-0 to Nasarawa United in their previous outing.
Both teams will recognise the fixture’s importance, with a positive result potentially providing the momentum needed to improve their positions in the coming weeks.
Home advantage could be significant for Kun Khalifat, but Inter Lagos will be determined to make amends for their recent setback.
The Matchday 10 programme has also been affected by rearrangements.
Ranchers Bees’ scheduled meeting with Doma United has been postponed. Meanwhile, the encounter between Sporting Lagos and Enugu Rangers has also been moved to a later date due to Rangers’ continental commitments. New dates are to be confirmed.
The absence of those fixtures means the two clubs involved will have to wait to add to their points tallies, while the remaining teams can take advantage of the situation.
Rangers, who remain among the early pacesetters despite having played fewer matches than some rivals, will monitor the results closely as the top-of-the-table race intensifies.
Matchday 10 arrives as early standings begin to reveal which teams can sustain a challenge and which still have significant work to do.
Rivers United have established themselves as a difficult side to beat, but their trip to Bendel Insurance will provide a stern examination of their unbeaten run. The People’s Elephant, Enyimba, face a demanding assignment in Lafia. Meanwhile, the Southwest derby between Ikorodu City and Shooting Stars offers both teams a chance to claim local bragging rights and valuable points.
With Katsina United and Plateau United already sharing the spoils, attention now turns to Sunday’s fixtures, where the leading sides will look to strengthen their positions, and those lower down the table will be desperate to avoid falling further behind.
As the 2026/2027 NPFL season gathers momentum, every point matters, and Matchday 10 could provide another important twist in an increasingly competitive title race.

title: Explosions Heard In Saudi Capital As Fight With Houthis Continue
body: Explosions rang out in the Saudi capital on Sunday, as the kingdom was due to reopen Riyadh international airport despite repeated attacks by Yemen’s Houthis. Saudi Arabia, which leads a military coalition fighting the Iran-backed Houthis, has faced a barrage of strikes from the group in recent weeks. The fighting erupted after a years-long truce between the Houthis and Yemen’s Riyadh-backed government fell apart. Riyadh’s international airport said flights would resume on Sunday after a two-week closure following the Houthi strikes. However, it remained unclear to what extent the airport was operational. The Houthi fighters have carried out waves of strikes on the airport, including an attack this month that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade. The group has also targeted oil infrastructure and other sites, with the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen announcing on Sunday it had intercepted 10 Houthi missiles fired at southern Saudi Arabia. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree warned that Riyadh airport was still “unsafe” and a “military target”. “The Yemeni Armed Forces warn all international, regional and local airlines — as well as staff and travellers — against using King Khalid Airport in Riyadh, as it is unsafe and serves as a military target for our forces,” he said. “The Saudi regime shall bear the consequences of any operations at the airport.” Attack warning An AFP journalist in the city heard three explosions in the early hours of Sunday, with residents receiving alert messages for a “hostile aerial threat” urging them to stay in a safe place. The warning came as the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it had downed a ballistic missile launched by the group towards Riyadh, as well as two drones in the capital area. “Air defences intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward Riyadh,” the coalition posted on X. Later Sunday morning, the coalition said its forces intercepted a cruise missile fired by the Houthis at the kingdom’s southern city of Khamis Mushait. Attacks appeared to target areas across the south, with warnings also issued for Abha city and Namas Governorate. “The bombardment has been very heavy since this morning — may God keep us safe. Everything is shaking because of the explosions,” one resident in Khamis Mushait told AFP Sunday on condition of anonymity. The attacks came after the Houthi fighters said that — in the space of 24 hours — they targeted three Saudi airports, including in Riyadh, energy installations, a pipeline and an air base. The Saudi civil defence agency said it had also responded to falling debris in the Mecca and Medina regions on Saturday after intercepting two Houthi missiles. The Houthis denied targeting the cities, the two holiest in Islam, calling the Saudi claim a “huge lie”. The Houthis also fired at the southern Yemeni city of Aden, the interim seat of the Saudi-backed government, saying they targeted a naval base and military camp overseen by Saudi forces. The flare-up in Yemen, with the Houthis taking control of the entire Red Sea coast in a lightning offensive last month, has further destabilised the region and disrupted oil markets. The Houthi attacks have dealt a blow to Saudi Arabia, the world’s biggest exporter of crude, disrupting businesses, airlines and residents, and rattling its drive to shift its international image. AFP The post Explosions Heard In Saudi Capital As Fight With Houthis Continue appeared first on Channels Television .

title: North Korea Expands Missiles and Drones With Russian Help
body:
North Korea has advanced its ballistic missile systems and established mass production lines for strike drones with technical and operational assistance from Russia, The New York Times reported.
Moscow is transferring military technologies, telemetry feedback, and operational expertise to Pyongyang in exchange for North Korean ammunition, labor, and combat troops deployed in support of Russia’s war effort in Ukraine.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
In early October, North Korea conducted a test launch of a tactical ballistic missile that Pyongyang claimed is capable of delivering a nuclear warhead.
South Korean and Japanese defense tracking systems recorded the munition traveling approximately 700 kilometers (435 miles), whereas state media in Pyongyang asserted the missile achieved an operational flight range of 1,000 kilometers (621 miles).
Departing from routine diplomatic protocols that traditionally limit Seoul to brief statements of condemnation following Northern missile tests, South Korea conducted its first operational test of a domestically developed hypersonic ballistic missile five days later.
The test launch was observed in person by South Korean President Lee Jae-myung, reflecting growing institutional concern in Seoul regarding Pyongyang’s accelerated technological timeline.
Western intelligence and defense analysts observe that Pyongyang is leveraging Russian operational data detailing how North Korean weapons perform in real combat environments against modern Western-supplied air defense systems.
Defense analyst Anton Ponomarenko noted that telemetry and performance feedback provided by the Russian military have enabled North Korean engineers to refine the guidance accuracy and terminal maneuverability of tactical ballistic missiles, increasing the conventional and nuclear strike risk posed to South Korea.
Concurrently, Moscow has assisted Pyongyang in establishing domestic industrial manufacturing lines for loitering munitions and strike drones.
Pyongyang has adapted lessons from the armed conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East , where cost-effective unmanned platforms have repeatedly saturated and depleted advanced, high-cost air defense networks.
During North Korean military drills conducted last month, an integrated swarm of unmanned aerial vehicles conducted synchronized saturation strikes against an island target while cruise and ballistic missiles launched simultaneous strikes from multiple vectors.
Defense specialists emphasize that countering coordinated drone-swarm and missile saturation tactics could compel South Korea and its regional allies to overhaul integrated air and missile defense postures at substantial financial cost.
The reciprocal technology transfers underscore the deepening military axis between Moscow and Pyongyang following the signing of a comprehensive strategic partnership agreement during Russian President Vladimir Putin’s visit to Pyongyang in June 2024, which codified a mutual defense clause.
In a birthday dispatch addressed to Putin on Oct. 7, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un reaffirmed “invariable support” for Moscow, characterizing Russia’s war in Ukraine as a “sacred war of justice” and pledging to expand bilateral strategic alignment.
The partnership encompasses significant conventional transfers and frontline force commitments. North Korea has supplied artillery munitions and ballistic missiles to the Russian military while deploying an estimated 14,000 to 15,000 military personnel to Russian, including roughly 10,000 combat infantry and 1,000 military engineers deployed in the Kursk region.
According to casualty assessments compiled by South Korea’s National Intelligence Service (NIS), approximately 6,000 North Korean soldiers deployed in support of Russian operations have been killed or wounded in combat , reinforcing Pyongyang’s reliance on Russian technological reciprocity to compensate for troop and material losses.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Zelensky: Russia launches 1,600 guided bombs, 48 missiles and nearly 2,300 attack drones at Ukraine in one week
body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky reported this on Facebook , according to Ukrinform.
“This week alone, Russia has fired approximately 1,600 guided bombs, 48 missiles of various types—including ballistic missiles—and nearly 2,300 attack drones at Ukraine. Unfortunately, there are casualties and injuries from these brutal strikes almost every day,” Zelensky said.
He noted that four people were killed and 22 others were wounded—including an 11-year-old girl—as a result of Russian shelling in the Dnipropetrovsk region that evening. In Vinnytsia, a Russian drone struck a high-rise building, wounding six people. In Kharkiv, the Russians first struck a construction supply store and then cynically launched a second strike against the emergency services that had arrived at the scene. Rescue workers were injured. “There were also strikes last night on thermal power plants, substations, coal mines, grain silos, shopping centers, and a postal terminal. There is damage in nine regions,” the President noted.
He emphasized that this is precisely how Russia responds to diplomacy and efforts to end its isolation, and it is very important that support for pro-life advocates not wane alongside the negotiation track.
“We need to unblock the delivery of interceptors for the ‘Patriots,’ which has already been agreed upon by the Europeans. We need to continue supporting Ukraine’s combat aviation to defend against ‘Shahed’ drones. Every such defense package, especially ahead of winter, helps save lives,” the head of state noted.
As reported by Ukrinform, Zelensky stated that the Russians will intensify their ballistic attacks against Ukraine, especially as supplies of interceptor missiles to Ukraine decrease.

title: Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark moves his prediction for self-improving AI forward to 2027
body:
A new benchmark called TasteVal measures how well AI systems design experiments on their own and interpret the results. The findings show an unusually steep improvement curve.

That capability has roughly doubled every three months since December 2025, according to Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark. The research lab P-Zero Research calls it "research taste," meaning the ability to pick the right experiments and draw the right conclusions from them. The best model tested outperformed a comparison group of 24 human experts at a fraction of the cost.
