Clark co-founded Anthropic and writes the Import AI newsletter. Based on the numbers, he now believes recursive self-improvement (RSI), where AI systems develop their own successors, could become possible as early as 2027. He had previously expected 2028.

The benchmark doesn't prove that AI systems are already improving themselves, since it only captures a narrow slice of scientific work. But it does show where the debate is heading, away from raw model performance and toward the question of how much independent research work language models can actually take on.
TasteVal only measures part of the picture
P-Zero Research defines research taste as three abilities: identifying which research questions are worth pursuing, designing experiments to answer them, and correctly interpreting the results. TasteVal only tests the last two. Choosing the most promising research direction is often considered the core of scientific intuition, but in TasteVal that decision is already made for the model.

Each of the eight tasks specifies a fixed research goal from AI model development, along with a measurable score. The tasks cover areas like training data selection, pretraining and fine-tuning language models, training on human preferences, and defending against adversarial prompts.

The model decides which experiment to run next and uses the results to guide its following step. To keep coding skill from skewing the outcome, a fixed coding agent runs all experiments on a single Nvidia H100 GPU. Each run ends after 40 GPU-hours of compute or 120 hours of wall-clock time.

The human baseline came from 24 experts who had recently worked at places like OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Nvidia, and Microsoft Research. They tackled the same tasks, with at least two people on each one. The best human attempt per task served as the benchmark.
Research taste measured through compute efficiency
To make research taste quantifiable, P-Zero Research translates it into compute efficiency. The reasoning is that experiment compute is scarce in AI research, so picking the right experiments and reading their results correctly means fewer runs and more progress on the same budget.

The lab draws on its "AI Futures Model," which predicts that experiment compute becomes the biggest bottleneck once coding is automated. So TasteVal measures how much compute a model needs to match the experts' scores. A model that gets there with half the compute has twice the research taste by this definition. P-Zero Research calls this ratio the compute multiplier.

The top model, Anthropic's Opus 5.5, hit a compute multiplier of 2.3, reaching expert-level scores with less than half the compute. The statistical range runs from 1.15 to 4.37, though. At the low end, the model would barely lead. A single run cost roughly one-thirtieth of what an expert attempt cost on average.

Across several model generations, the compute multiplier has roughly doubled every three months since December 2025. The uncertainty is large here too, with the reported doubling time ranging from 1.7 to 5.0 months.

[caption id="attachment_63367" align="alignnone" width="770"] According to P-Zero Research, the research taste of leading AI models has roughly doubled every three months since December 2025. | Image: P-Zero Research[/caption]

In prior years, model research taste grew much more slowly. The curve only steepened around the turn of 2025 into 2026. Whether that's a lasting trend can't be determined from a single benchmark, and the authors themselves admit their results may overstate "how quickly research taste is improving." The tasks can be checked quickly and cheaply, which is the kind of task AI labs find easiest to optimize for. The comparison group also didn't include any top-tier researchers.
Clark pulls his timeline forward
Clark has long called creativity the key factor in how fast AI systems can improve themselves. Earlier this year, he wrote that models hadn't shown this ability at any groundbreaking scale. He now points to progress in mathematical breakthroughs and benchmarks like TasteVal as signs that this is changing.

In a long essay in May, Clark had offered more cautious numbers. He put the odds of a system that independently trains a stronger successor at roughly 60 percent by the end of 2028 and 30 percent by 2027. That forecast comes from someone who co-founded the company whose model tops the benchmark, which adds a layer of bias to the prediction.
Critics had drawn the line at exactly this capability
TasteVal matters because it measures the exact capability that skeptics had flagged as a barrier to a major AI breakthrough. AI researcher Herbie Bradley pushed back on Clark's May essay, arguing that while models could plausibly take over the work of junior researchers, more demanding skills like research taste, creativity, and coherent long-term research planning were nowhere in sight.

When it comes to planning and evaluating experiments, TasteVal pushes against that assessment, though it says nothing about choosing a long-term research agenda.

How wide the practical gap remains shows up in a study on AI development using AI agents led by a team at Fudan University. The researchers analyzed the development of their own model and found that AI agents contributed up to 55 percent of methodology proposals, but humans still made over 85 percent of the final decisions. The authors noted it remains unclear how AI can generate diverse research directions and assess their value before results are in, and that's exactly the kind of decision TasteVal takes off the models' plate.
The debate is shifting
The benchmark arrives in the middle of a debate the major AI labs kicked off themselves. In June, Anthropic wrote that recursive self-improvement hasn't been achieved yet but "could come sooner than most institutions are prepared for" Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei now calls for a controlled slowdown in AI development, while OpenAI acknowledges that fully autonomous RSI isn't happening yet and says it should only be pursued if human oversight is guaranteed.

TasteVal shifts what counts as progress. For a long time, the focus was on how well models solve well-defined tasks like math problems or coding challenges, but now the question is increasingly whether they can make the decisions that push research forward.

If the trend P-Zero Research measured holds up in other tests, the implications cut both ways. AI development would get faster and cheaper, but at the same time a growing share of the research would become harder for humans to verify, because models would be planning and evaluating their own experiments.

title: Uba Sani: Bond Between North, Tinubu Strong
body: Governor Uba Sani of Kaduna State has assured President Bola Ahmed Tinubu that the northern part of the country stands firmly with him, saying the bond between the people of the region and the President remains strong. The governor stated this in a statement on Saturday, released after the flag-off of the All Progressives Congress (APC) 2027 presidential campaign in Kaduna. He said the event, which he described as historic, affirmed the strength of the APC and its shared resolve to ensure Tinubu’s re-election in the forthcoming general elections. Sani noted that the number of citizens who came out to welcome the President demonstrated the confidence they have in the Tinubu-led administration, saying the reception was an expression of the strong bond between the president and the people. Akume: Any Northerner contesting 2027 Presidency is the region’s enemy Bandits Kill 7 Vigilantes, Abduct Over 30 Residents in Zamfara Community “It was a profound honour for Kaduna State to host the historic flag-off of the All Progressives Congress presidential campaign, an occasion that affirmed the strength of our party, the cohesion of our leadership and our shared resolve to secure a second term for His Excellency, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, GCFR. “The presence of governors, party leaders, stakeholders and supporters lent this gathering exceptional significance. Above all, the multitude of citizens who lined the streets from the airport to the stadium to welcome Mr President gave eloquent expression to their confidence in his leadership. Their reception conveyed a message whose meaning was unmistakable: the bond between the President and our people remains strong.” Uba Sani said. He commended Tinubu for his administration’s interventions in Kaduna and other states in the North West subregion, adding that the north would mobilise to ensure his victory in the 2027 poll. “Across Kaduna and the wider North-West, the Renewed Hope Agenda finds practical expression in investments in infrastructure, education, healthcare, agriculture, transportation and other critical sectors. “These interventions speak to the everyday concerns of our citizens and the enduring aspirations of our communities. They have strengthened public confidence and deepened our conviction that the progress already achieved must be sustained and consolidated. “We recognise that continuity carries a responsibility: to build upon these foundations with renewed purpose, sustained commitment and an unwavering focus on the wellbeing of our people. This is the spirit in which we approach the task ahead. Our unity must now find expression in collective endeavour. “From Kaduna, our message is clear and unequivocal: the North stands firmly with President Tinubu. United in purpose and resolute in conviction, we are prepared to mobilise our people for a decisive victory in January 2027. “Together, we will work to secure his renewed mandate and advance the promise of a stronger, more prosperous Nigeria.” Sani added.

title: More Lula, Or Back To The Bolsonaros? Brazil Votes In Cliffhanger
body: Brazilians headed to the polls on Sunday, facing a stark choice: another four years under veteran leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva or a return to the right under Senator Flavio Bolsonaro. It is the final electoral battle for Lula, who turns 81 next week and is hoping to pull off a dramatic turnaround after a shock second-place finish in the first round to the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro. Final polls showed the two candidates neck-and-neck. Sunday’s runoff will determine whether Brazil remains one of Latin America’s few leftist nations or joins a regional swing to the right championed by US President Donald Trump, who has not openly endorsed the son of his ally. Lula, who is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, has pitched himself as a bulwark against US interference and democratic backsliding and promised to expand social protections. Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, has vowed to crack down on crime and slash government spending, while handing Brazil to “the Lord Jesus Christ,” with a message of change that won over Brazilians looking for something new. “This is about renewal, enough of the same old thing,” 67-year-old retiree Eduardo Viana told AFP, adding that Lula “says he governs for the poor… just look, people can’t even go to the supermarket.” Flavio Bolsonaro presents himself as more moderate than his firebrand father, who is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for an attempted coup bid after his 2022 election loss. He vows that, if elected, his first act will be to free Jair Bolsonaro, a deeply divisive figure in Brazil whose legacy loomed large over the campaign of his eldest son. After its first-round defeat, the left swung into action with massive rallies declaring “Never Again Bolsonaro,” where protesters recalled the former president’s chaotic handling of the Covid pandemic, devastation of the Amazon rainforest and cuts to public programs. Deforestation of the world’s largest rainforest has hit its lowest level in four decades under Lula. Yet, as the El Nino weather phenomenon fueled fires that choked Amazonian cities with smoke in recent weeks, climate change barely featured in the campaign. Polling stations will close at 5:00 pm local time (2000 GMT), and results are expected within hours. Fed up with crime Lula, revered for social welfare programs that lifted millions out of poverty, made a dramatic comeback to office in 2022 elections after a massive corruption scandal saw him jailed for over 18 months. The charges, annulled on procedural grounds, have continued to haunt him. In his third term he has overseen a drop in inflation and unemployment, and lifted millions out of hunger, but voters complain about the cost of living and a sense of insecurity. Lula’s famed social policies became a point of tension as he expanded welfare programs during the campaign. Critics want the government to rein in spending. “Even if people call it handouts, for us, they were an enormous help. Because anyone who has ever gone hungry knows not to take these programs for granted,” said Walter dos Santos, 56, who lives in northeastern Brazil, a bastion of support for the president, who hails from the same region. The day after After his first-round blow, Lula revamped his social media strategy, turning to video selfies and even buying his first cellphone. A fierce social media battle drew in Meta, parent company of WhatsApp, Facebook and Instagram, which Lula’s campaign accused of favouring his opponent with “algorithmic manipulation.” Meta has denied this but acknowledged that some of Lula’s campaign ads had been mistakenly deactivated due to technical errors. Whoever wins, Brazil is facing a bruising election aftermath. “If the left wins, it faces four years with a hostile Congress and threats of impeachment,” said political analyst Thomas Traumann, referring to sweeping legislative gains by the right. “If the far right wins, it will be a government of retribution, directed at the Supreme Court,” hated by the right after its conviction of Jair Bolsonaro over the attempted coup. Flavio Bolsonaro has said he would seek the impeachment of Supreme Court Judge Alexandre de Moraes, who led the case against his father. AFP The post More Lula, Or Back To The Bolsonaros? Brazil Votes In Cliffhanger appeared first on Channels Television .

title: UN urges probe into deadly Abyei drone attacks
body: The United Nations Security Council has called for those responsible for deadly drone attacks near Amiet Market and Todach in the disputed Abyei area to be held accountable, warning that attacks targeting civilians could constitute war crimes. South Sudanese officials have blamed the Sudanese Armed Forces for the attacks, which took place on Monday, 19 October, and killed and injured civilians, including women and children. In a statement issued on Friday, 23 October, the council condemned the attacks and expressed condolences to the families of those killed and the affected communities. It also wished those injured a full and speedy recovery. The council said it was gravely concerned that the death toll could rise as the United Nations Interim Security Force for Abyei (UNISFA) continued to verify the casualties. It said international humanitarian law prohibits attacks targeting civilians and civilian objects, reminding all parties to the conflict of their obligations to protect civilians. The council called for a full, transparent and prompt investigation into the attacks, stressing that those responsible must be held accountable. It also reaffirmed that Abyei must remain demilitarised and free of all forces other than UNISFA, calling on all actors to cease military operations and end any occupation of the area. The council reaffirmed its support for UNISFA and urged all parties to work with the mission to ensure the safety and security of civilians, humanitarian workers and peacekeepers. Abyei is a disputed area claimed by Sudan and South Sudan. A 2005 peace agreement provided for a referendum on whether the area should join Sudan or South Sudan, but the vote has never been held because of disagreements over voter eligibility and other issues. The UN Security Council established UNISFA in 2011 to help maintain security in the area. The post UN urges probe into deadly Abyei drone attacks appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: What happens at a polling unit? A step-by-step guide to voting in Nigeria
body: Sekinat Osundiji A polling unit is where voters go to cast their ballots during an election. It is also where election officials verify voters’ identities, issue ballot papers, and count votes after voting ends. For many Nigerians, understanding what happens at a polling unit can help them prepare for election day and know what to expect when they arrive to vote. Here is how the process works. Voters arrive at their polling units On election day, registered voters go to the polling units where their names appear on the voters’ register. They are expected to check their polling unit before leaving home to avoid going to the wrong location. At the polling unit, officials organise voters and direct them to the appropriate queues. Security personnel may also be present to maintain order and prevent disruptions. Election officials verify voters Before voting, officials check the voters’ register to confirm that each person is registered at that polling unit. The voter’s identity is then verified using the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS), which is used by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) for voter accreditation. The system checks the voter’s details and may use fingerprint or facial recognition, depending on the circumstances. If accreditation is unsuccessful, officials follow INEC’s prescribed procedures. Only voters who meet the accreditation requirements are allowed to proceed to vote. Voters receive their ballot papers After accreditation, election officials issue ballot papers for the elections taking place. Depending on the election, voters may receive separate ballot papers for positions such as president, governor, senator or member of the House of Representatives. Officials explain how to mark the ballot correctly. Voters must follow the instructions to ensure their choices are properly recorded. Voters mark their choices in private Voters proceed to the designated voting area, where they mark their ballot papers in secret. They select their preferred candidate or party by following the instructions printed on the ballot paper. Maintaining secrecy is important because no one should be forced to reveal their vote or told whom to support. After marking the ballot, the voter folds it as directed and places it in the appropriate ballot box. Voting closes and votes are counted When voting ends, officials follow INEC’s procedures for closing the poll. At the polling unit, ballot papers are sorted and counted in the presence of authorised party agents, observers and other permitted persons. The votes are counted according to the candidates or parties they represent. Officials also account for rejected ballots, which are ballot papers that cannot be counted as valid votes under the applicable rules. The counting process is expected to be transparent, allowing those present to observe and raise concerns through the proper channels. Results are announced at the polling unit After counting, the presiding officer records the results on the prescribed result sheet. The results are announced at the polling unit, and party agents and other authorised persons can observe the process. Where applicable, the results are uploaded electronically through INEC’s designated result-transmission system. The polling-unit result is then taken through the appropriate collation process, where results from different polling units are combined at higher levels. The result announced at one polling unit does not, by itself, determine the overall winner of the election. What can voters do if something goes wrong? Voters who experience problems, including difficulties with accreditation, disputes over voting procedures or suspected irregularities, can raise their concerns with the presiding officer. They can also report incidents to authorised election officials or security personnel where appropriate. Party agents and accredited observers may document incidents and report them through the relevant channels. Voters should avoid violence, intimidation or actions that could disrupt the process. Election complaints should be handled through the procedures established by INEC and the relevant legal authorities. Why the polling unit matters The polling unit is the starting point of the election results process. Every valid vote recorded there contributes to the results that are collated across the country. Understanding the process helps voters know their rights, follow the correct procedures and recognise when something may be wrong. For voters, election day is not simply about arriving at a polling unit and choosing a candidate. It also involves accreditation, ballot secrecy, transparent counting and the proper recording of results. Each stage plays a role in ensuring that the votes cast are properly accounted for. The post What happens at a polling unit? A step-by-step guide to voting in Nigeria appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Teodoro warns PMA of ‘weaponization of information’ as warfare moves beyond battlefield
body: BAGUIO CITY, Philippines – Wars are no longer fought only with guns, ships, and aircraft. Information itself can be weaponized, and future military leaders must know how to deal with it. Defense Secretary Gilberto “Gibo” Teodoro Jr. raised that warning during the Philippine Military Academy’s 128th Foundation Anniversary on Saturday, October 24, pointing to the “pervasive weaponization of information” as one of the security challenges that military institutions can no longer afford to treat as secondary. Teodoro said technological advances, geopolitical developments, disruptions to supply chains, and other changes can emerge quickly and carry consequences for the security of states and individuals. Some of these changes, he said, are not even the result of carefully planned government action but may come from technological breakthroughs or decisions by major global players that force everyone else to adjust. The military, he said, must be able not only to respond but also to build leaders capable of managing organizations through that uncertainty. For the Philippines, Teodoro said, that means strengthening the institutions needed to protect “our most sacred sovereignty, territorial integrity, and dignity as a Filipino people.” Teodoro is among the most vocal in the Philippine government over China’s actions against the Philippines in the West Philippine Sea, enough for China to bar him from entering the country as well as from engaging in “any transaction, cooperation or other activities” with organizations or individuals in China. ‘Tall order’ Teodoro said the changing security environment also affects what PMA is expected to produce. “We have to produce in this academy war fighters, make no bones about it. Every graduate of this institution is a war fighter,” he said. He was quick to explain that he was not referring only to soldiers engaged in combat. “War fighting is not confined to combat operations and kinetic operations. War fighting spans the whole gamut of activities that will preserve the national objectives of any state,” he said. That includes intelligence, analysis, logistics, personnel support, and the people who keep operations going behind the front line. “Every person in uniform is a war fighter. Every member of the civilian human resource team of the Department of National Defense and the Armed Forces of the Philippines is a war fighter,” he said. For PMA, this means doing two difficult jobs within the cadets’ four years at Fort del Pilar. The academy must give them an education that can meet Philippine standards and stand alongside peer institutions in countries the Philippines works with. At the same time, it must produce junior officers ready to serve in the Armed Forces and, beginning three years from now, the Philippine Coast Guard. Those graduates, Teodoro said, must leave with the proper military ethics, duties, responsibilities, and basic tactical skills required of their respective services. “That is a tall order,” he said. ‘Today is not fast enough’ Teodoro also had a message for defense planners: Think bigger. Move faster. “The Philippines cannot afford to be conservative in its planning,” he said. If the country plans cautiously while similarly situated states are more ambitious, he said, the Philippines risks falling behind. That is particularly dangerous when sovereignty and national security are involved. “Ambitious plans needed to have been laid down on the ground years ago,” Teodoro said. “But we cannot recoup the past. We can only make the present faster.” Then came one of his sharpest lines: “And today is not fast enough. Tomorrow is certainly unacceptable.” Teodoro said he had extensive discussions with PMA Superintendent Lieutenant General Michael Logico on the academy’s growth plans, infrastructure, curriculum, Corps of Professors, and the future design of the Cadet Corps, building on goals left by former superintendent Vice Admiral Caesar Bernard Valencia. Education is not the same as training Teodoro also questioned a habit he said he has seen in AFP education and training systems. “Education is for knowledge. Training is for skills,” he said. The two, he argued, should not simply be fused together. “Without knowledge, you cannot form skills. You cannot train skills.” Military officers need a continuing and current body of knowledge across different fields, he said, because conflict has become increasingly multidisciplinary, unpredictable, and difficult to structure neatly. That knowledge can then be translated into skills. Teodoro also took issue with educational opportunities being awarded without sufficient regard for merit, particularly in advanced study and research. “The opportunity for acquiring knowledge should be democratic,” he said. Once that opportunity has been made available fairly, however, he said “individual merit and excellence” should determine educational qualification. PMA cannot stay inside Fort Del Pilar Teodoro also challenged the idea that PMA education and training should remain confined to its Baguio home. “Fort Del Pilar houses the Philippine Military Academy. But the Philippine Military Academy should not be solely in Fort Del Pilar,” he said. The Philippines has too many different operating environments, he said, for future officers to depend on a single training venue. He linked this to the government’s push to secure military reservations for AFP use and to address infrastructure gaps that have affected operations, particularly in the maritime domain, as well as logistics, internal security, external defense, and disaster response. Teodoro said the Armed Forces must be ready to enforce Philippine laws across the country’s vast maritime domain and deal with state actors that may not always follow international law. That, he said, is why the defense establishment cannot afford timid planning. The task for PMA is no longer simply to teach cadets how to fight the wars previous generations knew. It is to give them enough knowledge, skill, and judgment to understand what the next threat looks like, especially when it may arrive not as a bullet, but as information. – Rappler.com

title: Coast Guard Icebreakers and the Finland Model: A Blueprint for the U.S. Navy?
body: Naval News visits Helsinki Shipyard to examine how the “Finland model” is driving icebreaker production, and questions if this strategy could solve the U.S. Navy’s surface combatant crisis. The ”Finland model” has been quoted as the one to be used by the U.S. Navy to solve the issue of a smaller and more affordable surface combatant than the fleet’s Arleigh Burke-class destroyers. The U.S. Navy has so far been unable to produce a replacement for the now-retired Oliver Hazard Perry-class frigates which entered service back in 1977, the latest failed programme being the Constellation-class FREMM-derivative cut short after two vessels . Naval News contributor Robin Häggblom had the opportunity to get a look at the work done at Helsinki Shipyard where coast guard icebreakers are being built under the Finland model. Revitalizing Helsinki Shipyard Under the ICE Pact The historical shipyard, now part of the UK-based Inocea Group, has been building ships in central Helsinki since 1865. Under different owners throughout its history, the yard has found a niche in building ice-reinforced vessels, both for the polar cruise industry, but also in the form of icebreakers. The latest chapter of the yard started with Canadian shipbuilder Davie acquiring it following the Russian full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and has seen it elevated to a key role in the trilateral US-Canadian-Finnish ICE Pact. The agreement outlines closer cooperation in the field of icebreaker design and production, as well as technology transfers. In practice this sees two consortiums build icebreakers for the US Coast Guard Arctic Security Cutter programme (ASC), with both building the first vessels in Finland to speed up delivery while at the same time investing in US industry to be able to build the rest of the series there. At the same time, the construction of the larger Polar Max icebreaker for the Canadian Coast Guard is also underway in Helsinki. Inocea’s Distributed Build Approach Inocea’s approach to the ASC is to build the first two vessels in Finland, followed by three more in Texas at Davie Defense’s facilities which currently are seeing significant investment. In the Finnish end, it is not just the Helsinki Shipyard that is employed, but also the facilities of Sata Shipbuilding in Pori on the west coast where hull construction of both vessels has started. Compared to the Helsinki Shipyard, Sata has better facilities for building large hull and superstructure blocks up to 500 tons in weight, which are then assembled in the main 280 m long drydock in Helsinki. For the Polar Max, the hull is being built in Helsinki where it currently occupies the drydock, before it is to be shipped to Canada where the superstructure will be added at Davie’s shipyard in Quebec. The Heavyweight: Polar Max When it enters service, the 22,800-tonne Polar Max will claim the title of the world’s heaviest non-nuclear-powered icebreaker. It reflects a growing trend of icebreakers serving as true multirole platforms. Designed for year-round Arctic operations, the ship can break up to 2.5 meters of ice and boasts a 90-day endurance. Alongside its icebreaking capabilities, the vessel features substantial cargo space and heavy-lift cranes for resupply missions. It can accommodate up to 250 personnel, allowing ample room for researchers and mission specialists alongside the core crew. Arctic Security Cutter. Davie Defense picture. The Agile Platform: Arctic Security Cutter The Arctic Security Cutters are smaller, measuring 100 meters in length with a normal operating displacement of 9,000 tons. Like the Polar Max, they feature a 90-day endurance, though with a smaller 124-person capacity. While the Canadian vessel is built to Polar Class 2 standards for year-round operation in moderate multi-year ice, the ASC requires Polar Class 3 (PC3) certification. PC3 denotes capability for year-round operation in second-year ice with multi-year inclusions. Even at PC3, this represents top-tier Arctic capability, outpacing several other operational and planned icebreaker classes. The Future of the Finland Model In addition to the three vessels currently being built, the Finnish part of Inocea also has the new Finnish civilian 96-meter long icebreaker Aino under contract for delivery in 2029, as well as another undisclosed project in the pipeline. While shipyard representatives note that running this kind of heavy industry in the middle of the capital is “Quite an adventure” and that the company face some issues with finding enough skilled workers, they are at the same time confident in the somewhat unique close cooperation between Finnish shipyards, academia, design bureaus, and system suppliers. The value placed on this is visible in the 200 million euro investment made into the yard during the upcoming years. Together with a comprehensive in-house design capability, the ecosystem has sped up the building process, allowing for an average time of delivery from contract of 30 months for their ice-capable vessels, compared to a global average approaching 60 months. This is backed up not only by the latest Finnish icebreaker Polaris delivered within 32 months of contract, but also by hull construction beginning within three months of contract for the Polar Max and four months for the ASC. While the programme currently is on track, it is important to remember that the first ICE Pact vessels are still a few years out and none of the vessels to be built in the US have yet to start production. As such, the final outcome is still open, but even more unclear is whether the promising-looking “Finland Model” may easily be adopted for the more complex and politically more sensitive world of naval surface combatants. With much of the benefits of the model stemming from trusting the expertise of the foreign shipyards and system suppliers, the experience from the Constellation-class raises questions about whether the U.S. Navy really is ready to accept a foreign design into its ranks. The post Coast Guard Icebreakers and the Finland Model: A Blueprint for the U.S. Navy? appeared first on Naval News .

title: Hunters kill 14 bandits in Bakori attack, two residents die
body:
The Katsina State Government says community hunters killed 14 suspected bandits during an attack on travellers in Bakori Local Government Area on Friday.
Two people, including a hunter and a traveller who was reportedly burnt to death inside his vehicle, died during the incident. Another hunter sustained gunshot injuries.
The Commissioner for Internal Security and Home Affairs, Nasir Mu’azu, disclosed this in a statement issued on Friday, 23 October.
According to the commissioner, security authorities received intelligence at about 1:28 a.m. that 26 armed men on 13 motorcycles were moving toward Dawan Laila forest in Bakori.
He identified the suspected leader as Isiya Kwashen Garwa. He said security personnel in the local government area were placed on alert over intelligence suggesting a planned mass abduction in neighbouring communities.
Mr Mu’azu said the authorities subsequently received reports at about 1:31 p.m. that the armed men had attacked travellers from Kakumi Ward who were heading to Illela market in Sokoto State.
The attackers reportedly set ablaze a private vehicle belonging to Jamilu Lawal, 50, who was travelling with three other people.
The commissioner said hunters from Gidan Wawo village, Kakumi Ward, mobilised to confront the attackers, resulting in a gun battle.
He said 14 suspected bandits were killed during the confrontation, while three of the travellers were rescued.
However, Mr Lawal was burnt inside the vehicle, according to the statement.
A 29-year-old hunter, Mohammed Jidda, was also killed, while another hunter, Usman Sunday, 25, sustained minor gunshot injuries and was receiving treatment.
The government did not explain how the traveller became trapped in the burning vehicle or whether the reported deaths of the suspected bandits had been independently confirmed by security agencies.
The casualty figures could not be independently verified by PREMIUM TIMES.
Mr Mu’azu said intelligence reports indicated that the armed group might launch a reprisal attack following the confrontation.
He said the state government was working with security agencies to prevent further attacks in the area.
The commissioner did not disclose the specific security measures introduced, but assured residents that the authorities were responding to the reported threat.
He commended the community hunters for confronting the attackers and urged residents to provide security agencies with credible information.
The government also appealed to residents to remain calm.

title: US Air Force considers giving bombers an air-to-air combat role
body:
The U.S. Air Force is studying the possibility of giving bombers an air-to-air combat role, an unusual concept that could eventually allow aircraft such as the B-21 Raider to engage enemy aircraft without operating as conventional fighters.
The proposal appears in a report on the future fighter force submitted to Congress in October. According to Air & Space Forces Magazine , the document lists “developing air-to-air capabilities on bombers” among options being considered as the service examines how to meet its future combat-aircraft requirements.
The Air Force estimates that it will need 1,509 aircraft coded for fighter missions by 2035, compared with 1,288 today. Budget and production constraints, however, could make it difficult to reach that number exclusively through aircraft such as the F-35A, F-15EX and future F-47 .
Using bombers for some air-to-air missions is one of the alternatives under study, alongside greater use of Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) and potentially another fighter design.
Follow Air Data News: WhatsApp | Instagram | LinkedIn | Twitter | Facebook
The report does not identify the B-21 as the aircraft that would receive the capability, nor does it establish a program to arm the Raider with air-to-air missiles. But previous Air Force discussions show that the service has already considered a larger role for stealth bombers in air superiority missions.
Such a mission would be fundamentally different from using the B-21 as a fighter. The Raider is a large, subsonic stealth bomber and was not designed for the speed, acceleration and maneuverability associated with traditional air combat.
Long-range weapons and networked sensors, however, increasingly separate the aircraft detecting a target from the aircraft launching the weapon.
A bomber could therefore operate as a stealthy weapons carrier, receiving targeting information from fighters, CCAs, airborne sensors or other platforms and launching air-to-air missiles without having to approach an enemy fighter for close combat.
The concept would exploit characteristics that are already central to the B-21: long range, low observability and a large internal weapons capacity. Instead of carrying only a handful of air-to-air weapons like a stealth fighter, a bomber could potentially serve as an airborne arsenal, although the payload and internal weapons-bay capacity of the B-21 remain classified.
The Air Force has also explored much longer-range air-to-air weapons. A recent request for information sought concepts capable of reaching targets at distances of at least 1,000 nautical miles, or about 1,850 km. A weapon in that class would radically change the relationship between the speed of the launching aircraft and the range at which an engagement could begin.
The concept also fits the Air Force’s move toward distributed combat networks. An F-47, F-35, CCA or another sensor could detect and track an aircraft while a bomber positioned elsewhere supplied the weapon.
That would allow a B-21 to contribute to air superiority without necessarily using its own sensors to find the target or exposing itself by approaching it.
CCAs could make the arrangement even more flexible. Air Force Global Strike Command officials have previously discussed the possibility of long-range collaborative aircraft accompanying bombers, extending their sensing, communications and defensive capabilities inside contested airspace.
The same architecture could also provide protection against unmanned aircraft and other airborne threats. Rather than relying exclusively on stealth to avoid interception, future bombers could have weapons capable of destroying threats approaching the formation.
The idea is not entirely new. The U.S. military has examined “arsenal plane” concepts in which a large aircraft carries substantial numbers of weapons while other platforms provide targeting information. A stealth bomber would add the ability to move such an arsenal considerably closer to defended airspace.
The Air Force has not disclosed which bombers it could use for the proposed air-to-air capability, what weapons they would carry or whether the concept will proceed to an acquisition program. The B-21 is still entering service as the centerpiece of the future U.S. strategic bomber force, while the B-52J is expected to remain in operation for decades.

title: Bill Gates warns the 'evolutionary' age of AI will be brutal for workers
body:
Autumn sale Get 60% off Autumn sale Get 60% off
People are going to keep on losing their jobs to AI because “the incentive structure [in business] is wrong: It’s ‘hire the robot, fire the human and don’t look back’,” Bill Gates tells The Observer in an exclusive interview.
Describing the AI age as an “evolutionary event” where humans are no longer the most intelligent things on the planet, he forecasts wholesale disruption to the labour market as almost all work skills – “skills of invention, skills of white-collar work and then with humanoids, the skills of physical human labour” – are replaced by AI.
Governments will need to find new sources of income to fund the needs of people put out of work, future education and re-skilling: “The revenue for the safety net to help us through this transition will actually be reduced, even though overall prosperity gets better.” He wants to see taxes on AI use, perhaps in the form of a “token tax”.
He also says that billionaires should pay more tax. He says he would have been willing to pay “a little more than double” the tax he has paid – he has paid $14bn in tax in his lifetime, but would have been willing to pay $40bn. “Governments [need to] figure out how to tax very wealthy people in a way that feels fair. It doesn’t solve the fact that government spending versus government tax collection in many rich countries, including the US, is out of whack… that disparity’s gotten larger in the last few years. So at some point, more taxes will have to be raised, and some spending will have to be curbed.”
While keen to stress the “good stuff” that could be enabled by AI, such as enhanced drug discovery, Gates warned that technological advances will present a “real test of quality of government”, at a time when developed countries are already fire-fighting on multiple fronts and geopolitical tensions are high. “You could say this isn’t the best time to say, hey, rich countries, let’s do the hardest thing you’ve ever done,” he said.
Bill Gates warns AI has exposed the internet’s soft underbelly
AI is not just stealing jobs from the young, it’s also taking from the managers of tomorrow
The philanthropist and Microsoft founder highlighted bioterrorism and cyberattacks as the most pressing short-term threats, but that, by the end of the 2020s, artificial intelligence could be operating beyond human control. Within three to four years, he says, “you hope that you’ve gotten very serious about the alignment control issues”, i.e. the risk of AIs operating in ways that no longer align with human interests.
The UK is perhaps better placed than most: its regulatory framework and state capacity on AI have been praised internationally and by industry insiders. Ahead of a budget that is expected to stress the importance of “resilience”, the chancellor made a flurry of AI-related spending announcements aiming to build on this strong start. There were two major themes: protecting Britain against emerging threats – including those highlighted by Gates – and promoting domestic innovation to avoid reliance on technologies developed overseas.
The government yesterday announced £100m of funding for a new AI Biosecurity Lab, the world’s first, with responsibility for monitoring biological threats and developing medical countermeasures. The lab will be supported by up to £200m of model credits from Anthropic and OpenAI.
The AI Security Institute, the UK’s internationally admired agency responsible for testing the capabilities of AI models, will receive a further £120m of funding. An additional £60m will go towards a National Cyber Shield, £70m towards a new National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (Nerv) Centre, and £23m towards the government’s new AI Economics Institute, which is chaired by Nobel prize winner Simon Johnson and tasked with analysing the emerging economic impacts of AI.
In keeping with the government’s interventionist inclinations, and its willingness to use the public sector balance sheet to “pick winners”, the UK’s Sovereign AI fund has also been backed with £120m of new funding, an increase of around 25%. Half will go towards direct investments in promising UK AI companies, and half towards an R&D procurement scheme, to foster innovative solutions in areas like cybersecurity and healthcare.
Kanishka Narayan, the minister for AI, has spoken repeatedly of the importance of the UK having strategic leverage over AI technology. That wouldn’t mean the UK duplicating all parts of the AI supply chain, but instead the pursuit of a small number of globally leading capabilities that other countries would struggle to manage without. A non-exclusive set of candidates include a global role for the AI Security Institute in safety evaluations, domestic computing capacity and expertise in chip design.
So-called “middle powers” like the UK are trying to pick a path through a world dominated by two AI superpowers. Gates warned in his interview that co-operation between those superpowers will be required to avert the AI-related risks that are causing so much worry inside the leading labs. “The US and China will, on a few of these issues, have to view it as a challenge to humanity, not a nation-state win-lose type situation.” he said.
Gates also spoke to The Observer of his regret over his links with the paedophile financier Jeffrey Epstein, which were the subject of a US Congressional committee hearing in June. “It definitely was a damaging thing to have spent time with him,” he said, adding that he has “lots of things where I look back and I say, okay, I hope what I learned from that is better than whatever pain or problems that it caused”.
What are your thoughts on this? Email us at letters@observer.co.uk

title: Anthropic Sued for Using Elvis Presley Music to Train AI Models
body:
Anthropic has been sued by the owners of Elvis Presley ‘s catalog for allegedly utilizing his songs to train AI models without permission.
The suit was filed Friday and claims the company infringed 274 songs of Presley’s, including “Can’t Help Falling in Love,” “A Little Less Conversation” and “Don’t Be Cruel.”
“The Elvis Plaintiffs bring this action to enforce these exclusive rights against the defendant that has built its entire business model based on copyright infringement at a scale never seen before,” wrote lead attorney Richard Busch. “The Elvis Plaintiffs are deeply protective of these iconic songs.”
Authentic Brands Group, which owns the rights to Presley , filed the lawsuit alongside other entities that also own rights to the “Jailhouse Rock” singer.
“‘Claude’ has created infringing output of copyrighted material of virtually every song from every catalog available on the internet, including the Works,” the lawsuit states. “Even after the Defendant supposedly put up ‘guardrails’ after being sued, in one of its latest iterations, Claude continues to infringe: when recently asked to recreate specific songs ‘for a modern audience,’ Claude did so and admitted: ‘These renders keep landing very close to the originals: same structure, same hooks reused with light rewording, and full sets of verses/choruses/bridges. That’s edging past ‘inspired by’ into reproducing the copyrighted song, even when the words are swapped out.’”
In August, Round Hill sued Suno and Anthropic, claiming mass copyright infringement. They alleged the AI companies used hundreds of the publisher’s songs to train their AI models without permission. Anthropic was also previously sued by Universal Music Publishing, Abcko, Concord and BMG for similar claims of lyrics being utilized to train Claude, an AI agent.
The suit is seeking $150,000 per infringed song.
An Anthropic spokesperson said in a statement to The Hollywood Reporter : “We disagree with the claims and intend to defend this case fully.”

title: Iranian people not to give in to US threats or pressures
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 25 (MNA) – Reacting to the intimidation of the US officials leveled against Iran, Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf has emphasized that Iranian people will not give in or surrender to the US military threats or pressures.
Speaking at the open session of the parliament on Sunday, he stressed that Iranian nation will not be intimidated by the United States.
“Iranian people will not give in to the US military threats or pressures under any circumstances,” Ghalibaf underlined.
“Until the US changes its behavior, stops its bullying and makes good on its broken commitments, its claims will have no credibility,” he said, adding, “We will deliver an unimaginable response to any violation of Iran’s territorial integrity.”
It was the US that miscalculated and plunged itself into a quagmire by waging war against Iran, the speaker continued.
Now, it is up to the Americans to take the necessary steps to get themselves out, he added.
Elsewhere in his remarks, the senior parliamentarian pointed to the US efforts to exert pressure on Iran, noting that Americans imagine that by employing certain media-based pressure tactics or military threats, they can force this great nation to submit, failing to realize that the Iran of today is not the Iran of the humiliating Pahlavi era. Rather, it is an impregnable fortress of self-belief, defensive capability, and ironclad resolve, which will never permit any foreign power to dictate terms regarding the honor of this land.
“We will not be intimidated, and we are prepared to deliver a crushing response, beyond what our enemies could ever imagine, to any act of aggression against the national sovereignty and territorial integrity of a greater Iran. Threats of large-scale war or assassination will not cause the Iranian nation to back down from their inalienable rights and interests,” the Iranian Parliament speaker maintained.

title: Drones Hit Omsky Kauchuk Deep in Russia, Belgorod Targeted
body:
Long-range strike drones struck the “Omsky Kauchuk” chemical enterprise and industrial infrastructure in the Siberian city of Omsk – located more than 2,500 kilometers from Ukraine – igniting a major fire across the manufacturing complex, open-source intelligence monitors reported on Saturday, Oct. 24.
According to Ukrainian OSINT project Exilenova+, unmanned aerial vehicles penetrated deep into Russian airspace, potentially traveling over 3,000 kilometers (1,860 miles) to reach Omsk’s northern industrial hub.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
The kinetic impacts sparked a large-scale fire across the production facilities of the chemical plant.
Omsk Region Governor Vitaly Khotsenko confirmed that air defense systems engaged aerial targets over the regional capital, stating that drones reached the northern industrial sector where major manufacturing complexes are concentrated. Khotsenko did not identify specific damaged enterprises in his official dispatch.
In addition to the chemical production plant, Exilenova+ reported that an Ozon e-commerce logistics hub in Omsk sustained damage during the aerial assault, while another unmanned platform struck a high-voltage electrical transmission tower in the municipality’s industrial perimeter.
The Omsky Kauchuk plant, a subsidiary of the Titan Group, functions as one of the Russian Federation’s primary petrochemical manufacturers, producing synthetic rubber, phenol, acetone, and organic chemical derivatives with an operating capacity of approximately 2,000 metric tons of output per day.
Beyond commercial rubber products, specialized synthetic polymers and chemical binders synthesized at the facility serve as critical raw materials in the production of solid rocket fuel.
Solid-propellant rocket motors utilizing such chemical binders are integrated into Russian strategic and theater missile platforms, including the 9M723 ballistic missiles of the Iskander-M system, alongside intercontinental ballistic missile systems such as the Topol-M and RS-24 Yars.
The strike marks one of the deepest recorded asymmetric aerial interdiction operations conducted against Russian defense-industrial supply networks since the beginning of the full-scale war.
Concurrently, Ukrainian strike drones engaged infrastructure in western Russia overnight into Sunday, Oct. 25, with detonations and debris falls reported in central Belgorod .
According to Exilenova+, incoming drones struck the MegaGRINN shopping and entertainment complex, a major commercial facility spanning approximately 163,000 square meters (1.7 million square feet) of housing more than 200 retail outlets, restaurants, and leisure venues.
The impact occurred overnight while the commercial center was closed to the public, preventing civilian visitor casualties, though blast waves shattered exterior glass facades and damaged passenger vehicles parked in adjacent residential lots.
The synchronized strikes on Omsk’s chemical production facilities and rear logistics hubs in Belgorod follow an expanding Ukrainian counter-infrastructure campaign targeting petrochemical suppliers, rocket propellant production nodes, and rear logistics nodes across Russia to degrade Moscow’s long-range strike capabilities.
Ukrainian Defense Forces struck key military-industrial facilities and an aviation base inside Russia overnight Friday-Saturday, confirming direct hits on the Proton-Elektroteks plant in Oryol, the Tolyattikauchuk industrial plant in Samara region, and an aircraft stationed at the Yeysk airfield, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported .
“Damage has been confirmed to the main production building of JSC Proton-Elektroteks in the city of Oryol, Oryol region of the Russian Federation,” the General Staff announced.
In the city of Tolyatti, located in Russia’s Samara region, Ukrainian units struck the Tolyattikauchuk chemical complex overnight into Saturday, Oct. 24, with military observers registering an explosion and a major industrial fire across the facility’s perimeter.
The kinetic strikes inside Russia coincided with a systemic blackout that plunged large swathes of Russian-occupied Crimea into darkness overnight into Saturday, Oct. 24.

title: Anthropic says one AI agent beats many subagents now that models can handle complexity alone
body:
Anthropic found that a single agent with on-demand context often outperforms multi-agent setups in quality, cost, and latency. The company is releasing a migration kit to help teams evaluate and make the switch.

Anthropic is recommending that companies evaluate whether they can consolidate sub-agents, because a single primary agent that loads context as needed often delivers better results than a fleet of specialized ones. Newer models starting with Opus 4.5, along with Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1, can manage complex plans directly in a single loop, which can also reduce costs and wait times. In one comparison, Anthropic says the single-agent architecture ran about twice as fast as the multi-agent setup.

The recommendation comes from hands-on experience across multiple enterprise deployments, where Anthropic's Applied AI team found that a single agent using so-called skills frequently beat both monolithic prompt designs and sub-agent setups on quality. One company, for example, had a dozen specialized sub-agents inside its customer-facing agent, which made it hard to keep a consistent brand experience and hurt usability with high latency.

[caption id="attachment_41956" align="alignnone" width="2024"] In the multi-agent workflow, context gets lost at every handoff between feature writing, test writing, and code review. In the single-agent workflow, one agent writes both the feature and the tests because it already has the context, while a separate verifier only runs the tests and reports results. | Image: Anthropic[/caption]
The model can now do much of the orchestration work itself
According to Anthropic, many agent designs follow a familiar pattern with intent detection, a fixed processing pipeline, user segmentation, separate recommendation branches, and an orchestrator sitting on top. Much of that is work the model can now handle on its own for the respective use case.

Anthropic calls it "Conway's Law" for agents. The architecture becomes a copy of the org chart, with each team shipping its own sub-agent until hundreds of overlapping agents pile up with no shared standards. What follows is what Anthropic calls a "Frankenprompt," where every team adds rules to the system prompt that end up contradicting each other. A clean system prompt, four or five lean data tools, and fixed output guardrails cover much of the respective use case, according to the company.

[video width="2024" height="884" mp4="https://the-decoder.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/orchestrator_vs_agent.mp4" loop="true" autoplay="true"][/video]

As one example, Anthropic cut the Claude Code system prompt for newer models by over 80 percent, partly because skills and tools now load only when needed. Newer models also comment on their own progress and check their own work, which can make some of the extra control layers unnecessary.

Anthropic says sub-agents still make sense when a single agent's context window shows measurable performance degradation, when multiple tasks need to run in parallel with separate context windows, or when a single agent struggles with tool selection.

[video width="2024" height="892" mp4="https://the-decoder.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/merge_subagents_to_agent_Anthropic.mp4" loop="true" autoplay="true"][/video]

For a step-by-step migration, Anthropic has published a migration kit on GitHub that walks teams through a workflow to identify existing patterns, evaluate alternatives, and verify the best approach. Anthropic warns against merging blindly, since in one test with a support agent, folding in a sub-agent did reduce latency but broke a previously working process. The primary agent started answering on its own instead of consulting the right specialist.
Teams should keep skill libraries from sprawling
Instead of giving every team its own agent, Anthropic recommends packaging workflows into skills and loading tools on demand through a tool search. A small central team should own the system prompt and overall quality. Separately, Anthropic notes that the model's tool selection tends to degrade beyond 30 to 50 tool definitions, so designated owners on each team should maintain the skill libraries to keep them from ballooning.

For reference material like guidelines, product specs, or metric definitions, Anthropic recommends knowledge bases that the agent queries only when needed through a search tool. That kind of information can also be embedded as reference files inside a skill. Anthropic advises against fetching context through code and injecting it directly into prompts.

Anthropic's findings are consistent with recent research. A study by Vals found that agent teams can be faster than single agents but don't deliver higher quality. Scaling from ten to 30 or 100 agents brought no quality gains but significantly higher costs, according to the study. OpenAI developer Eric Provencher has also questioned the value of agent swarms, calling them "almost certainly" wasted money.

title: SERAP drags FG to ECOWAS Court over N78.8bn cash transfer scandal
body: The Socio-Economic Rights and Accountability Project (SERAP) has sued the Federal Government at the ECOWAS Community Court of Justice over alleged financial irregularities involving more than ₦78.8 billion allocated to cash-transfer and social protection programmes. The organisation said the allegations involved the Ministry of Humanitarian Affairs and Poverty Reduction, the National Cash Transfer Office (NCTO) and the National Social Safety Nets Coordinating Office (NASSCO). According to SERAP, the issues were documented in the Auditor-General of the Federation’s 2024 Annual Report, published on August 7, 2026, covering various periods between January 2023 and December 31, 2024. In the suit, numbered ECW/CCJ/APP/42/26 and filed last week, SERAP is asking the court to declare that the government’s alleged failure to account for the funds allocated to federal cash-transfer and social protection programmes violates Nigeria’s international human rights obligations. The organisation is also seeking an order directing the government to provide a comprehensive and verifiable account of the questioned funds, including payment records, beneficiary details, verification documents and financial reconciliation records. SERAP further wants the court to order an independent investigation into the alleged irregularities, the recovery of any public funds found to have been improperly spent or diverted, and appropriate legal or administrative action against anyone found responsible, subject to due process. According to the organisation, the Auditor-General’s report questioned approximately ₦33.751 billion reportedly transferred to more than 3.2 million households across 35 states in 2023, citing inadequate records to verify payments and reconcile beneficiary information. The report also identified ₦36.744 billion in payments allegedly made without prepayment audits and ₦4.616 billion in unsupported expenditure. Other questioned payments included ₦350.182 million for enrolment, ₦89.511 million for store purchases and ₦17.422 million in diesel advances, SERAP said, citing the audit report. The organisation argued that the alleged financial irregularities raised concerns about whether the funds were properly managed and whether intended beneficiaries received the assistance meant to support vulnerable households. In its application, SERAP maintained that the government’s responsibility to protect human rights extended to the proper management of public resources allocated to social protection programmes. It argued that failures to verify beneficiaries, maintain accurate records, reconcile disbursements, investigate irregularities and recover misused funds could undermine the rights to social security and an adequate standard of living, including access to food, clothing and housing. “The failure to investigate the ₦78.8 billion cash-transfer scandal, account for the questioned funds and recover any unlawfully spent amounts violates Nigeria’s obligations to protect the human rights of vulnerable households,” the organisation said in its court filing. SERAP said the case was brought in the public interest to protect affected households and promote accountability for public funds allocated to social protection. The organisation also argued that the alleged failures could affect millions of Nigerians who depend on cash-transfer programmes to meet basic needs, particularly people living in poverty. The suit was filed on behalf of SERAP by its lawyers, Kolawole Oluwadare and Kehinde Oyewumi, under Article 9(4) of the ECOWAS Court Protocol. SERAP said it had previously urged President Bola Tinubu and relevant authorities, in a letter dated September 5, 2026, to account for the questioned funds, publish relevant audit records, investigate the expenditure and recover any money found to have been unlawfully spent or diverted. It also requested payment and beneficiary records, verification documents and explanations regarding missing REMITA records. According to the organisation, the deadline it gave the government to address the audit findings had elapsed without adequate action. SERAP is asking the court to direct the government to strengthen financial accountability, auditing, beneficiary verification and oversight mechanisms to prevent similar irregularities in future cash-transfer and social protection programmes. It also wants measures put in place to ensure eligible vulnerable individuals and households receive the benefits intended for them and that any established adverse effects on their rights are appropriately addressed. The organisation is relying on provisions of the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights and the United Nations Convention against Corruption in arguing that governments have obligations to protect public resources, ensure transparent financial management and investigate suspected misuse of public funds. No date has been fixed for the hearing of the suit. The post SERAP drags FG to ECOWAS Court over N78.8bn cash transfer scandal appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: NDC to unveil campaign council, present financial statement at NEC meeting
body: The Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) says it will unveil its National Campaign Council and present its statement of account at its third National Executive Committee (NEC) meeting scheduled for Monday, October 26, in Abuja. The party said the presentation of its financial statement was part of its commitment to transparency and accountability, challenging other political parties, particularly the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC), to disclose details of their finances. The announcement was contained in a statement signed by the NDC National Publicity Secretary, Osa Director, Esq. According to the statement, the meeting will hold at JD Event Centre, Kashim Ibrahim Way, opposite A-Class Park, Maitama, Abuja, at 10am. “A major highlight of the meeting will be the release and presentation of the party’s Statement of Account by the National Treasurer. This is in deference to our avowed commitment to the principles of transparency and accountability,” the statement said. The party challenged the APC and other political parties to follow its example in the management and disclosure of their finances. “In this regard, we challenge other political parties, especially the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC), to emulate this level of openness and transparency in the management of their finances,” it added. The NDC also addressed speculation about its finances, saying its resources would have been more substantial but for the inability of many of its candidates to pay for nomination forms. The party attributed the situation to the economic hardship in the country, claiming that about 80 per cent of its candidates could not afford the expression of interest forms. “However, contrary to speculations in the public domain, and due to the level of poverty, hunger and deprivation in the country occasioned by the rudderless APC and its amorphous economic policies, about 80% of our candidates could not afford the Expression of Interest forms,” the statement said. It added that the party issued the forms free of charge to the affected candidates. The NDC further disclosed that the meeting would feature the unveiling of its National Campaign Council (NCC), which it said would cover campaigns for the presidential, National Assembly, governorship and state Houses of Assembly elections. The party also said its candidates would receive certificates of return for their respective offices. Describing itself as prepared for the 2027 general election, the NDC said it was determined to offer Nigerians what it called altruistic leadership. “The NDC is turbo-charged and ready to give Nigerians the altruistic leadership the nation deserves,” the statement said. title: Ukrainian Attacks Kill 3 in Belgorod, Hit Perm Industrial Plant
body:
Overnight Ukrainian drone attacks killed four people in southwestern Russia’s Belgorod region, one in the Lipetsk region and damaged an industrial site in the Perm region of the Ural Mountains, officials said Sunday.
In the city of Belgorod near the Russian border with Ukraine, an attack killed three people and injured 13, said Belgorod regional governor Alexander Shuvayev.
The overnight attack on Belgorod damaged 30 apartment buildings, 35 cars, four houses, three administrative buildings, eight commercial premises and three social facilities, Shuvayev said.
In a separate incident on Sunday morning, one person was killed and another injured when a Ukrainian drone struck a car in the village of Voznesenovka near the town of Shebekino, local authorities said.
A drone attack on Russia's Perm region damaged an industrial facility, injuring five of its workers, regional governor Dmitry Makhonin said on Sunday.
Emergency services were at the scene and the injured people received the necessary medical help, he said on the state-backed MAX messaging app without providing further detail on the nature of the damage.
Meanwhile, Russia’s Defense Ministry said that its drones had struck a cargo vessel bound for the Black Sea port of Chornomorsk during an overnight attack.
The ministry said the vessel was being used to supply the Ukrainian army.
Russian forces also hit a logistics center, a distribution center and a logistics terminal in the Ukrainian city of Kharkiv. The ministry said the facilities had been used for storage and distribution of dual-use cargo for the Ukrainian military.
Reuters could not independently verify the Defense Ministry's information.
Later on Sunday, southwestern Russia's Lipetsk region Governor Igor Artamonov said a Ukrainian missile strike on an industrial zone in the city of Yelets killed a security guard and injured a paramedic.
Artamonov said the security guard worked at one of the industrial facilities located on the site. The paramedic at the medical center was taken to hospital, where she was receiving the necessary treatment, the governor said.
The governor did not identify the facility that was hit in the strike.
Reuters could not independently verify the report. There was no immediate comment from Ukraine.
