title: Could Russia attack NATO? Estonian general identifies two dangerous scenarios
body:
Russia has suffered heavy losses in Ukraine, but that does not make it harmless. Retired Estonian Major General Veiko-Vello Palm warns that Moscow could see an opportunity if NATO fails to respond quickly and together — and points to a vulnerable seam in the Alliance’s Baltic command structure.
In an interview with Dr Aleksander Olech for Defence24.com, Maj. Gen. (Ret.) Veiko-Vello Palm discusses the Russian threat to Estonia and the wider Baltic region, NATO’s readiness for a high-intensity conflict and the lessons of Ukraine. He also explains why Europe needs to rethink weapons production and industrial resilience and outlines three priorities for defence cooperation between Poland and the Baltic states.
Dr Aleksander Olech, Defence24.com: How do you assess the Russian military threat to Estonia and the Baltic states today? Has the war in Ukraine reduced Russia’s ability to threaten NATO, or is Moscow already rebuilding capabilities that could become a serious challenge in the coming years?
Maj. Gen. (Ret.) Veiko-Vello Palm: For Estonia, the military threat is straightforward: Russia is the only existential threat, and our defence planning has been based on that assessment for decades. What worries me is not a lack of discussion about the Russian threat; quite the opposite, more Europeans now acknowledge it. But I am not convinced that everyone who says this actually believes it, or at least believes in the immediacy of that threat. It is a little like telling someone who eats too much sugar every day that, if he continues, he may eventually develop diabetes. He understands the concept perfectly well. He agrees that diabetes is dangerous. He may even tell others that people should eat less sugar. And then he takes another piece of chocolate. The problem is that the consequence remains theoretical and distant, while today’s piece of chocolate is real. I sometimes see the same psychology in our approach to Russia. We recognise the threat intellectually, but many of our decisions still suggest that, somewhere deep inside, we treat the actual consequences as distant and theoretical.
For Estonia, this is not an abstract debate. We are simply too close to Russia and too small. The same is true, to varying degrees, for several other countries on NATO’s eastern flank. Any major disturbance in Russia, any escalation, and particularly any Russian miscalculation can have a disproportionately large impact on us. A larger country further away may have strategic depth, time and room to correct an error. Estonia has very little of any of these. For years, another misconception made that situation even more difficult: the idea that the security problem somehow lay partly with us. There used to be a strange tendency to look at our region and say: if your security environment is so bad, surely the problem cannot be entirely Russia’s. Perhaps you have also done something wrong. And then the implicit answer was that others would come and help us organise our countries better, moderate our behaviour, or improve our relationship with Russia. It was essentially the geopolitical equivalent of telling a rape victim that perhaps her skirt was too short. That thinking was complete nonsense, of course. Fortunately, there is much less of it today, although it has not disappeared entirely.
The truth is much simpler: the poor security situation in our region is created by Russia. One hundred per cent. Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland or Finland cannot solve that fundamental problem by behaving differently. The security environment will improve only when Russia itself changes. Until Russia changes, our task is to survive, but survival does not mean sitting quietly and waiting. It means being so well prepared – militarily, politically and societally – that Russia itself believes that if anyone in Moscow has a stupid idea, the consequences will be immediate and extremely painful. That is the essence of deterrence. It is not enough that we believe we can defend ourselves. Russia must believe it too.
One dangerous misconception is that Russia’s enormous losses in Ukraine mean it has ceased to pose a serious military threat. Russia can be weaker than it was before the war and still be extremely dangerous to us. Russia continues to use military force, continues to rebuild its military capabilities and continues to frame its relationship with the West in terms of confrontation. Parts of Western societies are increasingly tired of the war, and there is more talk of peace. Everybody wants peace, myself included, but the terms matter. At the moment, I see very little evidence that Russia understands peace as a compromise in which it accepts the sovereignty and choices of its neighbours. The Russian proposition still looks much closer to: give me what I want now, and be prepared to give me more when I want more. That would not be a sustainable peace; it would merely be an intermission.
That is why I am wary of trying to predict when Russia might attack NATO. The more useful question for a defence planner is under what conditions Moscow might believe that such an attack could succeed. I see two particularly dangerous conditions. First, if Moscow believes NATO will be unable to produce a sufficiently rapid and unified political and military response. Second, if Russia believes it can achieve surprise and create a military fait accompli before the Alliance can react effectively. Our task is to prevent those conditions from arising, rather than predict the date of the next war.
Dr Aleksander Olech: What is the most important lesson Estonia and the other Baltic states should draw from the war in Ukraine? Is it primarily about manpower, ammunition, air defence, drones, logistics, or the ability to sustain a long conflict?
Maj. Gen. (Ret.) Veiko-Vello Palm: I would challenge the premise slightly, because there is no single decisive lesson or capability. Modern warfare is a system. Command, intelligence, fires, manoeuvre, protection, air defence and sustainment are interdependent. You can have excellent drones, but without ammunition they achieve little. You can have ammunition, but without sensors and functioning command systems you cannot employ it effectively. You can have both, but without logistics you cannot sustain them. And ultimately somebody still has to hold the ground. If I had to single out two lessons from Ukraine, however, they would be mass and speed. War consumes an extraordinary amount of everything: people, ammunition, equipment, drones, fuel, spare parts and entire organisations. Ukraine has again demonstrated something European militaries had largely been allowed to forget during several decades of relatively small expeditionary operations: in a high-intensity war, quantity matters enormously. But I am always slightly uncomfortable with the famous phrase that “quantity has a quality all of its own”. It is too simplistic. A large amount of useless equipment remains useless.
For Estonia, this also has consequences for procurement. We need to reconsider the logic that has guided much of our defence procurement for years: that what primarily matters is price and delivery time. In peacetime, this can look economically rational. In a major war it can become a strategic vulnerability. I do not mean that Estonia should try to become self-sufficient in everything. That would be neither possible nor sensible. But we need to be much more deliberate about what must be produced in Estonia, what must be available in our immediate region, and which supply chains we are prepared to depend on during a war. This is also a lesson for the West more broadly. It is difficult to consider your ammunition supply genuinely secure if the explosives needed to manufacture that ammunition come from the other side of the world. That creates an additional defence problem. You are no longer only defending your territory and your military forces. You also depend on the security of global supply routes, ports, shipping, production facilities, and political relationships thousands of kilometres away.
What we preserve at home cannot be limited to assembly, although manufacturing capacity is important in itself. Putting a drone together does not necessarily require years of training. Configuring that drone to operate effectively in a heavily contested electronic-warfare environment is a completely different matter. That requires engineers, operators, testing, accumulated experience and, in some areas, very high levels of education. Most importantly, it requires practice. The critical national capability is therefore not only the ability to manufacture things. It is the ability to understand, modify and improve them. If you lose that competence, having an assembly line is not enough. In war, yesterday’s drone may no longer work tomorrow because the enemy has changed frequencies, tactics or countermeasures. You need people who understand why it stopped working and can change it quickly.
There is also a tendency to confuse innovation with developing a new drone or testing a new technology. Those things are necessary, but they are not innovation in themselves. Innovation is implemented change. The real challenge is organisational. We need readiness to change – not as an exceptional response to a crisis, but as part of the normal way our Defence Forces, government and industry operate. Ukraine demonstrates this every day. A successful tactic, frequency, drone, protection measure or technical solution immediately creates a countermeasure. That countermeasure creates another adaptation. The cycle never stops. An organisation that waits for the battlefield to stabilise before introducing the perfect solution will always be behind.
At the same time, Ukraine accepts a level of risk in innovation that we cannot simply reproduce in peacetime. Ukraine is at war. If a new and insufficiently tested technology creates a risk of injury, that risk has to be weighed against the much greater risk of being killed by an enemy using better technology. Under those circumstances, accepting a very high level of technological and operational risk is entirely rational. Our situation is different. European societies understandably have a much lower tolerance for serious training accidents in peacetime. We cannot simply import wartime Ukrainian risk acceptance into every peacetime activity.
If introducing a new munition or combat system requires several years of testing before soldiers can actually use it, then the battlefield may have changed several times before the testing process is complete. I do not claim to have a perfect answer to this problem, but I think we need to reconsider what constitutes sufficient evidence of safety and performance. Particularly with lethal systems, we should be more willing, where technically and legally appropriate, to rely on component-level qualification and accumulated evidence instead of automatically repeating the entire end-to-end explosives qualification chain for every modification. The objective should not be to remove safety requirements. It should be to understand which tests genuinely reduce meaningful risk and which procedures we repeat simply because that is how the system has always worked. We have to balance two risks: the risk of introducing something too early and the risk of introducing it too late. For decades, our peacetime systems have concentrated overwhelmingly on the first. Ukraine demonstrates the potentially fatal consequences of the second.
For this reason, innovation cannot be confined to one unit somewhere inside the defence organisation. Readiness to change has to be part of the DNA of the entire system – the Defence Forces, procurement, government, research institutions and industry. In a prolonged war, what matters is who can still fight on day one hundred — who can produce what they consume and adapt faster while doing so.
Dr Aleksander Olech: Is NATO’s current posture sufficient to defend the Baltic region? What should change in terms of allied forces, command arrangements, reinforcement plans and infrastructure to make deterrence more credible?
Maj. Gen. (Ret.) Veiko-Vello Palm: Judging by public discussions and reporting, NATO’s approach to the Baltic region has changed fundamentally. Not so long ago, much of the discussion was about reassuring the eastern flank. Allied presence was largely about demonstrating solidarity. Today, we are talking about something much more serious: preparing to fight and win a real war. That is progress, but NATO’s readiness cannot be measured simply by counting allied troops, headquarters or equipment. What matters is whether they can operate as a single fighting force. Any allied unit arriving in the Baltic region should be able to integrate into the existing defence system almost immediately. Command relationships, communications, intelligence, fires, logistics and infrastructure must already be prepared and regularly exercised. We cannot afford to spend the first days of a crisis figuring out how to work together.
There is a famous saying attributed to Eisenhower: “Plans are nothing; planning is everything.” I think this is particularly relevant here. We can spend years developing detailed defence plans, but the circumstances of a future war will inevitably differ from our assumptions. The real value of planning lies in creating shared understanding, relationships and the ability to adapt quickly. One issue that genuinely worries me is NATO’s command structure in our region. The boundary between two NATO Joint Force Commands runs through the Baltic Sea. Every military commander knows that boundaries between formations are potential vulnerabilities. When planning an attack, you deliberately look for seams between enemy units, because that is where coordination and responsibility can become less clear. And now we have such a seam in one of the most strategically important areas for the defence of the Baltic states. I sincerely hope that this will eventually be addressed by changing the command arrangements themselves, rather than simply promising better coordination between the two headquarters. Cooperation is necessary, but it is not a substitute for clear and coherent command responsibility.
We should also use an important advantage that we already have. Russia may choose when to attack, but it must come to us. We are already here. We know the terrain and can prepare our future battlefield today. The Baltic Defence Line is a good example. It must not become merely a construction programme of bunkers and obstacles. It has to be an integrated military system connecting fortifications, minefields, surveillance, artillery, drones, electronic warfare, air defence and logistics. An obstacle not observed and covered by fire is simply an engineering problem for the attacker.
The Baltic Defence Line must also involve society as a whole. Local governments, state agencies, private companies, infrastructure operators and hospitals all have essential roles. Roads must remain usable and be repaired when damaged. Heavy machinery, construction materials and fuel must be available. Hospitals must be prepared to receive military and civilian casualties, while municipalities must maintain essential services and support military operations. These responsibilities cannot be improvised after a crisis begins. They must be assigned, resourced and exercised in peacetime, together with the military. Preparing the defensive system in advance can reduce the time needed to establish a fortified battalion position from approximately two weeks to just one or two days. For Estonia, that difference can be decisive. And the system must connect across national borders, with the Baltic states sharing both their preparations and practical experience. Ultimately, deterrence is not about how impressive our plans look. It is about whether Russia believes we can fight effectively from the very first moment of a conflict.
Dr Aleksander Olech: How far should Europe go in rebuilding mass and preparing its societies for high-intensity conflict?
Maj. Gen. (Ret.) Veiko-Vello Palm: Preparing society for war does not mean militarising it. It means ensuring society can keep functioning during a war. There is a psychological challenge here. Constantly talking about war can create anxiety, and one natural response to fear is to ignore the problem. But avoiding the subject does not make the danger disappear. I believe people are often most afraid of what they do not understand. A good friend of mine organised a visit for Estonian healthcare professionals to Ukraine to see how civilian healthcare was functioning under wartime conditions. Before the visit, there was considerable fear and uncertainty. Afterwards, the attitude was completely different. People returned confident and determined. They had seen what war actually meant for their profession and concluded: we can manage under similar conditions, but we know what we need to change and prepare beforehand.
A high-intensity war would affect every part of society. Hospitals must treat casualties, municipalities must keep essential services running, companies must maintain infrastructure, and industry must continue producing. We cannot expect the armed forces to do all of this. For Estonia, with our limited manpower, this division of responsibilities is especially important. Every soldier assigned to a task that a civilian organisation could perform is one less soldier available for military operations. But civilian organisations need clear responsibilities, the necessary authority and practical experience before a crisis begins.
The same principle applies to military mass. Mass is not simply the number of soldiers, weapons or vehicles. It is also the capacity to keep them operational. Consider military vehicle maintenance. In wartime, we want damaged or broken equipment repaired as close to the fighting units as possible. That requires a distributed network of companies with the necessary skills, equipment and experience. But such a network cannot be created overnight. In peacetime, it means signing maintenance contracts with many different companies, including small contracts and trial assignments, so that they learn to work with military equipment and understand our requirements. From a purely financial perspective, this may be more expensive than concentrating all maintenance in one large facility. It creates additional administrative work and sacrifices some economies of scale.
But the cheapest peacetime solution is not necessarily the most effective wartime solution. We need to start evaluating procurement decisions not only by price, but also by the military capability and resilience they create. The logic extends to industrial production, transport, construction and other services. We need more companies capable of supporting defence, and we need to exercise that capability while we still have time. We need to make different decisions today, including some that seem less economical, so our countries can keep functioning and fighting when normal conditions disappear.
Dr Aleksander Olech: Has Europe focused too much on sophisticated, expensive platforms while neglecting mass production?
Maj. Gen. (Ret.) Veiko-Vello Palm: I would be careful with generalisations, because individual weapon systems need to be assessed case by case. The fact that a weapon system is expensive or produced in small quantities does not necessarily mean it cannot be manufactured in much larger numbers at a significantly lower unit cost. Sometimes the problem is simply insufficient orders. Unfortunately, in many other cases, the system was never designed for affordable, large-scale production. If we develop a weapon system with performance as the overriding priority and only start thinking about production volumes and costs afterwards, we should not be surprised when scaling becomes difficult or prohibitively expensive.
But not every weapon system should be mass-produced. Some high-end capabilities are inherently complex, expensive and available only in limited numbers. We absolutely need them. The British 20–40–40 approach offers one useful way of looking at this: a relatively small proportion of high-end capabilities, a larger proportion of affordable reusable systems, and a substantial proportion of inexpensive, often expendable capabilities. We also need to be more demanding about what we call battle-winning technology. If a country has twenty tanks or thirty artillery pieces, these systems may be extremely valuable, but their technological sophistication does not compensate for their limited numbers. We need to understand what military effect they can actually deliver and for how long.
That does not mean producing as many weapons as possible. It is about having enough weapons to achieve the required military effect, absorb losses, sustain operations and continue fighting. A weapon system that performs brilliantly in a demonstration but is available in quantities sufficient for only a few days of fighting may be an impressive technological achievement. It is not necessarily a meaningful military capability. Equally, producing thousands of inexpensive weapons that cannot survive the battlefield or defeat their intended targets achieves very little. The relevant question is not simply whether a weapon is cheap or expensive. It is how much effective combat power we can generate and sustain with the resources available.
This should fundamentally influence how we define military requirements. If a capability must be employed in thousands or tens of thousands, then unit cost, production rate, supply-chain resilience and ease of replacement are not secondary industrial considerations. They are essential military performance requirements. The real mistake is not buying expensive weapons. It is buying weapons without being clear about the military effect we need, the quantities required to achieve it, and whether we can afford to sustain that effect in war.
Dr Aleksander Olech: You are involved in Frankenburg Technologies and Wolfram Europa. What role can new defence companies play in rebuilding Europe’s industrial capacity, particularly in ammunition, explosives, warheads and mines? How can Europe turn innovation into production at scale?
Maj. Gen. (Ret.) Veiko-Vello Palm: Frankenburg Technologies and Wolfram Europa address different parts of the same problem: Europe needs to rethink not only what weapons it develops, but also what it considers an acceptable solution. At Frankenburg, we started developing an affordable counter-drone missile because we recognised a requirement that traditional procurement systems had not yet properly formulated. A few years ago, nobody was seriously asking for interceptors that could be manufactured in enormous quantities at a price that made sense against cheap drones. The technology was not necessarily the obstacle. The requirement itself was missing. With Wolfram Europa, we are addressing another part of the same problem. Europe has spent decades reducing its explosives production capacity and allowing essential industrial capabilities to disappear. We assumed that future wars would require relatively small quantities of ammunition and that global supply chains would provide whatever we needed.
Many European defence companies are rightly proud of being the tip of the spear. They develop extraordinarily sophisticated weapons, pushing technology to its limits and aiming for 99.99% performance. They have every reason to be proud. We need those capabilities, and we will continue to need them. At Frankenburg and Wolfram Europa, we approach the problem differently. We may be satisfied with a solution that delivers 80% of the desired performance, provided we can manufacture it in sufficient quantities, at an affordable price, and get it into service quickly. This does not mean lowering quality standards. Our products can still be sophisticated, technologically advanced and manufactured to demanding specifications. The starting point is different. We do not automatically assume that every weapon must meet every conceivable requirement before it becomes useful.
Imagine facing a serious battlefield problem without any effective solution. A company approaches you with a new weapon system. There are limitations. It needs at least some visible light. It cannot operate in very strong winds or heavy rain. And, for some inexplicable reason, it does not work on Saturday evenings. A traditional Western procurement response might have been: Interesting, but this does not meet our requirements. Come back when it also works in complete darkness and a snowstorm.
But a week has 168 hours, and until now you have had no solution for any of them. Now somebody offers you a weapon that can solve the problem for 130 of those 168 hours. My reaction would be: Excellent. Get it into service. Then we have two options. We can improve the existing system to cover more conditions, or we can develop another, complementary system that covers the remaining 38 hours. This approach is not appropriate for every weapon system or safety-critical requirement. But it illustrates a fundamental difference in how we think about military capability. We should stop asking only whether a weapon meets every requirement and start asking how much of the operational problem it can solve today.
At Frankenburg, the challenge is to produce affordable interceptors in quantities that correspond to the scale of the drone threat. At Wolfram Europa, we are developing capabilities in Latvia to manufacture and fill warheads and mines, develop new products and ultimately produce explosives. The ambition is European, not merely Latvian. We are not simply trying to recreate the industrial capacity Europe had thirty years ago. We want to combine modern technology with production methods designed for affordability and scale.
New defence companies can play an important role because they are often more willing to question established requirements and accept that an imperfect but useful solution today may be more valuable than a theoretically perfect solution years from now. For this to work, governments must change as well. Procurement must allow for faster introduction, continuous improvement and larger production volumes. Industry needs real orders, not just expressions of interest. A successful prototype is not yet an industrial capability. Manufacturing thousands of reliable products requires investment, qualified people, suppliers and functioning production processes. We should ask whether a system that addresses 80% of an urgent operational problem today may be more valuable than one that promises 99.99% performance but arrives too late or in too few numbers.
Dr Aleksander Olech: If you were advising Poland and the Baltic states, what three capabilities or areas of cooperation should they prioritise over the next five years?
Maj. Gen. (Ret.) Veiko-Vello Palm: I would focus on three areas that would make our armed forces more effective together, even if they are not politically attractive investments. The first is genuine interoperability across all our command-and-control systems — and I mean all of them. Not just the systems used by our national headquarters, but those operating at different levels of command, across different services and between allied formations. We should be able to exchange information automatically, without manually transferring data between incompatible systems or creating separate arrangements every time a new allied unit arrives. We should go a step further. Our military systems must also communicate with civilian networks and information systems. Modern warfare does not take place in an isolated military environment. We depend on civilian infrastructure, telecommunications, transport and other services. We need to exchange relevant information with these systems securely and reliably. This is not primarily a technological challenge. Much of the technology already exists. It is a question of common standards, organisational decisions and the willingness to abandon national or institutional solutions that do not work with others.
My second priority would be the large-scale introduction of artificial intelligence. I believe AI will drive the next major leap in military capability, so we should stop treating it mainly as an experimental technology confined to a few specialist projects. I would start with command and control. AI can help process enormous quantities of information, identify relevant developments, support decision-making and reduce the administrative burden on commanders and staffs. It can also help overcome something surprisingly persistent in multinational operations: language barriers. Perhaps we can finally stop using NATO’s unofficial third language – broken English. Joking aside, the ability to translate, interpret and exchange information rapidly between national systems and personnel could significantly improve multinational operations.
We often discuss unmanned platforms as though removing the human operator from the vehicle is the main achievement. But replacing a crew with a remote operator does not necessarily solve our manpower problem. To employ unmanned systems in truly large numbers, we need increasing levels of autonomy, which makes AI essential. Of course, decisions about the use of lethal force require appropriate human control, legal safeguards and clear responsibility. But that should not prevent us from automating the many other functions that consume manpower and slow down operations.
My third priority is to clarify what the armed forces must provide to society during a crisis and what support they can expect in return. We need a shared understanding of what information civilian authorities, infrastructure operators, emergency services and the wider population require from the military during a crisis or war. The armed forces will have information about threats, damaged infrastructure, dangerous areas, and the security situation that others need to continue functioning. We must be prepared to share the relevant information quickly, in usable formats and at the appropriate level of classification. The more effectively civilian organisations perform their own functions, the more our armed forces can concentrate on fighting the enemy.
Some years ago, I argued that an allied formation should be able to deploy anywhere within allied territory while moving perhaps only one-third of its normal logistical footprint. The remaining support should, wherever practical, come from the host nation. I call this “living off the land”, not in the traditional military sense of requisitioning whatever is available, but by using prearranged support from the host nation. Consider an Estonian unit deploying to Poland. Why bring an entire medical support structure if it can rely on Poland’s extensive, capable hospital network? Conversely, if a Polish unit deploys to Estonia, does it really need to bring all its mechanics, recovery equipment and heavy engineering machinery? Some of those services could be provided by Estonian military and civilian organisations. And surely we do not need to transport water and fuel across Europe as though we were deploying to Afghanistan.
Naturally, this requires advance planning, agreements, financing arrangements and practical exercises. Host-nation resources cannot simply be assumed to be available, particularly when the host country is also fighting a war. The potential benefit would be enormous. We could deploy combat power faster, with fewer vehicles and personnel tied up in support functions. Our aim should be to move fighting capability without transporting an entire self-contained support system behind every formation. Poland and the Baltic states will never have unlimited resources. But we can become much more effective by using the systems, people and infrastructure we already have as one integrated regional capability.
Veiko-Vello Palm is a retired Major General of the Estonian Defence Forces with more than 30 years of military service, during which he held a number of senior positions, including Deputy Chief of Defence, Chief of the General Staff, Commander of the Estonian Division and Commander of the 1st Infantry Brigade. Since retiring from active service in 2024, he has worked in the European defence industry and currently serves as a Member of the Management Board of Frankenburg Technologies, which develops cost-effective counter-drone missile systems, and as Chairman of the Supervisory Board of Wolfram Europa, a defence company focused on explosives, advanced munitions and warheads.

title: Independent candidates sense a moment. Some Democrats hope they're right.
body:
Pins and bumper stickers supporting Dan Osborn's candidacy for U.S. Senate sit on a campaign table on Sept. 3 at Pals Brewing Company in North Platte, Neb. Osborn, a 51-year-old Navy veteran, is running as an independent. Austin Johnson/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
BURWELL, Neb. — Tucked in the rolling Sandhills, the largest sand dune formation in America, sits Morgan Ranch, a 15,000-acre, family-run operation home to 1,000 cows and thousands of offspring.
"There's a lot of mouths to feed — both animals and two-legged," laughed Dan Morgan. His ranch has one of the largest privately owned Wagyu herds in the U.S.
He said his job has given him a front row seat to what he calls the "uncertainty" of President Trump's policies.
"To raise a piece of meat takes me three years," Morgan said. "Well, look at the changes in the past two years: costs, tariffs, reciprocal tariffs because half of our business is export — it's just hell," he said.
He's a Democrat — a self-described small blue dot in a sea of red, in a county and state that Trump dominated two years ago.
There's no Democrat running for the Senate in Nebraska, but Morgan is excited by independent candidate Dan Osborn.
"Osborn makes the case that somebody needs to represent the working family," Morgan said. "And he can effectively do that."
Osborn is one of four independents running for Senate in states President Trump won handily, including Idaho, South Dakota and Montana. Buoyed by the president's sinking approval ratings and public frustration over affordability, independent candidates argue they bring a winning case to voters.
It is an argument that some Democrats hope will resonate with voters as the party looks to retake control of Congress, betting that these candidates can help topple Republicans in parts of the country where their own brand is hurting.
"I'm a partisan Democrat. I believe in the Democratic Party. I also believe in building coalitions so we can win elections and then do the work of the people," said Jane Kleeb, the chair of the Nebraska Democratic Party. "And if that means creating coalitions with independents in some of our states, then that's exactly what we need to do."
But while these independents are generally unified in their political philosophy that the two-party system is toxic and has led to legislative intransigence, the challenges they face in their respective races are different, in large part because of the role the Democratic Party has decided to play.
Seth Bodnar, a former Green Beret running for Senate in Montana , said voters he talks to are fed up with politics as usual — and that he offers a viable alternative as an independent.
"When I go to Washington, D.C., I'm not going to put on a red jersey with an 'R' or a blue jersey with a 'D.' I'm going to have a jersey with an 'M' on it, and I'm going to work for Montana," Bodnar said in an interview from the homecoming parade at the University of Montana, where he used to be president.
Like Osborn, Bodnar said if elected, he won't caucus with either party. The current two independents in the Senate, Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Angus King of Maine, both caucus with Democrats.
His theory of the case is that in a closely divided Senate, an independent willing to work with either party — but beholden to neither — actually holds significant strength.
Seth Bodnar, an independent candidate for a U.S. Senate seat in Montana, speaks to supporters and the press outside the Yellowstone County Courthouse, Aug. 7, in Billings, Mont. Mathew Brown/AP hide caption
"I think there is real power in an independent or multiple independents that can work together, even with people who maybe don't leave their caucus but form an independent-minded bloc, that can move forward common sense solutions that this country so desperately needs," Bodnar said.
The race has been marked by frustration among Democrats — at either Bodnar for not running as a Democrat himself, or at the Democratic nominee, Alani Bankhead, for not dropping out and creating a glide path for Bodnar.
"Had Bodnar run as a Democrat, he'd be leading in this election," said former Democratic Gov. Brian Schweitzer.
"At the end of the day, there will be a lot of people that look in the mirror and say, 'Oh, my God, if we would have just run a Democrat without an independent, we would have won this election,'" Schweitzer said.
Many prominent Montana Democrats — like former Sen. Jon Tester and former Gov. Steve Bullock — have endorsed Bodnar, setting up a divide between Democrats supporting their own party's nominee and those supporting the independent.
"It's just been really, really contentious and quite a bitter thing within the state party," said Rob Saldin, political science professor at the University of Montana.
Saldin said unlike states like Idaho, which has deep Republican entrenchment, Montana Democrats aren't as "beat down" and look at the election as a chance to rebuild the brand in the state.
"They want somebody who, for years into the future, is going to be able to help bring money into the state Democratic Party, to help down-ballot candidates for the legislature, to be the face of the party in the state," he said. "And when you've got an independent candidate who's saying, 'a pox on both your houses,' this is not the guy who's going to be able to do that work in the trenches for the party."
There was an effort to get Bankhead to exit the race before the August deadline. Bankhead said she and her family were harassed. She also said "white gloved politicians" were subtly trying to tell her to drop out of the race.
Alani Bankhead, the Democratic candidate for Senate in Montana, is seen preparing for a rally in East Helena, Mont. on Aug. 10, 2026 — the last day that ballots could be changed. Bankhead verified she was not dropping out of the race. Clayton Murphy/Montana Public Radio hide caption
"They were very polite. They didn't ask me to drop out, but it was subtle — like, 'Well, what's the goal and what kind of job do you want down the road?'" she said, adding she heard from a sitting senator, sitting governor and former cabinet official. "Nobody from the [Democratic National Committee] was like, 'drop out' but that was certainly the nudge."
Bankhead claimed in an interview with Montana PBS that she was offered a DNC job if she dropped out of the race. The DNC denies this.
Bankhead said if Democrats want to support independents — there's a better way to do it.
"Nebraska was very transparent, right? The Democratic nominee said they would step aside in favor of the independent if the people voted for them. And that's very transparent — that's great."
Kleeb, the Nebraska Democratic Party chair and a DNC vice chair, said Nebraska Democrats were very conscious about being transparent regarding their intentions to support the independent on the ticket.
"We were very honest with voters," said Kleeb. "And I think if you're going to do this as a Democratic Party, that's what you have to do — you have to be honest with voters, explain the strategy and make sure that Democrats support that."
She said Democrats had high hopes for Osborn, a mechanic who got his start in politics leading a strike at the Kellogg's plant in 2021, and raised eyebrows two years ago when he came within seven points of incumbent Republican Sen. Deb Fischer.
The choice for Democrats to support Osborn led to the party running someone in the primary with the stated intention of having her drop out to clear the path for Osborn. There was then a lawsuit attempting to force the party to replace that winning primary candidate who dropped out.
Dan Osborn, an independent candidate for U.S. Senate from Nebraska, speaks with Maranda Lee, co-owner of Lee's Crossroads Cafe, at the cafe after a town hall meeting Sept. 3, in Arapahoe, Neb. Austin Johnson/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
Kleeb said the decision to back Osborn is part of a long-term goal, which includes repairing the damage to the Democratic brand in a redder state like Nebraska.
"It's right that people have pushed back on our brand — it's a problem. We are working on it," Kleeb said, adding there will be a time when Nebraska builds up its Democratic base so it's competitive statewide.
In the meantime, Democrats like Kleeb are hoping Osborn can help the party deny Republicans a majority in the Senate.
Osborn has been crisscrossing the state on a 93-county tour. His town halls have a distinctly populist pitch to voters denouncing money in politics.
"We are at a turning point in our country where we have to take it back for ourselves — for the workers, for the people," he said to a group of 30 in Taylor. "Because the powers that be — the money interests — have taken control."
In between stops in five counties on one day, Osborn said in an interview he's not only running against incumbent GOP Sen Pete Ricketts.
"I'm running against the entire establishment that is stuck in this system that's working exactly the way it's supposed to work for them," he said. "I represent something that's going to throw a wrench in."
As Osborn travels the state, Ricketts has been working to convince constituents that the independent is actually a Democrat.
"Dan's a Democrat. Open borders, take our guns, higher taxes, that's no fun — vote for Osborn and you'll see, the Democrats will run D.C.," croons a radio ad from the Ricketts campaign. In their debate , Ricketts called Osborn "Democrat Dan" so many times the independent suggested they should bring out a third podium.
This 2010 photo shows the Sandhills in north central Nebraska. Independent candidate Dan Osborn, who's running for U.S. Senate, recently held a series of meet and greets and town halls in the Sandhills, trying to form a broad coalition of Republicans and Democrats alike. Nati Harnik/AP hide caption
Sue McNeil, a lifelong Republican voter in Loup County, said she doesn't like the nickname.
"I think they're just using that 'Democrat Dan' to scare people, because Nebraska is a Republican state and I feel like a lot of people are a little nervous about supporting a Democrat," she said. "But Dan Osborn is not a Democrat — he's an independent."
She's supporting Osborn, citing frustration with the Trump administration and GOP-controlled Congress.
"Why did we start the war with Iran? Our fuel prices have skyrocketed," she said, noting she recently paid $159 to fill up the pickup. "How are we supposed to make it?"
But other conservative voters say they agree with Ricketts.
"Osborn is a fraud," said Rich Sherbeck from Ansley. "He's not really an independent — he's a Democrat, DSA-aligned."
Casey Stengel, who said he always votes Republican, was curious about Osborn and came to a meet and greet at a coffee shop in Thedford. He told Osborn he was on the fence and asked him to convince him to vote for him.
Osborn launched into a discussion about uplifting workers and building bridges with both parties to bring about real change.
"Yes, there's good ideas," he said. "But we all know one man ain't going to go fix the deal."
Sam Gringlas contributed to this report.

title: In Arkansas, Democrats see an opening at the edge of the competitive midterms map
body:
Arkansas Democratic Senate nominee Hallie Shoffner speaks with voters at a campaign stop in Hope, Ark. Friday, Oct. 23, 2026. Stephen Fowler/NPR hide caption
HOPE, Ark. — For Senate candidate Hallie Shoffner, the most important political label she wears isn't that she's a Democrat. Or that she's not a Republican. Instead, it's that she is an Arkansan.
As a lunchtime crowd ate at Tailgater's Burger Company Friday, Shoffner decried what she called a historically unproductive Congress driven by extreme voices in each party and pitched herself to receptive — if skeptical — voters as a candidate who would better serve their needs.
Arkansas is one of the most conservative states in the country, with nearly two out of three voters supporting President Trump in 2024 and Republican Sen. Tom Cotton in 2020.
But in the final days of the 2026 midterm election, Shoffner and other Arkansas Democrats are crisscrossing the state with a message that seeks to capitalize on the Trump administration's unpopularity, stubbornly high prices and anti-incumbency vibes.
"We're the sleeper race," Shoffner told NPR. "I mean, we're the race that no one's noticed and that no one is going to see coming."
Republicans have taken some notice, pre-emptively pouring millions of dollars into the Senate race, the Little Rock-based 2nd Congressional District and robust get-out-the vote efforts to try and stem the rising tide of dissatisfaction with the party.
But even in a midterm cycle where Senate races in states like Kansas, Iowa, Ohio and Texas are viewed as tossups, and where the landscape of potentially competitive House races stretches deep into conservative territory, Arkansas seems a bridge too far for election forecasters.
Arkansas' 2nd Congressional District is considered "Likely Republican," according to the Cook Political Report, and its Senate race is "Solid Republican."
Hallie Shoffner, the Democratic Senate nominee in Arkansas, has emphasized her farming background and belief that both parties have ignored the people's needs in the state. Stephen Fowler/NPR hide caption
At an outdoor coffee shop in Arkadelphia, Vanilla Hannah said she was there to support Shoffner and talk about her own reelection bid to be a local justice of the peace. She said it's possible that Arkansas could elect Democrats this year because the crop of candidates seems willing to work with people to meet their needs — and there are a lot of them.
"When it comes down to basic needs or whatever, the 'D' or the 'R' after your name don't mean a thing, because we're all suffering and all having the same issues and everybody's ready for a change," she said. "And running for an election is not just running specifically on the Democratic policies or the Republican or the libertarians or whatever. It's just what you believe in, and it seems like more and more people are having a common belief now."
Later, Shoffner visited a small family farm in nearby Bierne where several members of the Hatley family cooked sorghum to make syrup and talked about why they were supporting her campaign.
Shoffner is a multigenerational farmer who decided to shut down her family's operation in 2025, citing financial headwinds from rising input costs and Trump administration tariff and trade policies. That in turn inspired her Senate run and influenced much of her campaign's focus.
Sliding behind the wheel of a side-by-side utility vehicle, Shoffner takes off across the property and recounts her life story that led her away from the farm, into nonprofit work and back home when her dad got sick.
She doesn't buy the argument that her chances are low to win.
"This race isn't about Democrats or Republicans or independents or any of that," she said. "This isn't some kind of weird political alignment, this is a values alignment. This is reorienting representation in Arkansas based on common sense, based on compassion and based on showing up."
She said national Republicans — and Democrats — have made the mistake of ignoring the needs of Arkansas residents, especially with agriculture and trade policies.
"I come from a place, a community, that died in my lifetime," she said. "I was the last one left and I felt left behind. I felt like no one was really talking to me or talking about me. I felt like folks were making decisions about me, but without me, and ultimately they were rewriting the rules."
Now, with record diesel prices, the war in Iran and tariffs, Shoffner said she believes that Arkansas voters of all stripes want something different. She's also glad that the race hasn't seen an influx of outside air support from national Democratic groups.
"I don't need them, I really don't," she said. "This is an Arkansas First campaign, and I'm an Arkansan, and I want to talk directly to Arkansans, and I want them to know that when I go to D.C., the only letters that will mean anything next to my name are the "A" and the "R."
Chris Jones, the Democratic nominee for Arkansas' 2nd Congressional District, says voters are frustrated with promises made by the Trump administration that haven't been kept. Stephen Fowler/NPR hide caption
On the flip side, Chris Jones has the backing of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee as one of dozens of "Red to Blue" flip targets.
At an outdoor jazz night held at a brewery in Little Rock, Jones worked the crowd between visits to polling sites and a high school football homecoming game on a campaign that has seen millions of dollars in outside spending by Republicans.
"They understand that people are in pain," he said. "Folks are hurting. They can't afford gas. They can't afford groceries. And our campaign has always been about affordability and accountability for all. So prices are way too high."
Jones also ran for governor against Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders in 2022 and lost, so he started off with higher name recognition as a serious challenger to Rep. French Hill.
He knows it's a tall task, even in a national environment more favorable to Democrats. Hill is a longtime incumbent whose district only became more conservative after the last Census-led redistricting in 2021.
But he also knows that Democrats, Republicans and independent voters alike are open to looking for something other than the current leadership.
"Here's what's so fascinating: a lot of folks here voted for the president and this administration because they wanted lower prices, they wanted to end foreign wars, and they wanted to end corruption, particularly with the Epstein files," he said. "None of that has happened, so they're super frustrated."
Like many states that have seen the potential for close races next week, Arkansas has a longer history of single-party control that has led to anger and frustration at the status quo and incumbency in a way that extends beyond typical partisan labels or voting history.
"One of the things that we forget, because there's so much that comes out of this administration: It wasn't but 15 years ago that the entire federal delegation of Arkansas was Democrat," he said. "So it's not that long ago. The reason they got in office was because of the conditions that existed, the economic anxiety and pain that people feel — and folks feeling like what they wanted to happen out of Washington was not happening. We're in that same place now."
In addition to the DCCC support, Jones has had campaign visits from former DNC Chair Jaime Harrison, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and Rep. Jasmine Crockett of Texas. Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker and Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear have both endorsed his run. And he's heard from people who don't normally support Democrats saying they'll back his campaign.
"Folks are literally hurting, and it's to the point where they're saying, 'my life is so bad that I don't care about party anymore'," he said.
Another factor working in Democrats' favor this election cycle is a surge in Black turnout following a Supreme Court decision that weakened part of the Voting Rights Act.
Multiple states across the South rushed to redraw House maps to gain a partisan advantage, with many of the new districts crafted in a way that minimized Black voting power. Arkansas lawmakers did not redraw their maps — the state has an entirely Republican congressional delegation — but after the 2020 Census did split Little Rock up in a manner that made Hill's district more Republican.
In primaries following the ruling, and early voting this month ahead of the midterms, there has been sustained higher Black turnout in states like South Carolina, Georgia and Louisiana in ways that could affect the outcome in key races across the region.
"I think part of it is that folks realized that there was an imminent threat to their right to vote," Jones said. "And people realized across the country that if we don't show up now, and Black folks realize if we don't speak up now, then our ability to do it later might not be there."
Marcus Hatley, one of the people who met with Shoffner at his family farm, said the increased turnout seemed like a "course correction."
"People are dissatisfied with the way that that happened, and some are crossing sides and voting in a different direction," he said. "And a lot of it has to do with removing, in some of those states, the ability for people of color to have equal representation in their districts. So it looks like to me there's going to be a course correction. I could be wrong, but I believe there's going to be a change."

title: More dads taking paid family leave for a new baby, sometimes as much as moms are
body:
Karlo Campana plays Magnatiles with his daughters Gianna and Giselle, while his 5-month-old son Gianluca watches. Campana is one of the growing number of California men taking advantage of the state's paid bonding leave program. Dania Maxwell for NPR hide caption
Karlo Campana is usually outnumbered these days. He has three young kids under age 4.
On a recent Saturday, he played a mini-game of basketball with his two older kids in their Southern California home, shooting a ball into a hoop on the door, while his baby boy watched from his bouncy chair.
This story was produced in partnership with KFF Health News .
Campana took paid time off in May after the birth of his son — just as he did for his daughters.
It's sometimes called "bonding" or "family" leave, to distinguish it from the paid leave ("maternity" or "disability" leave) that mothers can take to physically recover from childbirth.
"You need that adjustment period," he said. Campana, who works at an ad agency, said having the time off not to think about work — or worry about losing income during that time — was crucial for him and his family during a sleep-deprived period.
"My wife isn't doing it on her own," he said. "She doesn't feel like she's alone on this journey. She feels like she has support." He jokes that by kid No. 3, he thought he had nailed diaper changes without too much mess — but he was wrong.
"The benefits are I get to spend time with each of them when they were in the infant stage, the baby stage, and I get to hold them and, you know, change the poopy diapers," he said. " It's like the funny moments of, like, being a parent, like, 'This is it right here, you're in the thick of it.'"
Karlo Campana plays with his daughter Giselle and his infant son Gianluca at home on October 12 in Santa Ana, Calif. With three children under 4, paid paternity leave gave him something invaluable: time to bond with his kids and support his wife in the thick of early parenthood. Dania Maxwell for NPR hide caption
Campana is among a growing number of fathers who take leave to bond with a new child in the states that offer paid family leave programs — and are part of a larger cultural shift that has seen dads handle more caregiving duties.
In California — as in several other states — men make up about half of bonding claim applications . Last year, men even surpassed women — as in Colorado and Washington — for the first time in the state's history. This trend comes at a time when the federal government has said it wants Americans to have more babies, and families report affordability is an obstacle in raising them.
There's no federal law guaranteeing paid parental leave, but California is one of 14 states, plus Washington, D.C. , that have passed legislation to enact paid family leave programs — and in many of those places, more dads are opting in.
"We're in a very different place in terms of our understanding of gender roles, of paternity leave, of dads' roles than we were 20-plus years ago," said Molly Weston Williamson, policy director at Paid Leave for All , an organization that advocates for paid family leave policies.
California's program offers , within a year, up to eight weeks of paid bonding leave for parents after a birth, adoption, or foster care placement. That's on top of six to eight weeks of paid disability leave that moms get to recover after birth.
Karlo Campana at dinner with his wife Lily and their three children. His experience reflects a broader shift across California, where fathers accounted for 51% of paid bonding leave claims in 2025, surpassing mothers for the first time. Dania Maxwell for NPR hide caption
Campana said he initially wasn't sure if he should take paternity leave because of lingering gender stereotypes.
" I felt guilty, for sure," Campana said. " I think dads maybe feel they need to be the provider. They need to be the ones that are only helping their family by bringing money or working."
Campana said that when he was growing up, his father worked three jobs. "It was hard for him to be present, and I think that's the one thing now — it's like, 'No, be present. Be there for your kids.'"
Research has shown that paternity leave confers benefits beyond allowing a father extra time to bond with a new child: It has positive effects on the whole family, including better health outcomes for both parents.
Paid parental leave has also been linked to lower odds of postpartum depression and a decrease in infant mortality rates .
In California, men accounted for 51% of bonding claims filed in 2025. It's a massive shift from when the state program started in 2004, and men made up about 18% of claim applications.
States fund their paid family and medical leave programs with different combinations of employer and employee contributions; California is among six states where family leave is entirely funded by employee payroll deductions.
Karlo Campana poses for a portrait with his wife Lily and their three kids (from left to right) Gianna, Gianluca, and Giselle. Dania Maxwell for NPR hide caption
In addition to changing gender norms, Williamson said other factors are likely contributing to the increase in claims by men in the state: greater awareness about the program, and recent changes to the benefit.
In 2025, the state boosted the amount of income a worker can recoup while on family leave. Now, in California and in other states, the leave benefit can be as high as 90% of their regular salary.
"That makes it a realistic option for a lot more families, and I think we're seeing dads and moms responding to that change," Williamson said. Still, she said, there's a lot the new data about dads isn't telling us.
"We're getting one particular vantage point into this data, which is useful and valuable, but it's only telling us sort of part of the story, and we'd need other kinds of information to better understand the full picture," Williamson said.
"Is it that more dads are working and therefore are potentially eligible for these benefits? Is it that women are deciding not to take leave?"
While private employers can offer their own paid leave as a benefit, this data also reflects only people who took leave through California's paid family leave program.
Karlo Campana washes Giselle's hands after dinner on October 12 at home in Santa Ana, Calif. "My wife isn't doing it on her own," he said of his decision to take paid leave from his job after the birth of their third child. "She doesn't feel like she's alone on this journey. She feels like she has support." Dania Maxwell for NPR hide caption
A spokesperson for the California Employment Development Department, which administers the state's family leave program, said the department couldn't provide definitive reasons for the increase in male bonding claims.
One thing is clear: The growth in these states comes as more parents are feeling strained economically.
President Trump has said, "We want more babies," and has promoted policy initiatives like expanding access to in vitro fertilization and offering investment accounts for newborns.
"People really are very worried about the affordability of kids," said Jeremy Pope , a professor of political science at Brigham Young University, and a principal investigator of the American Family Survey .
Karlo Campana plays with his new son Gianluca as his wife Lily prepares dinner in Santa Ana, Calif. "You need that adjustment period," he said. Dania Maxwell for NPR hide caption
According to the latest survey in 2025, 7 in 10 Americans said raising children had become unaffordable, according to the survey . It was the biggest single-year jump since the survey started more than a decade ago.
"I don't think they want government involved in the decision to have kids," Pope said. "But they worry a lot about how much it costs and they would like to see ways of making those costs smaller or getting help with those costs."
The Pew Research Center found in a recent survey of full-time working parents who are not self-employed, 84% said paid parental, family, or medical leave would be "extremely or very helpful" to them, but only half said it was available to them.
This story comes from NPR's health reporting partnership with LAist and KFF Health News .

title: Disenchanted Netanyahu supporters are prize of Israel election campaign
body: DIMONA, Israel – In the remote Negev Desert town of Dimona, long a bastion of Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party, disenchanted voters are going door-to-door campaigning for his top rival, hoping to bring down the veteran prime minister in Israel’s election on Tuesday, October 27. The ballot is Israel’s first since Hamas’ October 7, 2023, surprise attack that shook the country and plunged the region into turmoil, as Israel went to war on the militant group in Gaza and its allies in Lebanon and Iran . The October 7 security breach saw Likud’s popularity plummet. Opinion polls for months have predicted Netanyahu’s coalition of right-wing, far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties losing its majority. But his top rival, centrist Gadi Eisenkot, has no clear path to power either, and the race has become tighter as the election nears. Dimona, where an Iranian missile wounded dozens in March, has become a political battleground. “We must have change. Bibi has to go,” said Yossi Assayag, 74, who says he has supported Likud most his life. “Bibi has brought disaster to Israel. “ Likud loyalists Assayag is part of a cohort of town residents trying to convince their community to vote for Eisenkot’s party Yashar, which is neck-and-neck with Likud in the polls. It’s a tough task in Dimona, where half the voters in the previous 2022 election cast a ballot for Likud. “I will never betray Likud,” said Ruti Ohana, a pensioner, who says she has voted Likud ever since immigrating to Israel from North Africa more than 60 years ago. She said Netanyahu was a cut above his rivals, and the blame he receives from detractors for October 7 was unfair. Right-wing Likud long ago formed a core voter base among Jews of Middle Eastern and North African descent, known as Mizrahis, who felt neglected by the European-influenced centre-left Labor Party that dominated Israel for generations. Labor has since dwindled to a rump as Israeli politics have shifted rightwards, and there are now around half a dozen other parties courting Likud voters, from the centre to the far right. But the link to the party among its past supporters remains strong. “Most people here vote for Likud just because that’s how they were raised,” said Oria Asaf, 25, a past Likud voter now backing Yashar. “The change will come when people start to think about their children’s future rather than their parents’ past.” Battle for wavering Likudnics While Netanyahu has a hard core of supporters that can’t be won over, the prize is undecided voters who “understand that we are in a state of crisis” and are open to persuasion, said Michal Elmalem Abu, elected as a member of the city council from Likud and now leading Eisenkot’s Dimona campaign. Some 13% of Israeli voters have yet to decide how they will vote, according to data collected by the Viterbi Family Center for Public Opinion and Policy Research at the Israel Democracy Institute. Of those who voted for Likud in 2022, just 55% now say they will vote for the party again on Tuesday. Fifteen percent will support parties aligned against Netanyahu, including 8% for Yashar. Another 14% will vote for alternative right-wing parties, and 9% are undecided. It is in places just like Dimona where Eisenkot stands a chance to bite a chunk out of Likud’s base, said Amotz Asa-El, a political scientist at the Hartman Institute. A child of Moroccan immigrants who rose through the ranks to become military chief of staff, Eisenkot, 66, has a personal story of humble origins from the Mizrahi community that “appeals to a big swath of the Israeli electorate, particularly Likud’s traditional electorate,” said Asa-El. In an electoral field crowded with ex-soldiers, his peerless security credentials are an asset. The loss of his son, killed in combat in Gaza in December 2023, resonates with voters. At a town hall during a visit to Dimona in July, residents said they were excited about the prospect of a leader of Mizrahi descent. Others approached him with hugs and tearful condolences for the loss of his son. But a week later Netanyahu held his own event, demonstrating his powerful appeal in the hardscrabble Negev, where Likud governments have long boasted of bringing development funds. “Look around you, look at your community, look at what was here then and what is here now, and ask yourselves which governments invested in this monumental effort. And I do this out of immense love,” he said. Lior Katzav, a Likud former mayor of Kiryat Malachi, another small-town stronghold, said party surveys show voters who had abandoned Likud are returning as the election nears. But even some who are sympathetic to Netanyahu say it may be time for a change. Israel’s youngest prime minister when he was first elected 30 years ago, he has since become its longest-serving, now 77, having governed for 18 years over six terms. “It’s time for him to go,” said Dimona software engineer David Iskali. “He’s done a lot for Israel but it can’t go on. I won’t give my vote to someone almost 80-years-old.” – Rappler.com

title: Kano ACF chair resigns, three-member interim leadership team appointed
body:
The Arewa Consultative Forum (ACF), Kano State Chapter, has appointed a three-member interim leadership team to steer its affairs alongside the remaining executive committee members after its chairman, Goni Umar, resigned.
The ACF’s spokesperson in Kano, Nasiru Ibrahim, said in a statement to PREMIUM TIMES that the interim team comprises Isyaku Tofa, Bala Sani and Rabia Adamu.
The appointments were announced by Haliru Akilu during a joint meeting of members of the ACF Board of Trustees representing Kano State and the chapter’s executive committee, held on Saturday at the Late Amina Habib ACF Secretariat in Kano.
Mr Akilu, a retired army general, said the three members would manage the chapter’s affairs for the remainder of the current executive committee’s tenure, pending the election of a new chairman.
He explained that the decision was intended to restore understanding, promote reconciliation and strengthen cooperation among members following disagreements that had affected the chapter.
He urged members to set aside their differences and work collectively in the forum’s interest, stressing that the meeting aimed to resolve outstanding issues rather than revive past controversies.
“The spirit that should guide every one of us is the same: consultation before decision, integrity before convenience and service before self,” Mr Akilu said.
He called on members to embrace patience, humility and constructive dialogue, adding that every contribution should help the chapter find lasting solutions to its challenges.
Mr Akilu also acknowledged receipt of Mr Umar’s resignation letter, in which the outgoing chairman cited the demands of his busy schedule.
He expressed appreciation for Mr Umar’s service to the chapter, commending his time, energy and commitment to the forum. He also wished him well in his other responsibilities and hoped he would continue to offer advice and support.
Mr Akilu further commended Assistant Controller-General of Narcotics Abubakar Ahmed for serving as acting chairman for approximately four months during the outgoing chairman’s absence.
He praised Mr Ahmed’s dedication and contributions to the chapter, noting that his service had helped sustain its activities during the period.
In their separate remarks, the three newly appointed interim leaders expressed appreciation for the confidence reposed in them and pledged to justify the trust through dedicated service.
Mr Akilu said a united and purposeful ACF Kano Chapter would be better positioned to contribute to the development of Kano State and northern Nigeria, particularly in addressing challenges relating to insecurity, poverty, education, youth empowerment and peaceful coexistence.

title: Sabic returns to profit in third quarter as revenue rises despite regional conflict
body: Saudi Basic Industries Corporation ( Sabic ), the Middle East’s largest petrochemicals company, returned to profitability in the third quarter as revenue increased and its operating performance improved despite challenging market conditions. Net profit attributable to shareholders of the company reached 500 million Saudi riyals ($133 million) in the three months to the end of September, up 16.3 per cent from the same period last year, Sabic said in a bourse filing on Sunday. The company swung to a profit in the July to September period after reporting a net loss of 833 million riyals in the second quarter this year due to the regional conflict. Revenue in the third quarter rose 14 per cent on a quarterly basis to 28.17 billion riyals, although it remained about 3 per cent below the year-earlier level. Adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda) increased 40 per cent quarter-on-quarter to 4.75 billion riyals, while adjusted net income reached 840 million riyals, reversing a loss of 380 million riyals in the second quarter. “In Q3 2026, Sabic demonstrated exceptional resilience, despite geopolitical developments and market headwinds, coupled with a clear and robust forward-looking vision and continued focus on strategic objectives, namely portfolio optimisation, transformation and selective growth, in efforts to support the company’s long-term profitability and value creation for shareholders, building on its historic journey of more than five decades,” said Sabic chief executive Faisal M Alfaqeer. Sabic’s results come against a backdrop of heightened security risks for Saudi Arabia’s energy industry , with the kingdom’s oil and petrochemical infrastructure facing repeated missile and drone attacks amid the widening regional conflict. Sabic has a major presence in Dhahran, primarily centred around its advanced research and innovation ecosystems. Earlier this month, a Houthi missile attack damaged Saudi Aramco’s headquarters complex in Dhahran. The attack sparked a fire in an administrative building in Aramco’s complex. Aramco owns a 70 per cent stake in Sabic. The developments have raised fresh concerns about the security of Saudi Arabia’s energy infrastructure as the Iran war continues to disrupt regional energy markets. For the first nine months of 2026, Sabic narrowed its net loss to 320 million riyals, from 4.84 billion riyals in the same period last year, although revenue declined nearly 11 per cent to 79.13 billion riyals. Sabic said it completed the sale of its engineering thermoplastics business in the Americas and Europe for an enterprise value of $450 million during the third quarter, as part of efforts to streamline its operations and improve long-term profitability. It also said its transformation programme had generated 3.56 billion riyals in recurring Ebitda benefits towards its 2030 target of 11.3 billion riyals.

title: Troops raid bandits enclave, rescue three kidnap victims in Kebbi
body: By Haruna Aliyu,Birnin Kebbi Troops of Sector 2, Operation Fansan Yamma, have rescued three kidnapped victims during an operation in Sakaba Local Government Area of Kebbi State. The victims were identified as Aisha Aminu, 46; Sumayya Aminu, 27; and Nana Abbas, 15. The rescue operation took place on Saturday, October 24, 2026, with two of the victims rescued at Makuku Village and the third at Dankolo Village. The development was disclosed in a statement made available to our correspondent on Sunday by the spokesman for the 8 Division, Nigerian Army, Lt. Col. Olaniyi Osoba. According to the statement, the operation was successfully concluded without any incident. “The victims were subsequently handed over to the District Head of Dirindaji, Alhaji Usman Muhammad, through the Chairman of Sakaba Local Government Area,” the statement said. The military described the operation as successful, noting that the rescued victims were transferred to the relevant local authorities after their recovery. “The operation was concluded successfully without any incident,” the statement added. Osoba reaffirmed the troops’ commitment to protecting residents and communities in the state, stressing that troops remained focused on their responsibility to safeguard lives and property. “Troops remain committed to the protection of lives and property,” the statement said. The rescue comes amid persistent security concerns in parts of Nigeria’s North-West, where kidnapping and other criminal activities have continued to threaten residents and disrupt community life.
