title: 4 Killed in Synelnykove Strike, Rescuers Hit in Kharkiv
body:
A Russian drone strike on a residential apartment building in the city of Synelnykove in Dnipropetrovsk region killed four people and injured 13 others, regional authorities confirmed, while separate drone attacks on Kharkiv killed one person and wounded four, including three emergency rescue workers.
Head of the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Military Administration Oleksandr Hanzha announced that incoming fire struck a multi-story residential complex in Synelnykove on Saturday evening, Oct. 24, igniting a blaze across the fourth floor and inflicting extensive structural damage on nearby retail shops and parked civilian vehicles.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Three civilians died immediately at the impact site, while a 62-year-old man succumbed to critical wounds in a local hospital on Sunday morning, Oct. 25, raising the casualty toll to four.
Regional health authorities confirmed that 13 civilians sustained injuries, including an 11-year-old girl.
Four patients remain hospitalized in serious condition, with surgical teams stabilizing two women and a man before arranging medical transfers to a regional clinical facility in the city of Dnipro. A 50-year-old woman and a 70-year-old man were among those admitted in critical condition.
Concurrently in northeastern Ukraine, Russian forces launched a sequence of drone strikes across three urban districts of Kharkiv on Saturday evening and overnight into Sunday, killing one civilian and wounding four others.
Head of the Kharkiv Regional Military Administration Oleh Syniehubov reported that a turbojet-powered strike drone hit the Novobavarskyi district, killing one person, injuring four others, and setting a single-story structure ablaze.
In Kharkiv’s Osnovianskyi district, strike drones targeted a commercial shopping center, triggering an extensive structural blaze. Concurrently, an unmanned aerial munition struck a civilian commercial enterprise in the Industrialnyi district, igniting secondary fires and injuring a civilian worker.
As units from the State Emergency Service of Ukraine (DSNS) deployed to contain the blazes and clear debris, Russian forces launched a secondary strike targeting the operational area of the responding emergency detachments.
The repeat impact wounded two rescue personnel and destroyed an DSNS fire-tanker truck, while a third firefighter sustained injuries while battling the major fire at the shopping center.
The bombardments in Synelnykove and Kharkiv coincided with broader Russian standoff strikes across Ukrainian residential settlements and emergency services over the weekend.
Early Sunday morning, an adversary strike drone struck a five-story residential building in the central city of Vinnytsia , injuring six civilians, destroying four apartments between the second and third floors, and forcing the emergency evacuation of 15 elderly residents from an adjacent private care home.
Earlier on Saturday, daytime drone strikes in Sumy region killed a 31-year-old female farm worker at a cattle-breeding facility in Konotop district , while a separate drone strike in Dnipropetrovsk region’s Pokrovske community left a 14-year-old boy in critical condition. Concurrently, a missile impact killed a 45-year-old commercial warehouse employee in Lozova, Kharkiv region.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: SERAP sues Nigerian govt at ECOWAS Court over ₦78.8bn cash transfer
body:
The Socio-Economic Rights and Accountability Project (SERAP) has filed a lawsuit against the federal government over “the alleged diversion, irregular expenditure and failure to account for over ₦78.8 billion in public funds involving the Ministry of Humanitarian Affairs and Poverty Reduction, the National Cash Transfer Office (NCTO) and the National Social Safety Nets Coordinating Office (NASSCO).”
The allegations are documented in the Auditor-General of the Federation’s 2024 Annual Report, published on 7 August 2026. According to the Auditor-General, the findings cover various periods between January 2023 and 31 December 2024.
In the suit number ECW/CCJ/APP/42/26 filed last week at the ECOWAS Community Court of Justice, Abuja, SERAP is seeking: “a declaration that the failure of the Nigerian government to account for over ₦78.8 billion in public funds allocated for federal cash-transfer and social-protection programmes is unlawful and a violation of Nigeria’s international human rights obligations.”
SERAP is seeking a declaration that “the government’s failure to ensure the lawful administration of public funds allocated for cash-transfer programmes intended to benefit vulnerable households undermines the enjoyment of the rights protected under the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights.”
SERAP is also seeking “an order of perpetual injunction restraining the government from administering or disbursing cash-transfer and social-protection funds without adequate financial accountability, beneficiary verification, auditing and oversight mechanisms consistent with Nigeria’s international human rights obligations.”
In the suit, SERAP is arguing that “the government has violated, and continues to violate, the rights to social security and an adequate standard of living, including food, clothing and housing, by failing to properly administer social-protection funds and ensure access to benefits intended to meet basic needs.”
SERAP is also arguing that “the failure to account for substantial public funds allocated for social protection, and to investigate and remedy deficiencies, undermines the socio-economic rights of millions of affected Nigerians.”
According to SERAP, “The funds were intended to benefit over 3.2 million households across 35 states, whose access to financial assistance has been affected by the allegations made by the Auditor-General.”
The suit filed on behalf of SERAP by its lawyers, Kolawole Oluwadare and Kehinde Oyewumi, read in part: “The failure to investigate the ₦78.8 billion cash-transfer scandal, account for the questioned funds and recover any unlawfully spent amounts violates Nigeria’s obligations to protect the human rights of vulnerable households.”
“SERAP brings this public-interest case to protect the interests of affected households and ensure accountability for public funds allocated for their benefit.”
“SERAP submits that failures to account for public funds allocated to socio-economic rights, coupled with a failure to take effective corrective action, engages the State’s human-rights obligations. Cash-transfer programmes help address extreme poverty and enable vulnerable people to meet their basic needs.”
“The suit relies on the Auditor-General’s 2024 Annual Report, published on 7 August 2026, which identified financial irregularities in federal institutions, including the National Cash Transfer Office and the National Social Safety Nets Coordinating Office.”
“The Auditor-General questioned approximately ₦33.751 billion reportedly transferred to over 3.2 million households across 35 states in 2023, as adequate records to verify the payments and reconcile beneficiary records were not provided.”
“The report also identified ₦36.744 billion in payments made without prepayment audits, ₦4.616 billion in unsupported expenditures, and other questioned payments, including ₦350.182 million for enrolment, ₦89.511 million for store purchases and ₦17.422 million in diesel advances.”
“SERAP brings this public-interest case under Article 9(4) of the ECOWAS Court Protocol to protect the interests of affected households and ensure accountability for public funds intended for social protection.”
“The issue is whether the government has discharged its obligations under applicable human-rights treaties to safeguard resources allocated for social protection, investigate documented financial irregularities, provide effective remedies and ensure that those resources are applied for their intended purposes.”
“The Auditor-General is constitutionally responsible for auditing and reporting upon the public accounts of the Federation and the offices and agencies of the Federal Government. His findings are recorded in annual reports submitted to the National Assembly and constitute important official records concerning public expenditure.”
“The obligation to recognise and give effect to the rights protected under the African Charter, guaranteed by Article 1 of the Charter, include the obligation to adopt legislative or other measures necessary to give effect to protected rights.”
“The right to equality and non-discrimination, under Article 2 of the African Charter and the corresponding obligations, would be violated where there are failures in administering or verifying social-protection programmes which result in discriminatory exclusion or unequal access to benefits.”
“The Nigerian government has the obligation to take effective measures to prevent and address corruption and related misuse of public resources. The government has failed to take appropriate measures in response to the allegations made by the Auditor-General.”
“The right to social security cannot be effectively realised merely by establishing a formal cash-transfer programme where the State fails to maintain reasonable systems for identifying beneficiaries, maintaining records, reconciling disbursements, monitoring expenditure, investigating irregularities and remedying losses.”
“Following publication of the Auditor-General’s Report, SERAP issued a public statement and, in a letter dated 5 September 2026, urged President Bola Tinubu and relevant authorities to account for the questioned funds, publish audit records, investigate irregular expenditures, recover any funds unlawfully spent or diverted, and take appropriate action against those responsible.”
“SERAP also requested payment and beneficiary records, verification documents and an explanation for the missing REMITA records.”
“The deadline given to the government to address the Auditor-General’s findings had elapsed without adequate action.”
“The financial irregularities and the government’s failure to address them raise human rights concerns, particularly the rights to social security, an adequate standard of living, and the right to economic, social and cultural development.”
“The government must properly manage public funds allocated for social protection in accordance with its human rights obligations and take reasonable measures to ensure that vulnerable households receive their intended benefits.”
“The Auditor-General’s findings on beneficiary verification, prepayment audits, supporting documents and financial reconciliation raise serious questions about whether these funds were properly managed and reached vulnerable households.”
“Articles 1 and 21 of the African Charter, alongside Article 9 of the UN Convention against Corruption, require effective measures to protect people’s rights and resources, ensure transparent public financial management, investigate irregularities and recover public funds where losses or improper expenditure are established.”
“SERAP relies on Kolawole Olaniyan’s Corruption and Human Rights Law in Africa (Hart Publishing, 2014) and Ownership of Proceeds of Corruption in International Law (Oxford University Press, 2023) as persuasive academic authority on the impact of corruption on human rights, public resources, victims’ rights, accountability and international legal remedies.”
“These works support principles grounded in applicable human rights treaties and jurisprudence.”
“SERAP accordingly submits that the Auditor-General’s findings cannot be treated merely as administrative irregularities where public funds allocated for social protection may have been lost, improperly spent or left unaccounted for, and the government fails to take effective corrective action.”
“The failures in public financial management that impair protected human rights may engage the right to an effective remedy. The government’s failure to adequately investigate, account for and recover misused funds, and provide appropriate remedies, may constitute a continuing failure to meet its human-rights obligations.”
SERAP is therefore asking the ECOWAS Court for the following reliefs:
1. A DECLARATION that the failure to take effective measures to investigate and remedy the financial irregularities identified in the 2024 Annual Report of the Auditor-General of the Federation, insofar as those failures impair or risk impairing access to intended benefits, violates the Respondent’s international human rights obligations.
2. AN ORDER directing the Respondent, through the National Cash Transfer Office (NCTO), the National Social Safety Nets Coordinating Office (NASSCO) and other relevant agencies, to provide a comprehensive and verifiable account of the questioned funds, including relevant payment, beneficiary, verification and reconciliation records.
3. AN ORDER directing the Respondent to conduct an independent, prompt and effective investigation into the identified irregularities; recover public funds improperly spent, diverted or lost where established; and take appropriate legal or administrative action against persons found responsible, in accordance with due process.
4. AN ORDER directing the Respondent to strengthen financial accountability, beneficiary verification, auditing, reconciliation and oversight mechanisms to prevent the recurrence of irregularities in federal cash-transfer and social-protection programmes.
5. AN ORDER directing the Respondent to take effective measures to ensure that eligible vulnerable persons and households receive the social-protection benefits intended for them and that any established adverse effects on their protected rights are appropriately remedied.
No date has been fixed for the hearing of the suit.

title: Eisenkot leads Netanyahu but deadlock looms, election polls show two days before Israelis vote
body: Just two days before Israelis head to the polls, the four latest election surveys show a similar picture: Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party leads Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud, but neither of the two major political blocs has enough seats to secure a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.With the election campaign entering its final stretch, the battle to cross Israel's 3.25% electoral threshold could significantly affect the distribution of seats and the balance of power in the next Knesset.A comparison of the four polls published over the weekend, along with their average results, shows that neither Netanyahu nor his political rivals currently has a clear path to forming a government.Ofer Winter fails to cross electoral threshold as Netanyahu bloc loses groundAccording to the final Maariv poll before the election, the opposition's change bloc has strengthened to 54 seats, compared with 48 for Netanyahu's bloc.The shift comes as Ofer Winter's People of Israel party fails to cross the electoral threshold, receiving 3% of the vote, just below the required 3.25%.The poll also shows United Torah Judaism and Otzma Yehudit losing one seat each, while Likud, Shas, and the Religious Zionist Party (RZP) each gain a seat. Overall, Netanyahu's coalition bloc has lost three seats compared with the previous week's poll.Among the opposition parties, the most significant change is the rise of former prime minister Naftali Bennett's B'Yachad party, which gains two seats to reach 15. The Democrats, led by Yair Golan, also gain one seat, bringing their total to 10.Meanwhile, Eisenkot's Yashar remains unchanged at 21 seats, and Avigdor Liberman's Yisrael Beytenu remains at eight.The poll also finds that the joint Reservists Party and Economic Party led by former communications minister Yoaz Hendel and economist Yaron Zelekha narrowly crosses the electoral threshold, securing four seats.Eisenkot leads but lacks majority to form governmentThe Channel 13 election poll gives Netanyahu's bloc 50 seats, compared with 54 for the opposition's change bloc.Eisenkot's Yashar leads with 22 seats, followed by Netanyahu's Likud with 19. Bennett's B'Yachad ranks third with 14 seats.Ofer Winter's People of Israel receives 3.1% of the vote, falling short of the electoral threshold. The joint Reservists Party and Economic Party receives 3%, while Moti Leitner's Haredi Public Party receives 1.3%.All three fall below the 3.25% threshold required to enter the Knesset.KAN 11 poll: Winter fails to cross threshold as neither bloc secures majorityA poll published by Israel's public broadcaster KAN 11 shows Eisenkot's Yashar losing one seat but maintaining its lead with 22.Netanyahu's Likud also loses one seat, falling to 20, while Bennett's B'Yachad gains two seats to reach 14.The joint Reservists Party and Economic Party secures four seats.Meanwhile, Winter's People of Israel fails to cross the electoral threshold, along with the Haredi Public Party and the Noam Party.The poll points to a further decline for Netanyahu's bloc, which falls to 50 seats, while Eisenkot's bloc stands at 52.The Arab parties gain one seat, bringing their combined total to 14, while the Hendel and Zelekha list holds four seats.Under this distribution, neither of the two major blocs reaches the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority without additional support.Eisenkot narrowly leads Netanyahu as Hendel and Zelekha fail to enter KnessetThe Channel 12 poll puts Eisenkot's Yashar first with 23 seats, followed by Netanyahu's Likud with 21.Bennett's B'Yachad ranks third with 15 seats.Three parties fail to cross the electoral threshold, according to the poll. The joint Hendel-Zelekha list gets 2.4% of the vote, while the Haredi Public Party gets just 0.5%.Winter's People of Israel drops to 2.5%, keeping it out of the Knesset.The seat distribution among the political blocs highlights the difficulty Netanyahu faces in securing enough parliamentary support to form a government.The coalition bloc holds 50 seats, compared with 56 for the opposition bloc, while the Arab parties win a combined 14 seats.Neither bloc, therefore, reaches the 61 seats required for a parliamentary majority without additional support.Opposition bloc leads Netanyahu bloc by 4.5 seatsAhead of the election for Israel's 26th Knesset, the average of the four latest polls published by Channel 12, Channel 13, Channel 14, and Maariv shows Eisenkot's Yashar holding a lead of just over two seats over Netanyahu's Likud.Across the four polls, Yashar averages 22 seats, compared with 19.75 for Likud.Bennett's B'Yachad follows with an average of 14.5 seats, ahead of Golan's Democrats with 9.5 and Liberman's Yisrael Beytenu with eight.The joint Reservists and Economic Party list crosses the electoral threshold in two of the four polls, securing four seats in each. Its estimated average support stands at 3.10%, just 0.15 percentage points below the 3.25% electoral threshold.By contrast, Winter's People of Israel fails to cross the threshold in all four polls, averaging 2.88% support.Among the parties in Netanyahu's coalition bloc, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit averages 7.75 seats, while Shas and United Torah Judaism each average 7.5. The joint RZP and Zehut list averages seven seats.The Arab Joint List averages 9 seats, while the Ra'am party averages 5.5.Across the four polls, the opposition parties average 54 seats, compared with 49.5 for Netanyahu's bloc. The Arab parties average 14.5 seats combined.The average gap between the two major blocs is 4.5 seats, and neither has reached the 61-seat majority needed to form a government.

title: 2027: Kano Hisbah Board commandant says he won’t campaign for anyone
body:
The Commandant-General of the Kano State Hisbah Board, Aminu Daurawa, says he will not campaign for any politician in the 2027 general elections.
Mr Daurawa expressed his stance in a message he published on his Facebook page on Saturday.
The Islamic cleric’s position follows ongoing criticism of his inclusion in the All Progressives Congress (APC) campaign advisory committee in Kano.
PREMIUM TIMES reported that Mr Daurawa and Abdullahi Saleh Pakistan, a former chairman of the National Hajj Commission of Nigeria (NAHCON), are among the Islamic clerics listed on the committee.
Their inclusion raised questions about religious leaders’ involvement in partisan politics.
In the Hausa-language post, Mr Daurawa distanced himself from political activities, saying, “I am not a politician, and I will not campaign for anyone.”
“I hope that whoever will be just, compassionate to the poor, defend their rights and work to ease the affairs of their lives be granted victory by Allah,” he said.
“May Allah grant us leaders who are truthful, trustworthy and God-fearing, who will put the interest of the people above their personal interests,” he added.
Although Mr Daurawa distanced himself from “campaigning for anyone”, he has not commented directly on his inclusion in the APC advisory committee or on serving under the APC-led government of Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf.
Some Islamic clerics in northern Nigeria have openly supported President Bola Tinubu’s re-election bid.
One of them is Sani Jingir, a senior leader of Jama’atu Izalatil Bid’ah Wa Iqamatis Sunnah (JIBWIS), who has repeatedly defended the APC’s Muslim-Muslim presidential ticket.
PREMIUM TIMES recalls that in August, Mr Jingir reaffirmed his support for the ticket in Kano, urging Muslims to prepare their permanent voter cards ahead of the 2027 elections.
Other religious figures and organisations have also endorsed Mr Tinubu for a second term.
In August, more than 500 Islamic scholars and clerics from northern Nigeria endorsed the president after a meeting with APC governors and other political stakeholders.
In September, the Muslim Intellectuals Forum, comprising Muslim women scholars, preachers and Da’awah leaders from the 19 northern states, including the Federal Capital Territory, also endorsed Tinubu’s re-election bid.
However, some Islamic organisations have also challenged Mr Tinubu’s 2027 presidential bid.
In October, more than 1,000 clerics under the “Ko Da Naka platform”, in collaboration with the AFAQ Educational Foundation, urged Mr Tinubu to reconsider his re-election ambition, citing insecurity, economic hardship and the migration of skilled professionals.
In a communiqué issued after a conference in Kano, the clerics criticised aspects of the administration’s economic policies and called for urgent action to address killings, kidnappings and terrorism.
They also urged religious scholars to defend justice and avoid becoming instruments of partisan politics.
Unlike other clerics and their organisations, Mr Daurawa’s recent statement suggested a non-partisan stance, expressing no support for any candidate.

title: 2027: Sowore slams NDC, accuses Obi of renting party every election
body: The presidential candidate of the African Action Congress (AAC), Omoyele Sowore, has criticised the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) and accused its presidential candidate Peter Obi of renting political parties during election seasons. Sowore alleged that Obi’s political moves were not aimed at liberating Nigerians but at helping the ruling establishment deflect public anger and avoid accountability ahead of the 2027 general election. In a statement posted on X, Sowore accused the NDC of exploiting the political process, claiming that its leaders made ₦9 billion from the sale of nomination forms while running the party from their homes. “The same opportunists and packaged political frauds who made ₦9 billion from selling nomination forms while running a political party from their living rooms,” Sowore wrote, referring to the NDC. He described Obi as an unprincipled politician who, according to him, changes political platforms ahead of elections without offering a genuine challenge to the political establishment. “This is the problem with unprincipled politicians like Peter Obi, who rent political parties every election season, not to liberate Nigerians, but to…. divert public anger and evade the revolutionary consequences of their actions,” he said. Sowore also accused supporters of Obi and other political figures of attempting to discredit critics and distract Nigerians from what he described as the country’s underlying social and political problems. He named Osun State Governor Ademola Adeleke and Abia State Governor Alex Otti among those he alleged had helped promote narratives that distract from these issues. “But we cannot be fooled,” Sowore said, insisting that the politicians he criticised were delaying what he described as the liberation of Nigerians. The AAC candidate further alleged that Obi and his allies were not genuinely opposed to Tinubu’s administration but were instead seeking to manage opposition to the president without mounting a strong challenge to his government. “They don’t oppose Tinubu; they simply don’t want anyone to oppose him strongly enough to bring his disastrous reign to an end. Their politics is about managing opposition, not confronting the system,” he said. Sowore also referred to a remark attributed to Datti Baba-Ahmed, Obi’s former running mate in the 2023 presidential election, describing Tinubu as their “favourite uncle”. Obi, who contested the 2023 presidential election on the platform of the Labour Party, has since moved to the NDC ahead of the 2027 election. The post 2027: Sowore slams NDC, accuses Obi of renting party every election appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: EU talking about negotiator but either cannot or does not want to appoint one — Kremlin
body:
MOSCOW, October 25. /TASS/. The European Union is not acting constructively as it keeps talking about appointing negotiators on the Ukrainian conflict but is doing nothing. Brussels either lacks the desire or the resolve to take such a move, Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov told TASS, commenting on reports of Finnish President Alexander Stubb to be potentially proposed for this role.
"The European Union has long wanted [to appoint a negotiator], but either it cannot, or it cannot bring itself to do so," he said, adding that "this position can hardly be described as constructive."
"For now, they are only talking, and they aren’t taking any action," Peskov noted.
Moscow would support the appointment of a negotiator by the European Union, though it is important to make sure than such an envoy is committed to a peaceful settlement, he stressed.
"It would be good to have a negotiator. It would be even better if that negotiator were someone genuinely committed to facilitating a peaceful settlement," Peskov said.

title: The Gulf’s unfinished defence infrastructure
body: The Gulf states find themselves at the centre of a regional war that is not of their making . A confrontation that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran has spread into a web of proxy conflicts, reaching from the Strait of Hormuz to the Red Sea and Bab Al Mandeb, through Iraq and Yemen. The members of the GCC now face a question they can no longer put off: will they turn their commitment to collective security from communiques into a working military deterrent? Over several decades, Gulf states have invested heavily in advanced military capabilities, but progress towards operational integration has not kept pace. They have weapons and institutions. What is missing is an integrated collective response. Despite existing GCC defence co-operation mechanisms, each state continues to rely on its own national defence arrangements, while regional threats increasingly operate through cross-border armed networks . As a result, states with some of the most sophisticated arsenals in the world can be threatened by armed groups using drones and missiles that cost a fraction of the interceptors fired at them. For decades, Iran has cultivated armed partners in Lebanon, Iraq and Yemen. These networks extend its reach and give it leverage well beyond its borders. Tehran’s control over each group varies, and Iran does not order every attack directly. The strategic effect is the same either way: a set of fronts from which neighbouring states can be threatened and drained. This model can become more dangerous as pressure on Tehran grows, particularly if Iran’s armed partners join the conflict. Armed non-state actors are now built into the region’s calculations of deterrence, coercion and bargaining. Civilian airports, seaports, energy installations and critical infrastructure have also been targeted by armed groups. The recent Houthi escalation against Saudi Arabia, and earlier attacks and threats against vital facilities in the UAE, Kuwait, Bahrain and Qatar, mark a dangerous shift, even though the actors and circumstances behind each incident have differed. The Iranian aim is no longer only to exchange strikes. It is to carry war into civilian and economic life, and to turn public safety, market stability, trade and shipping into tools of blackmail. Gulf cities run the risk of becoming open arenas for settling regional scores, with civilians and economies treated as legitimate targets by groups that answer to no state and respect neither sovereignty nor the laws of armed conflict. The greatest danger in the current crisis is that the Gulf becomes the arena where Iran, the US and Israel settle their accounts This leaves the Gulf with an uncomfortable irony. States that chose diplomacy and stayed out of the war may still pay for it. Staying neutral does not buy immunity, and restraint alone will not deter actors who see escalation as their best bargaining tool. The GCC does not need to invent collective defence, as the framework for it already exists . The Joint Defence Agreement declares that an attack on one member is an attack on all. The council has created the Peninsula Shield Force and a Unified Military Command, along with a range of security co-operation mechanisms. The challenge now is ensuring that these structures can respond effectively to current security threats. Can they counter missile and drone salvos, cyberattacks and simultaneous strikes on critical infrastructure? If several Gulf capitals came under attack on the same day, could a joint operational mechanism respond in hours rather than weeks? For the GCC, the effectiveness of collective defence depends on whether its military co-operation can credibly deter potential attacks. Armed groups are not deterred by statements of condemnation or by solidarity expressed after the fact. Deterrence begins when an aggressor understands that striking one Gulf state means facing an integrated defence system, not an individual state’s response. That requires moving from co-ordination to integration. In practice, this means making the Unified Military Command fully operational, with the authority to co-ordinate joint responses, and linking early-warning and air and missile defence systems across the six GCC states. It also means establishing mechanisms that facilitate intelligence sharing in real time, developing joint plans to protect critical infrastructure, including airports, ports, energy installations and desalination facilities, and strengthening shared counter-drone and cyber-defence capabilities. Greater investment in regional defence industries would further reduce dependence on external suppliers. Some may argue that strengthening Gulf joint defence risks escalating tensions with Iran. Yet the purpose of deterrence is precisely to prevent war. Credible, integrated defences can strengthen Gulf states’ ability to protect their interests and pursue diplomacy from a position of strength, while reducing their vulnerability to coercion and prolonged attrition. Collective defence does not mean that every attack on one member leads to a joint war. It means a clear, predictable mechanism for collective response: defensive, intelligence and logistical support, protection of critical infrastructure and co-ordinated diplomacy. That mechanism should rest firmly on international law and draw a clear line between legitimate self-defence and open-ended retaliation. The message to Tehran should be equally clear. Iran cannot seek normal relations with its Gulf neighbours while arming groups that threaten them. Regional dialogue depends on respect for sovereignty, and de-escalation cannot serve as cover for continued pressure through proxies. The greatest danger in the current crisis is that the Gulf becomes the arena where Iran, the US and Israel settle their accounts. Each has its own strategic calculations. But the Gulf states should not bear the costs of wars they can neither start nor end on their own. For this reason, a joint Gulf defence system is about more than military readiness. It is about strategic autonomy. Outside security partnerships will remain important, but they cannot permanently replace the Gulf’s own capacity to defend itself. GCC leaders have an opportunity to convene an extraordinary summit devoted solely to security and defence. Such a summit would produce binding decisions with clear timelines to activate joint defence, empower the Unified Military Command, and build an integrated system for early warning and crisis response. Collective defence cannot stay on hold until the next crisis arrives. Iran has expanded its influence through several fronts and a network of armed groups. The Gulf would do well to not respond by copying that model or by sliding into a war of attrition. It would prove more worthwhile in the long run to build shared institutional strength that makes any attack on a Gulf state costlier and less likely to succeed. Statements do not create collective security, good intentions do not protect sovereignty, and a peace without credible deterrence may prove to be nothing more than a pause before the next war.

title: The curious case of Nebius, publicly traded AI infrastructure 'startup' (2024)
body:
On October 21, a new ticker opened to Nasdaq traders: NBIS , a truncation of Nebius , a fledgling player in the AI cloud infrastructure space.
Casual observers could be forgiven for wondering where this company had come from, as there had been little in the way of the usual fanfare that surrounds most startups’ journey to IPO — no roadshows; no horn tootin’; no confetti-laden ceremonies; nothing, not a peep. That’s because Nebius is an unusual beast: a public company, but a startup in just about every sense of the word.
Nebius has actually been public for 13 years, floating in May 2011 as Yandex N.V. — the Dutch holding company of Russian internet giant Yandex (often dubbed the “Google of Russia”). At the tail end of 2021, Yandex N.V. hit a peak valuation of $31 billion, but in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in early 2022, everything changed. Nasdaq halted trading in Yandex N.V. shares that February due to sanctions imposed on Russian-affiliated companies, and a year later Nasdaq said it would delist Yandex altogether . But Yandex successfully appealed on the basis that it was restructuring — a process that would take an additional 16 months to fully complete.
Part of this included offloading all its Russian assets , which was where most of the real business value lay. What remained under Yandex N.V.’s ownership was a random assortment of infrastructure and business units that just happened to be located outside of Russia. This divestment concluded in July , with Yandex N.V. changing its name to Nebius AI , an AI cloud platform replete with its own Finnish data center.
The new business was to be spearheaded by Arkady Volozh (pictured above), the Russian Yandex co-founder and former CEO who was removed from a European sanctions list in March after he publicly condemned Russia’s assault on Ukraine.
The core Nebius business sells GPUs (graphical processing units) “as-a-service” to companies needing “compute” — that is, processing power and resources to carry out computational tasks such as running algorithms and executing machine learning models. Last month, the company debuted a holistic cloud computing platform designed for the “full machine learning lifecycle,” spanning data processing, training, fine-tuning, and inference.
With the restructuring complete, and Volozh free to run the show from the company’s new HQ in the Netherlands, Nasdaq green-lighted Nebius to recommence trading last month. The situation was pretty much unprecedented, though: a public company whose trading was put on pause, only to resume nearly three years later under a new name and entirely different business proposition?
In many ways, it would’ve made sense to have delisted and grown with private capital, the good old-fashioned startup way. But as Volozh explained to TechCrunch earlier this year, building infrastructure is capital intensive, and the easiest and cheapest way to access capital in what is currently one of the hottest spaces in tech is via the public markets. But there was never any certainty on how the public markets would respond to this strange new entity. Nobody really knew what to expect.
A month in, and Nebius has enjoyed a somewhat tepid re-entry to public life; it’s significantly down on its $18 billion market cap before trading halted in February 2022, which was to be expected, and it has since yo-yoed between $3.5 billion and $4.75 billion, with some signs that it is starting to settle.
“We couldn’t predict what would happen, it could be $5 per share, or it could be $50 per share — this has never happened before, nobody really knows how to treat it,” Volozh told TechCrunch in an interview in London this month. “It’s still volatile, but it’s stabilizing, and the good thing is that it has stabilized above the cost of the assets, which means that the market believes we will be able to build a business here. How big a business, we’ll see.”
Nebius competes with all the usual hyperscaler cloud behemoths, though arguably its more direct rivals are other alternative cloud startups such as CoreWeave, which has raised a ton of cash this year . With CoreWeave in the midst of expanding from the U.S. into Europe , Nebius is moving in the other direction, announcing plans this week to extend its presence to the U.S. with a new GPU cluster in Kansas City (on the Missouri side) scheduled to go live in early 2025. The company has also opened “customer hubs” in San Francisco and Dallas, with plans for a third in New York by the end of the year.
But while the cloud infrastructure business is its bread and butter (accounting for two-thirds of its revenue, as per its first earnings report last month), there’s a triumvirate of additional businesses under the Nebius Group umbrella. This includes an autonomous vehicle company called Avride , based in Texas; a Netherlands-based generative AI and LLM company called Toloka ; and edtech platform TripleTen , located in Wyoming.
Avride descends from the international division of Yandex’s self-driving unit, which spun out of a joint venture with Uber in 2020. While Alphabet’s Waymo is now leading the way in the burgeoning robotaxi realm, recently securing a $45 billion valuation , Yandex was an early trailblazer in Russia , with Volozh noting that the company had been on the cusp of beating Waymo to launch the first fully autonomous cars on public roads, before the war put the kibosh on plans.
“They [Yandex] were set to launch the first taxis on public roads with nobody at the wheel, in a real city (Moscow), several months before Waymo launched in San Francisco,” Volozh said. “Journalists were invited to a big event in March, ’22, but that launch never happened. People had to pack all their things and go in a matter of weeks.”
The team that had been working on Yandex’s autonomous vehicle project transitioned over to Avride, a new brand it launched last year, eventually moving to Austin via Tel Aviv.
“This is the same 250 people,” Volozh added.
Last month, Avride announced a significant multiyear partnership with Uber, which saw Avride’s sidewalk food delivery robots land on Uber Eats starting in Austin , though the partnership will also bring Avride’s self-driving cars to the Uber platform later (Uber has signed other similar deals, including with Waymo ).
While Yandex had sufficiently deep pockets to fund autonomous vehicle projects, Nebius doesn’t — it has a couple billion dollars in the bank from its Russian divestment, and it’s laser-focused on building its cloud infrastructure business. And this is why Volozh says that Avride will need to find additional partners in the longer term.
“They have enough budget for this year and next year,” Volozh said. “We’re financing them, but they need to use this time to find new partners, because it’s very capital intensive to build fleets. It needs real investment.”
Obvious partners might include car manufacturers, but it could be any entity that’s ready to invest billions, with Volozh adding that it would be willing to give up control in Avride if needed.
Toloka, meanwhile, is a platform that specializes in data labeling and quality control for large language models (LLMs) and related AI systems — it’s much like Scale AI , which was most recently valued at more than $13 billion . Toloka has clear synergies with Nebius’s core infrastructure business, but the customers aren’t the same. Nebius works largely with generative AI startups seeking compute, whereas Toloka works with bigger companies such as Amazon and Hugging Face that want to improve their LLMs.
Both Toloka and Avride could eventually follow a similar path to that of ClickHouse , creators of the eponymous open source database management system that spun out of Yandex in 2021 . While the commercial ClickHouse entity secured big-name backers such as Index Ventures, Benchmark Capital, and Coatue, Nebius has retained a minority stake.
“ClickHouse became very popular, and we were approached by investment funds to create a business around the open source project. Now they have revenues, and they’re growing,” Volozh said.
TripleTen, on the other hand, is something of an outlier in the Nebius group of businesses, in that it’s pretty much a direct-to-consumer product that offers online coding bootcamps for those wishing to transition into the technology sector. One idea Nebius is dabbling with is to position itself as a provider of a “full stack of services” to AI companies, from data centers and GPU infrastructure, to education. And this highlights the situation that Nebius has found itself in: It’s drawing lines between the different entities it has been left with, and trying to make it all make sense.
For now, TripleTen is breaking even, and Volozh acknowledges that it’s not going to be the big revenue driver that its infrastructure business is — but it has the potential to provide meaningful income and will remain part of the Nebius Group.
“Nebius is a billion-dollar scale business,” Volozh said. “TripleTen — it’s a nice model, but it’s maybe a tens or hundreds-of-millions of dollars business. It’s not a billion-dollar business.”
As for the core Nebius AI cloud business, the company already has its fully owned data center facility in Finland, with plans to triple its capacity to 75 megawatts. In tandem, the company is building out additional sites at co-location facilities, a move designed to not only increase its capacity, but also to reduce latency by bringing the processing closer to its customers. In addition to the Kansas location announced this week, Nebius had already unveiled a new GPU cluster in Paris that goes online this month.
Further down the line, Nebius plans to build more of its own data centers, both in Europe and the U.S., but given the time it takes, it’s quicker to plug the gap with co-location facilities, which is why it’s forging ahead with a hybrid approach.
“It’s more efficient if we build it ourselves, but to build means a year and a half or two years — it’s a long process, and we can’t wait,” Volozh said. “That’s why we have these co-locations in Paris and Kansas City.”

title: Russian attacks kill 8, injure 51 across Ukraine over past day as drone strikes residential building in Vinnytsia
body:
Russian attacks killed eight people and injured 51 others across Ukraine over the past day, local authorities said on Oct. 24-25.
A Russian drone struck a five-story residential building in the city of Vinnytsia overnight on Oct. 25, injuring six people, one of whom was hospitalized, Nataliia Zabolotna , head of the Vinnytsia Oblast Military Administration, said.
The strike caused structural damage between the second and third floors, completely destroying four apartments and damaging nearby parked cars, Zabolotna added.
Alongside attacks on Vinnytsia, Russia launched 153 Shahed-type drones at Ukraine overnight on Oct. 25, including 92 jet-powered drones, as well as low-cost Banderol cruise missiles, the Ukrainian Air Force said.
Ukrainian air defenses intercepted 119 drones, including 64 jet-powered ones. As of 8 a.m., efforts to intercept the remaining drones were ongoing, with at least nine still in Ukrainian airspace.
Some drones evaded Ukrainian air defenses and struck 15 locations, while falling debris was recorded at nine other locations, according to the Air Force.
In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast , Russian attacks on the Synelnykove District on Oct. 24 killed three people and injured 14 others, including an 11-year-old girl, Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said. Five of the injured were hospitalized in serious condition.
In the Nikopol District , Russian attacks over the past day killed two women and injured five people, including a 14-year-old boy, Hanzha added.
In Kharkiv Oblast , Russian attacks killed a 45-year-old man in the town of Lozova and injured two other men, aged 43 and 26, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said.
In Kharkiv, a 39-year-old man was injured. Russian attacks also wounded three men, aged 70, 54, and 47, in the town of Derhachi, and a 45-year-old woman in the village of Mala Danylivka, Syniehubov added.
In Donetsk Oblast , Russian attacks killed one person in the village of Yarova and injured six others elsewhere in the region, Governor Vadym Filashkin said.
In Sumy Oblast , a 31-year-old woman was killed in a Russian attack on a farm in the Buryn community, which also injured an 18-year-old man. In the Boromlia community, a Russian drone struck a car, injuring three women aged 68, 56, and 36, according to local authorities .
Russian attacks injured four people in Zaporizhzhia Oblast over the past day. Russian forces carried out 832 strikes on 52 settlements across the region using drones, artillery, aircraft, and multiple-launch rocket systems (MLRS), local authorities said.
In Kherson Oblast , Russian attacks targeted 43 settlements, including the regional center of Kherson, injuring two people, Governor Oleksandr Prokudin said.
In Chernihiv Oblast , two women suffered acoustic trauma in a Russian strike on the regional capital, Chernihiv, on Oct. 24, Governor Viacheslav Chaus said.
One person was injured in a Russian drone attack on Kyiv on Oct. 24, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.

title: Obama Blasts Trump Over Iran War, Cost of Living at Midterm Rallies
body: Former US president Barack Obama delivered scathing criticisms of current leader Donald Trump at rallies Saturday in Ohio and Michigan to support Democratic candidates ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. Democrats are attempting to wrest back control of one or both chambers of the US Congress, which are currently controlled by Trump’s Republican party. Obama retains considerable popularity among the Democratic base, which he is keen to leverage to support his party’s candidates. In both states, the 65-year-old former president blamed the Trump administration for the rising cost of living, a top voter concern. “The current president chose to make a series of bad decisions,” Obama said in Cleveland, Ohio, where he rallied in support of former Democratic senator Sherrod Brown. “Most importantly, he decided to start an unnecessary war that nobody asked for.” The war on Iran has sent oil prices soaring as Tehran effectively blocked the Strait of Hormuz after being attacked. “After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence, the likes of which we have not seen in the modern era, you get a chance to say, ‘Enough is enough,'” Obama declared. “We are voting for change right here in Ohio.” Later, in Michigan, Obama campaigned for Abdul El-Sayed, from the party’s left wing, who is in a close race with Republican Mike Rogers for the US Senate. “Imagine the power duo of Abdul and Elissa,” Obama said, referring to the incumbent Democratic Senator Elissa Slotkin, who is not up for election this year. “You got a Muslim man, you got a Jewish woman fighting for you in the United States Senate. That’s something, Michigan, you can be proud of.” Trump slammed Obama’s campaign in Michigan in a post on Truth Social on Sunday, urging voters to choose Rogers. “Obama was a grossly incompetent President! He paid off Iran with $Billions, and gave them a road to a Nuclear Weapon,” Trump said, referring to a 2015 deal negotiated under Obama that offered Iran sanctions relief in return for drastically scaling back its nuclear work. Trump withdrew from that deal during his first term and imposed sweeping sanctions, including on countries that bought Iranian oil. Western countries accuse Iran of seeking to acquire nuclear weapons, something Tehran denies, defending its right to what it insists is a civilian nuclear program. – ‘Don’t procrastinate’ – Obama also urged voters to cast their ballots as soon as possible since early voting is already open in both states. “Don’t procrastinate, don’t equivocate,” Obama said. In Ohio, Brown will attempt a comeback against incumbent Republican Senator Jon Husted, while the race for governor will be contested between Democrat Amy Acton and Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, a former presidential candidate in 2024. Polls for Ohio give Democrats a slight lead in both those races, but the results are expected to be close. Obama also took digs at Trump’s renovation projects across the US capital, including his botched renovation of the National Mall’s Reflecting Pool, his construction of a massive White House Ballroom and the gilded decorations he has adorned the Oval Office with during his second tenure. “He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory,” Obama said, referring to the popular but indulgent American restaurant chain. Nationally, polls also suggest that Democrats could regain control of the House of Representatives but face a much more competitive contest for the Senate. The post Obama Blasts Trump Over Iran War, Cost of Living at Midterm Rallies appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Sikorski Says Russia Running Out of Resources if Ukraine Survives Winter
body:
Russia’s resources will begin to run out if Ukraine survives the coming winter, Poland’s foreign minister said on Saturday, urging Europeans to provide the embattled country with more aid such as power generators for the upcoming cold months.
Ukraine’s 1,200-kilometer-long front line remains static, and Russia’s offensive has stalled amid rising casualty rates among its own soldiers, Radosław Sikorski said, speaking at an event in northern Poland.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Sikorski believes Russian President Vladimir Putin’s future actions are based on two main factors.
“He is currently carrying out a partially covert mobilization, hoping that if he throws another 200,000 cannon fodder into the fray, he might break through the front,” he said.
“And, as is traditional among Russians, he is counting on ‘General Winter,’ which is why he is destroying combined heat and power” facilities, the minister added, referencing Russia’s attacks on Kyiv’s critical infrastructure.
Sikorski called on the Polish public and European countries to provide additional humanitarian aid and energy equipment, including generators, to Ukraine to help its citizens get through the upcoming winter.
“If Ukraine survives this winter – and I am optimistic – Russian resources will begin to run out next year,” the foreign minister said.
Earlier this week, the organizers of a Polish fundraising campaign called Warmth from Poland for Kyiv, which saw 80,000 people donate to buy generators for the Ukrainian capital last winter, relaunched the initiative.
This year the campaign aims to raise 10 million zlotys (€2.5 million).
“Russia is counting on our exhaustion – on us growing used to the darkness and looking away,” the organizers wrote.
“Let’s answer with another convoy of generators. With practical help. With the warmth of people who refuse to stop caring.”

title: Final bridge at Dubai World Centre roundabout to open on Friday
body: The final bridge of the World Trade Centre roundabout project will open in Dubai on Friday, the emirate's transport authority confirmed. Stretching over a kilometre, the bridge has the capacity to carry 3,000 vehicles per hour and will reduce travel time between Al Majlis Street and 2nd December Street from six minutes to one, the Roads and Transport Authority (RTA) said on Sunday. The completion of the work means that five bridges, with a total length of 5km, will have been built as part of the project, which the RTA estimates will benefit at least half a million residents and visitors. The average delay at the intersection is expected to fall by 12 minutes to 90 seconds. The total cost of the work is estimated to be more than Dh696 million. “The completion of the World Trade Centre roundabout development project is in line with the directives of the wise leadership to continue upgrading Dubai’s road infrastructure, improve traffic flow on Sheikh Zayed Road and enhance connectivity between the emirate’s leading economic and commercial centres," said Mattar Al Tayer, director general of the RTA. تستكمل #هيئة_الطرق_و_المواصلات ، يوم الجمعة 30 أكتوبر، مشروع تطوير دوار المركز التجاري بافتتاح الجسر الأخير، الذي يمتد بطول 1,000 متر ويتألف من مسارين، بطاقة استيعابية تصل إلى نحو 3,000 مركبة في الساعة، لخدمة الحركة المرورية من شارع المجلس باتجاه شارع الثاني من ديسمبر. ويسهم… pic.twitter.com/kLGWECeYFT — RTA (@rta_dubai) October 25, 2026 “The project will also increase road network capacity to keep pace with Dubai’s rapid population, urban and economic growth, reinforce its global leadership in business, investment and tourism, and provide an integrated, sustainable mobility system that reinforce the emirate’s competitiveness, facilitates travel for residents and visitors, and enhances quality of life.” The World Trade Centre roundabout project complements Al Mustaqbal Street Development Project, due for completion in 2027 added Mr Al Tayer. Al Mustaqbal Street project includes bridges and tunnels spanning a total of 1.5km and expansion of the street to four lanes in each direction Both projects form part of a comprehensive approach to upgrading the area’s key road corridors, he said. “The World Trade Centre Roundabout Development Project is one of Dubai’s strategic road network projects, given its vital location on Sheikh Zayed Road, the emirate’s main traffic artery, and its role in linking key road corridors with key economic, commercial and residential areas.

title: Russian forces attack civilian infrastructure in Rivne region overnight
body:
According to Ukrinform, the Rivne Regional Directorate of the State Emergency Service of Ukraine reported this on Facebook .
"Tonight, State Emergency Service units responded twice to deal with the aftermath of enemy strikes on civilian infrastructure in the Rivne region," the statement said.
The strikes caused fires, which rescuers extinguished, the emergency service said.
Preliminary reports indicate that there were no deaths or injuries.
As Ukrinform reported, a residential building was damaged in a Russian attack in the Sarny district on October 22. A woman and her two daughters were injured.

title: Ex-Google CEO Eric Schmidt calls OpenAI and Anthropic modern colonial trading companies
body:
The US and China have spent the past few years building AI empires, and every other country that wants access to advanced AI is becoming dependent on them.
Who can afford the race matters more than who builds artificial general intelligence first. High debt, domestic resistance, and a potential war over Taiwan threaten both powers, argue historian Niall Ferguson, researcher Lisa Klaassen, and former Google CEO Eric Schmidt .
In their essay for Foreign Affairs , they ground the empire analogy in scaling laws . Because model progress depends on energy, minerals, chips, and capital, software has become a scarce and therefore geopolitical resource again. Anyone below a certain threshold "is not in the game at all." Raw materials from the Congo and data workers in Kenya earning a few dollars an hour amount to what they call "the plantation economics of the chatbot age." Ad
The authors compare OpenAI and Anthropic to the East India Companies , the powerful colonial-era trading firms that operated with government charters but built their own armies and ruled entire regions. Like them, today's AI labs negotiate with governments yet remain on a government leash. Ad
As evidence, they cite a case from June. The US Commerce Department ordered Anthropic to cut off foreign nationals from its two most capable models. Unable to verify users' nationalities in real time, Anthropic shut down Fable 5 and Mythos 5 worldwide. The government lifted export controls on Fable 5 about two weeks later, but Mythos 5 stayed restricted to a group of US organizations.
The two countries' strategies diverge sharply. Washington offers expensive, closed technology in exchange for political alignment; Beijing pushes freely available open-weight models to spread its standards. The US leads in chatbots by about six months, and China in robotics. Their bottlenecks mirror each other. China has power but no top-end chips, while the US lacks minerals and a reliable power grid. Ad
US tech companies plan to invest more than $600 billion in 2026, mostly funded through debt, according to the essay. Other estimates run even higher, with Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and Meta together planning roughly $725 billion in AI investment this year .
China's approach is state-driven. The country plans $295 billion over five years, funded through government bonds, according to a draft reported by Bloomberg . Yet both sides face fiscal walls. The US already paid more in interest in 2024, about $881 billion, than it spent on defense, about $874 billion. By 2036, interest costs could hit twice the defense budget. From those numbers, the authors draw what they call an "imperial trilemma." Defense, tech leadership, and a generous welfare state can't all survive at once. Ad
They flag other risks, too. Protests against data centers have flared in Texas and Utah. Open models could undermine China's grip on information. And then there's the problem of losing control over the technology itself. Recently, hundreds of autonomous agents from an OpenAI model attacked Hugging Face and many other websites , with other AI companies reporting similar incidents. Ad
The greatest danger, the authors warn, still lies in a potential "Taiwanese chip crisis." TSMC, the central node of the entire AI supply chain, sits 90 miles off the Chinese coast. New fabs in Phoenix , Kumamoto, and Dresden are meant to make the island replaceable, but until they run at scale, a dangerous window stays open.
The authors propose an AI détente modeled on the Cold War, including caps on model capabilities for cyberattacks and biodesign. Getting China to accept limits while it trails technologically would be difficult, the authors write.

title: Full speed returned to Ukraine’s satellite links on Saturday morning. “We simply enforced our terms,” Musk claims after blaming Washington for 10 days

Hours later, SpaceX owner Elon Musk, who earlier pointed at Washington, said his company had enforced its own rules. A Ukrainian presidential adviser and a drone volunteer replied that civilian Starlink could not fly such missions. Ukraine holds off Russia with American tools it doesn't control, so any pause decided abroad, like stalled Patriot deliveries or the Starlink cap, opens gaps in its defense. With no stated rule on what Ukraine's forces may do, the next cutoff could again come unannounced and unexplained. Kyiv records full speed again The ministry recorded stable connections above 400 km/h (250 mph). Before, Kyiv said , links on Starlink and its military version, Starshield, cut out above 161 km/h (100 mph). Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the restoration began overnight. " The speeds are now where they need to be ," he said , citing defense against jet-powered Shahed drones. He thanked US lawmakers, the media, the State Department, and the US President, but not Musk or SpaceX. A Ukrainian soldier installs a Starlink terminal. This is NOT a threat, it is simply a statement of fact ." Musk named no evidence, cases, or time frames. Overnight, he answered a headline on the US financial blog ZeroHedge saying he "admits" SpaceX throttled Starlink. " We simply enforced our terms of service when they were bypassed. There has been no change to our terms of service ," Musk wrote . Explore further Who capped Ukraine’s Starlink? “Ultimately POTUS,” Musk said. Ultimately Musk, reports now say When the cap hit on 14 October, Musk wrote that the US government owns and controls Starshield and that the US military and " ultimately POTUS " decide any limits. US President Donald Trump, who credited Musk with the fix while Kyiv still saw the cap, said on 24 October he had spoken to Musk about Ukraine but gave no details. US President Donald Trump and Elon Musk in the Oval Office on 11 February 2025. Photo: White House / Daniel Torok Ukrainians note contradiction to reality Ukrainian presidential adviser on defense technology Serhii Beskrestnov, known by the callsign Flash, wrote : " It is very strange that Elon Musk doesn't know about the restrictions on Starlink operations in Ukraine ." Since winter 2026, every Starlink terminal over Ukraine, occupied areas included, has been limited to 70–90 km/h (43–56 mph), he said, and over Russia, Starlink does not work. " So we PHYSICALLY CANNOT USE COMMERCIAL STARLINK for deep strikes and mid-range strikes ," Beskrestnov wrote. Deep strikes hit targets far inside Russia, mid-range ones targets closer to the front. Ukrainian activist and drone fundraiser Serhii Sternenko called Musk's claim untrue. He said Ukraine introduced whitelists of terminals in February, and any terminal used on the move had to be listed and connected to Starshield. " So using civilian Starlink for drone missions was technically impossible. All drone missions that needed satellite communication could be carried out only with Starshield ," Sternenko added. European governments help pay for Ukraine's Starlink service. Germany funds it under a contract that runs until April 2027. Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski, whose country pays around $50 million a year for the service, said on 23 October: " Mixing business with politics usually ends badly, especially when we talk about Elon Musk ." title: 'Fair game': Iranian officials say US diplomats, officials are targets for assassinations - report
body: Iran is planning to target United States diplomats and other officials in new assassination plots, according to two Iranian officials, including a member of the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), The New York Times reported on Saturday.The officials told NYT that Americans were "fair game" due to Israel and the US having attacked and killed many Iranian officials, as well as some family members.The Iranian officials also confirmed US intelligence reports that Iran was working to increase its ability to actually execute assassination plots against US officials and civilians.US officials expressed concern Iran was in the “advanced stages” of planning these attacks, while Iran is also preparing for the possibility of an Israeli or US strike against it, kickstarting a new phase in the ongoing war between them.One US official warned that evidence existed suggesting that Iranian operatives who are "not just simply Iranian nationals" were present in the US, but that these operatives often exaggerate their actual ability to conduct attacks when communicating with Iran.US intelligence reveals Iran increasing efforts to target AmericansA US official confirmed to The Jerusalem Post on Friday that US Secretary of State and National Security Adviser Marco Rubio received an intelligence memorandum warning that Iran has significantly increased its efforts to target American officials and citizens, with plots to carry out lethal attacks reaching advanced stages.The confirmation came after Axios obtained an October 23 memorandum that Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton sent to Rubio, with a copy to CIA Director John Ratcliffe.The intelligence chief warned that information concerning Iranian plots to target American government personnel was relevant to a wider group of individuals than those currently authorized to receive it.Idan Kweller contributed to this report.

title: China hosts forum to pool wisdom for better future
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 25 (MNA) – China is hosting a three-day inaugural global governance forum to pool wisdom for better global governance, one year after the country proposed the Global Governance Initiative (GGI).
The 2026 Global Governance Forum (Xiongan) opened on Friday in Xiongan New Area, north China's Hebei Province. Hosted by the Chinese People's Institute of Foreign Affairs, it is themed "Rebuilding Confidence and Cooperation: Reforming and Improving Global Governance in a Transforming World."
In a message to the forum, Chinese President Xi Jinping noted the world is undergoing accelerated transformation unseen in a century, and the deficits in peace, development, security and governance are growing rather than diminishing.
"I have put forward the GGI to promote the building of a more just and equitable global governance system and a better world," he said.
China stands ready to work with all parties to uphold the vision of global governance featuring extensive consultation, joint contribution and shared benefits, pool strength through confidence-building and tackle challenges through cooperation, Xi said.
He called for efforts to promote the implementation of the GGI to inject more certainty and positive energy into a world of turbulence and transformation, and jointly move toward a community with a shared future for humanity.
"The forum offers a window for the world to follow the developments of China's vision for global governance. One of the key points is to invite all countries to communicate together and build a world together and share the outcomes together," said Selcuk Colakoglu, director of the Ankara-based Turkish Center for Asia-Pacific Studies.
Nearly 400 representatives from strategic, political, academic, business, media, and youth sectors from more than 90 countries and international and regional organizations, including the UN, attended the event.
The GGI emphasizes sovereign equality, international rule of law, multilateralism, a people-centered approach, and practical outcomes, providing an opportunity for all parties to further engage in the global governance system, international cooperation and dialogue, former Nepali President Bidya Devi Bhandari said.
The world today faces severe challenges such as economic inequality, poverty, geopolitical tensions, armed conflicts, climate change, and food security, while rising protectionism and unilateralism further complicate international cooperation. No single country can address these shared challenges alone; they require dialogue, enhanced cooperation, and joint efforts among all countries, Bhandari said.
Former Kyrgyz Prime Minister Djoomart Otorbaev said countries of the Global South support the GGI and want a world of growth, cooperation and progress instead of hegemony or interference.
"Our system is still designed without giving developing countries sufficient weight. So we see the need in the United Nations to make reforms to our governance systems," UN under-secretary-general Guy Ryder said.
It is important to enhance the representation and voice of the Global South in international affairs, advance reform of the international financial system in accordance with the timetable and roadmap agreed by all parties, increase the representation of developing countries in the Security Council, and give full play to the important role of emerging multilateral cooperation mechanisms such as BRICS and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, Chinese foreign minister Wang Yi said.
Wang also called for improving governance rules in emerging fields, turning new frontiers such as the deep sea, the polar regions and outer space into areas for international cooperation, and evolving an artificial intelligence (AI) governance structure based on general consensus soon.
China and the United States have both the capability and the responsibility to jointly develop and govern AI well, ensuring that its development remains under human control and benefits the people, Wang said when meeting with co-chair of the Board of Trustees of the Asia Society John L. Thornton and The New York Times columnist Thomas L. Friedman on the sidelines of the forum.
Thornton and Friedman said that the international community is paying close attention to the upcoming APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting hosted by China, and expects that China will take this opportunity to play a unique and positive role in tackling global challenges.

title: Russian Drone Hits Vinnytsia Apartment Block, 6 Injured
body:
A Russian strike drone hit a five-story residential apartment building in the central Ukrainian city of Vinnytsia early Sunday morning, Oct. 25, injuring six people, destroying multiple apartments, and damaging a nearby private nursing home, regional authorities reported.
Head of the Vinnytsia Regional Military Administration Nataliia Zabolotna announced on Telegram that incoming fire struck the urban residential quarter shortly before dawn.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
The kinetic impact caused structural collapses between the second and third floors of the multi-story apartment complex, completely destroying four apartments and damaging passenger vehicles parked across the residential courtyard.
Regional authorities confirmed that six civilians sustained injuries in the strike, with one victim transported to a regional medical center for inpatient care.
More than 60 personnel from the State Emergency Service of Ukraine (DSNS) and 14 specialized vehicles deployed to the impact site to extinguish localized fires, clear structural rubble, and inspect the structural integrity of neighboring properties.
Concurrently with the residential strike, the aerial bombardment damaged an adjacent private elderly care boarding house. Emergency responders and civil defense detachments evacuated 15 elderly residents from the damaged care facility to ensure their safety, while specialized psychologists from the DSNS provided immediate psychological assistance to the displaced residents.
Zabolotna reported that the wider wave of strikes across Vinnytsia region also inflicted physical damage on critical municipal life-support installations, civil infrastructure facilities, and private residential homes.
Firefighting units suppressed all active combustion zones across the affected municipal sectors, with utility and recovery crews continuing debris-removal operations.
On Saturday, Oct. 24, Russian drone struck a cattle-breeding agricultural enterprise in the Konotop district of Sumy region, killing a 31-year-old female farm worker and injuring four other people, regional authorities reported.
Concurrently , Russian forces launched an aerial drone attack against the Pokrovske community in the Nikopol district of Dnipropetrovsk region, injuring four civilians.
In Kharkiv region, a Russian missile hit a commercial warehouse in the city of Lozova , killing a 45-year-old man and wounding two others aged 26 and 43. Emergency medical crews attempted resuscitation at the scene, but the victim died of severe blast trauma as specialized firefighting units worked to extinguish a fire that engulfed the storage facility.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: ICEYE and Nokia partner with The Ministry of Defence of Ukraine to develop sovereign satcom capability
body:
Helsinki, Finland, Oct 22, 2026. ICEYE, the European leader in sovereign intelligence from space, and Nokia, a global leader in connectivity infrastructure, today signed a Letter of Intent with The Ministry of Defence of Ukraine, to explore cooperation in space. The partnership aims to support Ukraine’s defense capabilities, particularly in building sovereign satellite communications.



The shared intent was announced on October 22, 2026 during the visit of the Prime Minister of Finland to Ukraine.

Earlier this month, ICEYE and Nokia announced a partnership to develop secure, sovereign and high-performance broadband low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite communications systems for governments, supporting missions from defense and border security to emergency services and disaster response. Built on trusted European technology, the jointly developed satellite communications systems will give nations ownership and control of the satellites, ground segment and terminals.

Rafal Modrzewski, CEO and Co-founder of ICEYE, said: “Ukraine needs secure, sovereign and high-performance satellite communications systems that it controls. We have a proven track record of delivering sovereign missions at speed to help build that capability. ICEYE has proudly supported Ukraine since 2022, and we remain committed to continuing that support today.”

Mikko Hautala, Chief Geopolitical & Government Relations Officer, and Chairman, Nokia Defense, said: “Nations need communications they can rely on in every situation. Satellite networks extend and protect connectivity when networks on the ground are disrupted. This makes them a key part of any secure communications system. Through this Letter of Intent, together with Ukraine and ICEYE, we will explore how trusted, sovereign satellite communications can strengthen Ukraine's resilience and give it control over the connectivity it depends on."

title: Brazil heads to polls in runoff between leftist Lula and Bolsonaro Jr.
body: SAO PAULO, Brazil – Brazilians head to the polls on Sunday, October 25, in a tight runoff vote that could shift Latin America’s largest nation sharply rightward, bringing it closer to the United States as part of a broader conservative shift across the region. The runoff pits leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva against right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro , the son of convicted former President Jair Bolsonaro . Flavio scored a major upset at the start of the month by defying pollsters to lead voting in the first round. A victory for Bolsonaro, 45, would extend a wave of right-wing victories for Latin American candidates friendly to US President Donald Trump , while a fourth mandate for Lula would be a disappointment in Washington, which has clashed with his government over trade and security. The election race has been dominated by corruption scandals, economic anxiety, and accusations of US meddling, which Washington denies. It has also been colored by fallout from Jair Bolsonaro’s 2025 conviction for plotting a 2022 coup, with Flavio pledging to free his father if he is elected. Trump has called the case a “witch hunt” and imposed a 50% tariff on Brazil in 2025, in a decision explicitly linked to Jair Bolsonaro’s trial. While many of those were later watered down, Trump unleashed new levies against Brazil this year, citing unfair trade practices. Lula has cast the Trump administration’s proximity to the Bolsonaro clan as part of an attempt to sway the election, while labeling tariffs and other punitive measures as bullying. On economic issues, despite falling inequality, and unemployment, Lula has struggled to win over an electorate grappling with high living costs and heavy household debt. Endemic gang violence also weighs on voters’ minds. Bolsonaro has sought to capitalize on cost-of-living concerns and has also promised a heavy-handed approach to fighting crime, pledging maximum-security jails and chemical castration for serious sexual offenses. Candidates are neck and neck Polls show the candidates are practically tied going into the runoff, as Lula has closed the gap in the final days. Historical precedent favors Bolsonaro, however, as no candidate has ever won the presidency after coming second in the first-round vote. Bolsonaro picked up 47% of ballots cast in the first round, while Lula trailed with 45%. The senator’s first-round win sent Brazil’s markets and currency soaring on expectations of pro-business reforms. His first-round success was mirrored in congressional elections for his Liberal Party and other right-wing politicians, which could pave a legislative path for him, or complicate governance for Lula. – Rappler.com
