title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,578,450 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
body:
Russia has lost 1,578,450 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 25.
The number includes 1,850 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report , Russia has also lost 12,447 tanks, 25,605 armored combat vehicles, 166,918 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,614 artillery systems, 2,237 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,725 air defense systems, 449 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 3,017 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy. Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action.
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

title: Soldiers guard center of Milan as thousands of protesters march in cities across Europe
body:
Members of right-wing student groups march through the streets of Rome, Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026, during a demonstration called "Unlock Everything," organized in opposition to recent left-wing student protests and one of several demonstrations held by groups across the political spectrum. Gregorio Borgia/AP hide caption
MILAN — Thousands of young people marched Saturday through the streets of several Italian cities, including Milan, Rome and Turin, as authorities deployed large numbers of police and soldiers in a largely successful bid to stave off a repeat of the violent clashes and looting that marred similar protests last week.
The demonstration in Milan remained peaceful, but there were brief clashes with police in both Rome and Turin.
In Milan, thousands of young people marched the streets as soldiers were deployed and luxury boutiques were boarded up, but by late afternoon, most shops had opened, Italian media reported.
Premier Giorgia Meloni announced a raft of measures, including sending an additional 500 soldiers to Milan and tougher penalties for minors, who police said made up a large part of the violent protesters last week. In Milan, police detained several minors as a preventive measure, media reported.
While protests in France have claimed most international attention, large demonstrations also rocked many European cities Saturday from Milan to Rome to Madrid, Lisbon and Tirana.
Members of right-wing student groups march through the streets of Rome, Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026, during a demonstration called "Unlock Everything," organized in opposition to recent left-wing student protests and one of several demonstrations held by groups across the political spectrum. Gregorio Borgia/AP hide caption
The protests encompass a broad range of issues from education and corruption to anti-war movements, pensions and housing.
In Milan, huge crowds of mostly young people gathered as night fell, chanting insults to Meloni and holding aloft banners such as "No to lies of the state."
A group of protesters dumped manure outside Italy's energy regulator and burned a symbolic, oversized electricity bill, images broadcast on local television showed.
The 500 soldiers deployed to Milan came in addition to hundreds already stationed there, supporting about 5,000 police and other security personnel. Authorities used drone surveillance, checks at railway stations, rapid-response units and online monitoring for potential calls to violence.
A mayoral hopeful, Pierfrancesco Majorino, who announced his candidacy Thursday, joined the marchers and remarked how peaceful the day was, according to Italian media. He will contest a center-left primary in early 2027. Milan's center-left Mayor Giuseppe Sala, who has held the role since 2016, is not running again.
Many stores, particularly luxury boutiques within Milan's fashion district including Omega, Tiffany and Gucci, boarded up their front windows. The Apple store also shut down and remained shut even as others reopened.
Protesters march during a demonstration against rising living costs in Paris, Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026. Thibault Camus/AP hide caption
Rioters last weekend smashed their way into stores, targeting sneakers, athletic wear and sporting goods on streets that run off the city's central Duomo square.
Security measures extended beyond the city center over concerns protesters could move into other neighborhoods.
The protesters ended their march peacefully Saturday evening outside the Milan Polytechnic, more than 3 kilometers (2 miles) from the city center.
Officials said Saturday they were investigating a 30-year-old freelance journalist said to be the "mastermind" of the newly formed Oct. 17 movement, which has been the main driver of the recent protests in Italy.
Milan police say last week's violence and looting involved about 2,000 very young protesters, many of them "naturalized, second-generation Italians," alongside foreign nationals. Over two days, police arrested 45 people, including 34 minors.
A group of about 30 far-right activists, described as hooligans linked to Inter Milan soccer club, made a brief appearance chanting anti-immigrant and anti-Muslim slogans but were isolated by police.
Defense Minister Guido Crosetto said the soldiers deployed Saturday were only recently allowed to use plastic restraint ties and only in areas around train stations, not throughout the city. They are not authorized to carry pepper spray or tasers, he said.
Security was also heightened in Rome, where authorities locked down luxury shopping streets and stepped up controls around the Circus Maximus and Piazza del Popolo.
A small number of protesters tried to force their way into the Colosseum, but were ushered out by guards. Elsewhere, several hundred students demonstrated peacefully to stress they were not rioters.
"I think the images from last week were truly something terrible, especially for the young people, for the students, for the vast majority of the younger generations who want to study ... and do not accept being represented by those who use issues and needs to devastate entire cities," said Riccardo Ponzio, national president of an Italian far-right student association.
A separate anti-war march took place in central Rome. Organizers sought to distance themselves from potential unrest, urging participants to keep their faces uncovered and hands visible.
But it was these marchers who briefly clashed with police near the Piazza della Repubblica, even as organizers were trying to hold the crowd back using batons and tear gas. In the end, the protesters pulled back when a water cannon was turned on. They retreated to a location about half a kilometer (mile) away.
In Albania's capital Tirana, riot police used water cannons on large groups of protesters, some of whom set government buildings on fire and threw projectiles at police. Authorities said 2,500 officers patrolled the streets Saturday.
A protester throws a projectile towards police after a demonstration against rising living costs in Paris, Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026. Thibault Camus/AP hide caption
For over a week, protesters have hurled rocks, flares, firebombs and fireworks at police who have used batons and tear gas in clashes in the city center.
High school and university students are demanding lower tuition fees, greater state investment in education and protesting corruption in the education system. Some have joined a broader anti-government movement calling for the resignation of Socialist Prime Minister Edi Rama.
A separate protest organized by the opposition outside the prime minister's office turned violent earlier, with some activists lighting fires on the street.
Rama said Saturday his government was preparing a response to the students' demands and called them to a dialogue. He warned that violent protesters will face penalties.
Thousands of retirees and others marched peacefully in Spain's capital Saturday to demand public pensions aren't meddled with.
"They are threatening us with privatizing pensions. It's just another thing they want to profit from," said Maria José Benito, 68.
The protests came ahead of next month's snap election as Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's Socialist Party criticized the conservative opposition Popular Party for making overtures about privatizing public pensions. Spain also has been roiled by protests this fall around the issue of housing, as rental and home costs have risen in recent years beyond what many Spaniards can afford.
Taking their cue from Spaniards, protesters in Lisbon demanding affordable housing marched across the city on Saturday.
They have also targeted recent measures announced by the government of Prime Minister Luis Montenegro that include easing the cap on yearly rent increases and facilitating the eviction of tenants who fail to pay rent.
Montenegro defends the measures, saying that they aim at reinforcing trust between tenants and landlords and boosting the rentals market. Protesters claim that the measures are not balanced and put tenants in a more vulnerable position.
NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.

title: Pakistan reopens key border crossing with Iran
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 25 (MNA) – Pakistan reopened the Gabd-Rimdan crossing with Iran on Saturday, allowing trucks carrying LPG and essential food supplies to resume movement after a suspension that began on October 17.
Pakistan reopened its border crossing with Iran at Gabd-Rimdan on Sunday, restoring bilateral trade and allowing stranded trucks carrying liquefied petroleum gas and essential food commodities to resume movement after a week-long suspension.
Trade operations resumed at the crossing, also known as Gate 250, in Balochistan's Gwadar district, with border officials clearing commercial consignments holding consignment notes dated October 16 or earlier to cross, according to the Dawn newspaper.
Mir Naveed Jan Kalmati, president of the Gwadar Chamber of Commerce and Industry, confirmed the reopening, saying trucks and other vehicles were allowed to move toward Iran and Pakistan with import and export goods. He said the resumption would bring immediate relief to traders and transporters stranded on both sides and is expected to ease a nationwide LPG shortage and reduce soaring energy and food prices across Pakistan.

title: Regional security must be ensured by countries of region
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 25 (MNA) – Referring to the destructive role of the occupying regime of Israel in the region, Iran's Foreign Minister Seyyed Abbas Araghchi has said that regional security must be provided by the countries of the region.
Iran’s top diplomat made the remarks at a ceremony held at the venue of the Iranian Foreign Ministry’s Institute for Political and International Studies (IPIS) on Sunday to commemorate martyr Kamal Kharrazi former head of Iran's Strategic Council on Foreign Relations
He stated that any security plan originating from within region itself is welcomed.
Foreign players should not be in the region as they're only seeking security of Israeli regime, he said, emphasizing that Zionist regime’s officials are trying to sow seeds of discord and division in the region.
“We still believe that our region should enjoy an indigenous peace, free from foreign interference. The wars of the past year represent a turning point in the region’s history and have disrupted all existing structures. This is the reality, and nothing will be the same as it was before,” he added.
Martyr Kharrazi, who was the then foreign minister of Iran, was assassinated following a terrorist attack by the US-Zionist enemy.
The Zionist regime is the only warmongering factor in the region that consistently pursues war and incites conflict, Araghchi said, noting, “We welcome any initiative aimed at fostering indigenous security. It is a positive step for countries to seek to ensure their own security. Our region must move toward a state where the presence of foreign forces is reduced to zero. These forces arrived in the region to ensure Israel’s security, and their continued presence brings nothing but insecurity.”

title: Air defenses down 532 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions overnight
body:
MOSCOW, October 25. /TASS/. Russian air defense systems intercepted and destroyed 532 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions overnight, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"On-duty air defense capabilities intercepted and destroyed 532 Ukrainian fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles over the territories of the Belgorod, Bryansk, Kursk, Voronezh, Tula, Oryol, Lipetsk, Kaluga, Ryazan, Rostov, Saratov, Samara, Penza, Volgograd, Ulyanovsk, Moscow, Perm, Krasnodar Regions, the Republics of Tatarstan, Adygea, Mari El, Crimea, the Udmurt Republic, and the waters of the Sea of Azov," the report said.

title: Obama blasts Trump’s ‘chaos and cruelty’ while campaigning for Democrats
body: Former US president Barack Obama delivered scathing criticisms of his successor, Donald Trump, at rallies Saturday in Ohio and Michigan to support Democratic candidates ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. Democrats are attempting to wrest back control of one or both chambers of the US Congress, which are currently controlled by Trump’s Republican party. The former president retains considerable popularity among the Democratic base, which he is keen to leverage to support his Democratic Party’s candidates. In both states, the 65-year-old former president blamed the Trump administration for the rising cost of living, a top voter concern amid soaring fuel prices. “The current president chose to make a series of bad decisions,” Obama said in Ohio, where he rallied in support of former Democratic senator Sherrod Brown. “Most importantly, he decided to start an unnecessary war that nobody asked for.” “After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence, the likes of which we have not seen in the modern era, you get a chance to say, ‘Enough is enough,'” Obama declared in Cleveland. “We are voting for change right here in Ohio.” Later, in Michigan, Obama campaigned for Abdul El-Sayed, from the party’s left wing, who is in a close race with Republican Mike Rogers for the US Senate. “Imagine the power duo of Abdul and Elissa,” Obama said, referring to the incumbent Democratic Senator Elissa Slotkin, who is not up for election this year. “You got a Muslim man, you got a Jewish woman fighting for you in the United States Senate. That’s something, Michigan, you can be proud of.” Obama also urged voters to cast their ballots as soon as possible since early voting is already open in both states. “Don’t procrastinate, don’t equivocate,” Obama said. In Ohio, Brown will attempt a comeback against incumbent Republican Senator Jon Husted, while the race for governor will be contested between Democrat Amy Acton and Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, a former presidential candidate in 2024. Polls for Ohio give Democrats a slight lead in both those races, but the results are expected to be close. Obama also took digs at Trump’s renovation projects across the US capital, including his botched renovation of the National Mall’s Reflecting Pool, his construction of a massive White House Ballroom and the guilded decorations he has adorned the Oval Office with during his second tenure. “He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory,” Obama said, referring to popular but indulgent American restaurant chain. Nationally, polls also suggest that Democrats could regain control of the House of Representatives but face a much more competitive contest for the Senate. rle-pnb/mjf The post Obama blasts Trump’s ‘chaos and cruelty’ while campaigning for Democrats appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: War update: 193 combat clashes on front line over past day, Russia presses hardest on three axes
body:
According to Ukrinform, the General Staff of the Ukrainian Armed Forces said this in a Facebook update on the battlefield situation as of 08:00 on Sunday, October 25.
The enemy carried out 83 airstrikes, dropping 281 guided aerial bombs.
In addition, Russian invaders deployed 10,010 kamikaze drones and carried out 3,276 attacks on settlements and Ukrainian military positions, including 24 using multiple launch rocket systems.
Enemy shelling targeted, among other places, Pavlivka, Koreniok, Sopych, Neskuchne, Bezsalivka, Kucherivka, Luzhky, Mala Korchakivka, Topolia, Nova Sich, Khrapivshchyna, Obody, Yastrubshchyna, Baranivka, Mala Slobidka, Myropillia, Khotin, Volfyne, Iskryskivshchyna, Fotovyzh, Potapivka, Hirky, Stara Huta, Ulanove, Kindrativka and Zapsillia in the Sumy region, as well as Mykhalchyna-Sloboda, Buda-Vorobivska, Khrinivka and Kliusy in the Chernihiv region. Airstrikes hit the settlements of Svesa, Paliivka and Pysarivka.
Ukraine's missile forces and artillery struck a Russian troop and equipment concentration area, a UAV control post and a command-and-observation post.
On the Northern Slobozhanshchyna and Kursk axes, the enemy carried out two airstrikes, using six guided aerial bombs, and shelled Ukrainian military positions and settlements 51 times.
On the Southern Slobozhanshchyna axis, Ukraine's Defense Forces repelled eight attacks. Russian invaders advanced toward the settlements of Ternova, Okhrimivka and Bochkove.
On the Kupiansk axis, the enemy made four attempts to improve its positions, including offensive operations toward Radkivka.
Attempts to penetrate Ukrainian defenses were repelled on the Lyman axis, where Russian invaders launched six assaults near Zarichne and toward Stavky, Dibrova and Novoselivka.
On the Sloviansk axis, Russian forces launched four attacks near the settlement of Kryva Luka.
On the Kramatorsk axis, the enemy conducted no assault operations.
On the Kostiantynivka axis, 13 attacks were recorded. Russian invaders conducted offensive operations near Kostiantynivka.
On the Pokrovsk axis, the enemy launched 16 attacks, including attempts to advance near the settlements of Sofiivka, Vilne, Novyi Donbas, Vasylivka and Molodetske, and toward Dobropillia, Krasnopodillia and Serhiivka.
On the Oleksandrivka axis, Russian forces launched one attack toward the settlement of Zaporizke.
On the Huliaipole axis, Russian forces made 13 attempts to advance near Dobropillia and Bilohiria and toward the settlements of Verkhnia Tersa, Kopani, Huliaipilske and Yehorivka.
On the Orikhiv axis, the enemy made one attempt to attack toward Novoiakovlivka.
On the Dnipro River axis, Russian invaders conducted no assault operations.
On the Volyn and Polissia axes, the situation remained largely unchanged. No signs of the enemy forming offensive groupings were detected.

title: What will happen to Russian military aviation after the war? These aircraft could be scrapped
body:
Regardless of when and how the ongoing war ends, Russia will have to retire several types of combat aircraft afterwards. Although many have already proved of little use, this will mean substantial reductions in combat capability — at least on paper.
The history of protracted armed conflicts shows that, once they end, much of the equipment worn out or rendered obsolete by technological advances is scrapped or sold to third countries as part of cost and force cuts. Only the most modern and newest weapons remain in service, while equipment that was fighting on the battlefield just a few years earlier is sent to the scrapyard. US military equipment left over from the Second World War provides a good example. Aircraft such as the P-38 Lightning, Dauntless bombers and the heavy B-17 Flying Fortress and B-24 Liberator bombers were withdrawn from service. They were scrapped or, in some cases, converted into transport aircraft.
Russia will find itself in a similar position after the war, regardless of the conflict’s outcome or when it ends — within a few years at most, although the same would apply even if the war ended tomorrow. Moscow does not have a surplus of combat aircraft comparable to that of the United States after the Second World War. It does, however, have a heavily worn fleet, with many aircraft so old that there is little justification for retaining them now, and there will be none at all after the war. Even today, they are often listed only on paper as supposed evidence of Russian military might. Many will have to be retired, however, and disposing of entire families of aircraft will make the most financial sense.
There is already a precedent in Russia’s recent history. Following the collapse of the Soviet Union, Moscow decided to retire all single-engined combat aircraft.
Within just a few years, between 1992 and 1998, entire aircraft families were withdrawn from operational service, including all MiG-21 and MiG-23 fighters, MiG-27 ground-attack aircraft, Su-17 fighter-bombers and the navy’s Yak-38 vertical take-off aircraft. Other twin-engined designs also faced the axe, including the infamous Su-15 interceptors and MiG-25 fighters.
Small numbers were reassigned to training duties. The aviation formations inherited from the Soviet superpower were thus substantially reduced. The savings, however, allowed Russia to concentrate on keeping its most modern and promising designs in service: the twin-engined Su-24, Su-25, MiG-29, Su-27 and MiG-31. The Tu-95 and Tu-160 strategic bombers also survived, as did the Tu-22M3 long-range bombers.
Thirty years have passed since then — the period typically planned for a combat aircraft’s entire service life. The aircraft retained in Russia during the 1990s have now exceeded their intended service lives. Successors have also emerged: the Su-30, somewhat by chance following successful exports to India, China and other countries; the Su-35, the planned successor to the Su-27; the Su-34, a replacement for the Su-24 based on the Su-27’s successful aerodynamic configuration; and, finally, the Su-57, which is being steadily introduced into service, albeit with difficulties. Nevertheless, hundreds of older aircraft remain in service, and the war has only accelerated their deterioration.
According to figures officially published by reputable sources covering the world’s armed forces, Russia still has around 260 Su-24-family front-line bombers in service, compared with more than 290 listed before the war. These aircraft did not, however, participate in the aggression against Ukraine — at least not from the outset or along the main axes of attack. This probably explains why their confirmed losses currently amount to just 13 aircraft destroyed and five damaged. They have been operated by the Wagner Group, among others, suggesting their secondary status, given the Russian state’s willingness to place them in „private” hands.
It appears that only 100–140 aircraft may actually be in service today, including those operated by the navy. Apart from the episodes involving Wagner, it is the naval aircraft that appear to be used in combat today. Su-24s have been lost over the Black Sea and at bases in Crimea. The wreckage of one was visible in the ruins of Bakhmut in 2023. The Su-24 remains in service only because Russia has been unable to expand its Su-30 and Su-34 fleets sufficiently to replace it.
One indication of its limited utility is that it has not been adapted to carry precision-guided glide bombs fitted with UMPK kits. These are currently carried exclusively by newly built aircraft, primarily the Su-34. Assistance from the Su-24 could ease their workload, but its fleet is apparently in such poor condition that this would make little sense. The same applies to installing newer self-protection systems. Its absence from these relatively safe bombing missions, conducted from behind Russian lines, is the clearest indication that the Su-24 is nearing the end. Interestingly, these aircraft are rolled out at bases in Crimea and elsewhere to serve as decoys for Ukrainian drones. Despite repeated hits, they neither explode nor burn because they contain no fuel or operating fluids. Su-24 production ended in 1993, making the youngest aircraft 33 years old today. The war has only accelerated their ageing, despite the limited use of aircraft belonging to the Black Sea Fleet.
With the Su-34 fleet remaining at roughly 130 aircraft — production offsets losses, or allows only modest fleet growth — the retirement and demise of the Su-24 will reduce Russia’s officially listed aircraft inventory by almost 300.
Unlike the Su-24, the Su-25 Grach has been actively employed in the aggression against Ukraine from the outset. Its fleet of 192 aircraft has consequently suffered substantial irrecoverable losses, which we estimate at no fewer than 39 aircraft destroyed, with a further two damaged. Interestingly, these losses resulted from shoot-downs and accidents. Virtually no Su-25s have been lost in Ukrainian missile and drone strikes on airfields. Irrecoverable losses exceeding 20 per cent, with no production to replace them, have been accompanied by wear and tear. We counted 23 Su-25s destroyed in 2022, six in 2023, six in 2024 — two of which may have been lost in earlier years — and four in 2025.
The last known shoot-down of a Su-25 over the front occurred in February 2025, and the last loss in an accident in June 2025. After that, the tally stops and the aircraft disappears from the front line. Instead, a formation of a few aircraft takes the place of a full flypast during the 9 May parades. In theory, the fleet is undergoing modernisation. In the war, however, glide bombs and drones of various classes have replaced the Su-25. This means that aircraft of this class currently have no place on the modern battlefield, or at least that, in positional warfare, their tasks can be performed by considerably less risky means. A decision to retire them or substantially reduce their numbers after the war should come as no surprise.
There is talk of a combat-capable Yak-130M succeeding the Grach. First, however, these aircraft would have to be manufactured, which would be far from straightforward given production of the type to date.
More than 200 MiG-29s are still officially listed, including a naval squadron. Despite the potential these aircraft offered in the 1990s, they did not receive funding comparable to that allocated to the Su-27. Nor did export customers come to their rescue, as India did with the Su-27, enabling the development of the Su-30.
In Russia, the aircraft remained neglected for much longer than its larger contemporary, and the technical condition of this underfunded fleet steadily deteriorated. The full extent of the problem became apparent in 2009, following a series of accidents involving these aircraft. An inspection was ordered, revealing that 90 aircraft had structures so worn or corroded that they had to be struck off charge. That was 17 years ago.
Despite the plans, the MiG-29 never acquired a multirole version that secured its future. The MiG-35 was supposed to fulfil that role, but with no interest from export customers, Russia itself ordered only six. Russia’s relatively modern MiG-29s also include carrier-borne variants and a squadron of MiG-29SMTs stationed in Armenia. Russia’s new light or medium fighter — all its other fighters are in the heavy category — will be the Su-75 Checkmate, if it materialises. This single-engined aircraft draws on experience gained with the Su-57. First, however, its development programme must be completed, and then it must be manufactured. Who will pay? There are no foreign customers, and Algeria alone, with potential demand for 50–70 aircraft, will not finance Russia’s programmes. Meanwhile, more than 200 MiG-29s are approaching the end of their service lives in training and test units across Russia.
Russian MiG-29 wartime losses probably comprise two naval aircraft destroyed by drones in Crimea — unless these were merely old airframes being moved around airfields, as is done with the Su-24.
Around 100 Su-27s remain in service, some of which have been modernised. Their numbers are declining as Su-35Ss and Su-57s replace them in the last regiments still operating the type. By Russian standards, this process is proceeding according to plan, with no signs of disaster. Nevertheless, these are still 100 aircraft that must be replaced. Meanwhile, the Su-35 and Su-57 fleets are growing relatively slowly. Russia delivered 14 Su-35s into service in 2025 and 16 aircraft in 2024 — eight Su-35s and eight Su-57s. So far this year, it has delivered 12: six of each type. Replacing 100 aircraft will therefore take a long time, particularly once losses are taken into account.
MiG-31 production ended in 1994, making the youngest aircraft 32 years old. Worse still for Russia, its performance subjects it to considerable wear, and there is no successor beyond concepts and drawings that appear periodically in various publications. Neither the funding nor, probably, the technical capacity is available for a new Russian interceptor, particularly since completion of a development programme would still have to be followed by production. Just over 100 MiG-31s remain in service, or around 130 according to some sources. Somewhere between a dozen and more than 20 have been converted to carry Kh-47M2 Kinzhal aeroballistic missiles. It is difficult, however, to assess how many aircraft in this family remain serviceable today.
Most of their wartime losses are known to have resulted from accidents, engine fires, undercarriage failures and similar incidents. The MiG-31 may remain in service after the war, but only because there is no alternative, and at the cost of cannibalisation and further reductions in fleet size. That is unless Russia changes its doctrine and approach to protecting its airspace, allowing conventional air-superiority fighters to take over the role. Either way, this means another reduction and even fewer resources to cover Russia’s vast territory.
In our assessment, the future of the Tu-22M3 bomber, which is no longer in production, may also be in doubt. Around 60 were available at the start of the war, but at least nine have been destroyed, including three in accidents, several more have been damaged, and the rest of the fleet has suffered wear and tear. The Tu-22M3 cannot carry potent heavy cruise missiles such as the Kh-101, unlike the Tu-95MS and Tu-160. It must approach closer to its targets to employ shorter-range Kh-15, Kh-22 and Kh-32 missiles. It can also carry Kinzhal missiles. In the latter case, however, it is unclear whether Russia is still producing the weapon. Reports this spring suggested that production had been halted because of its low effectiveness, owing to Ukrainian spoofing and its high manufacturing costs. Will these large, failure-prone jets, whose numbers are steadily dwindling, have a place in future wars? This is another question Russia will have to answer after the war.
Retiring older aircraft, or grounding them while retaining them on paper, will leave almost exclusively newer types whose introduction into service began after 2008. Withdrawing the older types will allow resources previously devoted to obsolete aircraft to be redirected towards their successors. The fifth generation will be represented by the Su-57, of which 76 are known to have been ordered, although only 20–30 have been delivered. The fourth generation will comprise the Su-30SM/SM2, with around 130 currently in service; the Su-35S, also with around 130; and the Su-34 front-line bomber, likewise numbering around 130. Russia’s tactical aviation fleet „of the future” therefore currently consists of around 400 aircraft. It should also be added that the extent of their wear after four and a half years of intensive combat operations is unknown. With considerable effort, Moscow will probably manage to increase the numbers of these aircraft, which remain in production. Investment in the Su-35S and Su-57 appears particularly warranted. In addition to their existing roles, these aircraft may have to take over those performed by the MiG-31.

title: What schools will do amid intense heat during El Niño
body: MANILA, Philippines – The education sector will not be spared when El Niño worsens in the coming months. Across the country, temperatures are expected to be warmer than usual, which would pose another threat to students’ learning. Education Secretary Sonny Angara previously said government protocols would ensure that El Niño’s effects are mitigated in public schools. How exactly is the Department of Education (DepEd) preparing for the impact of the weather phenomenon? Pending formal guidelines, here’s what we know so far: How to conduct classes In an interview with Rappler on Friday, October 23, Education Undersecretary Malcolm Garma said the DepEd is concerned that lost school days may increase due to high heat index levels. The heat index, or the temperature that the human body perceives, is measured using the air temperature and the relative humidity in a place at a given time. Garma noted that the DepEd’s existing class suspension guidelines , issued back in June, already spell out learning continuity plans for schools. The DepEd said that under Level 1-Hayo, face-to-face classes continue during manageable conditions. Schools can set scheduled water breaks, shift outdoor activities to early morning or shaded areas, and allow students to wear comfortable clothing or Physical Education attire. At Level 2-Hinay, schools may adopt modified class days with structured home-based or hybrid learning. Level 3-Hinga may be implemented when temperatures can cause heat cramps or heat exhaustion or there is loss of water supply. Learning packets, short activities, and broadcast resources may be used to reduce academic demands. Once the heat index reaches 42°C and above, academic activities are suspended at Level 4-Hinto, focusing on safety checks and psychosocial support referrals, according to the class suspension guidelines. Garma said self-learning modules, activity sheets, and other materials needed for alternative learning will be prepositioned before the peak months of intense heat. What if the heat is unbearable? In case actual conditions turn out to be worse than projected, Garma said school heads can adjust class schedules or recommend granular suspensions of face-to-face classes. But he added that the situation must be properly assessed. “Hindi naman ‘yung school head ay basta-basta na lang siyang magpapauwi o magsu-suspend. So kailangan mai-vet ito ng [schools] division office…or [they should] even coordinate with the local government unit. Para sa gano’n, talagang hindi naman maabuso din ‘yung pagsususpende ng klase,” the DepEd official said. (The school head cannot just decide to send students home or suspend classes. This must be vetted by the schools division office or they should even coordinate with the local government unit. This is to prevent abuse of class suspensions.) “While we are looking after…the welfare of our learners, we also have to ensure that learning continues. At alam naman natin na pinakamainam pa din na learning delivery natin ay kung school-based ito or face-to-face (And we know that the best learning delivery is school-based or face-to-face),” he added. Measures for water supply, health Garma said the DepEd has ordered schools to make hydration facilities and equipment, such as safe drinking stations and water dispensers, accessible to learners and personnel. The DepEd also told schools to repair water leaks immediately and coordinate closely with local water concessionaires for rationing contingencies. Social Welfare Secretary Rex Gatchalian earlier raised the possibility of deploying community water depots to public schools. These depots are rainwater catchment equipment with built-in filtration systems to provide potable water during shortages. Garma said the DepEd welcomes such proposals. Regarding health, Garma said school clinics will be ready to address medical concerns like heat stroke or dehydration. Additional support from local government units (LGUs) and the Department of Health will also be tapped for emergency response. With El Niño also threatening agriculture and food supply, schools division offices and schools were directed to develop contingency menus for the school-based feeding program, partner with LGUs and cooperatives for local food sourcing, and maintain buffer stocks of shelf-stable commodities. How about school buildings? Garma said public schools can use their funding for maintenance and other operating expenses to buy additional ventilators like electric fans. But the DepEd’s long-term solution is structural intervention. “For old classrooms, we cannot change their designs; we can only do mitigation. But for those classrooms under construction and for future ones, we’ll make sure that there will be structural intervention such as high ceilings, insulated ceilings, and wide airflow,” he said in Filipino. Garma also said the DepEd is exploring the possibility of institutionalizing the use of solar power in schools to reduce electricity costs and possibly provide air-conditioning. The DepEd said its upcoming formal guidelines for El Niño-related measures will mandate schools to conduct integrated school-level risk assessments covering water supply reliability, classroom thermal safety, electricity resilience, and fire hazard prevention. The set of guidelines is also expected to prohibit schools from charging or requiring parents to buy cooling equipment, connectivity, or specialized attire as a condition for alternative learning modalities. – Rappler.com

title: Ukraine, Russia Agree Ceasefire Timetable for Oleshky Mission
body:
Ukraine and Russia have agreed on a synchronized ceasefire timetable to conduct an emergency humanitarian mission in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in southern Kherson region, Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets announced .
Lubinets confirmed that he finalized the operational timeline during direct consultations with Yana Lantratova, head of the Russian negotiating team. Under the agreed framework, the localized silence regime will take effect across the designated sector on Tuesday, Oct. 27, at 3:00 a.m. Kyiv time (4:00 a.m. Moscow time).
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“I informed the Russian side that the ceasefire will take effect from Oct. 27 at 3:00 a.m. Kyiv time,” Lubinets stated.
“The Russian commissioner, for her part, informed me of the same – that from the Russian side, the regime of silence is established from Oct. 27 at 4:00 a.m. Moscow time. That is the exact same time.”
The Ukrainian ombudsman noted that preliminary arrangements are proceeding as planned, adding that both sides are adhering to their initial commitments to enable the arrival of relief convoys and organize civilian evacuations.
The bilateral agreement establishes a humanitarian framework encompassing an operational silence regime, the delivery of emergency food and medical consignments, and the phased evacuation of non-combatants trapped in the ruined Dnipro left-bank enclave.
Lubinets emphasized that the humanitarian operation will be executed in gradual phases given the extreme physical, tactical, and logistical hazards confronting the mission on the ground.
The ombudsman expressed formal gratitude to United States First Lady Melania Trump and her diplomatic team for facilitating technical consultations and mediating the dialogue between Ukrainian and Russian negotiating delegations.
The humanitarian corridor is engineered to relieve an estimated 1,700 civilians who have remained isolated under Russian military occupation in Oleshky since early 2022.
The enclave has been entirely severed from authorized commercial freight convoys and institutional humanitarian assistance since late May, while central municipal utilities – including municipal electrical networks, running water, and central heating – have suffered extensive damage ahead of freezing winter temperatures.
Earlier in the month, Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha warned that Russian forces had turned the municipal core into a “death trap,” noting that exit roads and river routes leading away from the city were mined and monitored by loitering strike drones.
Local residents reported severe food shortages, an exhaustion of essential pharmaceuticals, and the presence of unburied deceased in residential courtyards due to continuous operational hazards.
The worsening humanitarian collapse in Oleshky had previously drawn top-level international appeals, including a telephone consultation between Pope Leo XIV and Russian President Vladimir Putin urging a localized ceasefire to permit the evacuation of vulnerable non-combatants, alongside direct calls from United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk demanding unfettered access for international relief agencies.

title: OpenMobile-2 proves open-source smartphone agents can rival proprietary models
body:
More data alone doesn't make smartphone agents better. With the same amount of data, what matters most is how many different apps an agent trains on.
AI agents that operate apps on their own learn mainly through practice, but the data they need is mostly locked up at big companies. Open models lag behind as a result, write researchers from Nanjing University, AI company SenseTime, and several other universities.
OpenMobile-2 is their attempt to close that gap. They're releasing two agent models built on Qwen3.5 with 9 billion and Qwen3.6 with 27 billion parameters , along with the full training environment, data, and instructions to reproduce everything. The authors say their model ranks near the top among current smartphone agents. Ad
Training on real apps is painful because logins, real purchases, and no way to reset state make the process expensive and hard to repeat. So the researchers rebuilt 35 apps popular mainly in China, including Taobao, JD, DiDi, and Meituan, plus globally used services like Slack and Google Drive. Combined with existing simulations and apps running in an Android emulator, the practice ground covers more than 110 applications. Ad
Human reviewers compared the rebuilt apps to the originals and kept refining until workflows and interfaces matched. Orders, budgets, and travel plans persist across sessions, and data can pass between apps via the clipboard. Every simulation resets to its starting state automatically, while the agent only sees screenshots and has no access to internal app data, mimicking how a person would actually use them.
From this setup, the team generated about 11,600 example workflows and more than 2,000 practice tasks with automated success checks. Google's Gemini 3.1 Pro served as the teacher model that produced the examples, which means OpenMobile-2 is effectively learning from a closed system. Ad
Both models show clear gains on established benchmarks. On AndroidWorld, the larger model jumps from 67.1 to 79.9 points, while the smaller one goes from 54.3 to 74. The predecessor OpenMobile-1 scored 64.7 on the same test. On the harder MobileWorld benchmark, which covers longer tasks spanning multiple apps, the larger model improves from 35.9 to 50.4 points.
The biggest jump shows up on real Android devices, where the larger model climbs from 31.9 to 59.6 points on SPA-Bench. The researchers say that's the best score among open models. Ad
Training environment diversity matters more than sheer data volume here. The researchers held the amount of data constant and only increased the number of apps the agent practiced on, which pushed the success rate on unseen apps from 60.7 to 67.5 percent. With the same data budget, app variety beats extra examples from a handful of apps. Ad
Reinforcement learning on top brought only limited gains, mainly in environments that resembled the training setup. On AndroidWorld, the larger model actually scored slightly worse afterward, landing at 79.9 instead of 80.8 points.
An experimental part of the study goes beyond tapping and swiping. More than 50 of the simulated apps offer direct commands like "add to cart" so the agent can skip navigating through menus, and the agent freely switches between both approaches depending on what's available.
On its own, though, this doesn't help much because the models tend to ignore the shortcuts without targeted training. Once they've been trained on them, the agents use them well, solving up to 10.3 percentage points more tasks while needing about five fewer steps. The researchers say this ability also transfers to tools the models never encountered during training.
During the later reinforcement learning phase, tool use got a bonus factor whenever a run included at least one direct command, though the reward still depended on whether the task was actually completed. Penalties kicked in when the agent reported a success that wasn't real. These interfaces only exist in the simulated apps for now, and the researchers call the approach experimental themselves.
Some results come from a custom benchmark the team built with 215 tasks, nearly half of which span multiple apps. Task completion isn't judged by a language model but by a program that compares the app's stored data before and after each run. The authors also checked for overlap between training and test tasks and found only minor similarities.
Microsoft Research had already classified API agents as more reliable and GUI agents as more flexible in a 2025 study, pointing to mobile apps as a typical case where external interfaces don't exist. Oppo takes a different route with its open agent X-OmniClaw , which runs on real devices and replays previously shown paths in apps like Taobao or Meituan via deeplinks instead of clicking through menus again. Among closed models, Google has built smartphone control directly into Gemini 3.5 Flash .

title: Oman bans abalone fishing until November 2027
body:
Muscat: The Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Water Resources has issued a ministerial decision banning the fishing and collection of abalone in Oman until November 1, 2027. According to Ministerial Decision No. 264/2026, the ban will take effect from the date the decision comes into force and will remain in place until November 1, 2027. The decision also prohibits the possession, trading or handling of abalone during the ban period, including transportation, buying, selling and exporting. Furthermore, the possession of abalone harvesting tools and equipment of any kind will be prohibited aboard fishing boats and vessels near coastal areas and fishing grounds throughout the ban period. However, an exception has been granted for quantities of abalone legally harvested before the decision comes into effect. These quantities may be traded or exported, provided the necessary permits are obtained from the competent authorities. The decision was issued by Dr Saud bin Hamoud al Habsi, Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Water Resources, on October 20, 2026. The regulation will come into force on the day following its publication in the Official Gazette.

title: India seeks prosperity and strength alongside global peace: Rajnath Singh
body:
By R Anil Kumar

Dushanbe, Tajikistan, Oct 21. Defence Minister Rajnath Singh on October 20, said India was working to combine economic prosperity, knowledge and strength with a commitment to global peace and human well-being, as he addressed the Indian diaspora in Dushanbe, Tajikistan.



Guided by the philosophy of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam, or “the world is one family”, India’s development ambitions extended beyond national progress, Singh said. He credited economic reforms, technological advancement and the country’s growing international stature with supporting this vision.

Highlighting India’s economic performance, Singh said the country contributed more than 16 per cent to global economic growth and was expanding at approximately 7.8 per cent despite a slowdown in several major economies.

He said India had entered into free trade agreements with 38 countries, opening markets for manufacturers and producers. He added that the India-UK and India-EU trade agreements were expected to eliminate tariffs on 99 per cent of Indian exports to those markets.

Describing a shift in governance from “policy paralysis” to a “reform express”, Singh said: “For us, reforms are not a compulsion; they are a conviction.”

The Minister said the current account deficit had declined from more than four per cent of GDP 12–13 years ago to 0.61 per cent in the previous financial year. Foreign exchange reserves had crossed $700 billion, he added.

On defence manufacturing, Singh said exports had reached ₹38,424 crore, while production had risen to ₹1.80 lakh crore.

He also highlighted the expansion of India’s startup ecosystem to more than 2.5 lakh enterprises. Nearly half originated from smaller cities and towns, while more than 45 per cent had at least one woman director or partner, he said.

Singh credited affordable mobile data and wider connectivity with expanding access to opportunities. He said the value of UPI transactions had increased from ₹7,000 crore in 2016–17 to ₹314 lakh crore in 2025–26.

Around 25 crore people had been lifted out of poverty over the past decade, he said, highlighting the role of the Jan Dhan-Aadhaar-Mobile framework and Direct Benefit Transfer in improving the delivery of government assistance.

Rajnath Singh also outlined progress in renewable energy, semiconductor manufacturing, transport infrastructure and space technology. Referring to efforts under the Semicon India programme and India Semiconductor Mission, he said, “We’re moving towards manufacturing both ships and chips, strengthening our position in strategic sectors.”

Singh praised the Indian diaspora as cultural ambassadors who preserved India’s traditions while contributing to their host countries. He said India and Tajikistan shared longstanding friendly relations, reinforced by the popularity of Indian music, literature and cinema among Tajik people.

During the event, he felicitated Indologist Prof. Habibullo Rajabov, Tajikistan’s first Padma Shri recipient, for his contributions to Hindi literature, education and philology. Indian and Tajik artists also presented cultural performances.

title: Air defense neutralizes 119 of 153 drones Russia launched at Ukraine overnight
body:
According to Ukrinform, the Ukrainian Air Force reported this on Telegram .
Overnight on October 25, from 18:00 on October 24, the enemy attacked Ukraine with 153 strike UAVs, including Shahed drones (92 of them jet-powered), S8000 Banderol/Dan-T, Gerbera drones, and Parodiya-type decoy drones, launched from Bryansk, Oryol, Kursk and Millerovo in Russia, as well as the temporarily occupied city of Donetsk and the temporarily occupied Autonomous Republic of Crimea, from Hvardiiske.
The air attack was repelled by aircraft, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare units, unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine's Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 08:00, air defense forces had shot down or suppressed 119 enemy UAVs, including Shahed drones (64 of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones and other types of UAVs. Nine attack UAVs remained in the air, with combat operations ongoing.
Hits by enemy aerial attack weapons were recorded at 15 locations, while debris from downed drones fell at nine locations.

title: Pres. Pezeshkian congratulates Kazakhstan on National Day
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 25 (MNA) – Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has sent a message to President of the Republic of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev to felicitate him and the Kazakh people on the Independence Day of the Central Asian country.
In a congratulatory message on Sunday, President Pezeshkian emphasized developing and deepening friendly and amicable relations between the two countries.
In this message, the Iranian president referred to the positive and stable trajectory of relations between Iran and the Republic of Kazakhstan over the past years, stating that the amicable relations between the two countries have always been established based on friendship, mutual respect and trust.
Stressing the historical, cultural, and civilizational commonalities between the two countries, Pezeshkian highlighted that these shared ties, in tandem with the common will of the leaders of Iran and Kazakhstan, have paved suitable ways for expanding and deepening bilateral cooperation in various fields.
Turning to the geographical situation of Iran and Kazakhstan as two significant and influential countries in the region, he stipulated that the duo countries possess shared capacities and responsibilities for strengthening regional peace, stability, and security.
The Iranian president expressed hope that, by taking advantage of the existing capacities and unsparing efforts of high-ranking officials of the two countries, “we will soon witness a further expansion of cooperation and strengthening of friendly relations between Iran and the Republic of Kazakhstan.”
Pezeshkian, in his message, prayed to God Almighty and wished health, success, prosperity, and well-being for the President and people of the Republic of Kazakhstan.

title: Public Prosecution warns against offensive social media content
body:
Muscat:The Public Prosecution has urged the public to exercise caution and responsibility when expressing opinions, particularly on social media platforms, warning of legal action against content that offends other nations, their leaders or peoples. In a statement, the Public Prosecution called for greater awareness and wisdom in public statements and actions, stressing the importance of avoiding anything that could harm Oman's relations with other countries. It urged individuals to refrain from publishing or sharing content that could be considered offensive to nations, their leadership or citizens, or that could negatively affect diplomatic relations. The Public Prosecution affirmed that it would take all legally prescribed measures against those found violating the law, including through publishing, reposting, participating in or inciting unlawful activities on social media. It stressed that such actions would be dealt with in accordance with applicable legislation, particularly Articles 20, 23 and 26 of the Law on Combating Cybercrimes.

title: Airbus projects global freighter fleet to almost double by 2045
body:
Toulouse, France, Oct 21, 2026. Airbus' 2026 Cargo Global Market Forecast projects the worldwide fleet of dedicated freighter aircraft to grow 46% from 2,360 in 2026 to 3,460 aircraft by 2045, as announced at the Cargo Facts Symposium. According to the forecast, there will be a requirement for 2,670 freighters mainly to replace older models (1,580) and also for growth (1,090).



Of the 2,670 freighters required, 1,140 will be single-aisle, 860 mid-size widebodies, and 670 large widebody aircraft. Some 970 aircraft will be new-build and 1,700 will be converted from passenger aircraft.

With long-term trade projected to expand at a 2.9% Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR), global air cargo traffic is forecasted to grow at 3.2% annually over the next two decades. Despite high fuel prices, ongoing geopolitical disruptions, and supply chain constraints, air freight has demonstrated remarkable resilience.

While air cargo accounts for less than 1% of global trade volume by weight, it carries more than 30% of total trade by value, proving it to be a vital mode of transport for goods requiring the quickest routes to market. In the last three years, computers and high-technology goods in air cargo have doubled in value, reaching 15% in 2026. Other drivers include e-commerce and air cargo seen as an alternative to shipping for some goods.

Asia-Pacific will continue to be the leading region for international air cargo traffic, with routes to North America being the largest (3.8% annual growth rate), followed by Europe. These routes can be efficiently operated by the newest freighter, the A350F.

Regional demand for the 2,670 freighter deliveries will be led by North America and Asia-Pacific, requiring 925 and 850 aircraft respectively, together accounting for two-thirds of total global demand. Demand in Europe and CIS will reach 515 aircraft, followed by Latin America with 165, the Middle East with 125, and Africa with 90.

An increasing number of previous-generation freighters will be retired and replaced by highly efficient next-generation freighters in the next 20 years. This includes new-build models such as the A350F, as well as passenger-to-freighter conversions across the A320, A321, and A330 families, helping operators lower fuel consumption and reduce carbon emissions.

title: MUSIGA warns musicians against glorifying online fraud
body: The Musicians Union of Ghana (MUSIGA) has cautioned musicians against making public statements that could be interpreted as encouraging or glorifying online fraud and other cyber-related crimes. In a statement signed by its President, Bessa Simons, MUSIGA said it respected musicians’ right to express opinions on governance, unemployment, corruption and the administration of justice, but stressed that such concerns should not be used to justify criminal conduct. “While MUSIGA respects every musician’s right to express opinions on governance, unemployment, corruption, and the fair administration of justice, we state emphatically that no grievance against public institutions justifies statements that may appear to normalize fraud, portray suspected offenders as heroes, or discourage cooperation with lawful investigations,” the statement said. The Union’s statement follows comments Shatta Wale made during ShattaFest in Accra on 17 October 2026, which suggested that he was encouraging young people to engage in fraud. “Me I do my music for over 25 years. I buy Rolls Royce, I buy Lamborghini all from my music. Then somebody go go talk somebody say Shatta Wale he dey do fraud. “Make I tell you today. I get plenty fraud boys who be my friends but me I no be snitch wey I go snitch anybody. The country no good so if you go fraud, fraud,” he said in Pidgin English. Shatta Wale’s comments have since generated widespread discussion, with some critics expressing concern that his influence could negatively affect society, particularly young people. MUSIGA warned that online fraud causes real harm to victims, damages Ghana’s international reputation, threatens legitimate digital businesses and endangers the future of young people. It therefore urged musicians, particularly those with large followings and influence among young people, to avoid statements, performances and social media posts that could be construed as promoting or defending internet fraud, money laundering, romance scams, identity theft and other forms of cybercrime. “Musicians must understand that their words carry weight. A stage, concert platform, interview, or social-media account is not a private space; it is a powerful channel of public influence,” the statement added. The Union said using such platforms to excuse criminal conduct, attack lawful enforcement actions or indirectly encourage fraudulent activities was irresponsible and inconsistent with the values of the music profession. However, MUSIGA acknowledged that concerns about selective justice, corruption, youth unemployment and accountability were legitimate national issues that musicians had every right to raise. It maintained that criticism of public institutions and demands for justice should be pursued constructively without appearing to endorse unlawful behaviour. “However, criticism of injustice must never become a justification for crime,” the statement stressed. The Union called on artistes to channel their influence towards addressing the challenges confronting young people by advocating employment opportunities, supporting digital-skills training, promoting financial literacy and entrepreneurship, and speaking out against corruption and fraud. It urged the music industry to contribute to solutions that would help young people pursue lawful and productive livelihoods rather than expose themselves to criminal activities. MUSIGA also cautioned musicians against making statements that could expose them or their fans to legal, reputational or professional consequences. “Every musician must remember that fame does not place them above the law, and artistic freedom does not include the freedom to encourage unlawful conduct,” the statement said. The Union reaffirmed its commitment to protecting the rights and welfare of musicians but warned that it would not remain silent when public statements by members threatened the credibility of the profession and the safety of Ghanaian youth. It called on musicians to use their platforms responsibly, defend the dignity of Ghana’s creative industry and inspire young people to pursue success through lawful and productive means.

title: Ballon d’Or 2026: The five most historic winners – from Matthews to Messi
body: The 2026 Ballon d'Or winner will be announced on Monday night at a glittering ceremony in London. The 70th staging of the event will be the first to be held outside France, with it moving to England as a tribute to Sir Stanley Matthews, who won the first ever Ballon d'Or in 1956. Below, we pick out five of the most historically significant Ballon d'Or victories and list every winner, going back to the very start. Honourable mentions must go to Lev Yashin, the only goalkeeper to win the award (1963), and Cristiano Ronaldo , who, with five trophies at home, is second only to Lionel Messi's eight. 1. Stanley Matthews (1956) Matthews was the inaugural winner of the award and, notably, was aged 41 at the time. His victory established the Ballon d’Or’s place in the game and reflected the enormous respect he commanded across Europe. At 41 years, 10 months and 17 days, he remains the oldest-ever winner. 2. George Weah (1995) Weah became the first African player to win the Ballon d’Or after the rules were changed to allow non-European players representing European clubs to be eligible. He remains the only African winner of the men’s award, making his triumph a defining moment for football on the continent. 3. Ronaldo (1997) At 21, Ronaldo Nazario became the youngest winner of the award, a record that still stands. His explosive performances for Barcelona and Inter Milan made him a global phenomenon and cemented his reputation as one of the greatest No 9s of all time. 4. Fabio Cannavaro (2006) Cannavaro’s victory was largely down to his inspirational leadership of Italy as they lifted the 2006 World Cup. He had also won Serie A with Juventus, although the club was later stripped of the title following the Calciopoli scandal. Significantly, Cannavaro remains the last defender to win the award, two decades ago. Only three defenders have ever won the award: Franz Beckenbauer, Matthias Sammer and Cannavaro. 5. Lionel Messi (2009) Messi won the first of his record eight Ballon d’Or awards in 2009, with his most recent triumph coming 14 years later, in 2023. During the 2008/09 season, Messi scored 38 goals and provided 19 assists as Barcelona won the treble under Pep Guardiola. That was also the first of four in a row – also a record. title: Musk Claims Ukraine Breached Starlink Terms, Kyiv Rebuts
body:
American entrepreneur Elon Musk stated that the Ukrainian military violated the terms of service of SpaceX’s commercial Starlink network by deploying it for offensive drone strikes, claiming a “loophole” allowing such use was closed last week, while Ukrainian defense figures disputed the technical feasibility of the allegation.
Writing on X on Saturday, Oct. 24, Musk distinguished between commercial Starlink services and the US government-controlled Starshield military system, asserting that commercial satellite connectivity was never permitted for lethal offensive operations.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be,” Musk stated.
“Starshield, a different system, is controlled by the US government. What they decide to do is up to them. Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week.”
Musk maintained that Starlink remains vital to Ukrainian territorial defense, describing it as the only communications network resilient against Russian jamming and physical interdiction. He added that if the system were terminated, the Ukrainian front line would experience an immediate collapse, characterizing the assessment as a statement of fact rather than a threat.
The billionaire asserted that SpaceX had done more to defend Ukraine than any private enterprise globally, while expressing contempt toward figures advocating prolonged conflict without realistic diplomatic frameworks.
Correct. Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be. Starshield, a different system, is controlled by the US government. What they decide to do is up to them. Ukraine military violated… https://t.co/ZXBB8bYfPn
Musk’s assertions were contested by Ukrainian defense specialist, volunteer, and former defense ministry adviser Serhii Sternenko, who stated that technical architectures established earlier this year precluded commercial terminals from operating on dynamic strike platforms.
Sternenko explained that institutional mechanisms implemented in February established strict regulatory whitelists separating stationary commercial equipment from dynamic military systems.
Under those protocols, Ukrainian civilians and military units could register stationary terminals, but any terminal intended to operate while in motion required formal inclusion on a specialized registry connected to the Starshield network.
“In February of this year, whitelists were introduced,” Sternenko stated.
“Stationary terminals could be registered by both military personnel and civilians. But for any satellite terminal to function in motion, it had to be placed on a special list and connected to the military Starshield system. Otherwise, satellite communication terminals in Ukraine would not function.”
Sternenko emphasized that operating standard commercial Starlink devices on unmanned aerial vehicles was technically impossible under existing system protocols, stating that all Ukrainian drone missions requiring satellite guidance were routed exclusively through Starshield.
Presidential defense technology adviser Serhii Beskrestnov, known by the call sign “Flash,” similarly dismissed Musk’s allegations, outlining preexisting technical and geographical parameters that prevent commercial terminals from guiding deep strikes into Russia.
Writing on Telegram on Saturday evening, Beskrestnov noted that Starlink terminals across Ukraine and occupied territories have been subjected to strict operational constraints since early 2026, including an automatic velocity cutoff calibrated between 70 and 90 km/h (43–56 mph).
Furthermore, commercial Starlink connectivity is geofenced and deactivated across sovereign Russian territory.
“Very strange that Elon Musk does not know about the restrictions on Starlink operations in Ukraine,” Beskrestnov stated. “Thus, we are physically unable to use commercial Starlink for deep strikes and medium-range strikes.”
The dispute over Starlink’s terms of service follows days of operational friction across Ukraine’s front lines after President Volodymyr Zelensky disclosed on Oct. 17 that an artificial 161 km/h (100 mph) velocity limit had been imposed on satellite terminals operating within Ukraine.
Ukrainian military specialists reported that the sudden cutoff severed telemetry links and grounded domestic interceptor drones deployed to counter Russian jet-powered Shahed loitering munitions, which cruise at speeds exceeding 400 km/h.
Comparative trials conducted by Ukrainian engineers demonstrated that equipped vehicles operated normally above 180 km/h in neighboring EU territory, establishing that the restriction was geographically confined to Ukraine.
The dispute eased earlier on Saturday when Ukrainian defense officials confirmed that Starlink and Starshield speeds had returned to pre-restriction levels , allowing domestic interceptor units and uncrewed logistics platforms to resume standard operations.
