title: Spike NLOS Live‑Fire Validates Infantry Use and ISV-U Platform Integration
body:
WASHINGTON, Oct. 20, 2026. Lockheed Martin successfully completed a live-fire demonstration of the Spike Non-Line-of-Sight (NLOS) system from an Infantry Squad Vehicle – Utility variant (ISV-U) at Dugway Proving Grounds, Utah, validating the system’s performance in a ground-based operational environment and advancing the US Army’s Mobile-Long-Range Precision-Strike Missile (M-LRPSM) directed requirement.



THE BIG PICTURE

The three-day live-fire demonstration featured 17 precision engagements against simulated operational targets at varied combat ranges with the majority of shots conducted by US Army infantry soldiers. All shots were launched from an ISV-U, marking the first-time there was a firing of Spike NLOS from this mobile platform.

WHY IT MATTERS

 	Ground‑centric precision strike: The demo proved that soldiers can safely fire the Spike NLOS from a mobile platform, extending strike reach well beyond line‑of‑sight while maintaining the precision needed to neutralize high‑value targets.
 	Accelerated requirements shaping: Transformation‑in‑Contact (TIC) units were some of the first to handle the missile, providing real‑time feedback that will help shape M‑LRPSM requirements and ensure the system meets warfighter expectations.
 	Path to fielding: Completion of further validation testing over the next year will take place prior to Phase 3, which is when initial operational production begins and final system prototypes will be delivered to the Army.
 	Enhanced combat agility: Integrating Spike NLOS onto ISV-U platforms for the Army’s Mobile Brigade Combat Team gives warfighters a non-line-of-sight capability that enhances combat agility and reduces the decision cycle in high-intensity conflict.
 	Rapid training and ease of use: Soldiers completed system training and conducted live-fire missions within the same week, demonstrating that the Spike NLOS system is intuitive and enables rapid field adoption.

EXPERT PERSPECTIVE

 	“This demonstration represents a critical milestone for Spike NLOS, showing that our infantry partners can confidently employ a long-range precision missile,” said Casey Walsh, program director, Lockheed Martin Multi-Domain Missile Systems. “The live‑fire data and soldier feedback gathered here will support the shaping of the final M‑LRPSM requirements and accelerate the fielding of a game‑changing long‑range precision strike capability.”

ADDITIONAL DETAILS

TIC units will maintain a hands-on role in the continued validation testing of the Spike NLOS system, providing ongoing user feedback that will be captured through soldier touchpoint opportunities and used to help shape M-LRPSM requirements. Lockheed Martin’s continued progress with Spike NLOS builds on the successful Phase 1 demo and Phase 2 milestones. This recent demonstration underscores Lockheed Martin’s commitment to delivering innovative, warfighter-centric solutions for the Army in a rapidly evolving battlespace.

title: US's shift from military aggression to clash of civilizations
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 25 (MNA) – U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s claims on ancient Persia’s invasion of Greece reflect Washington’s attempt to reframe its confrontation with Iran as a clash of civilizations, rather than a military aggression.
The remarks made by Marco Rubio—the U.S. Secretary of State—at the Acropolis in Athens, in which he referenced the Persian king Xerxes’ expedition to Greece in 480 BC and alleged that the city’s holy sites were set ablaze and its temples looted, are noteworthy for several reasons.
1. These statements come at a time when U.S. President Trump is under intense pressure due to his failure in his confrontation with Iran. Seeking a way out of this predicament, he aims to present a narrative that diverges from reality by exaggerating Western power and portraying Iran as a warmonger. Such rhetoric, rather than signaling confidence or strength, actually betrays an underlying anxiety about his own future. The United States is attempting to reframe the nature of its confrontation with Iran—casting military aggression against Iran as part of a broader "clash of civilizations"—thereby providing an ideological excuse for pro-war factions within the U.S.
2. Under these circumstances, the United States cannot impose its dominance over other nations merely by invoking "civilizational" claims. Civilizations are forged upon historical legacies, culture, identity, and social capacities; they cannot be manufactured through military might or political maneuvering alone. Iran, China, and Egypt are examples of civilizations with deep historical roots. Iran, for its part, has defined a civilizational horizon and objective for itself, articulated through the concept of a "New Islamic Civilization." Ironically, attacking Iran’s civilization and historical identity may backfire, potentially strengthening national cohesion among Iranians. This is because Iran’s historical and civilizational identity transcends day-to-day political disputes and can serve as a foundation for fostering convergence across various segments of society.
3. By pointing to a historical event from centuries past, Americans attempt to portray Iran as inherently warmongering, all while ignoring their own history of global wars and military interventions. The United States has a history spanning approximately 250 years—since its independence in 1776—yet, throughout this period, it has engaged in numerous wars. Jimmy Carter, a former U.S. President, once noted this extensive history of conflict, stating that out of the 250 years of the nation's existence, it has been at war for 233 years. From the country's earliest days, Americans—alongside the British—fought against Native Americans, resulting in the massacre of approximately ten million indigenous people. Subsequently, the nation’s history has been marked by conflicts with Britain, Mexico, and Spain; in later eras, this record expanded to include the Korean War, the Vietnam War, and U.S. military interventions in Afghanistan and Iraq. This track record demonstrates that war and military intervention constitute a significant component of U.S. foreign policy—a phenomenon best understood as part of an effort to maintain global power and hegemony. Today, U.S. officials openly speak of war, the destruction of Iran, and the termination of its very existence. Such rhetoric—far from reflecting any civilizational superiority—largely serves as an attempt to justify the nation's own approaches and to mask the inherent contradictions within its foreign policy.
4. By invoking Xerxes’ attack on a European nation—namely, Greece—Rubio likely intends to rally European countries to his side in the current confrontation with Iran. He seeks to elevate the dispute beyond a mere bilateral issue, reframing it instead as a clash of civilizations. However, it is unlikely that Europe will automatically adopt Washington’s approach; European policymakers have their own distinct calculations and considerations, and they will not be swayed by such narratives alone. While some observers characterize the tensions between Iran and the United States as conventional state-to-state disputes—suggesting negotiation as the primary solution—Rubio’s rhetoric indicates that the conflict transcends mere politics. Rather, it is rooted in a specific American civilizational and ideological perspective toward Iran, which informs the decisions made by the White House.
5. The American push to compel Iran’s submission stems precisely from this ideological and civilizational worldview. The U.S. perceives Iranian civilization as possessing inherent capacities and attributes that could, in the future, challenge American hegemony. Consequently, a portion of U.S. policy is directed toward weakening the Iranian-Islamic civilization and the Iranian state itself. When a civilization is targeted, its core constitutive elements—national sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity—are inevitably placed under threat. Consequently, elites and decision-makers should not simply brush aside Rubio’s remarks; nor should they assume that the profound differences between the two nations can be resolved merely through negotiations, displays of flexibility, or the granting of concessions to the other side. Understanding the depth of the rift with the United States—which is rooted in divergent worldviews and civilizational perspectives—is essential for making sound decisions and safeguarding the nation’s independence and national interests.

title: Malversation, graft charges filed vs 2 ex-DPWH execs over GenSan right-of-way scam
body: MANILA, Philippines – The Office of the Ombudsman has filed malversation and graft cases against two former Department of Public Works and Highways officials, four DPWH personnel, and seven private individuals over their alleged involvement in a road right-of-way scam in General Santos City. The Office of the Ombudsman said in a press statement on Sunday, October 25, that it “found prima facie evidence with reasonable certainty of conviction” against former DPWH Region 12 regional director Subair Saro Diron, former assistant regional director Laureano B. Suan Jr., and DPWH personnel Tomas Marquez Rodriguez, David Lucena Padlan, Paisal Amerol Padate, and Ansare Mariga Busran. The Ombudsman also included seven private individuals in the cases filed before the anti-graft court Sandiganbayan: Wilma Mamburam, Nelson Ti, Evelyn Paloso, Rudy Hadji Ong, Marisa Seguirre, William Uy, Paul Michael Bagio. “The Ombudsman filed 18 informations for Malversation of Public Funds or Property through Falsification of Public Documents under Article 217 in relation to Article 171 of the Revised Penal Code, and another 18 informations for violation of Section 3(e) of Republic Act No. 3019, or the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act,” the Office of the Ombudsman said. In 2018 and 2019, the National Bureau of Investigation submitted three investigation reports to the Ombudsman in relation to the DPWH Region 12 payment for right-of-way for 18 parcels of land allegedly affected by the construction of the Digos-Makar National Road in Lagao, General Santos City. The witness, Roberto Catapang Jr., had admitted in his 2017 affidavit that he was involved in a syndicate that was allegedly “in collusion with respondent public officers, collected money from the government purportedly as payments for the acquisitions, by fabricating and submitting fake documents.” Investigators found that the claimants, which were paid a total of P491,931,120.20, had presented falsified documents. The DPWH Region XII technical working group had approved the disbursement of the amount to the claimants. “Investigators also uncovered the alleged unlawful use of a 2009 appraisal value of P3,500 per square meter to determine compensation for properties taken by the government in the early 1990s, resulting in inflated right-of-way claims,” the Office of the Ombudsman said. The press statement also said that in a separate administrative decision, the Ombudsman ordered the dismissal from service of former DPWH Region 12 legal officer Ansare Mariga Busran. – Rappler.com

title: Elbit Systems Awarded $235 Million Contract to Supply EXTRA-MR Rockets and PULS Launchers to a European Country
body:
Haifa, Israel. Elbit Systems Ltd. announced on October 19, 2026 that it was awarded a contract valued at approximately $235 million to supply EXTRA-MR (Medium Range) rockets and Precise & Universal Launching System (PULS™) rocket artillery systems to a European customer, under a government-to-government (G-to-G) agreement between the Israel Ministry of Defense and the customer country’s Ministry of Defense. The contract will be performed over a period of three years.



Under the contract, Elbit Systems will supply the medium-range variant of the Company’s EXTRA supersonic rocket system. The contract also includes the delivery of PULS launchers, additional rocket-artillery-related platforms, and integrated logistics support.

The EXTRA-MR (Medium-Range) is a precision-guided rocket munition designed for mid-range operational scenarios, enabling highly accurate engagement of high-value targets at ranges of up to 80 km. Fully compatible with Elbit Systems’ PULS and existing C4I architectures, the system provides a flexible and cost-effective capability across a broad range of mission profiles.

Bezhalel (Butzi) Machlis, President and CEO of Elbit Systems: "This contract award further strengthens Elbit Systems’ position as a global leader in rocket artillery systems and reflects the growing international demand for our advanced rocket and launcher capabilities. The PULS systems and precision rocket solutions are recognized among the leading systems in their category and have been selected by a growing number of customers worldwide, including European and NATO member states. We remain committed to delivering advanced operational capabilities that support our customers’ evolving defense requirements."

title: Mahama describes AfCFTA as Africa’s ‘greatest architecture for conflict prevention’
body: President John Dramani Mahama has called for deeper economic integration among African countries, describing the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) as a major instrument for preventing conflict and strengthening peaceful relations across the continent. Speaking at the 12th Tana High-Level Forum on Peace in Africa in Bahir Dar, Ethiopia, President Mahama presented the 2026 State of Peace and Security in Africa Report, covering developments from January 2025 to June 2026. He argued that the AfCFTA should not be viewed solely as a commercial initiative, but also as a framework for reducing tensions by making African countries more economically interdependent. “We often view the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) purely as a commercial project. That is a mistake. The AfCFTA is perhaps our greatest architecture for conflict prevention,” he said. President Mahama explained that stronger trade links could increase the economic cost of conflict and encourage countries to see their neighbours as valuable trading partners and suppliers rather than adversaries. He also said integrated and traceable value chains could help dismantle illicit economies associated with smuggled minerals, illegal taxation at roadblocks and the activities of warlords. The President further highlighted the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS), which facilitates cross-border payments in African currencies, as another mechanism for strengthening regional economic ties and reducing Africa’s exposure to external economic shocks. However, he cautioned that economic integration alone could not resolve conflicts, stressing that political agreements and settlements remained necessary for lasting peace. “Trade cannot replace political settlement, but poverty and border friction will always guarantee war,” he said. President Mahama urged African countries to strengthen regional cooperation and address the economic conditions that fuel instability, arguing that sustainable peace must be supported by both security measures and economic justice.

title: NASA Names Stephen Cash, Marshall Space Flight Center Director
body:
By R Anil Kumar 



Washington DC, Oct 17, 202. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman has named Stephen Cash director of the agency’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, effective October 19. Cash, a veteran NASA engineer and aerospace executive, returns to lead the center where he began his career more than four decades ago.

“Marshall contributions to NASA's missions are historic and it's no question why it's the Center of Excellence for propulsion,” said Isaacman. “Steve Cash is a Marshall legend, has spent his career around the hardware, the people and has been in the seat before making the decisions when human spaceflight is on the line. As Marshall continues its critical role in Artemis and takes on new challenges in advanced propulsion, nuclear power, and the systems that will carry us deeper into the solar system, Steve brings the experience, technical judgment, and mission focus needed to lead the center into that next chapter. I am also grateful to Rae Ann Meyer for the leadership she has provided to Marshall during this transition and for her continued service to NASA.”

“Leading a NASA center requires a commitment to its people and to the technical capabilities entrusted to them,” said Amit Kshatriya, NASA associate administrator and chief engineer. “Steve understands that the jewel of Marshall is its workforce and that engineering excellence is sustained by giving talented people the opportunity to design, build, test, and learn through hands-on work. As Marshall continues strengthening the manufacturing, structural loads and dynamics, and propulsion capabilities that underpin NASA’s exploration enterprise, Steve’s leadership will help ensure the workforce has opportunities to develop and apply the expertise needed to deliver the agency’s most ambitious missions.”

As center director, Cash will lead one of NASA’s largest field centers, overseeing a workforce of more than 5,000 civil service and contractor employees and a broad portfolio of propulsion, space systems, scientific research, and technology development activities. Marshall plays a critical role in NASA’s Artemis program, including the development of NASA’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket, management of the Human Landing System Program, as well as other capabilities supporting sustained exploration of the Moon and future missions to Mars. Further, Marshall plays a key role in the advancement of nuclear power and propulsion, an area of focus that is expected to grow as NASA works towards sending the first humans to Mars.

“It is a profound honor to be back home at the Marshall Space Flight Center,” said Cash. “I am humbled to stand alongside the brilliant minds here as we continue to turn the impossible into everyday history.”

Cash began his NASA career at Marshall in 1982 and spent 34 years with the agency, holding senior engineering and management positions supporting some of the nation’s most significant human spaceflight programs.

During his NASA career, Cash served as manager of Marshall’s Space Shuttle Propulsion Office, overseeing critical propulsion systems supporting shuttle through its final missions. He later served as director of Marshall’s Safety and Mission Assurance Directorate from 2011 until his retirement in 2016, providing leadership in safety, reliability, and quality engineering to support mission success across the center.

Following his retirement from NASA, Cash continued his work in the aerospace industry, including serving as vice president for advanced space systems at Axient, supporting the development and execution of major spaceflight programs. In 2024, he was inducted into the Alabama Engineering Hall of Fame in recognition of his contributions to engineering and the nation's space program.

Cash succeeds Rae Ann Meyer, who has served as Marshall’s acting center director since September 2025. Meyer, who previously served as Marshall’s deputy center director and associate director, has provided leadership and continuity across the center’s programs and operations during her tenure as acting director. Meyer will return to her role as Deputy Center Director.

Established in 1960, Marshall has played a central role in American space exploration for more than six decades, from developing the Saturn rockets that carried astronauts to the Moon during Apollo to advancing the propulsion systems, infrastructure, and technologies supporting the next era of human spaceflight.

title: Africa needs stronger digital payment links to unlock regional trade – Femi Osinbajo
body: Professor Yemi Osinbajo, a former Vice-President of Nigeria, has called for stronger cooperation among African countries to improve cross-border payments, strengthen digital integration and support trade and investment across the continent. He said although African countries had made progress in developing domestic payment systems, transferring money across borders remained difficult and costly for traders, businesses and individuals. Prof. Osinbajo was speaking at the opening of the Mobex Africa Conference 2026 on the theme: ” Resetting Africa’s Digital Identity and Sovereignty from Promise to Practice.” He said some transactions still depended on correspondent banking arrangements outside the countries involved, often introducing additional intermediaries and costs. The former Vice-President said the challenges could undermine efforts to deepen regional economic integration and expand opportunities for businesses operating across national borders. He said initiatives such as the African Continental Free Trade Area and digital transformation programmes demonstrated the continent’s commitment to integration, but their success depended partly on efficient, secure and accessible payment systems. He called for stronger collaboration among central banks, financial institutions, governments, and other relevant authorities to improve connections between national payment systems. He said integration required more than technical partnerships, stressing the importance of trust, common standards and effective regulatory cooperation among African countries. The former Vice-President said digital integration must also protect financial stability and ensure that improved connectivity did not introduce risks into national financial systems. He urged governments to establish supportive policy environments, while central banks strengthened the resilience of financial infrastructure and financial institutions developed services that responded to the needs of households and businesses. He said digital financial services could create opportunities for traders and small businesses by improving access to financial information and enabling lenders to make better-informed decisions. He, however, stressed the need to protect customers, ensure fair lending terms and provide safeguards when technology failed or payment transactions encountered problems. The former Vice-President said accessible digital identification and straightforward verification processes were also important to making financial services available to more people. He noted that concerns about data exposure and increased visibility to authorities could discourage some traders from participating in formal digital financial systems. He called for safeguards to protect personal and business information and ensure that users could benefit from digital services without compromising their privacy or rights. Mr Owureku Asare, Director of the Fintech and Innovation Office at the Bank of Ghana, highlighted Ghana’s experience in developing payment infrastructure to improve connectivity among banks, microfinance institutions and other service providers. He said Ghana’s experience demonstrated that public investment, strong institutional leadership and enabling regulation could support secure and accessible payment systems while allowing financial institutions to innovate and compete. Mr Asare said Ghana remained committed to working with other central banks, regional institutions and industry partners to improve the efficiency and connectivity of payment systems across Africa.

title: Widespread protests, clashes with police in Europe (+PHOTOS)
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 25 (MNA) – Widespread and massive protests across European countries, including France, Belgium, Albania, Italy, escalated into violent clashes on Saturday following intervention by security forces and the police forces.
In a report on the widespread protests across Europe, the Al Jazeera website wrote that a massive wave of protests, accompanied by clashes between the public and security forces, swept through Europe on Saturday. These protests have emerged in response to political, economic, and social issues.
In Italy, thousands of people, including students, truck drivers, and farmers, took to the streets to protest against rising living costs, particularly regarding housing and fuel, as well as a reduction in government support.
Protesters lashed out at the implementation of security measures in the country, rather than addressing their legitimate demands. Protests also took place in major Italian cities—including Rome, Turin, Bologna, and Milan—against the war in the Middle East.
During these protests, violent clashes occurred between citizens and security forces, and at least 371 people—including 110 minors—were detained.
In Albania, too, students spearheaded protests against government corruption, scandals, a decline in job opportunities, and the poor quality of education. Protesters in Albania demanded the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama and criticized a luxury project in the country involving the Trump family.
Protests in Albania escalated into clashes with security forces, with police using tear gas, water cannons, and rubber bullets to disperse the crowd.
Protesters also set fires near the entrance to the Ministry of Agriculture in the Albanian capital. In other cities, protesters set fires at government buildings and banks, and used fireworks. They also smashed the windows of several shops.
Hundreds of young people in Belgium took to the streets to protest against the country's austerity policies and educational reforms, calling for increased financial support for the education sector, as well as improvements to purchasing power and public services. They also criticized the violence employed by police forces.
Security forces also used tear gas and pepper spray to disperse these protesters. Demonstrators in Albertine Square voiced their opposition to the federal government's policies. In the Saint-Gilles area, protesters set fire to some of the barriers erected by security forces.
The French Interior Ministry issued a statement announcing that 410,000 people participated in nationwide demonstrations on Saturday (against high prices and the high cost of living).
Agence France-Presse (AFP), citing the country's police, reported that tear gas and water cannons have been used to counter unrest in Paris. A number of protesters have also been arrested.

title: Evzones Raise Greek Flag at OXI Day ANZAC Memorial Ceremony in Sydney
body: SYDNEY, Sunday 25 October 2026 — The Hellenic Presidential Guard (Evzones) raised the Greek flag at the OXI Day ANZAC Memorial ceremony in Hyde Park on Sunday 25 October, hosted by the Kalymnian Association of NSW. The Evzones marched from Elizabeth Street to the memorial, joined by community members in traditional dress, before the flag raising and wreath laying ceremony began. The Kalymnian Association of NSW hosted the ceremony with special thanks to Hellenic Club Sydney, which hosts the Guard’s Sydney visit with support from the NSW Government. The Evzones in Hyde Park, Sydney, with community members in traditional dress. Photo: Nick Bourdaniotis The OXI Day ANZAC Memorial ceremony marked the 86th anniversary of OXI Day, when Greece rejected the Axis ultimatum on 28 October 1940. It also honoured Australians and Greeks who fought together in the campaigns of Greece and Crete in the Second World War. George Karantonis, vice president of the Kalymnian Association of NSW, served as master of ceremonies. He opened with an Acknowledgement of Country to the Gadigal People of the Eora Nation and later thanked the President of the Hellenic Republic, Konstantinos Tasoulas, for consenting to the Guard’s visit. Karantonis noted the absence of Archbishop Makarios of Australia, who was leading 250 Australian pilgrims in Constantinople. The pilgrimage honours the 35th anniversary of Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew’s election in October 1991. The crowd gathered along the Pool of Reflection at the ANZAC Memorial. Photo: Nick Bourdaniotis OXI Day ANZAC Memorial flag raising Following the flag raising at the OXI Day ANZAC Memorial ceremony, combined students of All Saints Grammar, St Euphemia College and St Spyridon College performed the Australian and Greek national anthems. The Guard then moved to its ceremonial position at the memorial. Dignitaries and officers salute during the OXI Day ceremony. Photo: Nick Bourdaniotis Rev Father Dimitrios Papaoikonomou, representing Archbishop Makarios, gave the first address. Greek Ambassador to Australia Stavros Venizelos and Commander Michail Tzinieris, head of the Presidential Guard mission, followed him. Con Apoifis, president of the Greek Orthodox Community of NSW, also addressed the crowd. Finally, Kalymnian Association secretary Nectaria Melas delivered an address written by association president George Michailou, who was among the pilgrims in Constantinople. The ANZAC Memorial across the Pool of Reflection during the ceremony. Photo: Nick Bourdaniotis Commander Michail Tzinieris, Head of the Mission of the Hellenic Presidential Guard, addresses the ceremony in front of the Evzones. Photo: Nick Bourdaniotis During the wreath laying, Father Papaoikonomou laid the first wreath. Ambassador Venizelos, Consul General of Greece in Sydney Georgios Skemperis and Defence Attaché Colonel Kyriakos Kyriakakos then laid a joint wreath. The Evzones beside the Pool of Reflection during the ceremony. Photo: Nick Bourdaniotis The Evzones lined up in front of the Pool of Reflection. Photo: Nick Bourdaniotis Kalymnian Association treasurer John Billiris, Hellenic Club Sydney vice president James Stevens and director Bill Maloukis, as well as Apoifis, also laid wreaths. Karantonis then recalled the words of wartime British Prime Minister Winston Churchill: “Hence we will not say that Greeks fight like heroes, but that heroes fight like Greeks.” Winston Churchill, quoted by MC George Karantonis Guests and the Guard’s program After a moment of silence, Karantonis closed the OXI Day ANZAC Memorial ceremony and thanked the Evzones, the NSW Police Force and memorial staff. “It is the commemoration of a principle,” he said of OXI Day. Guests included Major Panagiotis Mimikos, deputy commander of the Presidential Guard, Lieutenant Evangelos Galanakis, NSW Police Superintendent Despa Fitzgerald and Bayside Councillor Fiona Douskou. Descendants of the 2nd/1st Infantry Battalion AIF also attended, alongside James Jordan, chair of the Committee of the Battle of Crete and Greek Campaign. Michael Kyriakou of the High Commission of the Republic of Cyprus in Canberra also attended. Members of the Kalymnian Association’s executive committee and the Kalymnian Youth Society, presidents of Greek community associations, students and staff of the three schools, and Greek dancing groups also attended. The Evzones and dignitaries on the steps of the ANZAC Memorial. Photo: Nick Bourdaniotis Community members and guests on the memorial steps. Photo: Nick Bourdaniotis The OXI Day ANZAC Memorial ceremony was the flagship event of the Guard’s Sydney program , which began with a Guard of Honour at the Martin Place Cenotaph on 22 October. Greek City Times reported the Guard’s arrival and its visit to NSW Parliament House. The Evzones in full dress uniform at the ANZAC Memorial. Photo: Nick Bourdaniotis The Evzones travel to Canberra for OXI Day on Wednesday 28 October, before an 11am Doxology at the Cathedral of the Annunciation of Our Lady in Redfern on Thursday 29 October. Visitor details are on the memorial’s official website . Photo gallery of the OXI Day ANZAC Memorial ceremony All photos are copyrighted by Nick Bourdaniotis for Greek City Times The OXI Day ceremony at the ANZAC Memorial in Hyde Park, Sydney. title: Africa must prove climate adaptation is saving lives, not just spending money
body: When floods leave roads impassable, water supplies become contaminated and children fall ill, the consequences of climate change are measured in more than damaged infrastructure or financial losses. They are measured in lives disrupted, household incomes lost and families struggling to cope. For Dr Richard Munang, Director of the United Nations University Institute for Natural Resources in Africa (UNU-INRA), these are the realities that must shape how Africa measures progress on climate adaptation. “Adaptation is not what we spend. Adaptation is who we protect,” he told participants at the African Technical Workshop on the Global Goal on Adaptation (GGA) Indicators in Accra. The three-day workshop, held from 22 to 24 October 2026 at the West African Genetic Medicine Centre, brought together African climate negotiators, government officials, technical experts and representatives of the United Nations University and the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). Its central task was to test whether the global adaptation indicators can adequately reflect Ghana’s national priorities, what existing data systems can measure and where gaps must be addressed. The exercise comes as countries begin working with the 59 Belém Adaptation Indicators adopted under the Global Goal on Adaptation process. For African countries, the challenge is no longer simply to agree on a framework for measuring adaptation, but to determine whether it captures the results that matter to people and communities. Measuring what matters to people Dr Munang argued that climate adaptation must be judged by its impact on people’s lives, rather than by the amount of money allocated or spent. Drawing on his childhood in north-western Cameroon, where failed maize harvests left his family struggling to find food, he recalled how climate pressures can deepen the vulnerability of households already facing economic hardship. That experience, he said, reinforced the need to connect adaptation policies and investments to tangible improvements in people’s lives. “Because if you don’t count what is failing, you cannot fix it,” he said, calling for evidence that identifies both successful interventions and those that fall short. He pointed to the links between disaster risks and public health, arguing that poorly maintained drainage systems, flooded roads and delayed early-warning messages can have consequences that extend well beyond the immediate disaster. A flooded road can prevent an ambulance from reaching someone in need. Contaminated water can expose children to waterborne diseases. When early warnings fail to reach communities in time, the consequences can be devastating. These connections underpin the workshop’s decision to focus on disaster risk reduction and health, two areas where the effectiveness of adaptation measures can have direct consequences for human wellbeing. For UNU-INRA, working with the United Nations University International Institute for Global Health offers an opportunity to examine these connections more closely and strengthen the evidence used to assess adaptation outcomes. Ghana’s national priorities take centre stage Ghana is serving as the pilot country for the exercise, providing an opportunity to compare its National Adaptation Plan and sector priorities with the global indicators. The assessment is intended to establish where national priorities align with the indicators, where important outcomes may be missing and whether the data and institutional arrangements needed for reporting are already in place. Director of the United Nations University International Institute for Global Health, Dr Revathi Phalkey, said the exercise should help countries determine whether their existing systems can adequately measure progress towards their adaptation ambitions. “What we really need to measure is where do we need to go and how fast we can get there,” she said. Her remarks underscored the importance of looking beyond historical performance to assess the pace and scale of action needed to meet future adaptation goals. Representing the Chair of the Africa Group of Negotiators, Stella Okoh of Ghana’s Environmental Protection Authority said the workshop would help institutions identify how existing national reporting systems could be used to track the indicators. “The conversation is not to create different reporting formats,” she said, explaining that the priority was to build on existing national systems, identify gaps and determine what needed to improve. She also highlighted the importance of monitoring whether adaptation interventions were actually building resilience in Ghana. The approach is expected to bring together institutions responsible for climate adaptation, health, disaster management and reporting, helping them assess what information is available and where additional work is required. From global indicators to national action For the UNFCCC Secretariat, the exercise forms part of the wider effort to establish how the global indicators can be applied across different national contexts. Motsomi Maletjane of the Secretariat’s Adaptation Division said countries had agreed to test the indicators voluntarily following their adoption at COP30. The resulting experience will help inform the development of indicator metadata and methodologies, as well as assessments of their applicability to national circumstances. “These exercises by Ghana, many other countries that are doing similar exercises are very key to being able to tell how countries can start to work with the indicators,” he said. The findings are also expected to contribute to countries’ reporting on adaptation progress and inform their own planning processes. For Ghana, the workshop’s practical work centres on mapping national adaptation priorities against the relevant indicators, examining data availability and identifying methodological, institutional, technical and financial gaps. Participants are also expected to develop recommendations for addressing those gaps and identify lessons that could be adapted by other African countries. Building an evidence-based African position Beyond the technical assessment, the exercise carries implications for Africa’s engagement in international climate negotiations. Dr Munang said the continent needed evidence to demonstrate whether adaptation investments were delivering results and whether the global indicators adequately reflected African priorities. He argued that indicators should not be accepted simply because they form part of an international framework. Where they fail to capture national ambitions or outcomes, countries should be able to demonstrate the shortcomings and make the case for improvement. “Africa is not poor. Africa is uncounted,” he said, stressing the importance of strengthening the evidence available to African policymakers and negotiators. The workshop is expected to produce an assessment of Ghana’s alignment with the indicators, a review of implementation gaps, practical guidance for future country-level exercises and policy messages to support African engagement ahead of COP31 and COP32. The wider ambition is to develop an approach that other African countries can use to assess the indicators against their own adaptation plans, priorities and reporting systems. For Dr Munang, however, the ultimate test remains whether adaptation makes a measurable difference to ordinary people. “We can only say we have adapted if that child who is playing aside today will not end up in a clinic tomorrow,” he said. That challenge places the focus firmly on outcomes of whether communities are better protected from disasters, whether health risks are reduced and whether public investments are building resilience where it is needed most. As Ghana undertakes the pilot assessment, its findings could help shape a more practical approach to measuring adaptation across Africa, one that connects international commitments to national priorities and, ultimately, to the lives those commitments are intended to protect.

title: PIAC seeks details of petroleum funds allocated to Big Push projects
body: The Public Interest and Accountability Committee (PIAC) released its 2026 semi-annual report on Ghana’s petroleum revenue management, noting that additional information on how the government uses petroleum revenues allocated to the national budget would strengthen its assessment of government expenditure. Mr Richard Ellimah, Chairman of PIAC, said the Committee had yet to receive information from the Ministry of Finance on the utilisation of the Annual Budget Funding Amount (ABFA), which limited its ability to fully assess expenditure under the programme. He made this known at the launch of PIAC’s 2026 semi-annual report in Accra, explaining that the Committee had requested the data from the Ministry but was still awaiting a response. Mr Ellimah said the information was particularly important for monitoring expenditure on infrastructure projects, including the government’s Big Push Agenda, which includes the construction of the Accra-Kumasi Expressway. He said the concentration of a significant proportion of the ABFA in the Big Push programme could also influence how PIAC conducted its project inspections. “We are hoping very much that the Ministry of Finance will give us the data so we can understand what is going on,” he said. “It is something new for us because it is going to change the way we also do our project inspections.” Mr Ellimah also called for greater attention to compliance with the legal provisions governing the provision of information to PIAC. He said in the Committee’s 15 years of operation, he was not aware of any prosecution for failure to comply with the Petroleum Revenue Management Act (PRMA). PIAC intended to engage the Attorney-General for guidance on addressing recurring compliance concerns, he said, noting that the Committee could not independently initiate legal action to enforce its recommendations or compliance with the Act. “These are clearly legal infractions,” he said, adding that the Attorney-General’s advice would help determine the appropriate course of action. PIAC was established under Section 51 of the PRMA to promote transparency and accountability in the management and use of petroleum revenues. Its mandate includes monitoring compliance with the Act and providing independent information to the public to support informed debate and Parliament’s oversight responsibilities. Mr Isaac Dwamena, PIAC’s Executive Secretary, said the Petroleum Revenue Management Regulations specified the timeframe within which institutions were expected to respond to the Committee’s requests for information. Regulation 25 requires institutions requested to provide information for PIAC’s annual and semi-annual reports to do so within 15 days of receiving the request. Despite the outstanding information, the report assessed developments in petroleum revenue collection, production, expenditure and the management of the country’s petroleum funds during the first half of 2026. It said petroleum revenue receipts increased to US$561.4 million in the first half of 2026, from US$370.3 million in the corresponding period of 2025. The increase was attributed largely to higher crude oil prices and a rise in corporate income tax receipts. The average achieved crude oil price was US$92.80 per barrel, above the benchmark price of US$76 per barrel. PIAC, however, cautioned that the increase in revenue was driven substantially by higher prices rather than a corresponding rise in production. It highlighted the vulnerability of petroleum receipts to fluctuations in the international oil market.

title: NRSA praises Sunyani inner ring road project, raises concern over tricycle speeding
body: The National Road Safety Authority (NRSA) in the Bono Region has lauded the quality of work on the Sunyani-Inner Ring Road Project, being funded by the government’s “Big Push” Road Infrastructure programme. Mr Gabriel Kwame Okyere, the Public Relations Officer at the Bono Regional Office of the NRSA, however, cautioned tricycle riders in particular against reckless riding. Kofi Job Constructions Limited, contractors executing the 9.2-kilometre Road Project from Fiapre Roundabout, connecting the Sunyani Technical University, has asphalted the road. In an interview with the Ghana News Agency (GNA) in Sunyani, Mr Okyere said: “Our major concern now is how tricycle riders are speeding on the road since it was asphalted”. “In fact, the office continues to receive complaints of recklessness by the tricycle riders, using portions of the asphalted road project”, he stated. He commended the government for the ‘Big Push’ programme, saying that the inner ring road project had opened the Sunyani Municipality for economic growth. Mr Okyere said small-scale businesses had started springing up along the road project, since it was asphalted, thereby creating economic opportunities for the locals. In a separate interview, Mr Kofi Kamkam, the site engineer of Kofi Job Construction Limited, said 2.5 kilometres of the road project had been asphalted for use, assuring that the project would be completed within the two-year stipulated period.

title: Bloodied suspect carrying samurai sword charged with brutal beating of woman, killing her dog
body: An indictment was filed on Thursday against Lior Saraf, 50, from Kfar Saba, for a severe assault on a female friend and the killing of her dog.Saraf, who walked out into the street carrying a samurai sword while covered in blood, is accused of punching his friend repeatedly until she lost consciousness. Upon returning home and finding the dog licking her wounds, he threw a hammer at the dog and subsequently stabbed it to death with a kitchen knife.The prosecution submitted the indictment to the Central District Court in Lod, requesting that Saraf be remanded in custody until the end of legal proceedings. Court documents indicate that after the assault and the killing of the dog, he washed the knife. During the course of events, he also showered to remove bloodstains from his body. His friend was left bleeding in the home without him calling for medical assistance.The incident took place during the night between October 8 and October 9. According to the indictment, the friendship between Saraf and the complainant had been severed after a dispute and was renewed about a month earlier. That evening, around 10:00 PM, he arrived at her home, where he met her and another guest. About an hour later, the three traveled to his home in Kfar Saba, where Saraf and his friend used drugs and drank alcohol. The guest left after midnight, leaving the two alone.Later, they entered the shower together. Afterward, the went to the bedroom and called for Saraf to join her. He initially refused, but after she called him again, he entered the room, approached her, and kissed her at her request. At that point, according to the indictment, he began punching her in the face repeatedly until she lost consciousness.Saraf escapes from hospital, returns home to kill his own dogSaraf then went to a storage room, retrieved a samurai sword, and walked out into the street. He went to another home in the neighborhood, placed the sword near the gate, and entered the yard, where three people were sitting and talking. They noticed the bloodstains on his body, face, and hands and offered to escort him to Meir Medical Center. Saraf agreed. However, upon arriving at the hospital entrance, he asked them to wait and said he would return immediately. Instead of entering, he fled. The three individuals alerted the police.Around 3:45 AM, Saraf returned home. According to the indictment, his friend was bleeding and severely bruised, while his dog, a Siberian Husky, was licking her wounds. Saraf pulled a hammer from a drawer and threw it at the dog. The dog fled to another room. He then took a large kitchen knife, followed it, and stabbed the dog in the abdomen, killing it.He then pulled the knife from her body and washed it in the kitchen sink. Documents describe how, during the events, he also showered to remove bloodstains from his body. He did not provide medical aid to his friend or call for help.Around 4:00 AM, police officers arrived at the home following a call to the 100 emergency hotline. They found the injured woman and summoned Magen David Adom paramedics. She was evacuated to Meir Medical Center, suffering from multiple facial fractures, including a comminuted nasal fracture with a damaged septum, a fractured cheekbone, and additional fractures in the sinus area. She also suffered eye trauma and contusions across her face, neck, and arm. She required stitches and was hospitalized for three days.The detention request details the various accounts Saraf provided during interrogations. Initially, he claimed his friend fell in the shower and that the dog attacked her. He later confessed to beating her and killing the dog. In one of his versions, he claimed God had revealed Himself to him and that he saw the complainant as a devil that he had to kill. Later, he claimed God instructed him not to kill her, but rather to offer a sacrifice like the binding of Isaac, which led him to stab the dog. In his third interrogation, he claimed he believed another person was present in the apartment and that his friend was planning to harm him.Alongside the testimony of the complainant, the prosecution presented body camera footage from the responding officers, photographs of bloodstains in the home and of the dog's body, and medical records documenting the woman's injuries. Security camera footage from a neighboring home captured Saraf carrying the sword on his back. Neighbors reported seeing him stained with blood and later hearing screams and barking that ceased before police arrived. The municipal veterinary report confirmed that the dog died from an abdominal stab wound inflicted by a sharp object.Police also seized 48.08 grams of cannabis and under two grams of hashish from the living room table. According to the indictment, Saraf possessed the drugs not for personal consumption.The indictment, filed by attorney Neta Fonis-Elharar of the Central District Attorney's Office, charges Saraf with aggravated assault, animal cruelty, obstruction of justice, possession of a knife, and drug possession not for personal consumption. He has been in custody since October 9.In the request to detain him until the end of the proceedings, the prosecution cited the severe assault of his friend and the killing of the dog as evidence of his dangerousness. The prosecution added that it would not oppose referring him for a psychiatric evaluation.Hammer, gasoline, a break-in and arsonIn a separate incident, Daniel Azaria arrived at the business where his ex-girlfriend used to work, his face covered and carrying a hammer and a gallon of gasoline.According to the indictment filed against him, he attempted to break the glass doors, poured gasoline near the entrance, and set the fire. As the flames caught, he fled to his home. Azaria, 35, from Rehovot, was arrested on October 7 and is charged with arson.The incident occurred on September 3, 2026, at the offices of the Pandoor Doors company in Rishon LeZion. Azaria's ex-girlfriend worked at the location between 2017 and 2022, but the reason why he chose to set fire to the business remains unknown to the prosecution, as noted in the indictment.According to the charges, Azaria prepared in advance by equipping himself with a hammer and a gallon of gasoline. Around 1:00 AM, he left his parents' home in Rehovot, where he was living at the time, and got into his vehicle. He drove to the business, parked nearby, and walked toward the entrance wearing a mask.Footage obtained by Walla shows the events at the entrance to the business: Azaria striking the glass doors with a hammer and subsequently pouring fuel. According to the indictment, after attempting to break the doors, he set fire to the area where he had poured the gasoline. As the fire broke out, he left the scene and fled home.A passerby who noticed the flames called the police. He alerted emergency crews, who arrived and helped extinguish the fire. Other businesses operate adjacent to the site. The fire activated the venue's sprinkler system. According to the indictment, the fire caused minor damage to equipment and the business's door. Additionally, the sprinklers that were activated following the arson required replacement.

title: My wife died two years ago, then grief opened door for madness
body: My Peju Akande Mywife died two years ago. Before then, she had been sick for a long time; the kind of sickness that drains everybody in the house. You know that saying: “The person caring for the sick is sometimes sicker than the sick person.” It’s true. It’s painfully true. I won’t stand here and claim I did all the caring. Her children, our children, carried that burden with full chest. They were her hands, her legs and her nurses. But she was still mywife. I did what I could, in my own small way. I put all my manhood on hold and accepted it as destiny. You know what I mean. When she died, the house became quiet in a way that frightens even an old man. There used to be noise, you know, the good kind. People trooping in and out. Neighbours, people from our mosque, alfas, children she helped, women she advised, men she encouraged. Big tree Mywife was a big tree. When she fell, the shade disappeared. People came for the burial, stayed for a while, then left one by one like leaves falling off a branch. And I was alone. My children begged me to come and stay with them, but grief is a stubborn companion. I said I wanted to be alone. I didn’t realise loneliness has teeth. Not that I feared ghosts, if mywife appeared, even as a ghost, she wouldn’t harm me. She would probably scold me for misplacing my glasses, or my phone or even money. Eventually, my children arranged someone to cook and clean. I was turning 80; I needed help. Even if it was someone to quarrel with. That’s how I met this woman at the mosque. The ‘eleha’ who hid her evil under a burqa. She was an eleha, fully covered, soft‑spoken, eyes lowered. But I was fooled in my old age! I’m not saying women who wear hijab or burqa are evil. No. But this particular one used that covering to hide her wickedness like a snake hiding under dry leaves. She was 45 when we met. She said her husband left her with three children. At my age, I wasn’t looking for romance. I have 11 grandchildren. My prostate is enlarged — so that department is closed for renovation. Companionship All I wanted was companionship, you know, someone to talk to. Someone to sit with, someone to keep me warm in the evenings. I told her clearly: “I will help you financially. But I cannot father your children. They cannot live with me.” She agreed, or she pretended to. We started “seeing” each other quietly. I didn’t introduce her to my children, they would never accept it. But I’m sure they suspected. That woman entered my life like a thief in the night and she has been stealing me blind. She stole more than Shina Rambo! Do you know Shina Rambo? Ah, you are young. Shina Rambo was the most notorious armed robber in Nigeria in the 80s and 90s. This woman? She stole more than him, without gun, without knife, without breaking the door. She would take my money and claim I gave her myself. She lies like someone who practices lying as a profession. I would put money on top of the fridge, she would take it and swear I took it myself. I don’t have an ATM card, so I withdraw large sums at once. Before I know what is happening, fiam! All the money is gone. I told her I would help her financially. I didn’t tell her to help herself to my money like a rat eating ‘breadi agege’. She turned me into an ATM machine, and that is what I will not accept. So I told her not to come to my house again. And I will stand by it. Because as old as I am, I have learned one bitter truth: loneliness is not enough reason to invite madness into your home! •Series, first published in thisislagos.ng, was written and edited by Peju Akande and based on true stories The post My wife died two years ago, then grief opened door for madness appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Mahama warns foreign powers against treating Africa as a ‘chessboard’
body: President John Dramani Mahama has urged African leaders to unite against foreign interference and protect the continent’s sovereignty, warning that external powers are seeking strategic influence and access to Africa’s resources. Speaking at the 12th Tana High-Level Forum on Security in Africa in Bahir Dar, Ethiopia, he said African countries must take greater control of their political, economic, and security priorities instead of allowing foreign interests to determine their future. “External powers, from the East, the West, and the Gulf, are actively seeking leverage, access, and client states on our soil,” President Mahama said. He warned that Africa risked becoming a battleground for competing foreign interests if its leaders failed to act collectively and establish a common vision for the continent. “Africa is not an empty chessboard for foreign powers to play their games. We are not spectators,” he added. President Mahama stressed that African countries must take the initiative in shaping their own future, cautioning that failure to do so could leave the continent at the mercy of decisions made by others. “But unless we consciously decide to take up the pen and write our own script, someone else will write it for us, and we will not like how the story ends,” he said. The President called for stronger continental unity and greater African ownership of political, economic and security decisions, arguing that the continent must define its priorities and safeguard its sovereignty amid growing competition for influence.

title: Thunderstorms, hail and strong winds forecast in parts of Oman
body:
Muscat: The Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) has warned of possible thunderstorms, strong downdraft winds and hail in parts of Oman on Sunday, October 25. According to the latest weather forecast, cumulonimbus clouds are expected to develop over parts of Musandam Governorate, the Al Hajar Mountains and surrounding areas, bringing scattered thunderstorms, strong winds and possible hail. The authority also warned of potential flash floods in wadis and low-lying areas due to heavy rainfall. Meanwhile, local cloud formations have already begun developing along the Al Hajar mountain range, with conditions expected to expand over the coming hours, bringing scattered rainfall that could be accompanied by thunderstorms. The forecast is based on the Omani numerical weather prediction model, which indicates varying rainfall intensities across the affected areas during the next 24 hours.

body:
