title: GoldBod will not compromise LBMA certification for galamsey – Minkah
body: The Ghana Gold Board (GoldBod) has rejected suggestions that it would support illegal mining, insisting that doing so would undermine its efforts to secure certification from the London Bullion Market Association (LBMA). The Board’s Head of Communications, Prince Kwame Minkah, said responsible sourcing was a key requirement for the certification, which demands that gold entering the market comes from legitimate sources and is produced without causing environmental destruction. He explained that GoldBod’s ambition to meet international standards meant it could not endorse mining activities that violate the law or damage the environment. “Nobody should fall under any delusion that the CEO of GoldBod, whose institution is aspiring for LBMA Certification, would endorse illegal mining, especially when the prerequisite for LBMA Certification is responsible sourcing,” he said. Mr Minkah’s comments follow public criticism of GoldBod Chief Executive Officer Sammy Gyamfi over remarks concerning efforts to formalise unlicensed small-scale miners. Mr Gyamfi subsequently clarified that his position was to bring eligible operators into a regulated system, rather than endorse illegal mining. Speaking on Channel One TV on Saturday, October 24, Mr Minkah said his intervention was intended to reinforce Mr Gyamfi’s position on transitioning eligible miners into lawful operations. The LBMA is a global authority in the precious metals market, with standards covering the quality of gold and silver as well as responsible sourcing.

title: GES, stakeholders call for stronger action against child marriage in Eastern Region
body: The Eastern Regional Directorate of the Ghana Education Service (GES) has marked the International Day of the Girl with a call for increased investment in girls’ rights and efforts to end child marriage. The celebration was held at Oyoko Methodist Senior High School on the theme: “End Child Marriage and Invest in Girls’ Rights.” It brought together students and stakeholders to promote girls’ education, protection and empowerment, while encouraging boys to play an active role in addressing teenage pregnancy and gender-based violence. Madam Patricia Birago Gyamfi, Eastern Regional Girls’ Education Officer, said the participation of boys was essential to efforts to protect and empower girls. She stressed that no girl under 18 years should be forced into marriage, adding that every child deserved the opportunity to learn, develop and make informed decisions about her future. She called on parents to keep their daughters in school and urged teachers, community leaders and other stakeholders to create safe learning environments and support programmes that promoted girls’ education, health, safety and leadership. Mr Kwasi Owusu Obeng, Eastern Regional Population Officer of the National Population Council (NPC), said teenage pregnancy and early sexual activity posed serious threats to girls’ education and prospects. He said the Eastern Region had a teenage pregnancy rate of about 14 per cent, describing it as a concern that required stronger interventions. Mr Obeng said reproductive health education often focused on girls, despite the role boys played in teenage pregnancies, and called for greater attention to educating boys on abstinence and responsible sexual behaviour. He said involving boys in reproductive health programmes would help reduce teenage pregnancies and promote shared responsibility among young people. Dr Moses Barima Djimatey, Eastern Regional Deputy Director of Public Health, said addressing teenage pregnancy required the active involvement of both boys and girls. He disclosed that more than 4,000 girls aged between 10 and 19 became pregnant between January and June, describing the situation as a concern with health, social and economic implications. Dr Djimatey called for stronger collaboration among district assemblies, religious and traditional leaders, schools, the police and health workers to guide young people and protect their future. Assistant Superintendent of Police Lydia Wemegah, Eastern Regional Coordinator of the Domestic Violence and Victim Support Unit (DOVVSU), highlighted the need to intensify efforts to end child marriage and protect girls from abuse. She called for stronger enforcement of laws against child marriage, community sensitisation and support for victims, noting that poverty, cultural practices and limited education contributed to the persistence of the practice. As part of the celebration, students were divided into nine groups and assigned mentors to share their life experiences and discuss decisions that could shape their future. Madam Diana Mintah, Headmistress of Ghana Senior High School (GHANASS), called for regular mentorship programmes for students, saying they would equip them with the knowledge and values needed to become responsible leaders and positive role models for future generations.

title: ADC launches campaign in Imo
body:
The African Democratic Congress (ADC), on Saturday, launched its campaigns in Owerri, ahead of the 2027 General Elections, promising transparent governance and rapid grassroots transformation.
Speaking at the ceremony, the former Governor of Imo State, Emeka Ihedioha, said the party is built on equality and trustworthy leadership.
Mr Ihedioha explained that he associated with the party’s candidates because of their integrity.
“I ran a government centred on the people, and drove the process of good governance with honesty and integrity,” he said.
He pointed out that the ADC candidates shared in his political philosophy.
He regretted that the construction of 27 local government stadia and the expansion of the Adapalm plantation initiated by his administration were abandoned by successive administrations in the state.
Mr Ihedioha also said that electing ADC candidates would guarantee full administrative autonomy to local government councils, “enabling them to execute emergency road rehabilitations across rural communities in the state.”
The National Chairman of the party, David Mark, represented by the National Vice Chairman, Bon Unachukwu, said the massive turnout of supporters signified widespread acceptance of the party.
Mr Mark urged the electorate to vote for all the ADC candidates “to end hardship and insecurity in Imo and Nigeria.”
“When you vote ADC, you vote for prosperity, progress, and success,” he said.
Addressing the gathering, the Owerri Zonal Chairman of the party, Ben Mere, urged supporters to take the party’s message to every ward and village across the state.
Mr Mere assured party members that the ADC structure in the zone was united and fully prepared to secure victory in all elective positions in the upcoming polls.
Also speaking, the Imo East Senatorial Candidate of the party, Uchenna Ofoegbu, said his primary agenda was to “rescue the people from poverty and provide effective legislative representation.”
According to Mr Ofoegbu, the citizens are suffering from the effects of bad governance.
“Youth and women empowerment, rehabilitation of rural roads, and improved community healthcare delivery will form the focus of our campaign promises,” he said.
He also said the party would soon roll out vote-protection strategies to ensure that the people’s votes count.
On his part, the House of Representatives Candidate for Owerri Federal Constituency, Okey Amadi, described his candidacy as a “divine mandate supported by the electorate.”
“We promise a different kind of leadership that will guarantee security of lives, good medical services, and accountability through periodic presentation of our scorecards,” Mr Amadi said.
He also promised to provide a strong legislative advocacy for his constituency, when elected.
Others speakers at the event included the House of Assembly candidates – William Merem (Owerri North), Chidiebere Mere (Owerri Municipal), Francis Ugorji (Owerri West), as well as the state Chairman of the party, James Okoroma.
A major highlight of the event was the presentation of the party’s flag to the state and national assembly candidates of the party.

title: NDC to investigate vote-buying allegations in constituency elections if evidence is provided
body: The National Democratic Congress (NDC) says it is prepared to investigate allegations of vote-buying in its ongoing constituency elections if credible evidence is brought before the party’s national executives. The party’s Deputy Director of Elections, Rashid Tanko-Computer, said the NDC would not condone conduct that compromises the integrity of its internal electoral processes. He cited the party’s response to a previous incident involving Ayawaso as an indication that it was willing to act when concerns about electoral conduct were brought to its attention. Mr Tanko-Computer, however, said the party had not recorded any incidents of vote-buying in the constituencies where voting had taken place, describing the elections overall as largely peaceful and successful. He acknowledged that the exercise had encountered difficulties in some areas, including Odododiodioo, where counting was suspended following violence but resumed after party officials intervened. He also disclosed that voting in some constituencies in the Ashanti and Eastern regions had been postponed until the following day to allow outstanding issues to be resolved. Speaking on Channel One TV, Mr Tanko-Computer said: “If somebody has any evidence of that and it’s brought to the notice of the national executives, why not? We’ll take notice of it.”

title: Transport Minister calls for efficient, competitive ports to boost regional trade
body:
Mr Nikpe said achieving the ambition required sustained collaboration among the Ghana Ports and Harbours Authority (GPHA), the government, private-sector operators, regulatory agencies, and other stakeholders across the transport and logistics value chain.
He made the call in a keynote address at the GPHA’s 40th Anniversary Dinner and Industry Awards, where he highlighted six priorities for building a more efficient, competitive, and sustainable port system.
The priorities include improving cargo handling and evacuation, reducing avoidable delays, strengthening coordination among port operators and regulatory agencies, and making port services faster, more reliable and cost-effective.
The Minister said port competitiveness depended not only on infrastructure but also on the quality and efficiency of services delivered to businesses and customers.
He also called for the adoption of integrated digital systems, automation, and data-driven operations to improve transparency, simplify procedures, and enhance customer experience.
On transport connectivity, he said stronger links among ports, roads, railways, inland terminals and logistics centres were essential to easing congestion, facilitating cargo movement, and improving access to regional markets.
Mr Nikpe urged stakeholders to prioritise environmental sustainability, energy efficiency, workplace safety and operational resilience as the country modernised its port infrastructure and services.
He said workforce development was equally important, calling for investment in professional training, digital skills, technical expertise and leadership development to prepare workers for the changing demands of the maritime and logistics industry.
On regional trade, the Minister said Ghana had an opportunity to strengthen its position as a preferred gateway for landlocked neighbouring countries and a leading logistics hub for West Africa.
He said realising that potential required reliable services, competitive costs, efficient transit procedures and deeper collaboration with regional partners.
The Minister said the six priorities reinforced the anniversary theme of service, partnership and progress, stressing that no single institution could achieve the objectives independently.
He encouraged stakeholders to sustain cooperation to improve the competitiveness and efficiency of Ghana’s transport sector.
The event also recognised individuals and organisations whose dedication, professionalism and contributions had advanced GPHA and the country’s maritime industry.
The Minister congratulated the award recipients and urged stakeholders to uphold high standards of service, integrity, and innovation.
As GPHA looked towards its next 40 years, he called for continued investment in digital transformation, transport connectivity and workforce development to expand Ghana’s contribution to regional trade.
He said the ambition to build West Africa’s premier trade and logistics hub must be reflected in service quality, strong partnerships and tangible results for businesses, communities and the country.

title: Soludo in Tinubu’s Campaign: ‘Bitter truth’ is South-East must align with centre — Sly Ezeokenwa, APGA National Chair
body: •Dismisses anti-party claim against Anambra gov By Dickson Omobola National Chairman of the All Progressives Grand Alliance, APGA, Sly Ezeokenwa, in this interview first aired on Arise News, speaks on the reasons Anambra State governor and national leader of APGA, Professor Charles Soludo, has pitched tent with President Bola Tinubu of the All Progressives Congress, APC, ahead of the 2027 elections, despite concerns over alleged anti-party activities. Excerpts: Your party, APGA, has adopted President Bola Tinubu, and your governor, Professor Charles Soludo, has now been named on APC list. What should this tell the average voter? Is this merely a symbolic show of strength and dominance by the APC? Would the allegation of anti-party activity apply to Professor Soludo? I think it would be good to state that the decision of Professor Charles Soludo, who, by the way, is the national leader of our party, to support the President transcends their personal relationship. Once you become the leader of a party, the Constitution imposes certain obligations and responsibilities on you. In a multi-party democracy such as ours, coalitions are inevitable. When you have about 22 political parties, as we currently do, with people from diverse ethnic groups and different religious backgrounds, you can be certain that any presidential candidate seeking to meet the constitutional threshold faces a considerable task. You must recall that to be elected president of Nigeria, the Constitution requires you to secure a simple majority and at least 25 per cent of the votes cast in at least two-thirds of the states in the country. You will agree with me that this is not an easy task for any presidential candidate in a multi-party democracy. That, therefore, calls for broader coalitions. Those who are well versed in our politics will know that such coalitions have historical precedents. There have been instances of alliances and coalitions before independence, after independence, during the 1979 elections and beyond. For me, this is nothing new. However, our decision as a party to support the President stems from three perspectives, and I must make that emphatically clear. First, it draws from history. APGA has a standing policy under which the party considers a cordial relationship with the ruling party part of its strategic alliances and survival. You know very well that this policy was adopted around 2011. Incidentally, the only governor on the platform of APGA at the time was the current presidential candidate of the NDC. That was when APGA adopted the presidential candidacy of the then President Goodluck Jonathan, a decision it repeated in 2015. Even in 2019 and 2023, when the party nominated its own presidential candidates, it did not derogate from that tradition of supporting the incumbent. Beyond the policy and historical perspectives, we come to the more germane issue. Our leader popularised an aphorism that, in a multi-party democracy, it does not make sense for every political party in the country to field a presidential candidate when some of those candidates are unlikely to secure even 50,000 votes. If our affiliations and alliances in a multi-party democracy should be ideologically driven, then there is nothing wrong with political parties that profess similar ideologies coming together to support a common presidential candidate. That was how our leader popularised the phrase that progressives are working together, which stemmed from his charge or call during the President’s visit to Anambra. For our party specifically, there is a strong, longstanding alliance with the administration of President Bola Tinubu. That alliance led to the appointment of a serving member of APGA’s Board of Trustees, BoT, Bianca Ojukwu, as a minister in President Tinubu’s cabinet, as well as the appointment of another APGA member. If you look at the 2023 elections, despite having much of the influence in the South-East, Peter Obi of the Labour Party secured over 90 per cent of the votes in the region. How will APGA’s influence change that result in favour of the APC, bearing in mind that Obi was once a member of APGA and would still have some supporters in your party? Obi is from Anambra and still wields that level of influence in the South-East. How would you turn the region in favour of President Bola Tinubu now that APGA has aligned with his candidacy? As a party, we have our position, which is that we have endorsed and adopted the candidacy of President Bola Tinubu. That is a fact. Now, we have a critical issue involving a proud son of Anambra, the first governor elected on the platform of APGA, who is also running in this election. However, in this context, it is better for us to be politically correct as we approach the 2027 presidential election. It is a question of whether to be politically correct or join the bandwagon of sensationalism surrounding a particular candidate. We believe that, before the advent of the current Fourth Republic in 1999, the promoters and founders of the ruling party, the PDP, came together and crafted an agreement. It was more or less an unwritten agreement on power rotation or power sharing between the North and the South. We believe that, whatever the circumstances, it is now the South’s turn. Someone from Southern Nigeria, President Bola Tinubu, is currently in office. So, the South has another four years, and it only makes sense to allow the South, through President Tinubu, to complete its tenure. That is one fact. For us as a party, we believe it is our responsibility to tell the people the bitter truth, regardless of whose ox is gored or how people feel about it. That bitter truth is that we believe it has not served the interests of the South-East to continue on this trajectory of political alienation. If you look at the data or statistics recently released by the Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, showing the percentage of registered voters across the country, the South-East accounts for, I think, about 11 per cent of registered voters. The question is whether the South-East, on its own, can produce a President without building a broader coalition with other regions. We believe that the roadmap to the presidency, for the foreseeable future, requires the South-East to find a way to align with the centre. If we align with the centre and other regions, we can return to the question at the appropriate time. For now, it is the South’s turn to complete its remaining four years through the incumbent President. We believe it serves the interests of the South-East better to align with other regions by supporting President Tinubu’s bid for re-election. We see this as a means of bringing the South-East back into the equation. Since 2015, it has been our belief that the South-East has been left out of the scheme of things in the country. No matter how anybody feels about it, that is the bitter truth. It ought not to be so, but that is the reality on the ground. You called Obi your precious son from Anambra and the first person to win the governorship on APGA’s platform. Why denigrate him openly for political reasons? Win or lose, the 2027 elections will be over by January 15, but the impact of the damage you people would do to your fellow Igbo man would never be forgotten. How do you react to that? Emotions will get us nowhere. I head a political party; I do not run a charity organisation. As a political party, we make decisions based on what our leaders believe serves our strategic interests at a particular time. At this point, that means supporting President Bola Tinubu’s candidacy. It is the party’s decision, and, as I said, it is driven by historical alliances, policy and other factors. I have not seen any former governor who was given the kind of pre-eminence Peter Obi enjoyed under APGA. When he joined the party, APGA gave him its platform on a platter of gold, and he contested the election. Barely six months after completing his tenure, he left the party. Since then, he has continuously worked against APGA. His only mission, in our view, is to annihilate the party. APGA has survived various attempts by Peter Obi to undermine it. Let us start from 2015. Barely a year after leaving the party, he joined the PDP and became part of the coalition forces working against APGA’s National Assembly candidates. This was despite the fact that APGA had adopted the candidacy of President Goodluck Jonathan at the time. In 2017, Peter Obi was instrumental in the emergence of Chief Willie Obiano. However, that same year, he backed another candidate and took that candidate across the state. We have videos of him calling the then governor of the state a drunkard at a campaign rally. In 2021, he repeated the same thing, supporting another candidate. Despite all this, Professor Charles Soludo, who became governor in 2022, recognised that Obi was a son of the state and a former member of the party. He invited him back to APGA because we believed that building that brotherly alliance was necessary if we were to have a shot at the presidency. President Bola Tinubu, the brother you referred to, built alliances across the South-West before taking office. Even when the time came for him to run for President, he stepped aside from his ambition to support another presidential candidate because he believed it was not the right time for him to contest. That is what a true leader who has the interests of his people at heart does. A quick flaw in your argument: you said that when Peter Obi left, he still returned to work with the party to ensure Willie Obiano’s emergence. Did he not? No, no, no. That is wrong. Who worked for Obiano’s emergence? He was still in the party when he worked for Obiano’s emergence. The part of the story you have not mentioned is that all this started when they fell out. You are wrong. They did not fall out before he left the party. Immediately after Peter Obi handed over to Obiano on March 17, 2014, some Peoples Democratic Party, PDP, governors visited him at his residence somewhere in Onitsha and invited him to join the party. If you recall, he never said at the time that he had fallen out with Obiano. He called APGA a special purpose vehicle. But you have just made my point. He was elected, helped APGA win re-election and handed over an APGA government in the state when he left… We have never denied that Peter Obi helped us to get re-elected. But you are putting the cart before the horse. The fact is that APGA first did someone a favour by offering him its platform in 2003. When he was rigged out, APGA members went to the tribunal to defend his mandate. They testified, presented certified true copies of result sheets and tendered them as evidence, leading to the historic overturning of the declaration of then Governor Chris Ngige. So, you must give APGA credit. Now that your party is supporting President Tinubu, we have heard that in Edo State, the APC expects to deliver 2.5 million votes. In Osun, the Accord Party says it will deliver 1.8 million votes. How many votes will APGA deliver? For me, it is not about figures. It is about presenting our people with the facts, the truth and, as it were, the bitter truth: that, in this election, there is no pathway for our so-called brother. As painful as it is, that is our position. It is in the strategic interests of Ndi Igbo to align with President Bola Tinubu’s aspiration. That is what APGA stands for, and we will do everything possible to convince our people why they should vote for President Tinubu. Vanguard News The post Soludo in Tinubu’s Campaign: ‘Bitter truth’ is South-East must align with centre — Sly Ezeokenwa, APGA National Chair appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Israel is right to support Britain-Argentina talks over Falkland Islands - editorial
body: Israel's call for direct negotiations between Britain and Argentina over the Falkland Islands deserves qualified support.According to The Jerusalem Post's report, Ambassador Danny Danon urged talks at the United Nations. However, the Israeli embassy in London denied that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had ordered a policy shift, as The Telegraph reported. That denial must remain part of the account.The position itself is defensible. Israel has reason to take Argentina's concerns seriously, and peaceful negotiations have an established international framework. Jerusalem should clearly explain its position, including its commitment to the wishes of the people whose future is being discussed.Under President Javier Milei, Argentina has been a consistent friend of Israel. His support during the war following the October 7 massacre deserves meaningful diplomatic recognition. A relationship in which Israel welcomes solidarity on its own concerns while showing little interest in its partner's priorities would be difficult to sustain.Israeli diplomacy should make friendship worthwhile. That means listening, engaging, and looking for responsible ways to reciprocate. Supporting a peaceful process on an issue important to Argentina offers such an opportunity. It also signals to other friendly governments that Jerusalem takes their concerns seriously.UK must understand Israel policy affects wider relationshipBritain, meanwhile, should understand that its choices toward Israel affect the wider relationship. Every government is entitled to scrutinize another country's policies, and Israel has an equal right to reassess the diplomatic support it extends. British officials should expect Jerusalem to exercise independent judgment on issues London considers sensitive.That principle requires discipline. A foreign policy guided by anger can produce expensive gestures with little practical return. Israel should be able to explain what its Falklands position achieves: a stronger relationship with Argentina, support for peaceful diplomacy, and a consistent approach to resolving disputes. Those objectives deserve public articulation.There is a foundation for talks. UN General Assembly Resolution 2065, adopted in 1965, recognized the sovereignty dispute over the Falklands and invited Britain and Argentina to negotiate a peaceful solution, taking the islanders' interests into account. Supporting negotiations therefore fits within a longstanding diplomatic framework.The islanders themselves present the strongest challenge to any broader Israeli endorsement. In the 2013 referendum, 99.8% of votes favored retaining the islands' status as a British overseas territory. That expression of democratic preference carries enormous weight. Any editorial judgment about the dispute must address it honestly.Israel should explicitly insist that the islanders participate meaningfully in discussions affecting their future and that any change in sovereignty requires their freely expressed consent. Jerusalem and London cannot make their homes, citizenship, and political institutions bargaining chips in a disagreement. Supporting Argentina's request for dialogue must come with that clear safeguard.This also serves Israel's interests. A country that asks others to respect its people's security and right to determine their future should uphold those principles consistently. Different territorial disputes have different histories. Consistency requires applying defensible standards while acknowledging those differences.Jerusalem should also consider its friends in Britain. Many people willing to defend Israel will strongly oppose any attempt to pressure the Falklanders into an unwanted settlement. Israel gains little by making their support harder to sustain. Its diplomats should engage them directly and explain the limits of the position.For the same reason, gratitude to Milei cannot settle the sovereignty question. Territorial claims require examination on their own merits. Argentina's friendship provides a reason for serious engagement; a judgment on ownership would require a separate, substantial case.Israel's government should publish clear account of Falklands policyThe government should now publish a clear account of its policy. It should state whether it supports negotiations, what role it envisages for the islanders, and whether its position on sovereignty has changed. Contradictory signals leave partners and critics to interpret them for themselves.Israel can defend this approach with confidence if it makes its conditions explicit and applies them consistently. The test will be whether its diplomacy creates room for voluntary agreement while preserving relationships that remain valuable to Israel.The Post supports a carefully defined Israeli call for peaceful dialogue. Argentina deserves a fair hearing. The Falklanders deserve control over their future.Britain should recognize that diplomatic goodwill depends on reciprocity. Israel must pursue those objectives together, with enough clarity that a gesture toward a friend can develop into credible policy.

title: Saudi Arabia flight cancellations: Which airlines are suspending services and until when?
body: Flight cancellations across Saudi Arabia continue as airlines extend suspensions amid continuing regional tension and attacks by Yemen's Houthi rebels . Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport has partially reopened following its closure earlier this month, but international services remain disrupted. The airport is operating terminals 1 and 2 from October 25. Terminal 1 is designated for domestic flights, with Terminal 2 operating international flights. Etihad Airways has extended cancellations on routes to Riyadh and Dammam into November, while flydubai and Emirates has suspended several Saudi services until October 29. Here is how major airlines have adjusted their operations and when flights are expected to resume. Etihad Airways Etihad Airways has cancelled flights between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh, Dammam and Jeddah until November 5 owing to the regional disruption. All services to and from Riyadh and Dammam are affected, along with four Jeddah services – EY601, EY602, EY603 and EY604. Emirates Emirates has updated its online flight schedules for routes operating to Saudi airports. The airline will resume flights between Dubai and Jeddah on October 30, with EK801, EK805 and EK803 scheduled to fly to King Abdulaziz International Airport, and EK802, EK806 and EK804 due to operate the return legs to Dubai. Flights to both King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and King Fahd International Airport in Dammam are due to resume on November 8. Flights EK815, EK819 and EK817 are all due to operate from Dubai to Riyadh daily, with EK816, EK820 and EK818 returning. To Damman, the airline will fly EK823, EK827 and EK821 and EK824, EK828 and EK822 returning. The airline's services to Medina Prince Mohammad Bin Abdulaziz Airport continue to operate. Flydubai The airline has cancelled flights to Riyadh, Dammam and Abha up to October 29. From October 30, it will operate two daily flights to Riyadh: FZ847 and FZ855, with FZ848 and FZ856 returning. Four daily flights will resume to Damman: FZ883, FZ869, FZ863 and FZ867, with FZ884, FZ870, FZ864 and FZ868 returning. One route will operate to Abha: FZ813 and FZ814. Air Arabia Air Arabia has cancelled services between Sharjah and several Saudi destinations including Riyadh, Abha, Dammam and Taif. No resumption date has been announced. Qatar Airways The airline has temporarily suspended flights to and from Riyadh up to and including October 25. Meanwhile, its services to Jeddah have been reduced from seven daily flights to four. Flights to Damman remain suspended. Oman Air Oman Air has announced that all flights to and from Riyadh are suspended until October 31. SalamAir The Omani low-cost airline has cancelled flights to and from Riyadh and Dammam until October 31, citing regional security developments. Air France The French airline has extended its suspension of flights to and from Riyadh up to and including November 14. British Airways British Airways is scheduled to return with a limited service to Riyadh on November 3, operating one flight daily, according to previously announced plans. The airline discontinued flights to Jeddah in April as part of wider changes to its Middle East operations. Air India and Air India Express Air India and Air India Express have suspended flights to and from Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam until November 7. The Pakistan Airports Authority said at the time that its other Saudi services were continuing as usual. title: GoldBod begins stakeholder consultations ahead of 2027 small-scale mining support programme
body: The Ghana Gold Board (GoldBod) has begun engaging industry stakeholders on a proposed programme to formalise artisanal and small-scale mining and provide financial support to eligible operators ahead of its planned launch in 2027. The initiative, known as the Artisanal and Small-Scale Mining (ASM) Formalisation and Financing Support Programme, is expected to bring eligible informal miners into a regulated system while improving their access to financing and strengthening oversight of their activities. GoldBod said the consultations involve relevant government agencies, small-scale miners’ associations, civil society organisations and other industry stakeholders. The engagements are intended to gather input to ensure the programme reflects industry needs and can be implemented sustainably. The Board is developing the programme in collaboration with the Ministry of Lands and Natural Resources, the University of Mines and Technology (UMaT) and the Mineral Income Investment Fund (MIIF), with technical support from South Africa’s Rand Refinery. According to GoldBod, the initiative is expected to increase gold production and mineral revenues, create jobs, reduce operational costs and limit environmental degradation associated with mining activities. The programme also forms part of efforts to tackle illegal mining by ensuring that eligible operators are licensed, monitored and held accountable for their environmental and operational practices. GoldBod has stressed that the objective is not to legitimise galamsey, but to help eligible informal miners transition into lawful operations and comply with the country’s mining regulations. In a statement issued by its Media Relations Unit, the Board said it had “commenced stakeholder engagements with key industry stakeholders, including relevant government agencies, small-scale miners’ associations, civil society organizations, among others, on the proposed ASM FFSP”. The consultations come amid public debate over comments by GoldBod Chief Executive Officer Sammy Gyamfi on the formalisation of unlicensed small-scale miners. GoldBod has rejected allegations that he endorsed illegal mining, arguing that a video of his remarks was selectively edited and omitted important context.

title: Nigeria’s ambassador presents Letters of Credence to Cypriot President
body:
Nigeria’s Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary to Israel with concurrent accreditation to Cyprus, Nkechi Ufochukwu, has presented her Letters of Credence to Cypriot President Nikos Christodoulides.
According to a statement issued on Saturday by the Nigerian Embassy in Israel, the ceremony took place on Friday at the Presidential Palace in Nicosia, in line with diplomatic tradition.
The event also marked the official start of Ufochukwu’s tour of duty as Nigeria’s principal envoy to Cyprus.
She conveyed the fraternal greetings of Nigerian President Bola Tinubu to Mr Christodoulides and pledged to boost relations between the two countries during her tour of duty.
Mr Christodoulides welcomed Ms Ufochukwu and reaffirmed the deep and enduring friendship between Cyprus and Nigeria.
He said the two countries share ties of friendship born of historical experiences, common principles and enduring links between their peoples.
He said Cyprus fully understands Nigeria’s significant role in West Africa and across the continent, as well as its contribution to regional dialogue, cooperation, integration and stability.
He assured her that the Cypriot government stands ready to work closely with Nigeria to advance diplomatic relations in areas of mutual interest.
These include the economy, trade and investment, education and political dialogue, while tackling common challenges bilaterally and multilaterally.
The presentation of the Letters of Credence is a significant milestone in bilateral relations and a formal accreditation to perform representational duties.
It also serves as the official channel of communication between Abuja and Nicosia.

title: IBSAMAR IX concludes in South Africa, boosts India-Brazil-South Africa naval cooperation
body:
By Aroonim Bhuyan
New Delhi. The ninth edition of the India-Brazil-South Africa Maritime (IBSAMAR) Exercise 2026 concluded at Simon’s Town, South Africa, on October 20 after 10 days of joint naval training and operational engagements aimed at enhancing interoperability and strengthening maritime cooperation among the three countries.

According to a statement issued by the Ministy of Defence, the exercise brought together the Indian, Brazilian and South African navies for professional exchanges, joint training and maritime manoeuvres designed to improve operational coordination and foster a deeper understanding of each other’s capabilities and procedures.
The closing ceremony marked the culmination of activities conducted during the harbour and sea phases. Personnel from the participating navies exchanged operational experience and gained insights into their counterparts’ methods of conducting maritime operations. The interactions helped build mutual trust and confidence, enhancing the ability of the three forces to work together at sea.

Addressing the gathering at the closing ceremony, the commanding officer of INS Tarkash highlighted the importance of IBSAMAR in translating longstanding diplomatic ties among the three countries into practical naval cooperation.
He emphasised that the exercise’s value extended beyond joint maritime operations, with shared experiences, professional exchanges and mutual learning helping forge lasting relationships among naval personnel.
IBSAMAR reflects the enduring maritime partnership between India, Brazil and South Africa, which, despite being located across three continents, share common interests in maintaining safe, secure and stable seas.
The trilateral exercise provides a platform for the three navies to address common maritime challenges, exchange best practices and strengthen their ability to conduct coordinated operations. Such engagements contribute to building confidence, improving operational compatibility and promoting a peaceful maritime environment.

The exercise also highlighted the importance of sustained interaction and joint training in developing interoperability. A shared understanding of maritime procedures, combined with repeated operational engagements, enables participating forces to coordinate more effectively and strengthens their preparedness for future cooperation.
The professional bonds established among the participating crews are expected to extend beyond the exercise, reinforcing institutional ties and providing a foundation for deeper naval engagement among the three countries.
The successful conclusion of IBSAMAR IX reaffirmed the shared commitment of India, Brazil and South Africa to strengthening maritime cooperation and enhancing interoperability in support of safe, secure and open seas. It also underscored their common interest in upholding a rules-based maritime order and promoting peace and stability across the global maritime domain.

title: Omani youth account for 52% of total youth population
body:
Muscat: Oman will mark Omani Youth Day on Monday, October 26, with more than one million people aged between 18 and 29, highlighting the importance of young people in the Sultanate’s development and their role in achieving Oman Vision 2040. A ceremony will be held at the Youth Centre in Muscat under the auspices of Sayyid Bilarab bin Haitham al Said, Minister of State and Governor of Muscat. The programme will include a youth address, a visual presentation, a tour of the centre and the signing of a funding agreement for its main branch in Muscat Governorate, alongside other agreements and a recognition ceremony. Figures from the National Centre for Statistics and Information (NCSI) show that Oman had 1,038,715 people aged between 18 and 29 in 2025. Omani youth accounted for 52 per cent of the total, with males making up 51 per cent of the Omani youth population. More than a third of young Omanis lived in Muscat and North al Batinah governorates. The number of Omani youth stood at 538,491 in 2025 and is projected to reach 914,609 by 2040, underlining the importance of developing their skills and expanding opportunities for their participation in the national economy and society. The Youth Centre has been working to support this goal through training, skills development and interactive spaces that encourage innovation and help young people turn ideas into projects and initiatives.

title: Food, Floods, Erosion: 16,140 households targeted with 5,380 tubewells, dams, irrigation projects in Kano
body: •Inside the Ecological Project Office interventions in dry-season farming By Nnamdi Ojiego For farmers in Kano State, the end of the rainy season often marks a difficult transition. As rainfall declines, access to water becomes a major concern, particularly for smallholder farmers who depend on seasonal rains to cultivate their land. In communities exposed to flooding and erosion, the challenges are even greater, with damaged roads, threatened homes and disrupted economic activities adding to the difficulties of rural life. In Sumaila Town, Sumaila Local Government, for instance, residents faced serious challenges due to a lack of accessible roads and the threat of gully erosion. Vehicles could not enter parts of the neighbourhood, forcing car owners to park outside. Against this backdrop, the Federal Government has embarked on a series of ecological and agricultural interventions across Kano State, combining flood control, erosion remediation, road improvement and irrigation infrastructure in a programme intended to support farming throughout the year. The projects, implemented by the Ecological Project Office under the leadership of Permanent Secretary, Office of the Secretary to the Government of the Federation, Dr. Aishetu Gogo Ndayako, include interventions in communities spread across several local government areas, as well as irrigation schemes linked to Tiga, Challawa-Gorge and Kafin Chiri dams. Project documents obtained by Sunday Vanguard indicate that the programme covers erosion control, flood mitigation, the construction of bridges and culverts, improvements to rural roads, the provision of tubewells and pumping machines, and the development of canal networks to supply water to farmland. A separate watershed management programme lists 18 projects involving the provision of 5,380 tubewells and an equal number of pumping machines, with 16,140 households identified as intended beneficiaries. The programme is reported to have achieved an average completion rate of 99.7 per cent, according to a brochure published by the Ecological Project Office. The interventions form part of the Federal Government’s special ecological programme for the Kano River Irrigation Project under President Bola Tinubu’s Renewed Hope Agenda. Beyond the number of projects and facilities listed, the programme raises important questions about the relationship between water management, agricultural productivity, rural infrastructure and the ability of farmers to sustain production beyond the rainy season. Ecological interventions The erosion and flood-control component of the programme covers a range of communities where the government has listed projects intended to address erosion, flooding and deteriorating road infrastructure. The project schedule contains 32 entries, including the construction of bridges and culverts for flood control, erosion-control works, remediation of affected areas and road improvement along selected routes. Among the locations listed are Zambur, Unguwar Gai in Kibiya Local Government Area, Rimmin Yamma and Sumaila, Rurum-Bunkini-Kazaurawa, Furuwa, Kibiya town bypass, Zango and Hanyar Kogo in Takai, Kachako, Karaye, Kukar Bashari and Kwanar Dan Goro. Other locations include Fulatan in Rogo Local Government Area, Kadabo Road, Darki bypass in Wudil, Kiru, Tiga-Runum Road, Gala, Wudil town, Daki community, Bebejii, Kadauji village and Magami. The programme also lists road improvement and erosion-control works along Sabon Gwandu, Kazaurewa-Gana Road in Rano, Unguwar Gora, Rano-Bunkure Road and Falali in Sumaila, among other locations. The projects vary in their stated purposes. Some are primarily concerned with erosion control, while others combine erosion remediation with road improvement. Several involve the construction of bridges or culverts intended to help manage flooding and improve movement within affected communities. Such infrastructure can be important in rural areas where roads provide links between farms, residential settlements, markets and other essential services. Where erosion damages roads or floodwaters cut off access, farmers may encounter additional difficulties moving produce to buyers, obtaining agricultural inputs or reaching their fields. The listed interventions therefore have potential implications beyond the physical structures being constructed. Their value to communities will depend on whether they address the problems for which they were designed and whether the infrastructure remains functional after construction. Challenge of flooding, erosion Flooding and erosion can place considerable pressure on communities whose livelihoods depend on agriculture and local trade. Heavy rainfall can wash away topsoil, damage roads, undermine structures and disrupt the movement of people and goods. Where water is poorly channelled, runoff can gradually erode the land, deepen gullies and threaten farmland and residential areas. Flooding can also make roads impassable, leaving some communities with limited access to markets and essential services. For farming households, the effects may extend beyond the immediate damage. The loss of productive land, interruption of cultivation and difficulty transporting harvested crops can affect household earnings and food availability. The Federal Government’s programme addresses some of these concerns through a combination of erosion-control structures, bridges, culverts and road improvement works. The inclusion of bridges and culverts in locations such as Zambur, Furuwa, Magami and Unguwar Gora suggests an effort to address specific points where water movement and access are important considerations. Other projects focus on erosion remediation or the improvement of roads in towns and rural settlements. However, without adequate maintenance, infrastructure intended to control erosion and flooding can deteriorate, reducing its effectiveness over time. The programme’s long-term value will therefore depend not only on construction but also on the quality of the works, their suitability for local conditions and the arrangements for monitoring and maintenance. Irrigation expansion While the erosion and flood-control projects address environmental and infrastructure challenges, the irrigation component seeks to improve access to water for agriculture. The EPO has listed interventions at Tiga, Challawa-Gorge and Kafin Chiri dams, with plans to open new sectors for irrigation and provide canal networks to serve designated areas of farmland. Together, the three schemes are designed to cover 1,279.91 hectares. The Tiga Dam intervention accounts for 875 hectares, Challawa-Gorge for 240 hectares and Kafin Chiri for 164.91 hectares. The proposed schemes combine main canals, distribution canals, field canals and pipe extensions, depending on the requirements of each location. The objective, according to the documents, was to make water available for cultivation beyond the main rainy season, giving farmers an opportunity to grow crops during periods when rainfall alone may not support production. Dry-season farming can provide an additional source of income for farmers and help maintain agricultural activity when rain-fed cultivation is no longer possible. Depending on local conditions, crops grown under irrigation can also supply markets at different times of the year. For the intervention to achieve these aims, however, the infrastructure must be completed, supplied with adequate water and operated in a way that allows farmers to use it reliably. Tiga Dam: 875 hectares earmarked for irrigation The Tiga Dam scheme is the largest of the three irrigation interventions listed in the project material. Completed in 1974, Tiga Dam is a major water-storage structure associated with the Kano River Irrigation Project. The supplied technical data describes it as a zoned earth-fill dam with a length of 6,000 metres and a maximum height of 48 metres from foundation level. Its reservoir capacity is listed at between 1,350 million and 1,450 million cubic metres, although the design capacity is given as two billion cubic metres. Under the current EPO intervention, 875 hectares have been earmarked for irrigation across three sectors identified as Renewed Hope Sector 1 at Yakasai, Sector 2 at Gawama and Sector 3 at Guriya. The project schedule assigns 46 hectares to Yakasai, 381 hectares to Gawama and 448 hectares to Guriya. The three sectors together account for the stated 875 hectares. To support irrigation across the designated area, the planned infrastructure includes 20.361 kilometres of distribution canals, 77.456 kilometres of field canals and a one-kilometre pipe extension. The proposed network is intended to convey water through the irrigation system and distribute it to the designated farming areas. The effectiveness of the scheme will depend on how the different components are connected, the availability of water and the arrangements for distributing it among farmers. The size of the area earmarked for irrigation gives the Tiga intervention particular significance within the programme. If the facilities become operational and farmers can use them consistently, the scheme could support additional cultivation during the dry season. Challawa-Gorge: another 240 hectares The second intervention is at Challawa-Gorge Dam, where the government plans to open an additional 240 hectares for irrigation. Completed in 1992, the dam is described in the supplied technical document as a rock-fill structure measuring 7,804 metres in length, with a maximum height of 42 metres from foundation level. Its total reservoir capacity is listed as 930 million cubic metres, comprising 904 million cubic metres of active storage and 26 million cubic metres of dead storage. The irrigation intervention involves an extensive network of canals, pipe extensions and access roads. According to the project schedule, the planned main canals measure 14 kilometres and 2.5 kilometres, while the distribution canals measure 13.5 kilometres and 3.5 kilometres. The listed canal works also include lengths of 25 kilometres and 4.5 kilometres under the description of additional canals, identified in the source material as “Reid Canals”. The project, marked as ongoing, includes a 1.37-kilometre pipe extension and 10.5 kilometres of access roads within the canal network. The inclusion of access roads alongside the canal network is significant because irrigation infrastructure must connect with the areas it is intended to serve. Roads can assist movement within the scheme, including access to farms and the transport of agricultural inputs and produce. The 240 hectares designated for irrigation could provide additional opportunities for cultivation if the scheme is completed and made operational. The actual benefits, however, will depend on the distribution of water, the number of participating farmers and the reliability of the infrastructure. Kafin Chiri: a smaller scheme with similar objectives At Kafin Chiri Dam, construction is listed as ongoing. The planned irrigation area is 164.91 hectares. The dam’s technical data lists a reservoir capacity of 31.12 million cubic metres and a reservoir area of 8.42 square kilometres at full capacity. The EPO intervention includes 9.474 kilometres of main canal, 7.106 kilometres of distribution canals and 2.748 kilometres of field canals. Although the area is smaller than those covered by the Tiga and Challawa-Gorge schemes, Kafin Chiri forms part of the same wider effort to expand irrigation infrastructure and support farming outside the rainy season. The proposed canals are intended to connect the water supply with designated agricultural areas. As with the other schemes, their usefulness will depend on the completion of the network and the availability of water when farmers need it. The three dam projects collectively account for almost 1,280 hectares of planned irrigation. That figure provides a measure of the scale of the government’s stated intervention, although the project documents do not establish how much of the land is already being irrigated. Tubewells, pumping machines for dry-season farming Beyond the dam-based schemes, the EPO’s watershed management programme is designed to provide water facilities for all-season farming across several local government areas. The brochure lists all the projects and states that the programme involves 5,380 tubewells, 5,380 pumping machines and 16,140 households. The listed locations include Garko, Sumaila, Gaya, Ajingi, Albasu, Karaye, Kiru, Rogo, Bunkure, Tudun Wada, Takai, Kibiya and Wudil. The project descriptions refer to drilling tubewells, providing water-harvesting facilities and installing watershed management systems to support dry-season cultivation and other agricultural activities. A tubewell can provide access to groundwater, while a pumping machine helps move water to a location where it can be used. When properly installed and managed, such facilities can give farmers a source of water that is less dependent on immediate rainfall. The provision of these facilities can be particularly relevant to smallholder farmers who cannot rely solely on rain-fed cultivation throughout the year. However, the usefulness of a tubewell depends on several factors, including the availability and quality of groundwater, the reliability of the pump, the cost of operation and the arrangements for repairs and maintenance. The distribution of the facilities among communities and households would also help clarify whether the programme is reaching its intended beneficiaries. Completion level One of the notable claims in the project material is the reported average completion rate of 99.7 per cent for the watershed management programme. If the figure reflects verified physical progress across all 18 projects, it would indicate that the programme is close to completion. However, the brochure does not explain whether the completion rate refers to construction, equipment installation, the delivery of facilities or the operational readiness of the schemes. What the programme could mean for farmers The potential benefits of the interventions extend beyond the construction of physical infrastructure. For farmers, reliable access to water can make it possible to cultivate land during periods when rain-fed agriculture is difficult. Additional cropping opportunities may help households spread their income across the year and reduce the gap between harvests. Irrigation can also support agricultural activity linked to produce handling, transportation, trading and the supply of inputs. Where production increases, the benefits may extend to other people who depend on farming for their livelihoods. The erosion-control and road improvement projects could complement these efforts by improving access to agricultural communities and reducing disruption caused by damaged roads and flooding. However, such outcomes are not automatic. They depend on whether the infrastructure is completed to the required standard, whether the water supply is sustainable and whether farmers can afford to use and maintain the facilities. Access to land, seeds, fertiliser, extension services, markets and suitable storage facilities can also influence the results. The project documents identify food security, employment, higher agricultural production and improved rural livelihoods among the expected benefits of the interventions. Beyond construction The programme’s wider significance will ultimately depend on the relationship between infrastructure delivery and the needs of the people it is intended to serve. For the flood-control component, this means determining whether the works have reduced the risk of flooding, protected affected settlements and improved access to roads. For the irrigation schemes, it means establishing whether farmers can obtain water when needed, whether the canals function as designed and whether the intended farming areas are being cultivated. For the tubewell programme, the key questions include how many facilities are working, how groundwater resources are being managed and whether communities have the means to keep the equipment in service. Maintenance is particularly important. Pumps require servicing, canals may need desilting and drainage structures can be damaged by heavy rainfall or the movement of debris. Without clear responsibility for maintenance, infrastructure may lose its usefulness before its expected lifespan. The government would also need to establish a system for monitoring the programme’s performance and publishing information on its results. The Ecological Project Office’s documents provide a broad outline of the intervention and the scale of the facilities planned. The programme represents a substantial stated effort to link ecological works with agricultural water supply across Kano State. Its lasting value will be measured by whether the infrastructure works, whether farmers can use it and whether communities experience a measurable improvement in their livelihoods. For now, the listed projects provide a framework for that effort. Their eventual impact will depend on implementation, accountability and sustained attention to the needs of the communities the programme is designed to serve. title: Trump says US ready to do business with Ukraine and Russia after war
body:
Trump told this to reporters in Palm Beach after voting early in the midterm congressional elections, according to Ukrinform's correspondent.
"We'd like to get back to life where Russia and Ukraine make a deal, and then we'd be able to do business with both," Trump said in response to a question about possible cooperation with Russia in the energy sector.
"We'll do business with Ukraine and with Russia after this war ends, I would think," he added.
Meanwhile, First Lady Melania Trump, commenting on a humanitarian truce to save people in Oleshky, said it was good that the Pope supported this initiative and expressed hope that everything would go according to plan.
Asked to clarify whether she had spoken with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Russian President Vladimir Putin, the first lady replied that agreements had been signed with both of them.
Trump added that his wife had achieved greater success than professional negotiators and suggested that she could join the negotiations.
"I think she's doing better than the professionals right now. She got a ceasefire. This has to do with children and people, elderly people," Trump said.
As Ukrinform reported, Melania Trump announced that she had secured a local truce concerning the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in the Kherson region.

title: INEC Figures: How North-West, South-West may hold key to Aso Rock
body: •Candidates’ performance in two regions has shaped presidential election since 1999 By Luminous Jannamike Behind the battle for the presidency lies a contest over voter numbers, party machinery and political alliances. Tinubu has a head start as incumbent, but Atiku, Obi and other challengers know that no region is anybody’s political inheritance. The road to Aso Rock in 2027 runs through two regions where elections can be won, lost or thrown wide open: the North-West and South-West. Their combined electoral strength gives them enormous influence over the calculations of President Bola Tinubu and the opposition figures seeking to unseat him. The Independent National Electoral Commission’s 2026 voter register puts the North-West at 25,083,411 registered voters and the South-West at 19,614,274. Together, they account for 44,697,685 registered voters, representing more than 43 per cent of Nigeria’s 103,428,715 registered voters ahead of the 2027 general elections. Those figures make the two zones central to the presidential contest. But the real battle is more complicated than regional arithmetic. Candidates must convert registered voters into ballots, hold their traditional strongholds, penetrate rival territories and build a coalition broad enough to survive the country’s political and geographical divisions. For Tinubu, the stakes are particularly high. His South-West political base helped launch his presidential ambition, while his 2023 victory also depended on support beyond the region. Former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar and Peter Obi must find ways to disrupt that balance if they hope to deny him a second term. The numbers that can make or break a candidate The North-West’s 25.08 million registered voters make it Nigeria’s largest geopolitical voting bloc. The South-West follows with 19.61 million, ahead of the North-Central, which has 16.97 million. The political significance is unmistakable. Kano, Kaduna and Katsina are among the country’s most populous electoral states, while Lagos leads the national register with 7,488,633 voters. A candidate who makes substantial gains across these states can dramatically improve his national tally. Yet neither zone is a political inheritance. The North-West contains competing party structures, influential local leaders and voters whose choices are shaped by security, economic conditions, personalities and the performance of elected officials. Kano’s political history, in particular, shows how a powerful state-level movement can disrupt calculations made in Abuja. The South-West presents a different challenge. Tinubu’s longstanding political network gives him an advantage, but it does not guarantee uniform support across the region. Lagos demonstrated this in 2023 when Obi defeated Tinubu there by 9,848 votes, polling 582,454 against the president’s 572,606. That result remains a reminder that even a candidate’s home territory can become a battleground. Party loyalty, local grievances, urban voting patterns and the credibility of candidates can all upset expectations. The numbers also require caution. INEC’s register measures people registered to vote, not the number who will eventually cast ballots. Turnout, voter accreditation, election-day logistics and the distribution of votes among candidates will determine how much of that numerical advantage translates into electoral power. What elections since 1999 reveal Nigeria’s presidential elections have repeatedly shown that regional strength matters most when it forms part of a wider national coalition. Olusegun Obasanjo’s victories in 1999 and 2003 rested on support extending beyond his South-West origins. Umaru Musa Yar’Adua’s 2007 victory reflected the strength of the Peoples Democratic Party’s national machinery, while Goodluck Jonathan’s 2011 success drew on substantial support in the South and parts of the North. The 2015 election changed the political landscape. Muhammadu Buhari’s victory demonstrated that an opposition alliance could defeat an incumbent when it combined a formidable northern base with support in other parts of the country. The merger that produced the All Progressives Congress brought together political interests that had previously competed against one another. Buhari’s re-election in 2019 again showed the importance of maintaining a broad electoral coalition, even as the contest exposed persistent regional divisions. Tinubu’s 2023 victory followed another complex pattern. He won the presidency with 8,794,726 votes, ahead of Atiku’s 6,984,520 and Obi’s 6,101,533. The result was not the product of one region alone. It reflected a combination of Tinubu’s South-West support, votes from the North and the fragmentation of opposition support across several candidates. The lesson for 2027 is not that a candidate must reproduce one previous election formula. It is that regional dominance, without alliances and sufficient support elsewhere, can leave a candidate short of victory. The 2023 result that changed the game The last election exposed the risks of treating Nigeria’s regions as predictable voting blocs. Tinubu secured 2,542,979 votes in the South-West and 2,652,235 in the North-West, according to zonal breakdown. The figures showed that his northern performance was at least as important as his home-region strength. But the North-West did not vote as a single political unit. Atiku won Kaduna with 554,360 votes against Tinubu’s 399,293, while Rabiu Kwankwaso carried Kano for the New Nigeria Peoples Party. The split deprived the opposition of a unified northern vote while also limiting Tinubu’s ability to sweep the region. In the South-West, Obi’s narrow victory in Lagos demonstrated that Tinubu’s political base could be challenged. Obi’s strength in the South-East, meanwhile, did not translate into enough votes across the country to secure the presidency. Atiku’s support in parts of the North also proved insufficient. The distribution of votes made the difference. Had opposition support been concentrated behind a single candidate, the contest could have looked very different. Instead, three major contenders divided the electorate, while Tinubu assembled enough votes across several regions to finish first. Simon Kolawole, veteran journalist and political analyst, captured the strategic calculation in his assessment of the 2023 presidential election result. “Tinubu did well in ‘two out of three’ – the South-West and the core North,” he surmised. Kolawole also noted that a winning candidate might need sizeable support from the North-Central or South-South, or both, in addition to strength in the South-West and core North. His point is central to the next contest: Commanding two major blocs may create a strong platform, but it does not remove the need to win elsewhere. The constitutional hurdle also remains. Under Section 134 of the Constitution, a presidential candidate must secure the highest number of votes cast and at least one-quarter of the votes in no fewer than two-thirds of the states and the Federal Capital Territory. Regional strength must therefore translate into both a national plurality and geographically distributed support. The road to Aso Rock runs through alliances Tinubu enters the race with the advantages of incumbency, an established party structure and a political network built over decades. But those advantages will be tested by the electorate’s assessment of his administration, particularly over the economy, living costs, jobs and insecurity. The North-West could become a referendum on the government’s handling of insecurity and economic hardship. In the South-West, the president will need to defend his political base against discontent and opposition efforts to make inroads in urban centres and states where local dynamics favour challengers. Atiku faces the challenge of converting northern support into a broader national coalition, while Obi must demonstrate that his strong following in parts of the South and among younger voters can expand into regions where he was less competitive in 2023. Both will also have to confront the consequences of opposition fragmentation, party defections and competing presidential ambitions. The choice of running mates, the strength of state party organisations and agreements with influential political figures could prove decisive. So could turnout: A candidate with a smaller but highly mobilised support base may outperform a rival whose larger pool of registered supporters stays away from polling units. The North-West and South-West will undoubtedly shape the arithmetic of 2027. But neither region can deliver the presidency by itself, and neither should be treated as a guaranteed bloc for any candidate. The contest will be decided by who can turn voter numbers into actual ballots, withstand local political surprises and build alliances beyond familiar strongholds. For Tinubu, the challenge is to defend the coalition that brought him to power. For his challengers, it is to break that coalition without splitting their own support. Vanguard News The post INEC Figures: How North-West, South-West may hold key to Aso Rock appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Israeli forces raid 400 points in West Bank, 2,200 displaced
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 25 (MNA) – The Zionist regime's forces have attacked a number of 400 sites in the West Bank, occupied Palestinian territory, in which, 2,200 Palestinians were displaced.
The Zionist regime’s Minister of War Israel Katz, announced that Israeli forces have expelled approximately 2,000 Palestinians from their homes in Hebron, located in the West Bank.
Israeli forces turned Palestinian homes into barracks and observation posts after forcing residents to leave the city of Hebron on Saturday, day two of a military operation in the southern occupied West Bank, the official Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.
Troops took over homes in the Khallat Manna and Dahiyat al-Zaytoun areas of southern Hebron to be used as barracks, official Palestinian news agency Wafa reported, citing sources.
They also forced residents from homes in other neighborhoods and used the properties as observation posts, said sources.
The evictions follow the forced displacement of hundreds of families since Friday, amid extensive raids, road closures, and tight restrictions on movement.
Near Bethlehem, Israeli forces blocked dirt roads leading to the town of Tuqu and fired tear gas and stun grenades toward Palestinian vehicles traveling along rough alternative routes, Wafa reported, citing Palestinian security sources.

title: India, US and UAE hold trilateral talks in Mumbai, focus on energy security, connectivity and economic cooperation
body:
By Aroonim Bhuyan
Mumbai. India, the United States and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) on October 20 held a trilateral meeting in Mumbai to explore avenues for strengthening cooperation in energy security, connectivity, trade, investment, technology and regional affairs, amid continuing geopolitical uncertainty and the growing importance of resilient economic and supply-chain partnerships.



The meeting brought together External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and UAE Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan. The three leaders exchanged perspectives on areas of common interest, including regional energy security, economic priorities and contemporary international developments.
The discussions underscored the potential for India, the US and the UAE to build on their respective bilateral relationships and translate shared interests into greater practical cooperation across economic and strategic sectors.
Announcing the meeting, Jaishankar described it as a “useful exchange of perspectives” on energy, connectivity and contemporary developments. Rubio said the discussions focused on regional energy security and advancing the three countries' shared economic priorities.
While the public statements did not announce a specific trilateral agreement or a new institutional mechanism, the meeting provided an opportunity for the three governments to assess common challenges and identify areas in which closer coordination could advance their economic and regional interests.
Energy security and supply-chain resilience at the forefront
Energy security was among the most significant subjects of the meeting, given the strategic importance of West Asia to global oil and gas supplies and the exposure of international energy markets to regional conflicts and disruptions to maritime trade.
For India, the world’s major energy-consuming economies, reliable access to affordable energy is essential to sustaining economic growth, industrial expansion and domestic consumption. Its substantial dependence on imported crude oil and liquefied petroleum gas makes the security of supply routes, diversification of sources and stability in global energy markets important national priorities.
The UAE occupies a significant position in this equation as a major hydrocarbon producer, an established energy partner of India and a regional economic hub. The United States, meanwhile, is an important source of energy supplies, investment and technology, giving Washington, New Delhi and Abu Dhabi overlapping interests in strengthening the resilience of international energy networks.
The three countries’ discussions on regional energy security therefore carry significance beyond their immediate bilateral relationships. Closer coordination could help them address common concerns relating to supply disruptions, price volatility, maritime routes and the broader stability of energy markets.
The importance of these issues is particularly evident in the wider West Asian context, where tensions can affect shipping, energy infrastructure, insurance costs and the movement of goods through strategically important waterways. For India, disruptions to maritime traffic in and around the Persian Gulf can have consequences for both energy imports and the wider economy.
However, the publicly available accounts of the Mumbai meeting did not specify any new oil or gas supply commitments, joint energy projects or agreed measures for securing maritime routes. The emphasis was on exchanging views and advancing shared priorities rather than announcing a detailed operational programme.
Trade, investment and technology cooperation
Beyond energy, the meeting examined opportunities to deepen cooperation in the economy, trade, investment, technology and artificial intelligence (AI), according to the UAE Foreign Ministry’s account. The discussions reflected an interest in expanding the relationship beyond conventional diplomatic engagement towards more integrated economic partnerships.
For India, closer economic engagement with the US and UAE could help attract investment, widen access to international markets and strengthen its position in technology-intensive industries. For Washington and Abu Dhabi, India’s expanding economy, large consumer market and growing technological capabilities offer opportunities for commercial partnerships and investment.
The three countries also have complementary economic strengths. The US brings advanced technology, financial resources and a substantial market; the UAE provides capital, international business networks and logistics infrastructure; while India offers manufacturing capabilities, digital services, a skilled workforce and a large domestic market.
Cooperation in AI and emerging technologies could become an important dimension of this relationship. Potential areas of mutual interest include digital infrastructure, advanced computing, innovation, technology investment and the development of applications across industry and public services. However, the official account did not identify specific AI projects, funding commitments or technology agreements concluded during the trilateral meeting.
The UAE Foreign Ministry said the discussions aimed to deepen economic integration, expand regional and international cooperation and promote sustainable development.
Connectivity and regional economic integration
Connectivity was another central theme, reflecting the importance of transport networks, logistics infrastructure and trade corridors in linking India with the Gulf and wider international markets.
For India, stronger connectivity with the UAE and the US could support efforts to diversify export destinations, improve supply-chain efficiency and expand access to markets in West Asia, Europe and beyond. The UAE’s position as a major aviation, maritime and commercial hub makes it a particularly important partner in facilitating the movement of goods, capital and people.
The subject also carries wider strategic significance because connectivity is increasingly viewed as an instrument of economic resilience. Reliable transport links, efficient ports and logistics systems can reduce bottlenecks, improve the movement of essential commodities and make trade less vulnerable to disruptions along individual routes.
The US, India and the UAE have a shared interest in ensuring that economic links across the Indo-Pacific and West Asia remain reliable and commercially viable. The three governments could potentially build on their respective partnerships to promote investment in logistics, digital connectivity and trade-enabling infrastructure.
US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor highlighted this potential after the meeting, identifying energy, trade, technology and regional connectivity as areas where the three countries could advance cooperation and turn close ties into concrete results.
Nevertheless, no new connectivity corridor, infrastructure project or trilateral investment programme was publicly announced as an outcome of the meeting.
West Asia and the pursuit of regional stability
The trilateral engagement also provided an opportunity to exchange views on regional and international developments and discuss ways to strengthen security and stability.
West Asia remains particularly important to all three countries, although their strategic interests and immediate concerns differ. India has extensive economic and people-to-people links with Gulf countries and depends heavily on the region for energy supplies. The UAE seeks stability to protect its economic development, commercial networks and regional position. The US maintains substantial diplomatic, economic and security interests across the region.
These overlapping interests make dialogue among the three countries valuable at a time when geopolitical tensions can have consequences well beyond the immediate conflict zones.
For India, regional stability is closely linked to energy security, the safety of its nationals working abroad, maritime commerce and the uninterrupted movement of goods. For the UAE and the US, the stability of regional trade and energy networks is likewise an important economic and strategic concern.
