title: Tehran threatens strikes on energy, civilian targets, and nuclear escalation if attacked
body: Tehran is threatening to respond to a renewed US and Israeli air campaign with strikes on an expanded list of targets, including civilian infrastructure, according to a report by The Wall Street Journal.The warnings, issued publicly and over diplomatic communications, said that Iran would attack not only American bases and warships, but also natural energy infrastructure, natural gas pipelines, airports, and other civilian targets in the Persian Gulf region.Tehran has also threatened to utilize a new array of weapons, including nuclear bombs.According to Iran International, a media outlet opposed to the regime, the head of the Iranian parliament's International Affairs Committee, Mohammad-Saleh Jokar, asked "The Islamic Republic's authorities, in defense of the country and for the purpose of deterrence, to permit the use of deterrent weapons, including nuclear weapons, in the event of a US attack on Iran.” Jokar called for the suspension of Iran's cooperation with the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty in the event of an attack by the United States, according to Iran International. He said that countries hosting the US in their territories or airspace would face a "harsh response" and "pay a heavy price."Iran maintains stockpile of hundreds of thousands of missiles, dronesAnalysts, according to the WSJ, estimate Iran to hold hundreds of thousands of ballistic missiles, having resumed production in underground facilities.Iran is apparently leveraging its stockpile of missiles and drones - which remains at significant levels even after Operation Roaring Lion, Operation Epic Fury, and the succeeding blockade on the country - in an effort to deter an attack.In the most recent bout with Iran, significant damage was inflicted on US air bases, embassies, and fleets throughout the region. Energy and industrial facilities in the UAE, as well as gas plants and airports in Qatar, Dubai, Kuwait, and Bahrain were also hit.Tehran aims to cause even more pain in the case of a renewed campaign, especially at a time when interceptor missile stockpiles are under pressure in Israel and in US-aligned nations in the Gulf, following a suspended period of hostilities.Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi wrote an op-ed in the Financial Times, warning that new attacks “will put civilian lives and the well-being of all regional states and the global economy at great risk.”Despite the fact that a major portion of Iran's weapons stockpiles and defensive capabilities were degraded in the recent operations (the Pentagon said that up to 90% of drones, missiles, and naval industry was destroyed), analysts told the WSJ that Iran is more than willing to expand its retaliatory efforts.IRGC runs risk of overextending in retaliatory efforts“The consensus in Tehran now believes that deterrence requires imposing immediate, sustained and substantial costs on its adversaries,” said Sina Toossi, an Iran expert at the Center for International Policy."Iran runs the risk of overreaching if it tries to make good on all its threats," an expert on the Revolutionary Guard, Saeid Golkarat, told the WSJ. The country needs to carefully manage its shrinking stockpile of missiles, he assessed.“They certainly have the capability to inflict major damage to the region's energy and internet infrastructure,” said Washington Institute senior fellow Farzin Nadimi. “But if Iranians do that, they'll most likely lose their own in reciprocal attacks.”Negotiations have been deadlocked for months, and US President Donald Trump has repeatedly warned Iran that failure to come to an agreement could result in the US attacking Iran after midterm elections in early November.Israel, too, has stepped up its preparations for potential strikes against the Islamic regime in recent weeks, with conflicting reports saying that the IDF was planning to strike Iran on October 10 before being reeled in by US President Donald Trump.

title: An American lawyer helped open a backchannel between Biden’s White House and Putin. A Financial Times report details the exchanges, a later unofficial peace bid, and how it fell apart.
body: The Financial Times has published details of back-channel talks between U.S. leaders and Vladimir Putin in 2022 and early 2023. The effort began with Richard Conn, an American lawyer who had worked in Russia for many years and, after the war began, grew concerned that Putin might use nuclear weapons, with unpredictable consequences. In the fall of 2022, Conn worked through several Russian and American intermediaries to deliver a “conciliatory” message from Joe Biden’s administration to Putin. He later received a response to subsequent peace proposals. But by early 2023, official negotiators Yuri Ushakov and Eric Green had effectively brought Conn’s channel to an end, even before the Biden administration left office. The many subsequent U.S. attempts to negotiate a peaceful end to the war have involved other people and have yet to succeed. Who is Richard Conn, and how did he get involved in talks between Russia and the U.S.? Richard Conn is an American corporate lawyer and investor who began working in Russia in 1992, when he founded the Russian office of the law firm Latham & Watkins. The back channel originated in early March 2022, when Conn received a call from an unnamed Russian businessman who feared that the failure to capture Kyiv was pushing Vladimir Putin toward using tactical nuclear weapons in Ukraine. Conn decided he could use his longstanding contacts among American investors in Russia to establish direct contact between Washington and the Kremlin, bypassing Russia’s Foreign Ministry and other officials. Richard Conn To reach Putin, Conn contacted Bob Foresman, an American investor specializing in Russia. Foresman had held senior positions at several banks and investment firms with ties to Russia, including ING Barings, Renaissance Capital, Barclays, UBS, and Dresdner Bank. Through his work at Dresdner, Foresman knew Matthias Warnig, a longtime friend of Vladimir Putin. Before the fall of the Berlin Wall, Warnig was an economist and an officer in the Stasi . He began doing business in Russia in the early 1990s and eventually became head of the Nord Stream and Nord Stream 2 projects. People who spoke to the FT said Warnig was one of the few people with direct access to Putin, thanks to their longstanding relationship. Bob Foresman, October 2019 Matthias Warnig in January 2025 On the U.S. side, Conn enlisted Eric Green, an acquaintance who oversaw Russia policy at the U.S. National Security Council. They had discussed the idea of a back channel as early as 2021, shortly after Green took on that role. Eric Green, adviser to the U.S. president on Russia and Central Asia at the National Security Council under the Biden administration How events unfolded Immediately after speaking with the unnamed Russian businessman, Conn contacted Eric Green and proposed establishing direct contact with Putin to deliver a message from Joe Biden’s administration. This would bypass officials who, Conn suspected, might be shielding the Russian president from outside information to serve their own interests. Green agreed, but Conn did not manage to reach Putin until September 2022, after official talks in Istanbul had failed and Russian troops had withdrawn from the outskirts of Kyiv. The threat of tactical nuclear weapons being used had not disappeared entirely, but by then it had become clear that the threat had not materialized in the war’s first six months. On October 4, 2022, Conn and Foresman met with Warnig in Zurich. Afterward, Conn received a White House message from Green and passed it to Warnig at a separate meeting in Germany. The FT quoted it verbatim: “The US is not pursuing regime change. We’re not trying to destroy Russia. There is no existential threat. We’re trying to support international order and the UN. We want peace.” On October 26, at Frankfurt Airport, Warnig relayed Putin’s response, which he had written down in a notebook, to Conn and Foresman. The FT also presented this as a quotation, though it is not entirely clear whether these were Putin’s words or Warnig’s understanding of them: “I have no choice but to conduct military operations, but I am entirely open to negotiations. I want to discuss ways to resolve the problem. I want peace for Ukraine. We need to resolve this problem. I want a solution that will last 100 years. If there is no other choice, I will press ahead, knowing it will be painful. But I cannot turn back, and I am ready to fight.” The next day, speaking at a plenary session of the Valdai Discussion Club, Putin took a much more conciliatory tone on nuclear escalation. Discussing the possibility of Ukraine using a “dirty bomb,” he stressed that using nuclear weapons made “no political or military sense” for Russia. Conn and Foresman took this as a sign that their efforts had succeeded and the nuclear threat had diminished. The FT noted, however, that confidential talks on the subject were also taking place through official channels at around the same time, between Joe Biden’s national security adviser, Jake Sullivan, and Yuri Ushakov. Encouraged by this apparent success, Conn and Foresman decided to go beyond delivering a U.S. message to Putin and act as unofficial mediators between Russia and Ukraine. To do so, Conn needed businessman Michael Calvey to put him in touch with Ukrainian producer Alexander Rodnyansky, who knew Volodymyr Zelensky. At Conn and Foresman’s initiative, Warnig and Rodnyansky delivered peace proposals to the leaders of Ukraine and Russia. Under the proposals, Russia would withdraw its troops from most of the regions Putin had just annexed, with the border following the boundaries of Crimea and the parts of Donbas occupied before 2022. Ukraine would recognize Russian control over Crimea and grant Russia free passage along the “land bridge” to the peninsula. To ensure compliance with the ceasefire, Ukraine would receive protection from NATO countries, while Russia would begin discussions with the U.S. on a separate agreement on security guarantees. The FT reported that Warnig delivered these proposals to Putin on February 1, 2023, and that Putin had “gone through the document line by line, circling passages and scribbling comments.” Putin ruled out Ukraine joining NATO but allowed for EU membership, with some other military security guarantee as an alternative to the alliance, “like the one discussed at the Istanbul talks .” Meanwhile, Rodnyansky had great difficulty persuading Zelensky and Andriy Yermak even to hear the proposals developed at Conn’s initiative, the FT reported. In early 2023, the Ukrainian military was riding high after liberating large parts of the Kherson and Kharkiv regions and was actively preparing for its 2023 counteroffensive. Zelensky and his chief of staff refused to make any of the concessions in Conn’s proposals. The parallel talks effectively ended on February 18, 2023, when Conn and Foresman met with Warnig again in Zurich. Warnig said Putin had told Ushakov and several other senior Russian officials about the back channel. Putin also demanded that Ushakov confirm with Jake Sullivan that the American businessmen really did represent U.S. interests. According to Warnig’s account of what Putin told him, Sullivan did not confirm that Conn’s channel was authorized and said official contacts between the U.S. and Russia were sufficient to discuss these issues. The success attributed to the negotiators Conn brought together thus rests solely on the timing: “nuclear de-escalation,” if it happened at all in October 2022, followed shortly after Matthias Warnig delivered a direct message to Vladimir Putin. The FT article includes one personal detail with no direct bearing on the talks or their outcome. It recounts a private meeting between Warnig and Putin after Warnig came under European sanctions and encountered many difficulties in his daily life in Germany. Even the approximate date of the meeting is unclear, except that it definitely took place after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. At the meeting, Warnig and Putin sat at opposite ends of the famous 33-foot table in the Kremlin that the Russian president used to keep his distance from others during the COVID-19 pandemic. Putin was sympathetic to Warnig’s difficulties under sanctions and suggested that he move his family to Russia, but Warnig declined. Warnig, for his part, said Putin’s strength had always been his personal touch, but prolonged isolation had robbed him of it. “Power is a drug,” Putin said in response. title: Kimi Antonelli takes pole in Austin: Here's what he need to be crowned champion at US Grand Prix
body: A little over two years ago, just after his 18 th birthday, Kimi Antonelli crashed at Monza in his first-ever Formula One practice session. Today, he stands on the brink of the world championship and could become the sport’s youngest title winner in Austin, Texas, this weekend. That dream moved a step closer after he claimed pole position on Saturday. The Mercedes driver beat Red Bull's Max Verstappen by 0.179 seconds, with the Dutchman's teammate Isack Hadjar third ahead of Ferrari's Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton. Five drivers can still beat him on paper, even if most of them are clinging to the faintest of hopes. Six races remain, and all of them are traditional grand prix weekends as Singapore was the last Sprint weekend. Each GP win is worth 25 points, second place is 18, third is 15 and so on down to a single point for finishing 10th. That leaves a maximum of 150 points on the table. If two drivers finish the season level on points, the title goes to the one with more race wins. Teammate George Russell remains Antonelli’s closest challenger, while seven-time world champion Hamilton, four-time champion Verstappen, Ferrari’s Leclerc and defending champion Lando Norris are still technically in contention. Here is what each of the six contenders needs to finish the season as world champion. Kimi Antonelli Where he stands: First on 340 points with eight GP wins. What he needs: Antonelli can win the title in Austin this Sunday if he wins the race and Russell finishes ninth or lower, and Hamilton finishes fifth or lower. Victory would take Antonelli to 365 points and nine GP wins this season. Even if Russell subsequently won all five remaining races to draw level on points, Antonelli would still prevail, as he has secured more race wins. If the Italian finishes second or lower in Austin, his next opportunity comes a week later in Mexico City, on November 1. View this post on Instagram George Russell Where he stands: Second on 238 points, 102 points behind. What he needs: Russell’s best-case scenario involves him winning all six remaining races, which would take him to 388 points. Even then, Antonelli would have to score 48 points or fewer across those six races, which is essentially finishing sixth every weekend. Russell began the year as favourite, considering his experience and the brilliance of the car, and things started brightly for the Briton, who won the opening race in Australia. Since then, reliability issues and his own style of driving have seen him usurped by his younger, more daring teammate. Lewis Hamilton Where he stands: Third on 229 points, 111 behind Antonelli. What he needs: If Hamilton wins all six remaining races, he will finish on 379 points. Antonelli would then have to score 38 points or fewer. In Austin, Hamilton would be eliminated from title contention if Antonelli wins and the Brit finishes fifth or lower. He is also out if Antonelli outscores him by 14 points or more. Hamilton’s second year at Ferrari has seen him be more competitive but he has still only won once this season. He would need six wins in a row and a total collapse from the young driver who replaced him at Mercedes for him to take the crown. Realistically, the chase for a record eighth title will have to wait another year. Six winners in 2026. Six still left in the fight. Can anyone hunt down Kimi? 🎯 #F1 #USGP pic.twitter.com/LwnEKW0ScR — Formula 1 (@F1) October 19, 2026 Max Verstappen Where he stands: Fourth on 221 points, 119 behind. What he needs: If Verstappen wins all the remaining races, he will finish on 371 points. Antonelli would then have to score 30 points or fewer, which is worse than seventh place every weekend. If Antonelli scored exactly 31 points, they would tie on 371 points with eight wins each and second places would settle it. In Austin, if Antonelli wins the race, Verstappen is eliminated from title contention wherever he finishes. There may be little hope for Verstappen. He spent most of the year struggling to get the car to compete and did not win a grand prix until October, in Sepang. Red Bull’s progress over the last few weekends has been exceptional, and the burst of form has dragged him back into the title conversation. Antonelli has admitted it unsettles him. It is a warning for next season, but it has probably come too late for this year. Charles Leclerc Where he stands: Fifth, on 215 points, 125 behind. What he needs: If Leclerc wins all six remaining races, he will finish on 365 points. Antonelli would then have to score 24 points or fewer, which is essentially finishing P8 in every remaining race. Leclerc has virtually no hope of winning the championship and his teammate Hamilton has produced better performances this season. His early exit at Monza, Ferrari’s home race, perfectly demonstrated how the season has drifted away from him. Lando Norris Where he stands: Sixth on 201 points, 139 behind What he needs: If Norris wins all six races, he finishes on 351 points. Antonelli would then have to score 10 points or fewer across six weekends. In Austin, Norris would need to outscore the Italian by at least 15 points just to remain in contention.

title: Russia turning temporarily occupied territories into criminal enclaves – Ukraine's intelligence
body:
That is according to the Ukrainian Defense Ministry's Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR), Ukrinform reports.
"The situation in Ukraine's temporarily occupied territories is deteriorating – Russian invaders are effectively turning the subjugated regions into criminal enclaves where banditry and lawlessness prevail," the statement reads.
The catastrophic situation in the temporarily occupied territories is being documented even in the aggressor state's classified reports and assessments.
In particular, Moscow considers the illegal arms and explosives trade, chronic alcoholism among Russian invaders, which leads to so-called street brawls and violent clashes, a rise in cybercrime, and the embezzlement of budget funds to be risk factors for maintaining control over the occupied territories. Due to Russia's economic problems, the so-called "administrations" are receiving increasingly less funding.
The population lives in constant fear because of the strict counterintelligence regime, the threat of violence from war criminals serving in the Russian army, and repression by security agencies. This further fuels negative attitudes toward the invaders.
Meanwhile, living standards are declining. Poverty and devastation, a lack of jobs, and shortages of food, medicines, fuel and basic necessities are accelerating the exodus of residents.
Against this backdrop, Russia is seeking to increase the volume of positive propaganda, particularly about so-called "socioeconomic projects," "birth rate promotion programs" and similar initiatives.
At the same time, the invaders are seeking to isolate residents of the temporarily occupied territories as much as possible from alternative communication channels, including those run by individuals and organizations designated as so-called "foreign agents" in Russia.
"To strengthen control over the temporarily occupied territories, the Kremlin's leaders intend, among other measures, to tighten oversight of Russian occupation administrations, including collaborators holding positions in the occupation authorities. Moscow does not fully trust even the most pro-Russian among them," HUR said.

title: Conflict with Russia to cost Ukraine over $470 mln per day
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 25 (MNA) – Ukraine’s military spending in 2027 will amount to $473 million per day if the conflict with Russia continues, according to a media estimate.
Ukraine’s military spending in 2027 will amount to $473 million per day if the conflict with Russia continues, according to TASS calculations based on the Ukrainian Finance Ministry’s reports.
This figure refers solely to military expenditures, that is, costs related to payments to active-duty service members and the procurement of military equipment, ammunition, and gear. It does not include social spending to support former servicemen and the families of those killed in action, the construction of fortifications (if not carried out by the Defense Ministry), or any other government expenditures. Total military spending for the year will amount to nearly $173 billion.
In 2026, Ukraine’s military spending averaged about $300 million per day, excluding the Defense Ministry's additional requests at the end of the year. If these requests are included, the total rises to $370 million.

title: UFC 333: Volkanovski weighs up options as he and Yan retain titles after night of Abu Dhabi brilliance
body: Two champions walked into Abu Dhabi on Saturday. By Sunday morning, both had left with their title belts still wrapped firmly around their waists. Alexander Volkanovski cemented his place as the greatest featherweight in history with a TKO victory over Movsar Evloev at UFC 333, while Petr Yan retained his bantamweight belt with a unanimous decision over Merab Dvalishvili. Volkanovski had promised his wife he would not make her suffer on the sidelines at Etihad Arena, and the Australian was as good as his word with a second-round stoppage of Evloev. “It feels good to get a finish. I actually promised the missus – it was our wedding anniversary on Wednesday – I promised her a quick one so she wasn't stressing on the sidelines, so there you go.” Evloev looked way out of his league as he suffered the first defeat of his 21-fight career. Volkanovski looked better than ever. “He’s a great fighter. He was undefeated for a reason, but I just said I’m the right guy for that job,” Volkanovski said. Evloev conceded it was a “terrible fight” but that he was grateful to have shared a cage with the champion. “He’s a good one. Older, stronger, better, he’s truly a legend. I’m grateful for this opportunity to be here. Alex … great champion.” It was billed as striker against grappler. Volkanovski had encouraged Evloev to stick to his wrestling, saying no one could take him down, let alone keep him there. The Russian put that to the test three times in the opening round. The champion was up to the task every time. Evloev went to the well again in the second. Volkanovski showed the cunning of a fox in reversing it, proving he is no slouch on the ground either. It didn’t take long for Volkanovski to find his rhythm on his feet. He sliced Evloev open with a sledgehammer left hand that dropped the Russian. Volkanovski smelt blood, and after some vicious ground-and-pound that rendered Evloev helpless, the fight was waved off. COOKED HIM 😎 @AlexVolkanovski closes out #UFC333 with a RD2 finish! [ LIVE NOW on @ParamountPlus ] pic.twitter.com/noP5sd8ISz — UFC (@ufc) October 24, 2026 “I knew the ref would have to stop it when he covered up like that,” Volkanovski said, adding that he had no plans to retire after extending his record to 29 wins against four losses. “I’m choosing to do this. I said if I didn’t take too much damage, we probably keep going, so maybe we keep going.” Victory meant Volkanovski, 38, surpassed the great Jose Aldo for the most title wins in the featherweight division, with nine. “I don't really care about this,” he said, pointing to his belt, one that he has now defended six times across his two title reigns. “I really don't. “I just care about overcoming challenges. A guy that was undefeated in front of me, to overcome that and beat him, and again, getting through camps, means so much more to me.” The question now turns to who is next. Volkanovski says he has no plans to retire while also suggesting he could step up a division to fight lightweight champion Justin Gaethje, with the loser calling time on their career. Jean Silva or the winner of the bout between Aljamian Sterling and Kevin Vallejos is also a potential opponent at 145 pounds. “I guess we've just got to weigh the options. I’m in a pretty good position when you’ve got the president [ Dana White ] saying that you could pretty much do whatever you want.” Yan and Dvalishvili's epic third fight If the main event was a mismatch, the co-main event was an epic. Yan-Dvalishvili 3 lived up to its billing, with two of the greatest bantamweights delivering a fight for the ages. The head-to-head record read one win apiece, with the previous encounter seeing Yan dethrone Dvalishvili as bantamweight champion. The Russian took his time to get going, forced to fend off the relentless Georgian’s takedown attempts for the first two rounds. When he did let his hands go midway through the third round, they found their mark. Dvalishvili was slowed by punishing combinations and body shots that took the wind out of his sails. All three judges gave it to Yan, much to the delight of the crowd, who clearly backed the Russian. Debate's over 🫳 @PetrYanUFC puts on an instant classic to retain his belt! @VisitAbuDhabi | @InAbuDhabi | #InAbuDhabi [ #UFC333 | LIVE NOW on @ParamountPlus ] pic.twitter.com/wFfqFYrsCS — UFC (@ufc) October 24, 2026 “I’m really happy about the way the fight went, about getting the victory, about being able to do it in front of all of these fans that came out to support me,” Yan said. “It's an incredible feeling. I feel great.” Dvalishvili’s game plan was clear from the outset: to continually shoot at the champion. He scored a few towards the end of the first round, with Yan unable to set himself or fire anything in return. The second round followed much the same pattern, with Dvalishvili shooting at every opportunity. He took Yan down several times, although the champion was quickly back to his feet. Dvalishvili began the third energetically, but was left wincing from a punishing kick to the liver. It was a tactic that served Yan well in their second fight in December. Dvalishvili backed off and attempted to shake it off, but it gave Yan confidence, and his punches started to find their target more frequently. Round four saw the pendulum swing in Yan’s favour. Dvalishvili’s takedown attempts lacked conviction, with Yan easily able to fend them off. His striking accuracy proved decisive, with his left hand, in particular, finding the mark at will. Yan closed out the fight strongly, landing pummeling combinations punctuated by one flying knee that busted open Dvalishvili's forehead. On weathering Dvalishvili’s early storm, Yan said: “Diamonds are made under extreme pressure. I could have just given up, but I had to go through it. This is what I do.” For Dvalishvili, it was a second successive defeat to Yan. “The Machine” never stopped coming forward but again had no answer to the champion’s superior striking. “I can do better,” he said. “Congratulations to Petr Yan. He beat me today; he’s the better man. Congratulations to him.”

title: Saudi strikes martyr 193 in Yemen, wound 468
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 25 (MNA) – Saudi attacks on Yemen since the escalation began have martyred 193 people and wounded 468, including 62 children martyred and 122 wounded, Yemen's health ministry spokesman said.
Saudi attacks on Yemen since the escalation began have martyred 193 people and wounded 468, Yemen's health ministry spokesman said, according to Al-Masirah network.
He said 62 children were martyred and 122 others wounded in the attacks. The ministry also said 24 women were killed and 59 others wounded.

title: Obama unloads on Trump while stumping for Democrats ahead of midterms
body: US President Donald Trump has been telling voters to view the midterm elections as if he were on the ballot, and on Saturday, October 14, one of his Democratic predecessors did just that. Ten days out from the elections that will determine control of the closely divided Congress, Barack Obama took to the campaign trail to accuse the Republican president of corruption, deride his strategy for Iran , and skewer the gilded aesthetic he has applied to White House renovations. Obama stumped for Democratic candidates at rallies in Cleveland and Detroit, lampooning the Trump administration. Campaigning in Michigan for US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, Obama framed the November 3 vote as a “circuit breaker” to “at least rein in some of the foolishness” of Trump’s presidency. “We got to flip that circuit breaker, bring some accountability to this government,” Obama said. Obama, president from 2009 until Trump began his first term in 2017, remains one of the most popular figures among Democrats. They hope that bringing him into the race can fire up their supporters for a tight US Senate race in which El-Sayed faces Republican Mike Rogers, a former US representative. The former president obliged the Michigan crowd by playing to Democrats’ frequently repeated criticisms of Trump and of Republicans’ willingness to go along with him. “We have never seen a president excel in straight-up grifting, on your dime, like this,” Obama said. “Never seen a president so intent on selling favors like this…. Now the party seems to stand for corrupt government, or inept government, or no government.” Must Read Three issues defining the 2026 US midterm elections The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. A Reuters/Ipsos poll in August found that 63% of Americans think the president and his family have inappropriately profited from cryptocurrency since he returned to the White House last year and that 69% believe his policy decisions are influenced by his private business dealings. Obama also ridiculed the administration’s claims of victory against Iran. He argued that the war has given Iran more economic leverage because its threats to attack shipping in the Strait of Hormuz have unsettled oil exporters. “Iran now has veto power over the Strait of Hormuz, where oil goes through to get to the world,” Obama said. The former president also accused the Trump administration of emphasizing unimportant matters, sarcastically calling Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth someone “laser-focused on important matters like the jawline and testosterone levels of our troops” and ridiculing White House renovations as tacky. “He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory,” Obama said. – Rappler.com

title: Drought, fire and high diesel prices 'addin' up tough' for Oregon ranchers
body:
Katie Baltzor rides her side-by-side among the black angus cattle she raises near her home outside of Hines, Oregon. Anna King/NWPB hide caption
HARNEY COUNTY, ORE. - Late bloomin' rabbitbrush – wads of swaying ochre – stud the roadsides and steep eroded-basalt buttes rising up from the basin floor outside of Hines, Oregon.
In a broad open field, horses munch standing hay as Katie Baltzor watches her black angus cattle on this fall day.
We've ridden out here in a side-by-side vehicle – it's like an overgrown golf cart with a pickup bed in the back made for rough ranch work.
All the animals are quiet. Happy. With their heads down grazing.
"You see that horse, how he's got speckled colors?" said Baltzor with a smile in her voice. "Looks like country gravy, I guess that's why they called him Gravy."
Diesel prices remain near record highs , despite recent actions by President Trump as the mid-term elections get closer.
The high prices are adding to pain for cattle ranchers in western states, who were already struggling with persistent drought . And in Harney County, where bovines outnumber the people – by a lot - there's many mouths to feed.
Sir Yukon Gold, or just Yukon – like the potato – is a 10-year-old palomino Quarterhorse gelding. He's grazing with the other Baltzor geldings in a field south of Hines, Oregon. Anna King/NWPB hide caption
"Fuel costs, parts costs, everything has gone up," Baltzor said. "People say that prices have gone up, but calf prices (paid to ranchers) have (too).
"But calf prices still have not kept up with inflation – and so that's what makes it tough for ranchers to keep in business. If everything else goes up and cattle prices don't, you're just spinning your wheels a bit – you better like what you do."
Baltzor's face shows a life spent working in the desert sun. Her long ponytail glints a bit reddish in the afternoon light.
Baltzor and her husband Keith, had just finished riding a bunch of about 150 hundred head of their cattle down Highway 205 on horseback from another pasture.
"Sometimes it is dicey," she said. "There were cars starting to come through our bunch of cows … unfortunately a woman opened up her door and jumped out. And those cows would not go near her. It scared them, they wanted to come back anyway. Then she got out again and still was stopped. People just don't understand, they don't know. When you see a herd of cows and they're coming towards you, don't stop, just keep coming through them."
Baltzor was moving the cattle so they could work them closer to home. They are going preg-check the mother cows to make sure they're carrying new babies, and give all the cattle and calves vaccinations and dewormer.
Dramatic steep eroded-basalt buttes rise up from outside Crane, Oregon. Drought has heavily impacted Oregon with low snowpack and little rain meaning little irrigation water, and fueling massive wildfires this year. Anna King/NWPB hide caption
But for Baltzor, this year is already addin' up tough. The places where Baltzor typically ranges her cattle in the mountains were ravaged by record-size wildfires this summer, robbing them of the grass the herds usually eat. Baltzor, and hired riders, had to hoof it through heavy smoke into the mountains to extract their cattle from the path of the fires.
"So all our cows, instead of coming home the second week of September, we had to bring them home the third week in July," Baltzor said. "Other folks had to do the same. And some people had to start feeding – we didn't, we had the rakebrunch."
Rakebunching means just raking pasture hay into piles, and leaving it in the field for animals.
Now, it's gonna take time 'til the mountain grass comes back. In some areas where her neighbors' ground has been burned over, it's taken years for them to be able to return their animals to graze, Baltzor said.
"Where are we gonna run cows?" she said. "Some of those fields that burned, the allotments you can't go back on them for a couple of years. And because so many acres burned in Harney County, it's not just my husband and myself that have this issue."
With no grass, ranchers need hay to feed their cattle. But the drought that set the stage for the fires has dried up Baltzor's hay meadows, too.
"So, the meadows were very short," Baltzor said. "Some of them got some water and you were able to cut a little bit. Some of them didn't even get water and you couldn't even cut some of the fields."
A round bale of hay sits waiting to be collected near New Princeton, Oregon. Anna King/NWPB hide caption
Here's where the high diesel prices add up tough – what little hay there is, is a lot more expensive to harvest.
"The tractors, you know everything is diesel, and it's expensive and it costs a lot to keep them running," she said.
Haying typically takes several passes with a tractor – you have to cut it, turn the windrows to sun dry, and then bale them and stack them. Each time they fill the tractor with diesel now, it's about $300.
"And so just like this year when we were trying to decide, 'Should we try to run and bale some of this hay? Or it's not very good, it's very light, should we just rakebunch it?" she said. "Part of that was looking at the cost of diesel."
Rakebunching means going over it fewer times with the tractor. They also rakebunched because they feared more wildfire would force them back to their homeplace with the drought. Rakebunching is a good solution for the late summer and fall, but it will leave them short of hay later.
"But the bigger problem becomes next year," Baltzor said. "If we don't get the precipitation, then we don't have the irrigation water and then we'd be looking at purchasing hay."
Purchasing hay can mean driving long distances to get it, or having it delivered, in big trucks that burn a lot of diesel.
Baltzor drives her side-by-side through grass the color of a flaxen palomino.
Allen Farnsworth leans in for a closer look at some cattle at the auction in Vale, Oregon. This year's calves are penned and weighed after being sold at auction Anna King/NWPB hide caption
This year's high diesel prices come at a time when the price of beef in the supermarket is also way up. Ranchers can sell their calves now for pretty good money. But, "It's not something you just do," Baltzor said. "You keep a heifer."
Heifers are young females, ranchers like to keep some or all of the ones born every year, so they can produce more calves, and replace cows that are too old for that. It's a longer term investment.
"It's two years [for a heifer to be bred and] before you have a calf," she said. "You know, a product. It's not that they're going to have a calf right away. And sometimes people don't understand that."
Auctioneer Phil Roe auctions off a group of cattle to buyers in Vale, Oregon. Anna King/NWPB hide caption
Baltzor said she and her husband and ranch partner have switched to gas pickups to try to save a little on diesel. But she said every ranch here has a different break point
"Do you have vehicle loans?" Baltzor said. "Do you have cow loans? Do you have land loans?"
Baltzor said she and her husband worked outside jobs for years to be able to build their herd and accumulate land.
"It will pencil for us," Baltzor said. "Because we're lucky we worked really hard not to have debt. But not everyone's that lucky. And when we first started out we had a lot of debt …. Nobody gave it to us. We had to find places to rent, and we had to buy cattle. And we had to take out loans to do all of that."
On the way out of the pasture, a metal gate squawks a lot as it's closed and then clanks shut, held fast by a rope.
"There's different ways to get into the cattle business, and ours wasn't the easiest way," Baltzor said. "But I think it's very worthwhile. Because you appreciate what you have."
But times are lean for many in southeast Oregon, and now – here comes winter.

title: How Manny Pacquiao impacted UFC’s Aaron Pico
body: MANILA, Philippines – Manny Pacquiao’s influence stretches far beyond boxing, reaching athletes across combat sports. Among them is UFC featherweight Aaron Pico, who once came close to sharing the ring with the Filipino boxing legend. Pico, known for his elite freestyle wrestling, trained with Pacquiao’s longtime coach Freddie Roach at the renowned Wild Card Boxing Club in California, where he sharpened his striking skills. In 2017, the highly touted American prospect even had a chance to travel to the Philippines and serve as Pacquiao’s sparring partner ahead of his bout against Australian boxer Jeff Horn. But the plan fell through because Pico had a professional fight scheduled around the same time. “The first time I sparred at Wild Card, or during one of the few times I sparred there, Freddie was watching,” Pico told Rappler. “When he was preparing for the fight against Jeff Horn, Freddie asked me, ‘Do you want to go to the Philippines and be a sparring partner for Manny? I think you’d be a good look for Manny in preparation for Jeff Horn.’” Looking back, Pico wishes he had taken the opportunity to work with Pacquiao, who went on to lose to Horn by controversial unanimous decision in Brisbane. The chance would have been about more than just a sparring session for Pico. For him, it would have meant learning from a living legend whose intensity and passion made him one of the most exciting fighters of his generation. “Looking back, I probably would have just said, ‘Hey, I’ll go and spar Manny,’ because he’s a living legend. It would have been a great experience for me,” Pico said. “His intensity was something I could really pick up. It’s just unfortunate it did not happen, but I got a taste of that passion from Freddie.” Pico returned to the UFC spotlight on Sunday, October 25 (Manila time), needing just over a minute to TKO Guinea’s Losene Keita in their featherweight fight, an event made available in the Philippines via ESPN on Disney+. Pico improved his MMA record to 15-5, winning back-to-back fights. Keita, who previously split his last four, slipped to 17-3. The 30-year-old American was originally scheduled to fight Arnold Allen, who withdrew because of an injury, paving the way for Keita to step in on short notice. Even without getting the chance to spar with Pacquiao, Pico has carried fond memories of watching the Filipino icon fight. Growing up in California, Pico experienced the same fight-night tradition familiar to many Filipino families. Whenever Pacquiao competed, relatives and friends gathered to watch, turning his bouts into major occasions. As Pacquiao took on some of the best Mexican and American fighters of his era, his relentless pace and explosive style captivated a young Pico. “He didn’t really influence my fighting style, but as a fan, I enjoyed watching him,” Pico said. “Whenever Manny fought, my family would get together for big barbecues, and everyone would get really excited, especially me.” “He was such an exciting fighter to watch.” As Pico looks to establish himself among the UFC’s top featherweights, he hopes to deliver the same kind of excitement that made Pacquiao a global attraction. He knows the sports are different, but the goal remains the same: give fans a fight worth watching. “His fights were never boring. You knew that when you paid for the pay-per-view, you were going to get your money’s worth,” Pico said. “That’s what I’m trying to do, too, here in the UFC.” – with a report from Drew Lo/Rappler.com

title: Almost 283,000 Russian soldiers killed in Ukraine identified by media investigation
body:
Russian independent media outlet Mediazona, in collaboration with the BBC Russian service, has confirmed the identities of 282,993 Russian military personnel killed in Ukraine.
Since Mediazona last updated the figures in early October, the names of 6,880 Russian soldiers were added to the list of those killed. The latest count covers confirmed military deaths from Feb. 24, 2022, through Oct. 23, 2026.
The Kyiv Independent cannot immediately verify the reporting.
The journalists caution that the actual figures are likely significantly higher, as their findings are based on publicly available information, including obituaries, social media posts by relatives, regional news reports, and statements from local authorities.
As of Oct. 23, 2026, the deaths of 7,920 officers serving in the Russian military and other security services had been independently verified.
Officers have accounted for a shrinking share of confirmed Russian military deaths since the start of the full-scale invasion, according to Mediazona. During the initial phase of the war, when Russia relied heavily on professional contract troops, officers represented as much as 10% of those killed. By November 2024, their share had fallen to just 2–3%.
The decline reflects changes in battlefield tactics and Russia's growing reliance on recruited volunteer infantry, who face a substantially higher risk of being killed than their commanding officers.
Although estimates differ, Western intelligence assessments and independent research have generally put Russian military casualties significantly above Ukrainian losses. The Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimated in July 2026 that Russia had suffered approximately 1.4 million casualties since the start of the full-scale invasion, compared with 525,000–625,000 for Ukraine.
"Russian fatalities in Ukraine are more than four times greater than all U.S. fatalities in all wars combined since World War II, and more than nine times greater than all Soviet and Russian fatalities in all wars combined since World War II," CSIS wrote.

title: Ukraine loses nearly 14% of its locomotives in less than two years
body:
MOSCOW, October 25. /TASS/. From January 2025 through September 2026, Ukraine lost about 500 locomotives, about 14% of its total, according to TASS calculations based on the Ukrainian government’s information.
The majority of the losses, around 300, occurred in 2026. Since February 2022, Ukraine has lost approximately 600 locomotives, roughly 17% of its total.
As of February 2022, Ukraine had nearly 3,500 locomotives of various types and ages, including electric and diesel, making it difficult to estimate the cost of the losses. However, replacing the lost units with new ones will cost Kiev at least two billion dollars.

title: Almost 1,000 arrested as clashes follow another day of mass protests across France
body: Nearly 1,000 arrests were made as hundreds of thousands of people took part in another day of protests across France which were followed by some clashes late on Saturday, officials have said. After a day of largely peaceful demonstrations, police fired tear gas and water cannon to disperse protesters in a number of cities including Paris, while barricades were set alight in Marseille and people ripped boards from a shop in Bordeaux. But officials have so far managed to avoid rioting and looting on the scale seen last weekend, which resulted in some of the worst scenes of disorder in France’s modern history. The interior ministry said an estimated 410,000 people protested on Saturday, while the unions put the number at about 800,000. Some 70,000 police officers were deployed and restrictions imposed in several cities to prevent the latest protests over the cost of living and poor school conditions from descending into the kind of chaos which saw officers outnumbered, hundreds of businesses looted and buildings torched. President Emmanuel Macron had decreed earlier this week that only demonstrations organised by a recognised trade unions would be permitted. Hundreds of people have been jailed for vandalism, arson and looting after fast-track court hearings in recent days. Clashes between protesters and riot police in Paris erupted at the end of a peaceful march from the city’s Porte d’Italie towards Porte de Vincennes on Saturday, where the police operation included an elite unit that usually deals with organised crime and counter-terrorism. Some protesters were seen erecting makeshift barricades and pelting officers with projectiles, while police baton-charged groups of masked youths who were smashing the windows of a car dealership. French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said that “several thousand radical activists gathered at the rear of the march, including around 500 individuals identified as rioters”, the AFP news agency reported. In the southern port of Marseille, rubbish bins were set ablaze and metal sheets used to block streets. A law enforcement vehicle was seen driving through a burning barricade in France’s second-largest city. Meanwhile, some protesters in dark clothing and face coverings were seen taking boards off a building to build a street barricade in the southern city of Bordeaux. In Lyon, police used tear gas grenades to disperse a crowd which had reportedly gathered in an area deemed off-limits by the local prefecture. “There were around 150 of us, mostly secondary school and university students. Then the tear gas came almost immediately. You could barely see anything in the street,” said one protester in France’s third-largest city. Nuñez said late in the day that nearly 1,000 people had been arrested, a number he said would increase. The minister also said two people had been “seriously injured”: one in the south-western city of Toulouse, and another one in Clermont-Ferrand, central France. Earlier, a peaceful protester in Paris who gave her name as Zelie told the BBC people had taken to the streets because they were “really frustrated” and had been “suffering a lot” since Macron came to office. “They keep us quiet. They take our money, they tax us a lot and we can’t say anything. Today we are in the streets because it’s been too long, it’s been too much,” the 26-year-old said. Two masked teenage protesters, who did not want to give their names, also said their generation was in despair and felt abandoned by the government. “I think looting is really not good,” one of the demonstrators said of last Saturday’s disorder. “But it’s because of poverty and the violence of the police.” He added that the protests would end “when we have a response to our demands. We really want a change in France”. Meanwhile, some 13,000 people joined a rally against the hard-right National Rally party in the north-central city of Orléans which proceeded peacefully. Mass protests triggered by similar issues as in France also rocked several other European cities on Saturday. In Albania’s capital Tirana, riot police fired tear gas to disperse thousands of anti-government demonstrators, while clashes were also reported in Belgium’s capital Brussels. In Milan, northern Italy, a major security operation including hundreds of soldiers alongside police prevented protesters gathering in the city. Many had feared a repeat of violent scenes last week when some started fires, smashed windows and looted shops.

title: Microsoft Open-Sources Agensh: A Multi-Agent Harness for 1,024 Agents
body: Microsoft Research has open-sourced Agensh , a decentralized harness for large teams of coding agents. The Agensh multi-agent harness removes the central orchestrator that most agent frameworks depend on. Every worker picks its own sub-task, shares findings and merges code into a common Git repo. On ProgramBench, the team scaled the setup from 1 agent to 1,024 agents. TL;DR A Harness : Tested from 1 to 1,024 agents. Each worker gets a 272,000-token input and 128,000-token output limit. Runs on: Linux with Docker Compose. Single node by default (8 workers). The 1,024-agent run used 16 nodes, 64 agents each. Workers have a 64 GiB memory ceiling. Performance: more agents raised scores on all 5 hardest ProgramBench tasks, and reached them sooner. Best: 79.59% pandoc pass rate with 32 agents on GPT-6.1-sol. GPT-5.6-sol hit 55.06% with 1,024 agents. Worst: the 5-task mean reached only 28.78% at 128 agents. Going from 1 to 8 agents added 1.37 points. What is Agensh? Agensh is a multi-agent harness from Microsoft Research that coordinates many LLM agents without a lead agent. The target problem is the orchestrator ceiling. In orchestrator-worker designs, a lead agent plans, assigns and merges all work. The research paper cites Claude Code agent teams, Codex sub-agents, Copilot fleet and Kimi Agent Swarm as examples. Agensh lets the workers do that coordination themselves. How does the Agensh cooperation loop work? Each worker runs the same 5-step loop, concurrently and asynchronously: Gather context: read the goal, peer progress, messages and findings. Claim a sub-task: post a CLAIM, then settle overlaps by direct message. Take action: work locally with tools and post useful findings early. Verify results: check the work against the sub-task’s acceptance criteria. Merge progress: merge into the shared repo, post an update, then repeat. Three services connect the workers. Gitea hosts the shared workspace, with branches, PRs and merge conflicts. Mattermost carries a team channel plus direct messages for urgent collisions. A shared context board, adapted from DeLM , stores typed notes: OBSERVED, FACT, FAIL, CLAIM and PATCH_SUMMARY. The loop lives in the prompt, not in runtime code. Every worker gets the same prompt except its ID. Agensh sits on top of a single-agent harness. The experiments used GitHub Copilot CLI . The research paper states thin adapters can connect other harnesses, such as Claude Code. (function(){var f=document.getElementById("agx-frame");window.addEventListener("message",function(e){if(e.data&&e.data.agxHeight&&f&&e.source===f.contentWindow){f.style.height=e.data.agxHeight+"px";}});})(); How well does Agensh scale on ProgramBench? Microsoft team tested the 5 hardest ProgramBench tasks: FFmpeg, gromacs, pandoc, PHP-src and ctags. Agents rebuild each program from its observed behavior. They work offline, within 6 hours. Reference repos range from 2,767 files (pandoc) to 26,266 files (PHP-src). With GPT-5.6-sol at high reasoning effort, the mean final test-pass rate moved as follows: 1 agent: 19.31% 8 agents: 20.68% 32 agents: 26.52% 128 agents: 28.78% That is a 9.47-point gain, about 49% relative. On pandoc alone, scores were 33.89% (1), 41.75% (8), 43.11% (32), 50.94% (128) and 55.06% (1,024). Speed improved too: on pandoc, 128 agents passed 30% at the 30-minute checkpoint. 32 and 8 agents needed 60 and 90 minutes. The README adds a newer model. With GPT-6.1-sol, pandoc rose from 56.19% (1 agent) to 79.59% (32 agents). That is a 41.64% relative gain. These GPT-6.1-sol figures are not in the v1 paper. What behaviors emerged as the team grew? The research team traced worker trajectories at each scale: 8 agents: peers agreed on interfaces and resolved overlapping claims themselves. 32 agents: peers reviewed shared work; one approval was withdrawn after a counterexample. 128 agents: workers reused trusted reviewers and standardized an integration protocol. 1,024 agents: several workers acted as integrators, and peers recovered failed work. None of these roles was hard-coded. How does Agensh compare with other multi-agent harnesses? Feature Agensh Claude Code agent teams Kimi Agent Swarm Copilot CLI /fleet Coordination No orchestrator; peers self-claim work Fixed lead session coordinates teammates Orchestrator decomposes tasks Copilot assigns parts to subagents Agents shown 1,024 tested No hard limit; 3 to 5 recommended Up to 100 sub-agents Not disclosed Shared state Gitea repo + shared context board Shared task list with file locking Not disclosed Plan from plan mode Messaging Mattermost channel + direct messages Mailbox messages between teammates Not disclosed Not disclosed Models Model agnostic; tested GPT-5.6-sol, GPT-6.1-sol Claude models Kimi K2.5 Not disclosed Speed claim 30% on pandoc at 30 min (128 agents) Not disclosed 4.5x faster than sequential (self-reported) Not disclosed Availability Open source, MIT In Claude Code; experimental, off by default Top-tier subscribers, research preview In Copilot CLI How do you run Agensh? The release includes a single-node Docker Compose team and a single-agent baseline. Both use native Copilot ACP sessions. You need Linux with Docker Engine, Compose v2, systemd, cgroup v2 and Python 3.11+. Defaults are 8 workers, 6 hours per task and gpt-5.6-sol at high effort. You also need ProgramBench (v1.2.5 was validated) and a model API token. Full steps sit in the reproduction guide . Key Takeaways Agensh coordinates up to 1,024 agents with no central orchestrator. Workers self-claim tasks via Gitea, Mattermost and a shared findings board. 128 agents lifted the 5-task ProgramBench mean from 19.31% to 28.78%. GPT-6.1-sol with 32 agents hit 79.59% on pandoc. Code is MIT licensed, but token cost is not disclosed. Check out the Paper , GitHub Repo and Project Page .
