[{time.time() - t0:.1f} s]") json.dump({"results": RESULTS, "claims": CLAIMS}, open(os.path.join(WORK, "results.json"), "w"), indent=1) return run return wrap def claim(text, held): CLAIMS.append((CURRENT[0], text, held)) return held banner("1. Platform, pins and helpers") SYSTEM, MACHINE = platform.system(), platform.machine() ON_CUDA = SYSTEM == "Linux" and shutil.which("nvidia-smi") is not None assert ON_CUDA or (SYSTEM == "Darwin" and MACHINE == "arm64"), "needs an NVIDIA GPU on Linux (Colab T4) or an Apple-silicon Mac" WORK = os.environ.get("SALUKI_WORK") or ("/content/saluki" if os.path.isdir("/content") else os.path.abspath("saluki_work")) for d in ("models", "llama", "bfcl", "runs"): os.makedirs(os.path.join(WORK, d), exist_ok=True) # Everything the notebook downloads is pinned by size and SHA-256. LLAMA_TAG = "b11565" # llama.cpp release of 2026-10-12, commit f9a95aeb2 LLAMA_ASSET = {"Linux": ("llama-b11565-bin-ubuntu-cuda-12.8-x64.tar.gz", 171559844, "61b8cf4e49739afe4008b06a92390dff999e706e9e7e9749c015544a9f241627"), "Darwin": ("llama-b11565-bin-macos-arm64.tar.gz", 12105509, "19289548468babcd5131cecccf3a9bc7c67030cc7f0a978dafc0db1ba7891068")}[SYSTEM] MODELS = { "Saluki": dict(repo="ConwayResearch/Underdog-Saluki-27B-1.0", rev="4f60eba09f4b6db63c72915d328d97e1d93edb8c", file="Underdog-Saluki-27B-1.0-IQ2-mix.gguf", size=7898369152, sha256="4a673518b11b1c4445f9b9a9d3c40356f5ba39f6a6260dcb25f3fbfd475d9efb"), "ISTA": dict(repo="ISTA-DASLab/Qwen3.8-27B-GSQ-RCO-GGUF", rev="d562806dbafae37109975e970aae91b43e73b440", file="Qwen3.8-27B-GSQ-RCO-IQ2_XS.gguf", size=8422841472, sha256="f0ae5006da0ce6225935339e4e989369f94de95d2263cf969519f8420c9ae02c"), } # BFCL v4 data and BFCL's own checker code, at one gorilla commit. GORILLA = ("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ShishirPatil/gorilla/6ea57973c7a6097fd7c5915698c54c17c5b1b6c8/" "berkeley-function-call-leaderboard/bfcl_eval/") BFCL_FILES = { "data/BFCL_v4_simple_python.json": "82dd63ba502eb2520c6b5d1d9a5c4b590e03ff261565175561f6228a367d1991", "data/BFCL_v4_multiple.json": "aef168155ebd74b7ac2401198b201343bc7d16d7a3d7e0d4e6d8ee82c6969b2a", "data/BFCL_v4_irrelevance.json": "2b6ed4c2e992cdcf5f1678a701851f944bef7550ee026ed1ddb89efed5be01a6", "data/BFCL_v4_parallel.json": "19f51a82eff42e5d62541aa500115a056eb78f437c2ba1f10415fd7c8e5dda84", "data/BFCL_v4_parallel_multiple.json": "8863ea8433239f55c5f016154cf0830853c89f693c6ea270396a2fa121960579", "data/possible_answer/BFCL_v4_simple_python.json": "90cd5bc653690ee8e459b5b3f3fc9458606f7f3fcbf795bb51b7dc581f8c86dc", "data/possible_answer/BFCL_v4_multiple.json": "244e00ce9395df948bcafc7bee64e8f9c87ef70887587d83cae45b13699f3047", "data/possible_answer/BFCL_v4_parallel.json": "8a6aa19c1adddc6a5a2f7e40f9dbf30cc7e95815e7b830c90589ab318229e0f0", "data/possible_answer/BFCL_v4_parallel_multiple.json": "5ebf24f458c1f16300c05505d83d6f0a1b68b79be273a033febd0d4f840507e3", "eval_checker/ast_eval/ast_checker.py": "2aae7a68461a8f76c0be3894c8901b66b56967a1989d3ab066051e3fb97f1538", "constants/enums.py": "2182becfa2a1d071ee1db30db593b4758c6bf866aa12d2d4b8daf09175ea518a", "constants/type_mappings.py": "1702fb67afbe2c492608e58e2b7d02e46381f50166b47f3c952f76e34c7cd3bd", "utils.py": "3703b9bb63f83581c60b8e0b82aac74c360c9ca781e99e7d4eb28b0cce2285dd", "model_handler/utils.py": "f78fd3edce603b333dc9a88ee2c041dc547d51f71aa449ffebc044c4b1e353f3", } # Underdog Bench's five kinds of tasks, 24 each; we draw our own seeded sample because its task list is not published. KINDS = [("simple_python", "Call the one right function"), ("multiple", "Pick the right function from several"), ("irrelevance", "Know when no tool fits"), ("parallel", "Same function, several calls"), ("parallel_multiple", "Several different functions")] N_PER_KIND, SEED, CTX, PORT = 24, 2026, 16384, 8080 # llama-server's own defaults are temperature 0.8 and top_k 40, so every request states its sampler. GREEDY = dict(temperature=0, top_k=0, top_p=1.0, min_p=0) def sh(cmd, **kw): return subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True, **kw) def sha256_file(path, chunk=1 << 22): h = hashlib.sha256() with open(path, "rb") as f: for b in iter(lambda: f.read(chunk), b""): h.update(b) return h.hexdigest() def fetch(url, dest, size=None, sha=None, quiet=False): """Resumable download with curl, then a size and SHA-256 check. Returns seconds spent downloading.""" t0 = time.time() if not (os.path.exists(dest) and (size is None or os.path.getsize(dest) == size)): for attempt in range(5): r = sh(["curl", "-fsSL", "-C", "-", "--retry", "5", "-o", dest, url]) if r.returncode == 0 and (size is None or os.path.getsize(dest) == size): break time.sleep(5 * (attempt + 1)) got = os.path.getsize(dest) assert size is None or got == size, f"{os.path.basename(dest)}: {got} bytes, expected {size}" if sha: assert sha256_file(dest) == sha, f"{os.path.basename(dest)}: SHA-256 mismatch" return time.time() - t0 print(f"platform : {SYSTEM} {MACHINE}, Python {platform.python_version()}, glibc {platform.libc_ver()[1] or 'n/a'}") if SYSTEM == "Linux": print("os :", open("/etc/os-release").read().split('PRETTY_NAME="')[1].split('"')[0]) gpu = sh(["nvidia-smi", "--query-gpu=name,memory.total,driver_version", "--format=csv,noheader"]).stdout.strip() print("gpu :", gpu) # The CUDA 12.8 build of llama.cpp ships without the CUDA runtime; Colab's image has it as pip wheels. import importlib.util if importlib.util.find_spec("nvidia.cuda_runtime") is None or importlib.util.find_spec("nvidia.cublas") is None: subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "-q", "nvidia-cuda-runtime-cu12==12.9.79", "nvidia-cublas-cu12==12.9.2.10"], check=True) import nvidia.cuda_runtime, nvidia.cublas CUDA_LIBS = [os.path.join(list(m.__path__)[0], "lib") for m in (nvidia.cuda_runtime, nvidia.cublas)] else: chip = sh(["sysctl", "-n", "machdep.cpu.brand_string"]).stdout.strip() mem = int(sh(["sysctl", "-n", "hw.memsize"]).stdout) / 2**30 print(f"gpu : {chip}, {mem:.0f} GB unified memory (Metal)") CUDA_LIBS = [] HW = gpu.split(",")[0] if SYSTEM == "Linux" else chip print(f"work dir : {WORK} ({shutil.disk_usage(WORK).free / 1e9:.0f} GB free)") Everything the notebook touches is pinned before anything runs. The setup cell records the llama.cpp release, both model files and fourteen BFCL files by size and SHA-256, and it fixes the sampler for every request, because llama-server otherwise falls back to defaults we did not choose. It detects the platform, an NVIDIA GPU on Linux or an Apple-silicon Mac, and on Colab it ensures the CUDA 12 runtime libraries the prebuilt llama. cpp needs are importable.cpp needs are importable. Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser @section("2. Download llama.cpp b11565 and both 2-bit files, and check every byte against its pin") def download_step(): global LLAMA_DIR, SERVER_BIN, SERVER_ENV name, size, sha = LLAMA_ASSET tar = os.path.join(WORK, "llama", name) fetch(f"https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/releases/download/{LLAMA_TAG}/{name}", tar, size, sha) with tarfile.open(tar) as t: t.extractall(os.path.join(WORK, "llama"), filter="data") SERVER_BIN = glob.glob(os.path.join(WORK, "llama", "**", "llama-server"), recursive=True)[0] LLAMA_DIR = os.path.dirname(SERVER_BIN) for b in glob.glob(os.path.join(LLAMA_DIR, "llama-*")): os.chmod(b, 0o755) SERVER_ENV = dict(os.environ) if CUDA_LIBS: SERVER_ENV["LD_LIBRARY_PATH"] = ":".join(CUDA_LIBS + [LLAMA_DIR, SERVER_ENV.get("LD_LIBRARY_PATH", "")]) missing = [l for l in sh(["ldd", SERVER_BIN], env=SERVER_ENV).stdout.splitlines() if "not found" in l] assert not missing, f"unresolved libraries: {missing}" r = sh([SERVER_BIN, "--version"], env=SERVER_ENV) ver = re.search(r"version: .*", r.stdout + r.stderr).group(0) print(f"llama.cpp: {name} (SHA-256 checked) -> {ver}") for rel, digest in BFCL_FILES.items(): dest = os.path.join(WORK, "bfcl", rel.replace("/", "__")) fetch(GORILLA + rel, dest, sha=digest) print(f"BFCL v4: {len(BFCL_FILES)} files from gorilla@6ea5797 (5 task files, 4 answer files, 5 checker sources), all SHA-256 checked") for tag, m in MODELS.items(): path = os.path.join(WORK, "models", m["file"]) had = os.path.exists(path) and os.path.getsize(path) == m["size"] url = f"https://huggingface.co/{m['repo']}/resolve/{m['rev']}/{m['file']}" dl = fetch(url, path, m["size"]) # size check now, hash below t0 = time.time() ok = sha256_file(path) == m["sha256"] how = "already on disk" if had else f"downloaded in {dl:.0f} s ({m['size'] / dl / 1e6:.0f} MB/s)" print(f"{tag:7s}: {m['file']} {m['size']:,} bytes, {how}; SHA-256 {'matches' if ok else 'DOES NOT MATCH'} " f"the Hub's LFS pin ({time.time() - t0:.0f} s to hash)") claim(f"{m['file']} is byte-identical to the file pinned at {m['repo']}@{m['rev'][:7]}", ok) assert ok return f"llama.cpp {LLAMA_TAG}; Saluki 7.90 GB and ISTA IQ2_XS 8.42 GB verified by SHA-256" download_step() We download the CUDA build of llama.cpp b11565, both 2-bit files and the BFCL data, and check every byte against its pin. The Hugging Face downloads are resumable, and the hashes are the Hub’s own LFS digests at a fixed revision, so a silently replaced file would stop the notebook rather than change its results. BFCL’s task files, answer files, and checker code all come from one gorilla commit. The cell prints how long the downloads took, which is the slowest part of the run on Colab. Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser GGML_TYPES = {0: ("F32", 1, 4), 1: ("F16", 1, 2), 8: ("Q8_0", 32, 34), 10: ("Q2_K", 256, 84), 12: ("Q4_K", 256, 144), 16: ("IQ2_XXS", 256, 66), 17: ("IQ2_XS", 256, 74), 18: ("IQ3_XXS", 256, 98), 19: ("IQ1_S", 256, 50), 21: ("IQ3_S", 256, 110), 22: ("IQ2_S", 256, 82), 23: ("IQ4_XS", 256, 136), 29: ("IQ1_M", 256, 56), 30: ("BF16", 1, 2)} # name, values per block, bytes per block (ggml-common.h) def read_gguf(path): """GGUF v3 header: metadata, tensor table (name, dims, type, offset) and where the tensor data starts.""" f = open(path, "rb") u = lambda fmt: struct.unpack("<" + fmt, f.read(struct.calcsize(fmt)))[0] s = lambda: f.read(u("Q")).decode("utf-8", "replace") scalar = {0: "B", 1: "b", 2: "H", 3: "h", 4: "I", 5: "i", 6: "f", 7: "?", 10: "Q", 11: "q", 12: "d"} def val(t): if t == 8: return s() if t == 9: et, n = u("I"), u("Q") return [val(et) for _ in range(n)] return u(scalar[t]) assert f.read(4) == b"GGUF" version, n_tensors, n_kv = u("I"), u("Q"), u("Q") kv = {} for _ in range(n_kv): k = s() kv[k] = val(u("I")) tensors = [] for _ in range(n_tensors): name = s() dims = [u("Q") for _ in range(u("I"))] ttype, off = u("I"), u("Q") n = math.prod(dims) _, per, nbytes = GGML_TYPES[ttype] tensors.append(dict(name=name, dims=dims, type=GGML_TYPES[ttype][0], n=n, bytes=n // per * nbytes, off=off)) align = kv.get("general.alignment", 32) data_start = (f.tell() + align - 1) // align * align return kv, tensors, data_start def tensor_class(name): if not name.startswith("blk."): return name.split(".")[0] # token_embd, output, output_norm kind = name.split(".")[2] if kind in ("attn_q", "attn_k", "attn_v", "attn_output"): return "full-attention " + kind[5:] if kind in ("attn_qkv", "attn_gate", "ssm_out", "ssm_conv1d"): return "linear-attention " + kind if kind in ("ssm_alpha", "ssm_beta"): return "linear-attention gates (alpha, beta)" if kind in ("ffn_gate", "ffn_up", "ffn_down"): return kind return "norms and small vectors" @section("3. What Saluki changes: a tensor-by-tensor diff of the two GGUF headers") def header_diff(): global HDR HDR = {tag: read_gguf(os.path.join(WORK, "models", m["file"])) for tag, m in MODELS.items()} (kv_s, t_s, start_s), (kv_i, t_i, start_i) = HDR["Saluki"], HDR["ISTA"] assert [t["name"] for t in t_s] == [t["name"] for t in t_i] and [t["dims"] for t in t_s] == [t["dims"] for t in t_i] n_params = sum(t["n"] for t in t_s) print(f"both files: {len(t_s)} tensors with the same names and shapes, {n_params:,} weights, " f"architecture '{kv_s['general.architecture']}', {kv_s['qwen35.block_count']} blocks") for tag, (kv, ts, start) in HDR.items(): data = sum(t["bytes"] for t in ts) size = MODELS[tag]["size"] print(f" {tag:7s}: header {start:,} B + tensor data {data:,} B = {start + data:,} B " f"({'equals' if start + data == size else 'DIFFERS FROM'} the file size); {8 * data / n_params:.3f} bits per weight") claim(f"{tag}: header plus tensor bytes computed from the type table equals the file size exactly", start + data == size) rows = collections.OrderedDict() moves = collections.Counter() up = down = 0 for a, b in zip(t_i, t_s): r = rows.setdefault(tensor_class(a["name"]), dict(k=0, n=0, bi=0, bs=0)) r["k"] += 1; r["n"] += a["n"]; r["bi"] += a["bytes"]; r["bs"] += b["bytes"] if a["type"] != b["type"]: moves[(a["type"], b["type"])] += 1 up += b["bytes"] > a["bytes"]; down += b["bytes"] < a["bytes"] print(f"
{'tensor class':34s} {'count':>5s} {'weights':>9s} {'ISTA bpw':>9s} {'Saluki bpw':>10s} {'change MB':>10s}") for c, r in sorted(rows.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1]["n"]): if r["n"] < 1e6: continue print(f"{c:34s} {r['k']:5d} {r['n'] / 1e9:8.3f}B {8 * r['bi'] / r['n']:9.3f} {8 * r['bs'] / r['n']:10.3f} {(r['bs'] - r['bi']) / 1e6:+10.1f}") changed = sum(moves.values()) print(f"
{changed} of {len(t_s)} tensors change type: " + ", ".join(f"{n} {a}->{b}" for (a, b), n in moves.most_common())) print(f" {down} get fewer bytes, {up} get more") claim("every tensor whose type changes gets fewer bits; none gets more", up == 0 and down == changed) untouched = [c for c, r in rows.items() if r["bi"] == r["bs"] and r["n"] >= 1e6] print(f" classes with no change at all: {', '.join(sorted(untouched))}") proj = lambda c: c.startswith(("full-attention", "linear-attention")) and "gates" not in c claim("every attention and DeltaNet projection matrix keeps its type (only the small alpha/beta gates change)", all(a["type"] == b["type"] for a, b in zip(t_i, t_s) if proj(tensor_class(a["name"])))) keys = sorted(k for k in set(kv_s) | set(kv_i) if kv_s.get(k) != kv_i.get(k) and not k.startswith("tokenizer.ggml.t")) print(f"
metadata keys that differ: {keys}") print(f"Saluki's header still reads: general.name = {kv_s['general.name']!r}, quantized_by = {kv_s['general.quantized_by']!r}") print(f"sampling stored in both headers: temp {kv_s['general.sampling.temp']}, top_k {kv_s['general.sampling.top_k']}, " f"top_p {kv_s['general.sampling.top_p']:.2f} (these are Qwen's thinking-mode settings; step 5 shows what the server does with them)") saved = (MODELS["ISTA"]["size"] - MODELS["Saluki"]["size"]) / 1e6 return f"{changed} of {len(t_s)} tensor types changed, all downgrades; {saved:.0f} MB smaller" header_diff() Reading the two GGUF headers in plain Python shows exactly what Saluki changed. Both files have the same 851 tensors with the same shapes, and the type table predicts each file’s size in bytes. Saluki changes the type of 146 tensors and every change cuts bits: most fall on the feed-forward down projections and the output layer, and the small DeltaNet gate vectors drop from BF16 to Q8_0. No attention or DeltaNet projection matrix changes, and the header still names ISTA DASLab as the quantiser. Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser @section("4. Byte-level provenance: are the unchanged tensors ISTA's own bytes?") def provenance(): import numpy as np (_, t_s, start_s), (_, t_i, start_i) = HDR["Saluki"], HDR["ISTA"] ms = np.memmap(os.path.join(WORK, "models", MODELS["Saluki"]["file"]), dtype=np.uint8, mode="r") mi = np.memmap(os.path.join(WORK, "models", MODELS["ISTA"]["file"]), dtype=np.uint8, mode="r") q = dict(k=0, same=0, eq_bytes=0, bytes=0) f32 = collections.defaultdict(lambda: [0, 0, []]) # kind -> [identical, differ, relative L2 changes] for a, b in zip(t_i, t_s): if a["type"] != b["type"]: continue x = mi[start_i + a["off"]: start_i + a["off"] + a["bytes"]] y = ms[start_s + b["off"]: start_s + b["off"] + b["bytes"]] if a["type"] == "F32": kind = re.sub(r"blk\.\d+\.", "", a["name"]) u, v = x.view(np.float32).astype(np.float64), y.view(np.float32).astype(np.float64) same = bool(np.array_equal(u, v)) f32[kind][0 if same else 1] += 1 if not same: f32[kind][2].append(np.linalg.norm(u - v) / np.linalg.norm(u)) else: eq = int(np.count_nonzero(x == y)) q["k"] += 1; q["same"] += eq == a["bytes"]; q["eq_bytes"] += eq; q["bytes"] += a["bytes"] print(f"quantised matrices that keep their type: {q['same']} of {q['k']} byte-identical, but " f"{100 * q['eq_bytes'] / q['bytes']:.1f}% of their {q['bytes'] / 1e9:.2f} GB of bytes are equal") print(f"
unquantised F32 vectors (never re-encoded, so any change means the weights changed):") print(f" {'kind':28s} {'identical':>9s} {'changed':>8s} median relative change") for kind, (same, diff, rel) in sorted(f32.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1][1]): med = f"{sorted(rel)[len(rel) // 2]:.1e}" if rel else "-" print(f" {kind:28s} {same:9d} {diff:8d} {med}") changed = sum(v[1] for v in f32.values()) total = sum(v[0] + v[1] for v in f32.values()) claim("Saluki's unchanged-type tensors are byte-for-byte ISTA's (a pure type re-mix)", q["same"] == q["k"] and changed == 0) claim("Saluki's F32 norm and gate vectors differ from ISTA's, so its weights were changed, not only re-encoded", changed > 0) return (f"{q['same']}/{q['k']} same-type matrices byte-identical, {100 * q['eq_bytes'] / q['bytes']:.1f}% of their bytes equal; " f"{changed}/{total} F32 vectors changed") provenance() Same types don’t mean the same weights, so we compare the bytes of the 705 tensors that keep their type. Only one of 352 quantized matrices is byte-identical, yet 98.4% of their bytes match, consistent with small edits to the underlying weights followed by re-quantizing on the same grids. The unquantized norm and gate vectors settle it: most changed by a median of a few parts in ten thousand. Saluki is a lightly changed model, not a re-encoding of ISTA’s file. Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser SERVER = {} def start_server(tag): """One llama-server per model, one slot, all layers on the GPU, debug log kept for unparsed replies.""" stop_server() log_path = os.path.join(WORK, "runs", f"server_{tag}.log") cmd = [SERVER_BIN, "-m", os.path.join(WORK, "models", MODELS[tag]["file"]), "--host", "127.0.0.1", "--port", str(PORT), "-c", str(CTX), "-np", "1", "-ngl", "99", "-fa", "on", "--jinja", "--reasoning-format", "deepseek", "-lv", "5"] t0 = time.time() proc = subprocess.Popen(cmd, stdout=open(log_path, "w"), stderr=subprocess.STDOUT, env=SERVER_ENV) while True: try: if urllib.request.urlopen(f"http://127.0.0.1:{PORT}/health", timeout=5).status == 200: break except urllib.error.HTTPError as e: assert e.code == 503, e except urllib.error.URLError: pass assert proc.poll() is None, f"llama-server exited; see {log_path}" assert time.time() - t0 < 900, "server did not become healthy in 15 minutes" time.sleep(2) SERVER.update(tag=tag, proc=proc, log=log_path, load_s=time.time() - t0) return SERVER["load_s"] def stop_server(): if SERVER.get("proc") and SERVER["proc"].poll() is None: SERVER["proc"].terminate() SERVER["proc"].wait(timeout=60) SERVER.clear() def api(path, body=None, timeout=1800): req = urllib.request.Request(f"http://127.0.0.1:{PORT}{path}", None if body is None else json.dumps(body).encode(), {"Content-Type": "application/json"}) with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=timeout) as r: return json.loads(r.read()) def memory_report(): """Buffer sizes from the server's load log, plus what the GPU reports.""" text = open(SERVER["log"]).read() out = {} for label, what in (("weights", "model"), ("KV cache", "KV"), ("recurrent state", "RS"), ("compute", "compute")): last = {} # llama.cpp sizes every buffer in a dry run first; keep the final value per device for dev, mib in re.findall(rf"(\S+) +{what} buffer size = +([\d.]+) MiB", text): last[dev] = float(mib) out[label] = sum(last.values()) if ON_CUDA: out["GPU in use (nvidia-smi)"] = float(sh(["nvidia-smi", "--query-gpu=memory.used", "--format=csv,noheader,nounits"]).stdout.split()[0]) return out @section("5. title: Crude Oil Price Surges Above $117 Over Fears of Fresh US Strikes on Iran
body: • Oil theft slumps 82.9% to 17,600bpd in five years amid fresh uptick in losses • Navy uncovers 132,000 litres of stolen crude oil in Bonny Emmanuel Addeh and Linus Aleke in Abuja Crude oil prices surged above $117 a barrel at the weekend, reaching their highest level since April, as fears of renewed US military strikes on Iran and escalating threats to energy infrastructure across the Middle East heightened concerns about global crude supplies. This comes as oil theft and pipeline losses in Nigeria fell by 82.9 per cent in five years, from 102,900 barrels per day (bpd) in 2021 to 17,600 bpd in the first seven months of 2026, amid fresh concerns about further increases in lost volumes after years of decline. Meanwhile, the Nigerian Navy has uncovered 132,000 litres of stolen crude oil in Allison community, Bonny Local Government Area (LGA) of Rivers State, disrupting a potential storage point in the illicit petroleum supply chain as troops of Operation Delta Sentinel intensified their clampdown on oil theft and economic saboteurs in the Niger Delta region. Nigeria’s oil benchmark, Brent crude, climbed by about 3.5 per cent to cross $117 a barrel during trading before easing to just above $116, still up approximately 2.7 per cent. The latest rally followed reports that Washington was considering fresh military strikes against Iran after the November 3 midterm elections, raising concerns that the conflict, now in its eighth month, could escalate further rather than move towards a diplomatic resolution. Iran had threatened to attack oil facilities, undersea cables, data centres and artificial intelligence infrastructure across the Gulf if the United States and Israel launched a new offensive against the country. Brent crude traded at about $72 a barrel in February, before the war began, but surged to about $126 a barrel by the end of April as the conflict intensified and concerns mounted over supply security. Tensions rose again during the week following claims by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) that it struck four commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday. The US ordered some diplomats and family members of American government employees to leave Saudi Arabia, which had faced continued attacks by Houthi rebels operating from Yemen.

title: Oil Theft Slumps 82.9% to 17,600bpd in Five Years Amid Fresh Uptick in Losses
body: Meanwhile, official operational statistics published by the Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission (NUPRC) showed that daily crude oil losses, which fell to a five-year low of 9,100 bpd in 2025, rose by 93.4 per cent to 17,600 bpd between January and July 2026. The figures in the commission’s fifth anniversary publication, ‘The Upstream Gaze’, highlighted both progress in curbing crude theft and the ongoing challenge of protecting oil production and transportation infrastructure. According to the data, daily losses declined from 102,900 bpd in 2021 to 55,000 bpd in 2022, representing a 46.5 per cent reduction. The downward trend continued in 2023 when losses dropped to 22,900 bpd, before falling further to 11,200 bpd in 2024 and 9,100 bpd in 2025. The federal government attributed the cut in crude losses to the combined efforts of the military, local pipeline surveillance groups in the Niger Delta, and the introduction of modern crude measuring devices in the region. The figures showed that Nigeria’s total liquid hydrocarbon production, comprising crude oil and condensate, gradually recovered from the lows recorded in recent years. Output averaged 1.63 million bpd in the first seven months of 2026, compared with 1.62 million bpd in 2025, 1.56 million bpd in 2024, 1.47 million bpd in 2023 and 1.38 million bpd in 2022. Production stood at 1.62 million bpd in 2021, the NUPRC data highlighted. Crude oil production alone averaged 1.46 million bpd in the period under review, up from 1.43 million bpd in 2025, 1.35 million bpd in 2024, 1.24 million bpd in 2023 and 1.14 million bpd in 2022. The figure for 2021 was 1.31 million bpd. In contrast, blended condensate production continued its downward trend, averaging 170,000 bpd in the first seven months of 2026, compared with 190,000 bpd in 2025, 210,000 bpd in 2024, 230,000 bpd in 2023, 240,000 bpd in 2022, and 310,000 bpd in 2021. The gradual improvement in crude production also coincided with a significant shift in how the country allocates its oil, particularly the growing share supplied to domestic refineries as Nigeria expands its local refining capacity. Supply to domestic refineries climbed to 460,000 bpd in the first seven months of 2026, up from 280,000 bpd in 2025, 220,000 bpd in 2024, 20,000 bpd in 2023, and just 10,000 bpd in 2022. Domestic refinery supply was virtually non-existent in 2021. At 460,000 bpd, local refineries accounted for approximately 29 per cent of the 1.61 million bpd in total crude oil lifted during the period. The allocation represented a 64.3 per cent increase over the 280,000 bpd supplied to domestic refineries in 2025, underscoring growing demand for locally processed crude. Similarly, the shift coincided with a decline in crude available for export, as the government struggled to meet local supply. Average daily crude exports fell to 1.15 million bpd in the first seven months of 2026, from 1.33 million bpd in 2025; 1.31 million bpd in 2024; 1.47 million bpd in 2023; 1.32 million bpd in 2022 and 1.51 million bpd in 2021. The latest export figures were down 13.5 per cent from the 2025 level and 23.8 per cent from the 2021 volume. In the same vein, total crude lifting averaged 1.61 million bpd in the first seven months of 2026, marginally below the 1.62 million bpd recorded in 2025. The figures suggested that the growing allocation to domestic refineries has been accompanied by a reduction in export volumes, rather than a comparable increase in total crude lifted.

title: Navy Uncovers 132,000 litres of Stolen Crude Oil in Bonny
body: Meanwhile, the Nigerian Navy has uncovered 132,000 litres of stolen crude oil in Allison community, Bonny LGA of Rivers State. According to a statement by the Director of Naval Information, Navy Captain Abiodun Folorunsho, the Forward Operating Base Bonny discovered the stolen crude oil under Operation Delta Sentinel, following actionable intelligence. He said the operation uncovered 10 dugout pits, adding that the site and the recovered products were handled in accordance with extant regulations. “The operation reinforces the importance of intelligence-led action in identifying concealed petroleum stockpiles and disrupting the infrastructure that enables crude oil theft and the unauthorised movement of petroleum products. “The Nigerian Navy will sustain efforts to locate and dismantle illegal refining infrastructure and disrupt the networks facilitating crude oil theft across the Niger Delta,” the statement said. The Navy urged community leaders, residents, traditional institutions and other stakeholders to promptly report crude oil theft, illegal refining, suspicious petroleum storage and the unauthorised movement of petroleum products to the nearest security agency. Timely, credible information, the statement said, could enable swift intervention and prevent illicit activities from expanding. “Safeguarding the nation’s critical petroleum assets requires vigilance and active cooperation between security agencies and the communities they serve. The Navy therefore urges the public to remain alert and support lawful efforts to protect national resources,” Folorunsho concluded.

title: Amid Improved Economic Indicators, Foreign, Domestic Investors’ Transactions on NGX Hit N15.06tn
body: Kayode Tokede Foreign and domestic investors’ transactions on Nigeria’s stock market reached N15.06 trillion in the first nine months of 2026, amid key reforms and improved economic indicators. The Nigerian Exchange Limited’s (NGX) report on domestic and foreign portfolio participation in equity trading revealed that domestic investors continued to dominate transactions, accounting for 89.74 per cent of the total. In comparison, foreign investors contributed 10.26 per cent. Foreign investors’ share of transactions declined from 21.56 per cent in the corresponding period of 2025 to 10.26 per cent in 2026. Conversely, domestic investors, comprising retail and institutional investors, increased their share from 78.44 per cent to 89.74 per cent. The report disclosed that domestic investors’ transactions rose to N13.52 trillion between January and September 2026, representing a 102 per cent increase over the N6.69 trillion recorded in the corresponding period of 2025. Foreign investors, however, accounted for N1.55 trillion, representing a 16.01 per cent decline from N1.84 trillion recorded between January and September 2025. The shift suggests that the surge in activity on Nigeria’s stock market this year has been driven largely by local capital, particularly institutional investors. Capital market analysts attributed the growth in institutional investors’ transactions partly to the National Pension Commission’s (PenCom) decision to raise equity investment limits for pension funds in February 2026. They said the policy had helped inject fresh liquidity into the stock market, supporting gains in the share prices of some blue-chip companies. On February 9, 2026, PenCom revised the investment limits for ordinary shares in Retirement Savings Account (RSA) Funds I, II, III and VI (Active). The commission amended Section 9 of its investment regulations, raising equity allocation limits for RSA Fund I from 30 per cent to 35 per cent; RSA Fund II from 25 per cent to 33 per cent; RSA Fund III from 10 per cent to 15 per cent; and RSA Fund VI (Active) from 25 per cent to 33 per cent. Institutional investors accounted for N8.36 trillion of domestic transactions between January and September 2026, compared with N5.15 trillion from retail investors. In the corresponding period of 2025, institutional and retail transactions stood at N4.09 trillion and N2.60 trillion, respectively. The report also showed that foreign portfolio outflows rose to N913.61 billion between January and September 2026, up from N810.39 billion in the corresponding period of 2025, a 12.7 per cent increase. Foreign portfolio inflows, however, fell to N632.35 billion, down about 38.6 per cent from N1.03 trillion in the corresponding period of 2025. Capital market analysts said FTSE Russell’s 2023 downgrade of Nigeria contributed to foreign investors’ exit from the stock market. They described the upgrade in September 2026 as a first step towards attracting them back. The report put foreign investor inflows in September 2026 at N925.20 billion, up 249.53 per cent from the N264.70 billion recorded in August. Investors on the Nigerian stock market recorded strong returns in the first nine months of 2026, with market capitalisation gaining N63.73 trillion despite volatility. Market capitalisation rose from N99.376 trillion at the beginning of the year to N163.105 trillion on September 30, 2026, representing an increase of N63.73 trillion, or 64.13 per cent. Similarly, the NGX All-Share Index gained 95,598.64 points, or 61.43 per cent, rising from 155,613.03 points at the beginning of the year to 251,211.67 points at the end of September. With fewer than five new listings, the NGX has recorded substantial growth in 2026, with market capitalisation reaching the N164 trillion mark amid improving macroeconomic indicators. The report added: “Over 19 years, domestic transactions increased significantly by 160.83 per cent from N3.5560 trillion in 2007 to N9.2747 trillion in 2025, whilst foreign transactions also increased significantly by 329.87 per cent from N0.6156 trillion to N2.6475 trillion over the same period. “Total domestic transactions accounted for about 78 per cent of the total transactions carried out in 2025, whilst foreign transactions accounted for about 22 per cent of the total transactions in the same period. “As at 30 September 2026, year-to-date domestic transactions amounted to approximately N13.5159 trillion, representing 89.74 per cent of total market transactions, whilst foreign transactions amounted to approximately N1.5460 trillion, accounting for 10.26 per cent.”

title: APC Accuses Atiku, ADC of Plotting to Discredit Tinubu’s Campaign Flag-off in Kaduna With Fake News
body: • Keyamo: ADC presidential candidate jittery over losing north to Tinubu • Tinubu’s panic cannot erase APC’s terrible record, says ADC Chuks Okocha, Adedayo Akinwale in Abuja and Chinedu Eze in Lagos The All Progressives Congress (APC) Presidential Campaign Council (PCC) has accused the African Democratic Congress (ADC) and its presidential candidate, Atiku Abubakar, of orchestrating a fake news campaign to discredit its presidential campaign flag-off in Kaduna yesterday. Similarly, the Minister of Aviation and Aerospace development, Festus Keyamo, said Atiku was jittery over the flag-off of the presidential campaign of APC in Kaduna because he was afraid of losing the bulk votes which he was hoping to get from the north. But is swift reaction, the ADC accused the APC of using allegations of fake news to divert attention from the economic hardship Nigerians were facing under President Bola Tinubu. The APC-PCC in a statement issued statement by its spokesperson, Mr Dele Alake said it uncovered a “well-orchestrated, devious plan” to misinform the public through AI, deepfake videos and counterfeit documents targeted at the APC rally, President Tinubu, Governor Uba Sani of Kaduna State and APC leaders. According to the council, the plot began with the circulation of a picture of a security vehicle on routine patrol near an APC campaign billboard in Kaduna metropolis, which was twisted to claim security agents were deployed to protect APC billboards. The council said the story was planted in a national newspaper and subsequently shared by Atiku on his social media handles. Alake added that the second leg was the circulation online of a fake letter purportedly written by Sani to the Director-General of the APC Presidential Campaign Council, Senator Abdulaziz Yari, on the purported release of N2.3 trillion by the Kaduna State Government to host the rally. He added: “We are still at a loss as to how anyone can imagine and concoct this senseless and utterly baseless lie that defies logic and basic common sense. “How much is the entire annual revenue of Kaduna State, or any state, for that matter, that a state would spend N2.3 trillion to host a rally?” Alake queried. Alake noted that the alleged N2.3 trillion was more than Kaduna State’s annual budget for three years combined, citing the state’s budgets for 2024 at N458.271 billion, 2025 at N790.439 billion and 2026 at N985.9 billion, which he said were still less than N2.3 trillion. The council claimed Atiku and ADC had also perfected plans to circulate old, doctored and deepfake videos during the rally to show purported resentment by the people. Alake said: “We hereby use this opportunity to alert the general public about this malicious and ignoble plan. It is a fact that Atiku Abubakar and the ADC, his special-purpose vehicle, are incapable of winning any election. “They will pull any strings, no matter how despicable and atrocious, to stay afloat in their desperate bid to grab power at all costs.” The APC Campaign Council urged Nigerians to be vigilant and reject what it described as machinations of the opposition.

title: Keyamo: ADC Presidential Candidate Jittery over Losing North to Tinubu
body: On his part, Keyamo, in a statement titled, ‘Why Atiku Abubakar is Particularly Jittery About the Kaduna Flag-off,’ posted on his verified Facebook account, alleged that the former Vice President had launched ‘blistering online attack’ against APC as the date of the launch got closer. The minister accused Atiku of being behind the destruction of APC posters in Kaduna and other parts of the north. “The common but cheap tactic is to position cameras in certain places, procure individuals to tear down the posters of the President, and then post the videos online. The other tactic is to disseminate disinformation claiming that any support the President is seen to receive in the North is procured only through the massive deployment of financial resources. Hence the fake letter alleging a N2.3 trillion deployment for the Kaduna rally. The intention is to generate a hoopla that will create a groundswell of public opinion that President Tinubu has been “massively rejected” in the North,” Keyamo said. The Minister also said the reason why Atiku was allegedly doing this was because he did not want to lose the bulk votes which he was hoping to get from the north. “The reason for this is simple: Atiku Abubakar was seriously banking on the bulk of Northern votes to see him through in 2027, knowing full well that he has no inroads at all into the South, given the mood of the country that the South deserves to complete eight years of the Presidency. Tinubu’s Panic Cannot Erase APC’s Terrible Record, Says ADC Meanwhile, the ADC has accused the APC of using allegations of fake news to divert attention from the economic hardship Nigerians were facing under President Tinubu. The ADC Presidential Campaign Council said the ruling APC should focus on defending its record in government rather than accusing it and Atiku of plotting to discredit the APC’s presidential campaign flag-off. In a statement, the council’s Director of Strategic Communication, Phrank Shaibu, described the APC’s allegations as an attempt to distract Nigerians from rising living costs and the administration’s economic policies. Shaibu challenged the APC to provide evidence linking Atiku and the ADC to the alleged circulation of forged documents, manipulated images and deepfake videos ahead of the Kaduna rally. “Until then, his ‘fake news alert’ is an empty political stunt,” Shaibu said, referring to the statement by Alake. The ADC spokesperson argued that the economic difficulties confronting Nigerians could not be dismissed as propaganda, citing high petrol and diesel prices, food inflation and growing poverty. He said the APC’s allegations would not change the daily struggles of households grappling with the cost of food, transportation and other essential needs. On the security presence near an APC campaign billboard in Kaduna, Shaibu questioned the explanation that the vehicle was on routine patrol, asking why the issue had become a subject of political controversy. He also raised concerns about reports that some APC supporters had travelled long distances to attend the rally and were left sleeping on the streets of Kaduna. Shaibu further referred to reports of accidents involving APC supporters travelling from Sokoto and Abuja to the event. However, he acknowledged that details of the reported incidents remained unconfirmed. The ADC spokesperson called on the APC to account for the safety of supporters travelling to the rally, arguing that political mobilisation should not come at the expense of citizens’ welfare. “Making citizens endure long, hazardous journeys and sleep outdoors simply to create rally optics is political exploitation, not leadership,” he said. Shaibu also questioned the scope of Tinubu’s campaign activities, alleging that the president was campaigning in only 12 states and suggesting that supporters were being moved between rallies. He argued that the size of a rally crowd should not automatically be interpreted as evidence of widespread public support, particularly where attendees had been transported from other locations. “You can hire buses, assemble a crowd and plaster the streets with billboards. You cannot hire consent,” he said.

title: YPP Presidential Candidate, Agada, Faults FG’s 90-Day Action Plan to Ease Cost of Living
body: Onyebuchi Ezigbo in Abuja The presidential candidate of Young Progressives Party (YPP), Mr Peter Agada, has faulted the federal government’s 90-day action plan to ease cost of living, describing it as a campaign strategy that did not reflect economic reality. Agada said the President Bola Tinubu’s administration had failed after introducing numerous economic measures without results. The Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of Economy, Mr. Taiwo Oyedele, had announced that the National Executive Council (NEC) approved a 90-day plan to cushion the high cost of living on Nigerians. Reacting in an interview in Abuja, Agada said the economic team of the President had lost focus. “I align with those who opine that the economic team of Mr. President has failed to address Nigeria’s numerous economic challenges. I have listened to many analysts, but none spoke positively in support of the economic team,” he said. He noted that the minister had earlier announced subsidy intervention and a 17-point plan, including reduction of pump price, removal of illegal levies, but nothing was done, prompting resort to a 90-day timeline. “These promises back and forth are for Nigerians to believe and vote them back into office. If you believe in the rules of the game they are playing, there are just 85 days to election, and you are saying a 90-day timeline to cushion the cost of living. So, after the election, what happens? These guys are playing mind games,” he said. Agada questioned feasibility of reversing hardship created in past three years within 90 days, recalling previous interventions announced in 2023, including N75 billion injection in manufacturing, N75 billion for micro SMEs, N50 billion conditional grants, grain and fertilizer distribution, two metric tonnes release, N200 billion to cultivate 500 hectares, N50 billion each to rice farmers, N100 billion to CNG initiative, state infrastructure fund and minimum wage increase, which he said were never fully implemented. He said the government later removed tariffs on food importation which did not fight food inflation but only affected calculation. “If you said you were fighting food inflation, then return food prices to where they were before you took office,” he said. He further alleged that import waiver cuts pushed customs revenue to N35 trillion with about 60 per cent for military hardware importation without accounting. As an alternative, Agada recommended his Labour-Direct ward-to-ward development strategy, which he said can empower Nigerians with N40 million monthly and capture all Nigerians within 60 days of implementation. “Labour-Direct, ward-to-ward strategy remains an option that can capture all Nigerians within 60 days. At the moment, they have to take a look at our ward-to-ward plan. If they approach me to implement a 60-day development plan, Nigerians will have more confidence,” he said.

title: Military Tanks, Personnel Stationed at Abuja City Gate Ahead of Obi-Kwankwaso Mega March
body: Security operatives yesterday stationed trucks and vans around the Abuja City Gate ahead of the “mega march” to be headlined by the presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Mr Peter Obi, and his running mate, Senator Rabiu Kwankwaso. At the city gate, armed personnel were seen milling round the landmark, effectively restricting a convergence on the premises or surrounding areas. Security agencies deployed in the area included officers of the Nigeria Police Force, Nigerian Army, Civilian Joint Task Force (CJF), the Department of State Services (DSS), and the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC). The heightened security presence follows a plan to hold a mega march and national rally in Abuja yesterday by a coalition of support groups backing Obi and Kwankwaso. The rally was scheduled to begin at 8am, with the city gate designated as the take-off point. Speaking to journalists on the development, one of the mobilisers of the rally, Saint Samson, said members were prevented from gathering at Unity Fountain amid heavy security presence in the city. “We got to Unity Fountain, but there was a security presence when we arrived, and some of our members were repelled from converging. We have decided to move to another location,” Samson said. “What we want to do is to mobilise support and campaign for the candidates of our party, as the constitution requires us to do, and gather to tell Nigerians what we have for them.” The mobiliser said the march was peaceful and was not intended to oppose or attack the government. “We are not against the government or attacking the government, so sending security to chase us and attack us is not democracy,” he said. He added that the group was regrouping to prevent casualties, insisting that its members were not violent or aggressive. “We don’t want any casualties, so we are putting our men together. We are not violent people; we are not aggressive,” he said.

title: Conclude Our Agreement Without Further Delay Or We Act, CONUA Tells FG
body: • TUC demands immediate conclusion of collective bargaining agreement with congress Kuni Tyessi in Abuja The President of the Congress of University Academics (CONUA), Dr. Niyi Sunmonu, has warned that the union will pursue appropriate lawful trade union actions if the federal government fails to conclude its Collective Bargaining Agreement without further delay. In the same vein, the Secretary General of the Trade Union Congress of Nigeria (TUC), Dr. Nuhu Toro, has demanded immediate action to finalise the collective bargaining agreement with CONUA. Sunmonu gave the warning yesterday in Abuja while addressing journalists after the National Executive Council (NEC) meeting of the union held at the University of Abuja. He said NEC reviewed the latest draft of the proposed FGN-CONUA Agreement of September 2026 and condemned the failure of the federal government to treat CONUA fairly. “CONUA has consistently pursued constructive engagement and believe that dialogue must lead to tangible outcomes. The recognition of a trade union must translate into meaningful collective bargaining and a concluded agreement that provides an effective framework for representing its members,” Sunmonu said. He called on the Federal Ministries of Education and Labour and Employment, and all relevant negotiating authorities, to conclude the process as a mark of government’s commitment to democratic process and sustained industrial harmony in Nigerian universities. “While CONUA remains committed to dialogue, the union reserves the right to pursue appropriate lawful trade union actions in pursuit of the welfare of its members, should the circumstances warrant it,” the CONUA President warned. He also demanded the prompt settlement of outstanding entitlements, including three and a half months of withheld salaries, promotion arrears, irregular payment of recently approved entitlements and arrears arising from the 25% and 35% wage awards. “University academics must not be subjected to indefinite delays, the trauma resulting from trivialization of its well-being and inconsistent implementation or administrative uncertainty,” he said. He commended the federal government for resolving the pension-entitlement issue, recalling the collaborative programme organised by CONUA and PENCOM on 26 September 2024. On representation, Sunmonu said CONUA’s exclusion from programmes associated with TETFund and NEEDS Assessment was unfair. On university education, the CONUA President said Nigeria cannot build a competitive knowledge economy on inadequately funded and poorly equipped universities. He called for reliable electricity, internet connectivity, functional laboratories and digital transformation, while condemning reported practices of hiring or renting academic staff and equipment for accreditation. “Accreditation must reflect an institution’s genuine and sustainable capacity to deliver its programmes. It must not become an exercise in appearances that conceal deficiencies in staffing, facilities or equipment,” Sunmonu stated. Meanwhile, the Secretary General of the TUC, Dr. Toro, has demanded immediate action to finalize the collective bargaining agreement with CONUA. Toro, who spoke on behalf of the TUC leadership said the congress would not tolerate any unnecessary delay by the relevant university authorities and government agencies responsible for concluding and signing the agreement. According to him, collective bargaining agreements are not political favours or administrative conveniences, but serious commitments that must be respected in accordance with the laws of the land. Toro further declared the solidarity of the TUC with CONUA, saying the university academics must not stand apart from the wider struggles of the Nigerian working class. “CONUA must not stand alone in defending university academics and university academics must not stand apart from the wider struggles of the national working class,” he said.

title: Makinde to Tinubu: Rising Foreign Reserves Can’t Feed Hungry Nigerians
body: •Faults economic recovery claims, demands reset of economy, security, education Wale Igbintade Oyo State Governor and presidential candidate of the Allied Peoples Movement (APM), Mr Seyi Makinde, has faulted President Bola Tinubu’s economic recovery narrative, arguing that rising foreign reserves meant little when millions of Nigerians were struggling with hunger and worsening economic hardship. Makinde accused the federal government of creating a misleading impression of economic progress by highlighting improvements in financial indicators without demonstrating corresponding improvements in citizens’ living conditions. The governor made the remarks yesterday in a video message at the official launch of the Makinde and Daura for Better Nigeria (MAD) Resetter Movement in Lagos, where he called for a comprehensive overhaul of Nigeria’s economy, security architecture, education system and political environment. The event attracted APM leaders, party loyalists, stakeholders and candidates preparing for the 2027 general elections in Lagos State and other parts of the country. Makinde argued that the government’s economic performance should be measured by the ability of ordinary Nigerians to afford basic necessities, achieve financial independence and access opportunities to improve their lives, rather than by official statistics alone. He likened the situation to a household whose head boasts of substantial savings while members of the family go hungry. “We have heard stories that Nigeria’s foreign reserves are going up. I liken it to a household where the head is telling the people that we have a lot of money in our savings accounts, but everyone in that household is hungry,” he said. The governor maintained that genuine economic recovery should translate into better living standards and enable young Nigerians to pursue their aspirations without struggling merely to survive. Expressing support for the movement’s agenda, he said the country needed fundamental changes across key sectors to improve the welfare of its citizens. “I am with you 101 per cent towards the reset agenda for Nigeria. We need to reset our economy, our security architecture, our educational system and the socio-political environment,” he said. Makinde also called for a return to the principles of federalism and multiparty democracy, arguing that these formed the foundation of Nigeria’s political arrangement and remained essential to building a country that worked for everyone. “Nigeria was negotiated on the basis of a federalism arrangement. Nigeria was negotiated on the basis of multiparty democracy. So, join myself and Alhaji Lawal Daura in the agenda to make Nigeria work for everybody,” he said. He urged Nigerians dissatisfied with the country’s direction to join the movement, encouraging its members to extend their mobilisation beyond Lagos and the South-west to other geopolitical zones. The governor expressed optimism about the initiative, praying that the efforts of those working towards a better Nigeria would not be in vain. Also speaking at the event, the Director-General of the Makinde-Daura Presidential Campaign Organisation, Hon. Hassan Felix, called for a change of direction, citing unemployment, insecurity and economic hardship as major challenges confronting the country. Felix questioned claims that the government’s economic policies were improving living conditions, arguing that persistent hardship and the departure of companies from Nigeria contradicted such assertions. Comparing Nigeria’s economic fortunes with those of Ghana, he lamented that the country had failed to translate its abundant resources into widespread prosperity. The Director of Volunteers, Support and Special Interest Groups of the MAD Political Campaign Organisation, Dr Emmanuel Dennis, said the movement intended to run an issue-based campaign focused on the country’s economic and governance challenges rather than rallies and entertainment. Dennis said rising petrol prices, worsening hardship and stagnant salaries had made it increasingly difficult for Nigerians to provide for their families. He also criticised the National Assembly, describing it as a rubber stamp, and expressed concern that court decisions were increasingly determining electoral outcomes instead of voters’ choices. The APM governorship candidate in Lagos State, Adelaja Adeoye, promised an inclusive administration that would cater for residents irrespective of gender or social background. He also urged voters to reject vote-buying, describing their permanent voter cards (PVCs) as instruments of political power and warning that money offered in exchange for votes would provide only temporary relief. Meanwhile, APM local government chairmen in Lagos State endorsed the Makinde-Daura presidential ticket, Adeoye’s governorship candidacy and the party’s candidates for senatorial, House of Representatives and other legislative seats. Speaking on behalf of the chairmen, Hon. Isiaka Sodeinde reaffirmed their commitment to the reset agenda and declared support for the APM-PDP alliance. He expressed confidence that the alliance’s candidates would emerge victorious in the 2027 elections.

title: NDC Fixes Monday for Third NEC Meeting, Presidential Campaign Council Unveiling
body: •Says 80% of candidates received free nomination forms amid economic hardship Sunday Aborisade in Abuja The Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) will unveil its National Campaign Council on Monday as part of preparations for the 2027 general election, while presenting its financial accounts to demonstrate its commitment to transparency and accountability. The party disclosed this in a statement issued yesterday by its National Publicity Secretary, Osa Director, announcing that its third National Executive Committee (NEC) meeting would be held at 10 a.m. on October 26 at JD Event Centre, Kashim Ibrahim Way, Maitama, Abuja. A major highlight of the meeting, according to the party, will be the National Treasurer’s presentation of the party’s statement of account, a move it said is intended to distinguish its financial management practices from those of other political parties. The NDC challenged other political parties, particularly the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC), to adopt similar measures to promote transparency in managing party finances. The party also attributed its financial limitations partly to the economic difficulties facing Nigerians, claiming that approximately 80 per cent of its candidates could not afford the fees for expression-of-interest forms. It said it had consequently issued the forms to the affected candidates free of charge to enable them to participate in the electoral process. The party blamed the situation on what it described as widespread poverty, hunger and deprivation under the APC-led federal government, criticising its economic policies. Beyond the financial disclosures, the NEC meeting will give the party an opportunity to unveil its National Campaign Council, which it said would coordinate its campaign activities across all levels of government. According to the statement, the council will encompass the presidential, National Assembly, governorship and state Houses of Assembly campaign structures. The party also announced plans to present certificates of return to its candidates contesting the various elective positions. The developments come as political parties intensify preparations for the 2027 general election, with campaign structures, candidate mobilisation and party organisation expected to play important roles in the contest. For the NDC, the planned unveiling of its campaign council and disclosure of its accounts are intended to project organisational readiness and distinguish the party’s approach to internal financial accountability. The NDC expressed confidence in its preparations for the forthcoming elections, saying it was determined to offer Nigerians what it described as altruistic leadership. The statement read, “The leadership of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) wishes to announce that its 3rd National Executive Committee (NEC) meeting will hold on Monday, 26th October 2026, at JD event centre, Kashim Ibrahim Way, opposite A-class park, Maitama, Abuja. The time is 10 am prompt. “A major highlight of the meeting will be the release and presentation of the party’s Statement of Account by the National Treasurer. This reflects our avowed commitment to the principles of transparency and accountability. In this regard, we challenge other political parties, especially the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC), to emulate this level of openness and transparency in managing their finances. “For the NDC, it is no longer politics as usual. “Our finances would have been more robust. However, contrary to speculations in the public domain, and due to the level of poverty, hunger and deprivation in the country occasioned by the rudderless APC and its amorphous economic policies, about 80% of our candidates could not afford the Expression of Interest forms. The party had to issue forms to such candidates free of charge. “The party will also use the opportunity of the NEC meeting to unveil its National Campaign Council (NCC). “As a party of innovation, our NCC is all-encompassing. It covers the Presidential, National Assembly, Governorship, and State Houses of Assembly Campaign Councils. “Our various candidates will be presented with Certificates of Return for their respective offices. “The NDC is turbo-charged and ready to give Nigerians the altruistic leadership the nation deserves. A New Nigeria is Possible. We can do it!”

title: 30 Feared Dead in Attack on Taraba Community as Hunters Kill 14 Bandits in Katsina
body: Wole Ayodele in Jalingo and Francis Sardauna in Katsina About 30 people have reportedly been killed in an attack by suspected bandits on Binnari community in Karim Lamido Local Government Area (LGA) of Taraba State, with several houses burnt and food crops destroyed. In Katsina, the state government announced the successful foiling of a planned mass kidnap operation in Gidan Wawo village, Kakumi Ward of Bakori LGA following a coordinated security response that resulted in the elimination of 14 suspected bandits. The attack in Taraba, which occurred shortly after Friday’s Juma’at prayers, reportedly claimed the lives of children and elderly persons, while several residents fled their homes for safety. However, the Taraba State Police Command said only 10 bodies had been recovered as of Friday evening, while residents reported that more bodies were discovered yesterday morning. Some residents also expressed fears that several victims remained missing following the attack. Local sources said the assailants might have entered the community from neighbouring Plateau State, although the claim has not been independently verified as well as their identities. The attack has compounded the hardship facing residents, many of whom are now mourning lost relatives and struggling to recover from the destruction of their homes and food supplies. Confirming the incident, the Police Public Relations Officer of the Taraba State Command, ASP Victor Mshelizah, said preliminary information indicated that the attackers initially targeted food items and other valuables. “There was an incident like that yesterday, immediately after Friday’s prayers. “From the preliminary report, it was revealed that the people initially came to steal food stuff and other valuables,” he said. ASP Mshelizah said security operatives had recovered 10 bodies as of Friday evening, as the identities of the attackers had yet to be established. He assured residents that the police would continue to intensify efforts to protect lives and property of the people. Reports said the attack has further renewed concerns over the vulnerability of rural communities in Karim Lamido and other parts of Taraba State to armed violence, with residents calling for stronger security measures to prevent further attacks. Meanwhile, in Katsina, a statement signed by the state Commissioner for Internal Security and Home Affairs, Dr. Nasir Danmusa, said intelligence reports had indicated that 26 heavily armed bandits riding on 13 motorcycles, under the leadership of a notorious kingpin identified as Isiya Kwashen Garwa, were advancing towards Dawan Laila Forest in preparation for coordinated attacks on neighbouring communities when community hunters from Gidan Wawo were promptly mobilised to engage the fleeing criminals in a fierce gun battle. According to Danmusa, the encounter ended in a decisive victory for the security volunteers, with 14 bandits neutralised and three victims rescued alive. The operation, however, came at a painful cost. A brave community hunter, Mohammed Ibrahim Jidda, 29, was killed while defending the community, while another hunter, Usman Sunday, 25, sustained minor gunshot injuries and is currently receiving medical treatment. One of the travellers, Jamilu Lawal, 50, tragically lost his life after being burnt in the vehicle during the attack. The government disclosed that intelligence reports indicated possible reprisal attacks by the bandits following the heavy losses they suffered. It assured residents that comprehensive countermeasures had already been activated in collaboration with security agencies to forestall any further threats. The Katsina State Government commended the courage, resilience and sacrifice of security personnel and community hunters whose swift intervention prevented what could have been a devastating mass kidnap. The state government urged residents to remain calm, vigilant and continue providing timely and credible intelligence to security agencies. It reaffirmed its unwavering commitment to safeguarding lives and property across the state.

title: Amupitan: Nigerians will Decide Outcome of 2027 Elections, Not Algorithms
body: Adedayo Akinwale in Abuja The Chairman of the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), Prof. Joash Amupitan, has said algorithms will not determine the outcome of the 2027 general election. Amupitan made the remark at the AI and Democracy Forum 2026 in Abuja. Addressing the question, “Will algorithms decide the 2027 vote?”, he said artificial intelligence (AI) would not replace the will of the electorate. “Let me, as the chair of INEC, answer it unequivocally: no! Algorithms will not and must never decide the 2027 votes,” he said. “Algorithms will not decide the votes because the choice of who leads Nigeria belongs exclusively to the Nigerian people.” Amupitan, however, said AI-driven geospatial analysis and predictive modelling could improve electoral logistics and help the commission meet its operational demands. He said since assuming office on October 23, 2025, he had overseen five major elections and more than 16 by-elections, during which INEC tested predictive logistics optimisation. The INEC chairman said the commission recorded improvements in the early deployment of election materials and the commencement of voting. “Reports from civil society and observers reported significant improvement in terms of early deployment of materials and early commencement of voting in all the elections we’ve conducted,” he said. Speaking during a panel session, Amupitan said AI components were already embedded in some of the technologies the commission used, including the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS). He said facial recognition and fingerprint technology used for voter accreditation involved AI components, adding that similar technologies were incorporated into the smart card readers that preceded BVAS. The INEC chairman said the commission was refining its systems to address AI-related challenges and ensure the technology was used for lawful purposes. He added that it could not disclose some details of its preparations publicly because of cybersecurity concerns. At a press conference on October 6, Amupitan said INEC had established a dedicated AI division within its information and communication technology department to support result verification and strengthen cybersecurity ahead of the 2027 elections. He also said the commission had integrated automated AI auditing tools into its result verification process under a five-pillar AI governance framework, with mandatory human oversight. Amupitan said the commission was finalising its AI governance policy to guide the use of the technology in the electoral process.

title: 2027: Akume Berates Atiku, Says Former VP’s Presidential Ambition Could Hurt North’s Interests
body: Olawale Ajimotokan in Abuja The Secretary to the Government of the Federation (SGF), Senator George Akume, has criticised former Vice President Atiku Abubakar over his ambition to contest the 2027 presidential election. The former governor of Benue State described the presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) as a pretender and warned that the move could undermine the collective political interests of Northern Nigeria. Akume spoke yesterday in Kaduna with gloves in his hands, at a pre-campaign meeting with Benue State indigenes resident in the state. He urged northerners to rally behind President Bola Tinubu’s re-election bid, insisting that the region should wait until 2031 before seeking to return to the presidency. The SGF argued that individual presidential ambitions should not be allowed to disrupt the power-rotation arrangement between the North and South, which he said had helped sustain Nigeria’s unity and territorial integrity. “Anybody who is from the North and running for the presidency is an enemy of the North. Don’t allow that pretender to deceive you. It is not yet our turn. The North’s turn is in 2031. Prepare to vote for Tinubu. Do not allow anyone to destroy the country because of a vaunting personal ambition,” he said. Akume maintained that the North stood to gain more by supporting Tinubu for a second term than by pursuing competing political ambitions that could divide the region and weaken its collective influence ahead of the next general election. He also defended the president’s record on political appointments and religious inclusiveness, urging northerners not to be swayed by what he described as misleading narratives about the administration. “Let us remember that the president has been fair to all in terms of appointments and others. He doesn’t favour one religion over the other. Just look at the figures. So be careful about what people tell you,” Akume said. The former Benue State governor further faulted Atiku’s position on fuel subsidy, accusing the former vice-president of inconsistency. “Forget that other one making noise that he was going to remove fuel subsidies. He is always flip-flopping. He says something today and changes gear the next minute,” he said. Akume argued that the political understanding reached by Nigerian leaders on the rotation of presidential power should remain a guiding principle in managing the country’s political differences. He recalled that the agreement reached in Kaduna was designed to preserve national cohesion and ensure a sense of inclusion among the country’s diverse political constituencies. “Remember that it was in this same Kaduna State that we agreed on power rotation between the North and the South. You cannot doubt the credentials of those that reached this agreement at that time, and it was done to keep this country together. We agreed on a power shift, and that is what has kept this country going,” he said. Akume also cited federal government projects in Benue State, covering healthcare, roads and education, as evidence of Tinubu’s commitment to the state.

title: LCCI Demands Constant Electricity Supply for Industrial Clusters, Commercial Centres, Technology Parks
body: Dike Onwuamaeze The President of Lagos Chamber of Commerce and Industry (LCCI), Mr. Leye Kupoluyi, has called for the development of constant electricity supply hubs in industrial clusters, commercial centres, markets and technology parks across the country. Kupoluyi made this call during the LCCI’s power sector group’s conference with the theme “Gas to Power: Unlocking Nigeria’s Energy Potential for Sustainable Economic Growth.” He said: “I advocate the development of 24/7 electricity supply hubs in industrial clusters, commercial centers, markets and technology parks. “Through partnerships between government and private investors, these hubs can combine gas-fired generation, renewable energy, battery storage and dedicated distribution infrastructure to provide more reliable electricity. “Such arrangements can reduce businesses’ dependence on individual generators, lower operating costs and improve productivity.” According to him, Nigeria possessed substantial gas resources that could be deployed to strengthen electricity generation and support industrial development. He stated that gas-fired power plants could provide “dispatchable” electricity and complement renewable energy sources, helping to meet the needs of businesses that require dependable power. Kupoluyi, however, emphasised that “gas-fired generation alone will not resolve all our electricity challenges,” stressing that “it must be accompanied by improvements in transmission, distribution, metering, market liquidity, and operational efficiency. “The ultimate goal is to translate our natural resources into dependable electricity, competitive businesses and sustainable economic growth.” The LCCI’s president stated that currently businesses, particularly manufacturers and small and medium-sized enterprises, were documenting the burden of frequent power outages in their financials as high energy costs, increased production costs, reduced capacity utilisation and weakened profit margins. He said: “Electricity is the lifeblood of modern economic activity. Unfortunately, unreliable electricity supply remains a major constraint to business competitiveness and economic growth in Nigeria. “Businesses, particularly manufacturers and small and medium-sized enterprises, continue to bear the burden of frequent power outages, high energy costs, and dependence on petrol- and diesel-powered generators. “These challenges increase production costs, disrupt operations, reduce capacity utilization, weaken profit margins and undermine the competitiveness of Nigerian products in domestic and international markets. “They also discourage investment, constrain job creation and contribute to higher consumer prices.” He added: “For a country seeking accelerated industrialisation, economic diversification and inclusive growth towards a $1 trillion economy, this situation is unsustainable. “Nigeria must move decisively towards a power sector that supports productivity, attracts investment and enables businesses to thrive.” The president of LCCI said that Nigeria must explore how it can harness its abundant natural gas resources to deliver reliable, affordable, and sustainable electricity to businesses and households. “Our objective must go beyond generating electricity to ensuring that dependable power reaches businesses and households at affordable and commercially sustainable prices. “To achieve this, we need best-practice regulation that promotes competition, transparency, investor confidence and accountability. Regulatory institutions must provide predictable rules, enforce service standards, protect consumers and ensure that electricity market participants fulfill their obligations. “Tariff frameworks must support the sector’s financial sustainability while addressing affordability and the need for efficient service delivery,” he said. In his keynote address at the conference, the Lagos State Commissioner for Energy and Mineral Resources, Mr. Biodun Ogunleye, said that Nigeria did not lack energy resources but must address the infrastructure, commercial structures and institutional frameworks required to convert those resources into reliable electricity for industries, businesses and households. Ogunleye said that gas remained fundamental to achieving improved electricity supply, particularly for Lagos, Nigeria’s largest commercial and industrial hub. He said that Lagos was receiving approximately 1,000 megawatts from the national grid against its electricity requirement of over 6,000 megawatts. “This enormous supply gap has encouraged widespread dependence on expensive self-generation, increasing production costs, weakening competitiveness and placing considerable financial pressure on households and businesses. “However, our ambition is to deliver approximately 6,000 megawatts of electricity capacity, comprising 4,000 megawatts of gas-fired generation and 2,000 megawatts from renewable energy sources.”

title: Soludo: Supporting Tinubu’s Re-election Could Pave the Way for Igbo Presidency in Future
body: Chuks Okocha in Abuja The Governor of Anambra State, Prof. Chukwuma Soludo, has said supporting President Bola Tinubu’s second-term bid could pave the way for an Igbo presidency in the future. In a video that circulated on X at the weekend, Soludo, speaking in Igbo, said backing Tinubu in the 2027 election could encourage other regions to support an Igbo presidential candidate when power returns to the South. He said the South-east should support the incumbent southern president, noting that power would shift to the north after Tinubu’s tenure before eventually returning to the south. “You have to engage in discussions. Now that it is a southerner holding the power; it’s remaining four years. It is now left for us (Igbos) to support him so that when it goes to the North and comes back, we can now trust that every southerner and northerner will support us,” he said. The governor said political power should rotate among different groups, adding that he had no intention of seeking a third term. “What am I vying for? I’ve gotten a governorship position; will I go for a third term? Everyone must be given the opportunity to be able to rise,” he said. Soludo also said the All Progressives Grand Alliance (APGA), the party under which he was elected governor, would support the prevailing political direction in the interest of the south-east. “As for APGA, we will support the moving train because that is where we can get our share that we would bring home in our own interest,” he said. His remarks followed his appointment to the revised presidential campaign council of the All Progressives Congress (APC), unveiled recently. Soludo was appointed to the council alongside Osun State governor, Ademola Adeleke, and the Minister of Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Nyesom Wike. APGA described the governor’s inclusion as a testament to his consistent advocacy for a strategic partnership between Anambra State and the federal government for the collective good of Ndi Anambra and Ndigbo at large. In a statement, APGA’s National Publicity Secretary, Ejimofor Opera, said the partnership had yielded tangible benefits for Anambra, including federal collaboration on critical infrastructure projects and economic development initiatives.

title: Denmark handed Greenland over to US — Trump
body:
WASHINGTON, October 25. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump believes that the Danish government has agreed to transfer control of Greenland to Washington.
"By the way, Denmark was so great. They gave us Greenland," he told Republican Party supporters at a rally in Georgia ahead of the November 3 midterm congressional elections. "It's going to go down as the greatest real estate deal in history, probably after Venezuela," Trump emphasized, referring to the agreement he signed in September with Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenland’s Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen. The agreement involves transferring responsibility for ensuring the security of the Arctic island to Washington.
"We got them both for zero," the US president added, referring to Greenland and Venezuela.
Trump had previously stated that Washington was assuming temporary control of Venezuela. On January 3, the US attacked civilian and military targets in Venezuela, seized President Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores and removed them from the country. Vice President Delcy Rodriguez, who served as executive vice president under Maduro, is currently acting as head of state in Venezuela.
Greenland is part of Denmark as an autonomous territory. In 1951, Washington and Copenhagen signed the Greenland Defense Agreement in addition to their NATO alliance commitments. Under this treaty, the US undertook to defend the island from potential aggression.

title: Court Bars Eunisell from Enforcing 177% Default Charges against Halkin
body: Wale Igbintade The High Court of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Abuja, has permanently restrained Eunisell Limited from demanding or enforcing late-payment charges imposed on Halkin Exploration and Production Limited under a contractual clause prescribing a default fee equivalent to 177 per cent annually. Justice SB Belgore, in a judgment delivered on October 22, 2026, declared the provision, which imposed a daily charge of 0.5 per cent on outstanding payments, an unconscionable penalty that was unenforceable and contrary to public policy. The judge also nullified all invoices, bills and assessments issued under the disputed clause in the service agreement executed by the two companies on January 20, 2022. The ruling has significant financial implications for the parties, as Eunisell had previously instituted a separate debt-recovery action against Halkin, seeking $10,240,679.98 in outstanding contractual fees, including $7,624,171.51 in late-payment charges calculated at the disputed rate. However, the judgment did not dismiss the entire $10.24 million debt claim, which is distinct from the substantive relief granted in the present suit. The dispute arose from a service agreement under which Eunisell was engaged to provide specialised engineering services and operate a modular Early Production Facility for Halkin’s operations at the Atala Marginal Oilfield, also known as Oil Mining Lease (OML) 46. Under the agreement, Halkin was required to pay a fixed daily service fee of $9,900, while Clause 10.4 stipulated that the payments made after the contractual deadline would attract a default charge of 0.5 per cent daily. Halkin approached the court to challenge the provision, arguing that the rate was excessive, oppressive and designed to punish it for delayed payments rather than compensate Eunisell for any genuine financial loss. In resolving the dispute, Justice Belgore acknowledged the freedom of commercial parties to negotiate contractual terms but held that such freedom did not oblige courts to enforce unconscionable penalty clauses. Relying on the Supreme Court’s decision in Oyeneyin v. Akinkugbe and the Court of Appeal’s decisions in Awutolo v. Okolo and Chevron Nigeria Limited v.
