Titan Energy Limited, the judge explained that a penalty clause was unenforceable where it was intended to frighten a party into performing its contractual obligations rather than serve as a genuine pre-estimate of the loss arising from a breach. Applying these principles, the court found that the disputed provision imposed an excessive financial burden on Halkin. Justice Belgore also noted that the agreement was denominated in United States dollars, reasoning that this insulated Eunisell from local inflation and currency fluctuations. The judge further observed that Eunisell had failed to file a response to Halkin’s amended originating summons within the time permitted by the applicable rules. Consequently, the material averments in Halkin’s affidavit evidence remained unchallenged. Citing judicial authorities on unchallenged affidavit evidence, the judge held that the claimant’s evidence was deemed admitted and accepted by the court. The court also dismissed Eunisell’s preliminary objection challenging the competence of the suit. Eunisell had argued that the action constituted an abuse of court process because the parties were already involved in a separate debt-recovery suit, marked FCT/HC/CV/5599/2024. The company also contended that the dispute involved contested facts that required a trial commenced by a writ of summons rather than an originating summons. Rejecting the objection, Justice Belgore distinguished between the earlier action, which sought to recover outstanding contractual fees, and the present suit, which sought an interpretation of a specific provision in the service agreement. He held that an originating summons was appropriate because the central issue concerned the construction of a written contract. The judge also rejected Eunisell’s argument that the existence of the separate debt-recovery action rendered Halkin’s suit an abuse of court process. In another aspect of the judgment, Justice Belgore dismissed an application by Eunisell challenging the accuracy of the court’s record of proceedings on May 18, 2026. The company had alleged that the court failed to consider its opposition to Halkin’s application to amend its originating summons and incorrectly recorded its counsel as having no objection. The judge, however, recalled that Eunisell’s counsel, PL Osakwe, had initially expressed opposition to the amendment but subsequently informed the court that he was not objecting after the judge sought clarification on the grounds for his opposition. According to Justice Belgore, the court had explained that the issues raised in the preliminary objection could be addressed after the amendment was granted. He maintained that the record accurately reflected counsel’s eventual position and faulted the company for failing to follow the prescribed procedure for challenging a court record. Relying on the Supreme Court’s decision in Andrew v. INEC, the judge held that a party seeking to challenge a court’s record must first file an affidavit disputing its accuracy and subsequently bring a formal application, supported by a separate affidavit, seeking an order to amend it. The judge dismissed the application as incompetent and rejected it on its merits. He consequently ordered Eunisell to pay N1million in costs to Halkin over the unsuccessful application, which had delayed the delivery of the substantive judgment. The judge made no order as to costs in the substantive suit.

title: Attack on ADC Supporter: Atiku Accuses Tinubu, Okpebholo of Encouraging Political Violence
body: Chuks Okocha in Abuja The presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Atiku Abubakar, has accused President Bola Tinubu, Edo State Governor Monday Okpebholo, and the All Progressives Congress (APC) of creating an environment that encouraged political violence. The accusation followed an alleged attack on comedian Osagie Daniel Idedia, popularly known as Porkupyne, in Benin City. In a post on X yesterday, Atiku alleged that the comedian was attacked because he supported him and his demand for good governance and accountability in Edo State. He condemned the incident and called for an urgent police investigation into the circumstances surrounding the attack. “I condemn in the strongest possible terms the brutal attack on comedian Osagie Daniel Idedia (aka Porkupyne), in Benin City, Edo State,” Atiku said. He added that the incident was politically motivated, alleging that the comedian was targeted because he was his supporter. Atiku held Okpebholo, Tinubu and the APC leadership responsible for what he described as a climate of impunity in which opposition supporters were allegedly intimidated and assaulted. “Governor Okpebholo must explain what happened to Porkupyne, stop hiding behind official silence and prove that his government is not shielding political thugs,” he said. The former vice-president also called on Tinubu and the APC to stop what he described as the brutalisation of opposition supporters, insisting that political differences should not expose citizens to violence. He urged the police to identify those responsible for the alleged attack and investigate whether any individuals sponsored or facilitated it. “The police must urgently investigate allegations of political involvement, identify the perpetrators and expose whoever sponsored or facilitated this cowardly attack,” Atiku said. Atiku also appealed to Amnesty International and foreign missions in Nigeria to monitor the treatment of opposition supporters and document cases of alleged politically motivated violence ahead of the 2027 general election. “I am formally drawing the attention of Amnesty International and all foreign missions in Nigeria to this deeply troubling incident,” he said. He called for justice for Idedia and protection for Nigerians exercising their right to political choice and peaceful dissent. “I demand immediate justice for Porkupyne and protection for every Nigerian exercising the right to political choice and peaceful dissent,” he added.

title: Soldiers Kill 15 Terrorists in Borno Air Strike
body: Linus Aleke in Abuja Troops of Operation Hadin Kai have neutralised 15 terrorists in a precision air strike north-west of Pulka in Gwoza Local Government Area (LGA) of Borno State. The Nigerian Army said the terrorists were neutralised during an operation conducted at about 11:50 pm on October 23, 2026. The Acting Military Information Officer of the North-east Joint Task Force, Operation Hadin Kai, Captain Mohammed Goni, disclosed this in a statement issued yesterday. Goni said the operation followed credible intelligence and confirmed sightings of terrorist movements in the Pulka area. The statement read, “The Joint Task Force (North East), Operation HADIN KAI (OPHK), has recorded another operational success with the neutralisation of 15 terrorists in a precision air strike north-west of Pulka in Gwoza LGA of Borno State. “The operation was conducted at about 11:50 p.m. on 23 October 2026, following credible intelligence and confirmed sightings of terrorist movements in the general area of Pulka.” According to Goni, the air strike was followed by ground operations to exploit the area and consolidate the operational gains. He said the engagement demonstrated the effectiveness of intelligence-driven targeting and coordinated military action in disrupting terrorist movements and degrading their operational capabilities. “It also reflects the unwavering commitment of Operation HADIN KAI to denying terrorist groups freedom of action and preventing them from threatening communities within the theatre,” he added. Goni said the operation formed part of the sustained offensive operations by troops, supported by intelligence gathering and the coordinated deployment of available military capabilities. “Through these efforts, the Theatre Command continues to maintain pressure on terrorist elements, disrupt their activities and strengthen the security environment across the North East,” he stated. He assured the public that Operation Hadin Kai remained committed to defeating terrorism and insurgency, protecting law-abiding citizens and creating conditions for the restoration of normalcy and socio-economic activities in affected communities. “The Theatre Command reassures the public that troops will sustain the momentum of ongoing operations with vigilance, determination and professionalism,” he said. Goni urged members of the public to continue cooperating with security agencies by providing timely and credible information about suspicious movements and activities. “The continued partnership between the military and the civilian population remains essential to consolidating operational gains and achieving lasting peace and security across the North East,” he said.

title: Leafs scorch Oilers 7-2 for fourth win in a row
body:
EDMONTON – William Nylander had two goals, including the 300th of his career, as the Toronto Maple Leafs scorched the Edmonton Oilers 7-2 on Saturday.
Jack Roslovic, Auston Matthews, Troy Stecher, Zack MacEwen and Vinni Lettieri also scored for the Maple Leafs (7-4-2) who have won four straight.
Anthony Stolarz made 30 stops to earn the win in the Toronto net.
Leon Draisaitl scored twice for the Oilers (8-2-1) who had a three-game winning streak halted. With his league-leading 12th goal, Draisaitl recorded his third consecutive two-goal game and extended his goal-scoring streak to six games, during which he has nine goals.
Tristan Jarry recorded 25 saves for Edmonton.
Maple Leafs: Matthews and Kirill Marchenko both extended their season-opening road point streak to five games. Matthews now needs just one point to reach 800 in his career, which will make him the fastest player in franchise history to reach the milestone, in addition to the NHL’s third quickest American skater to hit the mark.
Oilers: Connor McDavid had two assists to extend his season-starting points streak to 11 games — giving him an incredible 33 points in 11 games. McDavid entered the contest scoring at a staggering 3.10 points-per-game rate.
Just 54 seconds after going up 2-0, Kirill Marchenko made a nice pass to hit Stecher in flight in the slot and he scored his second goal of the season in as many games.
No team has had more success in Rogers Place in Edmonton than the Maple Leafs. Since the Oilers moved into their new arena, Toronto has gone 12-2-1.
The Maple Leafs have been impressive this season on the PK. They had killed 40 of 41 opposition power plays and 30 in a row until Edmonton got one late in Saturday’s game.
Maple Leafs: Visit the Calgary Flames on Monday.
Oilers: Host the Detroit Red Wings on Monday.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 24, 2026.

title: Ebola: Lagos Upgrades Isolation Centre, Targets 24-Hour Test Results
body: The Lagos State Government has intensified preparedness against Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) following the confirmation of an index case in Abuja, upgrading its isolation centre and targeting laboratory test results within 24 hours. The state Commissioner for Health, Prof. Akin Abayomi, disclosed this in a statement, saying Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu had directed relevant agencies to maintain a high level of alertness and preparedness. Abayomi said Lagos was treating the situation as a priority because of the constant movement of people between Lagos and Abuja. He said the state’s Emergency Operations Centre had been working ahead of the confirmed case, with teams conducting simulation exercises to ensure responders understood their roles. According to him, the state’s isolation centre has been upgraded, while additional capacity is being developed. Training for health workers in public and private facilities is also ongoing, with emphasis on infection prevention and control. The commissioner said the state was establishing a clear pathway for laboratory testing, targeting results within 24 hours. “Our isolation centre has been upgraded, and additional capacity is ongoing,” Abayomi said. “We are defining a clear pathway from sample to result, targeting results within 24 hours.” He added that a dedicated Ebola Research Committee was reviewing the latest evidence on treatments and vaccines to guide decisions. Abayomi said the state was also refining screening at airports and other points of entry in collaboration with federal partners. He noted that disease surveillance was being digitally enhanced on SHIP to improve the detection, tracing and real-time response to suspected cases. The commissioner urged residents to wash their hands regularly with soap and water and avoid contact with the blood and body fluids of anyone who was ill. He advised anyone experiencing fever, weakness, vomiting, diarrhoea or unexplained bleeding, or who suspected exposure to the virus, not to self-medicate but to call health authorities before visiting a health facility. Abayomi also urged health workers to maintain a high index of suspicion, ask patients about their travel history and use personal protective equipment. Residents were advised to report suspected cases or exposure through the Lagos State emergency numbers, 112 and 767, or the Directorate of Epidemiology, Biosecurity and Global Health on 0802 316 9485. He urged residents to remain calm, stay alert and rely on official information from the Lagos State Ministry of Health.

title: Okpebholo Threatens to Sign Death Warrant of Condemned Kidnappers, Cultists If …
body: Governor Monday Okpebholo of Edo State yesterday said he would not hesitate to sign the death of the four convicted Vegetable Market kidnappers if they did not appeal against the judgment within the stipulated time. He said even if they appealed they were just postponing what would still come on them. Speaking during a fellowship at God’s People Worldwide Prayer Ministry, while reviewing his administration’s efforts to curb kidnapping, cultism and other violent crimes in Edo State, said insecurity was one of the biggest worries he met on assuming office. Okpebholo said that he raised the state of the roads and the security situation with President Bola Tinubu at their meeting who he said give him the approval to resolve the issues. The governor said that when the gunmen struck at the Vegetable Market in Benin City, he called the President, who asked if he could handle it, and he said he could. “I called the Commissioner of Police and told him I wanted these guys arrested, because I already have an approval from God, and they were caught within that time. “They are already sentenced to death, and I pray they don’t appeal the judgment. Even when they appeal the judgment, they are only delaying time. If within the days stipulated, they don’t appeal, I will execute,” he said. An Edo State Special Criminal Court on September 29 2026 sentenced four defendants to death for the abduction of a woman at the Vegetable Market along Airport Road, Benin City. The governor said that before he began the campaign against kidnapping and cultism, he met prominent traditional rulers across the state to warn them against interceding for anyone involved in the crimes. He recalled many strange incidents linked to spiritual forces after his administration pulled down a building associated with a cult group: “A black bird died in my office when I demolished their building. A vulture also died in my bed while contesting for governorship,” he said. Founder of God’s People Worldwide Prayer Ministry, Apostle Ehijele Umuahia, during the event urged church members to vote for the governor and his preferred candidates in the 2027 elections. Citing Proverbs 29:2, he told the congregation that prayer for the governor should go together with active participation in the electoral process. Christians, he said, should come out in large numbers to vote. Umuahia described Governor Okpebholo as a humble man whose commitment to the things of God predates his time as governor. He said he has known him for over 15 years, from the days of the late Chief Tony Anenih. “Whenever Chief Tony Anenih came to visit me, he was one of those who accompanied him. That was how we came to know each other,” he said.

title: War Rhetoric? Not Again, Pat Utomi
body: In the run-up to the 2011 presidential election, political tension in Nigeria was intense. President Olusegun Obasanjo had done eight full years in office, and power had gone to the north in 2007. The zoning policy of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) envisaged that the north would also keep power for eight years. But President Umaru Musa Yar’Adua, Obasanjo’s successor, died less than three years into his tenure, and Vice-President Goodluck Jonathan succeeded him, as required by the 1999 Constitution. Yar’Adua’s death in May 2010 truncated that understanding, and power was back to the south by default. There was intense internal strife in the ruling party over power rotation. In some quarters, Jonathan was not expected to run in 2011 — so that a northerner would complete what was considered the north’s allotted eight years. The people of the Niger Delta insisted that they too deserved to produce the president, and this was a rare opportunity in Nigeria’s history. Gen Ibrahim Babangida, the former military president who spent eight years in power, Lt Gen Aliyu Mohammed Gusau, a former national security adviser (NSA), Alhaji Atiku Abubakar, former vice-president, and Dr Abubakar Bukola Saraki, then governor of Kwara state, entered a process within the PDP to produce a northern consensus candidate to confront Jonathan in the presidential primary. The political tension intensified as soon as Atiku was picked as the consensus candidate. Speaking at the THISDAY Dome, Abuja, in December 2010, during a conference organised by the Northern Political Leaders Forum (NPLF), the body that picked him as the northern candidate, Atiku attributed a famous JF Kennedy line to philosopher Frantz Fanon, warning: “Those who make peaceful change impossible make violent change inevitable.” He cleverly added a caveat: “This is not what we want for Nigeria.” As it turned out, Jonathan still defeated him to win the PDP’s ticket. Gen Muhammadu Buhari, candidate of the Congress for Progressive Change (CPC), became the sole northern hope. The ensuing tension along our fault lines was choking. And as results showed Jonathan heading for victory over Buhari, violence broke out in the north. Ten youth corps members, who were part of INEC ad hoc staff, were murdered in Bauchi for allegedly rigging for Jonathan, even though he got only 16 percent of the votes in the state. More than 800 people were killed in 12 northern states. Mr Abubakar Malami, then CPC national legal adviser, condemned the violence but said it was a reaction to the “determination” of the PDP to win the election “by any means”, citing the post-election riots of 1965 and 1983 as precedence. Malami later became the attorney-general of the federation. Meanwhile, Boko Haram, which had been carrying out deadly attacks since 2009, revved up its terror campaign, leading to unsubstantiated allegations that northern politicians were taking their pound of flesh over the zoning dispute. In April 2012, at a summit in Asaba, Delta state, Gen Andrew Owoye Azazi, then NSA, said: “The extent of violence did not increase until when there was a declaration by the current president that he was going to contest. The PDP got it wrong from the beginning by saying Mr A can rule, Mr A cannot rule… according to PDP’s convention, rules and regulation and not according to the constitution and that created the climate for what has manifested itself this way.” Why this excursion into history? Because I am beginning to hear echoes of 2011 as we approach another presidential election. And, disturbingly, one of those raising the spectre of violence is Prof Pat Utomi, a man I respect very highly and to whom I devote an entire chapter in my forthcoming book. In an X post last Sunday, he wrote: “I am in the middle of an accidental town hall meeting in Manchester… They were energized to ask for how they could own fighting rigging. The determination to do whatever will prevent election malpractice suggest we may see a civil war if power tries to muscle the will of the people this time.” Notice the phrase: “will of the people”. Which people? For some people, if their preferred candidate is not declared the winner, then the election must have been rigged. True, rigging is a fact — it is undeniable — but it is not always the reason people lose elections. For instance, until his death, Buhari believed that he won the 2003, 2007 and 2011 elections but was rigged out. In 2011, he even alleged that a software in INEC’s computers reduced his votes by 40 percent. He was convinced his huge popularity in the core north was enough to make him president. But no candidate has ever won the presidential election by being popular in just one section of the country. You need other sections as well — as Buhari eventually realised in 2015. It is worrisome that many people do not countenance the fact that Nigeria has 36 states, the FCT, six geopolitical zones and 774 local government areas. More than 20 million Nigerians regularly vote in presidential elections. Different interests motivate them. Some are moved by ethnic and religious sentiments; some, political affinity; some, party affiliation; some, ideals and policies; and some, “stomach infrastructure”. Moreover, voters in rural areas, semi-urban towns and big cities behave differently when it comes to voting. Social media and WhatsApp cannot capture every sentiment. But many voters project the voices of thousands as the choices of millions. The stuff of echo chambers. Not every allegation of rigging is backed by evidence. Sometimes, allegations arise from genuine irregularities. At other times, they are driven by an exaggerated sense of a candidate’s popularity. Electoral fraud is real, but so is political delusion. In an emotionally charged atmosphere, many find it difficult to believe that a candidate so overwhelmingly popular in their region could lose in another region. That was part of what happened in 2011. Buhari was hugely popular in the north. He polled 1,315,209 votes in Bauchi, while Jonathan had just 258,404. To his supporters, rigging was the most convenient explanation for him not being declared the president-elect, and violence was the redress. To be clear, we must stamp out rigging. We must talk tough and act tough. But there is a line we must not cross. We must never make bloodshed an acceptable response to electoral disappointment. Nor should those in power think they can rig with impunity. Those who rig elections and those who resort to violence in response are both enemies of democracy. One steals the people’s mandate; the other threatens their lives and property. Neither deserves our sympathy. No candidate is worth dying or killing for — in my opinion. As Jonathan would say, “My ambition is not worth the blood of any Nigerian.” Politicians should spend more time canvassing for votes instead of inciting violence. I am for free and fair elections any day, anytime, anywhere. I am for one person, one vote. I am against the manipulation of figures, voter suppression and vote trading. While I accept that voters cannot tell who will perform best in office, at least they can assess the candidates and their records and weigh their promises. Nobody has a crystal ball. Theirs is to vote. They cannot guarantee what the winner will do in office, but they can hold the government accountable and vote out the incumbent at the next opportunity if they have the numbers. The reality of electoral democracy is that everybody may have their say, but not everybody will have their way. Life is not fair, is it? Utomi would say he did not explicitly call for civil war but was only warning about the possible consequences of rigging, but reckless language has consequences too. Putting ideas in people’s heads has consequences. Those who use the language of violence are hardly victims in the end. Even their family members are hardly affected. It is the people on the street who bear the scars. Some families have not recovered from the violence of the past that led to killings and destruction of property. I am troubled by the ease with which some people invoke the possibility of another civil war in a delicately balanced country like Nigeria. Such wild language can take on a life of its own. Indeed, the Ahmed Lemu panel that investigated the 2011 post-election violence identified inflammatory political statements among the factors that fuelled the killings. Words matter, especially when the political atmosphere is already combustible. INEC, the security agencies and the political authorities must be put on their toes to ensure a free and fair election in 2027. They are not doing us a favour by ensuring a credible process. And politicians must learn to handle defeat rather than attribute every electoral failure to rigging. It is so predictable and has almost become part of the formality. Nobody should threaten us with civil war or bloodshed over an election. Not again, please. AND FOUR OTHER THINGS… EBOLA ALERT The wife of a Swiss diplomat has become the index case of Ebola in Nigeria, 12 years after the first incident. She had just returned from Uganda when she started showing symptoms of the deadly disease, which kills about half of those infected on average. The comforting part is that Ebola does not spread through the air like COVID-19. It is transmitted mainly through direct contact with the bodily fluids of infected people who have developed symptoms, or with contaminated materials. The scary part is that early Ebola symptoms look like malaria or flu, so they can be easily seen as normal. I must commend the federal government for its prompt public enlightenment campaign. Kudos. AAC VS APC I was surprised that many laughed off the request by the African Action Congress (AAC) to use the State House banquet hall for the inauguration of its presidential campaign council. The party, which is fielding Comrade Omoyele Sowore as its presidential candidate, also requested the provision of food, drinks, and logistical support for an estimated 5,000 participants attending from Nigeria and abroad. Why? The ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) used the same hall, which belongs to Nigeria and not to any party, to inaugurate its own campaign council. What is sauce for the goose should be sauce for the gander. The request may be ignored but AAC has made its point. Simple. VALUE DECLINE I fly ValueJet regularly and I have always recommended it to my friends because of its promptness and efficiency. I am now forced to admit that its standards have been falling for a while, which I can live with for now. What I cannot live with is to book an Abuja-Lagos flight, only to find myself in Iperu, Ogun state, as I did on Wednesday. No indication there would be a stopover during booking. No such information on my ticket. No such announcement when the flight was called. I believe some people just think Nigeria is a jungle where anything goes, where they can do anything and get away with it. This is quite unprofessional and I suppose it is actionable in a court of law. Impunity. NO COMMENT Chief Samuel Ortom, former governor of Benue state, has been complaining about the failure of his successor to give him befitting benefits. “I was supposed to be provided with a house,” he said, with the sense of entitlement that has become a culture for our politicians. “You have seen me here in my Games Village house. Which ex-governor is living in Games Village? The whole of this country, in Abuja here, which governor is living in Games Village?” Can you imagine a whole former governor, His Excellency, living in Games Village when his mates have mansions in Banana Island, Maitama, Asokoro, New York, Dubai, Tokyo, Doha, Acapulco, Bahamas and Cairo? What a pity. Hahahaha…

title: The Evolving Character of the 2027 Campaigns
body: Postscript by Waziri Adio Nigeria’s potentially historic presidential election is 83 days away. The political parties chose their presidential candidates about five months ago, in line with the electoral timetable. The presidential campaign window officially opened on 19 August, more than two months ago. Yet the campaigns have not fully come to life. Many parties have yet to inaugurate their presidential campaign councils or unveil their policy documents. By now, the parties and their candidates should be criss-crossing the country, generating excitement and selling themselves and their ideas to potential voters, rather than largely making the rounds of television stations and issuing a flurry of press statements and social media posts. More than 40% of the campaign window has elapsed, but the campaign machinery has yet to get into full gear across the board. At this stage of the 2023 electoral cycle, the energy in the air was so thick it could be sliced. Indeed, many candidates had started campaigning before the official kick-off. The lull in the first two months of the present campaign window could create two impressions: that the stakes are lower than they were in 2023, and that the 2027 presidential election is all but settled. Both impressions would be wrong. So much rides on the January 2027 election for the leading candidates and the country, and its outcome is far from settled. The relatively quiet start is not indicative of how the rest of the campaign or the election itself might unfold. In my column of 7 June, I argued that the 2027 presidential election would be more bitterly contested than the 2023 one. I have seen no reason to revise that position. So, what is happening, and what does it tell us about the likely character of the 2027 presidential campaigns? I will make five broad observations. First, we are likely to see a greater emphasis on virtual campaigns and smaller events than on physical campaigns and mega rallies in this electoral cycle. Physical campaigns cost a lot of money. The current cash crunch makes fundraising even harder for the opposition in an election with an incumbent on the ballot. Opposition parties and their candidates have to be strategic, concentrating their energy and resources when these are likely to make the greatest impression on voters: closer to election day. Media appearances and events staged for broadcast are not always free, but they are generally cheaper than mega rallies. So, don’t expect sustained, intensive campaigning until about four to six weeks before the presidential poll. My second point follows from the first: we do not need a campaign period of five to six months. Earlier in this republic, elections were held within three to four months of the conclusion of party primaries. Advocates of a longer electioneering period argued that it would give the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) more time to prepare and citizens more time to get to know the candidates. They cited examples from other countries. I was never persuaded and saw the change as an attempt to fix what was not broken. A longer campaign does not necessarily level the playing field. It can further advantage those who already have the most resources. Nor does it automatically produce a more searching examination of the issues. It may simply prolong the distraction for everyone. The more useful priority is to hold elections early enough for all election petitions and appeals to be resolved before a new administration is sworn in. Third, despite the slow start to public rallies, this campaign season is going to be heated, especially in the traditional media and on social media. What we have seen so far suggests that the rancour and savagery could surpass even the levels of 2023, which I consider the worst in the Fourth Republic. Desperation on all sides, and a willingness to stoop low in pursuit of electoral advantage, will drive this. Intemperate language, gratuitous insults and attacks, fake news aided by artificial intelligence, and incitement are becoming more common. Ridiculing opponents and discrediting their ideas have always been part of electioneering. But there must be limits. For me, fake news and incitement cross the line. Fourth, the cost-of-living crisis will be the central issue of this campaign season. I expect it to receive more attention and resonate more widely than insecurity. The recent surge in the prices of food, transport and other essentials is fresh in people’s minds, while terrorism has afflicted the country since Boko Haram began its campaign of violence. This does not make insecurity any less grave. But the rise in living costs can also be linked directly to key policies of the current administration, even where external shocks, such as the global energy crisis, have compounded the pressure. This is a boon to the opposition, and it would be unreasonable to expect it not to exploit the issue to the hilt. I support the economic reforms, as I will never tire of saying. Nigeria was inches away from complete collapse, though this was not apparent to everyone. The shock therapy administered by President Bola Tinubu’s administration was necessary and proper. However, the government could have done much more to help Nigerians cope better with the shocks. It should have prioritised social protection and targeted relief against the expected increases in food and transport costs, which absorb a disproportionate share of poor households’ incomes. The government should be taken to task over how it has managed the pain of the reforms. Election time is precisely the time to do so. But the opposition should also be pressed on what it would do differently, how it would do it and what it would cost. The opposition seems to have found a magic bullet for the affordability crisis: the petrol subsidy. Leading the charge is former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar, the presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC). He has promised a production subsidy rather than the familiar consumption subsidy, with support tied to verifiable barrels to prevent the usual sharp practices. But he has yet to provide the figures needed to establish the cost of the subsidy, how it would be funded and what other spending would have to give way. Moving the subsidy to the supply side does not, by itself, resolve these questions or guarantee lower food and transport costs. For his part, Mr Peter Obi, the candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), now says he would restore the petrol subsidy while eliminating the corruption associated with it. This marks a shift from his earlier support for subsidy removal. He has pointed to personal and family probity and promised to be in charge. But these assurances do not amount to a detailed plan for tackling corruption in the subsidy system. Some other candidates have joined the petrol subsidy-restoration bandwagon, mostly by clowning around. The opposition has alighted on something to which many Nigerians have a deep emotional attachment: subsidy on petrol, rather than on kerosene, diesel or aviation fuel. Yet unsubsidised petrol can be affordable when crude prices are low and other costs are favourable. It is also worth bearing in mind that restoring petrol subsidy does not automatically send the prices of other goods tumbling. Opposition candidates sometimes seem irritated when asked for the details of their plans. But both the incumbent and the challengers deserve scrutiny. Voters need to know that the candidates understand the issues and that their proposals will not make things worse. My fifth observation extends the last point: this campaign is shaping up to be heavy on vibes and soundbites and light on deep policy discussion. Given where Nigeria stands, we need a serious discussion about the country’s direction more than ever. Should we stay the course, make adjustments or take a different path? What are the candidates proposing to address the country’s key challenges and how workable are those options? About five months after the candidates emerged, more than two months into the campaign and less than three months before this consequential election, there is still too little clarity about where the leading candidates stand, especially the challengers. Yes, they have made announcements and delivered some memorable lines. But announcements are not policies. Voters need detailed manifestoes and policy documents setting out what the candidates intend to do, why and how. The apparent calculation is that few Nigerians care about policy, that most are eager to choose anyone but the incumbent, and that catchy lines are the easiest way to excite them. Some of these may be true. But there are also voters who want a credible basis for choosing among the candidates. To fulfil all righteousness, manifestoes and policy documents will be unveiled at some point. Yet the fact that this has not been done so far, with less than three months to the presidential election, says much about the priority of the leading candidates and the character of this campaign season.

title: Cornell student named in Jane Doe's civil suit seeks to be dropped from case
body:
The defense attorney argued it is now too late for Jane Doe to bring a claim.
One of the Cornell students who was named in a civil lawsuit by a former undergraduate student known as Jane Doe, has asked a judge to drop him from the suit.
The lawsuit claimed that during an alleged 2024 gang rape, Diego Sarabia approached Jane Doe, "grabbed her face and started kissing her, all without her consent," before she pushed him away.
Doe's lawsuit also alleged Sarabia was among the Chi Phi fraternity brothers who allegedly snorted ketamine off her body.
In a motion Friday to dismiss Jane Doe's complaint, James Knox, Sarabia's attorney, wrote that Doe did not allege in her suit that Sarabia "supplied her with drugs or alcohol, participated in any of the alleged sexual encounters described elsewhere in the complaint, or was even present for most of the conduct that forms the basis of plaintiff's broader allegations."
All seven frat brothers have denied wrongdoing and Sarabia argued he was not part of the most severe conduct alleged in the lawsuit.
"As far as defendant goes, this is essentially a lawsuit about an allegedly forced kiss," Knox wrote in a Friday motion to dismiss Jane Doe's complaint.
The lawyer argued it is now too late for Jane Doe to bring a claim against Sarabia.
"Any intentional tort arising out of that alleged conduct is foreclosed by a strict one-year statute of limitations because plaintiff commenced this action nearly two years after the alleged events," Knox wrote.
Doe's attorney has not yet filed a response to the motion.
The motion came a week after a New York judge rejected a request by Sarabia's attorney to impose a gag order .
Knox argued that a gag order would limit "possible juror prejudice" and prevent the potential release of sensitive information that could lead to " threats, doxing, intimidation, and extrajudicial contact."
Judge Phaedra Perry-Bond called the request a "side show" that's "meant to muddy the waters and distract from the merits of the claims and defenses involved in this case."
New York Attorney General Letitia James, who was appointed special prosecutor by Gov. Kathy Hochul, is conducting an investigation into the incident. Cornell, which said it fully supports the appointment of a special prosecutor, is also conducting an internal probe of its response to the allegations.
Cornell has said it takes allegations of allegations of sexual violence "extremely seriously" and that it "investigated and adjudicated the allegations consistent with university policies."
At the same time, the university has said it is committed to taking additional steps to improve campus safety.
The case has rocked the university and started conversations about treatment of sexual assault allegations on college campuses across the country.
24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

title: Amy Acton says Trump, Vance should 'look at the facts' after Ramaswamy attack ad
body:
Former President Barack Obama also railed against Trump at a campaign rally.
CLEVELAND -- Ohio Democratic gubernatorial nominee Amy Acton told ABC News in an interview Saturday that she hopes President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance will "look at the facts" of the abuse she says she endured as a child after they defended an attack ad made by GOP nominee Vivek Ramaswamy's campaign.
Bipartisan backlash has hit Ramaswamy's campaign after the release of the ad featuring Acton's estranged mother whom Acton says stood by the man who was criminally charged with sexually abusing her as a child. Acton said she hasn't seen her mother since she was 12 years old.
In the ad, Acton's mother, Donna Arthur, said Acton has lied about her past, though it doesn't mention the allegations of sexual abuse.
In response to Trump and Vance, who have doubled down on and defended the ad, Acton told ABC News, "My job is to work with anyone on any side of the aisle to solve problems instead of making them, and I would say I do hope they would look at the facts."
Acton spoke to ABC News after a rally in Cleveland with former President Barack Obama.
Acton has alleged her mother's second husband molested her between the ages of 9 and 12. Charges were filed against her stepfather and Acton testified against him. He pleaded not guilty, but fled the state before trial and never appeared before a judge. He died in 2004.
Acton said she and her brother endured "extreme child abuse and neglect" in their childhood.
"We were frequent flyers in children's services ... There are facts in this case: a grand jury indictment, fugitive out against bail, and that behavior went on and on," Acton said.
Speaking to reporters this week about the ad, Trump dismissed questions about the allegations of Acton's sexual abuse, asserting at multiple points that the ad has "nothing to do" with Acton's stepfather.
Similarly, Vance told rally attendees in Ohio earlier this week that he is "a little bit disgusted when I see Republicans across the country who are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America."
The Cleveland Plain Dealer, Ohio's largest newspaper, endorsed Acton for governor on Sunday, saying that it was reversing a previous decision to not endorse in the race in the wake of the ad.
"Vivek Ramaswamy, seeking the highest office in this state, has produced a campaign advertisement that weaponizes the sexual abuse his opponent, Amy Acton, suffered as a child. People across the political spectrum have rightly condemned it," the paper's editorial board wrote , in part.
"A candidate who uses childhood sexual abuse as a weapon against the person who endured it has crossed a line that Ohioans should defend, whatever their party. We are better than this. We have a responsibility to show it. Today, we endorse Democrat Amy Acton for governor."
The paper also wrote that Acton's other achievements further prompted their endorsement, declaring that Ramaswamy "has offered Ohioans far less reason to trust him."
"[Acton] has earned consideration on her own record, her preparation and her commitment to the people she seeks to serve," the paper wrote.
Ramaswamy's campaign on Sunday dismissed the paper's endorsement in a statement to ABC News, referring to its editor Chris Quinn by name.
"Anyone who thought Chris Quinn's paper wouldn't back the liberal in this race is fooling themselves," campaign spokesperson Evan Machan wrote.
GOP Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine, who on Thursday told reporters in Columbus, Ohio, that the ad is "deeply, deeply troubling" and that the Ramaswamy campaign "needs to take it down," but he did not withdraw his endorsement of Ramaswamy.
Asked whether she was disappointed that DeWine didn't withdraw his endorsement, Acton said it was "an honor and a privilege" to work with him during COVID-19 pandemic as the director of the Ohio Department of Health.
"I really do appreciate him calling out the facts of the case," Acton said. "That this was an indictment he knows better than others. He's a prosecutor. He started his career prosecuting cases like this, and he knew more than anyone. He knows who I am and knows my story."
Speaking to reporters on Friday, Ramaswamy said the ad had nothing to do with childhood abuse.
"We ran an ad about lying," he said. "Amy Acton is lying. She has been lying this entire campaign about me, about her record, about her history in this state."
In a statement to ABC News, Connie Luck, a spokesperson for Ramaswamy said: "Ohioans can't afford a liberal governor who shows up for Obama but never shows up for them."
Ramaswamy and Acton have never met in person. Asked what she would say to him, Acton said: "I really have no words for Mr. Ramaswamy. I think there is no low that he wouldn't sink to."
Speaking to survivors of abuse, Acton said: "For those out there going through it now, hold on, please. If there's someone you feel safe with, say something about it."
Acton campaigned Saturday alongside former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown, who's running to win back his seat, and Obama, who was the last Democratic presidential candidate to win the state of Ohio in a presidential election in 2012.
Democrats are eyeing the Senate and gubernatorial races as key pickup opportunities given the headwinds facing Republicans.
In his remarks, Obama delivered a scathing rebuke of the Trump administration on a variety of issues, from the economy to immigration to the war in Iran.
Regarding the GOP candidate for governor, Obama called Ramaswamy "thirsty" for attention.
"Vivek's own supporters know it's all about what's in it for him," Obama said. "We all know that guy, you know, who ... just wants to get attention no matter what, willing to do anything. And in recent days, we've seen there is no line he will not cross, no low he will not sink to."
Obama emphasized what he called a "moral component" to this election and said that "basic decency" is missing from the current public discourse.
ABC News' Diana Paulsen and Oren Oppenheim contributed to this report.
24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

title: What does luxury sound like? Inside the growing world of sonic branding
body: Those fortunate enough to own Ferrari’s new all-electric Luce may be preoccupied with whether the supercar can retain the Italian manufacturer’s famed engine sound. But listen more closely and it becomes clear that just as much thought has gone into the sounds inside the cabin, as Emmy-winning composer Nick Wood knows well. “From the engine start to indicators and warning tones, these are very simple noises. But they had to have a Ferrari feel to them, not sound generic like your open fridge door,” says Wood, who designed what he calls the Luce’s “sonic universe”. Every sound the car makes is the product of live recordings of organic sounds – from pianos and cellos to banging wood on pipework and the growl of vintage Ferraris – manipulated in the British composer’s Tokyo studio. “The importance of sound can come across as so nebulous that it can be hard to validate,” says Wood. “Brands are unsure about how to approach it. They’re all about cool video but have, until recently, no consistent identity for the way they sound. But, from product sounds – like those the Luce makes – to the music played at events, the idea of what’s called sonic branding is something more of them are waking up to.” Wood, one of the field’s pioneers, has worked with Chanel, Fiat, Uniqlo, Apple and the spa at Claridge’s hotel, and writes pieces of sound lasting anywhere from a second or two to several hours. Of course, the idea that brands should associate themselves with a sound is nothing new. Russell Boiarsky of Texas-based Stephen Arnold Music, which has worked on sonic identities for Airbnb, CNN and UPS, points out that the first radio jingle, for General Mills’ Wheaties cereal, was broadcast in Minneapolis a century ago this year. “But the difference is that jingles were meant to be earworms that you couldn’t forget whether you liked them or not, which is not always a positive thing. Sonic branding is about expressing the values of a brand through sound,” he explains. Think of Netflix’s start-up “ta-dum”, which suggests drama and a sense of occasion, or McDonald’s “I’m Lovin’ It” riff, designed to evoke fun and positivity. “The challenges,” Boiarsky adds, “are that it’s already a noisy world, so brands don’t want to bombard their customers with yet more.” There is already talk of a “sound-off economy”, in which more people keep their devices silent. “And audiences are already stretched thin for attention, so brands may have less than a couple of seconds to cut through.” When sonic branding succeeds, however, studies suggest it can be remarkably effective. Hearing is among the fastest senses our brain processes, while sound is closely connected to emotion and memory. As Wood points out, sounds can stay with us long after imagery has been forgotten – allowing a brand associated with them to resonate too. Repetition helps embed that association, but fewer iterations may be required than imagined: if a sound is well designed, as few as five exposures can be enough. And if the idea of a brand having a sound as much as a look still seems somewhat woolly, research is putting the effectiveness of this approach on a more scientific footing. “Brands are excited to hear that there is science behind this, that it’s not just witchcraft,” says Boiarsky with a laugh. Stephen Arnold Music works with UK-based SoundOut, a platform specialising in music testing and sonic brand analysis, to establish how closely a sonic logo or track matches a brand’s personality, its emotional impact and how distinctive it is. The company’s annual benchmark study tracks recognition and recall of sonic brands, while the company is now working with AI models to map particular kinds of sounds to certain feelings. “I don’t see that [insight] being used aggressively or to manipulate,” Boiarsky says – not, at least, in the way background “muzak” has been said to influence consumer choices or worker behaviour in shops and factories. Instead, he sees artificial intelligence as a starting point for a composer’s creativity, much as it can now generate a potential hit song that may lack the human element required for longevity. That is why, although sonic branding can be developed using synthesisers, Stephen Arnold Music often records with orchestras in pursuit of a more authentic sound. The human touch matters personally, too: both Wood and Boiarsky are recording artists in their own right. It is an approach shared by Unmute, a Copenhagen-based “creative sound agency”, which devised the sound logo for Imax cinemas globally. The team have spent the past year developing a new sonic identity for Danske Bank, which is now being rolled out. To create something that felt suitably Nordic for Denmark’s largest retail bank without sounding generic, Unmute even commissioned a bespoke piano using inherently intuitive audio cues. Built with two strings for every note, rather than the standard range of one to three, it produces what the agency describes as a “cleaner” sound. The instrument now stands in the lobby of the bank’s headquarters. “The work here is to translate a brand into meaningful sound, which will become part of that brand for years to come, so actually it’s a very big decision, rather like changing a logo,” explains Unmute co-founder and sonic director Simon Kringel. Sound may only have come to be regarded as a fundamental part of a brand’s ecosystem in the past five years or so, but Kringel believes its importance will continue to grow as our lives become increasingly digital. It is no coincidence that some of the most recognisable examples of sonic branding belong to technology companies such as Google and Nintendo, which have had a head start. “The move from print to digital platforms, and the fact that the way we interact with so many brands now is through websites and increasingly ‘gamified’ apps, means that the opportunity for sound is there, as well as the need for a sonic identity and user-friendliness,” says Kringel. “The questions for any brand to understand are: ‘How do we sound as a company?’, ‘How do we sound different from our competitors?’ and ‘How can people make a connection to us when they’re only listening?’”

title: Batherson nets hat trick as Senators sink Rangers
body:
OTTAWA – The Ottawa Senators survived a late rally by the New York Rangers to earn a 7-4 win Saturday night.
Drake Batherson had three goals and an assist for the Senators, who were outshot 27-25.
Jake Sanderson’s first of the season proved to be the winner and Michael Amadio added an empty-net goal for insurance.
Tim Stutzle and Dylan Cozens also scored for the hosts. Jonas Johansson made his Senators debut stopping 23 of 27 shots.
Will Cuylle, J.T. Miller, Alexis Lafreniere and Pavel Dorofeyev scored for the Rangers. Dylan Garand, making his seventh consecutive start, stopped 18 shots.
Sanderson’s first of the season was a big one. Garand made an initial save on Ridly Greig and Sanderson buried the rebound to make it 5-3. But the Rangers got back within one on a Dorofeyev snap shot with 4:28 remaining.
Five goals in the second period saw the Senators holding a one-goal lead, 4-3.
Batherson gave the Senators a 3-0 lead 1:47 into the second, settling a rebound and beating Garand from in close.
The Rangers made it 3-1 scoring short-handed off a Cozens turnover that led to a 2-on-1. Noah Laba poked the puck ahead to send Cuylle in alone and beat Johansson.
Cozens scored his first of the season just over a minute later when a Batherson shot deflected off his skate.
New York then scored twice to pull within one. Miller found a loose puck out front and with 26 seconds remaining Lafreniere buried a pass from Miller.
Ottawa jumped out to a 2-0 lead in the first, scoring twice in a span of 66 seconds.
Batherson opened the scoring taking a pass from Sanderson at the side of the net and wristed it past Garand.
Just over a minute later, Claude Giroux snagged a turnover, found Fabian Zetterlund who dished it off to Stutzle on the rush and scored.
Senators: Despite Jake Sanderson’s return the Senators power play continued to struggle going 0-for-3.
Rangers: The Rangers dominated play in the offensive zone for long periods of time in the third.
The Senators own a 24-9-1 record when Batherson and Stutzle score in the same game.
Rangers: Host the Los Angeles Kings on Monday.
Senators: Visit the Vegas Golden Knights on Tuesday.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 24, 2026.

title: Serbia to hold early parliamentary elections
body:
BELGRADE, October 25. /TASS/. Early elections to the National Assembly (unicameral parliament) will be held in Serbia.
The Republic Electoral Commission has registered 6,451,292 voters who will elect 250 lawmakers to serve four-year terms.
Polling stations will open at 7:00 a.m. local time (6:00 a.m. GMT) and close at 8:00 p.m. (7:00 p.m. GMT). According to the REC, more than 16,000 observers, including 622 foreign observers, will monitor the voting process.
The ballots will feature 18 electoral lists. The main contenders are expected to be the United Serbia list of the ruling Serbian Progressive Party, led by Aleksandar Vucic, who stepped down as the country’s president on September 27, and the Student List coalition. The latter grew out of a protest movement that erupted in Serbia following the tragedy in Novi Sad in November 2024, when 16 people died when a concrete canopy at the train station collapsed.

title: Cerebras Deploys Trillion-Parameter AI Models
body:
Oracle Cloud Infrastructure plans to offer Cerebras inference to AI labs, enterprises, and developers. Read more >>
One of the most frequently asked questions we get is how we deploy large models on Cerebras wafer-scale chips. A single Cerebras WSE-3T wafer has 44 GB of on-chip memory, and trillion-parameter frontier models need terabytes for their weights alone.
In this post, we’ll explain how we split a large frontier model across multiple WSE-3T wafers, to run multi-trillion parameter models at 1000-2000+ tokens per second.
We’ll use the open source model Kimi K3, with ~3 trillion parameters, as an illustrative example.
Kimi K3 is an open source, 3T parameter model with 69 linear-attention layers and 24 dense layers.
It scores an impressive 88.3% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (vs. GPT-5.6 Sol's 88.8%) and 91.2% on BrowseComp (vs. GPT-5.6 Sol's 90.4%). These results demonstrate frontier-level coding and agentic capabilities, even outperforming leading proprietary models on some benchmarks. Read more about Kimi K3 here .

This gives us a total wafer count of 35 + 24 = 59 wafers.
Cerebras executes models in a pipeline. After the Cerebras compiler maps the model layers across regions of wafers, the runtime maps the path for tokens to flow between wafers. For ultrafast latency, only activations need to be passed between the wafers, and this can be done via RDMA over Ethernet. This is roughly 2 microseconds per hop.
It’s important to emphasize that because each Cerebras wafer has 44 GB of on-chip SRAM and each layer is only 16 GB, we are typically able to fit entire layers of the model directly on the chip.
This means that in most cases, the model weights never have to move, and layers don’t need to be split across wafers. Only activations cross from one wafer to the next.
Now that we have our wafers connected together and the model laid out, we can think of each wafer as one stage in an assembly line: the model’s weights for each stage stay in place, and the request’s intermediate results move through the layer stages.
For example, Wafer 1 runs model layers 1–2 and sends its activations to wafer 2. Wafer 2 runs layers 3–4 and passes its results to Wafer 3, and so on until the last wafer produces the next token.
This raises a common misconception. If a token has to travel through each wafer in order, doesn’t each wafer sit idle while it waits for its turn? In effect, wouldn't the system be running at a batch size of one?
No! If we only sent one request down the line at a time and waited for it to complete before starting the next request, this would be an inefficient use of the pipeline. Instead, we keep the entire pipeline full with different requests. Because the model is split into pipeline stages already, each stage can work on a different request at the same time.
While stage 3 processes a token for request A, stage 2 processes one for request B, and stage 1 one for request C. In our example, each stage is a layer. In production, Cerebras uses much finer-grained stages, and many more of them.
Each stage can also process a micro-batch , a small group of requests, rather than a single request. So the number of requests in flight is roughly the number of stages times the micro-batch size.
To understand the tradeoff, smaller micro-batches make each request even faster, while larger micro-batches increase total throughput.
The amount of on-chip memory allocated to KV cache determines the maximum number of concurrent requests. Every request in flight needs its own KV cache on each dense-layer wafer, so the size of on-chip memory sets the ceiling on concurrent requests. As explained above, we only need to calculate KV cache requirements for dense layers.
For each 44 GB wafer that already has one dense layer, we can calculate the remaining space for the KV cache with:
Total wafer storage - size of one dense layer. In this case:
Calculating the # of Concurrent Requests
To find the number of concurrent requests supported for any particular model mapping, we first calculate how much cache a single 256k request takes up:
To then calculate the total number of concurrent requests this configuration would support, we divide:
The total number of concurrent requests represents the number of simultaneous requests moving through the pipeline at any point in time. Unlike a GPU batch, those requests don’t wait for one another to finish, they stream through the pipeline continuously.
Of course, neither concurrency nor batch size tells you exactly how efficiently an inference system performs. When evaluating the throughput of an inference system, the more meaningful metric is total token throughput per unit of power (e.g. tokens per second per megawatt), when measured at the same output generation speed.
The same approach extends to larger models: calculate the memory needed for weights and request state, distribute the model across wafers, and connect them into a pipeline. Each additional wafer contributes compute and on-chip memory, allowing us to accommodate models that exceed the capacity of any single chip.

title: Military paramedic and veteran Olena Sharhovska dies at 43
body:
That is according to Suspilne Kultura , Ukrinform reports.
In 2015, she began traveling to the front with the Mykola Pyrohov First Volunteer Mobile Hospital and later joined the Hospitallers medical battalion.
"Having mastered tactical medicine, 'Jane' went out to evacuate the wounded from the hottest sections of the front line, snatching our soldiers from the clutches of death on the way to stabilization points," the medical battalion's members said on Facebook .
In September 2022, Sharhovska enlisted in the International Legion of the Ukrainian Armed Forces, where she also conducted tactical medicine training. At the same time, she continued serving on rotations with the Hospitallers battalion.
The team at Novynarnia, a media outlet with which the veteran had worked, said that health problems forced her to leave military service in August 2024.
In civilian life, the journalist also worked as a translator, social media specialist and editor, including in television and print media and on projects run by Ukraїner and Osvitoria.
According to Novynarnia, Sharhovska defended the rights of women in the military in 2015-2016, campaigning for women's right to serve in the Ukrainian Armed Forces and helping organize the "Invisible Battalion March."

title: IN BRIEF: Brazil to hold second round of presidential elections
body:
RIO DE JANEIRO, October 25. /TASS/. The second, decisive round of the general election will take place in Brazil. Voters will decide who will serve as head of state for the next four years: incumbent President and Workers’ Party leader Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva or the candidate from the right-wing opposition, senator Flavio Bolsonaro.
Voting in Brazil will take place from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. local time (11:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. GMT). More than 158.7 million Brazilian citizens are eligible to vote. Voting is mandatory for all literate Brazilians between the ages of 18 and 69.
Incumbent President Lula da Silva is seeking re-election for what would be the final term of his political career. He is building his campaign around strengthening Brazil’s international standing and expanding export opportunities, particularly with countries in the Global South and the BRICS. His domestic policy agenda includes tax reform, government funding for defense and technology initiatives, and actively developing hydrocarbon reserves.
Meanwhile, Flavio Bolsonaro is focusing his campaign on strongly condemning the government’s policies and drawing public attention to the excessive tax burden and rampant street crime. The right-wing opposition candidate has rallied the conservative electorate and powerful agricultural interests behind him. In foreign policy, he favors the US market and aims to restore bilateral relations to the level seen during the administrations of Jair Bolsonaro and Donald Trump.
The October 4 vote showed an advantage for conservative forces and fell short of the incumbent president’s expectations, falling short of the incumbent president’s expectations of a first-round victory. According to the results, Flavio Bolsonaro took the lead with 47.03% of the vote. Lula da Silva is in second place with 45.16%. The margin between the candidates was less than two percentage points. Given an electorate of 150 million, this is equal to nearly two to three million votes.
On the eve of the second round, the son of the former Brazilian leader is considered the frontrunner. Flavio Bolsonaro managed to seize the political initiative by successfully mobilizing voters in economically developed regions and the agricultural business sector.
Lula da Silva’s campaign shifted to a defensive strategy between the rounds, finding itself playing catch-up. The government passed emergency social measures, including debt relief for four million self-employed individuals and an unexpected increase in benefits for the poor.

title: Hellenic Club Centenary Gala Draws Albanese and Venizelos in Sydney
body: SYDNEY, October 2026 — The Hellenic Club centenary gala at the Hyatt Regency Sydney on Saturday drew Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Greek Ambassador Stavros Venizelos and NSW ministers to mark 100 years of the club. Albanese spoke at the black-tie ball marking the Hellenic Club centenary, which the club had said was sold out. He thanked club president Nikolas Hatzistergos for inviting him to the milestone event. Presenters at the podium during the Hellenic Club centenary gala. Photo: Nick Bourdaniotis Since the 1920s the club has served Sydney’s Greek community, and it says it is the last multicultural institution in the city centre. Albanese also praised the contribution of Greek Australians to the nation. “Australia without Greek Australians is simply beyond imagining,” he said. Albanese then traced the club’s origins to a small group of Greek shopkeepers in 1926: “What is most telling is that when we turn the clock back to 1926, there weren’t all that many Greeks in Sydney – at least not yet. Somewhere between 1000 and 1500 in a city of a million. But for a bunch of Greek shopkeepers who put their heads together, that was more than enough – and out of their vision, the Hellenic Club was born.” Anthony Albanese, Prime Minister of Australia He said the club later helped new arrivals settle and became “the heartbeat of Sydney’s Greek community” . The Prime Minister also linked the night to OXI Day on 28 October, which marks Greece’s refusal of an ultimatum from invading fascist powers in 1940. He said Australians joined the fight in Greece’s “most desperate hour of need” . Finally, Albanese closed his speech with a toast to the next century. “Happy anniversary. Here’s to your next hundred years,” he said. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese with members of the Hellenic Presidential Guard (Evzones) after they were presented with a Hellenic Club medallion. Photo: Nick Bourdaniotis Hellenic Club centenary guests Ambassador Venizelos and the club’s patron, Nick Politis AM, also attended the Hellenic Club centenary. The club’s board appointed Politis as patron in June, and the club said at the time that his appointment would be formally acknowledged at the centenary ball. Politis has chaired the Sydney Roosters since 1993 and was made a Member of the Order of Australia in 2014 for significant service to rugby league football as an administrator. Nick Politis AM, honorary patron of the Hellenic Club Sydney. Photo: Nick Bourdaniotis NSW Ministers Stephen Kamper, Courtney Houssos and Sophie Cotsis attended, as well as Consul General of Greece in Sydney Georgios Skemperis. The Hon. Stephen Kamper MP, NSW Minister for Lands and Property, Minister for Multiculturalism, Minister for Sport and Minister for Jobs and Tourism. Photo: Nick Bourdaniotis Father Stavros Ivanos represented Archbishop Makarios of Australia. Andrew Liveris AO, president of the Brisbane 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games Organising Committee, also joined the guests. Photo: Nick Bourdaniotis Former Australian officials Arthur Sinodinos AO and Arthur Spyrou, the former Australian Ambassador to Greece, attended too. In addition, past presidents and current board members of the Hellenic Club joined the Hellenic Club centenary celebrations. Photo: Nick Bourdaniotis During the evening, Nick Politis was made an honorary patron of the club. A tsarouchi, the traditional shoe of the Evzones, is presented on stage at the Hellenic Club Sydney centenary gala. Photo: Nick Bourdaniotis Greek singer Eleftheria Eleftheriou performed at the gala as a special guest. The club had announced her, together with Trio Mousikanti from Greece, as the headline entertainment. Eleftheria Eleftheriou, performing at the Hellenic Club Sydney centenary gala. Photo: Nick Bourdaniotis Early years and premises According to the club’s official history page , a group of Greek shopkeepers in inner-city Sydney began meeting in 1924. The club incorporated on 4 December 1926. Its first rooms stood at the corner of Castlereagh and Park streets. The club also helped raise funds for the Greek Orthodox church of St Sophia, which opened in September 1927. For many years the club limited membership to 60 people. During World War II, however, it made all Greeks serving in the armed forces honorary members. The Hellenic Club Sydney centenary cake at the gala dinner. Photo: Nick Bourdaniotis In the 1940s the club bought 195–197 Elizabeth Street under president Peter Soulos. Later, in 1954, it bought 251–253 Elizabeth Street, where Hellenic House opened on 19 October 1959 in the presence of NSW Premier JJ Cahill. In the late 1960s, club donations helped fund chairs in archaeology and modern Greek studies at the University of Sydney. The club bought 238–240 Castlereagh Street in 1979. Photo: Nick Bourdaniotis In 2013 the club converted the historic Australian Workers Union building there into Alpha Dining. Past presidents include John Comino and Jim Kospetas, who led the board in the 2000s. A speaker addresses the full ballroom at the Hellenic Club centenary gala. Photo: Nick Bourdaniotis The Hellenic Club centenary gala formed part of the club’s program for the Hellenic Presidential Guard (Evzones), whose Sydney visit the club hosts with support from the NSW Government. Video: Nick Bourdaniotis The Evzones attend the OXI Day ANZAC Memorial ceremony in Hyde Park on Sunday 25 October. They then travel to Canberra on 28 October. A historic photograph is shown on screen during the Hellenic Club centenary gala. Photo: Nick Bourdaniotis Guests dance at the Hellenic Club centenary gala ball. title: Kimberly Guilfoyle Posting to Greece Tied to Alleged Trump Family Feud
body: Kimberly Guilfoyle’s controversial departure from her role as US ambassador to Greece has taken a new turn, with reports alleging that a bitter personal dispute within Donald Trump Jr.’s inner circle influenced her diplomatic appointment to Athens. An investigation by Greek newspaper Kathimerini reportedly examined claims that Guilfoyle’s relationship with her former fiancé, Donald Trump Jr., deteriorated after messages allegedly sent about his partner, Bettina Anderson, triggered tensions within the Trump family. According to sources cited in the reporting, the fallout contributed to a decision to move Guilfoyle thousands of miles away from the president’s family by appointing her to a diplomatic post in Greece. The allegations have not been independently established, and the precise circumstances behind her appointment remain unclear. Alleged messages fuel claims of a family feud Guilfoyle, 57, was previously engaged to Donald Trump Jr. before their relationship ended and he became involved with Anderson, 39. The report alleges that private messages contained unflattering remarks about Anderson and her relationship with Trump Jr. It also refers to alleged exchanges between Guilfoyle and Trump donor Eric Deters concerning the president’s eldest son’s partner. The exact messages have not been made public in full, and the claims remain allegations. According to the reports, Guilfoyle also allegedly suggested that Anderson had supplied bikini photographs to the Daily Mail . The claims have added another layer to the dispute surrounding Guilfoyle’s personal relationships and her standing within Trump’s political circle. Sources cited in the investigation suggested that her appointment to Greece was intended, in part, to create distance between her and the president’s family. That interpretation has not been confirmed by the White House. Financial misconduct allegations add to the controversy The latest reporting follows separate allegations involving Guilfoyle and Deters, a Trump supporter and donor. According to reports cited by The New York Times , Deters alleged that Guilfoyle sought $100,000 to help cover her American Express credit card debt ahead of her Senate confirmation hearing in 2025. The allegations also concern communications in which Guilfoyle reportedly asked Deters to arrange the money. Deters has claimed that their relationship later involved discussions about assistance with tax and legal matters and access to senior Trump administration officials. Guilfoyle’s lawyer has challenged the authenticity of the correspondence and disputed Deters’ allegations, maintaining that she did nothing wrong. Deters has threatened to sue Guilfoyle for defamation and said he intends to subpoena Trump Jr. as part of a potential legal dispute. Any such claims would need to be tested through the legal process. Guilfoyle’s departure leaves questions over US relations with Greece Guilfoyle took up her role in Athens in November 2025, placing her at the centre of US-Greek relations during a period of defence cooperation and military modernisation. Her appointment initially attracted attention because of her longstanding connections to Trump and the administration. Following her departure, experienced diplomat Josh Huck, the deputy chief of mission, assumed responsibility for the embassy. Greek officials have largely treated the matter as an internal US issue. Deputy Prime Minister Kostis Hatzidakis has said relations between Greece and the United States remain at a high point, while opposition figures have criticised the limited public response to the controversy. The developments have raised questions about the circumstances surrounding Guilfoyle’s appointment and departure. However, claims that her posting was designed as punishment for a personal dispute remain unverified. For Greece, the priority remains maintaining its strategic relationship with Washington, particularly as the two countries deepen cooperation on defence, energy and regional security. title: Olympic Champion Eleftherios Petrounias Wins Fifth World Medal
body: Olympic champion Eleftherios (Lefteris) Petrounias took silver in the Rotterdam rings final on Saturday 24 October, scoring 14.333 with a flawless routine at the 54th World Artistic Gymnastics Championships. The 35-year-old finished behind China’s Lan Xingyu, who scored 14.766 and claimed his first world title on the apparatus. Armenia’s Artur Avetisyan completed the podium with 14.233. The Greek gymnast won Olympic gold on the same apparatus at Rio 2016. For Petrounias, it is a fifth medal at a world championship and his second silver, after Antwerp in 2023. He also won world gold in 2015, 2017 and 2018. How the Rotterdam rings final unfolded Petrounias had barely qualified, reaching the Rotterdam rings final in eighth place because of a poor dismount. Still, he showed his class and experience once again when it mattered. His 14.333 also put him ahead of Japan’s Shinnosuke Oka, who placed fourth with 14.133. Russia’s Ilia Zaika finished fifth on 14.100. Turkey’s Mehmet Ayberk Koşak came sixth with 13.800, while Great Britain’s Courtney Tulloch placed seventh on 13.366. Glen Cuyle of Belgium rounded out the eight-man field with 12.833. The men’s competition closes on Sunday 25 October with the vault, parallel bars and horizontal bar finals. Results from every session sit with the International Gymnastics Federation and the championship organisers . A growing medal collection The silver adds to a collection that already includes his 11th European Championship medal , a bronze in Zagreb in August, and a World Cup gold in April . In Zagreb, Avetisyan and Zaika had both edged him. This time, however, both men finished behind him in the Rotterdam rings final. Petrounias has now won world medals in 2015, 2017, 2018, 2023 and 2026. Only Lan stopped him from a fourth world gold.
