title: Trump admits to discussing situation in Ukraine with Elon Musk
body:
WASHINGTON, October 25. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump said he discussed the situation in Ukraine with US businessman and SpaceX founder Elon Musk.
"Yes, I have [spoken to him about it]," he said in response to reporters' questions in Florida. When asked to share details about his conversation with Musk, Trump replied: "No, I can’t."
On October 23, Trump stated that Musk "had done nothing wrong" in light of reports on restrictions on the operation of the Starlink and Starshield satellite communication systems in Ukraine. The day before, on October 22, the US leader announced that Ukraine’s access to the military-grade Starshield satellite service had been restored. Trump made these statements in response to media reports alleging that he had asked Musk to lift the restrictions.

title: We should be more ambitious with the software we build
body:
Since early this year, Michael Malis (of pgrust ) has been showing me interesting things he's done and saying
[W]e should be more ambitious 1 with the software we build
There is, understandably, a lot of skepticism about projects like pgrust because there are so many low-quality AI-generated projects out there. If I didn't know Malis and didn't look into it, I would just assume that pgrust was another vibe slopped project that's never going to work. But I know Malis well enough to trust his work without looking into it, and if you look into it a bit, you'll see that in testing pgrust, he's testing thoroughly enough that he's even uncovering real bugs in Postgres, such as this numerical bug that can cause valid SP-GiST operations to fail , this format cache bug that can cause incorrect results from JSONPath , this pgcrypto bug that can cause later operations to fail , multiple memory safety bugs in the dictionary loader 2 , this money overflow bug , etc.
This isn't to say that pgrust is bug free 3 , but it does indicate that there's a substantial amount of testing happening and, even if pgrust itself is never successful, just making the attempt will have improved Postgres in a durable way. The main pitch for pgrust is actually performance, and that's where the really interesting work is happening; if pgrust fails, it's possible that some of the optimizations they've demonstrated will make it into Postgres, Clickhouse, etc., but that's obviously less direct than filing Postgres bugs which get fixed.
That being said, I find it understandable that, every time I see pgrust discussed on a news aggregator, most people dismiss it as vibeslop garbage because almost all of these rewrite projects are slop. If I didn't know Malis, I would make the same assumption, because who has the time to look into all of these projects? Because I know Malis, I didn't bother to look at it; I just trusted him (I only found the above because I wanted to check on pgrust before using it as an example for this post).
As a consumer of software, everywhere you look, there's slow software that the creator is claiming is fast because the creator is touting some slop benchmark, e.g., here's one of multiple examples I saw yesterday , and of course low-quality software that doesn't work is more common than ever.
But, as a builder of software, it doesn't matter that almost all of these projects are vibeslop, that other people are out there shoveling out huge piles of crap and calling it gold . You can build things like pgrust or other projects that would've been too large to really be feasible in the past and, if you do a reasonable job with testing and benchmarking, that stuff can actually be good-enough quality to use.
If I were writing it, I would say "we can be more ambitious with the software we build" and not "we should", but Malis has been casually chatting with me when he's said this, so maybe he would say the same in an actual post; don't read too much into should vs. can here. What's interesting to me is how capabilities have advanced such that we can do a lot more.
Just for example, after hearing that OpenAI was going to use Cerebras for their SOTA models and not just fast-but-low-quality models like 5.3-Codex-Spark, I looked at where time on my computer would go if I was using a SOTA model, but 10x to 100x faster; some things that were already sometimes a bottleneck that would only get worse with a faster model were:
At the level of a "works for me" project, these are all things that can seriously be improved. I don't have much spare time at the moment but, even so, I built this regex engine that can be tweaked to be faster than other general-purpose regex libraries on any particular workload I care about , this ripgrep fork that uses the native code compiler from the regex engine and is faster for my codex ripgrep workloads (of course a text index is the better solution, but I've already worked on text indexing and this was a "just for fun" project where I wasn't trying to do the optimal thing), and a Rust that sped up builds for my projects (huge improvement for cold builds, moderate for warm, limited by wanting to avoid forking the Rust compiler front-end). For syscalls and filesystem overhead, just switching development from Mac to Linux improved this a lot, and of course this is another thing that can be sped up a lot as well, especially when agents are hammering lots of small filesystem operations (it's not uncommon to see my machine waiting on filesystem ops because the standard OS filesystem interface wasn't designed with modern disk performance in mind). With modern disks, there's no reason to use the *nix filesystem API. In the past, writing a developer toolchain that uses direct I/O instead of normal filessytem operations or building a custom OS or a funny layer that fakes out syscalls would've been an absurd endevaor, but that's totally doable now.
For someone like me who doesn't know anything about regexes, string matching algorithms, compilers, interpreters, etc., this set of projects would've taken a year or more to get to "works for me" quality. Instead, this was a low single-digit number of hours of my time. If I wanted to make any of these things meet a "useful product or open source project" quality bar, that would be a lot more work 0 , but it's still pretty incredible how much this process is sped up.
My read of Malis's meaning when he says “we should be more ambitious with the software we build”, is that it doesn't even occur to people to do these things that are now easy. For weeks, every time I logged into Twitter, I saw someone complain about how Rust compilation is slow and is limiting development velocity (I think this wasn't actually true when I saw the complaints, in that this was before 5.6 Sol and 6 Astra were available on Cerebras, and if you measured where the time actually went, Rust compilation time wasn't actually that much of a bottleneck at the time). Sure, Rust compliation is slow. You can just write a Rust interpreter as well as speed up compilation directly. There are problems like this which I see people complaining about daily that are solvable without a lot of time or effort now. As far as I can tell, these problems are problems because people are implicitly carrying around a pre-agentic cost model. Ten years ago, the kind of person who implemented a new compiler because their compiler was slow was the kind of person who started programming a new 3d game engine when they wanted to make an indie game, i.e., the kind of person who never ships anything. Most productive programmers I know still have an aversion to this kind of thing, even though it is now actually reasonable to implement this kind of thing now 4 .
Another project I previously mentioned was this Azul AI which is superhuman at matched time controls . When I did that (with GPT-5.1/5.2), with zero AI knowledge, it took about 5 hours of my time to get something superhuman, and about 20 hours of my time to become what appeared to be the strongest AI at the time, including being stronger against humans than this AI that was used to cheat on Board Game Arena . Gabriel Cangussu recently built an AI that demolishes my AI, and AFAICT, it took him substantially less time than my AI took me. From talking to him about it, one key difference is that Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 have a much better understanding of board game AIs. When I used GPT-5.1/5.2, pretty much every suggestion they had was wrong and I had to do a lot of steering to get things to be remotely reasonable. If I had GPT read a codebase or a paper to implement relevant techniques from the paper, it would fail. If I read the paper myself and named a technique, it would say it did the technique, but it would generally do something that superficially looked like the technique but wasn't the actual technique until I issued some corrections. When the model is that far from being able to do the right thing, if you have no background in the area, it's fairly time consuming to check if the model did the right thing since you have to learn enough about what it's supposed to do to be able to check that it did what was claimed.
When I did that project, I said to friends that I didn't think the state models were in could last. It seemed impossible that they wouldn't get good enough to be able to read a paper and implement the techniques soon, and it seemed like they should also be able to pick out codebases and papers to crib from as well. From my experience messing around a bit with Fable 5 and Cangussu's experience with Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5, that seems to have happened, which is a huge time saver for someone like me who doesn't know anything about board game AIs (I know a little bit now, but still less than any real AI researcher) 5 .
For any particular domain, like board game AIs, you can say, "who cares? Board game AIs don't matter", but I've found this increase in capability to be true in quite a few different domains. Just for example, I did this toy eval of verification and test techniques with GPT-5.6 Sol implementing zstd on medium and xhigh . I haven't had time to write it up, but when I published that post, I also re-did the evals with GPT-6 Astra. 6 Astra was so good that I had to find different evals because models had advanced too much. For zstd, 6 Astra succeeds at passing all of the registered tests more than 99% of the time across all conditions, even the ones that significantly impair performance, like using TDD (and, BTW, it does it more cheaply as well, taking about $1 to implement zstd). I ended up using the IMAP RFC, which 5.6 Sol couldn't do effectively, and Pandoc, which is a pretty major thing to implement as it needs to be able to read and write many different formats 6 .
BTW, when people have said they used the new model and everything just works, software is solved, etc., I haven't found this to be true at all. It's true that there are a lot more things the newer model can one-shot, where things basically just work, but this just means that I end up working on more ambitious things where models still struggle 7 . I'm more productive and can work faster , but I find that, in terms of what I'm doing, I get farther from "it just works" with each more capable model because the gap between what the model can verify effectively without significant handholding and what the model can implement has been increasing 8 . All of that is a long-winded and less eloquent way of saying: we should be more ambitious with the software we build.
Thanks to Laurence Tratt, Yossi Kreinin, Alex Kolovsky, Max Hawkins, David Turner, and Michael Malis for comments/corrections/discussion.
I've had this note on my recent posts, which also applies to this one. In order to get more posts out, I'm trying to crank posts out in half an hour and not review them much. This definitely means less well-supported posts. If I were writing this in my standard style, I would've had comprehensive benchmarks for all of my projects that I mentioned. Instead, I did a quick comparison that satisfied my curiosity and am writing this up without rigorous benchmarking, and there are maybe twenty or thirty things in this post that I'd like to do but haven't done.
I haven't even written up this Rust interpreter. If, five years ago, I'd cobbled together a Rust interpreter that got a 50x speedup on cold compiles and 2x on warm/cached builds (with much more being possible if edits to the Rust compiler were in bounds), that would be a super interesting thing that I'd want to write up, but even operating in this mode where I barely edit posts and just blast them out, this isn't interesting enough to write up because it's so easy to do things that would've been considered very interesting not all that long ago.
Here's a comment from Yossi Kreinin, quoted (with permission, of course):
If you publish this I will publish a response explaining that for most people they should be less ambitious with the software they build with AI or they'll experience abject failure. I think a lot of the problems don't lend themselves that well to "agentic loops" since you don't have clear pass/fail criteria, and even when you do most people have trouble reasoning about giant black boxes which they can impose constraints on but can't understand the innards of [I include myself in this set.] This is a little bit like microservices I guess, where some people both need it and are very good at using it but likely for most people, they need it less and can't use it well at all. I sort of envy the ones who should and actually can be this ambitious about the software they build of course; not saying you shouldn't be more ambitious at all but moderating said ambition is a big part of handling the current situation for most I think
I have a similar thought about " there's no reason for software to be slow " BTW; in many cases, if you use AI to speed up some flow, you will add a bunch of messy code that will be overfit for the use case you tested on and will neither generalize, perf-wise, for all the use cases you should care about, nor will be maintainable upon future changes. If you know what you're doing and you understand how the system should be decomposed into parts and when it makes sense to go all-in on optimizing some part or a combination of them working together and how to properly benchmark it, etc., then things are great, but if for instance you have a manager who thinks there's no reason for software to be slow and he pushes people to use AI to make random parts of the software fast... Run for cover
My feeling is that, overall, the situation here is a bit analogous to the discussion here about why I don't like when people talk about how AI gives a 100x or 1000x productivity increase . There are some things that are sped up by a very large factor, easily over 1000000x. And some things don't currently get sped up at all. If you do exactly what you would've done five years ago, but with AI, the speedup is fairly poor because of Amdahl's law . But, in the general case, you can choose what to speed up and if you're looking for things that are productive to do, this often seems to involve things that were previously too expensive to do.
And, I think that you can often set up systems that have some kind of self-checking property even when most people wouldn't. This discussion of the implementation of Guards of Atlantis 2 is an example of that. It's a poor choice for an AI project because the official rules are a mess of ambiguous and contradictory English text (it's probably the game I've seen humans misplay at the highest rate, and the rules are confusing enough that the designer has often changed their mind about what their own rules mean despite continually maintaining that the rules are perfectly clear and one can play the game by simply reading the rules as written). If you try to produce a working set of rules in a naive way, AI won't really help with this (although it can speed up implementation once you have a clean spec), but for that, I was able to set up some kind of janky set of consistency checks between all of the inconsistent explanations of the game rules, which got fairly close to a correct set of rules (approximately as close as what someone else did with much more human effort and less of a systematic approach), which was enough to compare it to someone else's implementation and get a working set of rules. This setup did cost a lot more in tokens than a more manual approach. But it was "only" a month or two of the $200/mo OpenAI subscription with GPT-5.1/5.2, which is a lower cost than the cost in time of me sitting down and writing a clean spec for the game, i.e., a copy of the rules that is actually consistent and correct.
I feel like a lot of problems are in something like this class of problem, where it's possible to set up some kind of at least partially self-checking setup that a human can spend a small amount of time on. This also feels analogous to the situation about software testing at large, where (before coding agents) I found fuzzing and property-based testing to be highly effective. For most domains, people told me some kind of reason this kind of testing wouldn't work, but when I've tried these techniques with all of the domains people told me these techniques don't work for, they work fine. They're somewhat more work to apply, but they're still applicable and, AFAICT, more efficient and effective than writing traditional unit tests.
Part of the gist of Yossi's comment is that people aren't doing this kind of thing. Considering how many more bugs I see now than I used to, e.g., the last time I opened up the web chat for a big AI lab, I ran into a double-digit number of bugs within one minute, it's hard to say that Yossi is wrong. But, to that point, I still have my original opinion. Just because other people are pumping out vast quantities of barely working slop doesn't mean that you have to do the same thing.
The examples in the body of the post I gave for things I've done are tooling things I never would've done. There are a lot more things like that as well since it's so easy to build "works for me" quality tooling that's intended solely for me. I do think it's possible to go further than is productive, e.g., Steve Yegge wrote a lot about Gas Town and how productive it was, but when he was building his next agentic framework, he noted that he never used Gas Town to successfully build anything other than Gas Town and here's someone playing his game that's been created with his next gen framework (the commenter's references to $1B are because Yegge says his game is in the running for being the first solo-run billion dollar company), people were into Ralph Loops for a while even though, when I tried comparing them, they seemed worse than just doing the naive thing I was doing at the time, normal loops with context where you sometimes clear context as appropriate instead of doing it by default at the completely arbitrary point of when a single turn is completed , etc., so I've tried to stick to things where the impact is pretty direct. Besides the obvious reason this has been effective, the dramatic change in model and harness capability over time means that what tooling it makes sense to build changes very quickly, so spending a lot of time working on any particular tool that will be suboptimal at best and quite possibly obsolete in three months doesn't really make sense.
And, for a lot of my personal tools, my assumption is that an AI lab will obsolete anything I make in short order. For a very silly example of this, I have a tool that was useful since the release of GPT-5.6 Sol that restarts codex when it finds a memory leak. Presumably, OpenAI will fix this at some point and this tool will become worthless. For a slightly less silly example, take the Rust interpreter I had some agent build. For token-budget reasons, a lot of things that ought to be done for a very high-performance interpreter haven't been done.
For example, the interpreter doesn't modify the actual Rust front-end compiler to make it easy to take updates; performance would be much better if I just made changes to the Rust front-end, but I don't have the token budget to maintain a compatible fork of the Rust compiler, but this shouldn't be a problem for OpenAI. OpenAI committed $10B+ on getting access to Cerebras while also preventing Anthropic from having access.
Funnily enough, for coding, on many tasks, if you actually use one of their SOTA models and compare it to what you get from Anthropic, the actual speedup isn't all that large because of time spent on things like compiling Rust. Given that they were willing to commit $10B+ on this, it stands to reason that they'll eventually do a better job at speeding up the relevant tools than anyone could feasibly do outside an AI lab, so there's not much point in spending too much effort on this (this could arguably be untrue if non-coding tasks are expected to completely dominate future OpenAI revenue in the short term, but even then, given what they pay for tokens vs. what I pay, it still seems like it would make sense for them to speed a lot of these things up given that I could do it outside of a lab; perhaps there's some kind of argument like, if you have access to their usage data, there are so many more important bottlenecks that this one doesn't make sense to prioritize, but it still seems like it should make sense for them at some point even if it doesn't fall into the top 100 bottlenecks for Cerebras-enabled coding agents).
Another kind of thing that one might not call ambitious, but that speaks to the kind of thing that's possible, are games that I've made. There are games I've thought about and wanted to make that I don't think are generally enjoyable enough that they make sense for a real audience, but that I've wanted to play. For example, ever since reading David Gerrold's Star Wolf books in the 90s, I've wanted to play a game that implements combat as described in the books, which is a sort of like submarine combat. At least among realistic war games, this genre is extremely niche because almost everybody finds naval combat boring, and submarine combat is a particularly boring subgenre of naval combat games, so this doesn't really make sense as a money-making game, but it's so easy to implement games that I had an agent implement the game so I could play it for an hour or two. I never would've spent 10-20 hours implementing a game so that I could play it for an hour or two, but I'd spend 5 minutes. I've also previously mentioned implementing a game with the same rules as Scout and Guards of Atlantis 2 and other board games. I was never going to take the time to implement these games by hand just so I have a way to play with my friends on the occasions where we can't get together in-person, but I'm happy to have an LLM bash these things out. And, of course, for people who want to make games with a wider audience, there's a game renaissance going on right now due to coding agents. It's amazing how many interesting and creative games are being made now that having programming skills and the time to put them to use is no longer a bottleneck for making games.
Data analysis is another thing where the productivity multiplier can be very high and I can do all sorts of things I never would've done. As I've mentioned in a number of my last posts, I have way too many of these projects to really be able to write them up, even when attempting to write very quickly and bash out posts in half an hour apiece.
When I've talked to people about their one-off tooling, there's a lot of fun stuff people have done. For example, here's something Peter Geoghegan mentioned a month or two back:
I had Fable implement a custom Neovim Lua function that formats code according to my very specific preferences. This is both something I don't want to maintain myself and inherently a Rube Goldberg device. Theoretically I could accomplish the same outcome in a principled way by patching clang-format, but my requirements are so exact that I think that approach would never be satisfactory.
We use a tool call pgindent, which is our fork of bsd_indent. You can approximate the same formatting rules using clang-format, but that isn't good enough. If I commit something that isn't perfectly formatted/indented according to pgindent, I get a CI failure that I'm expected to fix quickly -- something I'd really prefer to avoid ...
Practically speaking, getting slick, clang-format-style formatting that avoids nag emails about misindented code requires a total architectural mess (I also don't want to spend the time developing a principled approach, but that's really a separate issue). The function allows me to effortlessly format a given block of code from Neovim, similar to the clang-format LSP integration. I'm being unreasonably fussy here, of course, but I find that LLMs allow me to be this exacting about tooling.
The function performs multiple passes: an initial formatting pass using clang-format/clangd, and a separate formatting pass using pgindent. I need it to do both because clang-format handles some cases correctly that pgindent misses. This is brittle because I only want to format the code within a range of lines selected via block visual mode (I don't want to run clang-format on code not added by my patch). This conflicts with pgindent's design; it can only format whole C files.
Figuring out which relevant subset of the temp whole file buffer needs to be copied back into my working buffer is nontrivial. The initial line range I selected doesn't directly map to the affected C AST elements. So the function uses tree-sitter to intelligently delineate the exact subset of the temp indented C code that needs to be copied back. The rules need to be fuzzy in exactly the right way for cases where my selection straddles the same block of code. There are a bunch of edge cases.
Another complicating factor is that pgindent relies on a typedef file generated with objdump to identify types; without that file, the formatting looks wonky. The formatting function dynamically generates any extra typedefs from clangd, for that one file, so I don't have to worry about a stale typedef file (I might have created a new struct seconds before running the formatting tool, I don't want to run objdump on the whole postgres binary each time, that'd blow up latency).
This appears to work perfectly. The latency is totally acceptable. I have only a vague understanding of how all this works, though. I don't even know Lua. This will probably continue to work, even as further changes are made to our fork of bsd_indent that somewhat alter how code is formatted, which happens from time to time.
I'm skeptical of the saaspocalypse. But I do think that LLMs are writing a lot of useful software that would have been insanely uneconomical to write any other way. There's an interesting small subset of software that'd be impossibly tedious for any human to maintain, relative to the value that it creates.
I also caught with Malis while writing this and found out about all sorts of fun stuff he's been doing. It's enough that writing it all up in detail could be its own post, but one fun thing is that, the last time I taked to him about pgrust verification, he mentioned using Kani to verify some parts of the code. He's since switched to Lean and has been using Lean to verify things that are too complex to do in Kani. This would be another topic for another post, but I wonder why people have generally settled on Lean for LLM-driven proofs (as opposed to, say, ACL2 ). I wonder how Lean would look in an updated version of this theorem prover comparison , or if someone were to run a theorem prover eval that's analogous to this language eval .
Of course, you can think of plenty of examples out of AI labs, such as a mid-sized team Anthropic building an internal replacement for GitHub as well as some other tooling in five months
A team of seven people built both Scion and Antique (our code review tool, which we could easily write a whole other blog post about), not to mention half a dozen related systems, and fully migrated to them in five months.
I think these kinds of examples are interesting and they point to where the industry will be in the not-so-far future, but what you can do with unlimited tokens, while relying on other infrastructure and tooling built with unlimited tokens doesn't tell you much about what you can accomplish today without unlimited funds. Projects like pgrust as well as projects that people I know do in their spare time (of which I've probably mentioned something like 1%—there are just a lot of these, like David Turner creating an ad skipper for podcasts that's "works for me" quality that works better than anything he could find, the spare-time projects Dennis Snell mentioned here , etc.) are more representative of what you can do today.
One reason I trust Malis is that he's a lot more careful about what he claims than a stereotypical founder. For example, when I joined the pgrust discord to check out what people are saying, I saw this message from Malis (dated a month ago, 2026-09-17, an eternity in agentic coding land) in response someone asking about pgrust's readiness for use as a production database:
I would not recommend using it as your primary production database today. We are setting a production deployment for a company right now, but they are more tolerant to their production database going down than most people. We'll have good empirical evidence on how reliable pgrust is after they start running it
Malis doesn't seem like someone who would claim something is production ready when it's clearly wildly unready , like many well-known projects have, and it turns out he's not doing that.
I wrote the draft of this a week before publishing and didn't have time to publish it. Since then, there was this pgrust Clickhouse benchmark controversy . On looking into this, the accusations of nefarious cheating seem to be false, and the accusation that it was premature to submit the preview of pgrust to the benchmark is something Malis acknowledged. I do think this is the kind of thing that a project will never live down, in that regardless of the truth of the matter, people will be bringing this up years later. You can see this right now in discussions around that specific controversy, and as we discussed when we look at Ed Zitron's prediction track record and when we looked at futurist predictors like Kurzwil , almost nobody actually looks at what actually happened and people will repeat incorrect statements that were based on vibes indefinitely.
I don't think I can really present all of the evidence for why I trust Malis (technically, I could do it, but it would easily be a 20k+ word post), but if you look at how he discusses pgrust vs. how typical database founders market their new DB projects, it seems dramatically different to me. Of course there are extreme examples like MongoDB, which disputed correctness issues for years despite Kyle Kingsbury repeatedly showing that the anecdotes people had about data corruption were real. For an example that's more typical, a friend of mine worked as an early employee for a database startup. Their webpage bragged about doing some huge number of QPS. On testing it, my friend found that the claim was off by multiple orders of magnitude and suggested that the webpage get changed. The founder disagreed because they were going to hit the performance numbers, so it was still a true claim. After multiple years of performance improvements, the company eventually reduced the claim by one order of magnitude and they can still only hit that number with a very contrived, unrealistic, workload. This is, unfortunately, pretty normal for a company peddling a product based on its performance. By contrast, when I look at the pgrust discord to see what Malis is saying about performance, here's his most recent message:
Right now, the best way to help is to find bugs and performance issues in 0.4-beta. The new query engine is very fast on some workloads, but it causes performance regressions on others, and it doesn't support some more complex queries. We're trying to track down everything that's either slower than Postgres or errors out. It's not an easy thing to do given the massive space of queries you can run
We want to fix these things before the general release of 0.4-beta. Off the top of my head, there was a big performance regression in very fast queries. This is because we primarily optimized the new query engine for large-scale OLAP-like workloads. I'm doing optimization work to fix the very slow queries. I don't think there's any fundamental reason why the new engine should be slower than the previous one for fast queries
Even though he was a founder and exec of a successful startup prior to starting the pgrust project, he never really got into the mindset that most founders seem to, where they seem to be able to say anything and believe anything they say. You might say this is a low bar, and I'd agree, but I still think it's rare and it's why I trusted what he says about pgrust without looking into it and also why, when I looked into it, his claims seem to be borne out by reality.
Another way to look at it is [this framing from Thomas Ptacek]:
The last year in the technology industry has felt like 100 years all happening at once. Our industry is destabilized in a way nobody’s experienced since the advent of the personal computer. Every limit AI runs up against collapses within a month. Everything we do with frontier models today, in a few years we’ll be doing instantaneously and for free.
Given the pace of change recently, I find it understandable that most people, even most programmers, aren't quite aware of what's possible right now. Speaking to non-programmer responses, one of the things I thought was interesting was how many people objected to this review of Ed Zitron's prediction accuracy because they thought that AI capabilities hadn't increased in the past two years. For most people I talk to, the idea that AI didn't improve from February 2024 to September 2026 is baffling (even if you think of programming as an exception and look at other capabilities), but there's a lot of people out there who are perhaps looking at the Google AI summary at the top of search results or using Copilot integrated into some Microsoft suite, who don't realize that capabilities have advanced. At every scale, there seems to be an information gradient like this, where very few people outside of labs have a good idea of what productive people are doing with models today.
This comment about an increase in cheating online has come to pass . On re-reading the actual comment that I wrote, I didn't explicitly write that it seemed inevitable that there would be a large increase in cheating, although it can be inferred from connecting the statements there together, and I've been on the record in public on some discords, etc.
I don't follow the online game scene, but I'm told that for Azul (the most popular game on BGA, the biggest online board game platform for modern board games), 3 of the top 10 places last season were taken by cheaters, including top place. Also, as I've noted elsewhere in the past, BGA doesn't seem equipped to make reasonable policy decisions on almost any level. Things like the mechanics of their Elo ranking algorithm, their structure for game seasons, their policy for counteracting collusion, their policy for countering cheating, etc., are worse than the most naive straightforward solution you can think of so, as expected, they don't have a reasonable policy to counter cheating. The top ranks of the most popular game have been overrun with cheaters and this should be expected to spread to other games. As harms from AI go, this is a fairly benign one. It just happens to be one of a double-digit number of examples I saw last week of people being more ambitious in the software they create. I'm half mentioning this because it's easily quantifiable, and half because I predicted this would happen and it seems reasonable to follow up and see what happened. One side effect of people being more ambitious with the software they build is a rise in cheaters, scammers, and the like.
On the bright side, when it comes to board games, perhaps six months ago, I made the comment on a board game discord that there isn't really any reason to play games on Board Game Arena over some vibe coded app because the vibe coded app will have better performance, be less buggy, have things like a move timer policy that actually makes sense, etc., unless the game is something like Guards of Atlantis 2, where the rules are so poorly written that AI struggles to understand the rules. At the time, I was already playing games with friends on apps I vibe coded (legally, as game rules and mechanics aren't copyrighted), but people thought I was a madman when I said this. Since then, I've seen a number of other people build their own apps so they can play a better implementation of a board game than is publicly available. I would rate every board game I've implemented as fairly bad, but in the pre-coding agent world, most online board games were even worse. In a coding variant of this argument , the bar to displace old human-written code isn't very high because most old human written code is atrocious. I suspect people playing these new vibe coded implementations actually better for board game designers since people playing their games more means more physical game sales, although I think people would do this regardless of whether or not it benefits board game designers because the existing verisons of so many games are really terrible. For example, if two players click at the same time in a game on BGA, this is an error, which is absurd for an online game platform. But BGA won because it's much better than the alternatives, and it's also better than most custom implementations (e.g., see the reviews for online Brass: Birmingham , where the game actually doesn't work).

title: Small Programs and Languages
body:
My Implementing a Forth article got some great feedback, particularly around the subject of tiny Forth implementations. (And it was an excuse to list some of the tiniest Forths I’ve seen.)
I know I’m not alone in seeing the appeal of tiny Forths, tiny languages, tiny programs, and just small stuff in general. What’s up with that, anyway?
If I see that something is 200 lines of code, I’m much more likely to read it than if it’s 2,000 or 20,000 lines.
What’s more, if it’s a program that does something interesting in 20 lines when I was expecting 2,000, then I’m going to be very, very interested to read those 20 lines!
When I was researching DOM diffing libraries prior to creating RetroV , one of the repos I looked at was ijk by Luke Jackson.
I was pretty used to looking at fat JavaScript libraries at that point, so when I cracked open the source file for ijk, I was really surprised. Here’s the source: index.js (githubusercontent.com).
Just 25 lines! I was instantly intrigued.
More recently, one of the responses to my aforementioned Forth article was Philippe Brochard with a 46 byte "Forth".
It’s so small, I can just put the hexdump right here:
(See my update to Implementing a Forth for more about this artifact.)
Sure, very few people jump at a chance to read raw machine code. But that’s exactly my point. Something this small doesn’t feel so scary, right? I mean, 46 bytes. If you put the effort into it, you know you can figure out how it works eventually.
This next one almost serves as a counter-example because the code is so dense and frightening, but I can’t help mentioning it anyway.
One of my favorite software stories is Roger K.W. Hui’s Appendix A "Incunabulum" from An Implementation of J in which he describes Arthur Whitney writing an array-based language interpreter,
"…​on one page and in one afternoon â an interpreter fragment on the AT&T 3B1 computer. I studied this interpreter for about a week for its organization and programming style…​"
Hui can list the entire interpreter in the appendix because it’s just that single page, 122 lines of incredibly cryptic C, which you can view here:
https://code.jsoftware.com/wiki/Essays/Incunabulum
I haven’t personally tackled that puzzle yet, but it’s in my unwritten list of dense computer things that I would print out and take with me if I suddenly found myself cast out of society and forced to go live alone up on a mountain or something.
(By the way, J is in the family of array languages which include APL. If you enjoy brevity, cryptic programming puzzles, and high performance numerical computing, these languages have got you covered!)
Update July 2026: Speaking of Arthur Whitney, Alex (alexalejandre.com) sent me a link that I knew I’d have to add here. Check this out: https://fall.tr/kos
It’s a transcript of a Geo Carncross talk describing an operating system, kOS, featuring Whitney’s k array language, kdb database, and a GUI and window manager in a 90 Kb bootable image. Individual source code stats are just as impressive (such as 60 lines of C for the aforementioned GUI and window manager). And apparently kdb is 100 lines of C? Is that right? Even Whitney C, that’s still impressive. Now I’m even more intrigued by kdb than ever! And if any of that seems interesting, you’ll definitely enjoy the article Impending kOS (vector.org.uk).
Something else that would certainly need to be in the collection I take to that lonely mountain would have to be The Most Beautiful Program Ever Written , according to the title of a talk by William Byrd. Spoiler alert: It’s this Lisp interpreter in Lisp:
(The above is from Alberto Zaccagni’s transcription of the code (github.com) shown in Byrd’s slide.)
Now, we all know that code golfing (wikipedia.org) is a programmer’s recreational game, and just for fun, right?
I say yes. And I’ll go one step further: They are meaningful .
When you see a ray tracer that fits on a business card (fabiensanglard.net), it makes you realize that a ray tracer is something that can fit on a business card !
That’s an actual fact about the minimum complexity of ray tracers.
Kolmogorov complexity (wikipedia.org) is:
"…​the length of a shortest computer program (in a predetermined programming language) that produces the object as output."
(I learned about Kolmogorov complexity in a book about Kurt GÃ¶del and it was my favorite thing in what was otherwise a pretty dry and depressing book.)
The meaning I get from this is that code golfers, for the benefit of the whole human race, produce versions of programs that represent the minimum complexity of those programs. Way to go code golfers!
What do we know about the fundamental complexity of the Lisp programming language?
Thanks to Justine Tunney, we know that a LISP with garbage collection can be as small as 436 bytes (justine.lol).
That’s a fact about Lisps with garbage collection. When you strip everything else away, you can get the essentials down to 436 bytes!
I take comfort in this because that means the concept can be boiled down to this hand-held size. And that means I can probably fit it in my head.
Thanks to Frank Force, we know that a 3D browser game can fit in 2Kb of (insanely compressed) JavaScript source: A 3D game in 2Kb of JS (frankforce.com)
Martin Kleppe’s whole site (aem1k.com) is filled with wonders you can run right in your browser.
And we haven’t even scraped the surface of what the demoscene has to offer for computers going back to the 1980s. Here’s a good place to start: https://demoscene.assembly.org/
Mini-things are fun and useful and meaningful.
My point here is that you don’t have to actually study the intricate clockwork puzzle of a miniaturized/golfed program to benefit from it. The miniature simply serves to prove that the concept can fit on a business card and it can fit in your head. Go ahead and find a readable version to study instead. (The miniature will likely have many things to teach, but some of them will be about how to make miniature programs.)
Small programs are interesting. But I’m also interested in small programming languages.
Generally speaking, the smaller the language, the less expressive it is.
One of the most well-known, least expressive languages is assembly.
Assembly languages are very syntactically and conceptually simple. There’s not much language at all: it’s mostly a rigid sequence of opcode mnemonics. Even with macros, writing in assembly is mostly about understanding the puzzle of a particular CPU’s instruction set architecture, or ISA. (You can prove this by comparing the syntax of assembly for CISC and RISC processors. The puzzle is totally different, while the language remains practically unchanged.)
An honorable mention must be made here for SNOBOL , which is kind of like assembly language both for the rigid syntactic reasons listed above and also because it presents a similar control flow challenge. Like a CPU, it only understands jumps and call/return. (In every other way, SNOBOL is wildly different, being a string matching and replacing language. It’s weird and fun and highly effective.)
Moving on to syntactically tiny "high-level" languages, these three are brilliant:
Forths win just about any "smallness" contest. The only syntactical construct is the space character. Forths are mind-bendingly flexible and powerful in a way that is downright disturbing.
Lisps , (especially Scheme?), have small core languages with very simple syntax and enormous expressive power and flexibility.
Tcl deserves to be mentioned with Forth and Lisp. Tcl is wild because everything is a string in a way that is hard to appreciate at first. You can construct your own language in Tcl just as you can with Forth or Lisp.
Forth, Lisp, and Tcl only require you to understand a few core ideas and give you limitless power in return. You could fit the syntactic core of these languages on an index card or less.
And yet, to wield these tools effectively requires a massive shift in thinking if you’re used to "normal" Algol-like procedural languages.
So how about something that is both small and simple and doesn’t require a blood sacrifice?
I think the Lua programming language fits the bill. Check out how small the core language is:
I’ve got the printed book version of this document and it’s a thin book! The Lua language is covered in the beginning and it is just 27 pages. 27 pages! I have game manuals longer than that.
The C language is pretty small. I don’t think it’s super easy to program effectively and safely with C, but there’s no denying it’s compact and pretty expressive for its size.
Newcomer Zig is C-like. But I think it’s actually quite large and you need to know a lot of it to use it effectively. (I’m also a fan of Zig and think it’s totally worth it . The size is there for a reason.)
JavaScript has a core language that is quite small. Probably on par with Lua, actually. Functions, arrays, and objects (used as dictionaries) are pretty much all the JS I use and I like it that way!
As with the natural human languages, the trade-off with a bigger programming language is, hopefully, greater expressivity.
Small or expressive. Which way should you lean?
In a wonderful talk by David Ungar (wikipedia.org) titled Self and Self: Whys and Wherefores , he laments the mistake of Self’s multiple inheritance:
"It’s far better to make a system a little too simple so a person has to write extra stuff, even write it twice with a comment that says, 'Look over here,' than to have a system that acts in strange ways and nobody can understand why. So, simplicity trumps expressiveness."
Got that? Here’s the bullet from the slide to help you remember:
I think small languages can also be fairly expressive, but only with very, very careful design. Recall Forth, Lisp, and Tcl.
Microworlds: The idea of small, self-contained, learnable programming environments also has a David Ungar connection I discovered while watching his talk. See "ARK" on my Microworlds card. (Smith and Ungar co-created the Self language (selflanguage.org), which is a notable milestone in programming and still under active development to this day.)
Languages which come with full-featured interactive IDEs are obvious potential microworlds.
But I also think that traditional text file-based programming can give you the microworld experience as well. For that, a language needs high quality documentation that installs alongside the compiler/interpreter. And it should strive to have error output that can be understood by beginners, including explanations of what went wrong and hints for how to fix it or or where to find more information.
Libraries: Another easily overlooked aspect of a programming language’s apparent size is its "standard library" of functions, data structures, and methods.
I think function libraries are subject to the exact same size versus expressiveness challenge.
For example, learning the Ramda (ramdajs.com) functional programming library for JavaScript was very much like learning a new programming language and I never managed to learn all of it. The composability of Ramda and the consistency of its curried functions was extremely eye-opening to me. My advice: A little bit of Ramda goes a long way!
The feels: Concision in our tools has a certain quality that goes beyond utility. Little things just spark joy , you know?
I’ve always had a fascination with miniatures, dioramas, and tiny scale models.
Stephanie M. Langin-Hooper , author of Figurines in Hellenistic Babylonia writes in Tiny Things and Why We Love Them (cambridgeblog.org):
"…​the act of shrinking a life-size thing to a smaller scale has an influential effect. The object is now cute, more accessible, more delicate, more 'squee'. It is also more helpless, and thus controllable â comforting and completely non-threatening due to its diminutive size.
Which is exactly the reaction I have when I see a tiny bit of code that does something useful.
Also, I’m super okay with "controllable" in the context of a computer, but the feeling of that paragraph changes a bit if we’re talking about, say, dolls.
Small scale helps make "big" things approachable:
"What might be threatening to think about in the real-scale world can be more manageable and more conceivable in miniature."
Small things, "allow low-stakes experimentation," which is why we often build tiny models of things before we scale them up.
Simon Garfield , author of In Miniature: How Small Things Illuminate the World has many of the same answers. He writes in Small world: Why we love tiny things (theguardian.com):
"The answer lies in our desire for mastery and elucidation. The ability to enhance a life by bringing scaled-down order and illumination to an otherwise chaotic world â a world over which we may otherwise feel we have little control â cannot be overvalued. […​] At its simplest, the miniature shows us how to see, learn and appreciate more with less."
I think this is a big part of what I get out of Assembly Nights with the small scale and orderly logic and internal consistency. Unlike the vast, fathomless Real World, an offline computer is a fantasy place where I can believe I could understand everything if I just tried hard enough for long enough.
"The satisfaction of observing small things becomes a desire to make small things, and both stages address the human need for comprehension and order. We live in a huge and doomy universe, and controlling just a tiny scaled-down part of it restores our sense of order and worth."
I’ve been studying computer history for a little while and I’ve only scratched the surface. But one of the things I’ve been finding is that a lot of the "big" stuff in our field are just accumulations of lots of "little" victories as individuals have solved "little" problems in new and different ways.
"We create small universes in which we may bury ourselves to the exclusion of all else. Blocking out real life for a while â always the prerequisite of the dedicated domestic hobby, from dollâs house modeller to jigsaw enthusiast to adult book colourist â may be contemplative, meditative, blinkered and essential. The people crouching over tiny details as if the world depended on it are only doing it because their world does depend on it."

title: Deadly Russian drone strike targets apartment in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, killing 3, injuring 12
body:
A Russian drone hit a residential building in the Synelnykove district of Dnipropetrovsk Oblast on Oct. 24, killing three civilians and injuring another 12, Governor Oleksandr Hanzha reported.
The drone attack caused a fire on the fourth floor of an apartment building and also damaged nearby vehicles and a store, Hanzha said . Three victims were killed.
At least 12 other people were injured in Russia's strike on Synelnykove, according to Hanzha. One of the victims is an 11-year-old girl. Five injured individuals are being treated in the hospital.
Three of the injured victims — two women and one man— are reported to be in serious condition and undergoing surgery.
Lethal Russian drone strikes are a daily occurrence in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast , which borders Ukraine's front-line Kharkiv, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson oblasts. The region's Synelnykove district has endured frequent attacks, active fighting, and temporary incursions by Russian troops due to its proximity to Russian-occupied territory.
In October 2026, Russia has intensified aerial bombardments across Ukraine in its annual attempt to destroy the country's power grid as temperatures drop. Thousands of homes in Synelnykove and other parts of Dnipropetrovsk Oblast lost power after Russia attacked the region's critical energy infrastructure overnight on Oct. 21.

title: The Importance of Limitations for Creativity and Learning (2023)
body:
The other day, my kids started messing around (at home) with an online document writing platform their school uses. They’d discovered a fun little easter egg. I watched them laugh and play with the feature - pushing its limits and ultimately crashing the browser.
These same kids have messed about in Scratch (wikipedia.org) through the school as well, but they rarely stick with it for very long.
I think Scratch is brilliantly done and I don’t wish to speak ill of it.
But it struck me how the limitations of the easter egg made it more compelling to play with. The feature was a little buggy and did not handle multiple instances very well. This led to interesting behavior as they added more and more instances to the page.
This "toy" had way less features than Scratch, but it was pretty free-form in use and it was easy to invoke. It also had severe limitations and was easy to break.
I think Scratch is so featureful that it is intimidating to newcomers. The paradox of having so many toys is that it’s hard to know which one to play with.
In both learning and creativity, I think there’s a lot to be said for a very simple toolbox that invites play but doesn’t present too many options at first.
I think a lot of people can relate to this in the visual arts: Give me a nice set of paints and brushes and a big blank canvas and watch me agonize about what to paint. But put a ragged piece of scrap paper and a pencil in front of me and watch me start to doodle!
Are these the same principles at work? It feels like they might be.
Another type of limitation is the structure of a story. That structure could be anything , but it might be that the story is told in 3-acts or that it is entirely based on the motivations of the characters, or something else. It doesn’t have to be much of a limit, but it’s something.
I think the lack of limits in the form of structure is what makes people’s dreams (generally) so boring to hear about - there’s no limits and no structure and no rules. It’s just seemingly-random events.
A movie that breaks its own internal rules is frustrating, but dreams don’t even have rules to break, so it’s not even interesting to criticize them!
A big-budget movie can be clever and amazing. But I think that requires the style and restraint of the director. Otherwise, you can just make the first thing that comes to your mind - which is probably going to be the most obvious thing to come to your (and your audience’s) mind!
But a small-budget movie has to be clever to be any good at all. If you’ve got $300 for props, you’re going to have to come up with something different…​and that can lead to surprise and delight because you did something unexpected with the material available.
Again, big budget stuff can be surprising and delightful, too, but I think that requires a ton of willful determination on the part of the artists involved. That’s might be why the successful ones can be pretty forceful personalities. (Not that I think artistic genius and being a nasty person need to go hand-in-hand either. I’m not promoting that idea here. I don’t think that’s the same thing.)

title: Early voting begins in New York: What to know and the key races to watch
body:
Gov. Kathy Hochul and U.S. Rep. Mike Lawler are hoping to keep their seats.
Saturday is the first day of early voting in New York and Empire State voters could help decide which party will control the U.S. House of Representatives over the next two years.
Republicans are seeking to fend off attempts by Democrats to flip congressional seats in the suburbs north of New York City and in the Adirondack Mountains near the Canadian border.
New Yorkers will also decide whether Democrats Kathy Hochul and Letitia James should each be elected to an additional term in their respective roles as governor and attorney general.
Hochul became the state's first female governor in 2021 after then-Gov. Andrew Cuomo resigned amid sexual harassment allegations -- accusations he denied. She was New York's lieutenant governor at the time.
Unlike most New York governors, Hochul is not from New York City or its suburbs, but hails from the Buffalo area -- a more than six-hour drive away. A moderate Democrat, she was largely unknown to voters in the metropolitan area, where much of the state's population resides, until Cuomo's resignation. She defeated Republican Lee Zeldin in 2022, winning a full term in Albany.
In the time since, Hochul has spent a significant amount of time downstate, recently collaborating with current democratic socialist New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on initiatives like expanded childcare access. Mamdani campaigned with Hochul on Friday and has released videos on social media in support of her campaign.
Hochul's Republican opponent in 2026, Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman, has worked to tie Hochul to Mamdani throughout his campaign, issuing a statement at one point that referenced the "Hochul-Mamdani agenda."
Blakeman has centered his gubernatorial campaign on fighting crime and lowering taxes in New York State. He has received President Donald Trump's endorsement and been adamant in his support of the president, even campaigning with him at a rally in Syracuse in early October.
A recent Quinnipiac University poll of likely New York State voters found that 55% would support Hochul and 41% would Blakeman.
In the attorney general's race, incumbent Letitia James is facing a challenge from Republican former Drug Enforcement Administration Chief of Staff Saritha Komatireddy. James gained national attention through her 2022 lawsuit against Trump, his company and members of his family alleging net worth inflation. The lawsuit led to a $454 million civil fraud judgment that was thrown out by an appeals court in 2025.
While Komatireddy has not historically been a household name in the state, many of her campaign materials using the "just fight crime" branding have gained significant attention on social media.
One of the most high-profile races in the country is in New York's 17th Congressional District in the lower Hudson Valley, where incumbent Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Lawler is being challenged by Democrat Cait Conley.
The district is home to everyone from former President Bill Clinton to New York City investment bankers to thousands of police officers.
Trump attended a rally with Lawler in the district in May while former U.S. Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg came to the district in September to campaign with Conley.
The race in the 17th Congressional District is not the only potentially competitive race within a stone's throw of Manhattan. In the 3rd Congressional District, which straddles Nassau and Queens, incumbent Democratic U.S. Rep. Tom Suozzi is being challenged by Republican Michael LiPetri, a former state assemblyman who has run for Congress twice before.
In New York's 21st Congressional District, which stretches from the historically industrial Mohawk Valley along the Erie Canal to the Canadian border, Democrats are hoping that 2026 is their best chance to flip the seat currently held by Republican U.S. Rep. Elise Stefanik.
Stefanik previously planned to seek the Republican gubernatorial nomination, but ended up dropping out of the governor's race and announcing she would not seek reelection to the House.
Republican Anthony Constantino, a sticker company CEO endorsed by Trump, is facing off against Democratic farmer Blake Gendebien in the district. Trump endorsed Constantino in the Republican primary over a state lawmaker who had been endorsed by the head of New York State's Republican Party.
Tariffs and American relations with Canada have been top of mind in parts of the district.
Early voting concludes on Nov. 1. Election Day is Nov. 3.

title: World hopes Putin-Trump-Xi meeting to help overcome chaos — Russian diplomat
body:
MOSCOW, October 25. /TASS/. Many around the world are pinning their hopes on the upcoming meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin, US leader Donald Trump, and Chinese head of state Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the APEC summit in China, Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said.
"At a time that is extremely difficult in terms of international relations, when the entire planet is literally being shaken, the leaders of the three major powers will have the opportunity, within a multilateral framework <…>, to exchange views," the diplomat noted during a TV broadcast. "Of course, the eyes of millions, or even billions, will be fixed on this [meeting]. Naturally, people are pinning high hopes on such a meeting. Why? Because many want to begin moving away from this slide toward absolute chaos and return to stability, or, at the very least, to a path that could lead to that stability," she emphasized.
Earlier, Trump said that his trilateral meeting with Putin and Xi Jinping could be held in China. In turn, Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov told reporters that, during a meeting with US special presidential envoy Steve Witkoff, Putin discussed the possibility of holding a trilateral meeting with Trump and Xi Jinping at the APEC summit in Shenzhen on November 18-19.

title: Trade Minister urges laboratories, factories to work as partners
body: The Minister for Trade, Agribusiness and Industry, Elizabeth Ofosu-Adjare, has called for stronger collaboration between research laboratories and factories to enable Ghana to produce more of the goods it consumes and expand its manufacturing capacity. She made the call on Friday, October 23, 2026, at the 14th Global Biennial Congress and Alumni Homecoming of the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST) in Kumasi. Addressing alumni of the university from Ghana and across the world, the Minister urged them to contribute their expertise, time, resources and capital to support the institution’s development and strengthen its role in national industrial growth. “My message to our alumni is bring your problems, your time, your capital and your work home to KNUST. Our laboratories and our factories must work as partners if Ghana is to make what it consumes and sell what it makes,” she said. The Minister’s remarks highlighted the need for closer partnerships between universities, government and industry to translate research and innovation into practical solutions that support local production and economic development. The event was attended by the Asantehene, Otumfuo Osei Tutu II, and other distinguished guests.

title: SBU detains Donetsk woman who fought for Russia and planned to leave for EU
body:
The SBU said this in a statement seen by Ukrinform.
"The suspect was exposed at the Domanove international road border crossing as she was trying to enter Ukraine from Belarus to renew her Ukrainian international passport," the agency said.
Investigators established that, after renewing the document, the woman hoped to travel unhindered to one of the EU countries for permanent residence.
According to the investigation, before Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the woman worked as a nurse at the Donetsk Regional Clinical Psychiatric Hospital. In late February 2022, she voluntarily joined the 91st Separate Rifle Regiment of the 1st Army Corps of Russia's Southern Military District. She attained the rank of sergeant in the Russian army and served until August 2024.
"After subsequently leaving the Russian armed formations, the suspect decided to leave the temporarily occupied part of the Donetsk region for the EU. To enter the European Union, the woman needed to renew her Ukrainian international passport, which is why she came to Ukraine," the statement said.
SBU officers documented the suspect crossing the state border and detained her at a hotel in Kovel.
During a search, officers found a Russian passport, Russian army military documents, a veteran's certificate issued by the aggressor country and rubles, the agency said.
Investigators notified the detainee that she was suspected of high treason under Part 2 of Article 111 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine, committed under martial law.
The suspect is being held in custody without the right to post bail. She faces life imprisonment with confiscation of property.

BBC’s Blue Planet III is looking to prove its authenticity by leaving in the less-than-perfect shots. Previous incarnations of the nature series were defined by their gorgeous, crystal-clear footage that seemed almost too good to be real. But one dead giveaway of AI is when things look too polished and seamless. To counter that, Blue Planet III goes warts and all.
Executive Producer Elizabeth White told The Guardian in the past, “the amount of plankton and things” floating in the water would have caused them to cut a shot. Or “we might have framed out a boat or a buoy or gone: ‘Oh, actually … the water conditions are not really good enough for this.’” Instead, this time they’re leaving it all in to show a more authentic, organic version of the oceans.
The series features incredible displays of dolphins trapping fish by plugging holes with sea sponges, inter-species fish communication, and 200,000 crabs lining up in formation to feed. White says that real ocean creatures “are probably more remarkable than AI could imagine.”

title: Infantino Claims ‘Vast Majority’ Back Fourth Term As FIFA President
body: FIFA president Gianni Infantino has said he has the backing of the “vast, vast majority” of member associations in his bid for re-election despite criticism of his aborted World Cup selloff plan. The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) rallied behind Infantino on Friday in a significant boost to the 56-year-old’s hopes of winning a fourth term in charge. Infantino’s future in the role was in doubt two months ago when he faced a furious backlash to his plan to sell off a portion of the commercial rights of competitions run by football’s world governing body to private investors. The heads of European football’s governing body UEFA, the AFC and CONCACAF, which runs the game in North and Central America, signed a letter saying football “belongs to no individual”. But Infantino, who apologised last week for the failed private investment project, is now in a strong position to secure re-election in March. “I think what is important is that in an organisation like FIFA, there can be different views, different points of view,” Infantino told the BBC on Saturday. “But if we are serious about democracy, about the democratic process, about believing that everyone has the same vote and the same voice all over the world, that football belongs to everyone, if we are serious about that, then we need to respect as well the views of the vast, vast majority. “I’m just coming back off Tokyo where the Asian Football Confederation has fully endorsed me. I was in Cape Verde where all African countries have endorsed me. I’m speaking to all associations everywhere in the world.” No other candidate has yet come forward to oppose Infantino with the deadline to do so less than a month away on November 18. He added: “There are different points of view it’s not always easy to bring them all under one roof but we need to respect and I do respect all opinions all views and then it will be up to the FIFA member associations to decide who they want as a president and how they want FIFA to be run.” AFP The post Infantino Claims ‘Vast Majority’ Back Fourth Term As FIFA President appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Trade tariffs cause whiplash at Port Milwaukee
body:
Sacha Pfeiffer visits Port Milwaukee to see how President Trump's tariffs have affected the flow of goods and impacted the regional economy.
SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST: As we heard from those early voters in Texas and from coverage of the protests in France, the economy and affordability are surging concerns globally. It's also a concern locally in Milwaukee, where I'm hosting this program tonight. If you look at a map, you realize the city is located on a massive superhighway of water. Milwaukee is on Lake Michigan, part of the Great Lakes region, and that region is its own economy. Cargo from around the world is shipped across the Great Lakes, and all that maritime trade contributes to a regional economy worth about $9 trillion. Now look at that map again. Four of the five great lakes are shared between the United States and Canada. Those two countries are now in an economic battle due to President Trump's tariffs, and that fight is harming port cities like Milwaukee. That is why I found myself this week on a long concrete pier on the port of Milwaukee, overlooking the vast expanse of Lake Michigan and talking with port director Benji Timm. BENJI TIMM: So the boat is coming from the East. You can see the breakwater. There's a break in the breakwater out there. And there's... PFEIFFER: A little passage for boats to get through. Yeah. TIMM: Yes, between the light - the two lighthouses. That's where the vessels would come in. And if they're going into our inner mooring basin, they'd pass underneath the Hoan Bridge in the highway. If they're coming into one of our terminals here, they'd come straight in into one of these slips. PFEIFFER: So whether they're coming from Canada or Europe, that is the way they get in. TIMM: That's our gateway. PFEIFFER: Port Milwaukee does business with more than 300 ships a year that import goods from all over. TIMM: So there are steel beams on the terminal, and this steel came in from Luxembourg. It came in for a hospital project from Minnesota. It's unloaded from a vessel here, and then it's loaded up onto trucks and then trucked over to Minnesota. (SOUNDBITE OF STEEL BANGING) PFEIFFER: Can we not make this in the United States? TIMM: That was a special gauge of steel, I know. PFEIFFER: I mean, and is that partly what the Trump administration hopes for eventually, is that we can make this steel at home? And by these tariffs, we won't have to bring it in from Europe? TIMM: That's the idea, yeah, is that we increase our production here. And again, I don't think anybody would argue with that, but we have to put the components into place to get us to that point. PFEIFFER: Over the past year, Timm watched anxiously as the Trump administration added or threatened tariffs on all sorts of items - steel, auto parts, salt, agricultural commodities, timber. The tariffs could come at any time, and that affects the budgets and supply chains of countless companies that rely on this port. What is your distress level about the impact that tariffs are having on the Milwaukee economy? TIMM: It's kind of whiplash. You know, it's - it has not been consistent. When the administration makes an announcement, we listen very closely, and then we try and figure out how it'll affect us. We try not to freak out because oftentimes it'll change. PFEIFFER: Sometimes you're inclined to freak out? TIMM: Sometimes. You know, we try and reserve the freak out. But... PFEIFFER: Imported products were all around us in warehouses and silos and massive domed containers. So we got in a van with Benji Timm and the mayor of Milwaukee, Cavalier Johnson, to get an up close look. (SOUNDBITE OF CAR DOOR CLOSING) CAVALIER JOHNSON: This peanut butter spread of tariffs just, you know, across the board, it's kind of - it's harmful. PFEIFFER: Remember that steel? There is now a 50% tariff on foreign steel imports to the U.S. We are passing by a shipping bay where it looks like, I don't know, steel cord - what are we seeing stacked up there? TIMM: So those are coils of steel. That's the tin plate steel that's primarily imported from the Netherlands, and it comes here and is used in canning, like food cans. There are a number of canning... PFEIFFER: Things we see on grocery store shelves - that's how it starts, right there. TIMM: Exactly. Yep. PFEIFFER: One of the things that's been tariffed is steel, and a lot of steel comes into Milwaukee. How has that affected the steel coming and going? TIMM: So the steel that comes into Port Milwaukee is not produced by U.S. steelmakers, so it has to be imported. And the steel is down approximately 30%, and that's kind of systemwide. So it's expensive, and production is down. You know, costs are going up, so there are less sales overall. PFEIFFER: The goal of these tariffs by the Trump administration is to try to have more manufacturing done in the United States, and that will take time. When you talk to the businesses in your state and your city that are affected by the tariffs, how patient are they feeling about waiting to see if the tariffs have the payoff that the Trump administration hopes for? TIMM: Well, that's the thing, is that our businesses and our consumers - they shouldn't be subject to the whims, the ups and downs, the back and forth, the unpredictability, the instability that's happening out of Washington. PFEIFFER: And that instability can have international ripple effects. All right, so we are seeing a very large ship. It is not a container ship. What are we seeing? TIMM: So that's a bulk carrier vessel. It's from... PFEIFFER: Bulk carrier? TIMM: Bulk carrier, yeah. So they have bays within cargo holds within the vessel, where they store bulk materials. PFEIFFER: And did you start to say it's from Bulgaria? TIMM: So the vessel itself is from Bulgaria, and it's going to take the DDGs to Spain. PFEIFFER: Do you think people would be surprised to know that a ship from Bulgaria is stopping in Milwaukee to then deliver things to Spain? TIMM: I do. PFEIFFER: Near the Bulgarian boat are huge mounds of something covered with tarps. TIMM: So on the left, those are salt piles. So one of the biggest commodities that Port Milwaukee brings in is salt, and that salt is used for road safety. It's used for component animal feed. It's also used for water softeners. Last year, we had a pretty harsh winter, and states as far away as Kentucky, Minnesota, Iowa, were coming here to get salt. PFEIFFER: A lot of Milwaukee salt comes from Canada. The Trump administration wanted to put tariffs on that, too. When you heard that salt Well, salt and many other products may be tariffed, what was your concern for Milwaukee? TIMM: So because salt is the biggest commodity that we import here, that would have had a significant impact on not only the city of Milwaukee's budget, but also other municipalities' budgets. PFEIFFER: The Trump administration removed salt from its tariff list after lobbying from Congress. But back on the pier, Timm told me the uncertainty is destabilizing. TIMM: Everyone wants predictability. They want to be able to plan for the future. They want to be able to plan, you know, acquisitions, improvements, investments in their businesses. And that's hard to do when prices change so frequently. PFEIFFER: What is your worry level about whether this will take a change of administration to improve the situation, whether the Trump administration may eventually lower the tariffs and it will create some relief for Milwaukee? TIMM: Yeah, my biggest worry is our relationship with Canada and making sure that we keep that strong. So they're Wisconsin's largest trading partner. They're a significant part of our economy here in Milwaukee. PFEIFFER: What do they... The U.S. and Canada are so interlinked by the Great Lakes that a ship going between the two countries can cross the international border 27 times. They're partners. TIMM: It's really interesting. Because there's such a tight relationship between the United States and Canada, we have a lot of the same companies on both sides of the border, and essentially, we trade components, and we trade equipment back and forth. And when you have disruptions like tariffs, when you have other disruptions in the transportation network, it can be really harmful and really kind of just slow down business. So I'd... PFEIFFER: President Trump is trying to use tariffs to reshape global trade and protect the U.S. economy. But that's leaving people like Port Milwaukee director Benji Timm to reassure his city's foreign trading partners. He has to keep goods flowing nationwide and worldwide. He has to brace for products suddenly becoming more scarce or more expensive, and he has no idea when that volatility will end. (SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC) PFEIFFER: Stay with us for more coverage from Wisconsin, an important bellweather state, where we are this weekend just ahead of the midterm elections.
