title: Designing Ethical, Privacy-Preserving Sponsorships for a Static Web App
body: Designing Ethical, Privacy-Preserving Sponsorships for a Static Web App Can a free web application generate revenue without relying on behavioral advertising, intrusive pop-ups, or extensive user tracking? That is a question I have been exploring while working on SabrTime, an Islamic Progressive Web App focused on duas, prayer-related tools, tasbeeh, and spiritual reflection. The idea is to design a direct sponsorship system that allows suitable businesses to support the project through clearly labelled advertisements while preserving user privacy and keeping essential features accessible. This article documents the proposed architecture, security considerations, advertiser review process, and implementation roadmap. The system described here is a design under development, not a claim that a complete advertising platform is already live. Project: https://sabrtime.in/ The Problem: Monetization Without Compromising Trust Many independent applications depend on advertising networks, subscriptions, donations, or affiliate marketing. Each model has trade-offs. Third-party advertising can introduce external scripts, cookies, tracking requests, and limited control over the final advertisement. Subscription models may restrict access for users who cannot pay. Affiliate programs can introduce referral tracking and unpredictable revenue. For an application built around personal values, these trade-offs deserve careful consideration. The questions I wanted to investigate were: Can advertisements be selected by page context instead of personal browsing history? Can a publisher review every campaign before it appears? Can paid placements be clearly distinguished from editorial content? Can campaign performance be measured without building individual user profiles? Can essential application features remain free? These questions form the basis of the proposed sponsorship architecture. The Proposed Model: Direct, Contextual Sponsorship Rather than immediately integrating a conventional advertising network, the proposed system would allow businesses to apply for direct sponsorship placements. A campaign would be reviewed before publication. Approved advertisements could then appear in designated areas of the application, such as selected educational articles or non-essential tool pages. For example, a publisher of educational books might sponsor a relevant resource page. The placement would be labelled as sponsored, link to the advertiser's website, and remain separate from the article's editorial conclusions. The application would not need to infer the visitor's religious practices or create a behavioral profile to display that placement. This is contextual sponsorship: the placement is selected according to the page or section, rather than a profile of the individual visitor. A Simple Architecture for a Static Application A static frontend can display approved sponsorship content without requiring a complex advertising server. However, static hosting alone does not provide secure administrative authentication, private storage, payment verification, or campaign-management permissions. A practical architecture therefore separates public campaign delivery from private administration. Advertiser | v Campaign Application | v Human Review | v Approval and Publication | v Public Campaign Configuration | v Static Frontend | v Clearly Labelled Sponsored Placement | v Advertiser Website The diagram represents a proposed workflow rather than a deployed system. Public campaign configuration A small pilot could use a curated JSON configuration containing approved campaign information. For example: { "campaignId": "campaign-001", "advertiserName": "Example Book Publisher", "placement": "educational-content", "status": "approved", "startDate": "2026-11-01", "endDate": "2026-11-30", "label": "Sponsored", "destinationUrl": " https://example.com/ " } This is an illustrative schema. It does not represent a real advertiser or an active campaign. The frontend could use this configuration to decide which placement to render and whether the campaign is within its scheduled dates. The configuration should contain only information intended to be public. Credentials, payment secrets, private applications, and administrative tokens must never be placed in client-side files. Why not build an advertising platform immediately? A new project does not necessarily need real-time bidding, audience segmentation, an advertiser dashboard, or a sophisticated analytics pipeline. Those systems increase implementation complexity and create additional security and privacy responsibilities. A manually managed pilot can help answer the more important initial question: do suitable advertisers actually want this type of placement? Infrastructure should grow in response to demonstrated demand rather than assumptions about future scale. Security Boundaries Matter One of the most important architectural lessons is that a public frontend cannot be trusted to enforce private business rules. Suppose a campaign record contains: { "status": "approved" } That value is useful for rendering a public campaign, but it does not prove that an administrator approved the campaign. A user can modify client-side data and JavaScript in their own browser. The real approval process must be enforced by the publishing workflow or a trusted backend. A production implementation should account for: Authentication for campaign administrators. Authorization checks for approval and modification actions. Server-side validation of campaign dates and destinations. Protection against unauthorized campaign changes. Secure handling of payment credentials. A reliable mechanism to pause or withdraw a campaign. Audit records for important administrative actions. If a static file is updated manually, access to the repository and publishing process becomes part of the security boundary. A larger deployment should introduce an appropriate authenticated management service. For a broader introduction to web application security, the "OWASP Cheat Sheet Series" ( https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/ ) is a useful resource. Privacy by Design Privacy should influence the architecture before analytics and advertising scripts are added. The initial design would aim to avoid behavioral advertising, cross-site tracking, and persistent personal advertising profiles. Contextual selection A campaign can be selected according to a predefined placement identifier: function selectCampaign(campaigns, placement, now = Date.now()) { return campaigns.filter((campaign) => { if (campaign.status !== "approved") return false; if (campaign.placement !== placement) return false; const start = Date.parse(`${campaign.startDate}T00:00:00Z`); const end = Date.parse(`${campaign.endDate}T23:59:59Z`); return Number.isFinite(start) && Number.isFinite(end) && now >= start && now <= end; }); } This example demonstrates basic filtering logic. It does not implement secure approval, campaign storage, payment verification, or a complete production advertising system. Production code would also need to define time-zone semantics, validate campaign data, handle unavailable assets, and choose a deterministic display strategy when multiple campaigns match. The key point is that placement selection can be based on the current page without requiring a visitor's personal profile. Minimize external dependencies Even without an advertising network, privacy risks can arise from third-party images, analytics libraries, destination websites, and hosting infrastructure. A privacy review should examine network requests, cookies, browser storage, referrer behavior, server logs, and data-retention practices. A static frontend is not automatically tracking-free. Privacy claims should be based on the system that is actually deployed and tested. For implementation guidance, see the "MDN Web Security documentation" ( https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Security ). Screening Advertisers and Destination Pages Direct sponsorship offers greater control over advertising content, but it also creates a moderation responsibility. A campaign should not be approved solely because its banner looks appropriate. The proposed review process would examine: The advertiser's identity and contact details. The advertised product or service. The wording and imagery. The destination website. Pricing, material conditions, and commercial claims. Potential scams, misleading redirects, or unsafe payment flows. Whether the campaign follows the publisher's published eligibility policy. For SabrTime, the proposed policy would be informed by Islamic ethical principles and would exclude clearly unsuitable categories. However, a publisher should not claim that every approved advertisement has received independent religious certification unless that certification genuinely exists. Advertising approval is a review decision, not automatically a religious endorsement. Campaigns should also be reviewed again if the destination page or advertised product changes materially after approval. Make Commercial Content Explicit A sponsored placement should never imitate an editorial recommendation or a religious resource. The user interface should make the commercial relationship obvious. For example: Sponsored Example Book Publisher Explore the publisher's educational catalogue. Visit advertiser This is an illustrative HTML component, not an existing SabrTime production component. In a real implementation, the card would also need accessible styling, appropriate link behavior, content validation, and a reliable process for managing campaign expiration. The "rel="sponsored"" attribute identifies the commercial nature of the link. The "noopener noreferrer" attributes help control aspects of opening the destination in a new tab. Google's guidance on "qualifying outbound links" ( https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/qualify-outbound-links ) explains how paid links should be identified. The sponsorship label should remain visible even when the card is styled to match the rest of the application. Measuring Campaign Performance Without Individual Profiles Advertisers need evidence that a placement is working. That does not mean every click must be connected to a persistent user identity. A minimal reporting system could measure: Aggregate impressions. Aggregate clicks. Campaign start and end dates. Basic rendering errors. Campaign renewals. Moderation and approval outcomes. Click-through rate is calculated as: [ CTR = \frac{\text{Clicks}}{\text{Impressions}} \times 100 ] For example, 25 clicks from 1,000 measured impressions would produce a 2.5% click-through rate. This is an illustrative calculation, not a measured result from the project. The system must define what counts as an impression. A card being loaded is not necessarily equivalent to being visible to a user. A small pilot could use aggregate event counts without retaining individual click histories. Any analytics implementation should still be reviewed for unnecessary identifiers, IP-address retention, third-party requests, and applicable privacy requirements. What About Payments? Payment processing should be treated as a separate, trusted component. The browser must not be allowed to declare a campaign paid simply because a user reaches a success page or changes a client-side variable. A production payment flow should verify payment status through the payment provider's trusted mechanisms and reconcile the result with the campaign record. Other important requirements include: Clear campaign pricing and duration. Refund and cancellation terms. Payment receipts and accounting records. Protection of API secrets. A process for disputed or failed payments. Appropriate tax and consumer-law review. A small pilot could begin with manually agreed sponsorships and controlled campaign publication before introducing an automated payment workflow. The implementation choice should reflect the project's scale and available operational resources. A Practical Development Roadmap The proposed system can be developed incrementally. Phase 1: Define the policy Document eligible categories, prohibited content, review criteria, sponsorship labels, and privacy expectations. Phase 2: Build the display component Create an accessible sponsored card with a clear label, validated destination, and placement rules. Phase 3: Introduce controlled publishing Maintain an approved campaign configuration and restrict access to the publishing workflow. Phase 4: Run a limited pilot Test mobile layouts, keyboard navigation, campaign expiration, broken links, and the effect on essential application features. Phase 5: Evaluate the evidence Measure aggregate campaign performance, gather user feedback, and determine whether advertisers see enough value to continue. Phase 6: Expand only when justified If the pilot demonstrates demand, consider a secure administrative interface, campaign scheduling, payment reconciliation, and aggregate reporting. This approach avoids investing prematurely in a large advertising platform before the underlying business model has been validated. Applying the Approach to SabrTime SabrTime is an Islamic PWA focused on duas, worship-related tools, and spiritual reflection. Its proposed sponsorship model explores whether direct commercial support can help sustain free resources without making invasive tracking or intrusive advertising a requirement. The intended principles are: Essential worship features remain accessible. Sponsored content is clearly identified. Advertisers are reviewed before publication. Commercial placements do not control religious editorial content. Personal religious activity is not used to construct advertising profiles. Campaign administration and payment processing receive appropriate security controls. The sponsorship feature is a work in progress. These principles describe the intended design and should not be interpreted as proof that all the controls are already implemented. Project reference: https://sabrtime.in/ Lessons for Independent Developers The broader lesson is that monetization architecture should follow the product's values. Before choosing an advertising provider or building an ad server, developers can ask: What user data is actually necessary? Can page context replace behavioral profiling? Who approves commercial content? How can paid links be disclosed? What happens when a campaign becomes unsafe? Which components require server-side enforcement? What evidence would justify investing in a more complex platform? The answers may differ across products, but making these decisions early can reduce unnecessary complexity later. A static application can be a useful starting point for a small sponsorship pilot. A production commercial system still needs appropriate security, operational controls, and honest privacy disclosures. Conclusion Privacy-conscious sponsorship is not simply a matter of removing third-party advertising scripts. It requires a deliberate approach to campaign selection, moderation, disclosure, data minimization, security, and commercial accountability. The proposed SabrTime model explores a straightforward starting point: direct sponsorship, contextual placements, human review, and aggregate reporting. The next step is to validate the model through a limited implementation and real feedback before investing in more complex infrastructure. For independent developers, the most useful question may not be how many advertisements an application can display, but how it can generate sustainable revenue while preserving the trust of the people who use it. Disclosure: This article was prepared with AI assistance and describes a proposed feature under development. It does not claim that the complete sponsorship system is deployed or that any advertiser has been independently halal-certified.

title: A pre-flight checklist before domain continued pre-training
body: Your team picked an open weight checkpoint and a corpus. The tempting move is to schedule GPUs and iterate on the mix later. Joel Hron at Thomson Reuters and Fergal Reid at Intercom both describe training as staged pipelines where evaluation sits beside the data, and Hron treats retained capabilities as an explicit objective. I'd treat the run as blocked until you can answer the questions below. What training stage are you actually running? Most product teams are not pretraining from scratch. They adapt a base model in layers. Continued pre-training adds more unlabeled domain text on top of an existing checkpoint. Supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization teach labeled behavior. Agentic reinforcement learning teaches tool use inside a harness. Hron maps Thomson's stack in that order: realign the open source starting point (Imperial College's Snowdon model, from the Qwen 3.5 family), then continuous pre-training on selected Thomson Reuters content (Westlaw, Practical Law, Checkpoint, Reuters News Archive), then fine-tuning and direct preference optimization with human experts, then agentic RL with access to TR applications. Less than 10% of the content corpus had been used for continuous pre-training at the time of the interview, with room to grow. Reid's path at Intercom started with parameter-efficient experiments such as LoRA and moved toward distributed training on large GPU nodes, combining full supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning for harder policies. The stage label matters because each phase needs different eval slices and different failure modes. Why build the eval set before the run? Do not treat public benchmarks as a substitute for job-shaped tests. Hron pairs curated training data with "good evals that represent those jobs equally well." Thomson uses CoCounsel Bench (on the order of thousands of legal queries, growing almost daily) plus internal legal benchmarks and public legal benchmarks. For retention, the team tracks roughly ten or eleven general dimensions (legal, tax, journalism, math, coding, instruction following, general reasoning, long context, and others) and describes a technical-paper graphic, due the week after the interview, comparing Qwen, Snowdon, and Thomson on a spider-style plot. Reid is blunter about offline suites versus live traffic: however carefully a backtest or evaluation is built, what happens in production can deviate from it. Intercom still invests in backtests (real customer hallucination cases, LLM judges on answer quality) but A/B tests in production against resolution signals before shipping. I'd copy the split: freeze an internal suite that mirrors real tasks before training, plan a production gate for anything that touches users, and accept that backtests alone will not catch every confounder (Reid notes latency can shift resolution rates in ways you would never encode offline). Sketch for scoping eval buckets before CPT (illustration only, not TR or Intercom code): # Sketch: define eval lanes before any training job RETAIN = [ " coding_snippets " , " math_word_problems " , " instruction_following " ] GAIN = [ " domain_qa " , " tool_use_with_apis " , " citation_style " ] HOLDOUT = { " never_in_train " : True , " source " : " prod_failures_last_90d " } def gate_release ( scores : dict ) -> bool : for task in RETAIN : if scores [ task ] < scores [ f " baseline_ { task } " ] * 0.98 : return False # regressions block ship return all ( scores [ t ] >= scores [ f " baseline_ { t } " ] for t in GAIN ) What can regress during continued pre-training? Catastrophic forgetting stops being an abstract research term once your product depends on skills the base model already has. Hron says Thomson Reuters users still need coding, math, and general reasoning from the open source foundation, and a large share of engineering goes into adding TR data without losing that fluency. But I think the more important thing is that it does not regress in any of those other areas. Joel Hron, CTO, Thomson Reuters He was candid that the result was not zero: he described a very small regression in coding and in math. The glossary framing matches that practice: measure gains on the new domain and performance on capabilities you need to keep. Mixing general data with domain data can limit damage during continued pre-training, but the mixture ratio is a hypothesis until you eval it. Before you scale corpus coverage (Thomson started small on CPT fraction), I'd require per-checkpoint reports on both domain lift and retention lanes, not a single average score. Where can reward hacking show up in post-training? Once you add RL or multi-objective preference training, the score becomes a target. Reward hacking is when the model satisfies the score through a shortcut that misses the intended task, such as getting answers from an unauthorized source. That matters for agentic RL like Thomson's harness over Westlaw and Practical Law, and for Intercom's offline RL stack built around a resolution model plus additional LLM judges (answer length, bullet-point use, and others). Reid says designing the objective function is "relatively the smaller part" compared with the infrastructure for running models at scale. I'd read that as a warning: a clever proxy (resolution model, LLM judge, benchmark leaderboard) can drift from user value, and auditing how answers were produced is one way to catch it. Intercom also runs production A/B tests so soft resolutions do not rise while hard resolutions fall, which is one guardrail against turning the product into a deflection machine. If you augment scarce labels with model-generated examples, treat synthetic data as augmentation, validate against real failures, and do not assume more rows equal better training. Synthetic data inherits its generator's biases and blind spots, and heavy training on model output can amplify errors. Checklist Name the stage (continued pre-training, SFT or DPO, agentic RL) and match eval tasks to that stage before you launch jobs. Ship a retention panel (general skills you rely on from the base model) and a domain panel (jobs your product actually sells), both measured at every checkpoint. Block promotion when any retention lane drops materially, even if domain accuracy spikes. For RL or judge-heavy post-training, log how answers were produced and test for proxy gaming; keep a production or shadow A/B gate when live signal exists. If you use synthetic pairs, spot-check against real incidents and existing eval harnesses before they enter the training mix. More on this topic, with the related episodes, is on Chain of Thought . It draws on this episode . Subscribe to the Chain of Thought newsletter for new episodes and write-ups like this one. Drafted with AI assistance from the episode transcripts.

title: Day 9/100: AI Is a Tool, Not an Authority
body: 🎧 Listen to this episode Yesterday, Karan Balaji sat down with Ram K Pari, a friend since school who is now finishing a PhD in neural engineering, working on speech perception for elderly people. They did not plan a debate. They wanted to answer one question that keeps coming up in different forms: why does the same AI give a beginner and an expert completely different outcomes? The conversation kept circling back to one answer. AI is a tool, not an authority. And the difference between a good outcome and a bad one is almost never the model. It is the person holding it, and whether they check its work. AI remixes. It does not invent. Ram still codes optimization by hand. That surprised Karan at first, until Ram explained why. When you are trying to build something genuinely new, not a remix of something that already exists, a large language model is the wrong instrument. It is trained on what has already been done. It recombines it, rephrases it, and finds clever ways around the edges of a problem. It does not have the intuition to push a field forward. Ram gave the example of the Navier-Stokes equations. There is a well known 3Blue1Brown video on the subject, and the AI approaches that made headlines around it mostly found edge cases, weird ways of getting around the problem rather than solving the core of it. Ram's point was blunt: an approach like that reveals nothing the field can build on. If you are in a field that specific, you need hyper specific knowledge to move forward, and no prompt replaces it. This is the part most of the public conversation misses. For the average person on an average day, remixing is enough. Most of what we do is not new. It is a website, a report, a piece of code that already exists somewhere in a different shape. AI is excellent at that. The mistake is assuming that because it remixes well, it also creates. It does not, at least not yet. The axe and the chainsaw Karan offered Ram an analogy during the call, and it stuck. Give an expert lumberjack an axe and a beginner a chainsaw, and ask them to cut down a tree. The expert wins. Not because the axe is better, but because he knows where to cut, at what angle, and how deep. The beginner with the chainsaw will cut a circle all the way around the trunk, and the tree will not move. It is the same with Photoshop, which Karan has used as an analogy for years. Photoshop did not kill photographers. Photographers kept their jobs because they knew what a good photo looked like and how to direct the tool toward it. The tool made them faster. It did not make them unnecessary. AI is the same story at a bigger scale. A designer who knows UX can direct a model to a one step workflow instead of five. A researcher who knows their domain can spot the moment a model starts confidently drifting. A beginner who cannot tell the difference gets an output that looks finished and is not. The Dunning-Kruger trap Ram manages masters and bachelors students, and this is where the conversation got serious. He watches students paste an entire problem into an AI tool, receive a solution, and walk away believing they understand it. They do not. They have an answer, not knowledge. The learning outcome, which was the whole point of the assignment, never happened. A couple of model generations ago, Ram had a trick for this. He made assignments hard enough that the AI would fail to produce a perfect solution. Students had to debug why the AI went wrong, and that debugging was where the actual learning lived. He is not sure that trick still works with frontier models, but the principle behind it is more important than ever: if the tool does the thinking, the student does not. This is the Dunning-Kruger effect in its purest form. The less you know, the more you think you know, because you cannot see the depth of what you are missing. AI makes this worse, because it hands you fluent, confident output. Fluency feels like understanding. It is not. The one place a beginner might win Ram did name one edge case where a beginner could theoretically outperform an expert, and it is worth naming honestly: medical diagnosis. A doctor is trained to work through likely causes first and rare ones last, in a specific order. An AI tool has no such order. It might surface a rare diagnosis for a strange set of symptoms that the standard sequence would reach last, or never. But Ram put a large caveat on it, and Karan will repeat it louder: talk to your doctor first. Using AI for medical decisions without expert knowledge is a massive risk. The edge case is real but rare, and the statistical distribution exists for a reason. Most of the time, the common diagnosis is the right one, and the expert's priors are a feature, not a bug. Design still needs a designer Karan shared his own version of this from design engineering. Tell a model to improve a screen and it will do visible things: nicer fonts, a more modern look, a cleaner layout based on a design system. What it will not do on its own is real UX. It will not decide that five steps should become one step, or that a sidebar experience fits the workflow better than a multi page flow. You have to tell it that, precisely, and then you have to check whether it actually did it. Karan has run this loop at the frontier model level. The first output is rarely directly usable by a human. You direct it, you review it, you redirect it, and only then does it become good. The work did not disappear. It changed shape, from producing to directing and verifying. The PHP story: a million tokens, no patch Ram's best example came from security. Recently a large PHP vulnerability made headlines, one that touched a huge share of the web. Before the patch dropped, people rushed to find the exploit with AI. Ram described users burning a million tokens in two days, and a wave of people on Twitter claiming they had found the exact exploit. They had not. Their models were exploiting older vulnerabilities, or finding tricks that only worked on their own local machines. This is the validation problem in its most expensive form. You will always get an output. The model will tell you it did the task. The question is whether it actually followed your instructions, and whether what it produced is true. Those are two different questions, and only a human can answer them. Ram put it well: AI is like a colleague who tells you the work is done. There is only one way to find out if it is. You check. The bias that scares Karan most Here is the pattern Ram and Karan both keep seeing, and it is the one that worries Karan most. When nine out of ten AI tasks go fine, people quietly stop validating the tenth. The tool feels reliable, so the habit of checking fades. Then one task lands in a critical environment, a system exposed to the internet, a piece of code that touches real users, and the skipped check is the difference between a bad day and losing the business. That is not a hypothetical. Failing to validate AI generated code in production is a business risk, full stop. It can cost revenue, trust, and in the worst case the company itself. Validation is also recursive, which is the part people forget. You can write validation tests with an AI agent too. But then you have to verify that the tests themselves do what you think they do. There is no point in the chain where checking becomes unnecessary. The chain just moves. Working more, not less One more observation from the call, because it cuts against the loudest narrative. Ram mentioned a study finding that people are working more because of AI, not less. Everyone Karan has talked to in industry says the same thing. Expectations rise to fill the new capacity. The tool lets you do more, so more is expected of you, with the same hours. That reframes the jobs question. Bulk, middle tier coding work is genuinely at risk. But domain specific roles, the ones where the knowledge itself is the job, look safe for now. Not because AI cannot touch them, but because directing AI well requires the very expertise people feared would be replaced. The rule to take into tomorrow So here is the rule Karan is taking from this conversation, and the one he would hand to anyone starting out with AI: Treat every AI output as a draft from a confident colleague. Verify it against what you actually asked for. Verify it against reality. And the more it matters, the more carefully you verify. That habit is the difference between an expert and a beginner, and it will stay the difference no matter what the models are called next year. Ram joked that we will probably be calling it superintelligence by then. The name will change. The rule will not: the tool does the work, but you are still responsible for the outcome.

title: Legal expert calls out Trump’s threat to delegitimize Alaska senate vote
body:
A legal expert says a lawsuit by the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) doesn’t hold up and threatens to delegitimize the results if Republican incumbent Dan S. Sullivan loses November’s Senate race in Alaska.
“I see no possibility of any literate voter being unable to distinguish the two Daniel Sullivans on the ballot,” Emily L. Waters, a professor at the University of Alaska Anchorage, told Global News.
On Thursday, the DOJ filed a lawsuit to block Alaska from certifying its Senate election results if Sullivan, the incumbent, doesn’t win.
President Donald Trump said he ordered the lawsuit because there will be two Dan Sullivans on the ballot.
Both identify themselves as Republicans.
“They have two guys named Dan Sullivan running,” Trump said. “So the Democrats put up a guy, I don’t think he ever voted before. All of a sudden he decides to run for the Senate and his name is Dan Sullivan.”
In the court filings, the DOJ claims the second candidate, Daniel J. Sullivan, is running with the intention of misleading and confusing voters to benefit Democratic rival Mary Peltola.
The documents further argue that, should the incumbent Sullivan lose, certifying the results would compromise the integrity of the election.
The Alaska Supreme Court previously ruled that both names could stay on the ballot.
Even if the second Sullivan was running to misdirect voters, Waters said that does not justify a legal battle.
“Judge Zeman addressed this previously in state court and said there’s no problem if somebody enters a race to harass or distract, as long as they follow procedures, their motivations for being on the ballot are irrelevant.”
She added that credit needs to be given to the voter to be able to distinguish between the candidates.
“Sullivan has enriched himself at our expense for 12 years,” she said. “Now he’s using his DC allies to try to keep himself in power and put his own interests ahead of Alaskans.”
If Peltola wins the race in Alaska, it will give Democrats one out of four seats needed to gain control of the Senate.
– With files from Global News’ Candice Cole

title: Duma speaker arrives on working visit to New Delhi
body:
NEW DELHI, October 24. /TASS/. State Duma Speaker Vyacheslav Volodin on Saturday arrived on a working visit to India, his first foreign trip as the new Duma’s chairman, leading a delegation of Russian lawmakers, a TASS correspondent reported.
Volodin noted earlier that Russia appreciates the relations it maintains with India. He reiterated this during meetings with the republic’s leadership while on an official visit to India in February 2025.
The Russian delegation will take part in the 12th BRICS International Parliamentary Forum in New Delhi on October 26-27. This year’s forum is themed on "Strengthening Parliaments for People-Centric Development." Volodin is also scheduled to meet with his overseas counterparts on the sidelines of the event.
In addition, there are plans for the Duma speaker to meet with senior Indian officials and parliamentarians to discuss the development of Russian-Indian cooperation in the economic, social, and technological spheres as well as the further strengthening and intensification of interparliamentary dialogue.

title: Saudi Arabia says Houthi missile shrapnel falls in Jeddah, Taif, Rabigh after interceptions
body: Saudi Arabia's Civil Defense said on Saturday it intercepted two ballistic missiles launched by Yemen's Houthis toward the Mecca and Medina regions, with debris falling in several locations, including Jeddah, Taif, and Rabigh.This follows a Houthi announcement about attacks on Saudi oil facilities and airports on Saturday, including a Saudi Aramco facility in Yanbu, the Rabigh oil refinery, and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.The terror group's military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said it also targeted King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, as well as Najran airport and an air base in Khamis Mushait.Houthi media reports strikes on SanaaEarlier on Saturday, Houthi-linked Saba News Agency reported that Yemen's National Commission for Human Rights had condemned Saudi Arabia over strikes in the capital.The group described a “massacre” in the Asr neighborhood of Sanaa and an attack on a cement factory in the Hamdan district of Sanaa Governorate.US warns Americans about possible escalation in Middle EastThe latest round of strikes came amid warnings by the US State Department, which updated its travel advisory notice for Israel on Friday, warning of an increased threat of armed attacks by Iran-backed Houthi terrorists and the potential for a rapid escalation of regional hostilities.The update did not change Israel's overall travel advisory classification, which remains at Level 3, urging American citizens to reconsider travel due to terrorism and unrest. The existing risk indicators and restrictions on travel to certain areas of the country also remain unchanged.In its warning on armed conflict, the State Department cited previous Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia, including strikes on civilian airports and critical infrastructure that resulted in civilian casualties and major travel disruptions. Idan Kweller contributed to this report.

title: Akume: Any Northerner contesting 2027 Presidency is the region’s enemy
body: Secretary to the Government of the Federation (SGF), Senator George Akume, on Saturday branded any northerner contesting in the 2027 presidential election as an enemy of the region. The African Democratic Congress (ADC) presidential candidate, Atiku Abubakar, is the only prominent politician from the north battling to unseat President Bola Tinubu in the next year’s presidential contest. Speaking at a pre-campaign meeting with a large crowd of Benue State indigenes residing in Kaduna, Akume noted told Northerners that the agreement on power rotation between the North and the South was reached in Kaduna State to keep the country together. The APC flagged off its presidential campaign in Kaduna on Saturday. Kano ACF appoints interim leadership after chairman’s resignation Tinubu gave you succour when PDP chased you in 2007, Shettima tackles Atiku A statement by the SGF’s spokesman, Yomi Odunuga, quoted him to have said: “Remember that it was in this same Kaduna State that we agreed on power rotation between the North and the South. You cannot doubt the credentials of those that reached this agreement at that time, and it was done to keep this country together. We agreed on power shift, and that is what has kept this country going. That is what has retained our territorial integrity.” As a result, he declared that any Northerner seeking to contest the 2027 presidential election is an enemy of the North, insisting that President Bola Ahmed Tinubu remains the right candidate to lead Nigeria beyond 2027 Nigerian Politics Coverage “Anybody who is from the North and running for the presidency is an enemy of the North. Don’t allow that pretender to deceive you. It is not yet our turn. The North’s turn is in 2031. Prepare to vote for Tinubu. Do not allow anyone to destroy the country because of a vaunting personal ambition,” he said. The SGF urged the North to back Tinubu’s re-election bid and wait until 2031 before seeking to return to the presidency. He warned that individual political ambitions should not be allowed to undermine the region’s collective interests. The former Governor of Benue State urged Northerners to remain united and resist political manoeuvres capable of weakening the region’s influence. He cautioned against attempts to divide them along political, religious and personal lines, and recalled past political disagreements among Nigerian leaders, warning against repeating mistakes that could weaken the North in national politics. He said the North stands to benefit more from supporting Tinubu’s second-term ambition than from allowing individual political interests to create divisions ahead of the next general elections.Follow Politics Defending the president’s record, the SGF said Tinubu has been fair to all in appointments and does not favour one religion over another. “Let us remember that the President has been fair to all in terms of appointments and others. He doesn’t favour one religion over the other. Just look at the figures. So be careful about what people tell you,” he said. Akume also told his audience that the president has shown his love for Benue State through significant projects. “Let nobody deceive you; Asiwaju loves Benue, and he has displayed that in the number of significant projects the Federal Government is carrying out simultaneously in the state. These projects are diverse in healthcare, roads, education and others. This is being replicated throughout the federation. For example, in the area of education, over 65 per cent of NELFUND has been accessed, and most of them are from the North,” he said. Taking a swipe at Atiku, he said, “Forget that other one making noise that he was going to remove fuel subsidy. He is always flip-flopping. He says something today and changes gear the next minute.”

title: Will AI expose the rickety infrastructure of the internet?
body:
A startling announcement went out earlier this week: Due to recently discovered vulnerabilities in the open source programming language PHP, website owners had to immediately patch their sites — or if they couldn’t update right away, they should take the sites down to be safe.
On this week’s episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Kirsten Korosec, Sean O’Kane, and I discussed the significance of the PHP-ocalypse and whether we’ll see more incidents like this in the future.
Sean called this “a real reckoning moment” that highlights how “when you get down to the bone level of the internet,” everything seems to be “held together by glue and dreams.” And with widespread access to large language models and AI agents, it’s only going to become easier to find these vulnerabilities. (That said, these specific vulnerabilities were found by human researchers , not AI models.)
Kirsten, meanwhile, wondered if we’re about to see the “next level of prepper doom […] because you could see how banks could get exploited, and [with] data and privacy concerns, it just feels a lot bigger than we can fix right now.”
Keep reading for a preview of our conversation , edited for length and clarity.
Sean: The internet is breaking in lots of ways this week, it seems.
I think the best way to think about this, if people are coming into this kind of cold: How many times over the last 10 years have we had these moments where something breaks or something nearly breaks, where one person maintaining one tiny repro repository as a hobby or whatever happens to catch that something nefarious is going on and saves us from the infrastructure of the internet completely crumbling?
Now multiply that by a billion, when people have access to not only extremely advanced software in the form of these LLMs that everybody uses, but also the ability to task them to go out and do it themselves, with creating AI agents that are single-minded at accomplishing those things.
We’re seeing a balance of two things happening this week. One is a bunch of the labs and companies like Google and OpenAI actually had people go out and find a bunch of vulnerabilities, including the one with PHP. And then we also have a bunch of people seeming to rush to take advantage of those vulnerabilities to try and hack into websites. So we have governments taking down websites, we have really popular websites that are going down briefly to be able to fix this vulnerability.
This is a real reckoning moment, where we’re going to find out the downside risk of building so much of the internet on open source technology like PHP. When you really get down to the bone level of the internet, it is held together with glue and dreams.
Anthony: There’s so many things that were striking about this. One of them is the fact that — as I understand it, at least — this is not a new vulnerability. This is a vulnerability that has existed in PHP for decades.
And PHP has been used as a programming language to build so much of the web, so this vulnerability has been there for decades, but no one knew about it. What happened is, essentially, that these big AI companies — including Wiz, now owned by Google — they were able to find these vulnerabilities using LLMs. [As noted above, I got this wrong: Human researchers participating in OpenAI and Wiz’s Hack the Planet initiative found the vulnerabilities , though they used AI to exploit the bug.]
I guess part of the calculation is, we need to patch this, because if we can find this vulnerability using LLMs, so can other people. But the only way we can get the patch out there is to announce the vulnerability. And so it creates this very panicked situation where [they say]: “Okay, this vulnerability existed for decades. You have to patch right away, and if you can’t patch it right away, just take your website down. It’s that severe a vulnerability.”
Kirsten: I think that the important thing is, a lot of people don’t even realize that their websites have PHP — which is this, as you mentioned, decades-old open source programming language.
For those who don’t know, Hypertext Preprocessor is the official term, [it’s] this really the core ingredient behind content management systems that are used throughout WordPress, Drupal, something like 70% of websites. We’re talking tens of millions of websites. So to me, it’s the scale. It also made me immediately think two things: One, this is just the beginning. What other decades-old bad software is out there that is going to be exploited?
And the other one was something that 404 Media, which had a really great breakdown , mentioned, which is link rot. Because a lot of people, companies, governments, maybe that small neighborhood website, they’re shutting these [websites] down. And so we’re going to have so much link rot and also websites that maybe had a little piece of history out there that aren’t gonna be accessible anymore, as opposed to patching it.
Sean: Anthony, I think you made a really good point. I’ve seen a lot of people unhappy with the disclosure rollout here, a bit of the chest beating that OpenAI seems to have done in its post about it.
Also, it seems like a couple people got ahead of the embargo of this release, which set off a race among the hacker set. I think it was Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince [who] already posted about seeing it escalate to millions of attempted hacks of the PHP2Shell.
The thing with these vulnerabilities, the way in cybersecurity this typically works is, if you’re stress testing a company’s software, even if it’s a fundamental piece of software that helps run a lot of different computers or parts of the internet or whatever it might be, you can go to that company and disclose it and it sort of stays within that bubble. But when we’re talking about something that’s as deep as and as fundamental as this, you can’t go around and tell everybody discreetly.
I mean, maybe you could, if the AI was advanced enough and you could task a billion agents to go send an email to every single person who has control over some part of a website. We are now rueing the days when we had webmasters who were easily identifiable, and maybe that would have solved the problem to some extent. But there’s just no easy way to do this. I think this is the beginning of what’s going to be a lot of back and forth and clearly a new frontier in cybersecurity.
Kirsten: Matthew Prince’s social media post was to me really telling, and pretty scary. Also, I don’t know if either of you saw this, but Amazon also put out a blog post . This is a very well-capitalized company, so they have the tools and a team to sort of catch what’s going on. They operate, basically, a honeypot network, or a decoy, and they actually saw that there were attempts to exploit that vulnerability before it had been publicly announced.
To me, again, it goes back to this: Amazon has the tools and the capital and the know-how to fight these things. There’s so many websites and even potentially government websites that just don’t have that level of attention. And so to me, that’s really the scary part.
And there [are] some AI employees out there that are probably going to take this to the next level of like prepper doom, because you could see how banks could get exploited, and [with] data and privacy concerns, it just feels a lot bigger than we can fix right now. So I’m interested to see two things. One, how extreme people’s behavior gets — but also I’m wondering if some new startups are going to pop up as a result of this, or if we’re going to be turning to some of the open source tools [offered by companies like Nvidia] to create these security layers.

title: Democrat Scott Colom aims for deep-red Mississippi Senate seat
body:
Colom would be Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction.
Why are major Democrats and Republicans flocking to Mississippi in recent weeks?
In a climate where polls show President Donald Trump's approval ratings cratering, Democrats are unusually optimistic about Scott Colom's chances of flipping the Senate seat held by incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith -- even in deep-red Mississippi.
"We got to have a senator that looks out for Mississippi, that puts Mississippi farmers first, Mississippi small businesses first, represent our values by not allowing corruption to ruin our country and actually delivers on the commitments to put America first," Colom told ABC News in an interview earlier this week.
The incumbent's campaign dismisses the Democratic push as the last-ditch effort of a campaign that will fall short.
Colom is a district attorney for four counties along the Mississippi-Alabama border and a former nominee to become a U.S. district judge. He would be Mississippi's first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction.
Democrats have argued that Colom's prominent credentials, as well as voter pushback against Republican incumbents and motivation among Democratic-leaning Black voters, could help boost him. Mississippi's population is around 36% Black, according to U.S. Census data .
Colom faces an uphill battle, as Mississippi has not elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1982 and voted for Donald Trump in 2024 by around 20 points. ABC News rates the race solid Republican.
But he has gotten the attention of national Democrats; major party figures such as former former Vice President Kamala Harris and Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock have campaigned with him. Former President Barack Obama also recorded an ad for him released earlier this month.
Harris, during a rally with Colom on Thursday, told attendees, "I've been in those rooms where there's no cameras, it's senators talking to each other... When you have a voice like his in that room, just think about the impact that's going to have on the decisions coming out of that room. Think about that. This is no ordinary time, and this is no ordinary man."
Colom also went viral online last week after a social video he posted showed Hyde-Smith, during a local news interview from February, saying "You have so many proteins to choose from" while discussing how to deal with higher prices on meat and other goods. In the interview, Hyde-Smith also spoke about working on regulations that would help energy production, and tax incentives to help development.
But it was the proteins part that Colom's campaign seized on, with a punchy video that featured voters mocking the senator's words, with one saying, "Pick another protein ... I'd rather pick another Senator instead." (The campaign has confirmed to ABC News that the video has been turned into a campaign ad.)
One concrete sign of confidence among Democrats over Colom's chances came on Tuesday, when the Senate Majority PAC, an outside group aligned with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, announced it would spend $1.2 million on an ad campaign across broadcast TV and digital for ads for Colom.
Asked what signs the group sees in Mississippi that makes it worth investing in, spokesperson Lauren French wrote, "Cindy Hyde-Smith has spent a decade in Washington without passing a single piece of legislation, and Mississippians have noticed."
Hyde-Smith has cosponsored legislation that has passed into law but legislation she initially sponsored or reintroduced has not become law, according to congressional records . Asked to respond to Senate Majority PAC, Hyde-Smith's campaign pointed to how bills from lawmakers "are often passed as part of larger legislative packages," and that has been true for some of Hyde-Smith's bills, including the first one she introduced. The campaign also pointed out that she is running for only her second full term.
French said Colom is running a "disciplined campaign" with messages resonating with voters.
Colom and Hyde-Smith have some history, as she blocked his nomination for federal judge in 2023. She cited his support for transgender rights and having previously been boosted by a George Soros-linked PAC, according to the Mississippi Free Press .
He insists his bid for Senate is not motivated by a desire to get back at her.
"It has nothing to do with the run for me ... as a Christian, I forgive her. It's about the people in Mississippi," Colom told ABC News.
"We are confident that Mississippians will once again send Cindy Hyde-Smith back to the U.S. Senate on November 3rd. This is simply Washington insiders making a last ditch effort to give life to Scott Colom's failing campaign," campaign manager Jake Monssen told ABC News in a statement.
Hyde-Smith's supporters may be more motivated after a boost from President Donald Trump, who's set to hold a rally in Mississippi on Monday as part of a swing of campaign rallies mostly in red states.
The Republican National Committee announced the rally around a week after Colom's social video went viral, although Trump and the group have not indicated why they are doing the rally there and Trump has expressed confidence in Hyde-Smith.
"Cindy Hyde-Smith's very popular ... So if I need to get her over the top, I would go there [to Mississippi]. She's great. Cindy Hyde-Smith is great," Trump told reporters when asked Thursday about the Senate election.
Hyde-Smith will be attending the rally, according to her campaign.

title: 12 injured, including 6 children, in shooting near Florida university, police say
body:
At least 11 of those injured had gunshot wounds, police said.
At least 12 people were injured, including six children, amid a Saturday evening shooting in Tallahassee, near the campus of Florida A & M University, officials said.
Eleven of those who were injured had gunshot wounds, Tallahassee Chief of Police Lawrence Revell told reporters during a late-night press conference.
"Six are adults and six are juveniles," he said. "We know our youngest victim is 11 years old. At least three of our victims have sustained serious injuries and one of those is in critical condition. Eight of those are reported to be in stable condition."
The person who was injured but not from a gunshot was "a grandmother of one of the victims," the chief said, adding that she "injured herself fleeing from the scene."
In a Sunday morning update, the Tallahassee Police Department (TPD) said that six of the victims remain hospitalized, with one in critical condition. Five other victims have been released from the hospital, police said.
No arrests had been announced as of Sunday morning. Police said they are working to identify those responsible for the shooting and sought the public's help, asking anyone with information about the shooting to contact investigators immediately. Police also asked that anyone with photos or video share them with investigators.
"We will determine what happened, identify those responsible, and get answers for all of the victims, their families and everyone impacted by this tragedy," Revell said in a statement released on Sunday. "We know there are people who saw something, heard something or may have video that could help us piece together exactly what happened."
"We need our community's help. No detail is too small, and no piece of information should go unreported," Revell added. "If you know something, please share it with our detectives. Your information could be the key to holding those responsible accountable."
Police described the shooting as an "altercation [that] occurred between individuals" near the intersection of Perry and Manatee Streets, just outside Florida A & M University's Bragg Memorial Stadium.
FAMU President Marva B. Johnson released a video statement Sunday afternoon, describing the shooting as an "evil act."
Johnson said that while the shooting did not occur on her campus, the school is offering care and support to "members of our FAMU family who were injured in the tragic incident."
She did not say if any students or faculty were among those injured.
"To our Rattler family and our surrounding Tallahassee community, I share your outrage and profound sadness at the senseless and despicable shooting that took place near our FAMU campus last night," Johnson said in the statement.
She added that free counseling support will be offered to students, saying, "A horrific act of violence like this is traumatizing for our students, whether you were near the event or not."
24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

title: After Netanyahu meets police chief, Israel's elections head warns against vote interference
body: Police Commissioner Danny Levy pledged Sunday that police would protect voters and act impartially against attempts to disrupt the election, after meeting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu following a legal challenge over political involvement in police election preparations.In a public statement two days before Tuesday's Knesset election, Levy said police had completed months of preparations to safeguard voting.Police said those preparations included responding to terrorist threats in cooperation with the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) and maintaining public order when the results become known and in the days afterward.CEC stresses Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir have no authority to direct police on election integrity“We will not allow violence, threats, incitement or criminal activity to undermine the will of the voters,” Levy said. “Safeguarding Israeli democracy is our mission. We will fulfill it without bias and without compromise.”Earlier Sunday, Central Elections Committee chairman Noam Sohlberg rejected a petition to block the discussion with Netanyahu, while stressing that Netanyahu and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir have no authority to direct police on election integrity or preparations.The decision followed Netanyahu's assurance that the planned discussion was a telephone briefing on security threats, rather than election integrity as earlier reports had described it. The meeting subsequently took place in person.Levy attended with the heads of the police's Operations Directorate and Intelligence Division. During the meeting, he told Netanyahu that police would safeguard Israeli democracy and were prepared to respond to terrorist incidents and maintain public order.Sohlberg said the prime minister and national security minister could meet with the commissioner about general public-order issues and ask him to present police preparations. But responsibility for administering the election and safeguarding its integrity rests with the Central Elections Committee and its chairman, he noted.The petition was brought by the organization Bochrim BeYisrael, separately from Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party's appeal earlier Sunday to Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara and Sohlberg to stop the meeting.The organization argued that the meeting would violate prohibitions on interfering with elections and using public resources for election campaigning. Sohlberg found insufficient evidence that holding the discussion would itself constitute election interference.He nevertheless recorded Netanyahu's assurance that the call would not address election preparations or election integrity, and said all those involved were expected to take particular care not to exceed their authority on election matters.Netanyahu argues call concerns 'routine security preparations'Bochrim BeYisrael subsequently asked Sohlberg to reconsider, citing a clarification submitted on Netanyahu's behalf that the meeting would take place in person. It argued that this changed a premise underlying the decision and heightened concerns about election campaigning.The organization sought an immediate order blocking the meeting or, alternatively, a requirement that it take place under Sohlberg's oversight with all party leaders invited. It also asked that Levy provide a full account of its contents if it had already occurred.In the initial response submitted on Netanyahu's behalf by attorney Ilan Bombach, the prime minister argued that the briefing concerned security preparations against what the filing described as serious warnings of terrorist attempts to disrupt the election or influence its conduct.The response said Netanyahu had held a security assessment on Thursday with the IDF chief of staff and the heads of the Shin Bet and Mossad. Levy had not attended, it said, and the briefing was intended to obtain an update on police preparations.Baharav-Miara, whose position was summarized in Sohlberg's decision, said police act in coordination with and under the direction of the elections committee chairman on election administration and public order during voting. Political leaders and candidates should not intervene in those matters, she said.Sohlberg noted that he and the committee's acting director-general were due to meet Levy that evening to discuss police preparations and issue instructions as needed.Yashar had warned that Netanyahu's meeting could undermine public confidence in the results, accusing him of potentially seeking to pressure public servants to advance his political interests.Ben-Gvir's office defended the meeting as routine practice followed by previous ministers. Citing the state commission of inquiry into the Meron disaster, it argued that the minister had a duty to question police preparations, identify gaps, and prevent loss of life.

title: Cornell student named in Jane Doe's civil suit seeks to be dropped from case
body:
The defense attorney argued it is now too late for Jane Doe to bring a claim.
One of the Cornell students who was named in a civil lawsuit by a former undergraduate student known as Jane Doe, has asked a judge to drop him from the suit.
The lawsuit claimed that during an alleged 2024 gang rape, Diego Sarabia approached Jane Doe, "grabbed her face and started kissing her, all without her consent," before she pushed him away.
Doe's lawsuit also alleged Sarabia was among the Chi Phi fraternity brothers who allegedly snorted ketamine off her body.
In a motion Friday to dismiss Jane Doe's complaint, James Knox, Sarabia's attorney, wrote that Doe did not allege in her suit that Sarabia "supplied her with drugs or alcohol, participated in any of the alleged sexual encounters described elsewhere in the complaint, or was even present for most of the conduct that forms the basis of plaintiff's broader allegations."
All seven frat brothers have denied wrongdoing and Sarabia argued he was not part of the most severe conduct alleged in the lawsuit.
"As far as defendant goes, this is essentially a lawsuit about an allegedly forced kiss," Knox wrote in a Friday motion to dismiss Jane Doe's complaint.
The lawyer argued it is now too late for Jane Doe to bring a claim against Sarabia.
"Any intentional tort arising out of that alleged conduct is foreclosed by a strict one-year statute of limitations because plaintiff commenced this action nearly two years after the alleged events," Knox wrote.
Doe's attorney has not yet filed a response to the motion.
The motion came a week after a New York judge rejected a request by Sarabia's attorney to impose a gag order .
Knox argued that a gag order would limit "possible juror prejudice" and prevent the potential release of sensitive information that could lead to " threats, doxing, intimidation, and extrajudicial contact."
Judge Phaedra Perry-Bond called the request a "side show" that's "meant to muddy the waters and distract from the merits of the claims and defenses involved in this case."
New York Attorney General Letitia James, who was appointed special prosecutor by Gov. Kathy Hochul, is conducting an investigation into the incident. Cornell, which said it fully supports the appointment of a special prosecutor, is also conducting an internal probe of its response to the allegations.
Cornell has said it takes allegations of allegations of sexual violence "extremely seriously" and that it "investigated and adjudicated the allegations consistent with university policies."
At the same time, the university has said it is committed to taking additional steps to improve campus safety.
The case has rocked the university and started conversations about treatment of sexual assault allegations on college campuses across the country.
24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

title: Amy Acton says Trump, Vance should 'look at the facts' after Ramaswamy attack ad
body:
Former President Barack Obama also railed against Trump at a campaign rally.
CLEVELAND -- Ohio Democratic gubernatorial nominee Amy Acton told ABC News in an interview Saturday that she hopes President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance will "look at the facts" of the abuse she says she endured as a child after they defended an attack ad made by GOP nominee Vivek Ramaswamy's campaign.
Bipartisan backlash has hit Ramaswamy's campaign after the release of the ad featuring Acton's estranged mother whom Acton says stood by the man who was criminally charged with sexually abusing her as a child. Acton said she hasn't seen her mother since she was 12 years old.
In the ad, Acton's mother, Donna Arthur, said Acton has lied about her past, though it doesn't mention the allegations of sexual abuse.
In response to Trump and Vance, who have doubled down on and defended the ad, Acton told ABC News, "My job is to work with anyone on any side of the aisle to solve problems instead of making them, and I would say I do hope they would look at the facts."
Acton spoke to ABC News after a rally in Cleveland with former President Barack Obama.
Acton has alleged her mother's second husband molested her between the ages of 9 and 12. Charges were filed against her stepfather and Acton testified against him. He pleaded not guilty, but fled the state before trial and never appeared before a judge. He died in 2004.
Acton said she and her brother endured "extreme child abuse and neglect" in their childhood.
"We were frequent flyers in children's services ... There are facts in this case: a grand jury indictment, fugitive out against bail, and that behavior went on and on," Acton said.
Speaking to reporters this week about the ad, Trump dismissed questions about the allegations of Acton's sexual abuse, asserting at multiple points that the ad has "nothing to do" with Acton's stepfather.
Similarly, Vance told rally attendees in Ohio earlier this week that he is "a little bit disgusted when I see Republicans across the country who are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America."
The Cleveland Plain Dealer, Ohio's largest newspaper, endorsed Acton for governor on Sunday, saying that it was reversing a previous decision to not endorse in the race in the wake of the ad.
"Vivek Ramaswamy, seeking the highest office in this state, has produced a campaign advertisement that weaponizes the sexual abuse his opponent, Amy Acton, suffered as a child. People across the political spectrum have rightly condemned it," the paper's editorial board wrote , in part.
"A candidate who uses childhood sexual abuse as a weapon against the person who endured it has crossed a line that Ohioans should defend, whatever their party. We are better than this. We have a responsibility to show it. Today, we endorse Democrat Amy Acton for governor."
The paper also wrote that Acton's other achievements further prompted their endorsement, declaring that Ramaswamy "has offered Ohioans far less reason to trust him."
"[Acton] has earned consideration on her own record, her preparation and her commitment to the people she seeks to serve," the paper wrote.
Ramaswamy's campaign on Sunday dismissed the paper's endorsement in a statement to ABC News, referring to its editor Chris Quinn by name.
"Anyone who thought Chris Quinn's paper wouldn't back the liberal in this race is fooling themselves," campaign spokesperson Evan Machan wrote.
GOP Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine, who on Thursday told reporters in Columbus, Ohio, that the ad is "deeply, deeply troubling" and that the Ramaswamy campaign "needs to take it down," but he did not withdraw his endorsement of Ramaswamy.
Asked whether she was disappointed that DeWine didn't withdraw his endorsement, Acton said it was "an honor and a privilege" to work with him during COVID-19 pandemic as the director of the Ohio Department of Health.
"I really do appreciate him calling out the facts of the case," Acton said. "That this was an indictment he knows better than others. He's a prosecutor. He started his career prosecuting cases like this, and he knew more than anyone. He knows who I am and knows my story."
Speaking to reporters on Friday, Ramaswamy said the ad had nothing to do with childhood abuse.
"We ran an ad about lying," he said. "Amy Acton is lying. She has been lying this entire campaign about me, about her record, about her history in this state."
In a statement to ABC News, Connie Luck, a spokesperson for Ramaswamy said: "Ohioans can't afford a liberal governor who shows up for Obama but never shows up for them."
Ramaswamy and Acton have never met in person. Asked what she would say to him, Acton said: "I really have no words for Mr. Ramaswamy. I think there is no low that he wouldn't sink to."
Speaking to survivors of abuse, Acton said: "For those out there going through it now, hold on, please. If there's someone you feel safe with, say something about it."
Acton campaigned Saturday alongside former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown, who's running to win back his seat, and Obama, who was the last Democratic presidential candidate to win the state of Ohio in a presidential election in 2012.
Democrats are eyeing the Senate and gubernatorial races as key pickup opportunities given the headwinds facing Republicans.
In his remarks, Obama delivered a scathing rebuke of the Trump administration on a variety of issues, from the economy to immigration to the war in Iran.
Regarding the GOP candidate for governor, Obama called Ramaswamy "thirsty" for attention.
"Vivek's own supporters know it's all about what's in it for him," Obama said. "We all know that guy, you know, who ... just wants to get attention no matter what, willing to do anything. And in recent days, we've seen there is no line he will not cross, no low he will not sink to."
Obama emphasized what he called a "moral component" to this election and said that "basic decency" is missing from the current public discourse.
ABC News' Diana Paulsen and Oren Oppenheim contributed to this report.

title: Speleologist and traveler Borys Hora killed in action
body:
His daughter Alina reported this on Facebook , according to Ukrinform.
"On October 19, our father Borys Hora, the father of both me and Liubko Hora, was killed. We are awaiting the results of DNA testing," she said.
Borys Hora was born in Ternopil on March 10, 1969. In the 1990s, he founded the Krystal tourism club within the Plast scouting organization. He later settled in a village near Mlynky Cave, where he established a speleology base and worked as a guide. Among other activities, he organized rafting trips on the Dniester and Chornyi Cheremosh rivers, hiking trips in the Carpathians, and climbs in the Caucasus Mountains. He also volunteered and cared for animals.
After Russia launched its full-scale invasion, Hora volunteered to join the Ukrainian Armed Forces.

title: Early voting begins in New York: What to know and the key races to watch
body:
Gov. Kathy Hochul and U.S. Rep. Mike Lawler are hoping to keep their seats.
Saturday is the first day of early voting in New York and Empire State voters could help decide which party will control the U.S. House of Representatives over the next two years.
Republicans are seeking to fend off attempts by Democrats to flip congressional seats in the suburbs north of New York City and in the Adirondack Mountains near the Canadian border.
New Yorkers will also decide whether Democrats Kathy Hochul and Letitia James should each be elected to an additional term in their respective roles as governor and attorney general.
Hochul became the state's first female governor in 2021 after then-Gov. Andrew Cuomo resigned amid sexual harassment allegations -- accusations he denied. She was New York's lieutenant governor at the time.
Unlike most New York governors, Hochul is not from New York City or its suburbs, but hails from the Buffalo area -- a more than six-hour drive away. A moderate Democrat, she was largely unknown to voters in the metropolitan area, where much of the state's population resides, until Cuomo's resignation. She defeated Republican Lee Zeldin in 2022, winning a full term in Albany.
In the time since, Hochul has spent a significant amount of time downstate, recently collaborating with current democratic socialist New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on initiatives like expanded childcare access. Mamdani campaigned with Hochul on Friday and has released videos on social media in support of her campaign.
Hochul's Republican opponent in 2026, Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman, has worked to tie Hochul to Mamdani throughout his campaign, issuing a statement at one point that referenced the "Hochul-Mamdani agenda."
Blakeman has centered his gubernatorial campaign on fighting crime and lowering taxes in New York State. He has received President Donald Trump's endorsement and been adamant in his support of the president, even campaigning with him at a rally in Syracuse in early October.
A recent Quinnipiac University poll of likely New York State voters found that 55% would support Hochul and 41% would Blakeman.
In the attorney general's race, incumbent Letitia James is facing a challenge from Republican former Drug Enforcement Administration Chief of Staff Saritha Komatireddy. James gained national attention through her 2022 lawsuit against Trump, his company and members of his family alleging net worth inflation. The lawsuit led to a $454 million civil fraud judgment that was thrown out by an appeals court in 2025.
While Komatireddy has not historically been a household name in the state, many of her campaign materials using the "just fight crime" branding have gained significant attention on social media.
One of the most high-profile races in the country is in New York's 17th Congressional District in the lower Hudson Valley, where incumbent Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Lawler is being challenged by Democrat Cait Conley.
The district is home to everyone from former President Bill Clinton to New York City investment bankers to thousands of police officers.
Trump attended a rally with Lawler in the district in May while former U.S. Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg came to the district in September to campaign with Conley.
The race in the 17th Congressional District is not the only potentially competitive race within a stone's throw of Manhattan. In the 3rd Congressional District, which straddles Nassau and Queens, incumbent Democratic U.S. Rep. Tom Suozzi is being challenged by Republican Michael LiPetri, a former state assemblyman who has run for Congress twice before.
In New York's 21st Congressional District, which stretches from the historically industrial Mohawk Valley along the Erie Canal to the Canadian border, Democrats are hoping that 2026 is their best chance to flip the seat currently held by Republican U.S. Rep. Elise Stefanik.
Stefanik previously planned to seek the Republican gubernatorial nomination, but ended up dropping out of the governor's race and announcing she would not seek reelection to the House.
Republican Anthony Constantino, a sticker company CEO endorsed by Trump, is facing off against Democratic farmer Blake Gendebien in the district. Trump endorsed Constantino in the Republican primary over a state lawmaker who had been endorsed by the head of New York State's Republican Party.
Tariffs and American relations with Canada have been top of mind in parts of the district.
Early voting concludes on Nov. 1. Election Day is Nov. 3.
