title: Clashes Break Out In Paris, Other French Cities Amid Fresh Protests
body: Clashes broke out Saturday in Paris and other French cities amid demonstrations held a week after others that degenerated into street violence and prompted a robust security backlash as President Emmanuel Macron seeks to restore order. Police arrested nearly 1,000 people as officers were confronted with “an extremely elevated level of violence” from black-clad “ultra-left” extremists, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said. Riot squads fired tear gas at protesters in the capital as well as in Marseille, Lyon, Bordeaux, Lille, Toulouse, Montpellier and Nantes. Two people were “seriously” injured, Nunez said: one man in Toulouse, who reportedly had fingers blown off, and another person in Clermont-Ferrand. He did not give details of either case. Authorities had deployed 70,000 security forces across the country for the new marches, which were called to protest the cost of living. Protesters hold antifascist banners and flags as they face CRS riot police in a street by the Campo Santo Antifascist village set as part of a counter-mobilisation “against racism, fascism and imperialism” on the sidelines of the congress of the far-right party Rassemblement National (RN) in Orleans, central France, on October 24, 2026. (Photo by SIMON WOHLFAHRT / AFP) The violence came a week after rioting that saw public buildings vandalised, hundreds of shops looted and 2,700 people arrested, casting a pall over a country that goes to the polls in six months to choose a successor to President Emmanuel Macron after 10 years. Nunez said Saturday’s outcome was more “positive” than a week ago, with more police on the streets acting more rapidly, conducting more pre-demonstration checks and better protecting businesses. There was nevertheless widespread anger at the government over a protest crackdown viewed as repressive and as an assault on the right to protest. Police battle ‘rioters’ Saturday’s demonstrations drew between 410,000 and 800,000 people across the country, according to different estimates by authorities and the organising CGT union. The main Paris march had between 110,000 and 250,000 attendees, according to those sources. Macron’s government has ordered police to prevent protesters reaching city centres, where shops are concentrated, and in Paris and some other cities, partial curfews were imposed in certain urban zones. The French president had ordered non-union demonstrations be banned as “illegitimate”. In Paris, where many shops had boarded up windows to prevent looting, and the Louvre and the Musee d’Orsay museums shut for the day, the main demonstration passed off largely peacefully. The march had been pushed to the capital’s southeast rim under a last-minute order by authorities. Afterwards, though, clashes broke out as the crowd was dispersing. Nunez said the confrontations lasted two hours and involved “500 rioters” at the back of the march. AFP journalists saw police charge several times and vigorously use tear gas and batons against some, mostly young, protesters. Protesters hold antifascist banners and flags as they face CRS riot police in a street by the Campo Santo Antifascist village set as part of a counter-mobilisation “against racism, fascism and imperialism” on the sidelines of the congress of the far-right party Rassemblement National (RN) in Orleans, central France, on October 24, 2026. (Photo by SIMON WOHLFAHRT / AFP) “The police started moving towards everyone, telling them to get down and back off. They were just taking people down, you know, beating protesters,” one demonstrator bleeding from a baton blow to his face, who gave his first name as David, told AFP. “I hear the media talking about repression in Iran and China. And now I see that France is doing the same, if not worse,” said Victor Lejendre, a 22-year-old student. He said he was “asking myself a lot of questions about what is going to become of this country”, adding that it was “dystopian”. Ultra-right vs ultra-left In the western city of Nantes, thousands of protesters broke through lines of police firing tear gas and a water cannon to reach the city centre, an AFP journalist there witnessed. In Lyon, police used tear gas to disperse around 1,000 people gathered in the south of the city. “If they prohibit protests then that means we are heading more and more towards a regime that is fascist, that is dictatorial,” said one 20-year-old protester in Lyon, who gave only his first name, Silem. In the southern cities of Cannes and Montpellier, far-right activists came out onto the streets seeking confrontations with “ultra-left militants”, in what authorities said was an unprecedented development. Meanwhile, the Yellow Vests, who staged disruptive protests against Macron eight years ago, called for more demonstrations on October 31 for “the freedom to protest”. Far-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon, who marched in the Paris rally, said Macron “is going to understand that this is going to repeat itself every week”. Several protesters leaving after clashes in Paris taunted officers with a “see you next Saturday”. Protest against Le Pen’s party Tensions were heightened by a rally in the city of Orleans by far-right leader Marine Le Pen’s National Rally party to kick off her campaign for the presidential election. Thousands of counter-protesters chanting anti-fascist slogans marched in the city. Police put their number at 13,000 while organisers said twice as many participated. The unrest across France highlighted the febrile political atmosphere ahead of the vote, in which Le Pen leads in surveys. Inflation in France, particularly affecting the cost of fuel, has surged since the start of the Middle East war in February. Protests have also been taking place in Italy, Belgium, Spain and Portugal over different issues, yet with some overlap on inflation and education problems. Italy has mobilised 500 troops to Milan after street violence there. AFP The post Clashes Break Out In Paris, Other French Cities Amid Fresh Protests appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Mahama links Africa’s conflicts to struggle over natural resources
body: President John Mahama says the struggle for control of Africa’s natural resources and the profits from their extraction are central to the continent’s security crises, warning that powerful interests benefit from prolonged instability. Addressing the 12th Tana High-Level Forum on Peace in Africa in Bahir Dar, Ethiopia, President Mahama said Africa, the President said the continent risks remaining vulnerable if its leaders fail to take greater control of their resources and determine their own security priorities. He said “Let me be clear, Africa is not an empty chessboard for foreign powers to play their games. We are not spectators,” he said. “But unless we consciously decide to take up the pen and write our own script, someone else will write it for us, and we will not like how the story ends.” President Mahama said the importance of African minerals to the global green energy transition and digital economy should give the continent greater bargaining power, but communities endowed with these resources often bear the consequences of exploitation without enjoying the benefits. He argued that sovereignty must go beyond political independence and membership of international institutions. “Real sovereignty means having the administrative, legal, and economic power to govern your strategic assets, negotiate fair terms, and ensure the wealth beneath our people’s feet actually puts food on their tables,” he said. He added that anything less amounted to “cosmetic independence that masks economic subjugation.” He says African leaders must look beyond weapons proliferation and military operations to confront the political and economic interests that sustain conflicts across the continent. “The real disease is mostly in the arena of political economy,” President Mahama said when presenting the 2026 State of Peace and Security in Africa Report at the 12th Tana High-Level Forum on Peace in Africa in Bahir Dar, Ethiopia. He challenged leaders to examine who controls natural resources, who benefits financially from their extraction and whose political and financial interests are better served by continued instability than lasting peace. “In every single theatre of conflict across this continent today, if you want to understand why guns are firing, do not start by counting the rifles,” he said. “Ask three basic questions, who controls the resource? Who cashes the cheque from its extraction? And whose political and financial fortunes are better served by perpetual chaos than by stable peace?” President Mahama cited Sudan, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Somalia and Mozambique as examples of how resource competition, governance failures and economic marginalisation contribute to insecurity. In Sudan, he said, the battle lines were drawn as much around gold extraction sites as around Khartoum. In eastern DRC, he linked the resurgence and entrenchment of the M23 group to coltan, cobalt and the global competition for minerals needed for the green energy transition. He also attributed the continued presence of Al-Shabaab in Somalia partly to governance failures that have created openings for the group to exploit. In Mozambique’s Cabo Delgado region, he said, the area’s substantial gas wealth has not translated into meaningful benefits for local young people, who instead viewed it as another source of marginalisation. “These are not separate, random brushfires. They are symptoms of a single, continent-wide firestorm,” he said.

title: Democrats, voting-rights groups challenge Trump's bid to block Alaska Senate certification
body:
Democratic groups and voting-rights advocates are seeking to join a federal lawsuit to stop the Justice Department's effort to prevent Alaska from certifying its U.S. Senate election results if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses.
The requests come from Alaskans for Mary, the campaign for Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola, the Democratic Party's Senate campaign committee, and a separate group including the League of Women Voters of Alaska, Common Cause and two individual voters.
Together, the groups argue that the executive branch lacks legal authority to intervene in state-run elections and is attempting an unprecedented override of state election administration with early voting already underway.
In court filings submitted Friday, the groups contend that the litigation — which President Donald Trump confirmed he personally ordered — seeks an extraordinary remedy: an investigation into whether voters who selected another candidate named Daniel J. Sullivan actually intended to vote for the incumbent senator.
Trump told reporters on Friday that he directed the Justice Department to file the lawsuit: "I'm the one that said 'do it.'"
The move drew swift bipartisan backlash, including from Alaska's Republican Senator Lisa Murkowski, who said on social media , "The Department of Justice should never have filed this lawsuit."
The legal battle centers on Daniel J. Sullivan, a non-incumbent challenger sharing a near-identical name with incumbent GOP Senator Daniel S. Sullivan. Alaska election officials initially removed the challenger from the ballot after a complaint from the state Republican Party, but state courts ordered his inclusion on the ballot.
In June, the Alaska Supreme Court affirmed that decision and directed election officials to clearly distinguish the two men.
The ballot now lists Sen. Sullivan as the "incumbent" and Republican, while the other Sullivan has no party registration.
The Justice Department filed its lawsuit on Oct. 22, seeking an order to prevent Alaska from certifying the Senate election if the incumbent loses.
The proposed intervenors say the department's approach would force Alaska voters to choose between electing the president's preferred candidate and risking the state being barred from certifying its election results.
Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee argue that the lawsuit directly threatens their interests because it could prevent Peltola from taking office even if she wins the election under Alaska's ranked-choice system.
They also question whether Alaska state officials will mount a sufficiently vigorous defense, given that the state's Division of Elections previously tried to exclude Daniel J. Sullivan from the ballot before a state court overturned the move.
The DSCC and Alaskans for Mary are asking the court to grant them defendant-intervenor status so they can formally file motions to dismiss the lawsuit.
The Democrats argue that while the DOJ has cited the National Voter Registration Act as the legal basis for its lawsuit, the statute contains no provision authorizing the federal government to dictate candidate eligibility or ballot layout, which are state matters under the Constitution.
Legal experts have echoed those concerns, noting that relying on the NVRA's general preamble language to halt state election certification lacks precedent.
The League of Women Voters of Alaska and Common Cause filed separately, warning that the DOJ's demand to investigate voter intent presents severe constitutional hazards.
The filings note that the DOJ has offered no mechanism to determine whether voters who selected Daniel J. Sullivan intended to vote for the incumbent.
Blocking certification, the groups argue, would disenfranchise Alaskans by denying them representation and injecting chaos into the election outcome.
Both organizations are asking the court for permission to join the case as defendants. The Democratic groups say they intend to seek dismissal if the court grants their motion.

title: Saturday march in Tbilisi “against oligarch Ivanishvili’s rule”. ‘Protests in Georgia’ video podcast
body: Protest in Georgia against Ivanishvili, video The traditional “Saturday march” took place in Tbilisi on the evening of 24 October. Hundreds of people once again marched through the city centre, as they have done almost continuously for nearly two years, carrying Georgian, EU and Ukrainian flags. The main slogan was “Georgia against Ivanishvili’s one-party rule!” — a reference to billionaire Bidzina Ivanishvili, founder and honorary chair of the ruling party. Protest scenes in Georgia: full collection “Peace to Georgia”, “Glory to the heroes” and “Long live a Georgia without Ivanishvili!” the demonstrators chanted. Passing cars honked continuously in a show of support for the marchers. The “Saturday marches” are part of an ongoing protest movement that has continued in Georgia for more than 700 days. Protesters are demanding that Georgia return to the path of European integration and that all political prisoners be released. They are also calling for the repeal of all anti-democratic laws passed by the ruling Georgian Dream party over the past two years. Protesters and opposition parties point out that part of Georgian society still does not recognise the results of the parliamentary election held in autumn 2024. They are calling for early parliamentary elections. Over the course of nearly two years of protests, dozens of people have been arrested . Many have been charged with criminal offences and sentenced to prison. For the first time in independent Georgia’s history, the country has around 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli , founder of the independent media outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti. She was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. The protests continue despite an intensifying crackdown on civil society and the media. News in Georgia

title: CAGG demands retraction, apology from GoldBod CEO over alleged illegal mining remarks
body: The Ghana Coalition Against Galamsey (CAGG) has called on the Office of the Attorney-General to investigate the Chief Executive Officer of the Ghana Gold Board (GoldBod) over statements it claims encouraged artisanal miners to operate without licences, provided they avoid forest reserves and river bodies. In a press release dated October 24, 2026, the coalition condemned the reported remarks, describing them as unlawful and reckless, and warning that they could undermine efforts to combat illegal mining, popularly known as galamsey. CAGG argued that Ghana’s mining laws do not exempt miners from licensing requirements based on the location of their operations. Citing Section 99(2)(a) of the Minerals and Mining Act, 2006 (Act 703), as amended by Act 995 of 2019, the coalition said anyone who undertakes mining without a licence granted by the Minister commits an offence. It further cited Section 99, arguing that anyone who commands, instigates, employs or facilitates others to engage in illegal mining could face the same penalties as the illegal miner. According to the coalition, offenders could face fines ranging from GH¢120,000 to GH¢180,000 and imprisonment of between 15 and 25 years, or both. The coalition therefore wants the GoldBod CEO to immediately retract the alleged statement and issue an unqualified apology to the Ghanaian public. It has also urged President John Dramani Mahama, the Minister for Lands and Natural Resources, and the Minerals Commission to publicly reaffirm that mining without a licence is illegal, regardless of where the activity takes place. CAGG further called on the Attorney-General’s Office to investigate the matter for possible abetment of illegal mining, insisting that no individual should be exempt from the law. Beyond the legal implications, the coalition warned that the reported remarks could expose farmers and landowners to encroachment on their lands. It has consequently called on the Ministry of National Security, the Ghana Police Service and the Ministry of the Interior to strengthen protection for farmers and landowners and establish rapid-response channels for reporting encroachment. The group is also demanding a clear national plan to protect farmlands, including legal safeguards for agricultural lands, mapping and registration of farms, support for vulnerable farmers seeking to document their land rights, and compensation and restoration for those whose lands have been destroyed. CAGG said GoldBod was established to formalise and regulate artisanal mining, not to encourage unlicensed operations. It warned that normalising mining without licences would weaken the regulatory framework intended to distinguish legal small-scale mining from illegal mining. The coalition comprises civil society organisations, professional associations, environmental advocacy groups and other stakeholders.

title: Iran proposes reopening Hormuz in exchange for US lifting its blockade — TV
body:
CAIRO, October 24. /TASS/. Iran has proposed reopening shipping in the Strait of Hormuz to the United States in exchange for lifting the US blockade on the Islamic Republic’s ports, Al Arabiya reported.
Tehran has already conveyed this proposal to Washington through Pakistani mediators, sources told the TV channel. Iran also told Pakistan that it is "ready to resume negotiations with the United States."
The Iranian side has yet to comment on this information.

title: Kano ACF appoints interim leadership after chairman’s resignation
body: The Arewa Consultative Forum (ACF), Kano State Chapter, has appointed a three-member interim leadership team to oversee its affairs following the resignation of its chairman, Dr Goni Faruk Umar. ‎ ‎According to the state Public Relations Officer of the forum in Kano, Nasiru Yusuf Ibrahim, the development comes amid efforts to restore unity and resolve internal disagreements that had affected the smooth running of the forum. ‎ ‎He said the interim team comprises the District Head of Tofa, Alhaji Isyaku Umar Tofa; Ambassador Bala Mohammed Sani and Hajiya Rabia Husaini Adamu. ‎ ‎The appointments were announced on Saturday by retired General Haliru Akilu during a joint meeting of members of the ACF Board of Trustees representing Kano State and the chapter’s executive committee held at the Late Amina Habib ACF Secretariat in Kano. “Ba ma yi”, crowd boos Tinubu at APC campaign flag-off in Kaduna Bandits Kill 7 Vigilantes, Abduct Over 30 Residents in Zamfara Community Akilu said the three members would lead the chapter for the remainder of the current executive committee’s tenure pending the election of a substantive chairman. ‎ ‎He said the decision was taken to promote reconciliation, restore understanding and strengthen cooperation among members following differences that had affected the chapter’s operations. ‎ ‎“The spirit that should guide every one of us is the same: consultation before decision, integrity before convenience and service before self,” Akilu said. ‎ ‎He urged members to set aside their differences and work collectively in the interest of the forum, stressing that the meeting was aimed at resolving outstanding issues rather than revisiting past controversies. ‎ ‎Akilu also confirmed receipt of the resignation letter of Umar, who cited the demands of his busy schedule for stepping down. ‎ ‎He commended the former chairman for his service and contribution to the forum, expressing hope that he would continue to offer advice and support to the chapter. ‎ ‎The retired general also praised Assistant Controller-General of Narcotics, Alhaji Abubakar Idris Ahmed, for serving as acting chairman for about four months during Umar’s absence, saying his efforts helped sustain the chapter’s activities. ‎ ‎In their separate remarks, the newly appointed interim leaders thanked members for the confidence reposed in them and pledged to work toward restoring unity, confidence and effective administration of the chapter until a new chairman is elected. ‎ ‎Akilu said a united ACF Kano chapter would be better positioned to contribute to tackling challenges facing Kano State and Northern Nigeria, including insecurity, poverty, education and youth empowerment.

title: Show HN: Whistle Translator
body:
An app for Mac, Windows and Linux that turns your voice into text and translates it, entirely on your computer. Speak and translate in eight languages, including Arabic, record whole meetings, and hold a shortcut in any app to dictate. Nothing you say ever leaves your computer.
Free · Mac 0.5.1: Apple Silicon, macOS 12 or later, 6.5 MB · Windows 0.4.0: 10 or 11, x64, 5.6 MB · Linux 0.5.1: Flatpak, x64, 5.9 MB
Or with Homebrew : brew install --cask msdocs/tap/whistle-translator
Turn off the kitchen lights and set a timer for ten minutes.
Schalten Sie die Küchenbeleuchtung aus und stellen Sie einen Timer für zehn Minuten ein.
Speech recognition and translation both run on your computer's processor. After a one-time model download, it works on a plane, in a basement, or with Wi-Fi switched off.
Hold ⌥ Space ( Alt+Space on Windows) in Mail, Slack or a browser, speak, release, and your words are typed at the cursor.
Hold ⌥ ⇧ Space ( Alt+Shift+Space ) to speak in one language and type in another. A floating pill shows your words as you speak.
See the transcript appear as you talk. Each sentence is translated the moment you finish it.
No account, no cloud, no telemetry. Your audio and text are processed locally and never uploaded.
Play any translation aloud with your system's built-in voice for that language.
Meeting mode transcribes for as long as you talk, saves a timestamped transcript and its translation as it goes, and keeps your computer awake until you stop.
Open a WAV file of any length and get its transcript and translation.
The app isn't signed by Apple or Microsoft yet, so your computer asks you to confirm it the first time.
Update with brew upgrade --cask whistle-translator . Uninstall with brew uninstall --zap --cask whistle-translator , which also removes downloaded models and settings.
SHA-256 of the 0.5.1 download: b9dd995fe4e45ed2f76fb25b8020c8db0c52380ca11fe4a41be2d0bcefc2a4d5
Prefer Terminal? After copying the app to Applications, xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine "/Applications/Whistle Translator.app" lets it open normally.
The Windows version is still 0.4.0, which translates into Arabic but can't transcribe spoken Arabic yet; that comes with its next update.
Windows 10 or 11 on x64. SHA-256 of the 0.4.0 installer: 5d462d56543fe3a9580773df89c4c90879f1a57490f4ac25b671dc2731d7e8c1
x86_64 Linux with Flatpak. To hear translations, install speech-dispatcher . SHA-256 of the 0.5.1 Flatpak: 3a5b2b5719a5f2566454fbd17051bd45507be01cd9c35d73bf8d82523147cbf7
The app grew out of a small Python project: offline speech-to-text and translation in a few lines, from a WAV file, the microphone or a live stream.
Whistle and Argos Translate in Python. Transcribe, add word timestamps, and translate between the same seven spoken languages.

title: EPL: Tottenham hands Chelsea first home loss of season
body: Tottenham scored two second half goals to hand ten man Chelsea a 2-0 defeat in their EPL match at the Stamford Bridge. A Mike Penders own goal and Mathys Tel brilliant solo goal secured all three points for Roberto de Zerbi’s Tottenham as two expensively-assembled teams met in the London derby. Chelsea were missing the injured duo of striker Joao Pedro, and goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez who had surgery on a broken jaw. He was replaced by Penders who produced excellent saves to deny Omar Marmoush and Tel in the first half. However, the Belgian’s error handed Spurs the initiative when he punched a corner kick into his own net. EPL: Arsenal defeat Everton, Manchester City lose 100% record Tinubu: Opposition Created Hunger, Poverty, We’re Fixing Them Cole Palmer then lost his head with two poor challenges that led to two cautions and a red card, leaving Chelsea with ten players. Tottenham pounced on the advantage as Chelsea went in search of an equalizer, Tel picked up the ball in his own half and went on a mazy run that ended with an unstoppable low drive into the net to seal the 2-0 win. Victory is Tottenham’s second in five days- a second win of the season- and the club’s first consecutive league wins since May. They win at Chelsea for the first time since April 2018, and Tottenham rose to 12th place with nine points after eight matches. Xabi Alonso’s Chelsea remain in fourth place with 13 points.

title: Letter| We owe our children a different South Sudan
body: Letter one of seven letters to South Sudanese Dear fellow South Sudanese, A child’s life must be worth more than anyone’s ambition to lead. In a later oral history of the 1999 Wunlit peace conference, Deborah Yier Jany, a Nuer woman living among Dinka in Yirol, recalled challenging the men to account for the children killed in the conflict. She rejected the loss of children’s lives to advance someone’s claim to leadership. Her words about the liberation movement were direct: “SPLA/M didn’t liberate this country to kill.” Her challenge belongs at the beginning of any conversation about our future. 1 Why ask people to invest hope in a country that has failed to protect them? For those who have buried loved ones, fled their homes or struggled to feed their children, another appeal to national unity can sound like another demand for patience. That response deserves to be heard. We cannot ask people to believe in South Sudan while refusing to hear what living in it has cost them. I write to argue for a national dialogue in which those experiences can help shape how we are governed. Yet the failure of those who govern us does not extinguish our claim to the country. South Sudan belongs to its people. No leader, liberation movement or community owns its future. Those who have lost pride in the country retain the same right to shape it as those who still do. Refugees and displaced people have not forfeited that right by seeking safety. Young people are entitled to question the political arrangements they inherit. We can recognise those who contributed to liberation while judging how they exercise power today. Amílcar Cabral reminded his comrades fighting Portuguese rule that people sought “to live better and in peace”. That remains a test of what liberation has achieved. Past sacrifice cannot place today’s decisions beyond public judgment. The country belongs equally to those who fought, those who sustained families through war and those born after independence. 2 Our own Constitution gives this belonging a firm foundation. At independence, Article 9(1) of the Transitional Constitution described the Bill of Rights as a covenant among the people of South Sudan and between them and their government. In ordinary language, this is a binding promise about how we treat one another and how we are governed. A citizen should be able to seek justice without a powerful protector and to live safely outside their home community. Public authority must protect people regardless of political allegiance. 3 When that promise is broken, people should not have to bargain again for their right to life or equal protection. Those rights must be honoured. What we must confront together is the kind of country we want to build and the terms on which all its people can live together and govern themselves as equals. What kind of country did we seek through independence, and what must change for all its people to have an equal stake in it? On what terms can our different peoples live together, govern themselves and share the benefits of the country’s wealth, without domination or exclusion? How do we confront the wrongs of our past and build a common future in which no one must take up arms to secure a place, and losing political power does not mean losing the protection or the benefits of the state? The people expected to live with the answers must have a meaningful part in shaping them. This matters in daily life. When safety depends on a commander or an influential relative, it can disappear with that person’s fortunes. When a court answers to the powerful, a citizen’s case can depend on whom they know. A country governed that way leaves people searching for protection wherever they can find it. Institutions that protect us across community boundaries offer a more dependable basis for living together. Our differences should not decide whose life matters or who can obtain justice. This is the case I want to make for a Citizens’ Assembly on South Sudan’s Future. By an assembly, I mean a representative process through which our people can help decide what kind of country we want to build and the terms on which we can share it as equals. It would bring our different experiences and aspirations into a common effort to agree how we govern ourselves, use the country’s wealth and confront the wrongs of our past, while securing a future in which political competition threatens no one’s safety or right to belong. It must reach beyond bargains among those who already hold power. Citizens must have a meaningful say in setting its agenda and shaping its conclusions, with an agreed and credible route for turning those conclusions into political consensus, governing rules and structures. People must be able to help set its agenda, challenge proposals and see what becomes of their contributions. Free and credible elections allow citizens to choose their leaders. Courts can uphold rights, and civic action can press for change. Dialogue can help people address contested questions about power and belonging that a choice between candidates cannot settle on its own. It can also help identify what should be carried into constitution making through the proper legal process. Its value depends on strengthening citizens’ power to shape their lives. It cannot relieve public institutions of their existing duties. Wunlit offers a useful, limited lesson. Convened under the New Sudan Council of Churches, it brought Dinka and Nuer community representatives together to work out how neighbours could live after violence. Its covenant addressed movement, trade and access to shared grazing lands and fishing grounds. It also provided for bodies to help carry the agreement into practice. People whose lives depended on peace helped shape its terms. 4 Wunlit was a local process, with limited participation by women and a broad amnesty that we should not adopt as a national model. Its lesson is that agreements about peace must reach the realities of daily life and be supported by arrangements to carry them out. It offers experience we can examine, rather than a formula we can simply repeat. 1,4 Families with children are staying in rudimentary shelters at the Renk transit camp as they wait for a more permanent place to settle in June, 2023. (Photo: CNN) Sharing a country also requires room for difference. Our languages and community ties need not disappear, and we will not agree on every account of the past. Each community needs protection from domination. Within each community, women and young people must also be able to question those who claim to speak for them. Equal citizenship must protect the individual as well as the community. Today, any call for dialogue will be heard against an immediate political background. Elections are scheduled for 22 December 2026. President Kiir dissolved the transitional government and national legislature in September, and talks between political parties have been reported. People are entitled to ask whether another dialogue would give them a greater say or give those in power more time. 5 This letter makes no case for postponing the vote. Nor can an election date alone establish that citizens have a free and credible choice. The test of both dialogue and elections must be whether people can take part freely and hold those who govern them accountable. Dialogue must never provide cover for indefinite rule. We must also reckon with the 2017–2020 National Dialogue. Citizens have already given time and hope to tell the country what must change. We should examine its recommendations and what followed them, preserving useful work rather than asking people to begin again as though they had never spoken. Political parties have an essential place in any serious process. An agreement among them, however, cannot speak for everyone whose life it will affect. 6 The hardest objection remains: what if those with power ignore the outcome? A conference alone cannot answer that question. Before asking citizens to take part, those proposing a process must explain who will act on its decisions, under what authority and how the public can challenge inaction. Participants need protection from punishment for speaking honestly. A meeting that cannot influence decisions does not deserve support merely because it is called dialogue. Securing those conditions will require political work. People who benefit from existing arrangements may resist changes that threaten their advantages. Public organisation and pressure will matter, as will the willingness of political leaders to accept limits on their power. We must be honest about these difficulties. Asking people to speak carries a responsibility to protect them from retaliation. Some may reasonably prefer other routes to change. That disagreement belongs within the discussion. So do demands for justice. No one should have to forgive a perpetrator, accept equal blame for unequal wrongs or surrender a legal claim in order to participate. Seeking a future together cannot require silence about what has happened. I write as a South Sudanese, offering an argument for you to examine. I ask you to test it against your own experience and challenge where it fails. Support for a shared future must leave room for disagreement about how to build it. The next six letters will develop this case and examine its hardest questions, including why dialogue may be necessary, who must shape it and what could make its decisions count. The starting point is that every South Sudanese has an equal claim to the country’s future, including those whose grievances make us uncomfortable. For now, I ask you to discuss this letter with someone whose experience of our country differs from yours. What would have to change for each of you to enjoy equal protection? What would convince you that your voice could shape the outcome of a national dialogue? I invite your answers and your objections. If we leave these questions entirely to those who hold power, we leave them to decide the terms of our common life. Our children deserve a country in which their lives matter more than anyone’s claim to rule. Yours, Dr. Remember Miamingi The author is a South Sudanese human rights lawyer and governance specialist. Sources 1. John Ryle and Douglas H. Johnson, editors, What Happened at Wunlit? An Oral History of the 1999 Wunlit Peace Conference, Rift Valley Institute, 2021, printed pp. 75–76. Deborah Yier Jany’s retrospective account and women’s participation. Rift Valley Institute oral history 2. Amílcar Cabral, extracts from a 1965 party directive, reproduced as Tell No Lies, Claim No Easy Victories, translated by Richard Handyside, Revolution in Guinea, 1974, pp. 70–72. Cabral directive and publication details 3. Transitional Constitution of the Republic of South Sudan, 2011, Articles 9(1), 11 and 14. The covenant is cited as expressed at independence. Constitution text hosted by the International Labour Organization 4. Wunlit Dinka Nuer Covenant and Resolutions, 8 March 1999, reproduced in PA-X. See the covenant and the resolutions on institutional arrangements. Wunlit agreement and resolutions 5. Radio Tamazuj, “Ruto tells Kiir: Pursue dialogue ahead of elections”, 5 October 2026. Source for the scheduled election date, September dissolution and reported party talks. Radio Tamazuj report 6. United Nations Development Programme, “National Dialogue Reaches Consensus on Recommendations to Redefine Unity in South Sudan”, 17 November 2020. An account of the consultations and conference, rather than an independent assessment of implementation. title: EPL: Arsenal defeat Everton, Manchester City lose 100% record
body: Dominant Arsenal scored once in each half to defeat Everton 2-0 in the English Premier League on Saturday. The EPL champions were dominant to take apart Everton at the Emirates with goals from defenders Ezri Konsa and Gabriel Magalhaes. The Gunners took the lead on seven minutes from a corner kick delivery, Konsa arrived to slot home the loose ball at the back post. It is Arsenal’s first goal from set piece this season. Mikel Arteta’s side controlled proceedings and had to wait until the second half to seal the win on 68 minutes. Kano ACF appoints interim leadership after chairman’s resignation “Ba ma yi”, crowd boos Tinubu at APC campaign flag-off in Kaduna It arrived after a crisp passing sequence that ended with Ben White crossing for Gabriel to head beyond Jordan Pickford. The Brazilian who is the highest-scoring EPL defender since he joined Arsenal, scores on his 200th Gunners appearance. The win ensured Arsenal extended their unbeaten run at home to 11 matches, while Everton suffered a first away league defeat this season. They are now joint-top of the league on 21 points with Manchester City who lost 2-1 at Aston Villa. The Cityzens were put to the sword by Nicholas Jackson’s brace, the former Chelsea defending scoring once in each half. Erling Haaland’s goal briefly drew City level, but Enzo Maresca’s side lost their first league match of the season.

title: Bandits Kill 7 Vigilantes, Abduct Over 30 Residents in Zamfara Community
body: Bandits have killed seven members of a local vigilante group and abducted an unspecified number of residents during an attack on Kaura Namoda town in Zamfara State. The attackers reportedly operated for more than three hours after entering the town through a riverine route at about midnight on Friday. The Chairman of Kaura Namoda Local Government Area, Hon. Munnir Haidara, confirmed the killing of seven members of the Joint Task Force (JTF), saying the attackers struck two areas, including Kofar Zurmi and the Old market areas. He said the local government had recruited residents into the security outfit and provided them with weapons to protect their communities. Makinde Faults FG’s Economic Recovery Claims, Says Nigerians Still Hungry Bandits killed as hunters repel attack in Katsina The chairman added that some members of the outfit sustained injuries and were receiving treatment in hospitals. Haidara said the council was still compiling data to establish the number of residents abducted during the attack. “We don’t have the actual number of people abducted during yesterday’s attack. We are still gathering data, but we hope to get the exact figure between now and this evening,” he said. However, a resident who spoke to Daily Trust on condition of anonymity said the number of abductees could exceed 30, adding that a relative of one of the victims had confirmed the abduction to him. Another resident said the bandits exploited an alternative route near the river to enter the town, bypassing areas usually guarded by local vigilantes. He explained that vigilantes normally maintained positions around the outskirts of the town, where they built local clay fortifications and sometimes remained on duty until about 3 a.m., firing warning shots to deter attackers. According to him, the bandits adopted a different route during Friday’s attack, enabling them to enter the town directly. He further alleged that the attackers blocked access routes while engaging the civilian JTF members in a prolonged gun battle, making it difficult for security personnel to advance into the affected areas for fear of ambush. The resident said security operatives stationed along the road fired shots into the air but did not enter the area where the fighting was taking place. He attributed the vigilantes’ disadvantage to their limited firepower, saying they relied mainly on pump-action guns and locally made weapons. The resident also alleged that the attackers entered the house of an Islamic teacher, killed a young boy and abducted some of the cleric’s children. Meanwhile, another resident alleged that the movement of security personnel and vigilantes to Kaduna State for the launch of President Bola Tinubu’s second-term campaign contributed to the community’s vulnerability. “Almost all the security agencies, including the vigilantes, were transported to Kaduna for the campaign. Those left behind were mostly young boys, and the bandits took advantage of the situation to attack the town,” he said. The resident said the figure of more than 15 abductees being circulated was based on preliminary information, adding that residents were still trying to establish the actual number. However, Haidara dismissed reports that security personnel responsible for protecting Kaura Namoda had been taken to Kaduna for the political event. He said those who travelled were political supporters and party stakeholders, not security operatives. The chairman said he personally supervised the departure of those who travelled in 10 vehicles provided for the trip. “I am the chairman of the local government, and I was the one who assigned the people transported in the 10 vehicles given to us to attend the campaign launch of President Tinubu. “Everybody taken to Kaduna was a frontline political supporter. We did not take any security personnel,” he said. Haidara questioned why the council would withdraw personnel responsible for protecting residents to attend a political event, insisting that the local government would not deliberately leave the town without security. “We cannot take security personnel to a campaign launch when those people are responsible for protecting residents. If we take all of them away, do you expect us to leave the people without security?” he asked. He maintained that no member of the local security outfit was among those transported to Kaduna.

title: GH¢10,000 injection: Assafuah boosts Black Challenge’s World Cup campaign
body: The Member of Parliament for Old Tafo, Vincent Ekow Assafuah, has donated GH¢10,000 to Ghana’s national amputee football team, the Black Challenge, as part of efforts to boost their morale ahead of the 2026 WAFF Amputee Football World Cup in Mexico. Mr Assafuah made the donation during a visit to the team at their hotel in Achimota, Accra, where he also presented cartons of water and soft drinks to support the players. The visit served as a show of solidarity and encouragement to the team as they intensify preparations for the international tournament, scheduled to take place in San Juan de los Lagos, Mexico, from November 13 to 22, 2026. Mr Assafuah commended the players for their determination and commitment to representing Ghana on the international stage, stressing the importance of supporting their efforts to bring honour to the country. He also pledged to help mobilise additional support for the team in the coming days, urging other stakeholders to contribute to the Black Challenge’s World Cup campaign. The donation comes as the team continues preparations for the tournament, where Ghana will be seeking to make a strong impression against some of the world’s best amputee football nations. The gesture highlights the importance of collective support from individuals, corporate organisations and public institutions in helping the Black Challenge achieve their ambitions and proudly fly Ghana’s flag in Mexico.

title: Tinubu gave you succour when PDP chased you in 2007, Shettima tackles Atiku
body: Vice President Kashim Shettima on Saturday took a swipe at former Vice President Atiku Abubakar, reminding him that President Bola Ahmed Tinubu gave him political refuge and a platform to contest the presidency after he fell out with the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) in 2007. ‎ ‎Speaking at the flag-off of the APC presidential campaign in Kaduna, Shettima said Tinubu had consistently supported northern politicians over the years and therefore deserved the region’s backing for a second term. ‎ ‎The vice president said claims that Tinubu does not like the North were unfounded, citing the president’s role in supporting Atiku, who is also the presidential candidate of African Democratic Congress (ADC), former presidential candidate Nuhu Ribadu and late President Muhammadu Buhari at different times. ‎ ‎“President Tinubu is one person who has fiercely identified with the North over the years,” Shettima said. 2027: North will give Tinubu 100 percent support – Yari Ex-NAHCON chair: Over N9trn projects in Kano enough evidence for Tinubu’s re-election ‎“It is pertinent to mention that when former Vice President Atiku Abubakar was harassed and chased out of the PDP in 2007, he ran to the Lion of Bourdillon, Bola Ahmed Tinubu, who gave him political succour, support and a platform to contest for the presidency.” ‎ ‎Shettima also recalled that Tinubu backed Ribadu’s presidential ambition in 2011 and later played a key role in Buhari’s victories in the 2015 and 2019 presidential elections. ‎ ‎The Vice President said the APC’s appeal to northern voters was not based on sentiment but on the administration’s record in office. ‎ ‎According to him, the Tinubu government has invested in education through the establishment of the Federal University of Applied Sciences, Kachia, the upgrade of the Federal University of Education, Zaria, and funding for the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND). ‎ ‎He also highlighted progress recorded on major infrastructure projects, including the Ajaokuta-Kaduna-Kano (AKK) Gas Pipeline, Kano-Maradi railway, Lagos-Kano rail corridor, Abuja-Kaduna-Kano highway and the Sokoto-Badagry Super Highway. ‎ ‎“We have built a record of continuing projects initiated by our predecessors, and that is why substantial progress has been recorded on these strategic projects,” he said. ‎ ‎Also speaking, Director-General of the APC Presidential Campaign Council, Senator Abdulaziz Yari, defended Tinubu against allegations that he is unfavourable to northern interests. ‎ ‎Yari challenged critics to explain why the North should not support the president, arguing that Tinubu had repeatedly sacrificed personal ambition to support northern politicians. ‎ ‎“In 2007, when Atiku was chased out of the PDP, Tinubu gave him a platform. In 2011, he supported our son, Nuhu Ribadu, even though he could have contested himself. In 2015, he supported Buhari to victory. ‎ ‎“Today, what evidence do we have not to support him for a second term?” he asked. ‎ ‎Yari expressed confidence that Tinubu would secure re-election, saying the president’s record and longstanding relationship with the North would work in his favour at the polls.

title: Alyoshki residents await humanitarian corridor, on-ground situation unchanged — diplomat
body:
MOSCOW, October 24. /TASS/. Residents in Alyoshki are waiting for the humanitarian passageway agreement to come into force, but the situation on the ground has not changed so far, the Russian Foreign Ministry’s Ambassador-at-Large Rodion Miroshnik told Zvezda TV channel in a comment.
"I can cite only the information that we receive from locals, and the administration of the Alyoshki District. From 7:15 a.m. to 8:30 a.m. today, there was a mortar shelling at the town of Alyoshki. This shows that the situation on the ground has not changed, at least by now," the diplomat noted. "Also, roads were mined last night. New mines that still block both driveways in the town of Alyoshki were discovered. That is, people are waiting for the agreement to establish a humanitarian corridor to be implemented, but no changes on the ground have yet taken place," he added.
Chief of the General Staff of the Russian Army Valery Gerasimov announced earlier that Russian forces will enforce a localized ceasefire in the Kherson direction at 4:00 a.m. Moscow time (1:00 a.m. GMT) on October 27 to allow for a humanitarian operation near Alyoshki.
On Friday, the White House broke the news about a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in Alyoshki. The localized ceasefire will come into effect on October 29. The sides agreed to cease hostilities in Alyoshki to "allow for humanitarian aid to enter and to prepare a civilian evacuation through a designated safe passageway," the White House said. An independent US media organization will assist and document the actions of both Russia and Ukraine during the process.

title: UAE Shuts All Beaches As Neighbors Grapple With Oil Spill
body:
Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe.
Footage released by IRIB and attributed to the IRGC shows Gem No 2 ablaze, in this screengrab obtained from a video released on October 10, 2026. IRGC VIA IRIB/Handout via REUTERS.
Oct 24 (Reuters) – Ras Al Khaimah authorities said on Saturday that all beaches in the emirate would be closed until further notice, a day after anoffshore oil leak prompted beach closures in neighboring Umm Al Quwain and Sharjah.
The Public Services Department announced the closures in a statement shared by Ras Al Khaimah Police General Headquarters. No reason was given.
The United Arab Emirates said on Friday that efforts were underway to contain oil leaking from a tanker offshore, with its Ministry of Climate Change and Environment conducting an environmental assessment.
All beaches and coastal areas around the city of Umm Al Quwain were temporarily closed until technical teams completed their assessments and determined the necessary safety and marine protection measures, the ministry said.
The ministry also urged fishermen and other sea users to avoid affected areas and follow official instructions.
Authorities in Sharjah temporarily closed Al Hamriyah Beach, on the UAE’s northern coast near the border with Umm Al Quwain, as a precaution, the Sharjah Government Media Bureau said.
Since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran, attacks on commercial vessels in Gulf shipping lanes have heightened concerns about maritime security and the conflict’s environmental fallout .
Ras Al Khaimah, a northern UAE emirate known for its beaches and luxury resorts, is also home to Wynn Resorts’ planned casino resort on Al Marjan Island.
The Las Vegas-based operator, which won the UAE’s first commercial gaming license in 2024, said in February it expected the resort to open in the first quarter of 2027.
Wynn said in March it had resumed construction after a brief pause, even as the Iran war continued to disrupt businesses across the Middle East.
Residents reported unusual odors in parts of Sharjah, Ajman and Umm Al Quwain, but the UAE’s environment ministry said they posed no health risks. The smell remained pungent across Umm Al Quwain on Friday.
UAE authorities have not named the tanker involved in the incident or said what caused the spill.
(Reporting by Eman Abouhassira and Maha El Dahan; Editing by Mark Potter)
