title: The Goose Programming Language
body:
A memory-safe systems language with no heap allocator, garbage collector, or lifetime annotations. In this repository's benchmarks, Goose runs faster than C++ and Rust while using less memory.
Tutorial · Reference · Specification · Command line · Packages · Samples · Benchmarks · Standard library
Goose has syntax familiar to C and Rust programmers, but there is no heap . Every dynamic value lives inline on data stacks managed by the compiler. Growth advances a pointer, and memory is freed when its scope ends. The language's type and lifetime rules make this memory model safe to use.
The tutorial walks through all of this by example, the reference covers the whole language topic by topic, the specification has the exact rules, and the benchmarks have the numbers, including the cases where Goose loses.
This section focuses on what distinguishes Goose. The tutorial explains these features in more detail, and the samples show them in thirty-one complete programs.
A program has the native call stack, static data and N data stacks, where the compiler works out N. A data stack is a large address-space reservation with a bump pointer, and there is no other memory. At most one resizable value is live per stack and it is always on top, so growth never moves anything and never checks a capacity. All of this is proved at compile time; the runtime tracks only the bump pointers.
push returns a reference to the new element, so a program can link elements while building the array. A vector<T> or Vec<T> may reallocate and cannot provide this guarantee. Stable references account for several benchmark gains.
Every reference and slice has a static root : the variable that bounds its target's lifetime. A reference must not outlive the variable that owns its target or access that target through an incompatible type. The compiler infers roots and specializes functions for them, so no annotations are needed. There are no aliasing or exclusivity rules. When a lifetime check fails, the error names the reference's root and its destination:
A slice T[:] lets a function accept a range from any array kind without copying its elements. For example, split returns slices into its input, and a dictionary keyed by u8[:] stores views of strings rather than copies.
There is no single array type. Instead there is a family of array types that differ only in how their size can change. Every member is laid out as [metadata][elements...] , inline and packed, never as a pointer to a separate block of elements:
Strings are u8 arrays: u8[>..] is a builder, u8[] a finished string stored inline in whatever holds it, u8[..16] a small string inside a struct, u8[:] a view. A struct may contain variable-size parts, which are stored inline in declaration order, so a record is a sequence of bytes with no indirection in it:
That order is 29 bytes and 0 allocations . As C++ std::string + std::vector<Item> it is 160 bytes and 1 allocation, and as Rust String + Vec<Item> it is 153 bytes and 4 allocations. An entire order book is a single array, so reading it streams through the cache. The trade-off is that an array of variable-size elements is sequential: you can iterate it but not index it (unless you keep a second array of references into it as an index).
Algebraic data types are the only form of dynamic polymorphism; there is no inheritance and there are no vtables. Every ADT can be stored in two ways, chosen at the point of use. Fixed mode ( Shape ) stores a tag plus room for the largest payload, so values can be indexed and overwritten. Variable mode ( Shape.. ) gives each value exactly the size of its variant. An array of such values becomes sequential and a value never changes variant, but in exchange you may take references into a payload:
Case functions provide another way to dispatch on a variant: define one overload per variant. Calls dispatch on the tag through a jump table, and the compiler checks that the overloads cover every variant:
A T& is a machine address: it takes eight bytes and never dangles. A relative reference is the same link stored as a narrow offset. A T&<u32> is measured from the field itself to a target in the same array, so the structure is position independent. A T&<u32 in pool> is measured from the base of a named pool, so other arrays can link into the pool. T&<u32>? uses offset 0 as null. Here is a binary search tree in one grow-only array, with 12-byte nodes:
References are transparent (there is no * or -> ). .= binds or retargets a reference, and Node? is a nullable reference that if , guard and assert narrow. The insert is one push and one store, and the push cannot invalidate cur . When lifetimes are not nested, the standard library's slot_pool<T> pairs a grow-only items array with a freelist. alloc_ref reuses a free slot or pushes a new one, and free returns a slot to the pool. Since a slot's memory is never actually freed, a stale slot reads a different value of the correct type rather than corrupting memory.
slice_pool<T> provides contiguous runs with allocation, free and resize operations. The language features reusable and reusable[] are deprecated in favor of these pool types. They remain available for existing code and the remaining migration gaps ; removal is a later step.
The tree's links are self-relative, so the tree means the same thing wherever it is stored. Saving it writes its bytes and loading it reads them back, with no serializer, no schema and no pointer fixups. from_bytes checks the framing, every tag, every length and every link before the bytes become a value, so a corrupt or hostile file makes it return false , never a wild reference.
The copy-free construction guarantee ( spec §4.3 ) says a constructed value is always built at its final location, which is passed down through calls. A function returning a grow-only array by value writes its elements directly into the caller's variable, or into a field of the record being built inside another array, so out-parameters are rarely needed.
return E from f returns E as the result of the innermost active call of f , however many frames up that call is. Every function in between keeps its plain signature. The construct is checked statically: every call of parse_user must lie inside a load call, so nothing can go uncaught at runtime. It is implemented as a hidden discriminant checked in each frame rather than as an unwinder, and the message is built directly where load 's caller wants it. The parsers in the samples use it for every syntax error.
Everything is monomorphized. Type arguments are inferred from argument types; type parameters that do not appear in those types can be supplied explicitly. Function values are passed as generic parameters. Every call of a function value is direct and can be inlined, function values cannot escape, and there are no closure objects or function pointers, so a higher-order function compiles to exactly the loop it looks like. A block may return from its lexically enclosing function, and nested functions can use the enclosing function's locals.
There is no shared mutable memory. A thread_fn and everything it calls is compiled as its own program with its own data stacks and its own copies of the globals. Values are passed between threads through typed queues, one per type, and must be flat , with no references at any depth. Passing them is cheap because a flat Goose value is contiguous: a job or a result can carry real data, such as pixels, and passing it is a single memcpy .
A failed check or abort in a worker started with thread_spawn_contained ends only that worker. Its message goes to whoever waits for it, not to stderr, so a supervisor can log it and start another:
The first thread_wait(id, msg) for a worker takes the message; a caller that doesn't ask for it loses it.
An extern fn binds a Goose signature to a C symbol. The math and os modules use this interface. Only types with supported C representations may cross the boundary; unsupported signatures are rejected at the declaration. The compiler emits one C file for the whole program. The bundled TinyCC backend can compile and run that C inside the Goose compiler's process.
Much of the speed comes from the memory model: no heap allocation or per-object teardown, contiguous data, narrow links, and enums sized for the variant they contain. Every index is bounds-checked, and the compiler removes checks it can prove unnecessary. An assert on a slice length often lets the compiler remove the remaining checks in a kernel, so that the kernel can be vectorized. --bce-lines reports the checks that remain. checkfree fn rejects a kernel if any bounds check remains in it; index types let graph edges keep the validation done while the graph was built. Benchmark measurements use whole-process wall-clock time, including teardown.
The summary explains the gains and losses; results.md has every measurement, and design.md explains what the suite tests.
Prebuilt compilers for Windows (x64), Linux (x64) and macOS (Apple silicon and Intel) are on the releases page , with the graphics, audio, ui and physics packages compiled in. Unpack one anywhere and put its directory on PATH: the compiler finds the standard library, TinyCC's runtime and the packages beside itself, and keeps what it builds under ~/.goose ( GOOSE_HOME ). The archive also holds these docs, the samples and the VS Code extension.
Running a program in-process ( goose file.goose ) needs nothing else on Windows. On Linux it needs the C library's headers ( libc6-dev , or glibc-devel ); on macOS, the SDK of the Xcode command line tools ( xcode-select --install ). goose build also needs a C compiler: Visual Studio 2022 or later, or clang, on Windows; gcc or clang elsewhere. The Linux compiler needs glibc 2.35 or later (Ubuntu 22.04, Debian 12), and the macOS compiler needs macOS 13.3 or later. macOS keeps a downloaded archive's files from running until xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine is run on the unpacked directory.
You need CMake 3.27 or later, a C++20 compiler (MSVC, clang or gcc) and Python 3 for the test and sample runners. TinyCC, which the in-process backend is built from, is part of the tree. The graphics, audio, ui and physics modules are packages in repositories of their own ( goose_gfx and goose_physics ; docs/design/packages.md ). -DGOOSE_BUILTIN_LIBS=all fetches them with git at configure time, at the pinned tags, and compiles them into the compiler, so programs that use them run with nothing else installed. Without that option the compiler is built on its own, and the first time a program imports one of these packages, the package is built into ~/.goose , which needs git, cmake and a C compiler.
GOOSE_BUILTIN_LIBS can also name some of the packages ( physics , or gfx , which includes audio and ui too). On Linux, SDL needs the X11 or Wayland development packages ( third_party/SDL/docs/README-linux.md ); without them the build leaves the gfx module out and says what to install.
The runner scripts prefer build/Release , then build/RelWithDebInfo , then build , then build/Debug . Pass --exe to select a specific compiler; use an explicit Debug executable when testing with compiler assertions enabled. The compiler is build/goose ( build/Release/goose.exe with the Visual Studio generator), and it finds the standard library in the source tree it was built from. On Windows 10 version 1903 and later, its embedded manifest selects a UTF-8 process code page so compiler paths do not depend on the system locale. Earlier Windows versions retain their legacy code page. Generated native executables retain their own process settings.
Run a program directly from source, in-process, with no C compiler and no build step ( goose run is the explicit form of the same command):
Or build an executable, which is written beside the source. The compiler finds a C compiler on the machine ( goose toolchain shows which one) and links the generated C with the runtime and any native modules the program uses, including graphics. Programs that use threads must be built this way, since TinyCC cannot place thread-local storage.
goose check only typechecks. --debug turns on the overflow, range and tag checks, each of which names its source line when it fails, and --bce-lines reports the bounds checks that remain on each line. Every resizable value lives on a data stack of 2 GB of reserved address space, committed as it is used, and --stack-reserve 16G changes that size. The command line describes every command and option, including how to write the C for a build system or a C host of your own ( goose -o tour.c tour.goose ).
A program with C of its own lists that C in a sidecar file beside the source, foo.build beside foo.goose : c_sources = ["impl.c"]; . Both forms build that C, so an extern fn can call it either way. A program uses a library by writing import name from "source"; in its root file. The source is a directory ( "./lib" ), or a git repository at a tag or commit ( "owner/repo@v1" on GitHub, "host/owner/repo@ref" ), which is fetched into ~/.goose and built there once per C compiler ( packages ).
A program using audio plays procedural mono/stereo PCM through SDL3 without opening a graphics window. See the audio reference .
The test suite and the samples run on Windows, macOS and Linux:
For editing, the VS Code extension gives syntax highlighting, the compiler's language server ( goose lsp : errors as you type, hover, go to definition, completion, rename, symbols) and one-key runs through the JIT:
Other editors can run goose lsp themselves; editors has the configuration for Neovim, Helix and Emacs.
Goose is new. What exists today is a whole-program compiler of about thirty thousand lines of C++, the specification, the standard library, the samples, and a test suite that CI runs on Windows, macOS and Linux with an extra sanitizer job. These are deliberately out of scope for now: moves for resizable values, more than one resizable per struct, labeled break , namespace privacy, and more OS/library access. Open items are tracked in the specification's Appendix B .
Goose is licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0 .
Wouter van Oortmerssen : Language Design, Compiler Design, Coding standards. home page, twitter .
Claude Fable : Compiler implementation, Benchmarking, Sample & Doc writing.
This repo was produced almost entirely with AI, from a human language design. I had designed Goose several years ago, and had started to implement it, but running a game startup (which is built on another programming language of mine, Lobster ) there was no time to finish it. Which was sad, because I knew Goose could do things other languages can't, and it should exist.
I had not expected AI to help with this until Fable came out. I thought it might be capable enough to do a good job. I made it essentially clone the style and structure of my other recent compiler (Lobster), which is why if you look at the code, it looks rather similar to that. My initial design had left lots of things unspecified, and lots of back and forth with Fable made me decide on all of those, and it is now a better language for it.
It is also an experiment in using AI to implement a new language, rather than reproduce an existing one.
You may wonder why I had it work in C++, if clearly I could have used any language, like Rust, or my own Lobster, or.. Goose itself (that may still happen). With Fable, it was my observation that it is almost equally capable in any language, and the strong guardrails of Rust or other languages are not as pressing as they once were. Since the compiler emits C, you likely already need to have a C/C++ compiler around, so sticking inside one ecosystem would seem to simplify deployment and adoption. I've also integrated libtcc and who knows what other C libraries in the future. And, like I said, to have the compiler code mimic my existing Lobster compiler seemed fun, at least I can read it like it is my own.

title: Spurs Seal Rare Win At Chelsea As Palmer Sees Red
body: Tottenham clinched a Premier League win at Chelsea for just the second time in 36 years as a woeful own goal from Blues keeper Mike Penders was followed by Cole Palmer’s red card in Saturday’s 2-0 victory. Roberto De Zerbi’s side clinched their second successive league win thanks to Penders’s howler in the second half at a rain-lashed Stamford Bridge. Chelsea forward Palmer was sent off for a second booking moments later before Mathys Tel produced a superb solo effort to condemn the Blues to their first home defeat against Tottenham since 2018. Since 1990, Tottenham had won just once in 41 previous away matches against London rivals Chelsea in all competitions. Ending that miserable run gave Tottenham only their second win in their last 16 league games against Chelsea, both home and away, and their first since 2023. English referee Chris Kavanagh shows a red card to Chelsea’s English midfielder #10 Cole Palmer (R) during the English Premier League football match between Chelsea and Tottenham Hotspur at Stamford Bridge in London on October 24, 2026. (Photo by Glyn KIRK / AFP) After a dismal start to the season, Tottenham have climbed to 12th place after building on Monday’s win against Coventry, which ended their wait for a first league win this season. It was a bitter blow for fourth-placed Chelsea, who had beaten Bournemouth and Everton in their previous two league games. They were booed off at full-time and remain very much a work in progress under Xabi Alonso in the Spaniard’s first season in charge. With Joao Pedro sidelined by a late injury, Morgan Rogers was Chelsea’s central striker, but their revamped attack was short of bite. Teed up by Rogers after Pedro Neto stole possession from Mateus Fernandes, Palmer went close to an early opener with a curler that Antonin Kinsky tipped over at full stretch. Tottenham responded with a spell of probing pressure as Omar Marmoush met Andy Robertson’s cross with a shot that was repelled by Penders. Alonso’s men pieced together the best move of the half with a flurry of one-touch passes to reach Jordan Henderson on the edge of the area, but the midfielder’s low drive was palmed away by Kinsky. Tottenham Hotspur’s Egyptian midfielder #22 Omar Marmoush (C) vies with Chelsea’s Ecuadorian midfielder #25 Moises Caicedo (L) and Chelsea’s French defender #05 Maxence Lacroix (R) during the English Premier League football match between Chelsea and Tottenham Hotspur at Stamford Bridge in London on October 24, 2026. (Photo by Glyn KIRK / AFP) Spurs spring a surprise Neto tested Kinsky with a fierce blast but the Tottenham keeper was up to the task with a save at his near post. Tottenham suffered a blow when often-injured midfielder James Maddison limped off in a premature end to only his second start since May 2025. Maddison had already missed training sessions since his long-awaited start against Coventry and his latest fitness setback suggested it was a failed gamble to start him at the Bridge. In keeping with the sloppy fare, Neto fired straight at Kinsky from a dangerous position after Palmer pounced on Sandro Tonali’s wayward pass. When Palmer’s run was halted by Fernandes’s handball, the Chelsea star escaped with a yellow card after barging into his rival with such aggression that the Tottenham midfielder was sent crashing to the sodden turf. Tottenham exacted swift revenge in the 77th minute. Fernandes’s in-swinging corner should have been caught by Penders, but he opted for a punch that was completely mistimed as he diverted the ball into his net for a comical own goal. It was a horrible moment for the 21-year-old Penders, who was making his first league start in the absence of Emiliano Martinez following jaw surgery. Rubbing salt into Chelsea’s wounds, Palmer was dismissed three minutes later for an ugly stamp on Conor Gallagher. Tel wrapped up Tottenham’s memorable triumph in fitting style in the 87th minute, skipping away from Chelsea’s flat-footed defence to drill a fine finish into the bottom corner from the edge of the area. AFP The post Spurs Seal Rare Win At Chelsea As Palmer Sees Red appeared first on Channels Television .

title: The AI graveyard: a running list of projects and startups that didn’t make it
body:
Relay, an AI-powered workflow automation tool built as an alternative to Zapier, shut down entirely in August. The product let users automate email and task workflows using AI agents, but as OpenAI, Google, and other larger platforms built similar automation directly into their own tools, five-year-old Relay struggled to hold on to a reason to exist as a stand-alone product.
More recently, chatbot platform Character.ai filed for bankruptcy just five years after launching.
Aside from Character.ai and Relay, plenty of AI bets never even survive inside the companies that build them. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence , about 42% of AI initiatives are ultimately abandoned by their corporate parents. The reasons vary: insufficient funding, technical challenges, competition, difficulty scaling, or just weak user demand.
The result is a growing AI graveyard. Below is a look at some of the most notable AI products, startups, launches, and bets that have shut down, pivoted, or significantly missed expectations. Think of it less as a scorecard of flops than as a record of what these attempts can (hopefully) teach the rest of the industry.
Even the biggest players aren’t immune. OpenAI, one of the most valuable private companies in the world, has had its own share of casualties and missteps. One of the more recent examples was its attempt to turn ChatGPT into a broader “ super app .” On July 9, OpenAI updated the app to combine several experiences, including separate “Chat,” “Codex,” and “Work” modes, while renaming the traditional, familiar version “ChatGPT Classic.”
The redesign quickly drew criticism from users who found the new interface confusing and cluttered, and OpenAI rolled back the change soon after , bringing the familiar ChatGPT interface back.
That wasn’t OpenAI’s only attempt to pull everything under one roof. The company has also shut down several stand-alone apps and folded their features directly into ChatGPT — a strategy that’s worked out better than the redesign did. ChatGPT Atlas, a stand-alone AI-powered web browser, lasted less than a year before being discontinued on August 9, with its most useful features absorbed into ChatGPT.
The company did the same thing with Operator , an AI agent that could browse the web and complete tasks on a user’s behalf, and OpenAI has increasingly built image generation directly into ChatGPT, shrinking the role of DALL-E as its own separate destination for creating images.
We also can’t forget its video-sharing platform, Sora , which struggled with high operating costs and user-retention challenges and shut down in March 2026.
When Apple unveiled Apple Intelligence in 2024, an improved Siri was one of the highlighted features. The pitch promised a Siri that could understand context, know what was happening across apps, and get tasks done effectively.
However, Apple repeatedly pushed back the release of the new Siri, citing various reasons like engineering issues and bugs . This delay eventually contributed to a $250 million settlement over claims regarding how Apple marketed the AI capabilities of the iPhone 16.
Siri AI finally appeared in the iOS 27 beta this past July, with the new AI-powered version rolling out to English-language users first this month; support for other languages is expected to follow.
Announced at its 2024 Build developer conference, Microsoft’s Recall feature was pitched as an AI-powered “photographic memory” for Windows PCs, periodically taking screenshots of what a user was doing so they could later search back through their own digital history.
Predictably, the announcement triggered an immediate backlash over privacy and security. Critics argued that Recall could create a searchable archive of highly sensitive information, including passwords, private messages, financial details, and other activity. Microsoft delayed the feature for nearly a year, giving the company time to rethink its security and privacy protections.
Even after a redesign, the controversy hasn’t gone away. A cybersecurity researcher recently built a tool that could extract and display data that Recall had captured, reviving questions about whether Microsoft has actually fixed the underlying problem.
Notion Mail launched in April 2025 as an AI-focused email product designed to help users organize and automate their inboxes. However, the company noticed its users were using separate AI agents to handle their email inboxes instead. As a result, Notion Mail is scheduled to shut down on September 22 .
The Humane AI Pin is probably one of the most well-known failures in AI hardware. Designed to provide AI features through a wearable device rather than a traditional smartphone, Humane raised $230 million from investors and garnered significant attention.
But the product struggled mightily with performance, and the situation worsened when Humane warned customers to stop using its charging case because of a potential battery fire risk. Humane then shut down its AI Pin business in February 2025, with most of the company’s assets acquired by HP for $116 million.
The Rabbit R1 was another heavily hyped AI device. Unveiled at CES in January 2024, the AI companion was designed to perform tasks on behalf of its owner. Rabbit said it had sold 100,000 units shortly after launch.
However, strong initial sales didn’t mean it was a strong product. Early reviews described the device as unfinished, with unreliable performance and a limited number of useful integrations.
The company hasn’t given up, though. It has continued updating the R1, positioning it as a computer controller capable of performing agentic tasks. It also recently announced a new hardware project, dubbed “Project Cyberdeck,” aimed at creating a portable device built for vibe-coding.
Huxe was an AI audio app, built by former developers of Google’s NotebookLM, that turned written information into conversational, podcast-style audio.
The company shut down in May 2026, partly as larger platforms began offering similar experiences to large existing audiences. For instance, Spotify has been expanding its own AI-powered audio tools.
Yupp was an interesting AI product: a free playground that allowed users to compare responses from hundreds of AI models side by side. Users could also vote on responses and earn cryptocurrency through the platform.
At its peak, the platform let users test more than 800 models, including from companies such as OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic. But according to its founders, Yupp never achieved strong enough product-market fit to survive. The platform shut down in March 2026.
Figgs AI operated from 2023 to 2024, letting users create and interact with customizable AI characters for role-play and storytelling. The platform reportedly drew more than 1 million users, but its developers said keeping the service free became too expensive to sustain, and they shut it down .
Founded in 2021 by former Google researchers Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, Character.ai became a buzzed-about consumer AI app by letting people chat with customizable bots, many of them modeled on celebrities and fictional characters. It raised $150 million at a $1 billion valuation in 2023. Then, the next year, Google paid a reported $2.7 billion to license its technology and bring its founders back into its orbit, leaving the startup to carry on without them.
The trouble piled up after that. Families sued, alleging the chatbots contributed to teen suicides and self-harm, and Disney sent a cease-and-desist letter over unauthorized use of its characters. Character.ai barred under-18 users from open-ended chats late last year and agreed to settle several of the suits, along with Google, in early 2026. But it wasn’t enough. The company filed for bankruptcy in early October, citing legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds. In an ironic twist, Disney is now the opening bidder, offering $20 million for a license to some of its intellectual property. The app is still running during the process, and the sale is expected to wrap up by late November or early December.

title: Syria's Energy Comeback Could Reshape Middle East Oil and Gas
body: Syria is undergoing countrywide reconstruction after more than a decade of conflict, which caused extensive infrastructure damage and led to millions of people being displaced. As Syrians rebuild their lives, the government has big plans for economic diversification and growth to support long-term recovery. Thanks to its favourable geographic position, this includes the development of a strong energy sector that could help eventually establish Syria as a regional hub.  Syria is now led by President Ahmed al-Sharaa, who formed a transitional government on March 29, 2025, following the end of the Assad regime. The government has introduced a wide range of policies and reforms over the past year, across all sectors, aimed at improving living standards and supporting economic growth. The national strategy focuses on institutional reorganisation, security integration, economic stabilisation, and transitional justice ahead of planned national elections in 2030.  The transitional government has taken control over Syrian energy, including the Omar oil field and Tabiyeh gas complex. This follows over a decade during which Syria's energy sector was split, with Damascus situated far from the country's oil-rich northeast. For years, while the government still oversaw gas output in the country's central region, it lost control of some of the country's largest production sites.  A 2026 agreement between the transitional government and the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces SDF provides the potential to integrate SDF forces into state structures, which could further unify energy governance. Meanwhile, the lifting of United States and European Union sanctions on Syria, following the fall of the Assad regime, and the relaunch of the SWIFT transfer system have made it easier for international companies to invest in Syria.  Before the conflict, which commenced in 2011, Syria was producing an average of 380,000 bpd of crude and 900 million cubic feet of gas. However, the conflict dramatically reduced output, with oil production down 80 per cent and gas by half, according to figures from Wood Mackenzie. Nevertheless, Syria is still home to estimated reserves of 1.3 billion barrels of oil equivalent, in addition to having vast unexplored onshore areas and an entirely untapped offshore sector. Higher levels of foreign investment could support an accelerated recovery in the oil and gas sector.  In May, Syria announced that it had an offshore site for its first deep-water oil and gas exploration project to be developed by the U.S. major Chevron, Qatar's UCC Holding, and the Syrian Petroleum Company SPC. This supports the government's aim to attract greater foreign investment in Syria's energy sector. Other U.S. oil and gas firms have also expressed interest in Syrian oil and gas projects under the transitional government, opening the door to new investment opportunities.  There is significant potential for Syria's energy industry given the current geopolitical challenges to global energy. Iran's restrictions on energy trade through the Strait of Hormuz have spurred interest in Syria as a potential transit route for pipelines transporting Persian Gulf oil and gas to the Mediterranean. Syria's border with Turkey offers enhanced access to major pipeline networks, which could facilitate the transport of oil and gas from the Middle East to Europe. With greater investment, Syria could serve as an "energy land bridge" for Hormuz-bypass pipelines, according to the Baker Institute.  In addition to redeveloping its oil and gas assets and potentially acting as a regional energy trade hub, the transitional government also has major plans for Syria's renewable energy sector. Small-scale solar projects have already begun to emerge, with estimates suggesting that the country's off-grid solar capacity increased from around 250 MW in 2022 to over 2 GW in 2025.  Syria is looking to develop both its solar and wind power sectors. In June 2025, the government signed a $7 billion deal with a consortium from Qatar, Turkey, and the United States to rebuild its power sector, including four gas-fired power plants and a 1 GW solar park. The project is expected to add 5 GW of capacity, which will cover almost half of the current electricity demand.  The government signed a Joint Development Agreement with the Saudi energy group ACWA Power in September 2025, as they work to identify suitable locations for wind energy projects, aiming to develop 1 GW of solar PV capacity and approximately 1.5 GW of wind power, as well as utility-scale battery storage to enhance reliability.  In February, the Syrian Ministry of Energy also signed an agreement with the Dubai-based energy group Marv Energy to develop a 700-MW wind farm with plans to install 140 locally manufactured wind turbines across several sites to connect to the national electricity grid. Marv Energy plans to manufacture the turbines at its factory in the city of Homs in western Syria. It aims to complete the project within five to seven years.  In October, the Ministry of Energy issued a request for expressions of interest for the Halabiya-Zalabiya Dam project on the Euphrates River. The project would include the construction of an 81-MW hydropower plant and a 1.2-GW pumped-storage hydropower facility, with an estimated investment cost of $1.16 billion. The project would require the development of a 1,200-metre-long, 23-metre-high dam. Meanwhile, the hydropower plant would have three 27-MW turbines.  Syria has significant oil, gas, and renewable energy capacity, but it is highly dependent on foreign investment to support development. Due to ongoing limitations to energy trade via the Strait of Hormuz, several investors are looking to Syria to develop alternative trade routes between the Middle East and Europe, which could support the country's economic recovery.  By Felicity Bradstock for Oilprice.com

title: Russian attack on Synelnykove kills three people and injures eight others
body:
According to Ukrinform, Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Military Administration, reported this on Telegram .
“Three people were killed, and at least eight were injured. The Russians struck Synelnykove with a drone. A fire broke out on the fourth floor of a high-rise building. A store and several cars were destroyed,” Hanzha wrote.
According to him, all the victims are in the hospital, including an 11-year-old girl.
The head of the regional military administration added that a 50-year-old woman and a 70-year-old man are in critical condition.
As reported by Ukrinform, four people, including a child, were injured in the Nikopol region as a result of a drone at tack.

title: Biotech stocks are surging. How investors can play the new drug innovation boom
body:
Moderna gave investors a scare as its stock plunged on Thursday. But it's still one of the hottest biotechs this year. And it's hardly alone – the sector is on a roll and looks poised for more gains.
The iShares Biotechnology ETF (IBB) is up 24% through October 23, building on a 28% gain in 2025. Two dozen of the ETF's 233 holdings have more than doubled year-to-date. Moderna leads the pack with a 587% surge — even after an 18% decline following a leak of clinical data for its cancer vaccine (which was actually positive).
Analysts say a new biotech cycle is underway, fueled by clinical trial results, M&A activity, and promising technologies such as genomics, mRNA — and AI.
"We're in the midst of a powerful innovation cycle," said John Hall, portfolio manager of the T. Rowe Price Biotechnology ETF . "What's super exciting is we're seeing newer modalities start to make it to market." Companies "understand the disease biology better," he adds, and that could ultimately lead to more novel drugs making it to market.
Investors are excited about technologies like mRNA and genomics, along with a steady stream of new drug approvals. The FDA approved about a dozen novel biologic drugs in 2025, out of 46 approvals in total. Roughly 66 novel drugs are in the pipeline for FDA approval, including potential blockbusters like Moderna and Merck 's cancer drug for melanoma, and a next-generation obesity drug from Eli Lilly .
Analysts say AI could also lead to more approvals as companies deploy the software to speed up drug development.
"Biotech is a phenomenal application for artificial intelligence and machine learning," says Piper Sandler analyst Ted Tenthoff. "You can set up exciting predictive models that, frankly, can do things that we've never been able to do in the space in terms of novel drug discovery."
Granted, the industry is recovering from a fallow period. The sector's last strong performance was during the Covid era when ultra-low interest rates encouraged investment in early-stage drug developers, and mRNA vaccines fueled a revenue surge for companies like Moderna, Pfizer and Biontech .
The sector then went cold as many early-stage companies fizzled. Demand for Covid vaccines evaporated, and surging interest rates put a chill in IPOs and M&A.
The risks haven't evaporated – this is still a sector whose products take years to develop, resulting in far more failures than successes. But analysts say the outlook is healthier now. While that's reflected in strong performance and richer valuations, there's still good reason to invest.
Recent clinical trial results are stoking excitement that novel drugs in the works could tackle some of the toughest problems in medicine.
Moderna and Merck's melanoma drug, for instance, uses mRNA to trigger an immune response in patients, targeting tumors that have been surgically removed and genetically analyzed. It's not a preventive vaccine, but it uses a similar immunology mechanism and showed a 42% reduction in cancer recurrence or death (used in conjunction with Merck's cancer drug Keytruda).
While the Phase 3 results disappointed Wall Street, oncologists say the outcomes were still highly positive. And they see the technology as a potential game changer, ushering in an era of personalized treatments for cancers. Moderna and Merck have said they aim to submit the drug for FDA approval and get it launched in 2027.
Inflammation treatment is another promising area. AstraZeneca and Amgen recently released positive Phase 3 results for another use for their drug Tezspire, an injectable approved for nasal polyps and asthma. In clinical trials, it showed that it successfully relieved swallowing symptoms and healed microscopic and visual tissue damage in patients with severe throat inflammation.
Roche, meanwhile, notched a win after the FDA approved its drug Enspryng, a therapy to treat rare inflammatory and autoimmune diseases. It became the first and only at-home injection for adults with thyroid eye disease.
Obesity drugs are also advancing beyond the first generation of GLP-1s. Eli Lilly's retatrutide, a "triple agonist" targeting three different hormone receptors, cleared two more clinical trials over the summer. The drug produced 28%-30% weight loss at the highest doses in the study, Lilly said. The company plans to submit the drug for FDA approval in the first quarter of 2027.
Much of the innovation isn't just happening in drug-making – it's also in areas like gene sequencing, mRNA, and high-tech instruments.
Illumina has more than doubled this year. The DNA and gene sequencing company is seeing accelerating demand for its NovaSeq X high-end sequencing platform. Pharmaceutical companies including Bristol-Myers Squibb , Merck and Kura are working with Illumina to develop precision oncology solutions.
Another big winner is 10x Genomics , up more than 300%. The biotech firm offers its lab instruments to help scientists research cancer, immunology and neuroscience. The company's Atera platform is helping produce data sets to train AI models, a process that helps accelerate personalized therapies.
On the AI front, companies are using the technology for more efficient drug discovery, says Shreefāl Mehta, president of Guidant BioTherapeutics. Using AI, "you can now bring a drug to clinical trials with less capital. More investment is also going into companies that are demonstrating that," he said.
Global AI in drug discovery will grow from a $20 billion market in 2025 to more than $160 billion by 2035, according to forecasts by Towards Health, a research and consulting firm.
One other catalyst for the sector could be M&A. Dealmaking for biopharma hit $134 billion in the first half of 2026, up from $112 billion for all of 2025, notes Jeet Mukherjee, biotech analyst at BTIG. That's a positive signal, indicating more drugs in development are showing clinical promise.
It also helps that Big Pharma has a "patent cliff" ahead. Products representing $180 billion of revenue will lose exclusivity by 2030, according to research firm RTW Institute. Companies with looming expiries "are looking for novel products and innovative products to put into their pipeline," Mehta says.
GLP-1 blockbusters have also left some companies flush with cash for acquisitions. Eli Lilly alone has completed 10 acquisition deals in 2026 worth $25 billion.
ETFs can capture the investing theme, though they aren't all alike. The iShares Biotech ETF is one of the lower cost funds. It tracks a market-cap weighted index of biotech stocks, led by companies like Gilead Sciences , Amgen , Vertex Pharmaceuticals , and Moderna.
The State Street SPDR S&P Biotech ETF holds stocks in equal weight, offering more exposure to small- and mid-cap names. Its top holdings are Moderna, Natera, Twist Bioscience and Halozyme Therapeutics .
Piper Sandler calls Illumina and 10x Genomics the "primary infrastructure plays" in the life science arena, saying their technologies are "driving the next generation of precision medicine."
Piper analyst David Westenberg has a buy rating and $305 target on Illumina, implying 14% gains from recent prices around $267. He has a hold rating on 10X with an $80 target, above recent prices around $70.
Twist Bioscience is another name to consider. The company makes customized synthetic DNA and sells DNA sequencing tools. Twist has partnered with Eli Lilly's AI and machine-learning platform and linked up with Anthropic in August to start testing its AI model, Claude, for protein development.
Twist isn't expected to turn an EPS profit until 2029, according to consensus forecasts. But revenue is expected to go from $572 million in 2027 to $833 million in 2029. Analysts have an average target of $168 on the stock, implying 21% returns from recent prices around $138.
In the small-cap space, Piper Sandler's Tenthoff likes Monte Rosa Therapeutics , a pioneer in protein degradation that selectively destroys disease-causing proteins.
The firm has partnered with Novartis to develop a drug for inflammatory conditions and autoimmune diseases. The companies announced a Phase 2 clinical study in September for an autoimmune disease treatment, which has been "triggering milestones to Monte Rosa," Tenthoff said.
Tenthoff has a buy rating and $37 target on the stock, which recently traded around $10.70.
Also in the small-cap arena, BTIG's Mukherjee recommends Faeth Therapeutics .
The biotech is developing a novel two-drug regimen to treat breast cancer and other tumors. The regimen "has the potential to address safety and dosing limitations of another recently approved drug for breast cancer," he says. And it could become "a mainstay of the future breast cancer treatment paradigm and other cancers."
Faeth is a clinical-stage company that has yet to bring a drug to market. Yet the stock is up 93% year-to-date on positive clinical trial results, trading around $18. Mukherjee has a $55 target on it.
Kymera Therapeutics is worth considering too. The company is developing an oral version of the blockbuster drug Dupixent (made and co-developed by Regeneron Pharmaceuticals and Sanofi ). Dupixent is an injectable, however, and oral agents "are frequently preferred by patients," Mukherjee says. "The drug has the potential to not only take share from patients taking Dupixent for numerous immunological diseases but also expanding the market to those not taking systemic biologic drugs," he tells CNBC.
Kymera has said it doesn't expect a patent fight over Dupixent because its drug is distinct, not a biosimilar or biologic copy.
T. Rowe's Hall also likes Kymera for its potential "to unlock disease targets that have been classically considered un-druggable." The stock is the second largest holding in T. Rowe's Biotech ETF, accounting for 4.2% of the portfolio.

title: New-Age Tech Stocks Tumble This Week, Swiggy Leads Sell-Off With 24.5% Fall
body: New-age tech stocks lost over $11 Bn in combined market capitalisation this week, with Swiggy leading a broad sell-off amid weakness in the wider Indian equity market. Of the 67 stocks under Inc42’s coverage before this week’s listings, 63 declined between 1.03% and 24.5%. Only Yudiz, Capillary, ixigo, and Tracxn ended the week higher. Swiggy was the biggest loser, falling 24.5% to close at ₹176.70 after its Q2 FY27 results highlighted mounting losses at quick commerce arm Instamart. The stock touched an all-time low during intraday trade yesterday. Twelve other stocks, including Yatra, Turtlemint, FirstCry, Unicommerce, and IndiaMART InterMESH, hit fresh 52-week lows during the holiday-shortened week. The selling extended to Eternal, Ola Electric, Paytm, and Lenskart, dragging the combined market capitalisation of the 67 companies to $149.2 Bn. Meanwhile, B2B manufacturing company Zetwerk and defence tech company Tonbo Imaging made their public market debuts at a premium yesterday. Both came under pressure after listing, closing 13.02% and 2.44% below their respective BSE listing prices. The two additions took the combined market capitalisation of the 69 new-age tech stocks tracked by Inc42 to $152.32 Bn, equivalent to about 3.2% of the total market capitalisation of BSE-listed companies. Here are some of the key developments at listed new-age tech companies during the week. Eternal Reports Profit Jump Eternal reported a nearly 92% YoY jump in Q2 FY27 net profit and unveiled Dark, an end-to-end encrypted AI platform for advanced AI users. Founder Deepinder Goyal said a global launch is planned before the end of 2026. Eternal also announced a proposed merger between portfolio company AdOnMo and gated-community management platform Mygate. It expects to hold a 4.4% stake in the merged entity. Ecommerce Platforms Face Action The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) took action against seven ecommerce platforms, including IndiaMART and Justdial, over listings and sales of unauthorised hazardous explosives. The action led to the removal of 3,940 sellers and product listings across the platforms. ideaForge Terminates US Agreement Drone maker ideaForge’s wholly owned US subsidiary terminated its joint venture agreement with US-based First Breach Inc, citing the failure to complete the transaction within the agreed deadline and discussions between the parties. Signed on September 23, 2025, the agreement envisaged a joint venture to license, source, design, engineer, manufacture, and distribute unmanned aerial vehicles in the US. Unicommerce Logs Profit Growth Ecommerce SaaS company Unicommerce’s consolidated net profit rose 11% YoY to ₹6.4 Cr in Q2 FY27, while operating revenue grew 15% to ₹59.1 Cr. Expenses increased 19%, outpacing revenue growth, with a lower tax expense supporting profit growth. The company expects profitability to improve in H2 as incremental investments moderate. With that, here’s a look at the broader market trend this week. Markets End Winning Streak The Sensex declined 2.15% to 73,123.83, while the Nifty 50 fell 2.63% to 22,600 during the week. Both indices declined across all four trading sessions, with markets closed on Tuesday for Dussehra. Rising crude prices, geopolitical tensions in West Asia, and sustained FII outflows weighed on sentiment. Broader markets saw steeper falls. The Nifty Midcap 100 and Nifty Smallcap 100 declined 5.6% and 7.3%, respectively, while the Nifty Bank lost 2.8%. Brent crude approaching $115 per barrel heightened concerns over inflation, rupee depreciation, and corporate margins. Investors also scrutinised Q2 earnings, valuations, and management guidance. IT stocks remained relatively resilient, while metals, realty, and consumer durables faced selling pressure. Foreign investors sold equities worth ₹2,697 Cr, their tenth consecutive week of net selling, although outflows moderated from ₹8,991 Cr. Domestic institutional investors bought ₹10,942 Cr. “Going ahead, the steady moderation in FII selling offers some comfort, though elevated crude and sharp broader-market weakness keep the downside risk alive,” said Vinod Nair, head of research at Geojit Investments. Next week, investors will track Federal Reserve and Bank of Japan rate decisions, US GDP, India’s industrial production, and corporate earnings. West Asia developments, crude prices, US treasury yields, and India-US trade negotiations will also remain in focus. Now, let’s take a look at the performance of Swiggy and ixigo. ixigo Defies Market Sell-Off ixigo rose 1.45% during the week following its Q2 results on October 17. The online travel aggregator swung to a consolidated net profit of ₹63.4 Cr from a ₹3.5 Cr loss a year earlier. This included a ₹40.7 Cr exceptional gain from the partial sale of its Freshbus stake and remeasurement of its remaining investment. Operating revenue grew 12.9% YoY to ₹321 Cr, while gross transaction value (GTV) rose 22% to ₹5,304.5 Cr. However, adjusted EBITDA fell 17.2% to ₹23.6 Cr, with the margin narrowing to 7.3% from 10%. Hotel GTV surged 158.7% to ₹111.3 Cr, while revenue increased to ₹8.1 Cr from ₹1.3 Cr. Room nights exceeded 4.7 Lakh, and inventory topped 70,000 properties. However, the segment’s contribution loss widened to ₹1.2 Cr from ₹71 Lakh. Train revenue increased 16.4% to ₹149.1 Cr, while bus revenue rose 23.8% to ₹81 Cr. Flight revenue fell 7.5% to ₹82.7 Cr despite 37.2% GTV growth, with the gross take rate declining to 7% from 9.38%. Choice Equity retained its ‘ADD’ rating and ₹190 target, citing hotel growth but flagging margin pressure from planned investments of ₹10-12 Cr over the next couple of quarters. Swiggy Hits Record Low Swiggy’s 24.5% weekly fall left it 54.7% below its ₹390 IPO price, with widening Instamart losses weighing on sentiment. Its consolidated Q2 FY27 loss narrowed 16% YoY to ₹922 Cr but widened 17% sequentially from ₹791 Cr. Operating revenue rose 36% YoY to ₹7,571 Cr, while consumer-facing businesses’ gross order value (GOV) increased 25% to ₹20,793 Cr. Instamart’s adjusted EBITDA loss widened to ₹895 Cr from ₹849 Cr a year earlier and ₹778 Cr in Q1, despite GOV rising 31% YoY to ₹9,230 Cr. Swiggy cited pricing investments, customer and category mix changes, and new dark-store costs for contribution-margin pressure. It expects Q2 to mark peak adjusted EBITDA losses and anticipates around 100 basis points of margin improvement in Q3. Food delivery’s adjusted EBITDA rose to a record ₹341 Cr from ₹240 Cr, while revenue grew 22% to ₹2,338 Cr. Segment profit increased 39% to ₹349 Cr. Swiggy plans to shift Instamart to an inventory-led model over two to three quarters, targeting an 80-basis-point contribution-margin improvement. Brokerages largely retained ratings but cut targets over quick commerce losses and execution concerns. HSBC lowered its target to ₹240 from ₹315, while CLSA cut its target to ₹262. Edited by Vinaykumar Rai Creatives by Varshita Srivastava The post New-Age Tech Stocks Tumble This Week, Swiggy Leads Sell-Off With 24.5% Fall appeared first on Inc42 Media .

title: Two Wealthy Americans Face Off In Bitter Feud Over Panama Port
body:
Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe.
A view of the Balboa Port is pictured after Hong Kong's CK Hutchison agreed to sell its interests in a key Panama Canal port operator to a BlackRock Inc-backed consortium, amid pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump to curb China's influence in the region, Panama City, Panama, March 4, 2025. REUTERS/Enea Lebrun
By Devon Pendleton and Fabiano Maisonnave
Oct 22, 2026 (Bloomberg) –To hedge-fund billionaire Louis Bacon, the crystalline waters and densely forested riverways of the Gulf of Chiriqui in western Panama are an ecological oasis. To developer John McKeown, the gulf is a conduit to potential markets for the region’s prized produce and a boon for its economy.
Those clashing visions are at the heart of a bitter dispute between the two wealthy Americans, who both say they’re championing Panama’s best interests.
The feud centers on a $260 million port McKeown is seeking to develop on the country’s Pacific coast, just south of the city of David. Ocean Pacific Investments, the company McKeown leads, describes the project, Puerto Baru, as Panama’s first “green” port that will help relieve pressure on trading hubs in Panama City and integrate with trade routes to North America and Asia. Chiriqui, with a population of around 500,000, is Panama’s breadbasket, cultivating foods including coffee, papayas and shrimp.
The battle has escalated all the way to Panama’s Supreme Court, which is weighing the port’s environmental approval after a group of local nonprofits challenged it. Already, the fight has involved civil and criminal complaints against some of those NGOs. The outcome will dictate the fate of an unspoiled pocket of Panama that’s seen little of the wealth that flows through its high-flying capital.
To Bacon, the project poses an unacceptable risk.
“I am concerned that the principals behind this project have no experience developing or operating commercial ports, yet they are proposing a major port in one of the most environmentally sensitive areas in Panama,” he wrote in a statement to Bloomberg News. “A simple look at the map would tell you this is not a suitable development site.”
Ocean Pacific, for its part, said that it has addressed potential environmental impacts and that the campaign to stop the port may be motivated by personal interests.
“If I believed Puerto Baru would cause significant harm to a part of Panama, a country I not only love but call home, I would never have committed myself or my resources to developing this project,” McKeown said in a statement.
The site at issue is nested among the serpentine channels that hold a quarter of Panama’s mangrove forests. Mangrove trees and their dense root systems fortify coastlines, shelter sea life and suck up enormous amounts of carbon .
Ocean Pacific envisages a 124-hectare (306-acre) commercial port. It would be the biggest private investment in Chiriqui Province’s history, Ocean Pacific says, and the area would benefit not just from an increase in industry but also more tourism, since there will be a dock for leisure vessels. An economic assessment commissioned by the company in 2021 estimated that the project could create upwards of 1,100 jobs.
Six Panamanian environmental groups say the facility, and the resulting cargo-ship traffic, would irreversibly damage the local ecosystem through pollution , water churn and blocked sunlight. Juan Carlos Monterrey Gómez, chief executive officer of environmental consultancy VANGLabs and Panama’s former special representative for climate change, said some impact on the local environment from a project of this size is inevitable. (Monterrey isn’t affiliated with any of the groups opposing it.)
A spokesman for Ocean Pacific said the company “strongly disagrees” that the port will cause irreparable damage and said potential impacts were “studied extensively and addressed in detail” as part of the environmental review, which was approved two years ago and was comparable, he said, to reviews conducted for US infrastructure projects. The analysis took four years, according to Ocean Pacific, and included a well-attended public hearing. A website for the project describes it as designed to meet “high sustainability standards,” with solar panels for all its power needs and dedicated conservation zones.
The spokesman also said the company has always been clear that it is not a port operator itself, and intends to partner with one.
Ocean Pacific has continued to work on the port while the court considers the case. But it struck back at the nonprofits, filing criminal complaints against two of them for slander, libel and crimes against the economy.
Shortly afterwards, the two nonprofits said that their bank accounts were frozen due to a court order. Unable to pay staff or raise funds, the groups are struggling to stay afloat and the staff say the measures have spooked other charities that might otherwise be speaking out. The case is producing the kind of chill associated with so-called SLAPP lawsuits, which are meant to intimidate critics, said Joana Abrego, former legal manager and now an external consultant for CIAM, one of the affected groups.
Ocean Pacific declined to comment on ongoing litigation.
One reason that CIAM and the other accused nonprofit, Adopta Bosque, were able to voice such strong opposition in the first place is Louis Bacon. The 70-year-old financier made a fortune through his hedge fund Moore Capital Management and has poured some of it into land and various conservation efforts around the world. He’s the 70th-biggest landowner in the US, according to the Land Report , and has placed 94% of that land under conservation easements, a legal tool that permanently bans future development.
The term conservationist suggests quiet stewardship, but that’s not Bacon’s style. He co-founded Waterkeeper Alliance, a nonprofit formerly run by Robert F. Kennedy Jr. that aims to enforce environmental laws. Through his nonprofit, the Moore Charitable Foundation, he has often taken an activist approach, collaborating with local advocacy groups to oppose projects near his properties, such as a cement plant in North Carolina. He notably was involved in a bitter yearslong feud with Peter Nygard, the disgraced Canadian fashion mogul, that was tied to their neighboring properties in the Bahamas.
The fight over Baru, too, is personal. Bacon owns Islas Secas, an all-inclusive eco-tourism resort that sits on an archipelago about 30 miles southwest of the proposed port, and where nightly rates start at $3,500. He said the port, if built, is far away enough that it won’t directly affect his island, but the dredging and habitat disruption would have cascading consequences. He’s not fighting the project to defend his luxury hotel, he said, and his commitment to Panama won’t change even if the port goes ahead.
Bacon described Ocean Pacific’s legal action against the nonprofits as extraordinary. “I’ve never had to support environmental advocates facing criminal penalties simply for raising concerns about a development project,” he said. “Lawfare against whistleblowers is abominable.”
Bacon has personally covered Adopta Bosque’s legal costs and also helped fund the broader campaign against the project, which includes an online petition and a website articulating the six nonprofits’ mission, endorsed by nearly four dozen “supportive organizations,” many of which Bacon has funded in the past for their wider work. He paid for an alternative port plan that endorsed moving it about 50 miles west to the city of Puerto Armuelles, and his foundation funded an impact analysis that estimated the port’s environmental toll would come to around $30 million over 20 years.
McKeown also has personal ties to Panama. A part-time resident of the country, he said he first became interested in Chiriqui’s potential as a maritime hub while on a deep-sea fishing excursion; the captain had to travel seven hours to resupply because there was no suitable dock.
He has experience bridging enterprise and conservation efforts. As president of the closely-held Los Angeles-area energy company, Synergy Oil & Gas, he helped create one of California’s biggest protected wetlands with authorities by agreeing to decommission what had been an active oil field. Before Synergy, McKeown was a real estate broker and owned several container and logistics yards. He said he’s raised money for Puerto Baru from various US individuals, whom he declined to identify.
Bacon said he’s expressed his concerns about the project with Panamanian officials personally and through his local foundation, and that he reached out to Ocean Pacific with an offer to help pay for additional scientific analyses and a coastal modeling study but didn’t get a response.
An Ocean Pacific spokesman said McKeown exchanged emails with Bacon’s son Trevor and concluded that new analyses would duplicate work that had already been done. McKeown said Puerto Armuelles was too far from the region’s farms to be feasible.
Panama’s environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, said in a statement that the ministry is legally “obliged to respect” the environmental approval for Puerto Baru — which a previous administration signed off on — and that it will abide by the Supreme Court’s decision when it comes. He declined to comment on Ocean Pacific’s lawsuits against the NGOs but said the nature of the suits had ministry officials “deeply concerned.”
“Panama is a democratic country,” he said. “At the Ministry of Environment we value and promote active, robust citizen participation, as well as contributions from civil society and the scientific community to environmental management.”
Panamanian advocates say the port project exposes what they describe as a chasm between Panama’s reputation as a leader on conservation and the environment and its treatment of local nonprofits.
“Organizations like ours are on our own. We don’t have institutions that protect us in this situation,” said Abrego. Two environmentalists opposing Puerto Baru declined to speak on the record out of fear for their safety criticizing the state’s stance on a development project.
The dissonance isn’t that unusual, said Monterrey, the former climate envoy, given the knotty bureaucratic interests that complicate most countries’ policies.
In his view, the port likely wouldn’t deliver what its developers are promising for Panama. “These large projects are usually presented as bringing jobs and development,” he said, “but they often produce social conflict, extract wealth from the communities and send the returns elsewhere.” Whether Ocean Pacific gets the chance to change that narrative is now up to the high court.

title: Iran-backed militias in Iraq accuse US of violating airspace, as threats grow - analysis
body: Iran-backed militias in Iraq accused the United States of violating Iraqi airspace. The statement comes amid tensions between the Iraqi government and Iran-backed militias over efforts to bring weapons under state control, according to a report by Rudaw."Standing with the forces of righteousness against the forces of evil is a duty dictated by sound human nature," the IRI said, according to Rudaw. The group sees the conflict involving Iran as a struggle against the US and Israel. The IRI has attacked Israel in the past during the conflict in Gaza.The Islamic Resistance in Iraq, an umbrella group of Iran-backed militias, continues to support Iran. The group issued a statement amid speculation about a possible new war with Iran.The militias also accused Baghdad of appeasing the US due to Washington's pressure on Iraq. The IRI is unhappy that Baghdad has been reducing commercial flights and closing border crossings with Iran. The IRI claimed to have documented 171 violations of Iraqi airspace by US fighter jets and reconnaissance aircraft between September 30 and Friday. The allegations were not independently verified.The accusations come after the US-led anti-ISIS coalition formally ended its military mission in Iraq on September 30. Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has sought to use the transition to bring militia weapons under government control. However, several powerful factions have rejected the initiative. The plan is set to take effect by June 2027. Some militias have agreed, while others have rejected the policy.Some militias opposed to disarmament, others willing to cooperateAccording to Rudaw, Kataib Hezbollah and Harakat al-Nujaba remain opposed to disarmament, while Harakat Ansar Allah al-Awfiya and Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada have expressed willingness to cooperate with government measures.Zaidi has extended the disarmament deadline to June 30, 2027, by which time "no weapons will remain outside the framework of the state," he said in an interview with Iraqi state media, quoted by Rudaw.The dispute illustrates a central challenge facing Iraq. Even after the US-led coalition's withdrawal, Iran-backed factions continue to portray their weapons as necessary for confronting Washington and Israel. This puts them increasingly at odds with Baghdad's efforts to assert state authority over armed groups.The tensions come as the US State Department has warned of increasing regional threats that could affect security in Iraq. On Saturday, the US Embassy in Iraq published an update to the State Department's travel advisory, citing the threat of increased attacks by the Iranian-backed Houthis. The warnings also cite terrorist threats in Iraq, including those posed by Iran-backed militias.The advisory maintained the existing warning against all travel to Iraq. It noted that Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia, including strikes on civilian airports and critical infrastructure, could lead to wider regional escalation."The hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area," the State Department warned. It also noted that "the Iraqi government cannot guarantee the safety of US citizens against sudden outbreaks of violence and armed conflict."The advisory specifically highlighted threats from armed groups inside Iraq. "Terrorists, including ISIS and Iran-aligned militias, encourage and conduct attacks against US persons and interests in Iraq," the State Department said.State Department warns of threats to US citizens, companiesIt also warned that militias threaten American citizens and international companies, citing attacks involving drones, indirect fire, and improvised explosive devices. Potential targets include airports, energy infrastructure, hotels, and diplomatic facilities.The warning illustrates the broader security challenges facing Baghdad. While the Iraqi government seeks to consolidate control over armed factions, Washington continues to view Iran-aligned militias as a threat. The escalation involving the Houthis also highlights how regional conflicts could further complicate Iraq's efforts to maintain stability and avoid being drawn into new confrontations.The tensions in Iraq come amid other developments involving Iran and Iranian-backed groups across the region. On Saturday, Rudaw reported that US intelligence had warned of increased Iranian efforts to assassinate American diplomats and officials in the Middle East and elsewhere. Citing an Axios report, Rudaw said a memorandum dated Friday from US National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton to Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned that some alleged Iranian plots had reached advanced stages. The report comes as Washington reduces staffing at several embassies amid concerns about regional escalation.Meanwhile, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Saturday that it had targeted a gathering center belonging to the Kurdistan Free Life Party (PJAK), an Iranian Kurdish opposition group. The attack took place in Iran but could have implications for Iraq, where Tehran has previously targeted Iranian Kurdish opposition groups. According to Rudaw, clashes between the IRGC and PJAK's armed wing, the Eastern Kurdistan Units (YRK), have intensified over the last week. Iran has used drones and artillery against mountainous areas where the Kurdish fighters operate. Iran's Mehr News Agency described the latest operation as a preemptive strike against PJAK members allegedly preparing attacks.These developments also come as Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi continues to insist that his government will end the presence of armed factions operating outside state control. In an interview quoted by Rudaw on Friday, Zaidi said that "Iraq will soon, God willing, be a state free of factions, like other countries in the world, and weapons will be exclusively in the hands of the Iraqi security forces."The developments illustrate the competing pressures facing Iraq. Baghdad wants to consolidate state authority over armed groups, but Iran-backed militias continue to see themselves as part of a wider regional confrontation with the US and Israel. At the same time, Iran's operations against Kurdish opposition groups and reports of threats to American officials suggest that tensions could spread across several fronts.One example of Baghdad's progress is a new agreement with a Yazidi armed group called YBS in Sinjar in northern Iraq. Baghdad also says it has reached a deal with Turkey for Ankara to leave a base near Bashiqa. However, these may be low-hanging fruit because Iran-backed militias are, in some ways, more powerful. Iran shares a long border with Iraq. It views Iraq as a "near abroad," basically meaning it feels it should control Iraq. It has carried out 1,000 attacks on the Kurdistan Region of Iraq, but also 600 on the rest of Iraq, using militias in some attacks.For Iraq, the challenge is not only disarming militias. It is also preventing the country from becoming a battleground in a wider regional conflict. The coming months will test whether Zaidi can turn his government's commitments into reality, particularly as the June 2027 deadline approaches.

title: 2027: It’s our turn to repay Tinubu, Shettima tells northerners
body: Vice-President Kashim Shettima has urged eligible voters in the northern part of Nigeria to rally round President Bola Ahmed Tinubu and ensure his re-election in the forthcoming 2027 general elections. Speaking on Saturday at the All Progressives Congress (APC) presidential campaign launch in Kaduna, Shettima said Tinubu had consistently supported politicians from the north, including former President Muhammadu Buhari. He said it was only fair for the region to reciprocate the support by re-electing the President and other candidates contesting different positions under the APC. “We have come to ask you to renew a second time for the APC from top to bottom,” Shettima said. Some Persons Need Eyeglasses To See My Husband’s Achievements — Remi Tinubu 2027: Forget about social media news, Nigerians love Tinubu – Information minister He said Tinubu had at a time supported and provided a platform for former Vice President Atiku Abubakar to contest the presidency in 2007 after his exit from the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP). Shettima also recalled how Tinubu canvassed support for late President Buhari during his presidential campaigns in 2015 and 2019. “And you can bear witness that in 2015 and 2019, President Tinubu stood solidly behind the late President Muhammadu Buhari, throughout his first and second term victories. This is a mark of honour and our faith in a man of honour,” he said. title: ‘Blaming Opposition For Hunger Is Delusional,’ Atiku Replies Tinubu
body: Former Vice President Atiku Abubakar has accused President Bola Tinubu of shifting responsibility for Nigeria’s economic hardship to the opposition, insisting that the administration must account for its record ahead of the 2027 presidential election. Atiku, the presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), was reacting to Tinubu’s remark at the APC campaign flag-off in Kaduna on Saturday that the opposition created hunger and poverty in the country. In a statement issued by his Director of Strategic Communication, Phrank Shaibu, Atiku described the President’s comment as “either delusion or a staggering case of political amnesia”. “The APC governed Nigeria for eight years before you took office. You have added another three and a half years. Nigerians know who has been in power, and hardship did not begin when the opposition started talking about it. Stop insulting their intelligence and answer for your record,” he said. Atiku accused Tinubu’s administration of worsening the hardship faced by Nigerians, arguing that the President could not dismiss concerns about the cost of living by blaming political opponents. He also criticised Tinubu’s planned inauguration of a section of the Abuja-Kaduna Expressway, alleging that the ceremony showed how disconnected the President was from the daily realities of Nigerians. “A road cannot be completed with a speech or a ribbon cutting ceremony,” he said. The former Vice President challenged the administration to explain the removal of the petrol subsidy and the depreciation of the naira, which he claimed had fallen from about ₦471 to ₦1,329 to the dollar. He also cited a World Bank estimate that 63 per cent of Nigerians would be below the national poverty line in 2026, accusing the government of presiding over rising poverty. Atiku further questioned the extension of the 2024 budget into 2025 alongside a separate 2025 budget, as well as what he described as ₦7.13 trillion recorded under “energy security” in 2024 and ₦11.2 trillion in NNPC pipeline-related spending. He called on the government to explain the figures and disclose what was delivered, as well as who received the sums. Atiku also demanded an explanation for what he described as a $12.4 billion gap in Nigeria’s external accounts for the first half of 2026 and the payment of $22.5 million in “other charges” on an Abu Dhabi financing facility. He further blamed the administration for failing to address killings, kidnappings and displacement across the country, saying Nigerians were asking questions about the government’s response to insecurity. “You cannot govern for three years, make life harder, and then blame others for describing the hardship. You asked who created the hunger. Nigerians are asking what you have done to end it,” he said. Atiku said the 2027 presidential election would be a referendum on Tinubu’s record, arguing that voters would judge the administration by their experiences at home, in markets and in their communities rather than by its campaign promises. “The people will judge your government by the lives they are living, not by the excuses you offer at campaign rallies,” he said. He concluded by claiming that Nigerians had rejected the administration, adding that their verdict would be reflected in the next presidential election. The post ‘Blaming Opposition For Hunger Is Delusional,’ Atiku Replies Tinubu appeared first on Channels Television .

On Thursday, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act into law, requiring disclosures on AI-generated ads. The law requires any ad — whether it’s a still image, video, audio, or text — that “has been significantly modified or generated by artificial intelligence” to include a label in the same format as the ad itself. That applies to TV commercials from multi-billion-dollar companies , as well as restaurants’ ugly, crowded flyers about their wing specials.
Pennsylvania is one of the first states to require disclosures on AI content. And it requires those labels regardless of where an ad was created. So you might see disclosures pop up in commercials in other states if they’re also expected to air in Pennsylvania.
The law leaves many loopholes, though. For one, what constitutes “significantly modified” is subjective. There is also a carve-out for “parody, satire, commentary or criticism,” as well as anything that is “evidently fictional.” Again, what “evidently fictional” means is unclear. The wording also suggests only content that “uses synthetic content in a manner that creates a false consumer perception” about a product or service would require a disclosure. Again, leaving questions about what qualifies as “false” under the law and who makes those decisions.
The office of State Senator Nick Pisciottano, who introduced the bill , did not immediately return a request for comment.
